title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
6. Layers: nn.Linear and activation functions
nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) is the dense (fully connected) layer \(\mathbf z \mapsto \mathbf W\mathbf z + \mathbf b\). It creates and randomly initialises its own parameters weight (shape (n_out, n_in)) and bias (shape (n_out,)): by default all of them are drawn uniformly from \([-1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}},\, 1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}]\). The factor \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\) keeps the outputs of the layer of order one, independently of the number of inputs (the reason is given in Section 7). Input: a batch of shape (B, n_in); output: (B, n_out).
In the printout, .data gives the bare numbers of a parameter without its gradient bookkeeping; it is used here only for a shorter printout. In computations .data should be avoided, because changes made through it are invisible to autograd; the safe alternatives are .detach() and torch.no_grad().


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
layer = nn.Linear(in_features=3, out_features=2)
print(layer)
print("weight:", layer.weight.shape, "\n", layer.weight.data)
print("weight.requires_grad:", layer.weight.requires_grad)
print("bias  :", layer.bias.shape, layer.bias.data)

Z = torch.randn(5, 3)            # batch of 5 inputs with 3 features each
out = layer(Z)                   # calling the layer = forward pass
print("output shape:", out.shape)

# check: it is really Z @ W^T + b
print("same as manual:", torch.allclose(out, Z @ layer.weight.T + layer.bias))


Linear(in_features=3, out_features=2, bias=True)
weight: torch.Size([2, 3]) 
 tensor([[-0.0043,  0.3097, -0.4752],
        [-0.4249, -0.2224,  0.1548]])
weight.requires_grad: True
bias  : torch.Size([2]) tensor([-0.0114,  0.4578])
output shape: torch.Size([5, 2])
same as manual: True


layer.weight.requires_grad is True: these are trainable parameters, and PyTorch will compute gradients with respect to them.
Activation functions exist both as layers (nn.Tanh(), nn.ReLU(), …) and as functions (torch.tanh, torch.relu, …). The six plotted below are (in the plots, \(\sigma\) denotes a generic activation function)







name
formula




Sigmoid
\(1/(1 + e^{-z})\)


Tanh
\(\tanh z\)


ReLU
\(\max(0, z)\)


LeakyReLU(\(\alpha\))
\(z\) for \(z \ge 0\), \(\alpha z\) for \(z < 0\); the slope \(\alpha\) is a free choice (0.01 is PyTorch’s default, 0.1 is used here to make it visible)


GELU
\(z\,\Phi(z)\), with \(\Phi\) the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution


Softplus
\(\ln(1 + e^{z})\), a smooth version of ReLU



In the code, acts is a dictionary (name \(\to\) layer); acts.items() yields the pairs (name, layer). axes.flatten() turns the \(2\times3\) array of subplots into a list of 6, and zip walks through the two sequences in parallel. The range \([-4, 4]\) covers the region where the functions bend; 300 points are only needed for smooth curves.


Code
z = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 300)
acts = {"Sigmoid": nn.Sigmoid(), "Tanh": nn.Tanh(), "ReLU": nn.ReLU(),
        "LeakyReLU(0.1)": nn.LeakyReLU(0.1), "GELU": nn.GELU(), "Softplus": nn.Softplus()}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 6), sharex=True)
for ax, (name, act) in zip(axes.flatten(), acts.items()):
    ax.plot(z, act(z), lw=2)
    ax.axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5); ax.axvline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5)
    ax.set_title(name); ax.set_xlabel("$z$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\sigma(z)$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()






nn.Sequential: stacking layers
The single-hidden-layer network \(f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} W^{(2)}_i\,\sigma(W^{(1)}_i x + b_i) + b^{(2)}\), with \(\sigma = \tanh\), is Linear(1, N) → Tanh → Linear(N, 1). By the Universal Approximation Theorem (see the lecture), such a network can approximate any continuous function on an interval when \(N\) is large enough. The width \(N = 16\) is arbitrary.
The parameter count is \(3N + 1\): the first layer has \(N\) weights and \(N\) biases, the second \(N\) weights and 1 bias. In the code, model.parameters() yields the trainable tensors of the model one after another, named_parameters() yields them together with their names, and p.numel() is the number of elements of a tensor. sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) adds up p.numel() for every parameter tensor without first building a list.


Code
torch.manual_seed(1)
N = 16
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(1, N),     # W^(1), b      : x -> N hidden pre-activations
    nn.Tanh(),           # sigma, element-wise
    nn.Linear(N, 1),     # W^(2), b^(2)  : N hidden activations -> 1 output
)
print(model)

n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print("number of trainable parameters:", n_params, "= 3N + 1 =", 3 * N + 1)
for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    print(f"  {name:10s} {tuple(p.shape)}")


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=1, out_features=16, bias=True)
  (1): Tanh()
  (2): Linear(in_features=16, out_features=1, bias=True)
)
number of trainable parameters: 49 = 3N + 1 = 49
  0.weight   (16, 1)
  0.bias     (16,)
  2.weight   (1, 16)
  2.bias     (1,)


The untrained network evaluated on a grid of 400 inputs (a batch of shape (400, 1); range and number of points are arbitrary choices for the plot).
A with block switches a setting on for the indented lines only and restores it afterwards. Inside with torch.no_grad(): PyTorch does not record the operations needed to compute gradients, which saves memory and time when a network is only evaluated.


Code
x = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 400)[:, None]       # shape (400, 1): batch of 1D inputs
with torch.no_grad():                         # we only evaluate; no gradients needed
    y = model(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(x.squeeze(), y.squeeze())
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$f_\theta(x)$"); ax.set_title("an untrained network")
plt.show()





The curve is smooth, but its shape and its small values (here between about \(-0.14\) and \(0.01\)) are determined only by the random initial values of the 49 parameters; another seed gives another curve. .squeeze() turns the shapes (400, 1) into (400,) for plotting. Fitting such a network to a given function means changing its parameters until the curve follows the target: this is training.

title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
7. A model class: subclassing nn.Module
For anything non-trivial we write a class with two methods. __init__ creates the layers and parameters, and it must always call super().__init__() first. forward(x) describes the computation; the model is then called as model(x), not model.forward(x). Parameters wrapped in nn.Parameter (and all parameters of sub-layers) are registered automatically.
Both rules have a reason. super().__init__() runs the __init__ of nn.Module, which creates the internal lists in which parameters and sub-layers are registered; assigning an nn.Parameter before this call fails with AttributeError: cannot assign parameters before Module.__init__() call. Calling model(x) runs forward together with additional bookkeeping of PyTorch (so-called hooks), which a direct call of forward would skip.
Below, the UAT ansatz written explicitly — exactly the formula from the lecture. In def __init__(self, N, activation=torch.tanh) the argument activation has a default value: it is used when the caller does not give this argument. A function such as torch.tanh can be passed and stored like any other object.
For the initial values, W1 and b are drawn from the standard normal distribution. Neuron \(i\) switches (its \(\tanh\) changes sign) at \(x = -b_i/W^{(1)}_i\); with W1 and b of order one, most of these points (about 80 %) lie in \([-3, 3]\), the range of inputs used below, so most neurons are not saturated there. The output bias c (\(b^{(2)}\) above) only shifts \(f\) up or down; there is no reason to start with a shift, so it starts at 0.


Code
class UATNet(nn.Module):
    """f(x) = sum_i W2_i * sigma(W1_i * x + b_i) + c   (single hidden layer, N neurons)."""

    def __init__(self, N, activation=torch.tanh):
        super().__init__()
        self.W1 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N))        # input weights
        self.b = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N))         # biases
        self.W2 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N) / N**0.5)  # output weights, scaled by 1/sqrt(N) (explained below)
        self.c = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1))         # output bias
        self.activation = activation

    def forward(self, x):                             # x: shape (B,) -> output (B,)
        hidden = self.activation(self.W1 * x[:, None] + self.b)   # (B, N) by broadcasting
        return hidden @ self.W2 + self.c

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = UATNet(N=8)
print(net)            # prints only sub-modules (layers); our parameters are listed separately:
print("parameters:", [(n, tuple(p.shape)) for n, p in net.named_parameters()])
x = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 200)    # shape (200,): this class takes a 1D tensor, nn.Sequential above needed shape (200, 1)
print("output shape:", net(x).shape)


UATNet()
parameters: [('W1', (8,)), ('b', (8,)), ('W2', (8,)), ('c', (1,))]
output shape: torch.Size([200])


The output weights are divided by \(\sqrt N\) for the following reason. The output is a sum of \(N\) terms, \(f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} W^{(2)}_i h_i(x) + c\) with \(h_i = \tanh(\dots)\in[-1,1]\). If the \(W^{(2)}_i\) are independent random numbers with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma_W^2\), the terms are uncorrelated with mean zero and their variances add: \[\mathrm{Var}\, f(x) = N\,\sigma_W^2\,\overline{h^2}, \qquad \text{standard deviation of } f \;\propto\; \sqrt{N}\,\sigma_W ,\] where \(\overline{h^2} = \frac1N\sum_i h_i(x)^2 \le 1\) is the mean squared hidden activation (the variance is taken over random \(W^{(2)}\) at fixed \(x\), with \(c = 0\)). With \(\sigma_W = 1\) an untrained network with many neurons would produce outputs that grow like \(\sqrt N\), far from the order-one values of typical targets. With \(\sigma_W = 1/\sqrt N\) the variance of the output is of order one for every \(N\). The same rule, weights scaled by \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\) with \(n_{\rm in}\) the number of inputs of the layer, is the basis of the standard initialisations (LeCun, Xavier/Glorot), and nn.Linear uses it by default. For the first layer \(n_{\rm in} = 1\), so W1 is not scaled. The cell below measures the standard deviation of \(f\) over the inputs and 50 random initialisations, with and without the factor: the 50 outputs of shape (200,) are joined by torch.cat into one vector of \(50\times200 = 10\,000\) values, of which std() computes the sample standard deviation (normalised by the number of values minus one, which makes no difference for 10 000 values).


Code
x_test = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 200)[:, None]                   # shape (200, 1)
print("   N   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1)   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1/N)")
for n_hidden in [1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    stds = {}
    for scaled in [False, True]:
        outputs = []
        for seed in range(50):                                 # 50 random networks
            torch.manual_seed(seed)
            W1, b1 = torch.randn(n_hidden), torch.randn(n_hidden)
            W2 = torch.randn(n_hidden) / (n_hidden**0.5 if scaled else 1.0)
            outputs.append(torch.tanh(x_test * W1 + b1) @ W2)  # (200,) for this network
        stds[scaled] = torch.cat(outputs).std().item()
    print(f"{n_hidden:5d}   {stds[False]:20.2f}   {stds[True]:22.2f}")


   N   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1)   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1/N)
    1                   0.67                     0.67
   10                   2.77                     0.87


  100                   7.52                     0.75
 1000                  21.90                     0.69


Without the factor the standard deviation grows by roughly a factor of 3 for every tenfold increase of \(N\) (expected: \(\sqrt{10}\approx3.2\); with 50 random networks the estimate fluctuates); with the factor it stays of order one, independent of \(N\).
A model can be moved to the GPU with model.to(device), and switched to double precision with model.double().

title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
8. Summary
Tensors are NumPy arrays with GPU support and automatic differentiation. Their default dtype is float32; for precise physics we use float64. torch.from_numpy shares memory and torch.tensor copies; .numpy(), .item() and .cpu() lead back to NumPy and Python numbers. Among the shape operations, reshape/view change the shape (keeping the row-by-row order), transpose/permute reorder axes (giving non-contiguous views), unsqueeze/squeeze add or remove axes of length 1, cat joins along an existing axis and stack along a new one; batched products are written with @ or einsum. The device is chosen as "cuda" if available, else "cpu", and all tensors in one operation must be on the same device. nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) computes \(\mathbf W\mathbf z+\mathbf b\) on batches (B, n_in), nn.Sequential stacks layers, and our own models subclass nn.Module with __init__ and forward. When a network is only evaluated, we wrap the computation in with torch.no_grad():.

title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
9. Exercises

Exercise 1 — Ising chain energy in PyTorch
Implement the vectorised energy of a periodic Ising chain, \(E = -\sum_{i=1}^{L} s_i s_{i+1}\) with \(s_{L+1} = s_1\), in PyTorch (torch.roll, torch.sum(..., dim=1)). Generate the random spins with torch.randint(0, 2, (M, L)) * 2 - 1. Run it on 100 000 configurations with \(L = 64\) and check the mean and standard deviation of the energy (\(\approx 0\) and \(\approx\sqrt{L}\)).

Solution


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
M, L, J = 100_000, 64, 1.0

# torch.randint(0, 2, ...) gives 0 or 1; *2 - 1 maps them to -1 or +1.
# .float() converts integers to floats so that sums and std() work as expected.
spins = (torch.randint(0, 2, (M, L)) * 2 - 1).float()

# np.roll -> torch.roll, axis -> dims/dim (for readers who know NumPy)
E = -J * torch.sum(spins * torch.roll(spins, shifts=-1, dims=1), dim=1)

# .item() converts a one-element tensor to a Python number for printing
print(f"mean = {E.mean().item():.3f},  std = {E.std().item():.3f},  sqrt(L) = {L**0.5:.3f}")
# Why sqrt(L): with periodic boundaries the L products s_i s_{i+1} of independent random spins are pairwise independent
# (uncorrelated) numbers +-1 with mean 0 and variance 1, so their variances add: the sum has mean 0 and variance L,
# hence standard deviation sqrt(L).


mean = 0.050,  std = 7.986,  sqrt(L) = 8.000





Exercise 2 — Tensor shapes in a multilayer network
Build model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10)) — the classic network for MNIST (a data set of 70 000 grey-scale images of handwritten digits 0–9, each of \(28\times28\) pixels) from the next lecture. 1. Feed a random batch of 32 “images” of shape (32, 28, 28). It fails; read the error message and fix the problem with reshape. 2. Print the shape of the output. What do the 10 numbers per image represent? 3. Count the parameters (on paper from the formula \(\sum_l n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\) for layer sizes \(n_0, n_1, \dots\), and with sum(p.numel() ...)). 4. The softmax \(p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}\) turns the 10 outputs \(z_k\) into probabilities. Apply torch.softmax(out, dim=1) and check that each row sums to 1.

Solution


Code
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
images = torch.rand(32, 28, 28)               # 32 random 28x28 "images", values uniform in [0, 1) like pixel intensities

# 1) The first layer expects input of shape (batch, 784). A (32, 28, 28) tensor is interpreted as
#    32*28 = 896 rows of length 28, which does not match 784 -> error.
try:
    model(images)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("Error:", e)

# Fix: flatten every image into a vector of 28*28 = 784 numbers; with -1, PyTorch computes that size.
flat = images.reshape(32, -1)
print("flattened shape:", flat.shape)
out = model(flat)

# 2) One row per image, 10 numbers per row: one score (logit) per digit class 0..9
print("output shape:", out.shape)

# 3) Parameters: layer n_in -> n_out has n_out * n_in weights and n_out biases
by_hand = 128 * (784 + 1) + 64 * (128 + 1) + 10 * (64 + 1)
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()), " by hand:", by_hand)

# 4) Softmax over the class dimension (dim=1) turns the scores into probabilities: p_k = exp(z_k) / sum_j exp(z_j)
#    is positive and the p_k sum to 1. The unnormalised scores z_k that enter the softmax are called logits.
with torch.no_grad():                   # no gradient tracking needed here (otherwise the output shows grad_fn)
    probs = torch.softmax(out, dim=1)
print("row sums:", probs.sum(dim=1)[:5])


Error: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (896x28 and 784x128)
flattened shape: torch.Size([32, 784])
output shape: torch.Size([32, 10])
parameters: 109386  by hand: 109386
row sums: tensor([1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000])





Exercise 3 — Random networks of different depth
Using nn.Sequential, build networks \(1\to W\to\cdots\to W\to 1\) with \(\tanh\) activations, width \(W=64\) and depth (number of hidden layers) \(1, 3, 10\). For each depth draw 5 random initialisations and plot \(f(x)\) on \(x\in[-5,5]\). Do this twice: (a) with PyTorch’s default initialisation, (b) with all weights redrawn from \(\mathcal N(0, (3/\sqrt{n_\text{in}})^2)\), where \(n_\text{in}\) is the number of inputs of the layer. How does the shape of a random function change with depth in the two cases? (The factor 3 is one choice among many; for \(\tanh\) networks the boundary between the two kinds of behaviour shown by (a) and (b) lies at a factor of about 1, and any factor well above 1 shows the effect of (b).) Hint: build the list of layers in a loop and pass it as nn.Sequential(*layers); torch.nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, std=...) redraws the weights of a layer.

Solution


Code
def make_mlp(depth, width=64, activation=nn.Tanh, weight_std_factor=None):
    """1 -> width -> ... -> width -> 1 network with `depth` hidden layers.
    weight_std_factor=None: PyTorch default initialisation; otherwise weights ~ N(0, (factor/sqrt(n_in))^2)."""
    layers = [nn.Linear(1, width), activation()]                  # activation is a class (nn.Tanh); activation() creates a layer object
    for _ in range(depth - 1):                                    # remaining hidden layers
        layers += [nn.Linear(width, width), activation()]
    layers.append(nn.Linear(width, 1))                            # linear output layer
    if weight_std_factor is not None:
        for layer in layers:
            if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):                      # True if layer is an nn.Linear object; only these have weights
                n_in = layer.weight.shape[1]
                # the trailing underscore of normal_ marks an in-place operation: the existing weight tensor is overwritten
                nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, mean=0.0, std=weight_std_factor / n_in**0.5)
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)                                 # *layers passes the list elements as separate arguments

x = torch.linspace(-5, 5, 500)[:, None]                           # shape (500, 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 7))
for row, (factor, row_name, plain_name) in enumerate([(None, "default init", "default init"),
                                                     (3.0, r"std $3/\sqrt{n_{in}}$", "std 3/sqrt(n_in)")]):
    for ax, depth in zip(axes[row], [1, 3, 10]):
        ranges = []
        for seed in range(5):
            torch.manual_seed(seed)                               # a different random network for each seed
            with torch.no_grad():                                 # evaluation only, no gradients
                y = make_mlp(depth, weight_std_factor=factor)(x).squeeze()
            ax.plot(x.squeeze(), y)
            ranges.append((y.max() - y.min()).item())
        ax.set_title(f"{row_name}, depth = {depth}")
        ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$f(x)$")
        print(f"{plain_name:17s} depth {depth:2d}: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks:", np.round(ranges, 4))
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# (a) Default initialisation draws weights uniformly from [-1/sqrt(n_in), 1/sqrt(n_in)] (variance 1/(3 n_in)).
#     Every tanh layer then shrinks the signal, and depth does NOT increase complexity: the outputs of the
#     10-layer networks vary by less than 1e-2 over the whole interval, i.e. they are almost constant.
# (b) With larger weights each layer stretches the signal and folds it through tanh; deep random networks
#     then become rapidly oscillating functions; the larger the factor, the more local maxima and minima
#     the deep networks have on [-5, 5].
# Depth can produce complicated functions, but only if the weights have a suitable scale; this is one
# reason why the initialisation of deep networks matters.


default init      depth  1: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [0.9912 2.7868 0.471  1.1998 0.9899]


default init      depth  3: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [0.0978 0.1152 0.2639 0.3197 0.1088]
default init      depth 10: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [0.0015 0.0027 0.0035 0.0065 0.0054]
std 3/sqrt(n_in)  depth  1: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [ 1.1431  1.5322  3.401   5.2946 12.0745]
std 3/sqrt(n_in)  depth  3: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [ 4.3558  4.1454  3.6766 10.2046  6.8429]
std 3/sqrt(n_in)  depth 10: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [11.8048 10.9719  9.7572  8.4522 10.6725]








Exercise 4 (advanced) — A custom layer
Write an nn.Module called GaussianRBF implementing \(f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i\, \exp\!\big(-(x-\mu_i)^2 / (2 s_i^2)\big)\) with trainable \(a_i, \mu_i, s_i\) (nn.Parameter). Initialise \(\mu_i\) on a uniform grid on \([-3,3]\), \(s_i = 0.5\), \(a_i \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\). Plot the output and the individual Gaussians for \(N=6\). (Radial-basis-function networks are also universal approximators.)

Solution


Code
class GaussianRBF(nn.Module):
    """f(x) = sum_i a_i exp(-(x - mu_i)^2 / (2 s_i^2)) with trainable a, mu, s."""

    def __init__(self, N):
        super().__init__()
        # nn.Parameter registers the tensor as a trainable parameter of the module
        self.a = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N))                 # amplitudes
        self.mu = nn.Parameter(torch.linspace(-3, 3, N))      # centres on a uniform grid
        self.s = nn.Parameter(0.5 * torch.ones(N))            # widths; for N = 6 the centres are 1.2 apart, so neighbouring
                                                              # Gaussians of width 0.5 overlap and their sum is a smooth curve

    def basis(self, x):
        """The N Gaussians evaluated at all points: shape (B, N)."""
        return torch.exp(-(x[:, None] - self.mu)**2 / (2 * self.s**2))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.basis(x) @ self.a                         # weighted sum -> shape (B,)

torch.manual_seed(0)
rbf = GaussianRBF(6)
print("parameters:", [(name, tuple(p.shape)) for name, p in rbf.named_parameters()])

x = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
with torch.no_grad():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    ax.plot(x, rbf.basis(x) * rbf.a, lw=1, alpha=0.7)        # (400, 6): ax.plot draws one curve per column = one weighted Gaussian
    ax.plot(x, rbf(x), "k", lw=2.5, label="sum $f(x)$")
    ax.legend(); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$f(x)$ and its Gaussian terms"); plt.show()


parameters: [('a', (6,)), ('mu', (6,)), ('s', (6,))]








Exercise 5 — Reading and writing einsum strings

Without running code, write down the shape of the result and the formula for: "ij,jk,kl->il" with shapes \((2,3),(3,4),(4,5)\); "bij->bj" with \((6,3,4)\); "ij,kl->ijkl" with \((2,3),(4,5)\); "bii->b" with \((6,3,3)\). Then check with code.
Write einsum strings for: (a) \(\sum_i u_i^2\); (b) the matrix \(A^{T}A\); (c) for a batch of matrices \(A_b\) of shape \((B, n, n)\), the traces \(\mathrm{tr}\,A_b\);

the quadratic form \(\sum_{ij} x_{bi} Q_{ij} x_{bj}\) for a batch of vectors \(x_b\). Verify each against a computation without einsum.

Write a function quadratic_form(x, Q) that computes \(\sum_{ij} x_i Q_{ij} x_j\) for every vector along the last axis of x, whatever the number of batch axes in front (use ...). Test it with x of shapes (3,), (6, 3) and (2, 6, 3).


Solution


Code
torch.manual_seed(5)
# 1) shapes and formulas
a, b, c = torch.randn(2, 3), torch.randn(3, 4), torch.randn(4, 5)
r1 = torch.einsum("ij,jk,kl->il", a, b, c)      # r_il = sum_jk a_ij b_jk c_kl = (a @ b @ c)_il, shape (2, 5)
print("ij,jk,kl->il :", tuple(r1.shape), " equals a @ b @ c:", torch.allclose(r1, a @ b @ c, atol=1e-6))
t = torch.randn(6, 3, 4)
r2 = torch.einsum("bij->bj", t)                 # r_bj = sum_i t_bij, shape (6, 4)
print("bij->bj      :", tuple(r2.shape), " equals t.sum(dim=1):", torch.allclose(r2, t.sum(dim=1)))
r3 = torch.einsum("ij,kl->ijkl", a, c)          # r_ijkl = a_ij c_kl (nothing summed), shape (2, 3, 4, 5)
print("ij,kl->ijkl  :", tuple(r3.shape), " element check:", torch.allclose(r3[1, 2, 3, 4], a[1, 2] * c[3, 4]))
sq = torch.randn(6, 3, 3)
r4 = torch.einsum("bii->b", sq)                 # r_b = sum_i sq_bii (trace of every matrix), shape (6,)
print("bii->b       :", tuple(r4.shape), " equals traces:", torch.allclose(r4, sq.diagonal(dim1=1, dim2=2).sum(dim=1)))

# 2) writing strings
u = torch.randn(5)
A43 = torch.randn(4, 3)
As = torch.randn(6, 3, 3)
xb, Q = torch.randn(6, 3), torch.randn(3, 3)
print("(a) i,i->        :", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("i,i->", u, u), (u**2).sum()))
print("(b) ki,kj->ij    :", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("ki,kj->ij", A43, A43), A43.T @ A43, atol=1e-6))
print("(c) bii->b       :", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("bii->b", As), torch.stack([torch.trace(m) for m in As])))
print("(d) bi,ij,bj->b  :", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("bi,ij,bj->b", xb, Q, xb),
                                           ((xb @ Q) * xb).sum(dim=1), atol=1e-6))

# 3) one string for any number of batch axes: '...' stands for all axes before the last one
def quadratic_form(x, Q):
    return torch.einsum("...i,ij,...j->...", x, Q, x)

for shape in [(3,), (6, 3), (2, 6, 3)]:
    xs = torch.randn(shape)
    reference = ((xs @ Q) * xs).sum(dim=-1)
    print(f"quadratic_form for x of shape {str(shape):10s}: result shape {str(tuple(quadratic_form(xs, Q).shape)):8s}"
          f" agrees: {torch.allclose(quadratic_form(xs, Q), reference, atol=1e-5)}")


ij,jk,kl->il : (2, 5)  equals a @ b @ c: True
bij->bj      : (6, 4)  equals t.sum(dim=1): True
ij,kl->ijkl  : (2, 3, 4, 5)  element check: True
bii->b       : (6,)  equals traces: True
(a) i,i->        : True
(b) ki,kj->ij    : True
(c) bii->b       : True
(d) bi,ij,bj->b  : True
quadratic_form for x of shape (3,)      : result shape ()       agrees: True
quadratic_form for x of shape (6, 3)    : result shape (6,)     agrees: True
quadratic_form for x of shape (2, 6, 3) : result shape (2, 6)   agrees: True





Exercise 6 — Predicting shapes
For t = torch.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4), first predict on paper, then check with code: 1. the shapes of t.reshape(4, -1), t.transpose(0, 2), t.permute(1, 2, 0), t.flatten(1), t.unsqueeze(1), t[:, None, :, None]; 2. the value of t.permute(1, 2, 0)[2, 3, 1]; 3. which of the results in 1. are contiguous; 4. whether t.transpose(0, 2).view(-1) works.

Solution


Code
t = torch.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)

# 1) and 3): shapes and contiguity
results = {
    "t.reshape(4, -1)": t.reshape(4, -1),            # 24 / 4 = 6  -> (4, 6)
    "t.transpose(0, 2)": t.transpose(0, 2),          # axes 0 and 2 swapped -> (4, 3, 2)
    "t.permute(1, 2, 0)": t.permute(1, 2, 0),        # old axes (1, 2, 0) -> (3, 4, 2)
    "t.flatten(1)": t.flatten(1),                    # axes 1 and 2 merged -> (2, 12)
    "t.unsqueeze(1)": t.unsqueeze(1),                # new axis at position 1 -> (2, 1, 3, 4)
    "t[:, None, :, None]": t[:, None, :, None],      # new axes at positions 1 and 3 -> (2, 1, 3, 1, 4)
}
for name, r in results.items():
    print(f"{name:22s} shape {str(tuple(r.shape)):16s} contiguous: {r.is_contiguous()}")
# reshape, flatten and inserting axes of length 1 keep the row-by-row order of the elements (contiguous);
# transpose and permute only change the strides, so the elements are no longer stored row by row

# 2) element [2, 3, 1] of t.permute(1, 2, 0) is element [1, 2, 3] of t (old axis 0 is now last)
print("t.permute(1, 2, 0)[2, 3, 1] =", t.permute(1, 2, 0)[2, 3, 1].item(), "= t[1, 2, 3] =", t[1, 2, 3].item(),
      "= 1*12 + 2*4 + 3")

# 4) view on a non-contiguous tensor
try:
    t.transpose(0, 2).view(-1)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("view fails:", e)


t.reshape(4, -1)       shape (4, 6)           contiguous: True
t.transpose(0, 2)      shape (4, 3, 2)        contiguous: False
t.permute(1, 2, 0)     shape (3, 4, 2)        contiguous: False
t.flatten(1)           shape (2, 12)          contiguous: True
t.unsqueeze(1)         shape (2, 1, 3, 4)     contiguous: True
t[:, None, :, None]    shape (2, 1, 3, 1, 4)  contiguous: True
t.permute(1, 2, 0)[2, 3, 1] = 23 = t[1, 2, 3] = 23 = 1*12 + 2*4 + 3
view fails: view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and stride (at least one dimension spans across two contiguous subspaces). Use .reshape(...) instead.





Exercise 7 — A batch of rotations

For \(B = 6\) angles \(\varphi_b = b\pi/6\) build a tensor R of shape (B, 2, 2) of rotation matrices \(\begin{pmatrix}\cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi\\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi\end{pmatrix}\) using torch.stack (no loop).
Rotate the unit vector \((1, 0)\) by every angle in three ways: with @ and unsqueeze/squeeze, with torch.einsum, and with torch.bmm (which multiplies batches of matrices). Check that the results agree and plot the rotated vectors.
Verify \(R^{T}R = 1\) for all matrices at once.


Solution


Code
n_rot = 6
phi = torch.arange(n_rot) * torch.pi / 6                  # shape (n_rot,)
c, s = torch.cos(phi), torch.sin(phi)
# 1) stack the four entries: first the two rows (each of shape (B, 2)), then the rows into matrices
row1 = torch.stack([c, -s], dim=1)                        # (n_rot, 2)
row2 = torch.stack([s, c], dim=1)                         # (n_rot, 2)
R = torch.stack([row1, row2], dim=1)                      # (n_rot, 2, 2): R[b] = [[c, -s], [s, c]]
print("R shape:", tuple(R.shape))

# 2) rotate the unit vector e_x by every angle
e_x = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0]).expand(n_rot, 2)          # the same vector for every rotation (expand adds the batch axis)
rot1 = (R @ e_x.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2)                  # (n_rot, 2, 2) @ (n_rot, 2, 1) -> (n_rot, 2, 1) -> (n_rot, 2)
rot2 = torch.einsum("bij,bj->bi", R, e_x)
rot3 = torch.bmm(R, e_x.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2)
print("all three agree:", torch.allclose(rot1, rot2) and torch.allclose(rot1, rot3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 4))
angle_labels = ["$0$", r"$\pi/6$", r"$2\pi/6$", r"$3\pi/6$", r"$4\pi/6$", r"$5\pi/6$"]
for b in range(n_rot):
    ax.arrow(0, 0, rot1[b, 0].item(), rot1[b, 1].item(), head_width=0.04, length_includes_head=True, color=f"C{b}")
    ax.text(1.12 * rot1[b, 0].item(), 1.12 * rot1[b, 1].item(), angle_labels[b], ha="center", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(-1.3, 1.3); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.3); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
plt.show()

# 3) R^T R for all rotations at once: transpose the last two axes
RtR = R.transpose(1, 2) @ R                               # (n_rot, 2, 2)
print("max |R^T R - 1|:", (RtR - torch.eye(2)).abs().max().item())


R shape: (6, 2, 2)
all three agree: True





max |R^T R - 1|: 0.0





Exercise 8 — Applying a layer to every time step
A batch of \(B = 8\) time series, each with \(T = 50\) time steps and \(F = 3\) measured quantities per step, is stored as a tensor of shape (B, T, F). 1. Apply nn.Linear(3, 5) to every time step by reshaping to (B*T, F), applying the layer, and reshaping back to (B, T, 5). 2. Apply the layer directly to the (B, T, F) tensor and compare: nn.Linear acts on the last axis and treats all other axes as batch axes. 3. What goes wrong if the tensor is stored as (B, F, T) instead? Fix it with transpose.

Solution


Code
n_series, T, F = 8, 50, 3
torch.manual_seed(0)
series = torch.randn(n_series, T, F)
lin = nn.Linear(F, 5)

# 1) merge batch and time axes, apply the layer, split them again
out1 = lin(series.reshape(n_series * T, F)).reshape(n_series, T, 5)
# 2) directly: Linear acts on the last axis
out2 = lin(series)
print("shapes:", tuple(out1.shape), tuple(out2.shape), "  agree:", torch.allclose(out1, out2))

# 3) features before time: the last axis has length T = 50, not F = 3
series_ft = series.transpose(1, 2)                        # (B, F, T)
try:
    lin(series_ft)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", e)
    # Linear merges all leading axes into one batch axis, (8 * 3) x 50 = 24 x 50, and multiplies it with W^T, which is 3 x 5
    # (the stored weight has shape (5, 3)): the inner dimensions 50 and 3 do not match
out3 = lin(series_ft.transpose(1, 2))                     # back to (B, T, F) before the layer
print("after transposing back:", tuple(out3.shape), "  agrees:", torch.allclose(out3, out1))


shapes: (8, 50, 5) (8, 50, 5)   agree: True
RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (24x50 and 3x5)
after transposing back: (8, 50, 5)   agrees: True

title: Lab 003a: Working with trained networks in PyTorch
text:
1. Training and saving

1.1 The data: two tasks from one data set
MNIST contains \(28\times28\) grayscale images of handwritten digits, \(60\,000\) for training and \(10\,000\) for testing. We split it into two tasks. The source task consists of the digits 0–4, with all training images of these digits; the CNN is trained on it in this section. The target task consists of the digits 5–9 and is used in Section 5. Its labels are shifted, \(5\to0,\dots,9\to4\), so both tasks have 5 classes.
The files are in the raw IDX format: a short big-endian header (a magic number, then the sizes), followed by one byte per pixel; we read them with gzip and numpy. Pixels are scaled to \([0,1]\).
PyTorch convolutions expect image tensors in the layout (N, C, H, W): batch size, channels, height, width. Our images are therefore stored as (N, 1, 28, 28). (JAX/Flax uses (N, H, W, C), see Lab 003b.)


Code
MNIST_DIR = "data/MNIST_raw"
MNIST_FILES = ["train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", "train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz",
               "t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", "t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz"]
if not all(os.path.exists(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{f}") for f in MNIST_FILES):
    os.makedirs(MNIST_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    for f in MNIST_FILES:
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"https://storage.googleapis.com/cvdf-datasets/mnist/{f}", f"{MNIST_DIR}/{f}")

def read_idx(path):
    with gzip.open(path, "rb") as fh:
        data = fh.read()
    ndim = data[3]                                                  # 3 for images, 1 for labels
    shape = np.frombuffer(data[4:4 + 4 * ndim], dtype=">i4")        # big-endian int32 sizes
    return np.frombuffer(data[4 + 4 * ndim:], dtype=np.uint8).reshape(shape)

Xtr_all = read_idx(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{MNIST_FILES[0]}").astype(np.float32) / 255.0   # (60000, 28, 28)
ytr_all = read_idx(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{MNIST_FILES[1]}").astype(np.int64)
Xte_all = read_idx(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{MNIST_FILES[2]}").astype(np.float32) / 255.0   # (10000, 28, 28)
yte_all = read_idx(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{MNIST_FILES[3]}").astype(np.int64)

def task(X, y, digits):
    # images of the given digits as (N, 1, 28, 28) float32 and labels shifted to 0 .. len(digits)-1
    keep = np.isin(y, digits)
    return torch.tensor(X[keep][:, None, :, :]), torch.tensor(y[keep] - digits[0])

Xs_tr, ys_tr = task(Xtr_all, ytr_all, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4])     # source task: digits 0-4
Xs_te, ys_te = task(Xte_all, yte_all, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
Xt_pool, yt_pool = task(Xtr_all, ytr_all, [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]) # target task: labelled images are drawn from this pool in Section 5
Xt_te, yt_te = task(Xte_all, yte_all, [5, 6, 7, 8, 9])

assert Xs_tr.shape[1:] == (1, 28, 28) and Xs_tr.dtype == torch.float32
print("source task (digits 0-4): train", tuple(Xs_tr.shape), "| test", tuple(Xs_te.shape))
print("target task (digits 5-9): pool ", tuple(Xt_pool.shape), "| test", tuple(Xt_te.shape))
print("pixel range:", Xs_tr.min().item(), "to", Xs_tr.max().item())


source task (digits 0-4): train (30596, 1, 28, 28) | test (5139, 1, 28, 28)
target task (digits 5-9): pool  (29404, 1, 28, 28) | test (4861, 1, 28, 28)
pixel range: 0.0 to 1.0




1.2 The architecture: a convolutional body and a dense head
The network (conv–pool–conv–pool–dense–output) is split into two named parts, because Sections 4 and 5 treat them separately. The body (the convolutional feature extractor) maps an image to a feature vector of \(32\cdot7\cdot7=1568\) numbers, \[
(N,1,28,28)\xrightarrow{\text{conv }5\times5,\ 16}(N,16,28,28)\xrightarrow{\text{ReLU, max-pool }2}(N,16,14,14)\xrightarrow{\text{conv }3\times3,\ 32}(N,32,14,14)\xrightarrow{\text{ReLU, max-pool }2}(N,32,7,7)\xrightarrow{\text{flatten}}(N,1568).
\] The head (the classifier) is a dense layer with ReLU followed by an output layer, \((N,1568)\xrightarrow{\text{fc, ReLU}}(N,64)\xrightarrow{\text{out}}(N,5)\), giving 5 logits (unnormalised log-probabilities of the classes).
padding=2 for the \(5\times5\) kernel and padding=1 for the \(3\times3\) kernel keep the height and width unchanged, so only the pooling layers halve them. Both parts are nn.Sequential containers built from an OrderedDict: every layer gets a readable name (conv1, relu1, …), which appears in the parameter names (body.conv1.weight) and lets us address single layers later.


Code
class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_classes=5):
        super().__init__()
        self.body = nn.Sequential(OrderedDict([
            ("conv1",   nn.Conv2d(1, 16, kernel_size=5, padding=2)),    # (N,1,28,28)  -> (N,16,28,28)
            ("relu1",   nn.ReLU()),
            ("pool1",   nn.MaxPool2d(2)),                               # -> (N,16,14,14)
            ("conv2",   nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)),   # -> (N,32,14,14)
            ("relu2",   nn.ReLU()),
            ("pool2",   nn.MaxPool2d(2)),                               # -> (N,32,7,7)
            ("flatten", nn.Flatten()),                                  # -> (N,1568), order (channel, row, column)
        ]))
        self.head = nn.Sequential(OrderedDict([
            ("fc",      nn.Linear(32 * 7 * 7, 64)),                     # (N,1568) -> (N,64)
            ("relu3",   nn.ReLU()),
            ("out",     nn.Linear(64, n_classes)),                      # (N,64) -> (N,n_classes) logits
        ]))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.head(self.body(x))

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = SmallCNN()
out = model(Xs_tr[:8])
assert out.shape == (8, 5) and model.body(Xs_tr[:8]).shape == (8, 1568)
print("logits of 8 images:", tuple(out.shape), "| feature vectors:", tuple(model.body(Xs_tr[:8]).shape))


logits of 8 images: (8, 5) | feature vectors: (8, 1568)



Drawing the network
A picture of the architecture helps to keep track of the shapes, and in Sections 4 and 5 it will also show which parts of the network are changed. A dense network can be drawn node by node, each node a circle and each weight a line (Lab 007), but for a convolutional layer such a drawing is not readable: conv1 alone produces \(16\cdot28\cdot28=12\,544\) numbers, each computed from a \(5\times5\) patch of the image with the same 25 weights of its kernel. Convolutional networks are therefore drawn as block diagrams in which every intermediate result is a stack of feature maps. The function draw_cnn draws \(C\) maps of \(H\times W\) pixels as overlapping squares whose side is proportional to \(H\) and whose number grows with \(\log_2 C\), and writes the shape \(H\times W\times C\) under the stack and the name of the layer that produced it above the arrow. Once the maps are flattened into a vector, the dense head is drawn with nodes and edges: every node a circle, every weight a line, and a wide layer with a limited number of circles, three dots for the omitted nodes and its true width under the column. A dashed line can mark the place where the network is cut into two parts, and an optional list status colours every layer as frozen, trained or new, which we use from Section 5 on.
The first cell contains the helpers for the columns of nodes: nodes_shown decides how many circles a layer of a given width gets (all of them up to max_nodes, then a number growing with the logarithm of the width), draw_layer draws one column, connect draws the lines of a dense layer between two columns, and finish sets equal scales on both axes and a figure size proportional to the drawing.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Rectangle
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection

SCALE = 0.42          # inches of figure per drawing unit; neighbouring nodes of a layer are 1 unit apart
NODE_COLORS = {"input": "#8A929E", "hidden": "#005CA7", "latent": "#D35A05", "output": "#002B5C",
               "cond": "#2E8B57", "noise": "#F2B28A"}


def text_height(fontsize, lines=1):
    """Height of `lines` lines of text of the given font size, in drawing units (used to place labels)."""
    return lines * 1.25 * fontsize / 72 / SCALE


def nodes_shown(n, max_nodes=8, growth=1.5):
    """Number of circles drawn for a layer of width n.
    Up to max_nodes every node is drawn. A wider layer gets max_nodes circles plus `growth` circles for every
    doubling of its width, so the column height still grows with the width: with the defaults a layer of
    16 nodes is drawn with 10 circles, 64 with 12, 256 with 16 and 784 with 18."""
    if n <= max_nodes:
        return n
    return max_nodes + int(round(growth * np.log2(n / max_nodes)))


def draw_layer(ax, x, n, y0=0.0, color=NODE_COLORS["hidden"], max_nodes=8, growth=1.5, r=0.32,
               top=None, bottom=None, show_width=True, fontsize=12):
    """Draw one layer of width n as a vertical column of circles at horizontal position x, centred at height y0.
    Returns the heights of the drawn circles, from top to bottom (needed to draw the edges).

    The circles are 1 unit apart. If the layer is wider than the number of circles (see nodes_shown), one slot
    in the middle of the column stays empty and gets three dots, which stand for the omitted nodes; the true
    width n is then the number written under the column. `top` and `bottom` are optional texts above and below."""
    k = nodes_shown(n, max_nodes, growth)
    capped = k < n
    slots = k + 1 if capped else k                         # one extra slot for the dots
    y = y0 + (slots - 1) / 2 - np.arange(slots)            # heights of the slots, from top to bottom
    if capped:
        mid = slots // 2
        ax.scatter([x] * 3, y[mid] + np.array([-0.25, 0.0, 0.25]), s=6, color="k", zorder=3)
        y = np.delete(y, mid)                              # no circle in the dotted slot
    for yi in y:
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, yi), r, facecolor=color, edgecolor="k", lw=0.8, zorder=3))
    under = (f"{n}" if show_width else "") + (f"\n{bottom}" if bottom else "")
    if under.strip():
        ax.text(x, y0 - (slots - 1) / 2 - 0.55, under.strip("\n"), ha="center", va="top", fontsize=fontsize, linespacing=1.1)
    if top:
        ax.text(x, y0 + (slots - 1) / 2 + 0.55, top, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=fontsize, linespacing=1.1)
    return y


def connect(ax, x0, y0, x1, y1, one_to_one=False, color="0.45", alpha=0.35, lw=0.6, ls="-"):
    """Edges between two drawn layers at horizontal positions x0 and x1, whose circles are at heights y0 and y1.
    A dense layer joins every node to every node, one line per weight; an elementwise operation joins
    node j only to node j (one_to_one=True). The lines are thin and semi-transparent, and are drawn
    below the circles (zorder), so they seem to end at the circle boundaries."""
    pairs = zip(y0, y1) if one_to_one else [(a, b) for a in y0 for b in y1]
    segments = [[(x0, a), (x1, b)] for a, b in pairs]
    ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segments, colors=color, alpha=alpha, linewidths=lw, linestyles=ls, zorder=1))


def bracket(ax, x0, x1, y, text, color="k", fontsize=12):
    """A horizontal bracket from x0 to x1 at height y with a text above it; it marks a block of layers."""
    ax.plot([x0, x0, x1, x1], [y - 0.3, y, y, y - 0.3], color=color, lw=1.5)
    ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, y + 0.2, text, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=fontsize, color=color)


def finish(ax, title="", fontsize=12):
    """Equal scales on both axes (circles stay round), no axes, and a figure size proportional to the drawing."""
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.autoscale_view()
    ax.axis("off")
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=fontsize)
    (x0, x1), (y0, y1) = ax.get_xlim(), ax.get_ylim()
    ax.figure.set_size_inches(SCALE * (x1 - x0) + 1.0, SCALE * (y1 - y0) + 1.2)


draw_cnn goes through the list of stages from left to right. A stage is either a shape \((H, W, C)\), drawn as a stack of squares, or an integer \(n\), drawn as a column of \(n\) nodes; two consecutive vectors are joined by the edges of a dense layer, every other pair of stages by an arrow. The function smallcnn_stages writes down the stages of our SmallCNN once, so that the later drawings only change the colours.


Code
def draw_cnn(stages, cut=None, status=None, input_image=None, image_cmap="gray_r", map_height=6.0, shape_fmt="{H}×{W}×{C}", max_nodes=5, growth=0.75, gap=2.4, fontsize=12, title="", ax=None):
    """Block diagram of a convolutional network: stacks of feature maps, followed by columns of nodes.

    stages : list of (shape, text) from the input to the output.
             shape = (H, W, C): C feature maps of H x W pixels, drawn as a stack of squares whose side is
             proportional to H and whose number grows with log2(C); "H×W×C" is written underneath.
             shape = n (an integer): a vector of n numbers, drawn as a column of nodes (draw_layer);
             two consecutive vectors are joined by the edges of a dense layer.
             text = the operation that produces this stage, written above the gap leading to it
             (for the first stage: the name of the input).
    cut    : None or (i, left_name, right_name): a dashed line after stage i that splits the network into two
             named parts, e.g. (5, "body", "head")
    status : None, or one entry per stage saying how the parameters of the layer that PRODUCES this stage
             are treated: "frozen" (grey, hatched), "trained" (blue, orange edges), "new" (green: a new layer,
             trained) or None (a layer without parameters, e.g. pooling, drawn white); a legend is added
    input_image : optional 2D array shown in place of the first square (the input), with colour map image_cmap
    shape_fmt : format of the shape written under a stack, e.g. "{H}×{W}\n×{C}" for two lines
    map_height : height of the largest feature map in drawing units (the nodes of a column are 1 unit apart)
    """
    if ax is None:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    unit = map_height / max(s[0] for s, _ in stages if not np.isscalar(s))   # drawing units per pixel
    off = 0.25                                       # shift between neighbouring squares of a stack
    x, lefts, rights, tops, prev_vec = 0.0, [], [], [], None
    # colours for the status of a layer: (map face, map hatch, node colour, edge colour, edge alpha)
    STYLE = {"frozen": ("#E3E6EA", "///", "#B8BEC6", "0.6", 0.25), "trained": ("#9CC3E6", None, NODE_COLORS["hidden"], NODE_COLORS["latent"], 0.35),
             "new": ("#A8D5B9", None, NODE_COLORS["cond"], NODE_COLORS["cond"], 0.55), None: ("#9CC3E6", None, None, "0.45", 0.35),
             "none": ("#FFFFFF", None, "#FFFFFF", "0.45", 0.35)}       # "none": no parameters, drawn white
    for i, (shape, text) in enumerate(stages):
        state = None if status is None else (status[i] or "none")   # with a status list, layers without parameters are white
        face, hatch, node_c, edge_c, edge_a = STYLE[state]
        if np.isscalar(shape):                       # a vector: a column of nodes
            xc = x + 0.4
            color = node_c or (NODE_COLORS["output"] if i == len(stages) - 1 else NODE_COLORS["hidden"])
            yv = draw_layer(ax, xc, shape, color=color, max_nodes=max_nodes, growth=growth, fontsize=fontsize)
            if prev_vec is not None:                 # vector -> vector: the edges of a dense layer
                connect(ax, prev_vec[0], prev_vec[1], xc, yv, color=edge_c, alpha=edge_a)
            prev_vec = (xc, yv)
            left, right, top = xc - 0.4, xc + 0.4, yv.max() + 0.4
        else:                                        # a stack of C feature maps of H x W pixels
            H, W, C = shape
            s = H * unit
            k = 1 if C == 1 else 2 + int(round(np.log2(C)))
            for j in range(k):                       # back square first, each next one shifted right and down
                ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x + j * off, -s / 2 - 0.6 * j * off), s, s, lw=0.8, zorder=2 + j,
                                       facecolor=face if C > 1 else "#D0D4DA", hatch=hatch, edgecolor=NODE_COLORS["output"]))
            if i == 0 and input_image is not None:   # the input itself instead of a plain square
                ax.imshow(np.asarray(input_image), cmap=image_cmap, extent=(x, x + s, -s / 2, s / 2), zorder=3)
            left, right, top = x, x + s + (k - 1) * off, s / 2
            ax.text((left + right) / 2, -s / 2 - 0.6 * (k - 1) * off - 0.35, shape_fmt.format(H=H, W=W, C=C), ha="center", va="top",
                    linespacing=1.1,
                    fontsize=fontsize)
            prev_vec = None
        if i > 0 and not (np.isscalar(shape) and np.isscalar(stages[i - 1][0])):   # arrow from the previous stage
            ax.annotate("", xy=(left - 0.15, 0), xytext=(rights[-1] + 0.15, 0),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="k", lw=1.2), zorder=10)
        lefts.append(left); rights.append(right); tops.append(top)
        x = right + gap
    # the names of the operations, all at one height above the tallest stage
    y_text = max(tops) + 0.6
    for i, (shape, text) in enumerate(stages):
        xt = (lefts[0] + rights[0]) / 2 if i == 0 else (rights[i - 1] + lefts[i]) / 2
        ax.text(xt, y_text, text, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=fontsize, linespacing=1.1)
    ax.update_datalim([(0, y_text + text_height(fontsize, 2) + 0.4)])   # keep the names inside the axes (below a title)
    if cut is not None:                              # a dashed line between stage i and stage i + 1
        i, left_name, right_name = cut
        xc, y_name = (rights[i] + lefts[i + 1]) / 2, y_text + text_height(fontsize, 2) + 0.8
        ax.plot([xc, xc], [-max(tops) - 1.0, y_name + 0.4], color=NODE_COLORS["latent"], ls="--", lw=1.6)
        for name, side in [(left_name + " ←", -1), ("→ " + right_name, 1)]:
            ax.text(xc + 0.3 * side, y_name, name, ha="right" if side < 0 else "left", va="center",
                    fontsize=fontsize + 1, color=NODE_COLORS["latent"])
    if status is not None:                           # legend of the colours, under the drawing
        from matplotlib.patches import Patch
        shown = [k for k in ["frozen", "trained", "new"] if k in status]
        labels = {"frozen": "frozen", "trained": "trained", "new": "new layer (trained)"}
        ax.legend([Patch(facecolor=STYLE[k][0], hatch=STYLE[k][1], edgecolor=STYLE[k][2]) for k in shown],
                  [labels[k] for k in shown], loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=len(shown),
                  frameon=False, fontsize=fontsize)
    finish(ax, title, fontsize + 1)
    return ax


The diagram of SmallCNN uses one training digit as the input. The height and width of the maps are halved by each pooling layer, \(28\to14\to7\), while the number of channels grows from 1 to 16 and 32; the body ends by flattening the \(7\times7\times32\) maps into 1568 numbers, and everything right of the dashed line is the head of Sections 4 and 5. The count printed under the diagram shows that the head holds most of the parameters, almost all of them in the dense layer fc with its \(1568\times64\) weights.


Code
def smallcnn_stages(n_out=5, extra=False):
    # the stages of SmallCNN for draw_cnn; extra=True adds the dense layer inserted in Section 5.6
    stages = [((28, 28, 1), "input image"), ((28, 28, 16), "conv1 5×5\nReLU"), ((14, 14, 16), "pool1"),
              ((14, 14, 32), "conv2 3×3\nReLU"), ((7, 7, 32), "pool2"), (1568, "flatten"), (64, "fc\nReLU")]
    if extra:
        stages.append((64, "extra\nReLU"))
    return stages + [(n_out, "out\nlogits")]

draw_cnn(smallcnn_stages(), cut=(5, "body", "head"), input_image=Xs_tr[0, 0])
plt.show()
n_body = sum(p.numel() for p in model.body.parameters())
n_head = sum(p.numel() for p in model.head.parameters())
print(f"parameters: body {n_body}, head {n_head}, total {n_body + n_head}")





parameters: body 5056, head 100741, total 105797


The package torchview, a small Python library that draws PyTorch models, draws the same model from the code instead of from a list written by us. Its function draw_graph passes a batch of the given shape through the model, records every module it calls and returns a graph of the data flow; with expand_nested=True the modules of body and head are shown inside two boxes, the two nn.Sequential containers. Each module box lists the shapes of its input and output tensors, so the graph is a check of the shapes \((N,1,28,28)\to(N,1568)\to(N,5)\), while our diagram shows the sizes of the maps and of the dense layers at a glance. torchview draws with Graphviz, a program that lays out graphs of boxes and arrows, and is not part of the standard Colab installation (%pip install torchview installs it); if it is missing, the cell prints a message. The model drawn here is a separate instance created inside torch.random.fork_rng(), together with the random input batch, so the random-number generator of the rest of the notebook is not changed.


Code
try:
    from torchview import draw_graph
    with torch.random.fork_rng():                        # leaves the global random-number generator unchanged
        graph = draw_graph(SmallCNN(), input_size=(1, 1, 28, 28), expand_nested=True)
    display(graph.visual_graph)
except Exception as err:                                 # torchview or Graphviz not installed
    print("torchview drawing not available:", err)








1.3 Training on the source task
Standard supervised training: cross-entropy loss on the logits, Adam with learning rate \(10^{-3}\), minibatches of 128 images, one epoch (one pass over the \(30\,596\) training images, 239 steps). The minibatch order comes from a NumPy generator with a fixed seed, so Lab 003b sees exactly the same sequence of minibatches.
Two helpers are used for the rest of the notebook: train_steps performs a given number of gradient steps on randomly drawn minibatches, and accuracy evaluates in chunks of 2000 images under torch.inference_mode() (no computational graph is recorded). model.train() / model.eval() switch layers such as dropout or batch normalisation between their training and evaluation behaviour; our network has none, but calling them is a habit worth having.


Code
def accuracy(model, X, y, chunk=2000):
    # fraction of correctly classified images
    model.eval()
    with torch.inference_mode():
        pred = torch.cat([model(X[i:i + chunk]).argmax(dim=1) for i in range(0, len(X), chunk)])
    return (pred == y).float().mean().item()

def train_epochs(model, X, y, epochs, batch_size, lr, seed):
    # plain training loop: one random permutation of the data per epoch
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n_batches = len(X) // batch_size                  # the last incomplete batch is dropped
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        perm = rng.permutation(len(X))[: n_batches * batch_size].reshape(n_batches, batch_size)
        losses = []
        for idx in perm:
            idx = torch.from_numpy(idx)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(model(X[idx]), y[idx])
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
            losses.append(loss.item())
        print(f"epoch {epoch + 1}: mean training loss {np.mean(losses):.4f} | test accuracy (digits 0-4) {accuracy(model, Xs_te, ys_te):.4f}")

t0 = time.time()
torch.manual_seed(0)
model = SmallCNN()
train_epochs(model, Xs_tr, ys_tr, epochs=1, batch_size=128, lr=1e-3, seed=0)
acc_source = accuracy(model, Xs_te, ys_te)
print(f"training time: {time.time() - t0:.1f} s | final test accuracy on digits 0-4: {acc_source:.4f}")

1.4 Saving and loading the parameters
What is saved is model.state_dict(), an ordered dictionary {parameter name: tensor}, e.g. "body.conv1.weight" → tensor of shape (16, 1, 5, 5). It contains the numbers only, not the code of the class. torch.save writes it to a file (a zip archive of the tensors).
Loading requires the architecture: we create a fresh SmallCNN (random parameters) and copy the stored numbers into it with load_state_dict. The names and shapes must match; otherwise PyTorch raises an error listing the missing or unexpected keys. torch.load(..., weights_only=True) reads tensors only and refuses arbitrary Python objects, which makes loading a file from an unknown source safe.
(The alternative torch.save(model) pickles the whole object including a reference to its class; such a file breaks as soon as the class definition is moved or renamed, and is therefore not recommended.)
To confirm that nothing is lost, we compare logits on the whole test set. Before loading, the fresh model gives different logits; after loading, the logits should be bit-for-bit identical (torch.equal, not just close).


Code
os.makedirs("checkpoints", exist_ok=True)
CKPT = "checkpoints/cnn_digits04_torch.pt"
torch.save(model.state_dict(), CKPT)
print(f"saved {len(model.state_dict())} tensors ({os.path.getsize(CKPT) / 1e3:.0f} kB)")

torch.manual_seed(123)                                  # a different seed: different random parameters
fresh = SmallCNN()
with torch.inference_mode():
    print("fresh model, logits equal to the trained model before loading:", torch.equal(fresh(Xs_te), model(Xs_te)))

state = torch.load(CKPT, weights_only=True)             # dict {name: tensor}
fresh.load_state_dict(state)                            # copies the numbers into the existing parameters
fresh.eval(); model.eval()
with torch.inference_mode():
    same_logits = torch.equal(fresh(Xs_te), model(Xs_te))
assert same_logits
print("after load_state_dict, logits on all", len(Xs_te), "test images identical:", same_logits)
print(f"test accuracy of the reloaded model: {accuracy(fresh, Xs_te, ys_te):.4f}")

after load_state_dict, logits on all 5139 test images identical: True

2. Structure of a trained network

2.1 Layers, parameter shapes and counts
print(model) shows the module tree. model.named_parameters() yields every trainable array with its full name. PyTorch shapes follow the convention (output, input, …): a Conv2d weight has shape (out_channels, in_channels, kernel_height, kernel_width) and its bias (out_channels,), while a Linear weight has shape (out_features, in_features), so that \(y = x W^{T} + b\), with bias (out_features,).
The number of parameters of a layer is the number of weights plus the number of biases, e.g. for conv1: \(16\cdot1\cdot5\cdot5+16=416\).


Code
print(model)
print()
print(f"{'parameter':22s} {'shape':>18s} {'count':>8s}")
for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    print(f"{name:22s} {str(tuple(p.shape)):>18s} {p.numel():8d}")
n_total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"{'total':22s} {'':>18s} {n_total:8d}")

# per layer: weights + biases of each module that owns parameters
print()
for lname, layer in model.named_modules():
    own = list(layer.parameters(recurse=False))
    if own:
        print(f"layer {lname:12s} ({type(layer).__name__:6s}): {sum(p.numel() for p in own):6d} parameters")
assert n_total == (16*1*5*5 + 16) + (32*16*3*3 + 32) + (1568*64 + 64) + (64*5 + 5)

Almost all parameters (\(100\,416\) of \(105\,797\)) sit in the dense layer head.fc, which connects all \(1568\) outputs of the convolutional part to 64 units; the two convolutional layers together have only \(5\,056\), because a kernel is shared over all positions of the image.


2.2 Access to a single layer
A layer is reached by attribute access along its name: model.body.conv1. Its parameters are .weight and .bias, tensors with requires_grad=True. To use them as plain numbers, call .detach() (a tensor without a gradient history, sharing the memory) and .numpy(); to modify them directly, do it inside torch.no_grad() so that the change is not recorded by automatic differentiation.


Code

print("kernel 0 (5 x 5):\n", np.round(W1[0, 0], 3))
print("output layer weight:", tuple(model.head.out.weight.shape), "(out_features, in_features) | bias:", np.round(model.head.out.bias.detach().numpy(), 3))

2.3 Trainable and frozen parameters
A parameter is trainable in PyTorch if p.requires_grad is True: then loss.backward() computes its gradient and an optimiser can change it. Setting requires_grad=False freezes it. The function below counts both groups; we use it in Section 5. At this point everything is trainable.


Code
def count_params(model):
    # (number of trainable, number of frozen) parameters
    trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
    frozen = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if not p.requires_grad)
    return trainable, frozen

tr, fr = count_params(model)
print(f"trainable parameters: {tr} | frozen parameters: {fr}")


trainable parameters: 105797 | frozen parameters: 0


For the experiments of Section 5 two more views are useful. layer_table lists every layer that owns parameters (the Conv2d and Linear layers) with its number of parameters and its state, trainable or frozen, read from the requires_grad flags; the total line repeats the two counts of count_params. snapshot stores a copy of every parameter tensor, and max_change prints, for every tensor, the largest absolute change since the snapshot, \[\max_k\,\big|w_k^{\rm after}-w_k^{\rm before}\big| ,\] where \(k\) runs over the entries of the tensor. A value of exactly zero proves that the tensor was not touched, bit for bit; a frozen layer must show zeros, a trained one must not.


Code
def layer_table(model):
    # one row per layer that owns parameters: name, number of parameters, trainable or frozen
    rows = []
    for name, layer in model.named_modules():
        own = list(layer.parameters(recurse=False))            # the layer's own parameters only
        if own:
            flags = {p.requires_grad for p in own}
            state = "trainable" if flags == {True} else ("frozen" if flags == {False} else "mixed")
            rows.append((name, sum(p.numel() for p in own), state))
    print(f"{'layer':12s} {'parameters':>10s}   state")
    for name, n, state in rows:
        print(f"{name:12s} {n:10d}   {state}")
    n_tr = sum(n for _, n, s in rows if s == "trainable")
    print(f"{'total':12s} {sum(n for _, n, _ in rows):10d}   trainable {n_tr}, frozen {sum(n for _, n, _ in rows) - n_tr}")

def snapshot(model):
    # copies of all parameter tensors, to compare with after training
    return {name: p.detach().clone() for name, p in model.named_parameters()}

def max_change(before, model):
    # largest absolute change of every parameter tensor since `before`; exactly 0 means unchanged
    for name, p in model.named_parameters():
        change = f"{(p.detach() - before[name]).abs().max().item():.2e}" if name in before else "new"
        print(f"{name:22s} max|dw| = {change}")
