The accuracy, the fraction of correctly classified images, is what we are interested in, but it cannot be used as a loss: it changes only when an image switches class, so its gradient with respect to the parameters is zero almost everywhere. The cross-entropy changes smoothly with the parameters.
Before training we check the loss of the untrained network. It gives \(q_k \approx 1/10\) for every class (Section 6), so the loss should be close to \(-\log(1/10) = \ln 10 \approx 2.30\).


Code
ce_loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

def accuracy(logits, y):
    """Fraction of images whose largest logit is at the true class."""
    return (logits.argmax(dim=1) == y).float().mean().item()

torch.manual_seed(0)
clf = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
with torch.no_grad():
    z = clf(X_va)
    print(f"untrained: loss {ce_loss(z, y_va).item():.3f}  (ln 10 = {np.log(10):.3f}),  accuracy {accuracy(z, y_va):.3f}")


untrained: loss 2.303  (ln 10 = 2.303),  accuracy 0.108




14.3 The training loop
The loop is that of Section 11 with mini-batches, written out here because the loss and the recorded quantities differ. The images are processed in mini-batches of 64, in a new random order in every epoch (torch.randperm), with Adam at learning rate \(10^{-3}\), the default of Adam; 64 is a common batch size, and values from 32 to 256 work as well. After every epoch the loss and accuracy on the training and validation sets are computed for all images at once, inside torch.no_grad() (Section 10.4). The training loss is evaluated after the epoch, with the final parameters of that epoch, so that it can be compared with the validation loss. We train for 10 epochs (10 passes over the 50 000 training images), enough to show where the validation loss stops improving. The cell prints its total running time; divided by the 10 epochs it gives the time of one epoch, which depends strongly on the processor and on the number of CPU threads available to PyTorch.
model.train() and model.eval() (Section 11.2) make no difference for this network (no dropout or batch normalisation) and are written for completeness.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
clf = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(clf.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
batch_size, n_epochs = 64, 10
log = {"train loss": [], "val loss": [], "train acc": [], "val acc": []}

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
    clf.train()
    order = torch.randperm(len(X_tr))                     # new random order of the training images
    for start in range(0, len(X_tr), batch_size):
        idx = order[start:start + batch_size]             # indices of one mini-batch
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = ce_loss(clf(X_tr[idx]), y_tr[idx])
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    clf.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        z_tr, z_va = clf(X_tr), clf(X_va)
        log["train loss"].append(ce_loss(z_tr, y_tr).item()); log["train acc"].append(accuracy(z_tr, y_tr))
        log["val loss"].append(ce_loss(z_va, y_va).item());   log["val acc"].append(accuracy(z_va, y_va))
    print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}:  loss train {log['train loss'][-1]:.4f}  val {log['val loss'][-1]:.4f}   "
          f"accuracy train {log['train acc'][-1]:.4f}  val {log['val acc'][-1]:.4f}")
print(f"training took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")


epoch  1:  loss train 0.1856  val 0.2002   accuracy train 0.9473  val 0.9434


epoch  2:  loss train 0.1144  val 0.1393   accuracy train 0.9669  val 0.9581


epoch  3:  loss train 0.0860  val 0.1140   accuracy train 0.9747  val 0.9665


epoch  4:  loss train 0.0649  val 0.1044   accuracy train 0.9808  val 0.9691


epoch  5:  loss train 0.0504  val 0.0947   accuracy train 0.9847  val 0.9736


epoch  6:  loss train 0.0338  val 0.0844   accuracy train 0.9902  val 0.9747


epoch  7:  loss train 0.0353  val 0.0984   accuracy train 0.9891  val 0.9725


epoch  8:  loss train 0.0233  val 0.0852   accuracy train 0.9928  val 0.9753


epoch  9:  loss train 0.0205  val 0.0867   accuracy train 0.9940  val 0.9747


epoch 10:  loss train 0.0152  val 0.0898   accuracy train 0.9956  val 0.9770
training took 1204 s




14.4 Learning curves
The printed numbers are easier to read as curves. The figure shows the training and validation loss (left) and accuracy (right) after each epoch.


Code
epochs = np.arange(1, n_epochs + 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
axes[0].plot(epochs, log["train loss"], "o-", label="training")
axes[0].plot(epochs, log["val loss"], "s-", label="validation")
axes[0].set_ylabel("cross-entropy loss")
axes[1].plot(epochs, log["train acc"], "o-", label="training")
axes[1].plot(epochs, log["val acc"], "s-", label="validation")
axes[1].set_ylabel("accuracy")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.legend()
plt.show()





Both losses fall quickly during the first epochs. Afterwards they separate: the training loss keeps falling (from about 0.19 after the first epoch to about 0.015 after the tenth), while the validation loss reaches its smallest value after about 6 epochs (about 0.085) and then stays at that level or rises slightly. This is the onset of overfitting: the network begins to adapt to details of the 50 000 training images that do not carry over to new images. The same is seen in the accuracies: about 99.6% on the training set but about 97.7% on the validation set.
The validation accuracy still increases a little while the validation loss no longer decreases. The two measure different things: the accuracy counts only whether the largest probability is at the right class, the cross-entropy also measures how confident the network is. As training continues, the network gets a few more images right, but it also becomes more confident everywhere, and pays a large loss \(-\log q_y\) for every image on which it is confidently wrong.


14.5 Evaluation on the test set
The test set is used once, for the final numbers. Besides the accuracy, two views show which mistakes the network makes. The first is the confusion matrix \(C_{ij}\), the number of test images of true class \(i\) that were classified as \(j\), with the correct answers on the diagonal. It is computed with one bincount: the pair \((i, j)\) is encoded as the single number \(10i + j\), the occurrences of every number \(0, \dots, 99\) are counted, and the counts are arranged as a \(10\times10\) matrix with reshape. The second view is a gallery of misclassified images with their true and predicted classes.


Code
with torch.no_grad():
    pred_te = clf(X_te).argmax(dim=1)
print(f"test accuracy: {(pred_te == y_te).float().mean().item():.4f}   ({(pred_te != y_te).sum().item()} of {len(y_te)} test images misclassified)")

C = torch.bincount(10 * y_te + pred_te, minlength=100).reshape(10, 10)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5.5))
im = ax.imshow(torch.log10(C + 1), cmap="Blues")         # logarithmic colours: the diagonal (about 1000) would hide the rest
for i in range(10):
    for j in range(10):
        if C[i, j] > 0:
            ax.text(j, i, str(C[i, j].item()), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7,
                    color="white" if i == j else "black")
ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_yticks(range(10))
ax.set_xlabel("predicted class $j$"); ax.set_ylabel("true class $i$"); ax.set_title("confusion matrix (test set)")
plt.show()

wrong = torch.nonzero(pred_te != y_te)[:, 0]             # positions of the misclassified test images
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(12, 3.6))
for ax, k in zip(axes.flat, wrong[:16]):
    ax.imshow(images_raw[k], cmap="gray_r")
    ax.set_title(f"true {y_te[k].item()}, pred {pred_te[k].item()}", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


test accuracy: 0.9756   (244 of 10000 test images misclassified)








The test accuracy (97.6%, i.e. 244 misclassified images out of 10 000) agrees with the validation accuracy of the last epoch (97.7%): since neither set was used for training, both estimate the accuracy on new images.
In the confusion matrix almost all images lie on the diagonal. The largest off-diagonal entries in our run are true 5 classified as 3, true 9 classified as 4, and true 9 classified as 3: pairs of digits whose shapes are similar. The misclassified images show that a part of the mistakes concerns digits that are hard to read also for a human; others are well readable and are genuine errors of the network.
The network reaches this accuracy without any notion that the input is an image: it treats the 784 pixels as an unordered list of numbers. Convolutional networks, which use the two-dimensional arrangement of the pixels, reach above 99% on MNIST; they are the subject of a later lecture.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
15. Summary
A dense network is defined by its layer sizes \([n_0,\dots,n_L]\) and its activation; layer \(l\) has a weight matrix of shape \(n_l\times n_{l-1}\) and a bias vector of length \(n_l\). nn.Sequential(...) builds a chain of layers, while a class derived from nn.Module (layers in __init__, computation in forward) builds any architecture; both are used in the same way, through model(x), model.parameters() and model.state_dict(). Networks of arbitrary depth are built in a loop, either as a list of layers passed to nn.Sequential(*layers) or as an nn.ModuleList in a class, but never as a plain Python list.
A training step consists of the forward pass, the loss, zero_grad(), backward() and step(). Mini-batches are provided by DataLoader, and one epoch is one pass over the training data. The data are divided into three sets: the training set fits the parameters, the validation set is used to monitor training and to choose, and the test set gives the final estimate and is used once. The validation loss is monitored inside torch.no_grad(), model.train() and model.eval() switch between the two modes, and a model is saved with torch.save(model.state_dict(), ...). The most common silent bugs concern shapes ((B, 1) against (B,)), dtypes (float32) and the scale of the inputs. For classification (Section 14) the network has one output per class and is trained with nn.CrossEntropyLoss on the logits with integer labels, and the accuracy and the confusion matrix serve for evaluation.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
16. Exercises

Exercise 1 — One architecture, three constructions
Build the network with layer sizes \([2, 32, 32, 1]\) and \(\tanh\) activations in three ways: (a) nn.Sequential written out layer by layer, (b) make_mlp, (c) the class MLP of Section 7.2. Draw it with draw_network, check that all three have the same number of parameters, and compare it with the formula \(\sum_l n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\). Then copy the parameters of (a) into (c) and verify that both give the same output for a batch of 10 random points. Hint: the Linear layers of (a) are model_a[0], model_a[2], model_a[4]; those of (c) are model_c.layers[0], [1], [2].

Solution


Code
sizes = [2, 32, 32, 1]
draw_network(sizes, activations=["tanh", "tanh"], title="Exercise 1", input_labels=["$x$", "$y$"], output_labels=["$f$"])
plt.show()

# (a) written out layer by layer
model_a = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 1))
# (b) from the list of layer sizes
model_b = make_mlp(sizes)
# (c) the class with nn.ModuleList
model_c = MLP(sizes)

formula = sum(n_out * (n_in + 1) for n_in, n_out in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:]))
for name, m in [("(a) Sequential by hand", model_a), ("(b) make_mlp", model_b), ("(c) MLP class", model_c)]:
    print(f"{name:25s} parameters = {sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())}")
print("formula:", formula, "= 32*(2+1) + 32*(32+1) + 1*(32+1)")

# copy the parameters of (a) into (c): Linear layers of (a) are at positions 0, 2, 4 (the others are activations)
with torch.no_grad():
    for layer_c, layer_a in zip(model_c.layers, [model_a[0], model_a[2], model_a[4]]):
        layer_c.weight.copy_(layer_a.weight)
        layer_c.bias.copy_(layer_a.bias)
points = torch.rand(10, 2)
with torch.no_grad():
    print("max |output (a) - output (c)|:", (model_a(points) - model_c(points)).abs().max().item())





(a) Sequential by hand    parameters = 1185
(b) make_mlp              parameters = 1185
(c) MLP class             parameters = 1185
formula: 1185 = 32*(2+1) + 32*(32+1) + 1*(32+1)
max |output (a) - output (c)|: 0.0





Exercise 2 — Fitting a function of two variables
Fit the 2D double-well potential \(V(x, y) = (x^2 - 1)^2 + \tfrac12 y^2\) on \([-1.5, 1.5]\times[-1.5, 1.5]\). 1. Generate 2000 random points \((x, y)\) in the square with values \(V(x,y)\) and split them into training (1400), validation (300) and test (300) sets. Inputs have shape (B, 2), targets (B, 1). 2. Train make_mlp([2, 64, 64, 1]) with the function train of Section 12 (mini-batches of 64, 200 epochs, lr=1e-2). Plot training and validation loss versus epoch. 3. Compute the test MSE once at the end. Show the true potential, the network and their difference as images on a \(100\times100\) grid.
The inputs \(x, y\in[-1.5, 1.5]\) and the values \(V\in[0, 2.7]\) are already of order one, so no rescaling is needed. A function of two variables needs more samples than one of a single variable to cover its domain, hence 2000 points and a somewhat wider network. The batch size, the number of epochs and the learning rate are reasonable defaults, not tuned values: changing any one of them by a factor of 2–3 (measured: batch 32 or 128, 100 or 400 epochs, lr \(3\cdot10^{-3}\) or \(3\cdot10^{-2}\)) gives final validation errors between \(1\cdot10^{-4}\) and \(2\cdot10^{-3}\), all small compared with the range of \(V\).

Solution


Code
def V2d(x, y):
    return (x**2 - 1)**2 + 0.5 * y**2

# 1) data: random points in the square, split 1400 / 300 / 300
rng2 = np.random.default_rng(1)
P = rng2.uniform(-1.5, 1.5, size=(2000, 2))                  # each row is a point (x, y)
Z = V2d(P[:, 0], P[:, 1])
X2 = torch.tensor(P, dtype=torch.float32)                    # shape (2000, 2)
Y2 = torch.tensor(Z, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)     # shape (2000, 1)
X2_train, X2_val, X2_test = X2[:1400], X2[1400:1700], X2[1700:]   # the points are already in random order
Y2_train, Y2_val, Y2_test = Y2[:1400], Y2[1400:1700], Y2[1700:]

# 2) training
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_2d = make_mlp([2, 64, 64, 1])
t0 = time.perf_counter()
hist_2d = train(model_2d, X2_train, Y2_train, X2_val, Y2_val, n_epochs=200, batch_size=64, lr=1e-2)
print(f"training took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")

# 3) test loss (once) and images
model_2d.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    test_mse = loss_fn(model_2d(X2_test), Y2_test).item()
print(f"final training MSE {hist_2d['train'][-1]:.2e}, validation MSE {hist_2d['val'][-1]:.2e}, test MSE {test_mse:.2e}")

g1 = np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 100)
GX, GY = np.meshgrid(g1, g1)
# ravel() turns each 100 x 100 grid into a list of 10 000 numbers; stack(..., axis=1) puts them side by side as the
# columns x and y, giving the batch of shape (10000, 2) that the network expects. reshape(100, 100) undoes this for the image.
grid_points = torch.tensor(np.stack([GX.ravel(), GY.ravel()], axis=1), dtype=torch.float32)
with torch.no_grad():
    V_net = model_2d(grid_points).numpy().reshape(100, 100)
V_true = V2d(GX, GY)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 4))
axes[0].semilogy(hist_2d["train"], label="training"); axes[0].semilogy(hist_2d["val"], label="validation")
axes[0].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel("MSE"); axes[0].legend()
for ax, img, title in zip(axes[1:], [V_true, V_net, V_net - V_true], ["true $V$", "network", "network $-$ true"]):
    im = ax.imshow(img, origin="lower", extent=[-1.5, 1.5, -1.5, 1.5], cmap="viridis" if title != "network $-$ true" else "RdBu_r")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8); ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# The square root of the test MSE is the typical error of the network in the units of V: about 0.03,
# compared with values of V between 0 and 2.7. The difference image shows where these errors are located.


training took 324 s
final training MSE 8.47e-04, validation MSE 8.06e-04, test MSE 6.87e-04








Exercise 3 — A classification task
Points \((x, y)\) belong to class 0 if their distance from the origin is below 1 and to class 1 if it is between 1.3 and 2 (two rings, no point in between). 1. Generate 600 points of each class (sample the radius uniformly in the ring and the angle uniformly), shuffle them and split 800 / 200 / 200. 2. Train make_mlp([2, 16, 16, 2]) (two outputs = two class scores) with nn.CrossEntropyLoss, which takes the scores of shape (B, 2) and the integer labels of shape (B,) (dtype torch.long), and applies softmax internally. One score per class (rather than a single output) makes the same code work for any number of classes. The labels are integers because the loss uses them as indices, to pick the score of the correct class. Use Adam, lr=1e-2, full batch, 300 steps; record training and validation loss. 3. Report the accuracy (fraction of correctly classified points) on the validation and, at the end, on the test set. 4. Plot the decision boundary: the predicted class on a grid of points, with the data on top.
The function train of Section 12 uses nn.MSELoss, so the training loop is written out explicitly here.

Solution


Code
# 1) data: two rings
rng3 = np.random.default_rng(2)
def ring(n, r_min, r_max):
    r = rng3.uniform(r_min, r_max, n)
    phi = rng3.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n)
    return np.stack([r * np.cos(phi), r * np.sin(phi)], axis=1)

points_rings = np.concatenate([ring(600, 0.0, 1.0), ring(600, 1.3, 2.0)])
labels_rings = np.concatenate([np.zeros(600), np.ones(600)])
order = rng3.permutation(1200)                                      # shuffle points and labels together
Xc = torch.tensor(points_rings[order], dtype=torch.float32)
Yc = torch.tensor(labels_rings[order], dtype=torch.long)                  # integer class labels, shape (1200,)
Xc_train, Xc_val, Xc_test = Xc[:800], Xc[800:1000], Xc[1000:]
Yc_train, Yc_val, Yc_test = Yc[:800], Yc[800:1000], Yc[1000:]

# 2) model and training loop
torch.manual_seed(0)
clf_rings = make_mlp([2, 16, 16, 2])                                      # outputs: one score (logit) per class
ce_loss_rings = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(clf_rings.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
hist_tr, hist_va = [], []
for step in range(300):
    loss = ce_loss_rings(clf_rings(Xc_train), Yc_train)                         # scores (800, 2) vs labels (800,)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        hist_va.append(ce_loss_rings(clf_rings(Xc_val), Yc_val).item())
    hist_tr.append(loss.item())

# 3) accuracy: the predicted class is the one with the larger score.
# argmax(dim=1) gives, for every row, the index of the largest entry. Softmax does not change the order of the
# scores, so this is also the class of highest probability, and softmax need not be computed.
# (... == Y) is a tensor of True/False; .float() turns it into 1.0/0.0, and its mean is the fraction of correct answers.
def accuracy_of(model, X, Y):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (model(X).argmax(dim=1) == Y).float().mean().item()
print(f"validation accuracy: {accuracy_of(clf_rings, Xc_val, Yc_val):.3f}")
print(f"test accuracy (computed once at the end): {accuracy_of(clf_rings, Xc_test, Yc_test):.3f}")
# The two classes are separated by an empty ring (1 < r < 1.3), so a perfect classification is possible.
# Without the gap (e.g. class 1 for 1 < r < 2) points near r = 1 would be harder, and the accuracy would drop below 1.

# 4) decision boundary
g = np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 200)
GX, GY = np.meshgrid(g, g)
grid = torch.tensor(np.stack([GX.ravel(), GY.ravel()], axis=1), dtype=torch.float32)
with torch.no_grad():
    pred_class = clf_rings(grid).argmax(dim=1).numpy().reshape(200, 200)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
axes[0].plot(hist_tr, label="training"); axes[0].plot(hist_va, label="validation")
axes[0].set_yscale("log"); axes[0].set_xlabel("step"); axes[0].set_ylabel("cross-entropy"); axes[0].legend()
# the classes are the integers 0 and 1: boundaries at -0.5, 0.5, 1.5 give exactly one colour to each class
axes[1].contourf(GX, GY, pred_class, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5], colors=["C0", "C1"], alpha=0.25)
# Xc_train[Yc_train == 0]: indexing with a True/False tensor keeps the rows where the condition holds (shape (n, 2));
# .T turns it into two rows x and y, and * passes them as the two arguments of scatter
axes[1].scatter(*Xc_train[Yc_train == 0].T, s=5, color="C0", label="class 0")
axes[1].scatter(*Xc_train[Yc_train == 1].T, s=5, color="C1", label="class 1")
axes[1].set_aspect("equal"); axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$y$"); axes[1].legend(loc="upper right")
axes[1].set_title("predicted class (background) and training data")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


validation accuracy: 1.000
test accuracy (computed once at the end): 1.000








Exercise 4 — Boundary conditions built into the network
The ground state of a particle in a box \([0, 1]\) is \(\psi_\ast(x) = \sqrt2\sin(\pi x)\). Fit it from 15 noisy samples (\(\sigma = 0.05\)) at random points in \([0, 1]\) with (a) BoxWavefunction([1, 16, 16, 1]) of Section 8.2 and (b) an unconstrained make_mlp([1, 16, 16, 1]). Train both with Adam (lr=1e-2, full batch, 2000 steps). Compare the values at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\) and the maximal error on a dense grid, and plot both fits. Which model respects the physics, and where does the unconstrained one go wrong?
Few samples are used on purpose: the regions between the outermost samples and the walls are then not covered by data, which exposes the difference between the two models.

Solution


Code
rng4 = np.random.default_rng(3)
x_s = np.sort(rng4.uniform(0, 1, 15))
y_s = np.sqrt(2) * np.sin(np.pi * x_s) + 0.05 * rng4.normal(size=15)
Xs = torch.tensor(x_s, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
Ys = torch.tensor(y_s, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)

def fit(model, steps=2000):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    for _ in range(steps):
        loss = loss_fn(model(Xs), Ys)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return model

torch.manual_seed(0); constrained = fit(BoxWavefunction([1, 16, 16, 1]))
torch.manual_seed(0); free = fit(make_mlp([1, 16, 16, 1]))

x_dense = torch.linspace(0, 1, 401).reshape(-1, 1)
exact = np.sqrt(2) * np.sin(np.pi * x_dense.numpy())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(x_dense, exact, "k", lw=3, alpha=0.4, label=r"exact $\sqrt{2}\sin(\pi x)$")
ax.plot(x_s, y_s, "ko", ms=5, label="15 noisy samples")
for name, m in [("x(1-x) NN(x)", constrained), ("unconstrained NN(x)", free)]:
    with torch.no_grad():
        values = m(x_dense).numpy()
    ax.plot(x_dense, values, lw=2, label=name)
    print(f"{name:20s} psi(0) = {values[0, 0]:+.3f}   psi(1) = {values[-1, 0]:+.3f}   max |error| = {np.max(np.abs(values - exact)):.3f}")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\psi(x)$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()
# The constrained model vanishes exactly at both walls for any parameters. The unconstrained model is only
# determined where there are samples; between the outermost samples and the walls it is not forced to zero.


x(1-x) NN(x)         psi(0) = +0.000   psi(1) = +0.000   max |error| = 0.082
unconstrained NN(x)  psi(0) = -0.035   psi(1) = +0.793   max |error| = 0.793








Exercise 5 (advanced) — Deep plain and residual networks
Train on the damped-oscillation data of Section 10 two networks of the same depth (10 hidden layers of width 16): make_mlp([1] + [16] * 10 + [1]) and ResidualMLP(1, 16, 9, 1) (one input layer plus 9 residual blocks), both with train (300 epochs). Plot their validation losses versus epoch. Before training, print the norm of the gradient of the first layer’s weights for both models (one backward pass on the training set): what does it tell us about how the signal propagates backwards through a deep plain network?

Solution


Code
torch.manual_seed(0); plain = make_mlp([1] + [16] * 10 + [1])
torch.manual_seed(0); resnet = ResidualMLP(1, 16, 9, 1)
print("parameters: plain", sum(p.numel() for p in plain.parameters()), "  residual", sum(p.numel() for p in resnet.parameters()))

# gradient of the first layer before training
for name, m, first in [("plain", plain, plain[0]), ("residual", resnet, resnet.input_layer)]:
    m.zero_grad()
    loss_fn(m(X_train), Y_train).backward()
    print(f"{name:9s} |dL/dW of first layer| = {first.weight.grad.norm().item():.2e}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for name, m in [("plain, 10 hidden layers", plain), ("residual, 9 blocks", resnet)]:
    hist = train(m, X_train, Y_train, X_val, Y_val, n_epochs=300)
    ax.semilogy(hist["val"], label=name)
    print(f"{name:25s} final validation MSE {hist['val'][-1]:.2e}")
ax.axhline(0.05**2, color="gray", ls=":", label="noise variance")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("validation MSE"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
# In the plain network the gradient reaching the first layer is the product of many factors (one per layer), each
# typically smaller than one for tanh with the default initialisation: it is much smaller than in the residual network,
# where the skip connections pass the gradient directly. This is the vanishing-gradient problem.


parameters: plain 2497   residual 2497
plain     |dL/dW of first layer| = 8.37e-05
residual  |dL/dW of first layer| = 4.23e-01


plain, 10 hidden layers   final validation MSE 1.50e-02


residual, 9 blocks        final validation MSE 5.15e-03

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
1. The architecture

1.1 Drawing the network
The network analysed in this notebook has layer sizes \([1, 64, 64, 64, 1]\) with \(\tanh\) activations: one input, three hidden layers of 64 nodes, one output.
This network is deliberately much larger than the 30 training points of Section 2 require (8513 parameters, counted in Section 1.3), so that it is able to overfit them (Section 4). Three hidden layers make the effects of depth on activations and gradients visible, and \(\tanh\) is used because for it “saturated” has a simple meaning (Section 2.3). The width 64 itself is arbitrary: with widths 32 and 128 the same training run also shows a minimum of the validation loss followed by a rise.


Code
layer_sizes = [1, 64, 64, 64, 1]
torch.manual_seed(0)                 # fixes the random initial weights; Section 3 uses the same seed, so it trains exactly this network
model = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
draw_network(layer_sizes, activations=["tanh"] * 3, title="the network analysed in this notebook",
             input_labels=["$x$"], output_labels=["$f(x)$"])
plt.show()
print(model)





Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=1, out_features=64, bias=True)
  (1): Tanh()
  (2): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=64, bias=True)
  (3): Tanh()
  (4): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=64, bias=True)
  (5): Tanh()
  (6): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=1, bias=True)
)




1.2 A table of the layers
We pass a small batch through the layers one by one and record, for each layer, its type, the shapes of its input and output, the shapes of its parameters, and the number of parameters. A pandas.DataFrame is a convenient container for such a table.
An nn.Sequential behaves like a list of layers: for layer in model runs over them in order, and model[0], model[-1] select the first and the last layer. In the table, index is the position of the module in the Sequential; it is not the layer index \(l\) of Section 1.3. type(layer).__name__ gives the name of the class of an object as a string (e.g. 'Linear'), and p.numel() the number of entries of a tensor.


Code
def layer_table(model, x):
    """One row per layer of an nn.Sequential model, for the input batch x."""
    rows = []
    for i, layer in enumerate(model):
        x_in = x
        x = layer(x)                                            # pass the batch through this layer
        params = list(layer.parameters())
        rows.append({
            "index": i,
            "layer": type(layer).__name__,
            "input shape": tuple(x_in.shape),
            "output shape": tuple(x.shape),
            "parameter shapes": [tuple(p.shape) for p in params],
            "parameters": sum(p.numel() for p in params),
            "trainable": sum(p.numel() for p in params if p.requires_grad),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

table = layer_table(model, torch.zeros(8, 1))                   # 8 dummy inputs; batch size and values are arbitrary, only the shape (B, 1) matters
table

Each Linear layer from \(n_{\rm in}\) to \(n_{\rm out}\) nodes has a weight matrix of shape \((n_{\rm out}, n_{\rm in})\) and a bias of length \(n_{\rm out}\), while the activation layers have no parameters and keep the shape. The batch dimension (8) is carried through unchanged.


1.3 Counting parameters
The table already lists the parameters of every layer; the same numbers follow from a simple formula. The layers are numbered \(l = 0, 1, \dots, L\), with \(n_0\) the number of inputs and \(n_L\) the number of outputs; for \([1, 64, 64, 64, 1]\), \(n_0 = 1\), \(n_1 = n_2 = n_3 = 64\), \(n_4 = 1\). The Linear layer from layer \(l-1\) to layer \(l\) has \(n_l n_{l-1}\) weights and \(n_l\) biases, i.e. \(n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\) parameters. Below we compare the total from the table with the formula \(\sum_{l=1}^{L} n_l\,(n_{l-1}+1)\) and with PyTorch’s own count.


Code
by_formula = sum(n_out * (n_in + 1) for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:]))
by_table = table["parameters"].sum()
by_pytorch = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"formula: {by_formula},  table: {by_table},  PyTorch: {by_pytorch}")
for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:]):
    print(f"  Linear({n_in}, {n_out}): {n_out} x {n_in} weights + {n_out} biases = {n_out * (n_in + 1)}")


formula: 8513,  table: 8513,  PyTorch: 8513
  Linear(1, 64): 64 x 1 weights + 64 biases = 128
  Linear(64, 64): 64 x 64 weights + 64 biases = 4160
  Linear(64, 64): 64 x 64 weights + 64 biases = 4160
  Linear(64, 1): 1 x 64 weights + 1 biases = 65


All three counts agree, 8513 parameters, and the breakdown shows that the two \(64\times64\) hidden layers hold almost all of them.


1.4 Parameter count, width and depth
The formula tells us how the size of a network grows when we make it wider or deeper. For a network \([1, W, \dots, W, 1]\) with \(D\) hidden layers of width \(W\) the count is \(W(1+1) + (D-1)\,W(W+1) + (W+1)\). The three terms are the first layer (\(W\) weights and \(W\) biases), the \(D-1\) layers from width \(W\) to width \(W\) (\(W^2\) weights and \(W\) biases each) and the output layer (\(W\) weights and one bias). The count is therefore linear in the depth \(D\) and, for \(D\ge2\), quadratic in the width \(W\). On the log-log axes below a power law \(W^k\) is a straight line of slope \(k\).


Code
widths = np.array([4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for depth in [1, 2, 3, 5]:
    counts = [sum(p.numel() for p in make_mlp([1] + [w] * depth + [1]).parameters()) for w in widths]
    ax.loglog(widths, counts, "o-", label=f"{depth} hidden layer" + ("s" if depth > 1 else ""))
ax.loglog(widths, 3 * widths**2, "k:", label=r"$\propto W^2$")    # only the slope 2 matters; the factor 3 places the line near the data
ax.set_xlabel("width $W$ (nodes per hidden layer)"); ax.set_ylabel("number of parameters"); ax.legend()
plt.show()





With one hidden layer the count grows only linearly (\(3W+1\)); every additional hidden layer adds a \(W\times W\) matrix, so the deeper networks follow the \(W^2\) line.


1.5 Trainable and frozen parameters
Not every parameter of a network has to be trained. Setting requires_grad = False for a parameter freezes it: no gradient is computed for it, and an optimiser leaves it unchanged. Freezing is used, for example, when a pretrained part of a network is kept fixed. Here we freeze the first layer of a copy of the model and recount.
The copy must be made with copy.deepcopy. A plain assignment frozen_model = model only gives a second name to the same network, and a shallow copy.copy(model) creates a new container that still holds the same parameter tensors: freezing it would freeze model as well. copy.deepcopy duplicates every parameter.


Code
frozen_model = copy.deepcopy(model)              # an independent copy, so that `model` itself stays unchanged
for p in frozen_model[0].parameters():           # module 0 of the `Sequential`, i.e. the first `Linear` layer
    p.requires_grad = False

trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in frozen_model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
total = sum(p.numel() for p in frozen_model.parameters())
print(f"total parameters: {total},  trainable: {trainable},  frozen: {total - trainable}  (= 64 weights + 64 biases of the first Linear layer)")


total parameters: 8513,  trainable: 8385,  frozen: 128  (= 64 weights + 64 biases of the first Linear layer)




1.6 Memory and computational cost
The parameter count translates directly into the memory and the cost of the network. Every parameter is stored as a float32 number of 4 bytes. One forward pass for one input needs, in every Linear layer, \(n_{\rm in}\,n_{\rm out}\) multiplications and as many additions (a multiply-add per weight). These numbers set the scale for large networks: a model with \(10^9\) parameters needs 4 GB only to store its weights.
The count of multiply-adds includes only the multiplications by weights; the bias additions and the activations add about \(n_{\rm out}\) operations per layer, which is small compared with \(n_{\rm in}n_{\rm out}\) for wide layers. In the printout 1 kB is taken as 1024 bytes.


Code
n_bytes = sum(p.numel() * p.element_size() for p in model.parameters())     # element_size() = bytes per number
mult_adds = sum(n_in * n_out for n_in, n_out in zip(layer_sizes[:-1], layer_sizes[1:]))
print(f"memory of the parameters: {n_bytes} bytes = {n_bytes / 1024:.1f} kB")
print(f"multiply-adds per input sample in one forward pass: {mult_adds}")


memory of the parameters: 34052 bytes = 33.3 kB
multiply-adds per input sample in one forward pass: 8320


The network needs 34 052 bytes for its parameters and 8320 multiply-adds per input sample.


1.7 Ready-made summary tools
In Sections 1.1–1.6 every number was computed directly from its definition, because this shows what each number means. In practice the same information is obtained with ready-made tools. PyTorch itself offers the basic pieces: print(model), parameters(), requires_grad, modules(), and the operation counter torch.utils.flop_counter.FlopCounterMode, which counts the floating-point operations of a computation. A table of the layers and a drawing come from two small additional packages. The function torchinfo.summary of the package torchinfo prints a table of the layers with output shapes and parameter counts, the numbers of trainable and frozen parameters, and estimates of memory and cost. The package torchview draws the network as a graph of layers and tensor shapes, using the program Graphviz (installed in Colab).
The two packages are not part of Colab’s standard installation. %pip install installs Python packages from inside a notebook into the Python environment that runs the notebook (-q: print less); it takes a few seconds and is needed once per Colab session. The note printed by %pip about restarting the kernel concerns packages that were already imported before the installation; torchinfo and torchview are imported only after it, so no restart is needed.


Code
%pip install -q torchinfo torchview


Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.


We first ask torchinfo.summary for the table of the model of Section 1 with the batch shape \((8, 1)\) of Section 1.2. The function returns an object that is displayed as the table and whose attributes hold the numbers, so they can be compared with our own counts; verbose=0 prevents the table from being printed a second time.


Code
import torchinfo

info = torchinfo.summary(model, input_size=(8, 1), verbose=0)
print(info)
print("total parameters: torchinfo", info.total_params, "  our count", by_pytorch)
print("trainable:        torchinfo", info.trainable_params)


==========================================================================================

==========================================================================================
Sequential                               [8, 1]                    --
├─Linear: 1-1                            [8, 64]                   128
├─Tanh: 1-2                              [8, 64]                   --
├─Linear: 1-3                            [8, 64]                   4,160
├─Tanh: 1-4                              [8, 64]                   --
├─Linear: 1-5                            [8, 64]                   4,160
├─Tanh: 1-6                              [8, 64]                   --

total parameters: torchinfo 8513   our count 8513
trainable:        torchinfo 8513


The columns agree with the table of Section 1.2: 128, 4160, 4160 and 65 parameters in the four Linear layers, 8513 in total. The last lines of the table need a comment. “Params size (MB): 0.03” is the memory of the parameters, \(8513\times4\) bytes \(= 34\,052\) bytes, the number of Section 1.6, here in units of \(10^6\) bytes. “Total mult-adds”, on the other hand, is counted differently from Section 1.6: torchinfo counts one multiply-add per parameter, the biases included, and for the whole batch, which gives \(8 \times 8513 = 68\,104 \approx 0.07\) M. Section 1.6 counted only the multiplications by weights, for one sample: \(8320 = 8513 - 193\), where 193 is the number of biases. Such counts are estimates of the cost, and different tools use different conventions, so it is always necessary to check what a tool counts.
The same summary of the copy with the frozen first layer (Section 1.5) shows which layers are frozen if we add the column “Trainable”; the argument col_names selects the columns.


Code
print(torchinfo.summary(frozen_model, input_size=(8, 1), col_names=["output_size", "num_params", "trainable"], verbose=0))


===================================================================================================================
Layer (type:depth-idx)                   Output Shape              Param #                   Trainable
===================================================================================================================
Sequential                               [8, 1]                    --                        Partial
├─Linear: 1-1                            [8, 64]                   (128)                     False
├─Tanh: 1-2                              [8, 64]                   --                        --
├─Linear: 1-3                            [8, 64]                   4,160                     True
├─Tanh: 1-4                              [8, 64]                   --                        --
├─Linear: 1-5                            [8, 64]                   4,160                     True
├─Tanh: 1-6                              [8, 64]                   --                        --
├─Linear: 1-7                            [8, 1]                    65                        True
===================================================================================================================

Estimated Total Size (MB): 0.05
===================================================================================================================


Frozen parameters are shown in parentheses, and the totals (8385 trainable, 128 frozen) are those of Section 1.5.
The operation counter of PyTorch gives a third convention for the cost. FlopCounterMode records every operation executed inside the with block. For a matrix product it counts 2 floating-point operations (one multiplication, one addition) per multiply-add; bias additions and activations are not counted. For one input sample we therefore expect \(2\times8320\), twice the count of Section 1.6.


Code
from torch.utils.flop_counter import FlopCounterMode

with FlopCounterMode(display=False) as counter:   # display=False: no printed table (it would need the package tabulate)
    model(torch.zeros(1, 1))                      # one forward pass for one sample
print("floating-point operations:", counter.get_total_flops(), "  = 2 x", mult_adds)


floating-point operations: 16640   = 2 x 8320


The count is indeed \(16\,640 = 2\times8320\). The number of layers of each type is obtained from model.modules(), which runs over the model itself and all layers inside it.


Code
n_linear = sum(isinstance(m, nn.Linear) for m in model.modules())    # True counts as 1, False as 0
n_tanh = sum(isinstance(m, nn.Tanh) for m in model.modules())
print(f"Linear layers: {n_linear},  Tanh layers: {n_tanh}")


Linear layers: 4,  Tanh layers: 3


Finally torchview draws the network. draw_graph passes a batch of the given shape through the model and records every layer it meets; .visual_graph is the resulting picture, and display(...) (available in every Jupyter/Colab notebook without import) shows it, which is needed here because the picture is created inside a try block. Every box is one layer with the shapes of its input and output; the first dimension (8) is the batch. Unlike our draw_network, which draws individual nodes (up to max_nodes per layer), this drawing shows layers and shapes, and it works for any model, also for models with skip connections. If Graphviz is missing, the except branch prints a message instead.


Code
try:
    from torchview import draw_graph
    graph = draw_graph(model, input_size=(8, 1))
    display(graph.visual_graph)
except Exception as err:
    print("torchview drawing not available:", err)





The tools are faster to use, and they are the right choice for large models. Our own functions of Sections 1.1–1.6 remain useful: they show what the numbers mean, and they can be extended to any quantity a tool does not provide, such as the saturation of the activations in Section 2.3.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
2. The network before training

2.1 A noisy damped oscillation
To see the network at work we need data. We use noisy measurements of a damped oscillation \(y(t) = e^{-0.2t}\cos(2t)\), \(t\in[0, 10]\), with noise of standard deviation \(\sigma = 0.1\) and deliberately few training points, so that overfitting (Section 4) becomes visible: 30 points for training, 40 for validation, 40 for testing. The input is rescaled to \([-1, 1]\).
Each of these numbers serves this purpose. The noise \(0.1\) is about 10% of the amplitude of the signal (\(y(0) = 1\)): large enough for overfitting to be visible, small enough for the oscillation to remain recognisable. With only 30 training points the network of Section 1, with its 8513 parameters, can memorise the training set. The validation and test sets are larger (40 points each) because their losses are used to choose and to evaluate the model, and a larger set gives a less noisy estimate. The positions \(t\) are drawn uniformly at random, so the three sets cover the interval in the same way: all \(30+40+40 = 110\) points are drawn at once, and the first 30, the next 40 and the last 40 form the three sets.
Besides the data, the code defines t_plot, 400 equally spaced values, and the corresponding network input X_plot. They are not data but a dense grid on which functions are evaluated for plotting, and on which the hidden layers are examined in Section 2.3. Finally, the rescaling \(t \to t/5 - 1\) maps \([0, 10]\) onto \([-1, 1]\). It matters because \(\tanh\) changes only for arguments of order one: with the raw inputs (up to 10) and first-layer weights in \([-1, 1]\), 52% of the first-layer activations of the untrained network would be saturated (Section 2.3), with the rescaled inputs below 0.1%.


Code
def damped_oscillation(t):
    return np.exp(-0.2 * t) * np.cos(2 * t)

noise = 0.1
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t_all = rng.uniform(0, 10, 110)
y_all = damped_oscillation(t_all) + noise * rng.normal(size=110)

def to_tensor(t, y):
    """Inputs rescaled to [-1, 1] and targets, both of shape (B, 1), float32."""
    X = torch.tensor(t / 5.0 - 1.0, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
    Y = torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
    return X, Y

X_train, Y_train = to_tensor(t_all[:30], y_all[:30])        # the points are in random order already
X_val, Y_val = to_tensor(t_all[30:70], y_all[30:70])
X_test, Y_test = to_tensor(t_all[70:], y_all[70:])
print("training:", tuple(X_train.shape), " validation:", tuple(X_val.shape), " test:", tuple(X_test.shape))

t_plot = np.linspace(0, 10, 400)
X_plot = torch.tensor(t_plot / 5.0 - 1.0, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(t_plot, damped_oscillation(t_plot), "k", lw=1, label="true function")
ax.plot(t_all[:30], y_all[:30], "o", label="training (30)")
ax.plot(t_all[30:70], y_all[30:70], "s", ms=4, label="validation (40)")
ax.plot(t_all[70:], y_all[70:], "^", ms=4, label="test (40)")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2); plt.show()


training: (30, 1)  validation: (40, 1)  test: (40, 1)







2.2 Initial weights
Before training, the network is defined entirely by its random initial weights, so we look at these first. PyTorch initialises the weights of nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) uniformly in \([-1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}},\ 1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}]\). The first layer (\(n_{\rm in}=1\)) therefore has weights in \([-1, 1]\), the hidden layers (\(n_{\rm in}=64\)) in \([-0.125, 0.125]\). The histograms below show the weights of every Linear layer of the untrained model, with these bounds as dashed lines. The biases are drawn from the same interval.
The scale \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\) keeps the size of the weighted sum \(\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\rm in}} w_i x_i\) independent of the number of inputs: for independent \(w_i\) and \(x_i\) with zero mean its variance is \(n_{\rm in}\,{\rm Var}(w)\,{\rm Var}(x)\), which does not grow with \(n_{\rm in}\) when \({\rm Var}(w)\propto 1/n_{\rm in}\).


Code
linear_layers = [layer for layer in model if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(linear_layers), figsize=(16, 3.2))
for k, (ax, layer) in enumerate(zip(axes, linear_layers)):
    w = layer.weight.detach().numpy().ravel()
    bound = 1 / np.sqrt(layer.in_features)
    ax.hist(w, bins=30)                                         # bins: enough to show the shape, a matter of readability
    ax.axvline(-bound, color="k", ls="--"); ax.axvline(bound, color="k", ls="--")
    ax.set_title(f"Linear {k + 1}: {layer.in_features} -> {layer.out_features}\n{w.size} weights")
    ax.set_xlabel("weight value")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The weight histograms are flat between the dashed bounds, as expected for a uniform distribution; the panels with only 64 weights are irregular because 64 samples are few.


2.3 Activations and saturated nodes
The weights alone do not tell us what the hidden layers do with an input. To see this, we pass the 400 inputs of the dense grid X_plot through the network and record the output of every activation layer. A node computes \(h = \tanh(z)\), where \(z\) is its weighted input, and \(\frac{d}{dz}\tanh z = 1 - \tanh^2 z = 1 - h^2\). A node with \(|h| > 0.95\) is saturated: its derivative \(1-h^2 < 0.0975 \approx 0.1\) is small, so gradients passing through it are damped by a factor of ten or more. The threshold 0.95 is a convention; any value between about 0.9 and 0.99 gives the same qualitative picture. The saturated fraction of a layer, shown in the panel titles below, is the fraction of activation values \(h\) (over all nodes and all 400 inputs) with \(|h|>0.95\).


Code
def hidden_activations(model, x):
    """Outputs of all activation layers of an nn.Sequential model for the input batch x."""
    outputs = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for layer in model:
            x = layer(x)
            if not isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):     # keep the outputs of the activation layers only
                outputs.append(x.numpy().copy())   # .numpy() shares memory with the tensor; copy() makes the stored array independent
    return outputs

acts = hidden_activations(model, X_plot)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(acts), figsize=(15, 3.2))
for k, (ax, h) in enumerate(zip(axes, acts)):
    saturated = np.mean(np.abs(h) > 0.95)
    ax.hist(h.ravel(), bins=40, range=(-1, 1))     # the full range of tanh, the same in every panel so that they can be compared
    ax.set_title(f"hidden layer {k + 1}: std {h.std():.3f},\nsaturated {100 * saturated:.0f}%")
    ax.set_xlabel("activation $h$")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





With the default initialisation practically no activation is saturated (below 0.1%), and the spread of the activations shrinks from layer to layer: the signal becomes weaker with depth.


2.4 Gradients in every layer
The activations describe the forward pass; training is driven by the backward pass. One forward and one backward pass on the training set give the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight matrix, and its norm tells how strongly each layer would be changed by the first step of gradient descent.
model.zero_grad() first sets the stored gradients to zero, because PyTorch adds new gradients to those already in .grad. nn.functional.mse_loss(a, b) is the function form of nn.MSELoss()(a, b) and gives the same value. For a matrix, .norm() is the Frobenius norm \(\sqrt{\sum_{ij} g_{ij}^2}\), the length of the matrix viewed as one long vector.


Code
def gradient_norms(model, X, Y):
    """Norm of dL/dW for the weight matrix of every Linear layer (one backward pass)."""
    model.zero_grad()
    nn.functional.mse_loss(model(X), Y).backward()
    return [layer.weight.grad.norm().item() for layer in model if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)]

for k, g in enumerate(gradient_norms(model, X_train, Y_train)):
    print(f"Linear {k + 1}: |dL/dW| = {g:.2e}")


Linear 1: |dL/dW| = 1.41e-02
Linear 2: |dL/dW| = 4.85e-01
Linear 3: |dL/dW| = 5.12e-01
Linear 4: |dL/dW| = 7.12e-01


The gradient of the first layer is the smallest. Gradient norms of different layers are, however, not directly comparable: the first weight matrix has only \(64\) entries, the hidden ones \(64\times64 = 4096\), and the norm sums over all entries. Comparisons are meaningful for the same layer between different models or different epochs, as in Sections 2.5 and 3.2.


2.5 Initialisation scale
The shrinking activations of Section 2.3 raise the question of how the behaviour of the untrained network depends on the scale of its initial weights. We repeat the analysis of Sections 2.3–2.4 for a deeper network (6 hidden layers of width 64) whose weights are drawn from \(\mathcal N(0, (c/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}})^2)\), the normal (Gaussian) distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation \(c/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\), for three values of \(c\). The table lists, for every hidden layer, the standard deviation of the activations and the fraction of saturated nodes, and the gradient norm of every weight matrix.
The three values \(c = 0.5, 1, 3\) stand for a too small, a standard and a too large scale. Their effect is multiplied once per layer, which is why a network deeper than the one of Section 1 makes it easier to see. A normal distribution is used instead of PyTorch’s uniform one, since only the standard deviation matters for the argument. For comparison, the default uniform distribution on \([-1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}, 1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}]\) has standard deviation \(1/\sqrt{3n_{\rm in}}\), i.e. \(c = 1/\sqrt3 \approx 0.58\); this is why the activations of Section 2.3 shrink with depth.
In the code, the functions of nn.init overwrite the values of an existing tensor in place (in PyTorch a trailing underscore, as in normal_, marks an in-place operation). The biases are set to zero so that only the weight scale is varied. The activations are measured on the dense grid X_plot, which samples the input interval evenly, while the gradients are those of the training loss and need the training data. At the end, pivot rearranges the long table (one row per pair (\(c\), layer)) into a wide one with one row per layer and one column per quantity and value of \(c\), so that the three values of \(c\) stand side by side; round(4) only affects the display.


Code
def init_scaled(layer_sizes, c, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
    for layer in m:
        if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):
            nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, mean=0.0, std=c / np.sqrt(layer.in_features))
            nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)
    return m

deep_sizes = [1] + [64] * 6 + [1]
rows = []
for c in [0.5, 1.0, 3.0]:
    m = init_scaled(deep_sizes, c)
    acts = hidden_activations(m, X_plot)
    grads = gradient_norms(m, X_train, Y_train)
    for k, h in enumerate(acts):
        rows.append({"c": c, "hidden layer": k + 1, "activation std": h.std(),
                     "saturated (%)": 100 * np.mean(np.abs(h) > 0.95), "|dL/dW| of this layer": grads[k]})

init_table.pivot(index="hidden layer", columns="c", values=["activation std", "saturated (%)", "|dL/dW| of this layer"]).round(4)

The three columns of each quantity show three different regimes. For \(c = 0.5\) the activations shrink by about a factor of two per layer, and all gradients are more than twenty times smaller than for \(c = 1\), decreasing slightly towards the first layers: the signal fades in both directions (vanishing gradients). For \(c = 1\) the activations decrease with depth only slowly (for \(\tanh\) the derivative is below 1, so \(c=1\) does not exactly preserve the signal), and the gradients are of similar size in hidden layers 2–6; layer 1 has only 64 weights, so its norm is smaller (see Section 2.4). For \(c = 3\) a large fraction of the nodes, up to about half in the deeper layers, is saturated, and the gradients are tens of times larger than for \(c = 1\), so the first optimisation steps would be very large (exploding gradients).
The weight scale therefore has to be chosen with the depth and the activation in mind, and the standard choices are derived from such arguments. Xavier (Glorot) initialisation uses \({\rm Var}(w) = 2/(n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out})\), i.e. \(c = 1\) for square layers, and is meant for \(\tanh\)-like activations. He initialisation uses \({\rm Var}(w) = 2/n_{\rm in}\) (\(c = \sqrt2\)), which compensates for the rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation, \(\mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z)\), which sets negative inputs (about half of them) to zero.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
3. Monitoring training
We now train the network of Section 1 and watch what happens inside it. The training function below is a standard training loop (full batch, Adam) with additional bookkeeping: after every epoch it records the training loss and the validation loss, the norm of the gradient of every weight matrix, and the relative change of every weight matrix since the start, \(\|W(e) - W(0)\| / \|W(0)\|\), where \(e\) is the epoch. It also keeps a copy of the parameters at the epoch with the smallest validation loss so far, which we shall need in Section 4.
The records are kept in log, a dictionary of lists to which one entry is appended per epoch. For the gradients and weight changes each entry is a list of 4 numbers, one per Linear layer; at the end np.array turns this list of lists into an array of shape (number of epochs, 4), so that log["grad"][:, k] is the history of layer \(k+1\).
The 30 training points form one full batch, so every epoch is a single exact gradient step and the loss curves contain no noise from a random choice of mini-batches. The learning rate lr=1e-2 is a common starting value for Adam on small problems and was not tuned. With learning rates \(10^{-3}\), \(3\cdot10^{-3}\), \(10^{-2}\) and \(3\cdot10^{-2}\) the smallest validation loss is reached at epochs 753, 419, 293 and 281, and in every case the validation loss rises afterwards. The 3000 epochs are far more than needed to reach the minimum, so that the overfitting after it can be seen.
A few details of the code deserve attention, because getting them wrong silently produces wrong records. The initial weights are stored as W0 = [... .detach().clone() ...]: optimizer.step() changes the weights in place, so without clone() the list would hold the current weight tensors themselves and the relative change would always be zero, while detach() keeps the copy out of the gradient computation. The record of the best model starts as best = {"val": np.inf, ...}; starting from infinity, the validation loss of the first epoch is always smaller and becomes the first “best” model. The best parameters are stored with copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()), because state_dict() returns a dictionary of the parameter tensors themselves, not of copies; without deepcopy the stored “best” state would follow every later optimiser step and end up equal to the final parameters.
The calls model.train() and model.eval() switch layers such as dropout and batch normalisation between their training and evaluation behaviour. This network has no such layers, so here the calls change nothing; they are kept because a general training loop needs them. The training loss of an epoch is computed before optimizer.step(), the validation loss after it; the two curves are therefore shifted by one step, which is irrelevant on a scale of thousands of epochs. Finally, torch.manual_seed(0) before make_mlp gives the same initial weights as in Sections 1–2, so the model trained here is exactly the one analysed above.


Code
def train_monitored(model, n_epochs=3000, lr=1e-2):
    linear = [layer for layer in model if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)]
    W0 = [layer.weight.detach().clone() for layer in linear]          # initial weights, for the relative change
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
    log = {"train": [], "val": [], "grad": [], "change": []}
    best = {"val": np.inf, "epoch": None, "state": None}
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        loss = loss_fn(model(X_train), Y_train)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        log["grad"].append([layer.weight.grad.norm().item() for layer in linear])    # read the gradients before the step
        optimizer.step()

        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            val_loss = loss_fn(model(X_val), Y_val).item()
            log["change"].append([((layer.weight - w0).norm() / w0.norm()).item() for layer, w0 in zip(linear, W0)])
        log["train"].append(loss.item())
        log["val"].append(val_loss)
        if val_loss < best["val"]:                                     # remember the best model so far
            best = {"val": val_loss, "epoch": epoch, "state": copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())}
    log["grad"], log["change"] = np.array(log["grad"]), np.array(log["change"])
    return log, best

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
log, best = train_monitored(model)
train_time = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"training took {train_time:.1f} s;  smallest validation loss {best['val']:.3e} at epoch {best['epoch']}")


training took 2.7 s;  smallest validation loss 1.941e-02 at epoch 293


Training takes 2.7 s, and the smallest validation loss, \(1.941\cdot10^{-2}\), is reached at epoch 293.

3.1 Training and validation loss curves
The loss on the training and validation sets as a function of the epoch is the most important plot of every training run. The dotted line is the noise variance \(\sigma^2 = 0.01\), the smallest mean squared error (MSE) that any model can reach on new data; the vertical line marks the epoch with the smallest validation loss.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
ax.semilogy(log["train"], label="training loss")
ax.semilogy(log["val"], label="validation loss")
ax.axhline(noise**2, color="gray", ls=":", label=r"noise variance $\sigma^2$")
ax.axvline(best["epoch"], color="C3", ls="--", label=f"smallest validation loss (epoch {best['epoch']})")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print(f"at the end: training loss {log['train'][-1]:.2e}, validation loss {log['val'][-1]:.2e}")





at the end: training loss 3.65e-03, validation loss 8.35e-02


The curves show two phases. At first both losses decrease together: the network learns the function that the training and validation points have in common. Later the training loss keeps decreasing, below the noise variance, while the validation loss increases, ending at \(3.65\cdot10^{-3}\) and \(8.35\cdot10^{-2}\) respectively. Below \(\sigma^2\) the network can only improve on the training set by reproducing its particular noise, which is useless (in fact harmful) for new points. This is overfitting. With 30 points even the true function has a training MSE that fluctuates by about \(\sigma^2\sqrt{2/30} \approx 25\%\) around \(\sigma^2\), so only a training loss well below \(\sigma^2\), as here at the end of training, is a clear sign of fitting the noise.


3.2 Gradients and weight changes per layer
The per-layer records show how the training proceeds inside the network. The gradient norms vary over several orders of magnitude and are plotted on a logarithmic axis; the relative weight changes stay between 0 and about 3 and are readable on a linear axis.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4))
for k in range(log["grad"].shape[1]):
    axes[0].semilogy(log["grad"][:, k], lw=1, label=f"Linear {k + 1}")
    axes[1].plot(log["change"][:, k], label=f"Linear {k + 1}")
axes[0].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\|\partial L/\partial W\|$"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\|W(e) - W(0)\|\,/\,\|W(0)\|$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].axvline(best["epoch"], color="C3", ls="--")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The gradient norms (left) decay during long stretches, interrupted by sudden spikes: at a spike the Adam step overshoots, the loss jumps up for a few epochs and then decreases again. These episodes are also visible as small jumps in the right panel, which shows how far each weight matrix has moved from its initial values. Relative changes of order one mean that training has substantially rewritten the layer, and changes that keep growing after the best epoch (dashed line) are the parameters adapting to the noise of the training set.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
section: 4. Overfitting and the choice of the epoch
text:
4. Overfitting and the choice of the epoch
Since the validation loss rises after epoch 293, the parameters at that epoch are a better model than the final ones. train_monitored kept a copy of them, and loading it gives the model that would have been obtained by stopping the training there (early stopping). We compare both models with the data.
A state_dict contains only numbers, not the architecture. A network with the same layer sizes is therefore built first, and its random initial parameters are then overwritten by load_state_dict. final_model = model is not a copy, only a second name for the trained network.


Code
final_model = model                                   # parameters after the last epoch
best_model = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
best_model.load_state_dict(best["state"])             # parameters from the epoch with the smallest validation loss

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
ax.plot(t_plot, damped_oscillation(t_plot), "k", lw=1, label="true function")
ax.plot(t_all[:30], y_all[:30], "o", color="C0", label="training data")
with torch.no_grad():
    ax.plot(t_plot, final_model(X_plot), "C3", lw=1.5, label=f"after the last epoch ({len(log['train'])})")
    ax.plot(t_plot, best_model(X_plot), "C2", lw=2, label=f"at the best epoch ({best['epoch']})")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()





The model after the last epoch passes close to the training points and makes large excursions in the gaps between them (e.g. around \(t \approx 5\)). The model from the best epoch is smooth and follows the true function over most of the interval, but it misses the small oscillations for \(t \gtrsim 6\). The best epoch was chosen with the validation set: the test set has not been used yet.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
5. Evaluation on the test set
Now, and only now, the chosen model is evaluated on the test set. Its test loss is the estimate of the error on new data that would be reported. For illustration only, the test loss of the overfitted final model is printed as well; it was not used to make any choice. The three panels then look at the errors in detail: predictions against measured values, the histogram of the residuals, and the residuals as a function of \(t\).


Code
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
best_model.eval(); final_model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    test_best = loss_fn(best_model(X_test), Y_test).item()
    test_final = loss_fn(final_model(X_test), Y_test).item()
    pred_test = best_model(X_test).numpy().ravel()
print(f"chosen model (best epoch {best['epoch']}): test MSE = {test_best:.3e}")
print(f"final model (for comparison only)   : test MSE = {test_final:.3e}")
print(f"noise variance                       : {noise**2:.3e}")

residuals = pred_test - Y_test.numpy().ravel()
print(f"residuals: mean {residuals.mean():+.3f}, standard deviation {residuals.std():.3f} (noise level sigma = {noise})")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))
axes[0].plot(Y_test.numpy(), pred_test, "o")
lims = [Y_test.min().item() - 0.1, Y_test.max().item() + 0.1]      # the margin 0.1 only extends the diagonal beyond the data
axes[0].plot(lims, lims, "k--", lw=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("measured $y$ (test set)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("predicted $y$"); axes[0].set_title("prediction vs. measurement")
axes[1].hist(residuals, bins=12)                                  # few bins: only 40 residuals
axes[1].set_xlabel("residual (predicted - measured)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("count"); axes[1].set_title(f"residuals, std {residuals.std():.3f}")
axes[2].plot(t_all[70:], residuals, "o"); axes[2].axhline(0, color="k", lw=1)
axes[2].set_xlabel("$t$"); axes[2].set_ylabel("residual"); axes[2].set_title("residuals vs. input")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


chosen model (best epoch 293): test MSE = 3.197e-02
final model (for comparison only)   : test MSE = 7.065e-02
noise variance                       : 1.000e-02
residuals: mean -0.027, standard deviation 0.177 (noise level sigma = 0.1)





The chosen model has test MSE \(3.197\cdot10^{-2}\), the overfitted final model more than twice as much, \(7.065\cdot10^{-2}\); both are well above the noise variance \(10^{-2}\).
For an ideal model the points of the left panel lie around the diagonal, the residuals have a standard deviation equal to the noise level \(\sigma = 0.1\), and they show no trend with the input \(t\). Even for an ideal model the standard deviation of 40 residuals fluctuates by about \(\sigma/\sqrt{2\cdot 40} \approx 0.011\) around \(0.1\) (for \(n\) Gaussian values the sample standard deviation scatters by about \(\sigma/\sqrt{2n}\)). Note also that residuals.std() subtracts the mean residual, so a constant offset of the model does not enter it, while \(\sqrt{\text{test MSE}}\) includes it.
Here the residual standard deviation, 0.177, is larger than \(\sigma\) by much more than this fluctuation, and the right panel shows why: for \(t \gtrsim 9\) all residuals are negative, i.e. the model is systematically too low in this region (it misses the last oscillation, see Section 4), and between \(t \approx 7\) and \(8.3\) all residuals are positive (the minimum of \(y\) near \(t \approx 7.9\) is too shallow in the model). In the left panel the points with \(t \gtrsim 9\) form a horizontal row: the model predicts almost the same value, about \(-0.08\), for all of them, whatever the measured value. Residual plots reveal such systematic errors, which a single number such as the test MSE hides.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
section: 6. Characteristics of a model in one table
text:
6. Characteristics of a model in one table
The quantities of this notebook are collected for two models trained on the same data: the network analysed so far and a small network with one hidden layer of 16 nodes. Both are evaluated at their best epoch. The small network (\(16\cdot 2 + 17 = 49\) parameters) serves as a contrast: with one narrow hidden layer it can represent only smooth functions, so it overfits much more slowly; its smallest validation loss is reached only at epoch 2880, near the end of the 3000 epochs, and at that epoch its training loss, \(7.8\cdot10^{-3}\), is only slightly below \(\sigma^2\). (With 30 points the training MSE of even the true function fluctuates by about \(\sigma^2\sqrt{2/30} \approx 25\%\) around \(\sigma^2\).) Its width 16 is arbitrary.
DataFrame.style.format changes only how the numbers are displayed, not the stored values: "{:.2f}" means two decimal places, "{:.2e}" scientific notation with two decimals. The training time depends on the computer and on other running processes; it is useful only to compare models trained on the same machine.


Code
def characterise(sizes, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = make_mlp(sizes)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    lg, bst = train_monitored(m)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
    m.load_state_dict(bst["state"]); m.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        tr = loss_fn(m(X_train), Y_train).item()
        te = loss_fn(m(X_test), Y_test).item()
    return {
        "layer sizes": str(sizes),
        "parameters": sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters()),
        "memory (kB)": sum(p.numel() * p.element_size() for p in m.parameters()) / 1024,
        "best epoch": bst["epoch"],
        "train MSE": tr, "val MSE": bst["val"], "test MSE": te,
        "train time (s)": elapsed,
    }

summary_table = pd.DataFrame([characterise([1, 16, 1]), characterise(layer_sizes)])
summary_table.style.format({"memory (kB)": "{:.2f}", "train MSE": "{:.2e}", "val MSE": "{:.2e}", "test MSE": "{:.2e}", "train time (s)": "{:.1f}"})

Here, with few data, more parameters do not give a better model. The large network reaches its best validation loss early (epoch 293), when its training error is still above the noise variance; later it improves only on the training set. The small network has a lower training error at its best epoch, because that epoch comes much later.
Such a table is the minimum documentation of a trained model: architecture and size, how it was selected (best epoch by validation loss), and its errors on the three data sets. Only the test column is an unbiased estimate of the error on new data.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
7. Quantities that characterise a network
The architecture of a network is described by its layer table (shapes and parameters per layer), the total number of parameters and the number of trainable ones (requires_grad), the memory of the parameters (4 bytes per float32 parameter) and the number of multiply-adds per sample. The number of parameters grows linearly with depth and quadratically with width.
Before training, the histograms of weights and activations, the fraction of saturated nodes and the gradient norms per layer show the state from which the optimisation starts. The initialisation scale controls whether signals and gradients shrink, survive or saturate with depth.
During training we follow the training and validation losses as functions of the epoch, together with the gradient norms and relative weight changes per layer. Overfitting shows up as a training loss that falls below the noise level while the validation loss rises; the parameters at the epoch with the smallest validation loss are kept (early stopping). The test set is used once, for the chosen model, and residual plots show whether its errors are random or systematic.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network

8. Exercises

Exercise 1 — Analysing an image classifier
The image classifier nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10)) assigns a \(28\times28\) grey-scale image of a handwritten digit (the MNIST data set, Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology) to one of 10 classes, the digits \(0, \dots, 9\): it has \(784\) inputs, one per pixel, and 10 outputs, one per class. 1. Load the MNIST test images (torchvision.datasets.MNIST, train=False) and show one example of every class with its label. 2. Draw the network and produce its layer table with layer_table for a batch of 16 test images (pixel values divided by 255). 3. Find the layer that holds most of the parameters and its fraction of the total, and explain why it is this layer. 4. Compute the memory of the parameters and the number of multiply-adds per image. 5. Freeze everything except the last layer and report the number of trainable parameters. Check the totals with torchinfo.summary (Section 1.7).

Solution

import contextlib, io

# 2) drawing and table

             output_labels=[f"{k}" for k in range(10)])

# 3) share of the largest layer

# 4) memory and multiply-adds

Exercise 2 — Early stopping with patience
In practice training is stopped automatically once the validation loss has not improved for a number of epochs (the patience). Modify the training loop so that it stops after 200 epochs without a new minimum of the validation loss, restore the best parameters, and report the stopping epoch, the best epoch, the time saved compared with 3000 epochs, and the test loss of the restored model.
The patience must be longer than the temporary rises of the validation loss (the spikes of Section 3.2), otherwise training stops at one of them. With the network and data of this notebook a patience of 100 epochs stops at epoch 213 with the best epoch 113 and validation loss 0.036, nearly twice the minimum found in Section 3; patience 200 and 500 both find the minimum at epoch 293.

Solution


Code
def train_early_stopping(model, max_epochs=3000, patience=200, lr=1e-2):
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    best_val, best_epoch, best_state = np.inf, 0, None
    train_hist, val_hist = [], []
    for epoch in range(max_epochs):
        model.train()
        loss = loss_fn(model(X_train), Y_train)
        optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            val = loss_fn(model(X_val), Y_val).item()
        train_hist.append(loss.item()); val_hist.append(val)
        if val < best_val:
            best_val, best_epoch, best_state = val, epoch, copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
        elif epoch - best_epoch >= patience:          # no improvement for `patience` epochs
            break                                     # leave the loop; `epoch` keeps its last value
    model.load_state_dict(best_state)                 # restore the best parameters
    return epoch, best_epoch, train_hist, val_hist

torch.manual_seed(0)
m = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
stop_epoch, best_epoch, tr_h, va_h = train_early_stopping(m)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
with torch.no_grad():
    test_mse = loss_fn(m(X_test), Y_test).item()
print(f"stopped at epoch {stop_epoch}, best epoch {best_epoch}, {elapsed:.1f} s instead of about {train_time:.1f} s for 3000 epochs")
print(f"test MSE of the restored model: {test_mse:.3e}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.semilogy(tr_h, label="training"); ax.semilogy(va_h, label="validation")
ax.axvline(best_epoch, color="C3", ls="--", label="best epoch"); ax.axvline(stop_epoch, color="k", ls=":", label="stop")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
