title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
1. The original MNIST files

1.1 Download
MNIST is distributed as four compressed files (.gz): images and labels, each for the training part (\(60\,000\) images) and the test part (\(10\,000\) images). Libraries such as torchvision or keras download exactly these files and decode them for you. Here we do both steps ourselves, so that the data stop being a black box.
urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, path) downloads a file from the internet and saves it on disk. The original web page of Y. LeCun no longer serves the files reliably, so we use two public copies (mirrors) and take the first one that works. A file that is already on disk is not downloaded again.


Code
DATA_DIR = "data/MNIST_raw"
MIRRORS = ["https://ossci-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/mnist/",          # copy used by torchvision
           "https://storage.googleapis.com/cvdf-datasets/mnist/"]     # copy used by tensorflow
FILES = {"train_images": "train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz",
         "train_labels": "train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz",
         "test_images":  "t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz",
         "test_labels":  "t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz"}

def download(filename):
    # Download one MNIST file (only if it is not there yet) and return its path.
    path = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, filename)
    if os.path.exists(path):
        return path
    os.makedirs(DATA_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    for mirror in MIRRORS:
        try:
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(mirror + filename, path)
            return path
        except Exception as err:
            print(f"  {mirror} failed: {err}")
            if os.path.exists(path):
                os.remove(path)                 # remove a partially downloaded file
    raise RuntimeError(f"could not download {filename}")

paths = {key: download(name) for key, name in FILES.items()}
for key, path in paths.items():
    print(f"{key:13s} {os.path.getsize(path) / 1e6:5.2f} MB")


train_images   9.91 MB
train_labels   0.03 MB
test_images    1.65 MB
test_labels    0.00 MB




1.2 The IDX file format
After decompression each file is a sequence of bytes (ubyte = unsigned byte, an integer \(0\dots255\)) in the very simple IDX format:







bytes
content




0–1
always 0, 0


2
data type; 8 (hex 0x08) means unsigned bytes


3
number of dimensions \(d\): 3 for images (number, rows, columns), 1 for labels


4 … \(4+4d-1\)
the \(d\) sizes, each a 4-byte integer, most significant byte first (big-endian)


then
the data, one byte per pixel or label, row after row



gzip.open decompresses on the fly. We read the first 16 bytes of the training images:


Code
with gzip.open(paths["train_images"], "rb") as f:
    header = f.read(16)                                       # 4 bytes "magic number" + 3 sizes of 4 bytes
print("first 16 bytes:", list(header))

sizes = np.frombuffer(header, dtype=">i4")                     # ">i4" = big-endian 4-byte integer
print("as four big-endian integers:", sizes)
print("data type byte:", header[2], " number of dimensions:", header[3])


first 16 bytes: [0, 0, 8, 3, 0, 0, 234, 96, 0, 0, 0, 28, 0, 0, 0, 28]
as four big-endian integers: [ 2051 60000    28    28]
data type byte: 8  number of dimensions: 3


The four integers are \(2051\) (the “magic number” \(=\) 0x00000803: data type 08, \(3\) dimensions), \(60\,000\) images, \(28\) rows and \(28\) columns. For example, \(60\,000 = 0\cdot256^3 + 0\cdot256^2 + 234\cdot256 + 96\), which are bytes 4–7 above.
A complete reader is a few lines. np.frombuffer interprets raw bytes as an array without copying; offset skips the header.


Code
def read_idx(path):
    # Read an IDX file (gzip-compressed) into a NumPy array of unsigned bytes.
    with gzip.open(path, "rb") as f:
        raw = f.read()
    assert raw[0] == 0 and raw[1] == 0 and raw[2] == 0x08, "not an IDX file of unsigned bytes"
    n_dims = raw[3]
    shape = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=">i4", count=n_dims, offset=4)          # the d sizes
    data = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.uint8, offset=4 + 4 * n_dims)        # all the rest
    return data.reshape(shape)

X_train_full = read_idx(paths["train_images"])
y_train_full = read_idx(paths["train_labels"])
X_test_raw   = read_idx(paths["test_images"])
y_test_raw   = read_idx(paths["test_labels"])

for name, a in [("X_train_full", X_train_full), ("y_train_full", y_train_full), ("X_test_raw", X_test_raw), ("y_test_raw", y_test_raw)]:
    print(f"{name:13s} shape {str(a.shape):16s} dtype {a.dtype}   values {a.min()} ... {a.max()}")
print("first 20 training labels:", y_train_full[:20])


X_train_full  shape (60000, 28, 28)  dtype uint8   values 0 ... 255
y_train_full  shape (60000,)         dtype uint8   values 0 ... 9
X_test_raw    shape (10000, 28, 28)  dtype uint8   values 0 ... 255
y_test_raw    shape (10000,)         dtype uint8   values 0 ... 9
first 20 training labels: [5 0 4 1 9 2 1 3 1 4 3 5 3 6 1 7 2 8 6 9]


That is the whole data set: an array of \(60\,000\) images \(28\times 28\) with integer pixel values \(0\) (background) to \(255\) (ink), the corresponding labels \(0\dots9\), and the same for the \(10\,000\) test images. Everything that follows works with these NumPy arrays.

test counts    : [ 980 1135 1032 1010  982  892  958 1028  974 1009]


The classes are nearly balanced (between about \(9\%\) and \(11\%\) each), so a model that always answers the same digit would be right in only about \(10\%\) of the cases, and so would random guessing. Any useful model must do much better than \(10\%\).


2.3 The mean image of every class
Averaging all training images of one digit shows the “typical” shape and how much it varies (blurred regions = places where different writers put the ink differently).


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 10, figsize=(12, 1.6))
for k in range(10):
    axes[k].imshow(X_train_full[y_train_full == k].mean(axis=0), cmap="gray_r")
    axes[k].set_title(f"mean {k}"); axes[k].axis("off")
plt.show()







2.4 Flattening an image into a vector
The networks of this notebook (dense, or fully connected) take a vector as input. A \(28\times28\) image becomes a vector of \(m = 784\) numbers by writing the rows one after another: pixel \((i, j)\) (row \(i\), column \(j\)) goes to position \(28\,i + j\). This is what reshape does (NumPy and PyTorch store arrays row by row, so no data are moved). The cell below checks the index formula on one pixel and plots the image next to its flattened version.


Code

i, j = 6, 14
print(f"pixel (row {i}, column {j}) = {img[i, j]},   vector element {28 * i + j} = {vec[28 * i + j]}")

axes[1].plot(vec, lw=0.8)
for r in range(1, 28):
    axes[1].axvline(28 * r, color="grey", lw=0.3)              # boundaries between image rows
axes[1].set_xlim(0, 784); axes[1].set_xlabel("position in the vector  (= 28 * row + column)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("pixel value")
axes[1].set_title("the same image as a vector of 784 numbers (grey lines: start of a new image row)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


pixel (row 6, column 14) = 253,   vector element 182 = 253





Each bump in the right panel is one image row crossing the stroke. The network sees only this list of \(784\) numbers: it does not know which pixels are neighbours. (Convolutional networks, discussed later in Chapter 2, use the 2D arrangement.)

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
3. Splitting the data set (Box 2.10)

3.1 Training, validation, test
The available images play three different roles. The training set is used to change the parameters by gradient descent. The validation set is used during development, to watch for overfitting and to choose settings such as the number of epochs, the learning rate or the architecture. The test set is used once, at the very end, to report the final quality; if it were used to choose settings, it would no longer measure performance on new data. For teaching purposes the analyses and exercises below also look at the test set, whereas in a real project such comparisons would be made on the validation set.
The MNIST test file is our test set. The \(60\,000\) training images are split at random into \(50\,000\) for training and \(10\,000\) for validation. The split must be random: a data file may be ordered (by class, by writer, by date of collection), and the first images of a file need not be representative of the rest. rng.permutation(n) returns the numbers \(0,\dots,n-1\) in a random order; the first \(50\,000\) of them select the training images.


Code
n_full = len(X_train_full)
perm = rng.permutation(n_full)                     # a random order of 0, ..., 59999
idx_train, idx_val = perm[:50_000], perm[50_000:]
print("first 10 entries of the permutation:", perm[:10])
print("training indices:", len(idx_train), "  validation indices:", len(idx_val))
print("common indices:", len(np.intersect1d(idx_train, idx_val)),
      "  together they cover all images:", np.array_equal(np.sort(np.concatenate([idx_train, idx_val])), np.arange(n_full)))

X_tr_img, y_tr_np = X_train_full[idx_train], y_train_full[idx_train]
X_va_img, y_va_np = X_train_full[idx_val],   y_train_full[idx_val]
X_te_img, y_te_np = X_test_raw,              y_test_raw

training indices: 50000   validation indices: 10000
common indices: 0   together they cover all images: True


Indexing a NumPy array with an array of indices (X_train_full[idx_train]) picks the rows in that order. No image is in both sets, and together they use every image exactly once. The random split gives training and validation sets with the same class proportions, which also match the test file:


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
for shift, (name, y) in zip([-0.27, 0, 0.27], [("training", y_tr_np), ("validation", y_va_np), ("test", y_te_np)]):
    ax.bar(np.arange(10) + shift, np.bincount(y, minlength=10) / len(y), width=0.27, label=f"{name} ({len(y)})")
ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_xlabel("digit"); ax.set_ylabel("fraction"); ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
plt.show()







3.2 Flattening and standardisation
As in the chapter, the input vectors are standardised to mean \(0\) and standard deviation \(1\): \[\mathbf x \;\leftarrow\; \frac{\mathbf x - \mu}{s},\] with one number \(\mu\) (mean) and one number \(s\) (standard deviation) computed over all pixels of all training images. Inputs of order one keep the pre-activations \(\mathbf W\mathbf x + \mathbf b\) in the range where the sigmoid is not flat, which makes gradient descent work well.
\(\mu\) and \(s\) are computed from the training set only and then applied unchanged to validation and test data. Using statistics of the test set would let information about the test data leak into the model (data leakage); in a real application the test data are not even available when the model is built.
Finally the arrays are converted to PyTorch tensors: inputs as float32 (the default type of PyTorch parameters), labels as int64 (the type PyTorch expects for class indices).


Code
def flatten(images):
    # (N, 28, 28) uint8  ->  (N, 784) float32
    return images.reshape(len(images), -1).astype(np.float32)

X_tr_flat, X_va_flat, X_te_flat = flatten(X_tr_img), flatten(X_va_img), flatten(X_te_img)
mu, s = X_tr_flat.mean(), X_tr_flat.std()          # from the TRAINING set only
print(f"training-set pixel statistics: mean {mu:.2f}, std {s:.2f}  (on the 0..255 scale)")

X_tr = torch.from_numpy((X_tr_flat - mu) / s)
X_va = torch.from_numpy((X_va_flat - mu) / s)
X_te = torch.from_numpy((X_te_flat - mu) / s)
y_tr = torch.from_numpy(y_tr_np.astype(np.int64))
y_va = torch.from_numpy(y_va_np.astype(np.int64))
y_te = torch.from_numpy(y_te_np.astype(np.int64))

for name, X, y in [("train", X_tr, y_tr), ("val", X_va, y_va), ("test", X_te, y_te)]:
    print(f"{name:5s}  X {tuple(X.shape)} {X.dtype}  mean {X.mean():+.3f} std {X.std():.3f}   y {tuple(y.shape)} {y.dtype}")


training-set pixel statistics: mean 33.33, std 78.57  (on the 0..255 scale)
train  X (50000, 784) torch.float32  mean +0.000 std 1.000   y (50000,) torch.int64
val    X (10000, 784) torch.float32  mean -0.001 std 1.000   y (10000,) torch.int64
test   X (10000, 784) torch.float32  mean +0.006 std 1.008   y (10000,) torch.int64


The training inputs have mean \(0\) and standard deviation \(1\) by construction; validation and test inputs are close to that but not exactly, since they were transformed with the training statistics. The background pixels (\(0\)) become \(-\mu/s \approx -0.42\), full ink (\(255\)) becomes about \(2.8\).

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
4. Mini-batches

4.1 Mini-batches from a random permutation
The gradient of the loss is an average over images. Computing it over all \(50\,000\) images before every parameter update (full-batch gradient descent, as in the chapter’s equations) is expensive. Instead, each epoch (one pass over the training set) begins by putting the training indices in a new random order. This order is then cut into consecutive pieces of batch_size indices, the mini-batches, and for each mini-batch the loss and its gradient are computed on these images only and the parameters are updated.
Every image is thus used exactly once per epoch, and one epoch makes \(\lceil 50\,000/B\rceil\) updates (with \(B\) the batch size). The gradient of a mini-batch is a noisy estimate of the full gradient (stochastic gradient descent), but many cheap noisy steps are much faster than a few exact ones.
The function below produces the index arrays of the mini-batches. It is a Python generator: yield hands out one value and pauses the function until the next value is requested by the for loop, so the batches are produced one at a time.


Code
def batch_indices(n, batch_size, shuffle=True, generator=None):
    # Yield index tensors of consecutive mini-batches covering 0, ..., n-1 once.
    order = torch.randperm(n, generator=generator) if shuffle else torch.arange(n)
    for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
        yield order[start:start + batch_size]          # the last batch may be shorter

batch_size = 64
batches = list(batch_indices(len(X_tr), batch_size, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)))
print("number of mini-batches per epoch:", len(batches), "  ( = ceil(50000 / 64) =", int(np.ceil(50000 / 64)), ")")
print("sizes of the first three and of the last batch:", [len(b) for b in batches[:3]], len(batches[-1]))
print("first batch indices:", batches[0][:10].tolist(), "...")
all_used = torch.sort(torch.cat(batches)).values
print("every training image used exactly once:", torch.equal(all_used, torch.arange(len(X_tr))))


number of mini-batches per epoch: 782   ( = ceil(50000 / 64) = 782 )
sizes of the first three and of the last batch: [64, 64, 64] 16
first batch indices: [36044, 49165, 37807, 11341, 6091, 16904, 36293, 28026, 24681, 17849] ...
every training image used exactly once: True


\(50\,000 = 781\cdot 64 + 16\), hence \(782\) batches, the last one with \(16\) images. A batch of data is then X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]: a matrix \(X_i\in\mathbb R^{64\times784}\) (one image per row, as in the chapter’s feed-forward pass) and a vector of \(64\) labels.


Code
idx = batches[0]
xb, yb = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]
print("one mini-batch: inputs", tuple(xb.shape), "  labels", tuple(yb.shape))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 16, figsize=(13, 3.8))
for ax, x, y in zip(axes.flat, xb, yb):
    ax.imshow(x.reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r")        # back to 28 x 28 for display only
    ax.set_title(str(y.item()), fontsize=9); ax.axis("off")
fig.suptitle("the first mini-batch of 64 images (in random order, with their labels)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


one mini-batch: inputs (64, 784)   labels (64,)







4.2 PyTorch Dataset and DataLoader
PyTorch packages these two steps into two classes from torch.utils.data. A Dataset knows how many samples there are (__len__) and returns sample number i (__getitem__), here a pair (image vector, label). A DataLoader takes a Dataset, shuffles the indices in every epoch, cuts them into batches, calls __getitem__ for every index of a batch, and stacks the results into batch tensors (collate).
Writing our own Dataset shows that there is nothing more to it. (For tensors already in memory PyTorch also offers the ready-made TensorDataset, which does the same.) For large data sets that do not fit into memory, __getitem__ would read one image from disk; the DataLoader can then load batches in parallel processes (num_workers). This is the main reason the classes exist.


Code
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

class MNISTDataset(Dataset):
    # Pairs (image vector, label) stored as two tensors in memory.
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.X, self.y = X, y

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.X)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.X[i], self.y[i]

ds_tr = MNISTDataset(X_tr, y_tr)
x0, y0 = ds_tr[0]                                       # calls __getitem__(0)
print("len(ds_tr) =", len(ds_tr), "   ds_tr[0]: image", tuple(x0.shape), " label", y0.item())

loader_tr = DataLoader(ds_tr, batch_size=64, shuffle=True, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
print("batches per epoch: len(loader_tr) =", len(loader_tr))
xb_dl, yb_dl = next(iter(loader_tr))                   # the first batch of one epoch
print("one batch from the DataLoader:", tuple(xb_dl.shape), tuple(yb_dl.shape))


len(ds_tr) = 50000    ds_tr[0]: image (784,)  label 1
batches per epoch: len(loader_tr) = 782
one batch from the DataLoader: (64, 784) (64,)


With shuffle=False both methods must give identical batches, and indeed they do. The timing shows the price of the generality: the DataLoader calls __getitem__ \(50\,000\) times per epoch and stacks single images, while X_tr[idx] copies a whole batch in one operation.


Code
loader_fixed = DataLoader(ds_tr, batch_size=64, shuffle=False)
same = all(torch.equal(xd, X_tr[idx]) and torch.equal(yd, y_tr[idx])
           for (xd, yd), idx in zip(loader_fixed, batch_indices(len(X_tr), 64, shuffle=False)))
print("DataLoader(shuffle=False) gives the same batches as slicing X_tr[idx]:", same)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), 64):
    xb, yb = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]
t_slice = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for xb, yb in loader_tr:
    pass
t_dl = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"one epoch of batches: slicing X_tr[idx] {t_slice:.3f} s,  DataLoader {t_dl:.3f} s")


DataLoader(shuffle=False) gives the same batches as slicing X_tr[idx]: True


one epoch of batches: slicing X_tr[idx] 0.015 s,  DataLoader 0.199 s


Both ways are used below: the regression model of Section 5 uses our own batch_indices, the cross-entropy model of Section 6 the DataLoader. Each mini-batch has the same size and is drawn the same way, so the choice does not affect the comparison of the two models.

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
section: 5. Classification as regression with a single sigmoid output
text:
5. Classification as regression with a single sigmoid output

5.1 Digit recognition as curve fitting
The chapter imagines an unknown function \(G:\mathbb R^{784}\to\{0,\dots,9\}\) that maps the pixels of an image to the digit it shows, and treats learning \(G\) as non-linear curve fitting (regression), just as in the one-dimensional example of the Universal Approximation Theorem. The network, which we call model A, has one output node with a sigmoid, so \(\bar y = f_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf x)\in(0,1)\). The target of an image with digit \(y\) is the rescaled digit \(y/10\in\{0, 0.1, \dots, 0.9\}\), and the loss is the mean squared error over a batch of \(B\) images, \[\mathcal L = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B \big(\bar y_i - y_i/10\big)^2 .\] The predicted digit is obtained by turning \(10\,\bar y\) into an integer.
This last step needs care. int() in Python (and .long() in PyTorch) truncates, e.g. \(2.97\to2\), although the output is closest to the target \(3\). The correct choice is rounding to the nearest integer, followed by clipping to \(0\dots9\), because with the sigmoid \(10\bar y\in(0,10)\) and a value such as \(9.6\) would round to \(10\). The cell below compares the two rules on a few example outputs.


Code
outputs = torch.tensor([0.031, 0.297, 0.304, 0.649, 0.951])         # example values of the sigmoid output
print("10 * y_bar       :", (10 * outputs).tolist())
print("truncated (int)  :", (10 * outputs).long().tolist())
print("rounded + clipped:", (10 * outputs).round().clamp(0, 9).long().tolist())

def predict_digit_regression(y_bar):
    # sigmoid output in (0,1)  ->  digit 0..9
    return (10 * y_bar).round().clamp(0, 9).long()


10 * y_bar       : [0.3100000023841858, 2.9699997901916504, 3.0399999618530273, 6.489999771118164, 9.510000228881836]
truncated (int)  : [0, 2, 3, 6, 9]
rounded + clipped: [0, 3, 3, 6, 9]




5.2 Network with one output node
As in the chapter, the input is the flattened standardised image (\(m = 784\) numbers), followed by one hidden layer of \(N^{(1)} = 21\) nodes and the output node, all with the sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\): \[\bar{\mathbf h} = \sigma\big(\mathbf x W^{(1)T} + \mathbf b^{(1)}\big)\in(0,1)^{21},\qquad \bar y = \sigma\big(\bar{\mathbf h}W^{(2)T} + b^{(2)}\big)\in(0,1).\] The number of hidden nodes is kept in the variable N_HIDDEN, so that it can be changed in one place (Exercise 4 shows what wider and deeper networks do). nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) holds \(W\) of shape (n_out, n_in) and \(\mathbf b\) of length n_out, and computes \(\mathbf x W^T + \mathbf b\) for a batch of row vectors \(\mathbf x\). (The chapter has no bias in the output layer; with one extra parameter this makes no difference.)


Code
N_HIDDEN = 21                                     # nodes in the hidden layer, as in the chapter

def make_regression_model():
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(784, N_HIDDEN), nn.Sigmoid(),      # hidden layer
        nn.Linear(N_HIDDEN, 1),   nn.Sigmoid(),      # ONE output node, value in (0, 1)
    )

torch.manual_seed(0)
model_reg = make_regression_model()
print(model_reg)
for name, p in model_reg.named_parameters():
    print(f"  {name:9s} {str(tuple(p.shape)):11s} {p.numel():7d} parameters")
print("total:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_reg.parameters()))

with torch.no_grad():
    out = model_reg(X_tr[:5])
print("output for 5 images, shape", tuple(out.shape), ":", out.squeeze(1).tolist())


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=784, out_features=21, bias=True)
  (1): Sigmoid()
  (2): Linear(in_features=21, out_features=1, bias=True)
  (3): Sigmoid()
)
  0.weight  (21, 784)     16464 parameters
  0.bias    (21,)            21 parameters
  2.weight  (1, 21)          21 parameters
  2.bias    (1,)              1 parameters
total: 16507
output for 5 images, shape (5, 1) : [0.49288123846054077, 0.5091497898101807, 0.5078026056289673, 0.48742517828941345, 0.5129513144493103]


The output has shape (B, 1), one column. The targets will have shape (B,), so the output is reshaped with .squeeze(1) before the loss is computed: nn.MSELoss given shapes (B, 1) and (B,) would broadcast them to a (B, B) matrix and compute something else; PyTorch only prints a warning, which is easy to overlook (a classic bug).
The untrained network gives nearly the same output \(\approx 0.5\) for every image (small random differences): it has not learned anything yet.


5.3 Loss and evaluation
A function that evaluates a model on a whole data set (all images at once, without gradients) returns the loss and the accuracy, the fraction of images whose predicted digit equals the label. The accuracy is what we care about, but it cannot be minimised by gradient descent: it is piecewise constant in the parameters, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere. The MSE changes smoothly.


Code
mse = nn.MSELoss()

def evaluate_regression(model, X, y):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        y_bar = model(X).squeeze(1)                     # shape (N,)
        loss = mse(y_bar, y.float() / 10).item()
        acc = (predict_digit_regression(y_bar) == y).float().mean().item()
    return loss, acc

loss0, acc0 = evaluate_regression(model_reg, X_va, y_va)
print(f"untrained network on the validation set: MSE {loss0:.4f}, accuracy {acc0:.3f}")


untrained network on the validation set: MSE 0.0879, accuracy 0.087




5.4 The training loop
The optimiser is Adam with learning rate \(10^{-3}\). The chapter uses plain gradient descent; Adam is discussed in the section The Zoo of Optimization Algorithms and is much less sensitive to the choice of the learning rate, while plain gradient descent is the subject of Exercise 5. One epoch is one pass over the \(782\) mini-batches of Section 4.1. For each batch the loop computes the forward pass and the loss, clears the old gradients with zero_grad, computes \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\boldsymbol\theta\) with backward, and updates the parameters with step. The loss of every mini-batch is stored, since it is cheap and shows the noise of stochastic gradient descent, and after every epoch the loss and accuracy on the full training and validation sets are computed with evaluate_regression.
model.train() / model.eval() switch layers (such as dropout, which randomly switches off nodes during training) between training and evaluation behaviour. This network has no such layers, but the calls are a habit worth keeping.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_reg = make_regression_model()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model_reg.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
n_epochs, batch_size = 20, 64
shuffle_gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)           # random order of the batches, reproducible
hist_reg = {"batch loss": [], "train loss": [], "val loss": [], "train acc": [], "val acc": []}

t_start = time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
    model_reg.train()
    for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), batch_size, shuffle=True, generator=shuffle_gen):
        xb, yb = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]                    # one mini-batch: (B, 784) and (B,)
        target = yb.float() / 10                         # digit / 10
        y_bar = model_reg(xb).squeeze(1)                 # forward pass, shape (B,)
        loss = mse(y_bar, target)

        optimizer.zero_grad()                            # clear gradients of the previous step
        loss.backward()                                  # backpropagation
        optimizer.step()                                 # theta <- theta - (Adam step)
        hist_reg["batch loss"].append(loss.item())

    tr_loss, tr_acc = evaluate_regression(model_reg, X_tr, y_tr)
    va_loss, va_acc = evaluate_regression(model_reg, X_va, y_va)
    for key, v in zip(["train loss", "train acc", "val loss", "val acc"], [tr_loss, tr_acc, va_loss, va_acc]):
        hist_reg[key].append(v)
    if epoch == 1 or epoch % 2 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}:  MSE train {tr_loss:.4f}  val {va_loss:.4f}   accuracy train {tr_acc:.3f}  val {va_acc:.3f}")
print(f"training took {time.perf_counter() - t_start:.0f} s")

epoch  2:  MSE train 0.0126  val 0.0133   accuracy train 0.515  val 0.505


epoch  4:  MSE train 0.0094  val 0.0103   accuracy train 0.607  val 0.599


epoch  6:  MSE train 0.0084  val 0.0096   accuracy train 0.622  val 0.609


epoch  8:  MSE train 0.0077  val 0.0092   accuracy train 0.640  val 0.617


epoch 10:  MSE train 0.0076  val 0.0095   accuracy train 0.641  val 0.618


epoch 12:  MSE train 0.0070  val 0.0092   accuracy train 0.653  val 0.630


epoch 14:  MSE train 0.0068  val 0.0091   accuracy train 0.660  val 0.636


epoch 16:  MSE train 0.0067  val 0.0092   accuracy train 0.654  val 0.628


epoch 18:  MSE train 0.0066  val 0.0091   accuracy train 0.665  val 0.640

training took 9 s




5.5 Learning curves
Left: the MSE. The thin line is the loss of the individual mini-batches (x-axis converted to epochs: batch \(k\) is at epoch \(k/782\)); the markers are the losses on the full training and validation sets after every epoch. Right: the accuracies.


Code
def plot_history(hist, loss_name, title):
    n_ep = len(hist["train loss"])
    epochs = np.arange(1, n_ep + 1)
    batch_x = np.arange(1, len(hist["batch loss"]) + 1) / (len(hist["batch loss"]) / n_ep)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
    axes[0].plot(batch_x, hist["batch loss"], color="lightgrey", lw=0.5, label="mini-batches")
    axes[0].plot(epochs, hist["train loss"], "o-", label="training set")
    axes[0].plot(epochs, hist["val loss"], "s-", label="validation set")
    axes[0].set_yscale("log"); axes[0].set_ylabel(loss_name)
    axes[1].plot(epochs, hist["train acc"], "o-", label="training set")
    axes[1].plot(epochs, hist["val acc"], "s-", label="validation set")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("accuracy")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.legend()
    fig.suptitle(title); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

plot_history(hist_reg, "MSE loss", "Part A: single sigmoid output + MSE")





The network learns, but slowly and not far: the validation accuracy rises from about \(9\%\) before training and \(36\%\) after one epoch to about \(60\%\) after four epochs and then creeps up to about \(64\%\) after twenty. The loss on the validation set flattens after about seven epochs, while the training loss continues to decrease slightly: the small hidden layer cannot do much better with this formulation of the task. The accuracy curve is jagged: a small change of the parameters can push many outputs across a rounding boundary \(k\pm0.5\) at once.


5.6 Confusion matrix (Box 2.11)
The accuracy is a single number; to see which digits are confused with which, we use the confusion matrix \(C\). It counts, for every pair (true digit \(i\), predicted digit \(j\)), how many images of digit \(i\) (in a given set) were predicted as \(j\). We show it for all three sets: training (the data the parameters were fitted to), validation (used during training to monitor the model) and test (used only now). Each row is normalised to sum to one, so \(C_{ij}\) is the fraction of images of digit \(i\) that were classified as \(j\); the diagonal element \(C_{ii}\) is the fraction of digit \(i\) recognised correctly. The mean of the diagonal is the accuracy averaged over classes (Box 2.11); since the MNIST classes are nearly balanced it is almost equal to the plain accuracy.
The matrix is built with one bincount: the pair \((i, j)\) is encoded as the single number \(10i + j \in\{0,\dots,99\}\), the occurrences are counted and arranged as a \(10\times10\) matrix.


Code
def confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, k=10):
    C = torch.bincount(k * y_true + y_pred, minlength=k * k).reshape(k, k).float()
    return C / C.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)              # each row (true class) sums to 1

def plot_confusion(ax, C, title):
    im = ax.imshow(C, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    for i in range(10):
        for j in range(10):
            if C[i, j] >= 0.005:
                ax.text(j, i, f"{C[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5,
                        color="white" if C[i, j] > 0.5 else "black")
    ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_yticks(range(10))
    ax.set_xlabel("predicted digit $j$"); ax.set_ylabel("true digit $i$")
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nmean of diagonal = {C.diagonal().mean():.3f}", fontsize=10)
    return im

with torch.no_grad():
    y_bar_tr = model_reg(X_tr).squeeze(1)
    y_bar_va = model_reg(X_va).squeeze(1)
    y_bar_te = model_reg(X_te).squeeze(1)
pred_reg_tr = predict_digit_regression(y_bar_tr)
pred_reg_va = predict_digit_regression(y_bar_va)
pred_reg_te = predict_digit_regression(y_bar_te)
acc_reg_te = (pred_reg_te == y_te).float().mean().item()
C_reg_tr = confusion_matrix(y_tr, pred_reg_tr)
C_reg_va = confusion_matrix(y_va, pred_reg_va)
C_reg = confusion_matrix(y_te, pred_reg_te)
print(f"accuracy (regression):  training {(pred_reg_tr == y_tr).float().mean():.3f}"
      f"   validation {(pred_reg_va == y_va).float().mean():.3f}   test {acc_reg_te:.3f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5.3))
plot_confusion(axes[0], C_reg_tr, "Part A: regression, training set")
plot_confusion(axes[1], C_reg_va, "Part A: regression, validation set")
plot_confusion(axes[2], C_reg, "Part A: regression, test set")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


accuracy (regression):  training 0.677   validation 0.638   test 0.652





The test accuracy is about \(65\%\), higher than the \(56\%\) reported in the chapter, which uses full-batch gradient descent instead of Adam with mini-batches (see Exercise 5). The three matrices look almost the same. Training and test accuracies differ by only about 2–3 points, so overfitting is mild; validation and test agree, so the validation set, which we watched during training, was a reliable estimate of the performance on new data. The model is limited by the task as posed. The confusion matrix shows the characteristic pattern of the regression: the errors form bands next to the diagonal. A \(5\) is predicted as \(4\) or \(6\) in almost half of the cases, an \(8\) as \(7\) or \(9\) and a \(2\) as \(1\) or \(3\) in more than a third. Confusions between digits of similar shape but distant value (such as \(4\) and \(9\)) do not appear as such.
The continuous output shows why. For every true digit we plot the distribution of \(10\,\bar y\) over the test images (a violin plot: the width is the histogram of the values). The dashed horizontal lines are the rounding boundaries \(k\pm 0.5\); an image is classified correctly when its value lies in the band around its own digit.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
ax.violinplot([10 * y_bar_te[y_te == k].numpy() for k in range(10)], positions=range(10), widths=0.8, showmedians=True)
for b in np.arange(-0.5, 10, 1):

The output for each digit is centred near the target, but the distributions are wide, about one unit for most digits, and have long tails (the blue horizontal bars mark the minimum, median and maximum; the black bars the targets). title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
section: 6. Ten outputs, softmax and categorical cross-entropy
text:
6. Ten outputs, softmax and categorical cross-entropy

6.1 One-hot encoding, softmax and the cross-entropy
We now pose the task differently and call the resulting network model B. Instead of one number, the network returns \(K = 10\) numbers \(z_0,\dots,z_9\) (the logits), one per class. The softmax \[q_k = \mathrm{SoftMax}(\mathbf z)_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=0}^{9} e^{z_j}}\] turns them into a probability distribution \(\mathbf q\): \(q_k > 0\) and \(\sum_k q_k = 1\). \(q_k\) is read as the probability, according to the network, that the image shows digit \(k\). The predicted digit is the most probable one, \(\arg\max_k q_k\).
The label \(y\) is written as a one-hot vector \(\mathbf p\) with \(p_k = \delta_{k,y}\) (Box 2.7): the “true” distribution, all probability on the correct class. Two distributions are compared with the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (Box 2.8), \[\mathrm{KL}(\mathbf p\,\|\,\mathbf q) = \sum_k p_k\log\frac{p_k}{q_k} = \underbrace{\sum_k p_k\log p_k}_{-\,\mathcal H(\mathbf p)\ \text{(no }\boldsymbol\theta\text{)}}\;\underbrace{-\sum_k p_k\log q_k}_{\mathcal L_{\rm ce}} .\] (Here and below \(\log\) denotes the natural logarithm.) Only the second term depends on the network, so the loss is the categorical cross-entropy, averaged over the batch of \(B\) images. For a one-hot \(\mathbf p\) only the term of the true class survives: \[\mathcal L_{\rm ce} = -\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{k=0}^{9} p_{ik}\log q_{ik} = -\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\log q_{i,y_i} .\] It is \(0\) if the network gives probability \(1\) to the true class and grows without bound as that probability goes to \(0\).
In PyTorch, nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes the logits of shape (B, 10) and the labels as integers of shape (B,). It applies the softmax itself (in a numerically stable form, via \(\log\sum_j e^{z_j}\)), so the model must not end with a softmax layer. The cell checks on random logits that the formula above, written out with one-hot vectors, gives the same number.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
z = torch.randn(5, 10)                                  # logits for a batch of 5 images
y5 = y_tr[:5]                                           # their true labels

q = torch.softmax(z, dim=1)                             # probabilities, each row sums to 1
p = nn.functional.one_hot(y5, num_classes=10).float()   # one-hot labels, shape (5, 10)
print("labels:", y5.tolist())
print("one-hot p:\n", p.int())
print("row sums of q:", q.sum(dim=1).tolist())

ce_formula = -(p * torch.log(q)).sum(dim=1).mean()
ce_torch = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(z, y5)
print(f"cross-entropy from the formula: {ce_formula:.6f}   nn.CrossEntropyLoss: {ce_torch:.6f}")

6.2 Network with ten output nodes
The hidden layer is exactly that of model A. Only the output layer changes: \(10\) nodes instead of \(1\), and no sigmoid (the softmax is inside the loss).


Code
def make_classification_model():
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(784, N_HIDDEN), nn.Sigmoid(),      # hidden layer   (as in Part A)
        nn.Linear(N_HIDDEN, 10),                     # TEN output nodes: logits z_0 ... z_9
    )

torch.manual_seed(0)
model_ce = make_classification_model()
print(model_ce)
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_ce.parameters()),
      "  (Part A:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_reg.parameters()), ";  difference 9 * (N_HIDDEN + 1) =", 9 * (N_HIDDEN + 1), ")")


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=784, out_features=21, bias=True)
  (1): Sigmoid()
  (2): Linear(in_features=21, out_features=10, bias=True)
)
parameters: 16705   (Part A: 16507 ;  difference 9 * (N_HIDDEN + 1) = 198 )


An untrained network gives roughly equal probabilities \(q_k\approx 1/10\) to all classes, so the cross-entropy should start near \(-\log(1/10) = \log 10 \approx 2.30\):


Code
ce = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

def evaluate_classification(model, X, y):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = model(X)                               # shape (N, 10)
        loss = ce(logits, y).item()
        acc = (logits.argmax(dim=1) == y).float().mean().item()
    return loss, acc

loss0, acc0 = evaluate_classification(model_ce, X_va, y_va)
print(f"untrained: cross-entropy {loss0:.3f} (ln 10 = {np.log(10):.3f}),  accuracy {acc0:.3f}")


untrained: cross-entropy 2.356 (ln 10 = 2.303),  accuracy 0.072




6.3 Training with the cross-entropy
The loop is the same as for model A with three differences: the batches come from a DataLoader as in Section 4.2, the target is the integer label itself, and the loss is the cross-entropy of the \(10\) logits. Optimiser, learning rate, batch size and number of epochs are the same as for model A, so any difference in the learning curves comes from the output layer and the loss.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_ce = make_classification_model()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model_ce.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
n_epochs, batch_size = 20, 64
loader_tr = DataLoader(MNISTDataset(X_tr, y_tr), batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True,
                       generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(1))
hist_ce = {"batch loss": [], "train loss": [], "val loss": [], "train acc": [], "val acc": []}

t_start = time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
    model_ce.train()
    for xb, yb in loader_tr:                             # the DataLoader shuffles and batches
        logits = model_ce(xb)                            # forward pass, shape (B, 10)
        loss = ce(logits, yb)                            # target: integer labels, shape (B,)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        hist_ce["batch loss"].append(loss.item())

    tr_loss, tr_acc = evaluate_classification(model_ce, X_tr, y_tr)
    va_loss, va_acc = evaluate_classification(model_ce, X_va, y_va)
    for key, v in zip(["train loss", "train acc", "val loss", "val acc"], [tr_loss, tr_acc, va_loss, va_acc]):
        hist_ce[key].append(v)
    if epoch == 1 or epoch % 2 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}:  CE train {tr_loss:.4f}  val {va_loss:.4f}   accuracy train {tr_acc:.3f}  val {va_acc:.3f}")
print(f"training took {time.perf_counter() - t_start:.0f} s")

It then rises slowly to about \(94.6\%\). Training and validation curves stay close (training accuracy \(97\%\)), so this small network barely overfits.


Code

    pred_ce_tr = model_ce(X_tr).argmax(dim=1)
    pred_ce_va = model_ce(X_va).argmax(dim=1)

For correctly classified images the network is nearly certain (one bar close to \(1\)). Among the mistakes, some are confident (\(5\) read as \(6\) with probability \(0.88\), an image that is ambiguous to a human, too), others show the doubt explicitly: for the \(3\) read as \(2\) the true class receives almost the same probability as the prediction. title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
7. Output layer and loss function

7.1 Same hidden layer, different output layer and loss
Both networks have the same hidden layer, the same optimiser, learning rate, batch size and number of epochs; they differ only in the output layer and the loss. The cell below puts their validation curves and test confusion matrices side by side and counts the misclassified test images.


Code
epochs = np.arange(1, n_epochs + 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.2, 1, 1]})
axes[0].plot(epochs, hist_reg["val acc"], "s-", label="A: 1 output + MSE (validation)")
axes[0].plot(epochs, hist_reg["train acc"], "o--", color="tab:blue", alpha=0.5, label="A: training")
axes[0].plot(epochs, hist_ce["val acc"], "s-", label="B: 10 outputs + CE (validation)")
axes[0].plot(epochs, hist_ce["train acc"], "o--", color="tab:orange", alpha=0.5, label="B: training")
axes[0].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel("accuracy"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plot_confusion(axes[1], C_reg, "A: regression")
plot_confusion(axes[2], C_ce, "B: cross-entropy")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{'':28s} {'regression (A)':>15s} {'cross-entropy (B)':>18s}")
print(f"{'test accuracy':28s} {acc_reg_te:15.3f} {acc_ce_te:18.3f}")
print(f"{'misclassified test images':28s} {(pred_reg_te != y_te).sum().item():15d} {(pred_ce_te != y_te).sum().item():18d}")





                              regression (A)  cross-entropy (B)
test accuracy                          0.652              0.948
misclassified test images               3480                516


This is the central result of the notebook. With the same hidden layer, data and training, the single-output regression reaches about \(65\%\) test accuracy and the ten-output cross-entropy network about \(95\%\), with about seven times fewer errors. The difference comes from how the task is posed, that is, from the output layer and the loss together; Exercise 2 shows that the ten outputs account for most of the gain. Model B is better in every epoch: after one epoch it is already far beyond the best value model A ever reaches. The confusion matrices show two different kinds of errors: bands along the diagonal (A: neighbouring values) versus rare, scattered errors (B: similar shapes).


Code
top2 = q_te.topk(2, dim=1)                                # two largest probabilities and their digits
a, b = top2.indices[:, 0], top2.indices[:, 1]
doubtful = torch.nonzero((top2.values[:, 1] > 0.25) & ((a - b).abs() >= 3))[:, 0]
print("test images on which model B hesitates between two distant digits:", len(doubtful))

show = doubtful[:8]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(show), figsize=(2 * len(show), 2.9))
for ax, n in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), show):
    ax.imshow(X_te_img[n], cmap="gray_r"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(f"true {y_te[n].item()}\nB: {a[n].item()} ({q_te[n, a[n]]:.2f}) / {b[n].item()} ({q_te[n, b[n]]:.2f})\n"
                 f"A: 10y = {10 * y_bar_te[n]:.1f} -> {pred_reg_te[n].item()}", fontsize=8.5)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

mid = (a[doubtful] + b[doubtful]).float() / 2
between = ((10 * y_bar_te[doubtful] - a[doubtful]).abs() > 1) & ((10 * y_bar_te[doubtful] - b[doubtful]).abs() > 1)
print(f"fraction of these images where A's output is more than 1 away from both candidate digits: {between.float().mean():.0%}")
print(f"mean |A's output - midpoint of the two candidates|: {(10 * y_bar_te[doubtful] - mid).abs().mean():.2f}")


test images on which model B hesitates between two distant digits: 248





fraction of these images where A's output is more than 1 away from both candidate digits: 60%
mean |A's output - midpoint of the two candidates|: 1.42


In these hesitant cases the regression output tends to land between the two candidate digits: for about \(60\%\) of the images it is more than \(1\) away from both of them. For example, an \(8\) that model B reads as \(8\) (\(0.53\)) or \(2\) (\(0.44\)) gets \(10\bar y\approx5.9\) from model A, which rounds to \(6\), a digit nobody would read in it. This is exactly what the MSE asks for: when the network cannot tell whether the target is \(0.2\) or \(0.8\), the value minimising the expected squared error lies in between.
The comparison can now be summarised. The ten-output network with the cross-entropy treats the classes as unordered categories, returns a probability for each, and reaches a much higher accuracy with the same hidden layer (about \(95\%\) instead of \(65\%\)). The single-output regression must fit a function that jumps between the values \(0, 0.1, \dots, 0.9\) in an arbitrary order of shapes; the rounding then turns every small error into a neighbouring digit, and every hesitation into an average. The difference comes from how the task is posed, that is, from the output layer and the loss together, and Exercise 2 shows that the ten outputs account for most of the gain.

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
Summary
MNIST is stored as four binary files in the IDX format: a short header (data type, number of dimensions, sizes) followed by one byte per pixel or label. Ten lines of NumPy read them, and the data loaders of libraries do nothing more. To prepare the data, the images are flattened to vectors of \(784\) numbers and standardised with the mean and standard deviation of the training set only. The \(60\,000\) training images are split at random into training (\(50\,000\)) and validation (\(10\,000\)) sets, and the separate MNIST test file serves as the test set.
Training proceeds in epochs. An epoch is one pass over a random permutation of the training set, cut into mini-batches; Dataset and DataLoader implement exactly this and are most useful when the data do not fit into memory. For every batch the training loop performs the forward pass, the loss, zero_grad, backward and step, and after every epoch the model is evaluated on the training and validation sets without gradients.
The main message concerns the formulation of the task. With the same hidden layer, data and training, the single-output regression reaches about \(65\%\) test accuracy and the ten-output cross-entropy network about \(95\%\). The difference comes from the output layer and the loss together. One sigmoid output trained with the MSE on the rescaled digit imposes an order and a distance on the classes that do not exist, so its errors are mostly neighbouring digits and averages of two candidates. Ten outputs treat the classes as categories, and Exercise 2 shows that they account for most of the gain (ten sigmoid outputs with the MSE reach about \(94\%\)).

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
Exercises

Exercise 1 — Truncation instead of rounding
Evaluate the trained regression model model_reg on the test set with the prediction (10 * y_bar).long() (truncation, as Python’s int()) instead of rounding. How much accuracy is lost? Then train model A again (10 epochs suffice) with the targets \((y + 0.5)/10\) instead of \(y/10\): for which prediction rule (rounding or truncation) are these targets the natural choice, and do you recover the accuracy?

Solution


Code
with torch.no_grad():
    y_bar = model_reg(X_te).squeeze(1)
acc_round = (predict_digit_regression(y_bar) == y_te).float().mean().item()
acc_trunc = ((10 * y_bar).long().clamp(0, 9) == y_te).float().mean().item()
print(f"targets y/10:        rounding {acc_round:.3f},  truncation {acc_trunc:.3f}")

# targets in the middle of the interval [y/10, (y+1)/10): truncation is then the natural rule
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_shift = make_regression_model()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model_shift.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
for epoch in range(10):
    for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), 64, generator=gen):
        loss = mse(model_shift(X_tr[idx]).squeeze(1), (y_tr[idx].float() + 0.5) / 10)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
with torch.no_grad():
    y_bar = model_shift(X_te).squeeze(1)
print(f"targets (y+0.5)/10:  truncation {((10 * y_bar).long().clamp(0, 9) == y_te).float().mean():.3f}"
      f",  rounding {(predict_digit_regression(y_bar) == y_te).float().mean():.3f}")


targets y/10:        rounding 0.652,  truncation 0.445


targets (y+0.5)/10:  truncation 0.631,  rounding 0.470


With targets \(y/10\), an output slightly below the target (e.g. \(2.97\) for a \(3\)) is truncated to the wrong digit: truncation drops the accuracy from about \(65\%\) to about \(45\%\). With the shifted targets \((y + 0.5)/10\) the target sits in the middle of the interval \([y, y+1)\) that truncation maps to \(y\), so truncation is the right rule (and now rounding fails). After \(10\) epochs the shifted model reaches about \(63\%\) on the test set, comparable to model A after \(10\) epochs (\(62\%\) on the validation set). The rule turning the continuous output into a class must match the encoding of the targets.



Exercise 2 — Ten outputs with the MSE
Is the improvement of model B due to the ten outputs or to the cross-entropy? Train the network of model B with ten sigmoid outputs and the MSE between the outputs and the one-hot vectors \(\mathbf p\) (predicted digit: the largest output). Use 10 epochs and compare the test accuracy with models A and B.

Solution


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_onehot_mse = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, N_HIDDEN), nn.Sigmoid(), nn.Linear(N_HIDDEN, 10), nn.Sigmoid())
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model_onehot_mse.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
for epoch in range(1, 11):
    for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), 64, generator=gen):
        p = nn.functional.one_hot(y_tr[idx], 10).float()
        loss = mse(model_onehot_mse(X_tr[idx]), p)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    if epoch % 5 == 0:
        with torch.no_grad():
            acc = (model_onehot_mse(X_va).argmax(1) == y_va).float().mean().item()
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}: validation accuracy {acc:.3f}")
with torch.no_grad():
    acc_te = (model_onehot_mse(X_te).argmax(1) == y_te).float().mean().item()
print(f"test accuracy:  A (1 output, MSE) {acc_reg_te:.3f}   10 outputs + MSE {acc_te:.3f}   B (10 outputs, CE) {acc_ce_te:.3f}")


epoch  5: validation accuracy 0.922


epoch 10: validation accuracy 0.935
test accuracy:  A (1 output, MSE) 0.652   10 outputs + MSE 0.938   B (10 outputs, CE) 0.948


Most of the gain comes from the ten outputs: with one-hot targets there is no artificial order of the classes, and even the MSE gives about \(94\%\), close to the cross-entropy (\(95\%\)). The cross-entropy still has two advantages: its outputs form a probability distribution with a clear interpretation, and its gradient does not vanish when an output is confidently wrong (for a sigmoid output with MSE the gradient contains \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\), which is tiny when the sigmoid saturates at the wrong end), so it typically learns faster.



Exercise 3 — Batch size
Train model B for 5 epochs with batch sizes \(16\), \(64\), \(512\) and \(50\,000\) (full batch), always with Adam and learning rate \(10^{-3}\). Record the validation accuracy after 5 epochs, the number of parameter updates and the training time. Explain the result.

Solution


Code
for bs in [16, 64, 512, 50_000]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = make_classification_model()
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
    n_updates, t0 = 0, time.perf_counter()
    for epoch in range(5):
        for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), bs, generator=gen):
            loss = ce(model(X_tr[idx]), y_tr[idx])
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
            n_updates += 1
    _, acc = evaluate_classification(model, X_va, y_va)
    print(f"batch size {bs:6d}: {n_updates:6d} updates, {time.perf_counter() - t0:5.1f} s,  validation accuracy {acc:.3f}")


batch size     16:  15625 updates,   7.8 s,  validation accuracy 0.944


batch size     64:   3910 updates,   2.0 s,  validation accuracy 0.937


batch size    512:    490 updates,   0.4 s,  validation accuracy 0.897


batch size  50000:      5 updates,   0.2 s,  validation accuracy 0.360


All runs see the same number of images (5 epochs), but the number of parameter updates differs by a factor of \(3\,000\). The full batch makes only \(5\) updates and is still close to guessing (\(36\%\)); batch size \(512\) reaches about \(90\%\). Batch sizes \(16\) and \(64\) give similar accuracy (about \(94\%\)), but \(16\) is almost four times slower: more Python overhead and smaller, less efficient matrix products per image. Batch sizes of a few tens to a few hundred are the usual compromise. Giving the full batch the same number of updates as batch size \(64\) would require thousands of epochs.



Exercise 4 — Wider and deeper networks
The chapter’s network is small: \(784\cdot21 + 21 + 22 \approx 16\,500\) parameters. Train both models (regression and cross-entropy) for 10 epochs with the hidden layers [21] (models A and B), [128] (one wider layer) and [128, 64] (two hidden layers), all with sigmoids, and compare the test accuracies. Which of the two approaches profits more from a larger network? Does the conclusion of Section 7 change?

Solution


Code
def make_mlp(hidden, n_out, sigmoid_output):
    layers, n_in = [], 784
    for n in hidden:                                     # hidden layers with sigmoids
        layers += [nn.Linear(n_in, n), nn.Sigmoid()]
        n_in = n
    layers.append(nn.Linear(n_in, n_out))
    if sigmoid_output:
        layers.append(nn.Sigmoid())
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)

def train_quick(model, kind, n_epochs=10):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), 64, generator=gen):
            if kind == "regression":
                loss = mse(model(X_tr[idx]).squeeze(1), y_tr[idx].float() / 10)
            else:
                loss = ce(model(X_tr[idx]), y_tr[idx])
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        if kind == "regression":
            return (predict_digit_regression(model(X_te).squeeze(1)) == y_te).float().mean().item()
        return (model(X_te).argmax(1) == y_te).float().mean().item()

print(f"{'hidden layers':14s} {'parameters':>11s} {'regression':>11s} {'cross-entropy':>14s}")
for hidden in [[21], [128], [128, 64]]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    m_reg = make_mlp(hidden, 1, sigmoid_output=True)
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    m_ce = make_mlp(hidden, 10, sigmoid_output=False)
    n_par = sum(p.numel() for p in m_reg.parameters())
    print(f"{str(hidden):14s} {n_par:11d} {train_quick(m_reg, 'regression'):11.3f} {train_quick(m_ce, 'classification'):14.3f}")


hidden layers   parameters  regression  cross-entropy


[21]                 16507       0.631          0.943


[128]               100609       0.733          0.972


[128, 64]           108801       0.799          0.973


Both approaches profit from a larger network, the regression much more (from \(63\%\) to \(80\%\) in 10 epochs) than the cross-entropy (from \(94\%\) to \(97\%\)). The gap shrinks but remains large: the cross-entropy with the chapter’s tiny network (\(16\,500\) parameters) is still far better than the regression with a network almost seven times larger. A big network can partly compensate for a badly posed task, but it is cheaper to pose the task well.



Exercise 5 — Full-batch gradient descent
The chapter trains the smallest version of model A: \(784\to21\to1\), sigmoid everywhere, no bias in the output layer, loss \(\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^N(\bar y_i - y_i/10)^2\) with \(N = 50\,000\) training images, and full-batch gradient descent (all \(50\,000\) training images in every step) with a large learning rate. Build this network with nn.Sequential (nn.Linear(21, 1, bias=False) for the output), train it with torch.optim.SGD for 500 full-batch steps with \(\eta = 50\), and plot the training and validation accuracy against the step. This is the network of model A; only the optimisation differs. Compare the test accuracy with model A. Why is such a large learning rate needed?

Solution


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_book = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 21), nn.Sigmoid(), nn.Linear(21, 1, bias=False), nn.Sigmoid())
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model_book.parameters(), lr=50.0)
target_tr = y_tr.float() / 10
steps, acc_tr_book, acc_va_book = [], [], []
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for step in range(501):
    if step % 10 == 0:
        _, a_tr = evaluate_regression(model_book, X_tr, y_tr)
        _, a_va = evaluate_regression(model_book, X_va, y_va)
        steps.append(step); acc_tr_book.append(a_tr); acc_va_book.append(a_va)
    if step == 500:
        break
    model_book.train()
    loss = ((model_book(X_tr).squeeze(1) - target_tr)**2).mean() / 2    # ALL training images: full batch
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(f"training took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")

_, acc_book_te = evaluate_regression(model_book, X_te, y_te)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.plot(steps, acc_tr_book, label="training"); ax.plot(steps, acc_va_book, label="validation")
ax.set_xlabel("gradient-descent step (full batch = 1 epoch)"); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title(f"784-21-1, SGD full batch, eta = 50:  test accuracy {acc_book_te:.3f}")
plt.show()
print(f"test accuracy: full-batch gradient descent {acc_book_te:.3f}   Part A (same network, Adam, mini-batches of 64) {acc_reg_te:.3f}")


training took 9 s





test accuracy: full-batch gradient descent 0.461   Part A (same network, Adam, mini-batches of 64) 0.652


With full-batch gradient descent the same network reaches only about \(46\%\) after \(500\) steps, compared with \(65\%\) for model A (the chapter reports \(56\%\); the exact number depends on the initialisation and the number of steps). The curve shows the price of a large learning rate: around step \(160\) one step overshoots, the accuracy collapses to \(\approx 10\%\) and the network has to recover. A large \(\eta\) is nevertheless needed because the gradient is tiny: by the chain rule it contains factors \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(1-\sigma)\le 1/4\) (two factors for the hidden-layer weights, one for the output weights) and the small difference \(\bar y - y/10\). Model A makes \(15\,640\) updates (20 epochs × 782 mini-batches) with Adam on mini-batches: about 30 times more updates than the \(500\) full-batch steps, each with an adaptive step size.

2. The datasets
For every \(L\) we use 51 temperatures from 3.5 down to 1.0 (step 0.05). Forty independent chains are cooled through this grid, and at each temperature every chain contributes 5 configurations separated by \(2L\) sweeps, which gives 200 configurations per temperature. Each file stores

configs: int8, shape (n_T, 200, L, L), values \(\pm1\);
T: the temperatures (ascending);
the generation settings, so that every file documents itself.

Data sets that already exist are loaded; the others are generated, which takes several minutes for the largest lattices.


Code
L_LIST = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
T_GRID = np.round(np.arange(1.0, 3.5001, 0.05), 3)          # ascending, 51 values
N_CHAINS, N_SAMPLES, N_EQUIL = 40, 5, 1000

def generate(L, seed):
    k0, k1 = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed))
    s0 = jnp.where(jax.random.bernoulli(k0, 0.5, (N_CHAINS, L, L)), 1.0, -1.0)
    out = sample_chains(s0, jax.random.split(k1, N_CHAINS), jnp.asarray(T_GRID[::-1], jnp.float32), chessboard(L),
                        N_EQUIL, N_SAMPLES, 2 * L)                         # (chains, nT, samples, L, L), cooling order
    out = np.asarray(out)[:, ::-1]                                           # ascending T
    return out.transpose(1, 0, 2, 3, 4).reshape(len(T_GRID), N_CHAINS * N_SAMPLES, L, L)

data = {}
for L in L_LIST:

        np.savez_compressed(path, configs=data[L], T=T_GRID, L=L, n_chains=N_CHAINS, n_samples_per_chain=N_SAMPLES,
                            n_equil=N_EQUIL, n_between=2 * L, sampler="checkerboard Metropolis, cooled from T=3.5")
        how = "generated"
    print(f"L = {L:2d}: {how} {data[L].shape} in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

section: 3. Magnetisation and energy of finite lattices
text:
3. Magnetisation and energy of finite lattices
The exact results for the infinite lattice serve as the reference. Below \(T_c\) the spontaneous magnetisation is \(M(T) = \left(1-\sinh^{-4}(2/T)\right)^{1/8}\) (Yang), and the energy per spin is \(u(T) = -\coth(2\beta)\left[1+\frac{2}{\pi}\left(2\tanh^2(2\beta)-1\right)K(\kappa)\right]\) with \(\kappa = 2\sinh(2\beta)/\cosh^2(2\beta)\) (Onsager). On finite lattices \(\langle|m|\rangle\) stays non-zero above \(T_c\) and the transition is rounded; in the figure this rounding should shrink as \(L\) grows.


Code
def M_exact(T):
    T = np.asarray(T, float); out = np.zeros_like(T); low = T < TC
    out[low] = (1 - np.sinh(2 / T[low]) ** -4) ** 0.125
    return out

def u_exact(T):
    K = 1 / np.asarray(T, float); kap = 2 * np.sinh(2 * K) / np.cosh(2 * K) ** 2
    return -1 / np.tanh(2 * K) * (1 + 2 / np.pi * (2 * np.tanh(2 * K) ** 2 - 1) * ellipk(kap ** 2))

def energy(c):
    c = c.astype(np.float32)
    return -(c * np.roll(c, 1, -1) + c * np.roll(c, 1, -2)).mean((-1, -2))

colors_L = dict(zip(L_LIST, plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0.05, 0.85, len(L_LIST)))))
Tf = np.linspace(1.0, 3.5, 400)

        ax[0].plot(T_GRID, np.abs(data[L].mean((-1, -2))).mean(1), ".-", ms=2.5, lw=1.2, color=colors_L[L], label=f"$L={L}$")
        ax[1].plot(T_GRID, energy(data[L]).mean(1), ".-", ms=2.5, lw=1.2, color=colors_L[L])
    ax[0].plot(Tf, M_exact(Tf), "--", color="red", lw=1.2, label="exact"); ax[1].plot(Tf, u_exact(Tf), "--", color="red", lw=1.2)
    for a, lab in zip(ax, [r"$\langle|m|\rangle$", r"$\langle e\rangle$"]):

We start with a 1D chain. With \(h=0\) its bonds are independent: neighbours are parallel with probability \(p=e^{\beta J}/(e^{\beta J}+e^{-\beta J})\), so chains can be sampled exactly, bond by bond. The correlation length is \(\xi=-1/\ln\tanh(\beta J)\), and the three rows below, at \(T = 0.6\), \(1.0\) and \(5.0\), show domains whose length shrinks with temperature. The next cell turns to two dimensions and shows \(L=50\) snapshots across \(T_c\), followed by a second figure with a grid of configurations from the dataset.

title: The 2D Ising model and a CNN
section: 5. The critical temperature from CNN confidence
text:
5. The critical temperature from CNN confidence
The network is trained only where the answer is clear: configurations with \(T<1.5\) get the label 0 (ordered), those with \(T>3\) the label 1 (disordered), and nothing between 1.5 and 3 is used for training.
The network, built with Flax NNX, consists of two blocks of a \(3\times3\) convolution with 16 channels (with periodic boundaries, like the lattice), ReLU and \(2\times2\) max pooling, followed by global average pooling, a dense layer of 32 ReLU units and 2 outputs with softmax; it is trained with the cross-entropy loss and Adam. Global average pooling makes the same network work for every \(L\).
After training we predict at every temperature. For one configuration the network gives \(p_1\), the probability of “disordered”, and its confidence is \(\max(p_0,p_1)\). This yields two estimates of \(T_c\): the temperature where the average confidence is lowest, and the temperature where \(\langle p_1\rangle_T\) crosses \(1/2\). Each lattice size is trained with three seeds, and the printout gives the mean and spread of both estimates.


Code
class IsingCNN(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, *, rngs):
        self.c1 = nnx.Conv(1, 16, (3, 3), padding="CIRCULAR", rngs=rngs)
        self.c2 = nnx.Conv(16, 16, (3, 3), padding="CIRCULAR", rngs=rngs)
        self.d1 = nnx.Linear(16, 32, rngs=rngs); self.d2 = nnx.Linear(32, 2, rngs=rngs)
    def __call__(self, x):
        h = x[..., None]
        h = nnx.max_pool(nnx.relu(self.c1(h)), (2, 2), strides=(2, 2))
        h = nnx.max_pool(nnx.relu(self.c2(h)), (2, 2), strides=(2, 2))
        h = h.mean(axis=(1, 2))                                  # global average pooling
        return self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(h)))                     # logits

@nnx.jit
def train_step(model, opt, x, y):
    def loss_fn(m):
        return optax.softmax_cross_entropy_with_integer_labels(m(x), y).mean()
    loss, grads = nnx.value_and_grad(loss_fn)(model)
    opt.update(model, grads)
    return loss

@nnx.jit
def prob_disordered(model, x):
    return jax.nn.softmax(model(x))[:, 1]

T_MIN, T_MAX = 1.5, 3.0
def train_cnn(L, seed, epochs=8, batch=64):
    c = data[L]
    low, high = T_GRID < T_MIN, T_GRID > T_MAX
    X = np.concatenate([c[low].reshape(-1, L, L), c[high].reshape(-1, L, L)]).astype(np.float32)
    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(c[low].shape[0] * c.shape[1], int), np.ones(c[high].shape[0] * c.shape[1], int)])
    model = IsingCNN(rngs=nnx.Rngs(seed)); opt = nnx.Optimizer(model, optax.adam(1e-3), wrt=nnx.Param)
    X, y = jnp.asarray(X), jnp.asarray(y); key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        key, k = jax.random.split(key); perm = jax.random.permutation(k, len(y))
        for i in range(0, len(y) - batch + 1, batch):
            train_step(model, opt, X[perm[i:i + batch]], y[perm[i:i + batch]])
    acc = float(((prob_disordered(model, X) > 0.5) == y).mean())
    return model, acc

def predict_all(model, L):
    c = jnp.asarray(data[L].reshape(-1, L, L), jnp.float32)
    return np.asarray(prob_disordered(model, c)).reshape(len(T_GRID), -1)

def estimates(p1):
    conf = np.maximum(p1, 1 - p1).mean(1); p1m = p1.mean(1)
    i = int(np.argmin(conf)); T_conf = T_GRID[i]
    j = int(np.where(np.diff(np.sign(p1m - 0.5)) != 0)[0][0])
    T_cross = T_GRID[j] + (0.5 - p1m[j]) * (T_GRID[j + 1] - T_GRID[j]) / (p1m[j + 1] - p1m[j])
    return conf, p1m, T_conf, T_cross

SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]
results = {}
t0 = time.time()
for L in L_LIST:
    runs = []
    for seed in SEEDS:
        model, acc = train_cnn(L, seed)
        runs.append((acc,) + estimates(predict_all(model, L)))
    results[L] = runs
    Tc_conf = np.array([r[3] for r in runs]); Tc_cross = np.array([r[4] for r in runs])
    print(f"L = {L:2d}: training accuracy {np.mean([r[0] for r in runs]):.4f}; T_c from the confidence minimum "
          f"{Tc_conf.mean():.3f} +- {Tc_conf.std():.3f}; from <p1> = 1/2: {Tc_cross.mean():.3f} +- {Tc_cross.std():.3f}"
          f"   ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")

tc_conf = np.array([np.mean([r[3] for r in results[L]]) for L in L_LIST]); tc_conf_e = np.array([np.std([r[3] for r in results[L]]) for L in L_LIST])

    ax[2].plot(xx, np.polyval(fit, xx), "--", color=orange, lw=1)
    ax[2].axhline(TC, color=grey, ls=":"); ax[2].set_xlabel("$1/L$"); ax[2].set_ylabel("$T_c$ estimate")

title: Lab 010: Monte Carlo samples of the 2D Ising model
text:
1. The model and its observables
Spins \(s_i=\pm1\) sit on an \(N_x\times N_y\) square lattice with periodic boundary conditions (a torus), \(N=N_xN_y\). The energy is \[
H(\boldsymbol s) = -J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} s_i s_j , \qquad J=1,\ h=0,
\] where \(\langle i,j\rangle\) runs over the \(2N\) nearest-neighbour bonds. In equilibrium at temperature \(T\) (with \(k_B=1\), \(\beta=1/T\)) the configurations are distributed as \[
p(\boldsymbol s) = \frac{e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol s)}}{Z}, \qquad Z=\sum_{\boldsymbol s} e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol s)} .
\]
The figure below draws a small patch of the lattice. Each disc is a spin: a filled navy disc is \(s_i=+1\) and a white disc with an orange rim is \(s_i=-1\), the convention of every sketch in this course. A line between two neighbours is a bond, and its contribution \(-Js_is_j\) to the energy is \(-J\) when the two spins agree (solid blue line, a satisfied bond) and \(+J\) when they disagree (dashed purple line with a cross, a broken bond). The faded discs on the right and on the top are copies of the first column and of the first row: with periodic boundaries the right neighbour of a spin in the last column is the spin in the first column of the same row, and likewise for the top row, so the lattice has no edges and has the topology of a torus. Every broken bond raises the energy by \(2J\), so the two uniform configurations, all up and all down, are the ground states.


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;

# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (5.5 in = full text width) with 10-12 pt text,

def draw_spin(ax, x, y, s, r=0.26, sign=False, alpha=1.0, fs=10, lw=1.3):
    # one Ising spin at (x, y): navy disc for s = +1, white disc with orange rim for s = -1 (optionally with "+" / "-")

def draw_bond(ax, p, q, broken=False, lw=1.5, alpha=1.0, color=None, cross=True):

    c = color or (PURPLE if broken else BLUE)

def sketch_ising_model():
    # a 4 x 4 patch of the periodic lattice with a fixed, mostly ordered spin pattern; S[y, x], y = row from the bottom
    L = 4
    S = np.ones((L, L), int)
    S[2, 2] = S[2, 3] = -1                                          # a small domain of two flipped spins
    S[0, 1] = -1                                                    # and one isolated flipped spin
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.9))
    ax = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.0, 0.47, 1.0]); tx = fig.add_axes([0.47, 0.0, 0.53, 1.0]); tx.axis("off")

    # nearest-neighbour bonds inside the patch (right and up neighbours) and the periodic bonds to the ghost copies
    for y in range(L):
        for x in range(L):
            for dx, dy in [(1, 0), (0, 1)]:
                xn, yn = x + dx, y + dy
                s_n = S[yn % L, xn % L]                               # periodic boundaries: index modulo L
                ghost = xn == L or yn == L
                draw_bond(ax, (x, y), (xn, yn), broken=S[y, x] * s_n < 0, lw=1.6, alpha=0.35 if ghost else 1.0)
    # ghost copies of column 1 (right) and row 1 (top): the same spins seen again through the periodic boundary
    for k in range(L):
        draw_spin(ax, L, k, S[k, 0], alpha=0.3); draw_spin(ax, k, L, S[0, k], alpha=0.3)
    for y in range(L):

    ax.text(L, -0.45, "periodic\ncopies", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=10, color=GRAY)

    # one satisfied and one broken bond, annotated with their energies
    i, j = (0, 1), (0, 2)                                           # s_i = s_j = +1: a satisfied bond
    ax.plot(*zip(i, j), color=BLUE, lw=6, alpha=0.3, zorder=1)
    ax.annotate(r"$-J$", xy=(-0.05, 1.5), xytext=(-0.5, 1.5), fontsize=11, ha="right", va="center", color=BLUE,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=BLUE, lw=0.8))
    ax.text(i[0] + 0.3, i[1] - 0.1, "$s_i$", fontsize=11, ha="left", va="top", color=NAVY)
    ax.text(j[0] + 0.3, j[1] + 0.1, "$s_j$", fontsize=11, ha="left", va="bottom", color=NAVY)
    k, l = (1, 0), (2, 0)                                           # s = -1 next to s = +1: a broken bond
    ax.plot(*zip(k, l), color=PURPLE, lw=6, alpha=0.25, zorder=1)
    ax.annotate(r"$+J$", xy=(1.5, -0.08), xytext=(1.5, -0.6), fontsize=11, ha="center", va="top", color=PURPLE,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=PURPLE, lw=0.8))
    ax.set_xlim(-1.0, L + 0.6); ax.set_ylim(-1.15, L + 0.45); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

    # Hamiltonian and legend
    tx.set_xlim(0, 1); tx.set_ylim(0, 1)
    tx.text(0.0, 0.88, r"$H(\mathbf{s})=-J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}s_i\,s_j$", fontsize=12, color=NAVY, va="center")
    tx.text(0.0, 0.74, r"$J>0$, $\langle i,j\rangle$: nearest neighbours" "\nperiodic boundaries (a torus)", fontsize=10, color=GRAY, va="center")
    rows = [("spin", +1, r"$s_i=+1$"), ("spin", -1, r"$s_i=-1$"),
            ("bond", False, r"satisfied bond: $-J$"), ("bond", True, r"broken bond: $+J$")]
    for n, (kind, val, label) in enumerate(rows):
        yy = 0.55 - 0.13 * n

            tx.plot(0.085, yy, "o", ms=10, mfc=NAVY if val > 0 else "white", mec=NAVY if val > 0 else ORANGE, mew=1.3)
        else:
            draw_bond(tx, (0.04, yy), (0.13, yy), broken=val, lw=1.6)
        tx.text(0.18, yy, label, fontsize=11, va="center")
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_ising_model()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_ising_card.png")
plt.show()





For one configuration we measure the energy per spin and the magnetisation per spin, \[
e(\boldsymbol s)=\frac{H(\boldsymbol s)}{N}, \qquad m(\boldsymbol s) = \frac1N\sum_i s_i .
\] Thermal averages \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) are averages over samples drawn from \(p(\boldsymbol s)\), and two fluctuation quantities follow from the variances: \[
\begin{aligned}
c &= \frac{N}{T^2}\left(\langle e^2\rangle-\langle e\rangle^2\right) && \text{(specific heat per spin)},\\
\chi &= \frac{N}{T}\left(\langle m^2\rangle-\langle |m|\rangle^2\right) && \text{(susceptibility per spin)}.
\end{aligned}
\] The absolute value in \(\chi\) needs a word of explanation. On a finite lattice the two ordered states \(m\approx+M\) and \(m\approx-M\) have equal probability, so \(\langle m\rangle=0\) at every temperature, and the useful finite-size order parameter is \(\langle|m|\rangle\).
We cannot sum over all \(2^N\) configurations (\(2^{400}\) for \(20\times20\)), so we sample them.

title: Lab 010: Monte Carlo samples of the 2D Ising model
text:
2. The Metropolis algorithm
The idea is to build a Markov chain \(\boldsymbol s^{(0)}\to\boldsymbol s^{(1)}\to\dots\) whose stationary distribution is \(p(\boldsymbol s)\). A sufficient condition on the transition probabilities \(W\) is detailed balance: \[
p(\boldsymbol s)\,W(\boldsymbol s\to\boldsymbol s') = p(\boldsymbol s')\,W(\boldsymbol s'\to\boldsymbol s).
\] The Metropolis algorithm satisfies it as follows. We propose to flip one spin, \(s_i\to-s_i\). Only the four bonds of site \(i\) change, so with the local field \(\phi_i=\sum_{j\in\mathrm{nn}(i)}s_j\) \[
\Delta E = E(\boldsymbol s') - E(\boldsymbol s) = 2\,s_i\,\phi_i \in\{-8,-4,0,4,8\}.
\] The flip is accepted with probability \(A=\min\left(1,e^{-\beta\Delta E}\right)\). For \(\Delta E>0\) detailed balance holds because \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{W(\boldsymbol s\to\boldsymbol s')}{W(\boldsymbol s'\to\boldsymbol s)}
&=\frac{e^{-\beta\Delta E}}{1}
=\frac{e^{-\beta E(\boldsymbol s')}}{e^{-\beta E(\boldsymbol s)}}\\
&=\frac{p(\boldsymbol s')}{p(\boldsymbol s)} ,
\end{aligned}
\] and the case \(\Delta E<0\) is the same equation read backwards. The partition function \(Z\) cancels, which is why we never need it.
To make the algorithm fast we colour the lattice like a chessboard. All four neighbours of a black site are white, so the flips of all black sites are independent of each other and can be carried out at once, followed by all white sites. One sweep, black half plus white half, is one attempted flip per spin (one Monte Carlo step). With periodic boundaries the chessboard colouring is consistent only if \(N_x\) and \(N_y\) are even. We also update a whole batch of independent lattices (several chains times several temperatures) in one array operation, on arrays of shape (..., Ny, Nx).
The sketch below shows both ideas. On the left, the sites of a \(6\times6\) lattice are coloured like a chessboard; the four neighbours of the highlighted dark site are all light, so the new values of all dark spins depend only on light spins and can be drawn at the same time. On the right is a single proposed flip. The central spin \(s_i=+1\) has three neighbours up and one down, so its local field is \(\phi_i=2\). Before the flip three of its four bonds are satisfied and their energy is \(-2J\); after the flip three are broken and their energy is \(+2J\). The energy change \(\Delta E=2s_i\phi_i=+4J\) is positive, so the flip is accepted only with probability \(e^{-4\beta J}\), while the reverse flip, with \(\Delta E=-4J\), would always be accepted.
