Exercises

Plot PC 1 against PC 3, or PC 2 against PC 3. Find the digits that separate along each component and compare with the images of the principal directions \(\boldsymbol\lambda_l\).
Run PCA on the images of a single digit (e.g. Xtr[ytr == 1]). Describe what the first eigenvectors show now (slant, width, …).
Standardise every pixel (divide by its standard deviation, skipping pixels that are always zero) before PCA, i.e. diagonalise the correlation matrix. Compare the fraction of variance kept by 50 components with the unstandardised case, and explain why standardisation is a poor choice for images.

title: Lab 016: PCA, t-SNE and clustering in JAX
text:
3. t-SNE
PCA keeps the directions of largest variance, but a linear projection to 2D squeezes curved structure together. t-SNE (van der Maaten & Hinton, J. Mach. Learn. Res. 9, 2579 (2008), jmlr.org/papers/v9/vandermaaten08a) asks for something different: points that are neighbours in \(\mathbb R^{D}\) should be neighbours in the map. To make this precise, t-SNE turns distances into probabilities of being neighbours, once in the data and once in the map, and moves the map points until the two sets of probabilities agree.
In the data, around each point \(\mathbf x_i\) put a Gaussian of width \(\sigma_i\) and turn the squared distances \(d_{ij}^2=\lVert\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j\rVert^2\) into a probability over the \(n-1\) other points:
\[p_{j|i}=\frac{\exp(-d_{ij}^2/2\sigma_i^2)}{\sum_{l\ne i}\exp(-d_{il}^2/2\sigma_i^2)},\qquad p_{i|i}=0,\qquad p_{ij}=\frac{p_{j|i}+p_{i|j}}{2n}.\]
The symmetrised \(p_{ij}\) sum to one over all pairs. Each \(\sigma_i\) is chosen so that the distribution \(P_i=(p_{j|i})_j\) has a prescribed perplexity
\[\mathrm{Perp}(P_i)=e^{H(P_i)},\qquad H(P_i)=-\sum_j p_{j|i}\ln p_{j|i},\]
an effective number of neighbours. (\(e^{H}\) with the natural logarithm equals \(2^{H}\) with \(H\) in bits, the form used in the paper.) A point in a dense region gets a small \(\sigma_i\), a point in a sparse region a large one.
For the map points \(\mathbf y_i\in\mathbb R^{d}\) the similarities use a Student-t kernel with one degree of freedom (a Cauchy distribution):
\[q_{ij}=\frac{\tilde q_{ij}}{\sum_{l\ne m}\tilde q_{lm}},\qquad \tilde q_{ij}=\big(1+\lVert\mathbf y_i-\mathbf y_j\rVert^2\big)^{-1},\qquad q_{ii}=0 .\]
The map points are moved by gradient descent so that \(Q\) approaches \(P\), measured by the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, which is zero when the two distributions coincide and positive otherwise:
\[\mathcal L(\mathbf y_1,\dots,\mathbf y_n)=\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,Q)=\sum_{i\ne j}p_{ij}\ln\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}} .\]
Neighbours placed far apart (\(p_{ij}\) large, \(q_{ij}\) small) cost a lot; distant points placed close (\(p_{ij}\) small) cost little. t-SNE therefore keeps the local structure.
The map point \(\mathbf y_i\in\mathbb R^{2}\) is the new representation of \(\mathbf x_i\in\mathbb R^{D}\), but, unlike the PCA coordinates \(\mathbf w_i=\Lambda_k^{\top}\mathbf x_i\), it is not given by a formula: the \(\mathbf y_i\) are free parameters, found by minimising \(\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,Q)\) between the neighbour probabilities \(p_{ij}\) (Gaussian, in the input space) and \(q_{ij}\) (Student-t, in the map). There is therefore no map for new points, and only the neighbourhoods in the result are meaningful.
For gradient descent we need \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf y_i\). Write \(\mathcal L=\text{const}-\sum_{i\ne j}p_{ij}\ln \tilde q_{ij}+\ln\sum_{l\ne m}\tilde q_{lm}\) (using \(\sum p_{ij}=1\)) and use \(\partial \tilde q_{ij}/\partial\mathbf y_i=-2\tilde q_{ij}^2(\mathbf y_i-\mathbf y_j)\). Both terms combine into
\[\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf y_i}=4\sum_{j}\,(p_{ij}-q_{ij})\,\tilde q_{ij}\,(\mathbf y_i-\mathbf y_j) .\]
A pair with \(p_{ij}>q_{ij}\) pulls \(\mathbf y_i\) towards \(\mathbf y_j\) (attraction), a pair with \(p_{ij}<q_{ij}\) pushes it away (repulsion).
The reason for a different kernel in the map is the crowding problem: in 784 dimensions a point can have many neighbours at similar distances, and in 2D there is no room for all of them. The heavy tail of the Student-t lets moderately distant points sit far apart in the map, which opens gaps between groups. The figure compares the two kernels.


Code
r = np.linspace(0, 5, 300)
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(2.64, 1.9))
    ax.plot(r, np.exp(-r**2 / 2), color=blue, lw=2, label=r"Gaussian $e^{-r^2/2}$")
    ax.plot(r, 1 / (1 + r**2), color=orange, lw=2, label=r"Student-t $\frac{1}{1+r^2}$")
    ax.set_xlabel("distance $r$"); ax.set_ylabel("similarity"); ax.legend(frameon=False); clean(ax)
    save("gen_tsne_kernels.png"); plt.show()






3.1 t-SNE implementation in JAX
The implementation follows the three ingredients of the method: the bandwidths that define \(P\), the gradient of the loss, and the optimisation loop.

Bandwidths from the perplexity
The bandwidths are a root-finding problem. The entropy \(H(P_i)\) decreases monotonically with the precision \(\beta_i=1/2\sigma_i^2\), so for every point we find \(\beta_i\) by bisection until \(H(P_i)=\ln(\mathrm{Perp})\). We bisect in \(\ln\beta\), because the scale of \(\beta\) is unknown, with 64 halvings of the interval \([-23,23]\).
All squared distances are needed at once, and they come from one matrix product by the Gram identity \(\lVert\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j\rVert^2=\lVert\mathbf x_i\rVert^2+\lVert\mathbf x_j\rVert^2-2\,\mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x_j\), instead of an \(n\times n\times D\) array of differences; tiny negative values from rounding are clipped to zero. The bisection for one point is a lax.fori_loop(lo, hi, body, init), which runs body(i, state) for i = lo, ..., hi-1 inside the compiled program, with the pair of interval ends as the state. The function one_row is written for a single point, and jax.vmap(one_row) runs the bisection for all \(n\) rows at once, supplying to each its row of distances and its index. Inside, jax.nn.log_softmax computes \(\ln p_{j|i}\) stably (it subtracts the largest logit before exponentiating), and the point itself is excluded by setting its logit to \(-\infty\).


Code
@jax.jit
def sq_dists(X):
    # matrix of squared Euclidean distances, via the Gram matrix (good for many features)
    s = jnp.sum(X * X, axis=1)
    return jnp.maximum(s[:, None] + s[None, :] - 2.0 * X @ X.T, 0.0)

def sq_dists_lowdim(Y):
    # the same for a map with d = 1, 2 or 3 coordinates: exact differences, one coordinate at a time
    # (a Python loop over the d coordinates is unrolled when the function is traced)
    return sum((Y[:, None, a] - Y[None, :, a]) ** 2 for a in range(Y.shape[1]))

def conditional_p(D2, perplexity, n_steps=64):
    # rows p_{j|i} with the prescribed perplexity, and the precisions beta_i = 1 / (2 sigma_i^2)
    n = D2.shape[0]
    target = jnp.log(perplexity)

    def one_row(d_row, i):
        mask = jnp.arange(n) != i                              # exclude j = i

        def p_and_entropy(log_beta):
            logits = jnp.where(mask, -jnp.exp(log_beta) * d_row, -jnp.inf)
            logp = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits)
            p = jnp.exp(logp)
            return p, -jnp.sum(jnp.where(mask, p * logp, 0.0))

        def bisect(_, bounds):
            lo, hi = bounds
            mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
            too_wide = p_and_entropy(mid)[1] > target           # entropy too large: increase beta
            return jnp.where(too_wide, mid, lo), jnp.where(too_wide, hi, mid)

        lo, hi = lax.fori_loop(0, n_steps, bisect, (jnp.float32(-23.0), jnp.float32(23.0)))
        log_beta = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        return p_and_entropy(log_beta)[0], jnp.exp(log_beta)

    return jax.vmap(one_row)(D2, jnp.arange(n))

@jax.jit
def joint_p(X, perplexity):
    # symmetrised p_ij (sums to 1) and the bandwidths sigma_i
    n = X.shape[0]
    Pc, beta = conditional_p(sq_dists(X), perplexity)
    P = (Pc + Pc.T) / (2.0 * n)
    return jnp.maximum(P, 1e-12), jnp.sqrt(1.0 / (2.0 * beta))


We run the search on the 5000 digits in their 50 PCA coordinates, as is common: it is faster, and the noise of the last components is removed. To verify the search we recompute the perplexity of every row from the \(p_{j|i}\) that come out of it; all rows should hit the target 30. The histogram then shows how the bandwidths differ between two digits.


Code
t = time.time()
Pc_chk, beta_chk = jax.jit(conditional_p)(sq_dists(Z), 30.0)
Pc_chk.block_until_ready()
H_chk = -jnp.sum(jnp.where(Pc_chk > 0, Pc_chk * jnp.log(jnp.where(Pc_chk > 0, Pc_chk, 1.0)), 0.0), axis=1)
perp_chk = jnp.exp(H_chk)
sig_chk = np.asarray(jnp.sqrt(1 / (2 * beta_chk)))
print(f"binary search for 5000 points: {time.time() - t:.2f} s (including compilation)")
print(f"achieved perplexity: min {float(perp_chk.min()):.3f}, max {float(perp_chk.max()):.3f} (target 30)")
print(f"sigma_i: min {sig_chk.min():.3f}, median {np.median(sig_chk):.3f}, max {sig_chk.max():.3f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
for d in [0, 1]:
    ax.hist(sig_chk[y5 == d], bins=40, alpha=0.6, color=cmap(d), label=f"digit {d}")
ax.set_xlabel(r"bandwidth $\sigma_i$"); ax.set_ylabel("count"); ax.legend(frameon=False); clean(ax)
plt.show()


binary search for 5000 points: 6.64 s (including compilation)
achieved perplexity: min 30.000, max 30.000 (target 30)
sigma_i: min 0.619, median 1.451, max 2.263





The 1s are simple strokes that lie close to each other; at the same perplexity they get smaller bandwidths than the 0s. This is how \(\sigma_i\) adapts to the local density.


Gradient of the loss
The second ingredient is the gradient formula derived above. A derivation of this length is easy to get wrong by a sign or a factor of 2, and JAX offers an independent route: jax.grad(f) returns a new function that computes \(\partial f/\partial(\text{first argument})\) by reverse-mode automatic differentiation of the code of f. We therefore implement both the formula (tsne_grad_kl) and the loss written directly from its definition (kl_loss), and compare the analytic gradient with jax.grad(kl_loss) on 300 points. Agreement to float32 precision confirms the derivation.
The factor exag multiplies \(P\) during the first iterations (early exaggeration, explained below); it is 1 for the plain gradient.


Code
def tsne_grad_kl(P, Y, exag):
    # analytic gradient of KL(exag * P || Q) w.r.t. the map points Y (n x d), and KL(P || Q)
    n = Y.shape[0]
    W = 1.0 / (1.0 + sq_dists_lowdim(Y))
    W = W.at[jnp.diag_indices(n)].set(0.0)                 # w_ii = 0 (functional update of an immutable array)
    Q = jnp.maximum(W / W.sum(), 1e-12)
    PQ = (exag * P - Q) * W
    grad = 4.0 * (PQ.sum(axis=1)[:, None] * Y - PQ @ Y)   # 4 sum_j (p_ij - q_ij) q~_ij (y_i - y_j)
    kl = jnp.sum(P * jnp.log(P / Q))
    return grad, kl

def kl_loss(Y, P):
    # the loss alone, written directly from its definition, for jax.grad
    n = Y.shape[0]
    off = 1.0 - jnp.eye(n)
    W = off / (1.0 + sq_dists_lowdim(Y))
    Q = W / W.sum()
    return jnp.sum(off * P * jnp.log(P / jnp.where(off > 0, Q, 1.0)))

P_small, _ = joint_p(Z[:300], 30.0)
Y_small = jax.random.normal(section_key(4), (300, 2))
g_hand, kl_hand = tsne_grad_kl(P_small, Y_small, 1.0)
g_auto = jax.grad(kl_loss)(Y_small, P_small)
print(f"KL = {float(kl_hand):.5f} (formula) vs {float(kl_loss(Y_small, P_small)):.5f} (definition)")
print(f"largest |difference| of the gradients: {float(jnp.max(jnp.abs(g_hand - g_auto))):.2e}"
      f" (largest |gradient| entry: {float(jnp.max(jnp.abs(g_auto))):.2e})")


KL = 2.41138 (formula) vs 2.41138 (definition)
largest |difference| of the gradients: 1.16e-09 (largest |gradient| entry: 3.73e-03)




Optimisation
Plain gradient descent on the KL loss works poorly, and the standard t-SNE optimiser (van der Maaten & Hinton 2008; the same choices as scikit-learn) adds three ingredients. The first is momentum, \(\Delta\mathbf y^{(t)}=\mu\,\Delta\mathbf y^{(t-1)}-\eta\,\mathbf g^{(t)}\odot\nabla\mathcal L\), with \(\mu=0.5\) for the first 250 iterations and \(0.8\) afterwards. The second is early exaggeration: for the first 250 iterations \(P\) is multiplied by 12, the attractions dominate, and the clusters form while the map is still small and points can move freely. The third ingredient is a set of adaptive gains \(\mathbf g\), one per coordinate, increased by \(0.2\) when the gradient changes sign with respect to the last update and multiplied by \(0.8\) when it keeps its sign (minimum 0.01). The learning rate is \(\eta=\max(n/(4\cdot12),\,50)\), the rule behind scikit-learn’s learning_rate="auto". The map starts from the first \(d\) principal components of the data, scaled to a standard deviation of \(10^{-4}\), which makes the result deterministic; with init="random" a key is required instead.
The loop itself is a lax.scan(step, carry, xs), compiled once: it calls step(carry, x) for every x in xs, passes the new carry on, and stacks the second output of step over all iterations. Here the carry is (map, last update, gains), xs is the iteration counter, and the stacked output is the KL loss after every iteration. Inside a compiled function a Python if on a traced value is not allowed; jnp.where(it < n_exag, ...) selects the exaggeration and the momentum instead.


Code
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_iter", "n_exag"))
def tsne_optimise(P, Y0, lr, exaggeration=12.0, n_iter=1000, n_exag=250):
    def step(carry, it):
        Y, upd, gains = carry
        early = it < n_exag
        grad, kl = tsne_grad_kl(P, Y, jnp.where(early, exaggeration, 1.0))
        gains = jnp.maximum(jnp.where(upd * grad < 0.0, gains + 0.2, gains * 0.8), 0.01)
        upd = jnp.where(early, 0.5, 0.8) * upd - lr * gains * grad
        Y = Y + upd
        return (Y - Y.mean(axis=0), upd, gains), kl
    init = (Y0, jnp.zeros_like(Y0), jnp.ones_like(Y0))
    (Y, _, _), kl_history = lax.scan(step, init, jnp.arange(n_iter))
    return Y, kl_history

def tsne(X, d=2, perplexity=30.0, n_iter=1000, init="pca", key=None, exaggeration=12.0, n_exag=250):
    # exact t-SNE: returns the map (n x d), the KL loss per iteration and the bandwidths sigma_i
    X = jnp.asarray(X, jnp.float32)
    n = X.shape[0]
    P, sigma = joint_p(X, perplexity)
    if init == "pca":
        _, _, Vx = pca(X)
        Y0 = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) @ Vx[:, :d]
        Y0 = Y0 / jnp.std(Y0[:, 0]) * 1e-4
    else:
        Y0 = 1e-4 * jax.random.normal(key, (n, d))
    lr = max(n / exaggeration / 4.0, 50.0)
    Y, kl = tsne_optimise(P, Y0, lr, exaggeration, n_iter=n_iter, n_exag=n_exag)
    return Y, kl, sigma





3.2 Three hidden groups
Before the digits, an example small enough to understand completely. 450 points in \(\mathbb R^3\) form three groups (uniform balls of radius 1 whose centres lie on a diagonal, 2.4 apart), but the data come without colours. Seen along the diagonal the groups hide behind each other, and along every coordinate axis their values overlap, so no single coordinate reveals them. (From another angle the eye would find them in 3D; in 100 dimensions there is no angle to look from.) t-SNE with \(d=1\) gives each point one number \(y_i\), its position on a line, keeping close points close. On that line the three groups separate.


Code
def ball(key, n, r=1.0):
    k1, k2 = jax.random.split(key)
    v = jax.random.normal(k1, (n, 3)); v = v / jnp.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return v * r * jax.random.uniform(k2, (n, 1)) ** (1 / 3)

diag = jnp.ones(3) / jnp.sqrt(3.0)
keys3 = jax.random.split(section_key(5), 3)
X3 = jnp.concatenate([ball(keys3[k], 150) + (k - 1) * 2.4 * diag for k in range(3)])
g3 = np.repeat(np.arange(3), 150)                     # the true groups: used only to check the result

t = time.time()
Y1, kl1, _ = tsne(X3, d=1, perplexity=30.0)
Y1 = np.asarray(Y1[:, 0]); print(f"t-SNE of 450 points to d = 1: {time.time() - t:.1f} s (including compilation)")

# groups found on the line: cut at the two largest gaps between neighbouring points
order1 = np.argsort(Y1); gaps = np.diff(Y1[order1])
cuts = np.sort(np.argsort(gaps)[-2:])
found = np.zeros(len(Y1), int)
for c in cuts: found[order1[c + 1:]] += 1
purity = np.mean([np.bincount(g3[found == f], minlength=3).max() / (found == f).sum() for f in range(3)])
print(f"two largest gaps on the line: {np.round(np.sort(gaps)[-2:], 1)}  (median gap {np.median(gaps):.2f})")
print(f"each group found on the line contains points of a single true group: purity {purity:.3f}")
nums["tsne_line_purity"] = round(float(purity), 3)

X3n = np.asarray(X3); cols3 = [blue, orange, green]
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 1.75))
    a = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.0, 0.25, 0.86], projection="3d")
    a.scatter(*X3n.T, s=1.5, color="grey", alpha=0.6, lw=0); a.view_init(elev=35.26, azim=45)   # looking along the diagonal (1,1,1)
    a.set_xticklabels([]); a.set_yticklabels([]); a.set_zticklabels([])
    a.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=1.15); a.set_title("(1) data", y=1.0, pad=-2)
    a = fig.add_axes([0.28, 0.2, 0.2, 0.66])
    for ax_i in range(3):
        a.hist(X3n[:, ax_i] + 6.0 * ax_i, bins=20, color="grey", edgecolor="white", lw=0.3)
    a.set_xticks([0, 6.0, 12.0]); a.set_xticklabels(["$x_1$", "$x_2$", "$x_3$"]); a.set_yticks([]); clean(a)
    a.set_title("(2) $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$")
    a = fig.add_axes([0.52, 0.2, 0.2, 0.66])
    a.hist(Y1, bins=40, color="grey", edgecolor="white", lw=0.3); a.set_yticks([]); clean(a)
    a.set_xlabel("t-SNE $y_i$"); a.set_title("(3) t-SNE")
    a = fig.add_axes([0.75, 0.0, 0.25, 0.86], projection="3d")
    for f in range(3):
        a.scatter(*X3n[found == f].T, s=1.5, color=cols3[f], alpha=0.8, lw=0)
    a.view_init(elev=18, azim=-35); a.set_xticklabels([]); a.set_yticklabels([]); a.set_zticklabels([])
    a.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=1.15); a.set_title("(4) by peak", y=1.0, pad=-2)
    save("gen_tsne_3d_to_line.png"); plt.show()


t-SNE of 450 points to d = 1: 3.6 s (including compilation)
two largest gaps on the line: [13.3 14.3]  (median gap 0.10)
each group found on the line contains points of a single true group: purity 1.000





The three peaks on the line contain the three true groups exactly (purity 1.000). t-SNE kept the neighbours of every point, and that was enough to separate groups that no single coordinate and no view along the diagonal showed. What the line does not keep are the large distances, and the gaps between the peaks are not the distances between the groups in 3D. Only “who is next to whom” is meaningful in a t-SNE map.


3.3 t-SNE of the MNIST digits
Now the 5000 digits, again from their 50 PCA coordinates, mapped to the plane. Besides the map, the cell plots the KL loss after every iteration, so that we can watch the three phases of the optimiser at work.


Code
t = time.time()
E, kl_E, sigma_E = tsne(Z, d=2, perplexity=30.0)
E.block_until_ready(); print(f"t-SNE of 5000 points, d = 2: {time.time() - t:.1f} s (including compilation)")
nums["tsne_mnist_kl_final"] = float(kl_E[-1])
print(f"final KL(P||Q): {nums['tsne_mnist_kl_final']:.3f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
ax.plot(np.asarray(kl_E), color=blue)
ax.axvspan(0, 250, color=orange, alpha=0.15, label="early exaggeration")
ax.set_xlabel("iteration"); ax.set_ylabel(r"KL$(P\,\|\,Q)$"); ax.legend(frameon=False); clean(ax)
plt.show()

En = np.asarray(E)
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(2.7, 1.6))
    axs[0].scatter(En[:, 0], En[:, 1], s=0.6, color="grey", alpha=0.5, lw=0)
    axs[0].set_title("no labels")
    for d in range(10):
        m = y5 == d; axs[1].scatter(En[m, 0], En[m, 1], s=0.6, color=cmap(d), lw=0)
    for d in range(10):
        axs[1].text(*np.median(En[y5 == d], 0), str(d), fontsize=10, weight="bold", ha="center", va="center", path_effects=OUTLINE)
    axs[1].set_title("true digits")
    for a in axs: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); clean(a)
    plt.tight_layout(pad=0.2, w_pad=0.4); save("gen_tsne_mnist.png"); plt.show()
log("t-SNE 2D done")


t-SNE of 5000 points, d = 2: 132.6 s (including compilation)
final KL(P||Q): 1.335








[ 179.9 s] t-SNE 2D done


The loss is always evaluated with the true \(P\). During early exaggeration it changes little: the exaggerated attractions gather the clusters, but the map is still compact. Once the exaggeration is switched off, the clusters spread out, the loss falls quickly, and then it decreases slowly. In the map itself most digits form their own island, in contrast to the PCA projection of Section 2.


3.4 t-SNE in three dimensions
The same loss with \(\mathbf y_i\in\mathbb R^3\); only d changes. A third dimension gives the map more room, so we expect a lower final loss. Two viewing angles of the same map:


Code
E3, kl_E3, _ = tsne(Z, d=3, perplexity=30.0)
E3n = np.asarray(E3)
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(2.7, 1.6))
    for k_, (elev, azim) in enumerate([(20, 35), (20, 125)]):
        a = fig.add_axes([k_ * 0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0], projection="3d")
        for dgt in range(10):
            m = y5 == dgt; a.scatter(E3n[m, 0], E3n[m, 1], E3n[m, 2], s=0.4, color=cmap(dgt), lw=0)
        a.view_init(elev=elev, azim=azim); a.set_xticklabels([]); a.set_yticklabels([]); a.set_zticklabels([])
    save("gen_tsne_mnist_3d.png"); plt.show()
print(f"final KL(P||Q): d = 2: {float(kl_E[-1]):.3f} | d = 3: {float(kl_E3[-1]):.3f}")
log("t-SNE 3D done")





final KL(P||Q): d = 2: 1.335 | d = 3: 1.215
[ 305.6 s] t-SNE 3D done




3.5 Perplexity
The perplexity is the one parameter of t-SNE that changes the result qualitatively, because it sets how many neighbours each point tries to keep. The figure shows the first 2000 of the same digits with three perplexities. Small values keep only very close neighbours (many small fragments); large values smooth the map.


Code
Zs, ys = Z[:2000], y5[:2000]
maps_pp = {pp: np.asarray(tsne(Zs, d=2, perplexity=float(pp))[0]) for pp in [5, 30, 100]}
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(2.2, 0.95))
    for a, (pp, Ep) in zip(axs, maps_pp.items()):
        for dgt in range(10):
            m = ys == dgt; a.scatter(Ep[m, 0], Ep[m, 1], s=0.5, color=cmap(dgt), lw=0)
        a.set_title(f"{pp}", fontsize=10, pad=2); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); clean(a)
    plt.tight_layout(pad=0.2, w_pad=0.2); save("gen_tsne_perplexity.png"); plt.show()
log("perplexity scan done")





[ 344.8 s] perplexity scan done




3.6 Distances on a t-SNE map
The construction of the loss tells us which features of a map carry meaning. The position of a cluster carries none: the loss depends only on distances between map points, so a rotated, mirrored or shifted map is equally good, and another initialisation puts the clusters elsewhere. The separation between clusters carries little: pairs of distant points have \(p_{ij}\approx0\) and barely enter the loss, and the Student-t tail pushes groups apart, so a wide gap does not mean very different data. Cluster sizes carry little as well, because \(\sigma_i\) adapts to the local density and dense and sparse groups come out of similar size. Inside a cluster, only the nearest neighbours of each point (about as many as the perplexity) are kept, and larger distances are not to scale.
What the map shows reliably is which points are close neighbours. t-SNE places only the points it was given: there is no map for new samples.


3.7 t-SNE with scikit-learn
scikit-learn provides t-SNE as sklearn.manifold.TSNE. Its main parameters are the ones we met: n_components (\(d\)), perplexity, early_exaggeration (12), learning_rate="auto" (the rule \(\max(n/(4\cdot12),50)\)), max_iter (1000 by default) and init="pca". Since a t-SNE map cannot be applied to new points, the estimator has no transform; one calls fit_transform(X), which returns the map, and the final value of the loss is stored in kl_divergence_. The default method="barnes_hut" differs from our exact computation in two places: \(p_{j|i}\) is computed only for the \(3\cdot\mathrm{Perp}\) nearest neighbours of each point (all other \(p_{j|i}\) are set to zero), and the repulsive part of the gradient is approximated with a Barnes–Hut tree, which groups distant points into cells (L. van der Maaten, J. Mach. Learn. Res. 15, 3221 (2014), jmlr.org/papers/v15/vandermaaten14a). This reduces the cost per iteration from \(O(n^2)\) to about \(O(n\log n)\); method="exact" is also available.
Two runs of t-SNE never give the same map: different optimisers, or the same optimiser with a different approximation, end in different local minima, and even equally good maps differ by rotations and reflections. The two maps can therefore not be compared point by point. We compare instead what a t-SNE map is meant to preserve, the neighbours, with three measures. The first is the exact loss \(\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,Q)\) of both maps, evaluated with our \(P\). The second is the trustworthiness (J. Venna and S. Kaski, Neighborhood preservation in nonlinear projection methods: an experimental study, ICANN 2001, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 2130, 485 (2001), doi:10.1007/3-540-44668-0_68), available as sklearn.manifold.trustworthiness. With \(r(i,j)\) the rank of \(\mathbf x_j\) among the neighbours of \(\mathbf x_i\) in the data, and \(U_i^{k}\) the points that are among the \(k\) nearest neighbours of \(i\) in the map but not in the data, \[
T(k)=1-\frac{2}{nk(2n-3k-1)}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in U_i^{k}}\big(r(i,j)-k\big),
\] which equals 1 when every map neighbour is also a data neighbour and penalises intruders by how far away they really are. The third uses the labels only for scoring: the fraction of the \(k=10\) nearest map neighbours of a point that show the same digit, averaged over all points. For orientation, the same fraction is computed in the 50 PCA coordinates that both maps start from.


Code
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE, trustworthiness

t = time.time()
E_sk = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30.0, init="pca", learning_rate="auto", random_state=0).fit_transform(Zn)
print(f"scikit-learn t-SNE (Barnes-Hut) of 5000 points: {time.time() - t:.1f} s")

P_E, _ = joint_p(Z, 30.0)                                    # our exact P, the same for both maps
def knn_label_agreement(Y, labels, k=10):
    # mean fraction of the k nearest neighbours (in Y) that carry the same label
    D2 = np.array(sq_dists(jnp.asarray(Y, jnp.float32)))             # a writable copy
    np.fill_diagonal(D2, np.inf)
    nn = np.argpartition(D2, k, axis=1)[:, :k]
    return float(np.mean(labels[nn] == labels[:, None]))

tsne_cmp = {}
for name, Y in [("JAX, exact", En), ("scikit-learn, Barnes-Hut", E_sk)]:
    kl = float(tsne_grad_kl(P_E, jnp.asarray(Y, jnp.float32), 1.0)[1])
    tw = trustworthiness(Zn, Y, n_neighbors=10)
    tsne_cmp[name] = (kl, tw, knn_label_agreement(Y, y5))
    print(f"{name:25s}: exact KL(P||Q) {kl:.3f} | trustworthiness T(10) {tw:.4f} | same digit among 10 map neighbours {tsne_cmp[name][2]:.3f}")
print(f"{'50 PCA coordinates':25s}:                                              same digit among 10 neighbours {knn_label_agreement(Zn, y5):.3f}")
nums["tsne_sklearn_vs_jax"] = {k: [round(v, 4) for v in vals] for k, vals in tsne_cmp.items()}

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.9))
for a, Y, title in zip(axs, [En, E_sk], ["JAX implementation (exact)", "scikit-learn (Barnes-Hut)"]):
    for d in range(10):
        m = y5 == d; a.scatter(Y[m, 0], Y[m, 1], s=3, color=cmap(d))
        a.text(*np.median(Y[m], 0), str(d), fontsize=13, weight="bold", ha="center", va="center")
    a.set_title(title, fontsize=11); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); clean(a)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


scikit-learn t-SNE (Barnes-Hut) of 5000 points: 33.5 s


JAX, exact               : exact KL(P||Q) 1.335 | trustworthiness T(10) 0.9855 | same digit among 10 map neighbours 0.916


scikit-learn, Barnes-Hut : exact KL(P||Q) 1.379 | trustworthiness T(10) 0.9862 | same digit among 10 map neighbours 0.918
50 PCA coordinates       :                                              same digit among 10 neighbours 0.896





The two maps look different in detail, since the islands sit in other places and may be mirrored, as expected. The three measures, however, are close (exact KL 1.335 and 1.379, \(T(10)\) 0.9855 and 0.9862, same-digit fraction 0.916 and 0.918). Both maps keep the neighbours of the data to a similar degree, and the exact loss shows how far the approximate optimiser ends from our exact one. The fraction of same-digit neighbours is higher in either map than in the 50 PCA coordinates they were computed from (0.896), although t-SNE never saw a label. Keeping the nearest neighbours and discarding the large distances makes the digit structure easier to see.

Exercises

Rerun tsne(Z, init="random", key=jax.random.key(1)) and with another key. List the features of the map that stay and those that change.
Switch off early exaggeration (exaggeration=1.0). Compare the final map and the final KL loss with the default run.
Replace the Student-t kernel by a Gaussian in the map, \(\tilde q_{ij}=e^{-\lVert\mathbf y_i-\mathbf y_j\rVert^2}\) (this is symmetric SNE, stochastic neighbour embedding, the predecessor of t-SNE). Derive the new gradient, check it with jax.grad, and look at the crowding of the clusters.
Run t-SNE on the raw 784 pixels instead of the 50 PCA components. Compare the map with the one from 50 components and time joint_p.

title: Lab 016: PCA, t-SNE and clustering in JAX
text:
4. Clustering
The maps of Sections 2 and 3 show groups to the eye. Clustering algorithms make this precise and assign every sample to a group without being told what the groups are.

4.1 k-means
k-means splits the samples into \(k\) groups \(S_1,\dots,S_k\) with centres \(\boldsymbol\mu_1,\dots,\boldsymbol\mu_k\) by minimising the total squared distance of the samples to their centres,
\[\mathcal L=\sum_{c=1}^{k}\sum_{i\in S_c}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_c\rVert^2 .\]
Lloyd’s algorithm (S. P. Lloyd, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 28, 129 (1982), doi:10.1109/TIT.1982.1056489) alternates two moves until no sample changes cluster:

assign: every sample joins its nearest centre, \(c_i=\arg\min_c\lVert\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_c\rVert^2\);
update: every centre moves to the mean of its samples, \(\boldsymbol\mu_c=\frac1{|S_c|}\sum_{i\in S_c}\mathbf x_i\).

Each move can only lower \(\mathcal L\): the assignment minimises \(\mathcal L\) over the assignments for fixed centres, and the update minimises it over the centres for fixed assignments (the mean is the point with the smallest sum of squared distances, \(\partial_{\boldsymbol\mu}\sum_{i\in S_c}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu\rVert^2=0\)). There are finitely many partitions, so the algorithm stops, but possibly in a poor local minimum. Two remedies are used together. The first is the k-means++ initialisation (D. Arthur and S. Vassilvitskii, k-means++: the advantages of careful seeding, Proc. ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) 2007, 1027, dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/1283383.1283494). The first centre is a random sample, and each next centre is a sample drawn with probability proportional to \(D(\mathbf x)^2\), its squared distance to the nearest centre chosen so far, so that the centres start spread out over the data. The second is to run several starts (here 10) and keep the one with the lowest \(\mathcal L\).


4.2 k-means implementation in JAX
In the implementation, the iteration is a lax.while_loop(cond, body, state), which repeats body while cond(state) is true; the number of iterations is decided at run time, inside the compiled program. The update step uses a one-hot matrix \(H_{ic}=[c_i=c]\): the sums of the samples of each cluster are \(H^{\top}X\) and the counts are the column sums of \(H\), one matrix product without a loop over clusters (an empty cluster keeps its old centre). The k-means++ draw is jax.random.choice(key, n, p=...), which draws an index with given probabilities, and jax.vmap over keys runs the 10 independent starts in parallel. The number of clusters k is a static argument: it fixes the array shapes, so a new k compiles a new program.


Code
def sq_dists_xy(X, M):
    # squared distances between the rows of X (n x D) and of M (k x D)
    return jnp.maximum(jnp.sum(X * X, 1)[:, None] + jnp.sum(M * M, 1)[None, :] - 2.0 * X @ M.T, 0.0)

@jax.jit
def assign(X, mu):
    d2 = sq_dists_xy(X, mu)
    return jnp.argmin(d2, axis=1), jnp.min(d2, axis=1)

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames="k")
def update_centres(X, labels, mu_old, k):
    H = jax.nn.one_hot(labels, k, dtype=X.dtype)                 # n x k
    counts = H.sum(axis=0)
    sums = H.T @ X
    return jnp.where(counts[:, None] > 0, sums / jnp.maximum(counts, 1.0)[:, None], mu_old)

def kmeans_pp_init(key, X, k):
    n = X.shape[0]
    key, sub = jax.random.split(key)
    first = jax.random.randint(sub, (), 0, n)
    mu = jnp.zeros((k, X.shape[1]), X.dtype).at[0].set(X[first])
    d2 = jnp.sum((X - X[first]) ** 2, axis=1)                    # squared distance to the nearest centre
    def body(c, state):
        mu, d2, key = state
        key, sub = jax.random.split(key)
        idx = jax.random.choice(sub, n, p=d2 / d2.sum())
        return mu.at[c].set(X[idx]), jnp.minimum(d2, jnp.sum((X - X[idx]) ** 2, axis=1)), key
    mu, _, _ = lax.fori_loop(1, k, body, (mu, d2, key))
    return mu

def lloyd(X, mu0, max_iter=300):
    k = mu0.shape[0]
    def cond(state):
        _, _, changed, it = state
        return changed & (it < max_iter)
    def body(state):
        mu, labels, _, it = state
        mu = update_centres(X, labels, mu, k)
        new_labels, _ = assign(X, mu)
        return mu, new_labels, jnp.any(new_labels != labels), it + 1
    labels0, _ = assign(X, mu0)
    mu, labels, _, n_it = lax.while_loop(cond, body, (mu0, labels0, jnp.array(True), jnp.int32(0)))
    return mu, labels, jnp.sum(assign(X, mu)[1]), n_it

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("k", "n_init", "max_iter"))
def kmeans(key, X, k, n_init=10, max_iter=300):
    # best of n_init k-means++ starts: centres, labels, loss L, number of Lloyd iterations
    def one_start(kk):
        return lloyd(X, kmeans_pp_init(kk, X, k), max_iter)
    mus, labels, losses, iters = jax.vmap(one_start)(jax.random.split(key, n_init))
    best = jnp.argmin(losses)
    return mus[best], labels[best], losses[best], iters[best]

4.4 Silhouette score
A clustering algorithm always returns clusters, so we need a way to judge them without labels. In a good clustering each sample is close to its own cluster and far from the others (P. J. Rousseeuw, J. Comput. Appl. Math. 20, 53 (1987), doi:10.1016/0377-0427(87)90125-7). For a sample \(\mathbf x_i\) in cluster \(S_c\) we define
\[a_i=\frac{1}{|S_c|-1}\sum_{j\in S_c,\,j\ne i}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j\rVert,\qquad b_i=\min_{c'\ne c}\frac{1}{|S_{c'}|}\sum_{j\in S_{c'}}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j\rVert,\qquad h_i=\frac{b_i-a_i}{\max(a_i,b_i)}\in[-1,1].\]
A value \(h_i\approx1\) marks a sample well inside its cluster, \(h_i\approx0\) a sample on the border between two clusters, and \(h_i<0\) a sample closer to another cluster. For a cluster with a single sample \(h_i=0\) by convention. The mean \(\bar h=\frac1n\sum_ih_i\) scores the whole clustering. We write \(h_i\) for the silhouette because \(s_i\) denotes a spin in the physics notebooks of this lecture.
In JAX all mean distances to all clusters come from one product: with the distance matrix \(D_{ij}\) and the one-hot matrix \(H\), \((DH)_{ic}\) is the sum of distances from \(i\) to the members of \(c\).
The sketch shows the two distances for one point.


Code
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames="k")
def silhouette_samples(D, labels, k):
    # silhouette h_i for every sample, from the matrix of (not squared) distances D
    n = D.shape[0]
    H = jax.nn.one_hot(labels, k, dtype=D.dtype)
    counts = H.sum(axis=0)
    sums = D @ H                                           # sum of distances from i to each cluster
    own = counts[labels]
    a = sums[jnp.arange(n), labels] / jnp.maximum(own - 1.0, 1.0)
    mean_other = jnp.where((H > 0) | (counts[None, :] == 0), jnp.inf, sums / jnp.maximum(counts, 1.0)[None, :])
    b = mean_other.min(axis=1)
    return jnp.where(own > 1, (b - a) / jnp.maximum(a, b), 0.0)

def silhouette(D, labels, k):
    return float(silhouette_samples(D, labels, k).mean())

4.6 Rand index and adjusted Rand index
When the true classes are known, as for the digits, a clustering can also be scored against them. We then compare two partitions of the same \(n\) samples pair by pair, and the names of the groups do not matter. A pair agrees if both partitions put it in the same group, or both put it in different groups. The Rand index (RI) (W. M. Rand, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 66, 846 (1971), doi:10.1080/01621459.1971.10482356) is the fraction of agreeing pairs among all \(\binom n2\).
Everything follows from the contingency table \(n_{uv}\) = number of samples in class \(u\) and cluster \(v\), with row sums \(a_u\) and column sums \(b_v\):
\[\underbrace{\sum_{uv}\tbinom{n_{uv}}2}_{\text{same, same}},\qquad
\underbrace{\tbinom n2-\sum_u\tbinom{a_u}2-\sum_v\tbinom{b_v}2+\sum_{uv}\tbinom{n_{uv}}2}_{\text{different, different}},\qquad
\mathrm{RI}=\frac{\text{sum of the two}}{\binom n2}.\]
Random groups already agree on many pairs (most pairs are apart in both partitions), so the index is corrected for chance, which gives the adjusted Rand index (ARI) (L. Hubert and P. Arabie, J. Classification 2, 193 (1985), doi:10.1007/BF01908075):
\[\mathrm{ARI}=\frac{\mathrm{RI}-\mathbb E[\mathrm{RI}]}{1-\mathbb E[\mathrm{RI}]}
=\frac{\sum_{uv}\binom{n_{uv}}2-\big[\sum_u\binom{a_u}2\sum_v\binom{b_v}2\big]\big/\binom n2}
{\tfrac12\big[\sum_u\binom{a_u}2+\sum_v\binom{b_v}2\big]-\big[\sum_u\binom{a_u}2\sum_v\binom{b_v}2\big]\big/\binom n2},\]
where \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{RI}]\) is the mean over random relabellings that keep all group sizes. ARI = 1 for identical partitions, about 0 for random ones, and it can be negative.
In JAX the contingency table is again a product of one-hot matrices, \(N=H_a^{\top}H_b\). Labels are first renumbered \(0,\dots,K-1\) (np.unique(..., return_inverse=True)), so that DBSCAN’s noise label \(-1\) simply becomes one more group.


Code
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("ka", "kb"))
def _rand_indices(a, b, ka, kb):
    N = jax.nn.one_hot(a, ka).T @ jax.nn.one_hot(b, kb)             # contingency table
    comb2 = lambda x: x * (x - 1.0) / 2.0
    n = a.shape[0]
    s_ab, s_a, s_b, total = comb2(N).sum(), comb2(N.sum(1)).sum(), comb2(N.sum(0)).sum(), comb2(jnp.float32(n))
    ri = (total + 2.0 * s_ab - s_a - s_b) / total
    expected = s_a * s_b / total
    ari = (s_ab - expected) / (0.5 * (s_a + s_b) - expected)
    return ri, ari

def rand_indices(a, b):
    # (RI, ARI) of two labellings of the same samples
    ua, a_ = np.unique(np.asarray(a), return_inverse=True)
    ub, b_ = np.unique(np.asarray(b), return_inverse=True)
    ri, ari = _rand_indices(jnp.asarray(a_), jnp.asarray(b_), len(ua), len(ub))
    return float(ri), float(ari)

4.9 k-means with scikit-learn
In scikit-learn, k-means is the estimator sklearn.cluster.KMeans(n_clusters, init="k-means++", n_init, max_iter, random_state). After fit(X) it stores the centres in cluster_centers_, the labels of the training points in labels_, the loss \(\mathcal L\) in inertia_ and the number of Lloyd iterations in n_iter_; predict(X) assigns new points to the nearest centre, and fit_predict(X) returns the labels at once. Its k-means++ is the greedy variant, which draws several candidates for each new centre and keeps the best one, and its random numbers come from NumPy, not from our JAX keys. The scores live in sklearn.metrics: silhouette_score(X, labels) computes \(\bar h\) from the data and the labels, and rand_score(a, b) and adjusted_rand_score(a, b) compare two labellings.
The scores are deterministic functions of the data and the labels, so they must agree with ours exactly (up to float32 rounding), and the cell asserts it. k-means started from different random centres can end in different local minima, so there we compare statistically: the loss of the two solutions and the ARI between the two partitions. One exact statement about k-means remains: a converged solution is a fixed point of Lloyd’s algorithm. If scikit-learn is started from our final centres (init= an array of centres, n_init=1), it must stop at once with the same labels and the same loss.


Code
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score, rand_score, silhouette_score

# scores of the same labellings: exact agreement
_, lab10, _, _ = kmeans(section_key(13), E, 10)
checks = [("ARI, k-means on 50 PCA comp.", nums["kmeans_ari_pca50"], adjusted_rand_score(y5, np.asarray(lab_Z))),
          ("ARI, k-means on the t-SNE map", nums["kmeans_ari_tsne"], adjusted_rand_score(y5, lab_En)),
          ("RI, random groups", rand_indices(yk, parts[3][1])[0], rand_score(yk, parts[3][1])),
          ("silhouette, toy, k = 4", sil4[2], silhouette_score(Xkn, fits4[4][1])),
          ("silhouette, t-SNE map, k = 10", silhouette(DE, lab10, 10), silhouette_score(En, np.asarray(lab10)))]
for name, ours, sk in checks:
    print(f"{name:32s}: JAX {ours:.6f} | scikit-learn {sk:.6f}")
    assert abs(ours - sk) < 1e-4

# k-means from random starts: statistical agreement
t = time.time()
sk_km = KMeans(n_clusters=10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Zn)
print(f"\nscikit-learn KMeans on 50 PCA components ({time.time() - t:.1f} s, {sk_km.n_iter_} Lloyd iterations)")
print(f"loss: JAX {float(loss_Z):.1f} | scikit-learn {sk_km.inertia_:.1f}"
      f" | ARI with the digits: JAX {nums['kmeans_ari_pca50']:.3f}, scikit-learn {adjusted_rand_score(y5, sk_km.labels_):.3f}"
      f" | ARI between the two partitions {adjusted_rand_score(sk_km.labels_, np.asarray(lab_Z)):.3f}")
nums["kmeans_sklearn_pca50"] = {"loss_jax": round(float(loss_Z), 1), "loss_sklearn": round(float(sk_km.inertia_), 1),
                                "ari_digits_sklearn": round(float(adjusted_rand_score(y5, sk_km.labels_)), 3),
                                "ari_between": round(float(adjusted_rand_score(sk_km.labels_, np.asarray(lab_Z))), 3)}

# a converged solution is a fixed point of Lloyd's algorithm: exact agreement
fixed = KMeans(n_clusters=10, init=np.asarray(mu_Z), n_init=1).fit(Zn)
n_diff = int(np.sum(fixed.labels_ != np.asarray(lab_Z)))
print(f"started from our centres: {fixed.n_iter_} iteration(s), points with a different label: {n_diff},"
      f" loss {fixed.inertia_:.1f} (JAX {float(loss_Z):.1f})")
assert n_diff <= 2                                     # only float32 near-ties could differ
assert abs(fixed.inertia_ - float(loss_Z)) < 1e-4 * float(loss_Z)


ARI, k-means on 50 PCA comp.    : JAX 0.380302 | scikit-learn 0.380302
ARI, k-means on the t-SNE map   : JAX 0.757295 | scikit-learn 0.757295
RI, random groups               : JAX 0.626294 | scikit-learn 0.626294
silhouette, toy, k = 4          : JAX 0.691623 | scikit-learn 0.691623
silhouette, t-SNE map, k = 10   : JAX 0.468421 | scikit-learn 0.468421



scikit-learn KMeans on 50 PCA components (0.9 s, 30 Lloyd iterations)
loss: JAX 150274.5 | scikit-learn 150262.8 | ARI with the digits: JAX 0.380, scikit-learn 0.380 | ARI between the two partitions 0.930
started from our centres: 1 iteration(s), points with a different label: 0, loss 150274.5 (JAX 150274.5)


All scores agree to the printed digits. The two k-means solutions from random starts reach losses that differ by a small fraction, and their partitions agree closely without being identical: both are local minima of the same loss, found from different starting centres. Started from our centres, scikit-learn stops after one iteration with our labels and our loss, as it must.


4.10 DBSCAN
k-means cuts space into convex cells around the centres, so it finds round clusters. DBSCAN, density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (M. Ester, H.-P. Kriegel, J. Sander, X. Xu, Proc. KDD 1996, cdn.aaai.org/KDD/1996/KDD96-037.pdf), instead grows clusters from dense regions. It has two parameters, a radius \(r_{\rm D}\) and a minimum number of points \(n_{\min}\):

a core point has at least \(n_{\min}\) points (itself included) within distance \(r_{\rm D}\);
a border point is not a core point but lies within \(r_{\rm D}\) of one;
every other point is noise.

A cluster is a set of core points that can be reached from each other in steps shorter than \(r_{\rm D}\), together with their border points. The algorithm:

count the neighbours within \(r_{\rm D}\) of every point and mark the core points;
take a core point not yet in a cluster and start a new cluster with it;
add every point within \(r_{\rm D}\) of a core point of the cluster; repeat until no point is added (a breadth-first search; border points join but do not expand the cluster);
repeat 2–3 until every core point is in a cluster; the points never reached are noise.

DBSCAN needs no number of clusters, follows clusters of any shape and leaves isolated points unassigned.


4.11 DBSCAN implementation in JAX
The neighbour matrix is computed in JAX; the search itself is a short Python loop over a queue, which is easier to read than a compiled version and fast enough for a few thousand points.
The first figure shows the three kinds of points on a small example: 70 points on two half-moons and 8 scattered points, with \(r_{\rm D}=0.25\) and \(n_{\min}=4\).


Code
def dbscan(X, eps, min_pts):
    # labels (-1 = noise) and the core-point mask
    nb = np.asarray(sq_dists(jnp.asarray(X)) <= eps ** 2)        # neighbour matrix, itself included
    core = nb.sum(axis=1) >= min_pts
    labels = np.full(len(nb), -1)
    c = 0
    for i in np.flatnonzero(core):
        if labels[i] != -1:
            continue
        labels[i] = c; queue = deque([i])
        while queue:                                              # breadth-first search from core point i
            j = queue.popleft()
            if not core[j]:
                continue                                          # border points do not expand the cluster
            for q in np.flatnonzero(nb[j]):
                if labels[q] == -1:
                    labels[q] = c; queue.append(q)
        c += 1
    return labels, core

def make_moons(key, n, noise):
    n_out = n // 2; n_in = n - n_out
    t_out, t_in = jnp.linspace(0, jnp.pi, n_out), jnp.linspace(0, jnp.pi, n_in)
    X = jnp.concatenate([jnp.stack([jnp.cos(t_out), jnp.sin(t_out)], 1),
                         jnp.stack([1 - jnp.cos(t_in), 0.5 - jnp.sin(t_in)], 1)])
    return X + noise * jax.random.normal(key, X.shape), np.r_[np.zeros(n_out, int), np.ones(n_in, int)]

k1, k2 = jax.random.split(section_key(14))
Xd = np.r_[np.asarray(make_moons(k1, 70, 0.07)[0]),
           np.asarray(jax.random.uniform(k2, (8, 2), minval=jnp.array([-1.2, -0.8]), maxval=jnp.array([2.2, 1.3])))]
eps_d, m_d = 0.25, 4
lab_d, core = dbscan(Xd, eps_d, m_d)
noise_d = lab_d == -1; border = ~core & ~noise_d
nums["dbscan_sketch"] = {"clusters": int(lab_d.max() + 1), "core": int(core.sum()), "border": int(border.sum()), "noise": int(noise_d.sum())}
print(nums["dbscan_sketch"])

with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(2.75, 1.95))
    for i in np.flatnonzero(core)[::6]:
        ax.add_patch(plt.Circle(Xd[i], eps_d, fill=False, color="#999999", lw=0.6))
    ax.scatter(*Xd[core].T, s=9, c=cmap(lab_d[core]), label="core")
    ax.scatter(*Xd[border].T, s=9, facecolors="white", edgecolors=cmap(lab_d[border]), lw=1.0, label="border")
    ax.scatter(*Xd[noise_d].T, s=14, marker="x", color="k", lw=1.0, label="noise")
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=3, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), handletextpad=0.2, columnspacing=0.8)
    ax.set_title(rf"$r_{{\rm D}} = {eps_d}$, $n_{{\min}} = {m_d}$")
    save("gen_dbscan_sketch.png"); plt.show()


{'clusters': 3, 'core': 65, 'border': 6, 'noise': 7}





A harder test is a shape that k-means cannot represent. Two half-moons, points on two interlocking half-circles plus Gaussian noise, are a standard example. Each moon is a curved, elongated cluster, and the line that best splits the data into two round halves cuts both moons. We cluster 500 such points with k-means (\(k=2\)) and with DBSCAN (\(r_{\rm D}=0.2\), \(n_{\min}=5\)) and score both against the true moons with the ARI.


Code
Xm, ym = make_moons(section_key(15), 500, 0.06)
_, lab_km, _, _ = kmeans(section_key(16), Xm, 2)
lab_db, _ = dbscan(Xm, 0.2, 5)
nums["moons_ari_kmeans"] = rand_indices(ym, lab_km)[1]
nums["moons_ari_dbscan"] = rand_indices(ym, lab_db)[1]
nums["moons_dbscan_clusters"] = int(lab_db.max() + 1); nums["moons_dbscan_noise"] = int((lab_db == -1).sum())
print({k: (round(v, 3) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in nums.items() if k.startswith("moons")})

Xmn = np.asarray(Xm)
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(4.4, 1.7))
    for a, lab, title in zip(axs, [np.asarray(lab_km), lab_db],
                             [f"k-means, k = 2, ARI {nums['moons_ari_kmeans']:.2f}", f"DBSCAN, ARI {nums['moons_ari_dbscan']:.2f}"]):
        cols = np.where((lab >= 0)[:, None], cmap(lab % 10), np.array([[0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0]]))
        a.scatter(Xmn[:, 0], Xmn[:, 1], s=3, c=cols, lw=0); a.set_title(title)
        a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); clean(a)
    plt.tight_layout(pad=0.2, w_pad=0.4); save("gen_kmeans_moons.png"); plt.show()


{'moons_ari_kmeans': 0.241, 'moons_ari_dbscan': 1.0, 'moons_dbscan_clusters': 2, 'moons_dbscan_noise': 0}





DBSCAN recovers both moons exactly (ARI 1), while k-means, bound to convex cells, cuts them and reaches a much lower ARI, 0.241.


4.12 DBSCAN with scikit-learn
scikit-learn’s sklearn.cluster.DBSCAN(eps, min_samples) has the same two parameters; min_samples counts the point itself, like our \(n_{\min}\). After fit(X) the labels are in labels_, with \(-1\) for noise as in our implementation, and the indices of the core points in core_sample_indices_; fit_predict(X) returns the labels directly. There is no predict: DBSCAN, like t-SNE, describes only the points it was given.
DBSCAN is deterministic, and the core points and the noise points are fixed by the definitions, so they must agree exactly with ours. Only two details may differ: the numbering of the clusters, which the ARI ignores, and a border point within \(r_{\rm D}\) of core points of two different clusters, which joins whichever cluster reaches it first. The cell asserts that the core points and the noise points coincide, on the small example and on the half-moons, and prints the ARI between the two labellings.


Code
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

for name, X_, eps_, m_, ours in [("small example", Xd, eps_d, m_d, lab_d), ("half-moons", Xmn, 0.2, 5, lab_db)]:
    sk_db = DBSCAN(eps=eps_, min_samples=m_).fit(X_)
    core_ours = np.flatnonzero(dbscan(X_, eps_, m_)[1])
    same_core = np.array_equal(np.sort(sk_db.core_sample_indices_), core_ours)
    same_noise = np.array_equal(sk_db.labels_ == -1, ours == -1)
    ari_ = adjusted_rand_score(sk_db.labels_, ours)
    print(f"{name:13s}: {sk_db.labels_.max() + 1} clusters | same core points: {same_core} | same noise points: {same_noise}"
          f" | ARI between the two labellings {ari_:.3f}")
    assert same_core and same_noise


small example: 3 clusters | same core points: True | same noise points: True | ARI between the two labellings 1.000
half-moons   : 2 clusters | same core points: True | same noise points: True | ARI between the two labellings 1.000


Both implementations find the same core and noise points, and here also the same clusters (ARI 1 between the labellings).

Exercises

Run k-means with \(k=5\) and \(k=15\) on the t-SNE map. Use the contingency table to find which digits are merged and which are split.
Replace k-means++ by a uniformly random choice of the initial centres and use n_init=1. Run the toy example with four groups for 100 keys with jax.vmap and count how often it ends in a poor local minimum.
Run DBSCAN on the t-SNE map of the digits. Find \(r_{\rm D}\) and \(n_{\min}\) that give about ten clusters, and compare the ARI (on the non-noise points) with k-means.
Compute the silhouette for k-means with \(k=2\) on the half-moons, and for DBSCAN. Find the clustering the silhouette prefers and explain why this preference is misleading here.

title: Lab 016: PCA, t-SNE and clustering in JAX
text:
5. Summary
PCA projects the data on the directions of largest variance, the leading eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. It is linear, exact and fast, it can be applied to new samples, and its eigenvalues say how much variance a projection keeps. For the MNIST digits a few components keep the coarse shape of the images but do not separate all ten digits. t-SNE gives up the large distances to keep the neighbours. It turns distances into neighbour probabilities, in the data with a Gaussian of adaptive width and in the map with a heavy-tailed Student-t kernel, and minimises the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the two. Its maps separate the digits far better, but only the neighbourhoods in a map carry meaning, not the positions, gaps or sizes of the clusters.
Clustering turns such pictures into labels. k-means finds round groups by alternating assignments and centre updates, needs the number of clusters from outside, and can be guided by the elbow of its loss and by the silhouette score; DBSCAN grows clusters of any shape from dense regions and marks isolated points as noise. When true classes are known, the adjusted Rand index scores a clustering against them and is zero for chance. For every method the JAX implementation and scikit-learn agree exactly where the computation is deterministic, and statistically where random starts or approximations make the results differ.
Course book: T. Heightman and M. Płodzień, Deep Learning in Classical and Quantum Physics, arXiv:2508.10666.

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
1. The data
MNIST (Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology database) contains \(28\times28\) grayscale digits, \(60\,000\) for training and \(10\,000\) for testing. Each image is a vector \(\mathbf x\in[0,1]^{D}\) with \(D=784\) pixels. The files are in the raw IDX format, a simple binary format for multi-dimensional arrays: a short big-endian header (a magic number, then the sizes), followed by one byte per pixel. We read them with gzip and numpy only.
For the plots of latent spaces we use a fixed random subset of \(5000\) test images (X5, y5).


Code
MNIST_DIR = "data/MNIST_raw"
MNIST_FILES = ["train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", "train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz",
               "t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", "t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz"]
if not all(os.path.exists(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{f}") for f in MNIST_FILES):
    os.makedirs(MNIST_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    for f in MNIST_FILES:
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"https://storage.googleapis.com/cvdf-datasets/mnist/{f}", f"{MNIST_DIR}/{f}")

def read_idx(path):
    with gzip.open(path, "rb") as fh:
        data = fh.read()
    ndim = data[3]                                                  # 3 for images, 1 for labels
    shape = np.frombuffer(data[4:4 + 4 * ndim], dtype=">i4")        # big-endian int32 sizes
    return np.frombuffer(data[4 + 4 * ndim:], dtype=np.uint8).reshape(shape)

Xtr = read_idx(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{MNIST_FILES[0]}").reshape(-1, 784).astype(np.float32) / 255.0
ytr = read_idx(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{MNIST_FILES[1]}").astype(np.int32)
Xte = read_idx(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{MNIST_FILES[2]}").reshape(-1, 784).astype(np.float32) / 255.0
yte = read_idx(f"{MNIST_DIR}/{MNIST_FILES[3]}").astype(np.int32)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
sel = rng.choice(len(Xte), 5000, replace=False)                     # fixed subset of test digits for plots
X5, y5 = Xte[sel], yte[sel]
print("train", Xtr.shape, "test", Xte.shape, "plot subset", X5.shape, "| pixel range", Xtr.min(), Xtr.max())

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 10, figsize=(10, 2.4))
for d in range(10):
    for r in range(2):
        axs[r, d].imshow(Xtr[np.flatnonzero(ytr == d)[r]].reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r"); axs[r, d].axis("off")
    axs[0, d].set_title(str(d), fontsize=12)
plt.show()


train (60000, 784) test (10000, 784) plot subset (5000, 784) | pixel range 0.0 1.0





Before training we move the data to the device. jnp.asarray copies a NumPy array to the default device (here the CPU; on a GPU runtime, the GPU), and we do this once for the whole training set. Later a minibatch is taken on the device by indexing, X[idx], so that on a GPU no data travel between host and device during training. JAX arrays are immutable: we never modify them in place, we create new ones.


Code
Xtr_d = jnp.asarray(Xtr)                 # (60000, 784) on the default device
Xte_d = jnp.asarray(Xte)
X5_d = jnp.asarray(X5)
print(Xtr_d.devices(), Xtr_d.dtype, f"{Xtr_d.nbytes / 1e6:.0f} MB")

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
2. The autoencoder
An autoencoder is two neural networks trained together:

an encoder \(E_{\boldsymbol\theta_E}:\mathbb R^{D}\to\mathbb R^{d}\) with \(D\) inputs (the size of the data, \(784\) pixels), \(d\) outputs (the latent-space size, chosen by us) and its own parameters \(\boldsymbol\theta_E\) (weights and biases). Its output \(\mathbf z=E_{\boldsymbol\theta_E}(\mathbf x)\) is the latent vector;
a decoder \(G_{\boldsymbol\theta_D}:\mathbb R^{d}\to\mathbb R^{D}\) with \(d\) inputs, \(D\) outputs and its own parameters \(\boldsymbol\theta_D\). Its output \(\tilde{\mathbf x}=G_{\boldsymbol\theta_D}(\mathbf z)\) is the reconstruction.

\[
\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{784}\ \xrightarrow{\ E_{\boldsymbol\theta_E}\ }\ \mathbf z\in\mathbb R^{d}\ \xrightarrow{\ G_{\boldsymbol\theta_D}\ }\ \tilde{\mathbf x}\in\mathbb R^{784}
\]

The loss, pixel by pixel
There are no labels, and every input is its own target. The loss compares each image with its reconstruction pixel by pixel, \[
\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\theta_E,\boldsymbol\theta_D)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\underbrace{\frac1D\sum_{j=1}^{D}\big(x_{ij}-\tilde x_{ij}\big)^2}_{\varepsilon(\mathbf x_i)},\qquad \tilde{\mathbf x}_i=G_{\boldsymbol\theta_D}\big(E_{\boldsymbol\theta_E}(\mathbf x_i)\big),
\] with \(i\) the image and \(j\) the pixel. Two levels of averaging appear here, and both are used below:

\(\varepsilon(\mathbf x)=\frac1D\lVert\mathbf x-\tilde{\mathbf x}\rVert^2\) is the reconstruction error of one image, the mean of the per-pixel squared differences \((x_j-\tilde x_j)^2\). A map of these \(784\) numbers shows where the image is rebuilt badly. Later, \(\varepsilon(\mathbf x)\) will be our anomaly score.
\(\mathcal L\), the average of \(\varepsilon\) over the images, is the mean squared error (MSE) over all \(n\cdot D\) pixel values. It is the number we minimise, and the number we report as the “test MSE”.

\(\mathcal L=0\) only if every pixel of every image is rebuilt exactly. The MSE treats each pixel as an independent Gaussian measurement with a fixed noise. Up to constants, \(\mathcal L\) is the negative log-likelihood of \(p(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf z)=\prod_j\mathcal N(x_j;\tilde x_j,\sigma^2)\). Other per-pixel losses are equally valid choices. An example is the binary cross-entropy (BCE), \[
\mathrm{BCE}(\mathbf x,\tilde{\mathbf x})=-\frac1D\sum_{j=1}^{D}\Big[x_j\ln\tilde x_j+(1-x_j)\ln(1-\tilde x_j)\Big],
\] the negative log-likelihood of a model in which pixel \(j\) is “on” with probability \(\tilde x_j\in(0,1)\) (a Bernoulli distribution) and the pixel value \(x_j\in[0,1]\) plays the role of the observed outcome. For fixed \(x_j\) it is smallest at \(\tilde x_j=x_j\), and it punishes a confident wrong pixel (\(\tilde x_j\to0\) where \(x_j=1\)) without bound, while the MSE of a single pixel never exceeds 1. We use the MSE throughout.
\(\boldsymbol\theta_E\) and \(\boldsymbol\theta_D\) are updated together by gradient descent; the gradient flows from the loss through the decoder into the encoder (backpropagation).


Bottleneck and compression
If \(d\ll D\), the decoder has to rebuild \(784\) pixels from only \(d\) numbers. The encoder must therefore put into \(\mathbf z\) the features the decoder needs most, and the bottleneck is a lossy compression with ratio \(D/d\) (\(49\) for \(d=16\)). The loss does not ask for anything else, but similar images tend to get nearby latent vectors, because the decoder must rebuild them alike. The space of all \(\mathbf z\) is the latent space, a learned, low-dimensional description of the data.
Compression of this kind is part of everyday communication. Every photograph, video and voice call is compressed before it is sent. An encoder turns the signal into a few bits, these bits are transmitted, and a decoder rebuilds an approximation of the original at the other end. The JPEG and HEIC formats used by phone cameras do this with fixed, hand-designed transforms (a discrete cosine transform of small image blocks followed by quantisation, which rounds away the fine detail). Learned codecs instead train both halves on data: J. Ballé, V. Laparra and E. P. Simoncelli, End-to-end optimized image compression, arXiv:1611.01704; J. Ballé et al., Variational image compression with a scale hyperprior, arXiv:1802.01436, a variational autoencoder (VAE, an autoencoder with a probabilistic latent space) with a learned prior for the code; the JPEG AI standard for learned image coding, E. Alshina, J. Ascenso and T. Ebrahimi, IEEE MultiMedia 31 (2024), doi:10.1109/MMUL.2024.3485255; and learned speech coding, W. B. Kleijn et al., arXiv:2102.09660. An autoencoder is this idea with both halves learned from data, and with the short code itself as the object of interest.


Linear autoencoder and PCA
Take a linear encoder and decoder, \(\mathbf z=W_E(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x})\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf x}=\bar{\mathbf x}+W_D\mathbf z\), with \(W_E\in\mathbb R^{d\times D}\), \(W_D\in\mathbb R^{D\times d}\) and \(\bar{\mathbf x}\) the mean image. The reconstruction \(\tilde{\mathbf x}-\bar{\mathbf x}=W_DW_E(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x})\) is a matrix of rank at most \(d\) applied to the centred data. Stacking the centred images as rows of \(X_c\in\mathbb R^{n\times D}\), the loss is \(\frac{1}{nD}\lVert X_c-X_cW_E^\top W_D^\top\rVert_F^2\), and the best rank-\(d\) approximation of \(X_c\) in the Frobenius norm is given by its truncated singular value decomposition (Eckart–Young theorem). At the minimum, \(W_DW_E\) is therefore the orthogonal projector onto the span of the first \(d\) principal directions \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1,\dots,\boldsymbol\lambda_d\). These are the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix \(C=\frac1n X_c^\top X_c\), \(C\boldsymbol\lambda_l=\sigma_l^2\boldsymbol\lambda_l\) with \(\sigma_1^2\ge\sigma_2^2\ge\dots\), and the eigenvalue \(\sigma_l^2\) is the variance of the data along \(\boldsymbol\lambda_l\). These variances carry a component index \(l\) and are unrelated to the pixel noise \(\sigma^2\) above and to the sigmoid \(\sigma(u)\) introduced below. The loss at the minimum equals the PCA reconstruction error \[
\mathcal L_{\rm PCA}(d)=\frac1D\sum_{l>d}\sigma_l^2 ,
\] the sum of the discarded variances divided by \(D\). The linear autoencoder finds the same subspace as PCA, but not the same axes: any invertible \(A\) gives the same reconstruction with \(W_E\to AW_E\), \(W_D\to W_DA^{-1}\). With non-linear activations the autoencoder can follow curved low-dimensional structure, which a projection cannot. We check both statements numerically in Section 4.

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
4. Dense autoencoders on MNIST

A two-dimensional latent space
With \(d=2\) we can draw the latent space directly. We train for \(15\) epochs with Adam (learning rate \(10^{-3}\), minibatches of \(256\)). The labels are not used for training. They only colour the points of the plot.


Code
ae2, hist2 = train_autoencoder(DenseAE(d=2, rngs=nnx.Rngs(0)), Xtr_d, epochs=15, seed=0)
L2 = encode(ae2, X5_d)                                             # (5000, 2)
nums["ae2_test_mse"] = float(errors(ae2, X5_d).mean())
print("test MSE (d = 2):", round(nums["ae2_test_mse"], 4))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.0))
for d in range(10):
    m = y5 == d
    ax.scatter(L2[m, 0], L2[m, 1], s=3, color=cmap10(d), label=str(d))
ax.legend(markerscale=4, fontsize=11, ncol=2, loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 1))
ax.set_xlabel("latent $z_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("latent $z_2$")
ax.set_title("2D latent space, coloured by the true digit", fontsize=13)
save(fig, "gen_ae_latent_mnist.png"); plt.show()

test MSE (d = 2): 0.0389





Some digits occupy their own region of the plane (look at the 0s and the 1s), others overlap. The plane has no fixed scale, since the encoder is free to stretch it, and another seed rotates or mirrors it.


Sixteen latent numbers
Two numbers are a severe compression. With \(d=16\) the reconstructions become much sharper. The figure shows test digits (top), their reconstructions from \(16\) numbers (middle) and from \(2\) numbers (bottom).


Code
ae16, hist16 = train_autoencoder(DenseAE(d=16, rngs=nnx.Rngs(1)), Xtr_d, epochs=15, seed=1)
err16_X5 = errors(ae16, X5_d)
nums["ae16_test_mse"] = float(err16_X5.mean())
print("test MSE (d = 16):", round(nums["ae16_test_mse"], 4), "| (d = 2):", round(nums["ae2_test_mse"], 4))

show = X5[:8]
r16, r2 = reconstruct(ae16, X5_d[:8]), reconstruct(ae2, X5_d[:8])
fig, axs = plt.subplots(3, 8, figsize=(9, 3.6))
for j in range(8):
    for i, (img, lab) in enumerate([(show[j], "input"), (r16[j], "latent 16"), (r2[j], "latent 2")]):
        axs[i, j].imshow(img.reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r"); noframe(axs[i, j])
        if j == 0: axs[i, j].set_ylabel(lab, fontsize=12)
save(fig, "gen_ae_reconstructions.png"); plt.show()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
ax.plot(np.arange(1, 16), hist2, "o-", color=UJGray, ms=3, label="$d=2$")
ax.plot(np.arange(1, 16), hist16, "o-", color=UJBlue, ms=3, label="$d=16$")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("training loss (MSE)"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.legend()
plt.show()


  epoch   1: training loss 0.05061   (  1.3 s)


  epoch   5: training loss 0.01610   (  4.3 s)


  epoch  10: training loss 0.01347   (  9.0 s)


  epoch  15: training loss 0.01227   ( 13.0 s)
test MSE (d = 16): 0.0121 | (d = 2): 0.0389










PCA implementation in JAX
PCA is the best linear compression to \(d\) numbers, so it is the natural baseline for these errors. We compute it in JAX from the eigendecomposition of the \(784\times784\) covariance matrix of the training images (jnp.linalg.eigh returns the eigenvalues in ascending order, so we reverse them), project each test image on the first \(d\) principal directions, \(w^{(l)}=\boldsymbol\lambda_l^{\top}(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x})\), and rebuild it as \[
\tilde{\mathbf x}^{\rm PCA}=\bar{\mathbf x}+\sum_{l=1}^{d}w^{(l)}\boldsymbol\lambda_l .
\] The test error of PCA should be close to its training error, which by Section 2 is the sum of the discarded variances \(\sigma_l^2\) divided by \(D\); the cell prints both.


Code
xbar = Xtr_d.mean(0)
C = (Xtr_d - xbar).T @ (Xtr_d - xbar) / Xtr_d.shape[0]       # 784 x 784 covariance matrix
sig2, Lam = jnp.linalg.eigh(C)
sig2, Lam = sig2[::-1], Lam[:, ::-1]                         # descending variances sigma_l^2, principal directions lambda_l as columns

def pca_reconstruct(X, d):
    Lam_d = Lam[:, :d]
    return xbar + ((X - xbar) @ Lam_d) @ Lam_d.T

for d in (2, 16):
    nums[f"pca{d}_test_mse"] = float(mse_per_image(X5_d, pca_reconstruct(X5_d, d)).mean())
    nums[f"pca{d}_train_mse_from_eigenvalues"] = float(sig2[d:].sum() / 784)
print("test MSE    PCA       dense autoencoder")
print(f"d =  2      {nums['pca2_test_mse']:.4f}    {nums['ae2_test_mse']:.4f}")
print(f"d = 16      {nums['pca16_test_mse']:.4f}    {nums['ae16_test_mse']:.4f}")
print("PCA training MSE from the discarded variances sigma_l^2, d = 2 and 16:",
      round(nums["pca2_train_mse_from_eigenvalues"], 4), round(nums["pca16_train_mse_from_eigenvalues"], 4))


test MSE    PCA       dense autoencoder
d =  2      0.0557    0.0389
d = 16      0.0268    0.0121
PCA training MSE from the discarded variances sigma_l^2, d = 2 and 16: 0.056 0.0273


The dense autoencoders reconstruct better than PCA with the same number of latent numbers, with test MSE 0.0389 against 0.0557 for \(d=2\) and 0.0121 against 0.0268 for \(d=16\).


PCA with scikit-learn
The same baseline in scikit-learn takes three lines. PCA(n_components=16, svd_solver="full") creates the estimator; fit(X) computes the mean image mean_ and the principal components (the rows of components_) from a complete singular value decomposition of the centred training images; transform(X) projects images on the components and inverse_transform(Z) rebuilds them as \(\bar{\mathbf x}+\sum_l w^{(l)}\boldsymbol\lambda_l\). Since a model with 16 components contains the one with 2, we obtain the \(d=2\) reconstruction by keeping only the first two rows of components_.
Both programs compute the same projection, so the reconstruction errors must agree to float32 precision, and the cell asserts it. scikit-learn normalises the covariance with \(n-1\) instead of \(n\), so its explained_variance_ equals our \(\sigma_l^2\) times \(n/(n-1)\); the fractions explained_variance_ratio_ are the same.


Code
sk_pca = PCA(n_components=16, svd_solver="full").fit(Xtr)
Z_sk = sk_pca.transform(X5)
for d in (2, 16):
    rec = sk_pca.mean_ + Z_sk[:, :d] @ sk_pca.components_[:d]
    mse_sk = float(np.mean((X5 - rec) ** 2))
    print(f"d = {d:2d}: test MSE  JAX {nums[f'pca{d}_test_mse']:.6f} | scikit-learn {mse_sk:.6f}")
    assert abs(mse_sk - nums[f"pca{d}_test_mse"]) < 1e-4 * nums[f"pca{d}_test_mse"] + 1e-7
assert np.allclose(sk_pca.inverse_transform(Z_sk), sk_pca.mean_ + Z_sk @ sk_pca.components_, atol=1e-5)
n_tr = Xtr.shape[0]
ratio_jax = np.asarray(sig2[:16] / sig2.sum())
print("fraction of variance of the first 4 components: JAX", np.round(ratio_jax[:4], 5),
      "| scikit-learn", np.round(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_[:4], 5))
print(f"explained_variance_[0] / sigma_1^2 = {sk_pca.explained_variance_[0] / float(sig2[0]):.6f}   (n/(n-1) = {n_tr / (n_tr - 1):.6f})")
assert np.allclose(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_, ratio_jax, rtol=1e-3)


d =  2: test MSE  JAX 0.055712 | scikit-learn 0.055712
d = 16: test MSE  JAX 0.026838 | scikit-learn 0.026838


fraction of variance of the first 4 components: JAX [0.09705 0.07096 0.06169 0.05389] | scikit-learn [0.09705 0.07096 0.06169 0.05389]
explained_variance_[0] / sigma_1^2 = 1.000021   (n/(n-1) = 1.000017)




Linear autoencoder
The two implementations agree, and PCA is the baseline. Next we train a linear autoencoder with \(d=2\) (no activations, no sigmoid, input centred with the mean image) and compare it with PCA in two ways: its test MSE, and the principal angles between the plane spanned by the columns of its decoder \(W_D\) and the plane of \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1,\boldsymbol\lambda_2\). If \(Q_{\rm AE}\) and \(Q_{\rm PCA}\) are orthonormal bases of the two planes, the singular values of \(Q_{\rm AE}^\top Q_{\rm PCA}\) are the cosines of the principal angles; both angles are zero exactly when the planes coincide.


Code
class LinearAE(nnx.Module):
    """z = W_E (x - xbar),  xhat = xbar + W_D z  (no biases, no activations)."""
    def __init__(self, d, mean, D=784, *, rngs):
        self.mean = nnx.Variable(mean)                       # a fixed, non-trainable array stored in the model
        self.WE = nnx.Linear(D, d, use_bias=False, rngs=rngs)
        self.WD = nnx.Linear(d, D, use_bias=False, rngs=rngs)
    def encode(self, x, train=False): return self.WE(x - self.mean[...])
    def decode(self, z, train=False): return self.mean[...] + self.WD(z)
    def __call__(self, x, train=False): return self.decode(self.encode(x))

lin2, hist_lin = train_autoencoder(LinearAE(2, xbar, rngs=nnx.Rngs(2)), Xtr_d, epochs=30, seed=2, lr=3e-3, verbose=False)
nums["linear_ae2_test_mse"] = float(errors(lin2, X5_d).mean())

WD = lin2.WD.kernel[...].T                                   # (784, 2): the decoder columns span the AE plane
Q_ae, _ = jnp.linalg.qr(WD)
cosines = jnp.linalg.svd(Q_ae.T @ Lam[:, :2], compute_uv=False)
angles = np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(np.asarray(cosines), -1, 1)))
nums["linear_ae2_principal_angles_deg"] = [float(a) for a in angles]
print(f"linear AE (d = 2): test MSE {nums['linear_ae2_test_mse']:.4f}   PCA (d = 2): {nums['pca2_test_mse']:.4f}")
print("principal angles between the linear-AE plane and the PCA plane (degrees):", np.round(angles, 2))
print("first decoder column . lambda_1 and lambda_2 (normalised):", np.round(np.asarray(WD[:, 0] / jnp.linalg.norm(WD[:, 0]) @ Lam[:, :2]), 3))


linear AE (d = 2): test MSE 0.0557   PCA (d = 2): 0.0557
principal angles between the linear-AE plane and the PCA plane (degrees): [0.76 0.97]
first decoder column . lambda_1 and lambda_2 (normalised): [-0.494 -0.869]


The linear autoencoder reaches the PCA error and its plane is (up to a small angle) the plane of the first two principal components; its two decoder columns, however, are not \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1\) and \(\boldsymbol\lambda_2\) themselves, only some basis of the same plane. The non-linear autoencoder with the same \(d\) goes below the PCA error (0.0389 against 0.0557), so it compresses better than any linear projection to two numbers.
The mean image is stored in the model as an nnx.Variable, not an nnx.Param. Our training function differentiates only nnx.Param, so the mean stays fixed; variable[...] reads its value.

Exercise
Train the linear autoencoder with \(d=16\) and compare with pca16_test_mse. Then add a ReLU between its encoder and decoder layers and compare the error.



One digit through the autoencoder
We follow one clearly written test digit through the network, the 3 that the \(d=16\) autoencoder rebuilds best, and show the input, its \(16\) latent numbers and its reconstruction.

threes = np.flatnonzero(y5 == 3)
k3 = threes[np.argmin(err16_X5[threes])]                     # the 3 with the smallest reconstruction error
z3 = encode(ae16, X5_d[k3:k3 + 1])[0]

for arr, name in [(X5[k3], "gen_ae_in.png"), (x_out, "gen_ae_out.png")]:

ax.imshow(z3[:, None], cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-np.abs(z3).max(), vmax=np.abs(z3).max(), aspect="auto")

for s in ax.spines.values(): s.set_visible(True)

axs[0].imshow(X5[k3].reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r"); axs[0].set_title("input $\\mathbf{x}$")
