title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
5. Latent space
Every test image is now described by \(16\) latent numbers. We treat them as a new data set and view it with a linear projection, PCA (computed in JAX with a singular value decomposition, SVD, of the centred latent vectors), and with a non-linear map, t-SNE. The colours are the true digits, used only for plotting.
Lab 016 implemented t-SNE and k-means in JAX and compared them with scikit-learn. Here we use the scikit-learn estimators directly. TSNE(2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=0).fit_transform(Z) returns the two-dimensional map, and KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Z).labels_ the cluster of every point, the best of 10 k-means++ starts. t-SNE places the points in the plane so that the probabilities of being neighbours, computed from the distances in the 16-dimensional space and in the plane, agree as well as possible (it minimises the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the two sets of probabilities). k-means splits the points into \(k\) groups \(S_c\) with centres \(\boldsymbol\mu_c\) so that the sum of squared distances \(\sum_c\sum_{i\in S_c}\lVert\mathbf z_i-\boldsymbol\mu_c\rVert^2\) is as small as possible.
The agreement of a clustering with the true digits is measured by the adjusted Rand index (ARI), adjusted_rand_score(labels, clusters). The Rand index RI is the fraction of pairs of samples on which two partitions agree (both partitions put the pair in the same group, or both in different groups). Even random groups agree on many pairs, so the ARI corrects for chance, \(\mathrm{ARI}=(\mathrm{RI}-\mathbb E[\mathrm{RI}])/(1-\mathbb E[\mathrm{RI}])\), with \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{RI}]\) the mean of RI over random partitions with the same group sizes. The ARI equals \(1\) for a perfect match and is about \(0\) for a random assignment (Lab 016, Section 4.6).
The question is whether the digits form clusters in the latent space itself. We run k-means (\(k=10\)) directly on the \(16\) latent numbers and on their t-SNE map, and compare with k-means on the pixels (on \(50\) PCA components).


Code
def pca_2d(Z):
    """Projection on the first two principal components, via the SVD of the centred data (in JAX)."""
    Zc = jnp.asarray(Z) - jnp.mean(jnp.asarray(Z), 0)
    _, s, Vt = jnp.linalg.svd(Zc, full_matrices=False)
    return np.asarray(Zc @ Vt[:2].T), float((s[:2] ** 2).sum() / (s ** 2).sum())

def tsne(Z):
    return TSNE(2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=0).fit_transform(np.asarray(Z))

def kmeans_ari(Z, labels):
    return float(adjusted_rand_score(labels, KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(np.asarray(Z)).labels_))

def plot_two_maps(P_left, P_right, titles, labels, names=None):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6))
    for a, P2, t in zip(axs, [P_left, P_right], titles):
        for c in range(10):
            m = labels == c
            a.scatter(P2[m, 0], P2[m, 1], s=3, color=cmap10(c), label=(names[c] if names else str(c)))
        a.set_title(t, fontsize=13); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
    axs[1].legend(markerscale=4, fontsize=11, ncol=2, loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 1))
    plt.tight_layout()
    return fig

def label_medians(ax, P2, labels, fontsize=8, min_sep=1.4, n_iter=500):
    """Write each class at the median of its points. Labels closer than min_sep font heights are pushed apart
    (in inches on the drawn axes, so call after tight_layout); a moved label gets a thin line to its median."""
    x0, x1 = ax.get_xlim(); y0, y1 = ax.get_ylim()
    bb = ax.get_window_extent().transformed(ax.figure.dpi_scale_trans.inverted())
    w, h = bb.width, bb.height
    labels = np.asarray(labels); names = np.unique(labels)
    med = np.array([np.median(P2[labels == c], 0) for c in names])
    anchor = np.column_stack([(med[:, 0] - x0) / (x1 - x0) * w, (med[:, 1] - y0) / (y1 - y0) * h])
    pos, dmin = anchor.copy(), min_sep * fontsize / 72
    for _ in range(n_iter):                            # pairwise repulsion until no two labels are too close
        moved = False
        for i in range(len(pos)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(pos)):
                dv = pos[j] - pos[i]; r = np.hypot(*dv)
                if r < dmin:
                    u = dv / r if r > 1e-9 else np.array([np.cos(i + 2 * j), np.sin(i + 2 * j)])
                    pos[i] -= 0.51 * (dmin - r) * u; pos[j] += 0.51 * (dmin - r) * u; moved = True
        pos[:, 0] = np.clip(pos[:, 0], 0.4 * dmin, w - 0.4 * dmin); pos[:, 1] = np.clip(pos[:, 1], 0.4 * dmin, h - 0.4 * dmin)
        if not moved:
            break
    to_data = lambda p: (x0 + p[0] / w * (x1 - x0), y0 + p[1] / h * (y1 - y0))
    for c, a_, p in zip(names, anchor, pos):
        if np.hypot(*(p - a_)) > 0.25 * dmin:          # leader line from the moved label to the true median
            (xa, ya), (xp, yp) = to_data(a_), to_data(p)
            ax.plot([xa, xp], [ya, yp], color="0.15", lw=0.5, zorder=4)
            ax.plot(xa, ya, "o", ms=1.5, color="0.15", zorder=4)
        ax.text(*to_data(p), str(c), fontsize=fontsize, weight="bold", ha="center", va="center", path_effects=OUTLINE, zorder=5)
    ax.set_xlim(x0, x1); ax.set_ylim(y0, y1)

L16 = encode(ae16, X5_d)                                     # (5000, 16)
L16_pca, _ = pca_2d(L16)
L16_tsne = tsne(L16)
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(2.75, 1.45))
    for a, P2, t in zip(axs, [L16_pca, L16_tsne], ["PCA", "t-SNE"]):
        for c in range(10):
            m = y5 == c; a.scatter(P2[m, 0], P2[m, 1], s=0.6, color=cmap10(c), lw=0)
        a.set_title(t); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
    plt.tight_layout(pad=0.2, w_pad=0.5)
    for a, P2 in zip(axs, [L16_pca, L16_tsne]): label_medians(a, P2, y5)   # digits at their medians, pushed apart
    save(fig, "gen_ae_latent16_maps.png"); plt.show()

Z50 = np.asarray((X5_d - xbar) @ Lam[:, :50])                  # the pixels, on 50 principal components
nums["pixels_pca50_kmeans_ari"] = kmeans_ari(Z50, y5)
nums["ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_direct"] = kmeans_ari(L16, y5)
nums["ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_tsne"] = kmeans_ari(L16_tsne, y5)
print("k-means (k = 10), adjusted Rand index with the true digits:")
print(f"  pixels, 50 PCA components : {nums['pixels_pca50_kmeans_ari']:.3f}")
print(f"  16 latent numbers, directly: {nums['ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_direct']:.3f}")
print(f"  t-SNE map of the 16 latent numbers: {nums['ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_tsne']:.3f}")





k-means (k = 10), adjusted Rand index with the true digits:
  pixels, 50 PCA components : 0.384
  16 latent numbers, directly: 0.284
  t-SNE map of the 16 latent numbers: 0.696


In the PCA projection the digits overlap, because they differ along many of the \(16\) directions, and any two of them show only part of it. The t-SNE map keeps the neighbours of each point and shows groups. k-means directly on the 16 latent numbers agrees less with the digits than k-means on 50 PCA components of the pixels (ARI 0.284 against 0.384), and on the t-SNE map of the latent vectors it reaches 0.696. The latent space keeps the digits apart, but in groups whose shapes and sizes differ from the round groups of similar size that k-means looks for.

Exercise
Repeat the analysis with the latent space of the \(d=2\) autoencoder (L2), where no projection is needed. Compare the ARI of k-means there with the values above.

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
6. Convolutional autoencoders

A small convolutional autoencoder, \(d=2\)
A dense layer sees an image as a flat list of \(784\) numbers and does not know which pixels are neighbours. A convolutional encoder uses the 2D structure, like a convolutional neural network (CNN). The encoder has two convolutions with \(3\times3\) kernels and stride \(2\) (\(28\to14\to7\) pixels, \(16\) and \(32\) channels), followed by dense layers \(32\cdot7\cdot7\to128\to d\). The decoder mirrors it with dense layers back to \(32\cdot7\cdot7\), followed by two transposed convolutions with stride \(2\) (\(7\to14\to28\)), the last one with a single channel and a sigmoid.
nnx.Conv expects images with the channels last, of shape (batch, height, width, channels) (NHWC: number of images, height, width, channels), unlike PyTorch’s NCHW, which puts the channels before the height; our MNIST images become (n, 28, 28, 1) with a reshape, which costs nothing. nnx.ConvTranspose(..., strides=2, padding="SAME") doubles the height and width exactly.
On a CPU a convolutional layer costs far more arithmetic per image than a dense layer of similar size, and its gradient even more. To keep the notebook fast we use few channels and train the convolutional models on a random subset of the training images, for fewer epochs (N_CONV, EPOCHS_CONV below). To make up for the fewer images we use smaller minibatches of \(64\), which gives the same arithmetic per epoch and four times as many gradient steps. The dense autoencoders above used all \(60\,000\) images.


Code
class ConvAE(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=2, ch=(16, 32), *, rngs):
        c1, c2 = ch
        self.ch = ch
        self.c1 = nnx.Conv(1, c1, (3, 3), strides=2, padding=1, rngs=rngs)           # 28 -> 14
        self.c2 = nnx.Conv(c1, c2, (3, 3), strides=2, padding=1, rngs=rngs)          # 14 -> 7
        self.e1 = nnx.Linear(c2 * 7 * 7, 128, rngs=rngs)
        self.e2 = nnx.Linear(128, d, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1 = nnx.Linear(d, 128, rngs=rngs)
        self.d2 = nnx.Linear(128, c2 * 7 * 7, rngs=rngs)
        self.t1 = nnx.ConvTranspose(c2, c1, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)   # 7 -> 14
        self.t2 = nnx.ConvTranspose(c1, 1, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)    # 14 -> 28

    def encode(self, x, train=False):
        h = nnx.relu(self.c2(nnx.relu(self.c1(x))))
        return self.e2(nnx.relu(self.e1(h.reshape(h.shape[0], -1))))

    def decode(self, z, train=False):
        h = nnx.relu(self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(z)))).reshape(-1, 7, 7, self.ch[1])
        return nnx.sigmoid(self.t2(nnx.relu(self.t1(h))))

    def __call__(self, x, train=False):
        return self.decode(self.encode(x, train), train)

Xtr_img, X5_img = Xtr_d.reshape(-1, 28, 28, 1), X5_d.reshape(-1, 28, 28, 1)
N_CONV, EPOCHS_CONV = 20000, 8                              # training subset and epochs for the convolutional models
sub = np.random.default_rng(1).permutation(len(Xtr))[:N_CONV]
Xsub_img = Xtr_img[sub]
print("training images:", Xsub_img.shape[0], "| epochs:", EPOCHS_CONV)
cae2, hist_c2 = train_autoencoder(ConvAE(2, rngs=nnx.Rngs(3)), Xsub_img, epochs=EPOCHS_CONV, seed=3, batch_size=64)
print("parameters:", n_params(cae2))
Lc = encode(cae2, X5_img)
nums["cae2_test_mse"] = float(errors(cae2, X5_img).mean())
nums["ae2_latent_kmeans_ari"] = kmeans_ari(L2, y5)
nums["cae2_latent_kmeans_ari"] = kmeans_ari(Lc, y5)

with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(4.95, 2.05))
    for a, P2, t in zip(axs, [L2, Lc], [f"dense, k-means ARI {nums['ae2_latent_kmeans_ari']:.2f}",
                                        f"convolutional, k-means ARI {nums['cae2_latent_kmeans_ari']:.2f}"]):
        for c in range(10):
            m = y5 == c
            a.scatter(P2[m, 0], P2[m, 1], s=0.8, color=cmap10(c), lw=0)
        a.set_title(t); a.set_xlabel("latent $z_1$"); a.set_ylabel("latent $z_2$")
    plt.tight_layout(pad=0.2, w_pad=0.8)
    for a, P2 in zip(axs, [L2, Lc]): label_medians(a, P2, y5)        # digits at their medians, pushed apart (helper defined above)
    save(fig, "gen_ae_dense_vs_conv.png"); plt.show()
print({k: round(nums[k], 4) for k in ["ae2_test_mse", "cae2_test_mse", "ae2_latent_kmeans_ari", "cae2_latent_kmeans_ari"]})


training images: 20000 | epochs: 8


  epoch   1: training loss 0.07243   (100.7 s)


  epoch   5: training loss 0.04875   (157.2 s)


parameters: 413315





{'ae2_test_mse': 0.0389, 'cae2_test_mse': 0.0445, 'ae2_latent_kmeans_ari': 0.2409, 'cae2_latent_kmeans_ari': 0.2684}


With the same two latent numbers the convolutional encoder gives the higher ARI, 0.268 against 0.241 for the dense encoder, although it saw only a third of the training images and has the larger test MSE (0.0445 against 0.0389). Its layers compare neighbouring pixels, as in a CNN. Each number comes from a single training run. The labels are not used in training, so the ARI is a by-product of the reconstruction loss.


A deeper convolutional autoencoder, \(d=16\)
The deeper model has three convolutions (\(8\), \(16\), \(32\) channels, the last two with stride \(2\)), each followed by batch normalisation and ReLU, then dense layers \(32\cdot7\cdot7\to128\to16\). To save CPU time it is trained on a smaller subset (N_DEEP images, EPOCHS_DEEP epochs). The decoder mirrors it with transposed convolutions and ends with a \(3\times3\) convolution to one channel and a sigmoid.
Batch normalisation rescales every channel to zero mean and unit variance over the current minibatch, then applies a learned scale and shift. During training it uses the minibatch statistics and updates running averages of them; at evaluation it uses the running averages, so that the output for one image does not depend on the other images in the batch. In flax the running averages are nnx.BatchStat variables, which are not differentiated. They are part of rest in our training function and are carried through lax.scan next to the parameters. The argument train selects the mode (use_running_average=not train).


Code
class DeepConvAE(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=16, ch=(8, 16, 32), hidden=128, *, rngs):
        c1, c2, c3 = ch
        self.c3 = c3
        conv = lambda i, o, s: nnx.Conv(i, o, (3, 3), strides=s, padding=1, rngs=rngs)
        tconv = lambda i, o: nnx.ConvTranspose(i, o, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)
        self.enc_convs = nnx.List([conv(1, c1, 1), conv(c1, c2, 2), conv(c2, c3, 2)])     # 28 -> 28 -> 14 -> 7
        self.enc_bns = nnx.List([nnx.BatchNorm(c, rngs=rngs) for c in (c1, c2, c3)])
        self.e1, self.e2 = nnx.Linear(c3 * 7 * 7, hidden, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(hidden, d, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1, self.d2 = nnx.Linear(d, hidden, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(hidden, c3 * 7 * 7, rngs=rngs)
        self.dec_tconvs = nnx.List([tconv(c3, c2), tconv(c2, c1)])                       # 7 -> 14 -> 28
        self.dec_bns = nnx.List([nnx.BatchNorm(c, rngs=rngs) for c in (c2, c1)])
        self.out = conv(c1, 1, 1)

    def encode(self, x, train=False):
        for c, bn in zip(self.enc_convs, self.enc_bns):
            x = nnx.relu(bn(c(x), use_running_average=not train))
        return self.e2(nnx.relu(self.e1(x.reshape(x.shape[0], -1))))

    def decode(self, z, train=False):
        h = nnx.relu(self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(z)))).reshape(-1, 7, 7, self.c3)
        for t, bn in zip(self.dec_tconvs, self.dec_bns):
            h = nnx.relu(bn(t(h), use_running_average=not train))
        return nnx.sigmoid(self.out(h))

    def __call__(self, x, train=False):
        return self.decode(self.encode(x, train), train)

N_DEEP, EPOCHS_DEEP = 12000, 6
dcae, hist_d = train_autoencoder(DeepConvAE(16, rngs=nnx.Rngs(4)), Xtr_img[sub[:N_DEEP]], epochs=EPOCHS_DEEP, seed=4, batch_size=64)
print("parameters:", n_params(dcae))
LD = encode(dcae, X5_img)
nums["dcae16_test_mse"] = float(errors(dcae, X5_img).mean())
LD_pca, nums["dcae16_pca2_var"] = pca_2d(LD)
LD_tsne = tsne(LD)
nums["dcae16_kmeans_ari_direct"] = kmeans_ari(LD, y5)
nums["dcae16_kmeans_ari_tsne"] = kmeans_ari(LD_tsne, y5)
fig = plot_two_maps(LD_pca, LD_tsne, ["PCA of the 16D latent vectors (deep conv.)", "t-SNE of the 16D latent vectors (deep conv.)"], y5)
plt.show()
print({k: round(nums[k], 4) for k in ["ae16_test_mse", "dcae16_test_mse", "dcae16_pca2_var",
                                      "ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_direct", "dcae16_kmeans_ari_direct",
                                      "ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_tsne", "dcae16_kmeans_ari_tsne"]})


  epoch   1: training loss 0.07130   (  8.9 s)


  epoch   5: training loss 0.01287   ( 42.0 s)


parameters: 419249





{'ae16_test_mse': 0.0121, 'dcae16_test_mse': 0.0121, 'dcae16_pca2_var': 0.3886, 'ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_direct': 0.2838, 'dcae16_kmeans_ari_direct': 0.4558, 'ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_tsne': 0.6963, 'dcae16_kmeans_ari_tsne': 0.8153}


The two \(d=16\) models are the dense one (all training images, \(15\) epochs) and the deep convolutional one (a subset of the images, fewer epochs). Both reach the test MSE 0.0121, while k-means with \(k=10\) agrees better with the digits in the latent space of the convolutional model, with ARI 0.456 against 0.284 on the latent numbers directly and 0.815 against 0.696 on their t-SNE maps. A good reconstruction and a latent space that groups the digits are different properties, since the loss rewards only the reconstruction of the pixels.

Exercises

Train DeepConvAE with more channels, e.g. ch=(32, 64, 128), on all \(60\,000\) images (best on a GPU). Compare the test MSE and the ARI with the values above.
Remove the batch normalisation layers from DeepConvAE (replace bn(...) by the identity) and train again with the same seed. Compare the training curve and the test MSE with those of the original model.

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
7. Anomaly detection
An autoencoder trained only on normal data rebuilds similar samples well and unusual ones badly. The reconstruction error \[
\varepsilon(\mathbf x)=\frac1D\big\lVert\mathbf x-G_{\boldsymbol\theta_D}\big(E_{\boldsymbol\theta_E}(\mathbf x)\big)\big\rVert^2
\] is therefore an anomaly score, larger for samples that are more surprising for the model. No example of an anomaly is needed for training. To turn the score into a decision we choose a threshold \(\tau\) and flag every sample with \(\varepsilon(\mathbf x)>\tau\). A natural choice uses only normal data and sets \(\tau\) to the \(95\)th percentile of the scores of normal samples, so that \(5\%\) of the normal samples are flagged (the false-alarm rate).
To test this idea we train the dense autoencoder (\(d=16\), the same architecture and training as above) on all training digits except the 7s. For the network every 7 is then an unknown kind of image. We compute the score of all \(10\,000\) test digits and ask whether the 7s stand out.


Code
HELD_OUT = 7
aeA, _ = train_autoencoder(DenseAE(d=16, rngs=nnx.Rngs(5)), jnp.asarray(Xtr[ytr != HELD_OUT]), epochs=15, seed=5)
errA = errors(aeA, Xte_d)                                    # anomaly score of every test digit
is7 = yte == HELD_OUT
thr = float(np.percentile(errA[~is7], 95))                   # flags 5% of the normal test digits
nums["anom_err_normal"] = float(errA[~is7].mean())
nums["anom_err_seven"] = float(errA[is7].mean())
nums["anom_threshold"] = thr
nums["anom_frac7_flagged"] = float((errA[is7] > thr).mean())
top = np.argsort(errA)[::-1]
nums["anom_top16_sevens"] = int(is7[top[:16]].sum())
nums["anom_top100_sevens"] = int(is7[top[:100]].sum())
print(f"mean error: normal digits {nums['anom_err_normal']:.4f} | 7s {nums['anom_err_seven']:.4f}")
print(f"threshold (95th percentile of normal digits) {thr:.4f}: flags {nums['anom_frac7_flagged']:.3f} of the 7s")
print(f"fraction of 7s in the test set {is7.mean():.3f} | 7s among the 16 / 100 largest errors: "
      f"{nums['anom_top16_sevens']} / {nums['anom_top100_sevens']}")

with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(2.75, 1.95))
    bins = np.linspace(0, np.percentile(errA, 99.5), 50)
    ax.hist(errA[~is7], bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6, color=UJBlue, label="normal")
    ax.hist(errA[is7], bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6, color=DSOrange, label="7s")
    ax.axvline(thr, color="k", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.text(thr, 1.0, " threshold", transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("reconstruction error"); ax.set_ylabel("density"); ax.legend(handlelength=1.2, loc="center right")
    ax.ticklabel_format(axis="x", style="plain"); ax.set_xticks([0, 0.02, 0.04])
    save(fig, "gen_anomaly_hist.png"); plt.show()

with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(4.29, 1.5))
    for j, a in enumerate(axs.ravel()):
        t = top[j]
        a.imshow(Xte[t].reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r"); noframe(a)
        a.set_title(f"{yte[t]}", fontsize=10, pad=2, color=DSOrange if is7[t] else "k")
    plt.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.12, hspace=0.35)
    save(fig, "gen_anomaly_top.png"); plt.show()


  epoch   1: training loss 0.05458   (  1.1 s)


  epoch   5: training loss 0.01750   (  3.6 s)


  epoch  10: training loss 0.01444   (  6.7 s)

mean error: normal digits 0.0128 | 7s 0.0179
threshold (95th percentile of normal digits) 0.0268: flags 0.130 of the 7s
fraction of 7s in the test set 0.103 | 7s among the 16 / 100 largest errors: 3 / 22








The two histograms overlap strongly. The mean error is 0.0128 for the trained digits and 0.0179 for the 7s, and the threshold 0.0268, which flags 5% of the normal digits, flags 13% of the 7s. A 7 shares strokes with 1s and 9s, which the network has seen, so many 7s are rebuilt well. Among the 100 digits with the largest error 22 are 7s, against a share of 10.3% of 7s in the test set, and among the 16 largest 3 are. The others are badly written digits of the trained classes, which are anomalies for the autoencoder too.

ROC curve and AUC
Every threshold \(\tau\) gives one decision rule. For each we count

the true-positive rate \(\mathrm{TPR}(\tau)=\frac{\#\{\text{anomalies with } \varepsilon>\tau\}}{\#\{\text{anomalies}\}}\): the fraction of anomalies (here the 7s) found;
the false-positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}(\tau)=\frac{\#\{\text{normal samples with } \varepsilon>\tau\}}{\#\{\text{normal samples}\}}\): the fraction of normal samples flagged, the false alarms.

Lowering \(\tau\) from \(+\infty\) to \(-\infty\) traces the ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic, T. Fawcett, Pattern Recognit. Lett. 27, 861 (2006), doi:10.1016/j.patrec.2005.10.010) \(\big(\mathrm{FPR}(\tau),\mathrm{TPR}(\tau)\big)\) from \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\). A useless score lies on the diagonal (as many false alarms as hits), and a perfect one goes straight up to \(\mathrm{TPR}=1\) at \(\mathrm{FPR}=0\).
The AUC is the area under the ROC curve. It does not depend on any threshold. If \(\varepsilon_+\) is the score of a randomly chosen anomaly and \(\varepsilon_-\) that of a randomly chosen normal sample, \[
\mathrm{AUC}=P(\varepsilon_+>\varepsilon_-)+\tfrac12P(\varepsilon_+=\varepsilon_-) =\frac{1}{n_+n_-}\sum_{a\in+}\sum_{b\in-}\Big[\mathbb 1(\varepsilon_a>\varepsilon_b)+\tfrac12\mathbb 1(\varepsilon_a=\varepsilon_b)\Big].
\] \(\mathrm{AUC}=\tfrac12\) for chance, \(1\) for a perfect separation. (This is the Mann–Whitney \(U\) statistic divided by \(n_+n_-\), see J. A. Hanley and B. J. McNeil, Radiology 143, 29 (1982), doi:10.1148/radiology.143.1.7063747.)


ROC implementation in JAX
Our JAX implementation of the ROC curve sorts the samples by decreasing score. Walking down the sorted list lowers the threshold, and the cumulative counts of anomalies and normal samples give TPR and FPR. Samples with equal scores share one threshold and give one point. The area follows from the trapezoidal rule, and we compare it with the pairwise formula, a single vectorised comparison of all \(n_+\times n_-\) pairs. The two must agree, since the trapezoidal area of the ROC curve is exactly the Mann–Whitney statistic.


Code
def roc_curve(scores, labels):
    """ROC curve of `scores` for binary `labels` (1 = anomaly). Returns FPR, TPR (from (0,0) to (1,1)) and the thresholds."""
    s, y = jnp.asarray(scores), jnp.asarray(labels, dtype=jnp.float32)
    order = jnp.argsort(-s)                                  # decreasing score = decreasing threshold
    s, y = s[order], y[order]
    tp, fp = jnp.cumsum(y), jnp.cumsum(1.0 - y)              # counts above the threshold placed after each sample
    last_of_tie = jnp.append(s[1:] != s[:-1], True)          # equal scores: one threshold, one point
    tpr = jnp.concatenate([jnp.zeros(1), tp[last_of_tie] / y.sum()])
    fpr = jnp.concatenate([jnp.zeros(1), fp[last_of_tie] / (1.0 - y).sum()])
    return np.asarray(fpr), np.asarray(tpr), np.asarray(s[last_of_tie])

def auc_trapezoid(fpr, tpr):
    return float(jnp.trapezoid(jnp.asarray(tpr), jnp.asarray(fpr)))

@jax.jit
def auc_pairwise(s_pos, s_neg):
    """P(s+ > s-) + P(s+ = s-)/2 over all pairs (Mann-Whitney)."""
    diff = s_pos[:, None] - s_neg[None, :]
    return jnp.mean((diff > 0) + 0.5 * (diff == 0))

fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(errA, is7)
nums["anom_auc"] = auc_trapezoid(fpr, tpr)
auc_pairs = float(auc_pairwise(jnp.asarray(errA[is7]), jnp.asarray(errA[~is7])))
print(f"AUC (trapezoid on the ROC curve) = {nums['anom_auc']:.4f}  |  AUC (all {is7.sum()} x {(~is7).sum()} pairs) = {auc_pairs:.4f}")

with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(2.53, 2.3))
    ax.fill_between(fpr, tpr, color=DSOrange, alpha=0.15)
    ax.plot(fpr, tpr, color=DSOrange, lw=2, label=f"7s: AUC = {nums['anom_auc']:.2f}")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k:", lw=1, label="chance: 0.5")
    ax.plot(0.05, nums["anom_frac7_flagged"], "o", color="k", ms=4)
    ax.annotate("5% false\nalarms", (0.05, nums["anom_frac7_flagged"]), xytext=(0.06, 0.92), fontsize=10, va="top",
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=0.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("false-positive rate"); ax.set_ylabel("true-positive rate")
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02); ax.legend(loc="lower right", handlelength=1.2)
    save(fig, "gen_anomaly_roc.png"); plt.show()


AUC (trapezoid on the ROC curve) = 0.6958  |  AUC (all 1028 x 8972 pairs) = 0.6958





The black dot is the decision rule of the histogram, which at \(5\%\) false alarms finds 13% of the 7s. An AUC of about \(0.7\) means that a randomly chosen 7 has a larger reconstruction error than a randomly chosen normal digit in about seven cases out of ten, a real but weak signal.


ROC curve and AUC with scikit-learn
The same analysis is available in sklearn.metrics. roc_curve(y_true, y_score) takes the true binary labels (1 for the positive class, here the anomalies) and the scores, and returns three arrays, the FPR, the TPR and the thresholds, in decreasing order of the threshold, starting from the point \((0,0)\) with the threshold \(+\infty\). By default (drop_intermediate=True) it removes points that lie on a straight segment of the curve and do not change its shape; with drop_intermediate=False it keeps one point per distinct score, which is exactly our construction. roc_auc_score(y_true, y_score) returns the area.
Both are deterministic functions of the scores, so they must agree with ours exactly (up to float32 rounding of our cumulative sums), and the cell asserts it: the full curves point by point and the AUC.


Code
fpr_sk, tpr_sk, thr_sk = metrics.roc_curve(is7, errA, drop_intermediate=False)
auc_sk = float(metrics.roc_auc_score(is7, errA))
print(f"points on the curve: JAX {len(fpr)} | scikit-learn {len(fpr_sk)}"
      f" (with drop_intermediate=True: {len(metrics.roc_curve(is7, errA)[0])})")
print(f"largest difference of the curves: FPR {np.abs(fpr_sk - fpr).max():.1e}, TPR {np.abs(tpr_sk - tpr).max():.1e}")
print(f"AUC: JAX {nums['anom_auc']:.6f} | scikit-learn {auc_sk:.6f}")
assert len(fpr_sk) == len(fpr) and np.allclose(fpr_sk, fpr, atol=1e-5) and np.allclose(tpr_sk, tpr, atol=1e-5)
assert abs(auc_sk - nums["anom_auc"]) < 1e-5


points on the curve: JAX 9998 | scikit-learn 9998 (with drop_intermediate=True: 1799)
largest difference of the curves: FPR 3.8e-08, TPR 3.0e-08
AUC: JAX 0.695764 | scikit-learn 0.695764



Exercises

Hold out another digit instead of the 7 (change HELD_OUT). Find the digits that are easy anomalies and those that are hard, and relate the result to the shapes of the digits.
Use the deep convolutional autoencoder for the anomaly score. Compare its AUC for the 7s with that of the dense autoencoder.

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
8. CIFAR-10: photographs
CIFAR-10 contains \(32\times32\) colour photographs in \(10\) classes, \(50\,000\) for training and \(10\,000\) for testing, so \(D=32\cdot32\cdot3=3072\). Each image is stored as one row of \(3072\) bytes: first the \(1024\) red values, then the green, then the blue, each in row-major order. The files are Python pickles; we read them with pickle and numpy.


Code
CIFAR_DIR = "data/cifar-10-batches-py"
if not os.path.isdir(CIFAR_DIR):
    os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
    urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar-10-python.tar.gz", "data/cifar-10-python.tar.gz")
    with tarfile.open("data/cifar-10-python.tar.gz") as tf:
        tf.extractall("data")

def cifar_batch(name):
    with open(os.path.join(CIFAR_DIR, name), "rb") as fh:
        d = pickle.load(fh, encoding="bytes")
    return d[b"data"].astype(np.float32) / 255.0, np.array(d[b"labels"])

parts = [cifar_batch(f"data_batch_{i}") for i in range(1, 6)]
Ctr = np.concatenate([p[0] for p in parts]); cytr = np.concatenate([p[1] for p in parts])
Cte, cyte = cifar_batch("test_batch")
cnames = ["airplane", "automobile", "bird", "cat", "deer", "dog", "frog", "horse", "ship", "truck"]
to_img = lambda v: v.reshape(3, 32, 32).transpose(1, 2, 0)        # (3072,) -> (32, 32, 3) for plotting
rc = np.random.default_rng(5)
csel = rc.choice(len(Cte), 5000, replace=False)
C5, cy5 = Cte[csel], cyte[csel]
print("train", Ctr.shape, "test", Cte.shape)

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 10, figsize=(11, 1.6))
for c in range(10):
    axs[c].imshow(to_img(Ctr[np.flatnonzero(cytr == c)[0]])); axs[c].set_title(cnames[c], fontsize=11); axs[c].axis("off")
plt.show()

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
9. Summary
An autoencoder is an encoder and a decoder trained together to rebuild their input through a bottleneck of \(d\) numbers. The loss is the pixel-wise MSE, so no labels are needed, and the bottleneck acts as a learned, lossy compression. A linear autoencoder spans the PCA subspace, while the non-linear autoencoders trained here reach a lower reconstruction error than PCA with the same \(d\).
The latent space keeps the structure of the data, in the sense that similar images get nearby \(\mathbf z\), but its geometry is not designed for clustering. In our single runs the convolutional encoders, which see neighbouring pixels, gave latent spaces in which k-means agrees better with the digits. The reconstruction error of an autoencoder trained on normal data is an anomaly score. The ROC curve shows all thresholds at once, and the AUC is the probability that an anomaly scores higher than a normal sample. Anomalies far from the training data, such as photographs for an MNIST autoencoder, are easy to detect, while anomalies that resemble the training data, such as a held-out digit, are hard.
Course book: T. Heightman and M. Płodzień, Deep Learning in Classical and Quantum Physics, arXiv:2508.10666.

title: Lab 018: Classical spin models in JAX, the 2D Ising and the J1–J2 model
text:
1. The model
Spins \(s_i=\pm1\) sit on an \(L\times L\) square lattice with periodic boundaries. Every spin has four nearest neighbours (left, right, up, down) and four next-nearest neighbours (along the diagonals). The energy is \[
H(\boldsymbol s) = -J_1\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} s_i s_j \;+\; J_2\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle} s_i s_j ,
\qquad J_1>0,\quad J_2\ge 0,
\] with \(\langle i,j\rangle\) the \(2N\) nearest-neighbour bonds and \(\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle\) the \(2N\) diagonal bonds (\(N=L^2\)).

\(J_1>0\) is ferromagnetic: nearest neighbours want to be parallel.
\(J_2>0\) (with the \(+\) sign in \(H\)) is antiferromagnetic: diagonal neighbours want to be antiparallel.

We set \(J_1=1\) and use the single control parameter \[
g = J_2/J_1 .
\] Together with the temperature \(T\) (with \(k_B=1\)) this gives a two-dimensional phase diagram in the \((g,T)\) plane.
At \(g=0\) the model is the 2D Ising model, solved exactly by Onsager, with \(T_c=2/\ln(1+\sqrt2)\approx 2.269\). For \(g\to\infty\) (\(J_1\to0\)) only diagonal bonds remain. The diagonal bonds connect sites of the same chessboard colour, so the lattice splits into two independent square lattices (rotated by \(45^\circ\)), each an antiferromagnetic Ising model with coupling \(J_2\). Flipping every second spin of such a lattice maps the antiferromagnet onto a ferromagnet with the same partition function, so each sub-lattice orders at \(T = J_2\,T_c^{\rm Ising}\), i.e. \(T_c/J_1 \to g\,T_c^{\rm Ising}\) for large \(g\).
Between these limits the two couplings compete.

1.1 Ground states
At \(T=0\) the system sits in the configuration of lowest energy. Consider three candidate patterns and count the bonds per spin (2 nearest-neighbour bonds and 2 diagonal bonds per spin):









pattern
nearest-neighbour bonds
diagonal bonds
energy per spin \(E/N\)




ferromagnet (all up)
all satisfied: \(s_is_j=+1\)
all frustrated: \(s_is_j=+1\)
\(-2J_1+2J_2\)


Néel (chessboard)
all broken: \(s_is_j=-1\)
\(s_is_j=+1\)
\(+2J_1+2J_2\)


stripes (columns \(+,-,+,-\))
horizontal \(-1\), vertical \(+1\): net \(0\)
all satisfied: \(s_is_j=-1\)
\(-2J_2\)



The Néel state is never favourable for \(J_1>0\). The ferromagnet and the stripe state have equal energy when \(-2J_1+2J_2=-2J_2\), i.e. at \[
g = \tfrac12 .
\] For \(g<1/2\) the ground state is ferromagnetic (2 states, all up and all down). For \(g>1/2\) it is the stripe (also called collinear or super-antiferromagnetic) state, with 4 states (vertical or horizontal stripes, and the global flip).
At exactly \(g=1/2\) a single ferromagnetic row can be inserted into a stripe pattern at no energy cost, and many mixed patterns become degenerate. The system is frustrated, since it cannot satisfy both couplings, and the number of ground states grows exponentially with the system size.
The table only compared three guesses. On a small lattice we can check all \(2^{N}\) configurations, which is a good first exercise in JAX.


1.2 Exhaustive enumeration on a \(4\times4\) lattice
A \(4\times4\) lattice has \(2^{16}=65\,536\) configurations, few enough to compute the energy of every one of them; this is also a first look at vmap and jit. We write the energy of one configuration, then let jax.vmap turn it into a function of a whole batch, and jax.jit compile it.
Two building blocks are used throughout the notebook. The function jnp.roll(s, 1, axis) shifts the lattice by one site with periodic wrap-around, so s * jnp.roll(s, 1, 0) lists the products over all vertical bonds at once. And the energy splits into two integers, \(H = -J_1\,B_1(\boldsymbol s) + J_2\,B_2(\boldsymbol s)\), with \(B_1=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j\) and \(B_2=\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}s_is_j\); we compute \(B_1\), \(B_2\) once and then obtain \(H\) for every \(g\) without another sum over configurations.


Code
def bond_sums(s):
    # B1 = sum over nearest-neighbour bonds of s_i s_j,  B2 = same over diagonal bonds  (each bond counted once)
    b1 = jnp.sum(s * jnp.roll(s, 1, 0)) + jnp.sum(s * jnp.roll(s, 1, 1))
    b2 = jnp.sum(s * jnp.roll(s, (1, 1), (0, 1))) + jnp.sum(s * jnp.roll(s, (1, -1), (0, 1)))
    return b1, b2

def all_configs(L):
    n = L * L
    idx = jnp.arange(2**n, dtype=jnp.int32)
    bits = (idx[:, None] >> jnp.arange(n)) & 1
    return (2 * bits - 1).reshape(-1, L, L).astype(jnp.float32)

S4 = all_configs(4)
B1, B2 = jax.jit(jax.vmap(bond_sums))(S4)          # one call, 65 536 configurations
print(S4.shape, "configurations;  B1 range", int(B1.min()), int(B1.max()), "; B2 range", int(B2.min()), int(B2.max()))

g_scan = np.linspace(0, 1, 201)
E = -np.asarray(B1)[None, :] + g_scan[:, None] * np.asarray(B2)[None, :]     # E[g, config]
E0 = E.min(1)
degeneracy = (E <= E0[:, None] + 1e-9).sum(1)
for gv in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0):
    i = np.argmin(abs(g_scan - gv))
    print(f"g = {gv:.2f}:  E0/N = {E0[i]/16:+.4f}   ground-state degeneracy = {degeneracy[i]}")

NUMBERS["degeneracy_4x4_g025"] = int(degeneracy[np.argmin(abs(g_scan - 0.25))])
NUMBERS["degeneracy_4x4_g075"] = int(degeneracy[np.argmin(abs(g_scan - 0.75))])

1.3 Order parameters
Each ordered phase is characterised by a quantity that is non-zero in that phase and zero elsewhere, an order parameter. For ordering patterns that repeat with a wave vector \(\boldsymbol k\) the natural choice is the Fourier component of the spins, \[
m_{\boldsymbol k}(\boldsymbol s) = \frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol r} s_{\boldsymbol r}\, e^{i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r},
\] and its mean square defines the static structure factor \(S(\boldsymbol k)=N\langle|m_{\boldsymbol k}|^2\rangle\), which neutron scattering measures.








phase
ordering wave vector
order parameter




ferromagnet
\(\boldsymbol k=(0,0)\)
\(m = \frac1N\sum_r s_r\)


stripes
\((\pi,0)\) and \((0,\pi)\)
\(m_{\rm str} = \sqrt{m_{(\pi,0)}^2 + m_{(0,\pi)}^2}\)


Néel
\((\pi,\pi)\)
\(m_{(\pi,\pi)}\)



The stripe order parameter combines the two wave vectors because vertical and horizontal stripes have the same energy.
The magnetisation \(m\) is zero in the stripe phase, where half of the spins are up and half are down. A scan of \(\langle|m|\rangle\) over the \((g,T)\) plane therefore sees the stripe phase as “disordered”. To see it, one has to know that stripes exist and measure \(m_{\rm str}\). For the \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model we know this from the ground-state analysis. For a new material or a new model we often do not know which quantity to plot.


Code
def order_parameters(s):
    # s: (..., L, L) with values +-1.  Returns |m|, m_stripe, m_neel, and energy terms B1, B2 per spin.
    L = s.shape[-1]
    ph = jnp.where(jnp.arange(L) % 2 == 0, 1.0, -1.0)                 # e^{i pi x} = (-1)^x
    m = s.mean((-2, -1))
    m_pi0 = (s * ph[:, None]).mean((-2, -1))                           # k = (pi, 0)
    m_0pi = (s * ph[None, :]).mean((-2, -1))                           # k = (0, pi)
    m_pipi = (s * ph[:, None] * ph[None, :]).mean((-2, -1))           # k = (pi, pi)
    return {"m": jnp.abs(m), "m_str": jnp.sqrt(m_pi0**2 + m_0pi**2), "m_neel": jnp.abs(m_pipi)}

for name, p in patterns.items():
    o = order_parameters(jnp.asarray(p))
    print(f"{name:12s}  |m| = {float(o['m']):.2f}   m_str = {float(o['m_str']):.2f}   m_Neel = {float(o['m_neel']):.2f}")

1.4 Mean-field theory at finite temperature
The simplest approximation at \(T>0\) is mean-field theory, which replaces the neighbours of spin \(i\) by their thermal averages \(\langle s_j\rangle\). The spin then feels the field \[
h_i = J_1\sum_{j\in{\rm nn}(i)}\langle s_j\rangle - J_2\sum_{j\in{\rm nnn}(i)}\langle s_j\rangle, \qquad \langle s_i\rangle = \tanh(\beta h_i).
\] For the ferromagnetic ansatz \(\langle s_j\rangle = m\) this gives \(h = (4J_1-4J_2)m\), so \(m=\tanh(\beta(4J_1-4J_2)m)\), which has a non-zero solution below \(T^{\rm MF}_{\rm FM} = 4J_1-4J_2 = 4(1-g)\). For the stripe ansatz (columns alternate, \(\langle s_j\rangle=\pm m\)) the nearest-neighbour contributions cancel (two parallel, two antiparallel), and all four diagonal neighbours are antiparallel, so \(h = 4J_2 m\) and \(T^{\rm MF}_{\rm str}=4J_2 = 4g\).
Mean-field theory predicts the two lines meet at \(g=1/2\) at \(T=2\). This is wrong: fluctuations between the many degenerate ground states destroy the order, and the true transition temperature goes to zero at \(g=1/2\). Mean field also overestimates \(T_c\) at \(g=0\) (\(4\) instead of \(2.269\)), because it neglects fluctuations, which are strong in two dimensions.
Large-scale numerics give the following picture, although the questions are subtle and partly still debated. For \(g<1/2\) there is a continuous transition from the paramagnet to the ferromagnet, in the 2D Ising universality class, with \(T_c(g)\) decreasing to \(0\) at \(g=1/2\). For \(g>1/2\) there is a transition to the stripe phase. For \(g\) slightly above \(1/2\) it is weakly first order; above a multicritical point it is continuous, with exponents that vary along the line (Ashkin–Teller criticality) and approach the Ising ones as \(g\to\infty\). Kalz, Honecker, Fuchs and Pruschke (Eur. Phys. J. B 65, 533 (2008)) found weakly first-order transitions for moderate \(J_2>J_1/2\); Jin, Sen and Sandvik (Phys. Rev. Lett. 108, 045702 (2012)) and Jin, Sen, Guo and Sandvik (Phys. Rev. B 87, 144406 (2013)) placed the multicritical point at \(g^*\approx0.67\) and showed that continuous transitions above \(g^*\) can look first order on finite lattices; tensor-network calculations by Li and Yang (Phys. Rev. E 104, 024118 (2021)) suggest that the first-order window is narrower.
Even for a model this simple, the phase diagram required many studies, careful finite-size analysis, and knowledge of the right order parameters. In Lab 020 we ask how much of it an algorithm can find without being told what to look for.


1.5 Thermal averages and their estimators
In thermal equilibrium at temperature \(T\) (inverse temperature \(\beta=1/T\), \(k_B=1\)) a configuration \(\boldsymbol s\) occurs with the Boltzmann probability \[
p(\boldsymbol s)=\frac{e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol s)}}{Z},\qquad Z=\sum_{\boldsymbol s}e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol s)},
\] and an observable \(O(\boldsymbol s)\) of a single configuration has the thermal average \(\langle O\rangle=\frac1Z\sum_{\boldsymbol s}O(\boldsymbol s)\,e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol s)}\). The partition function also generates the thermodynamics: the energy per spin is the first derivative of \(\ln Z\) with respect to \(\beta\), and the specific heat per spin is the second derivative, which equals the variance of the energy, \[
\langle e\rangle=\frac{\langle H\rangle}{N}=-\frac1N\,\frac{\partial\ln Z}{\partial\beta},\qquad
c=\frac{\beta^2}{N}\,\frac{\partial^2\ln Z}{\partial\beta^2}=\frac{\beta^2}{N}\big(\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2\big)=N\beta^2\big(\langle e^2\rangle-\langle e\rangle^2\big).
\] On the \(4\times4\) lattice the sums over all \(2^{16}\) configurations can be done, and the function exact_4x4 below computes \(\langle e\rangle\), \(\langle|m|\rangle\) and \(\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle\) literally as these weighted sums. On larger lattices Monte Carlo draws \(n\) configurations \(\boldsymbol s^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol s^{(n)}\) with probability \(p(\boldsymbol s)\) at each \((g,T)\), and every average is estimated by the sample mean \(\overline{O}=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^nO(\boldsymbol s^{(k)})\). The table lists each observable in both forms; the estimators are those of the functions energy_per_spin, order_parameters and observables below. Here \(e_k=H(\boldsymbol s^{(k)})/N\) (computed as \(-\frac1{2N}\sum_i s_ih_i\), since every bond appears twice in \(\sum_is_ih_i\)), \(m_k=\frac1N\sum_is^{(k)}_i\), and \(\overline{x}\) is the mean over the \(n\) samples. On a finite lattice without a field \(\langle m\rangle=0\) by the symmetry \(\boldsymbol s\to-\boldsymbol s\), which is why \(|m|\) is used.

All variances in the maps of Section 5 are population variances (division by \(n\), jnp.var); the subsampling study of Section 5.1 uses the unbiased variance (division by \(n-1\), var(ddof=1)), which matters for its small subsets of 10 samples.
Section 2.2 also uses a dynamical quantity, the autocorrelation of \(|m|\) along a chain. With \(x_t=|m|\) after step \(t\) of one chain, \(\delta x_t=x_t-\overline{x}\) (mean over the chain) and \(v=\overline{\delta x^2}\), its definition and estimator are \[
A(t)=\frac{\langle x_sx_{s+t}\rangle-\langle x\rangle^2}{\langle x^2\rangle-\langle x\rangle^2},\qquad
\tilde A(t)=\frac{1}{n_{\rm ch}}\sum_{\rm chains}\frac{1}{v}\,\frac{1}{n-t}\sum_{s=1}^{n-t}\delta x_s\,\delta x_{s+t},
\] averaged over the \(n_{\rm ch}\) chains, and the integrated autocorrelation time is estimated as \(\tau=\tfrac12+\sum_{t=1}^{t^*-1}\tilde A(t)\), with \(t^*\) the first lag at which \(\tilde A(t)<0.05\).

title: Lab 018: Classical spin models in JAX, the 2D Ising and the J1–J2 model
text:
2. Metropolis Monte Carlo in JAX
The algorithm, derived in Lab 010, proposes to flip spin \(i\) and accepts with probability \(\min(1, e^{-\beta\Delta E})\). With the local field \[
h_i = J_1\sum_{j\in{\rm nn}(i)} s_j - J_2\sum_{j\in{\rm nnn}(i)} s_j ,\qquad \Delta E_i = 2\,s_i\,h_i .
\]
Spins can be flipped simultaneously only if they do not interact. For the Ising model the chessboard colouring works, but here diagonal neighbours have the same chessboard colour. We use four sub-lattices labelled by \((x \bmod 2,\, y \bmod 2)\): nearest neighbours differ in one parity, diagonal neighbours in both, so no two spins of one sub-lattice are coupled. In code a sub-lattice is the strided slice s[a::2, b::2], and we only draw random numbers for the spins we update. One sweep = four sub-lattice updates = one attempted flip per spin.
The JAX structure follows from this. A pure function sweep(s, key, g, beta) updates one lattice; randomness is explicit, a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) key goes in and a new key comes out. lax.scan repeats a step many times inside one compiled program, with no Python loop overhead. jax.vmap maps the whole simulation over chains, every chain with its own \(g\) and its own random key, so all values of \(g\) run at once. jax.jit compiles the result into a single program (XLA, Accelerated Linear Algebra, the compiler behind JAX, fuses the array operations; on a graphics processing unit, GPU, the same code runs unchanged).
Each chain is annealed: it starts at the highest temperature and is cooled through a decreasing sequence of temperatures. At each temperature it first equilibrates for n_equil sweeps and then stores n_samples configurations separated by n_between sweeps (to reduce correlations between stored samples). Slow cooling helps the chain find the ordered state at low \(T\).


Code
def local_field(s, g):
    # s: (..., L, L); the rolls act on the two lattice axes, so the same function works for one lattice or a batch
    nn = jnp.roll(s, 1, -2) + jnp.roll(s, -1, -2) + jnp.roll(s, 1, -1) + jnp.roll(s, -1, -1)
    nnn = (jnp.roll(s, (1, 1), (-2, -1)) + jnp.roll(s, (1, -1), (-2, -1))
           + jnp.roll(s, (-1, 1), (-2, -1)) + jnp.roll(s, (-1, -1), (-2, -1)))
    return nn - g * nnn                                     # J1 = 1, J2 = g

def energy_per_spin(s, g):
    return -0.5 * jnp.mean(s * local_field(s, g), axis=(-2, -1))   # each bond appears twice in sum_i s_i h_i

def sweep(s, key, g, beta):
    for a, b in ((0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)):          # the four sub-lattices (a Python loop, unrolled by jit)
        key, sub = jax.random.split(key)
        si = s[a::2, b::2]
        dE = 2.0 * si * local_field(s, g)[a::2, b::2]
        accept = jax.random.uniform(sub, si.shape) < jnp.exp(-beta * dE)
        s = s.at[a::2, b::2].set(jnp.where(accept, -si, si))
    return s, key

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_samples", "n_between"))
def anneal_chains(s0, keys, gs, Ts, n_equil, n_samples, n_between):
    # s0: (chains, L, L), keys: (chains, 2), gs: (chains,), Ts: (nT,) in the order visited.
    # Returns int8 samples of shape (chains, nT, n_samples, L, L).
    def one_chain(s, key, g):
        def at_T(carry, T):
            step = lambda c, _: (sweep(c[0], c[1], g, 1.0 / T), None)
            carry, _ = lax.scan(step, carry, None, length=n_equil)
            def store(c, _):
                c, _ = lax.scan(step, c, None, length=n_between)
                return c, c[0].astype(jnp.int8)
            return lax.scan(store, carry, None, length=n_samples)
        _, samples = lax.scan(at_T, (s, key), Ts)
        return samples
    return jax.vmap(one_chain)(s0, keys, gs)

def run(L, gs, Ts, n_chains, n_equil, n_samples, n_between, seed):
    # gs: (nG,) couplings; every g gets n_chains independent chains. Returns (nG, nT, n_chains * n_samples, L, L) int8.
    G = jnp.repeat(jnp.asarray(gs, jnp.float32), n_chains)
    k_init, k_run = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed))
    s0 = jnp.where(jax.random.bernoulli(k_init, 0.5, (G.size, L, L)), 1.0, -1.0)
    out = anneal_chains(s0, jax.random.split(k_run, G.size), G, jnp.asarray(Ts, jnp.float32),
                        n_equil, n_samples, n_between)
    out = np.asarray(out).reshape(len(gs), n_chains, len(Ts), n_samples, L, L)
    return out.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5).reshape(len(gs), len(Ts), n_chains * n_samples, L, L)



2.1 Exact benchmarks
Before producing data we test the sampler against two exact results. On the \(4\times4\) lattice we know the exact thermal averages for any \(g\) from the \(2^{16}\) states enumerated above. At \(g=0\) and large \(L\) the magnetisation must follow Yang’s exact result \(M(T)=\left(1-\sinh^{-4}(2/T)\right)^{1/8}\) below \(T_c\), and the energy per spin \(\langle e\rangle\) must follow Onsager’s exact result \(u(T)\).


Code
def exact_4x4(g, T):
    e = (-np.asarray(B1) + g * np.asarray(B2)) / 16
    o = order_parameters(S4)
    w = np.exp(-16 * (e - e.min()) / T); w /= w.sum()
    return (w * e).sum(), (w * np.asarray(o["m"])).sum(), (w * np.asarray(o["m_str"])).sum()

          f"(exact {m_ex:.4f})   <m_str> {float(o['m_str'].mean()):.4f} (exact {ms_ex:.4f})")

Code
def M_exact(T):
    T = np.asarray(T, float); out = np.zeros_like(T); low = T < TC_ISING
    out[low] = (1 - np.sinh(2 / T[low]) ** -4) ** 0.125
    return out

def u_exact(T):
    K = 1.0 / np.asarray(T, float)
    kap = 2 * np.sinh(2 * K) / np.cosh(2 * K) ** 2
    return -1 / np.tanh(2 * K) * (1 + 2 / np.pi * (2 * np.tanh(2 * K) ** 2 - 1) * ellipk(kap**2))

Away from \(T_c\) the Monte Carlo points lie on the exact curves. Near \(T_c\) the finite lattice rounds the transition: \(\langle|m|\rangle\) stays non-zero above \(T_c\) because a finite system always has a finite magnetisation fluctuation. This finite-size rounding is the subject of Lab 019.

Exercise
Set n_equil=50 in the cell above and look at the points just below \(T_c\). Explain why the agreement gets worse there first.



2.2 Critical slowing down and the Swendsen–Wang algorithm
Near \(T_c\) the lattice is made of correlated domains of all sizes up to \(L\). Metropolis flips one spin at a time, and a single flip inside a large domain is almost always rejected (it costs energy at every bond). To turn a whole domain around the chain must move its boundary one flip at a time, which takes very many sweeps, and consecutive samples are nearly copies of each other. This is critical slowing down, and the autocorrelation time grows with \(L\). Below we measure it for \(L=50\).
The remedy is to flip whole domains at once, but to choose them randomly in a way that keeps the Boltzmann distribution exact. The tool is a one-line identity for the weight of a single bond, with \(p = 1-e^{-2\beta J}\): \[
e^{\beta J s_is_j} \;=\; e^{\beta J}\Big[\,(1-p) \;+\; p\,\delta_{s_i s_j}\Big].
\] (For \(s_i=s_j\) the bracket is \(1\); for \(s_i\neq s_j\) it is \(1-p=e^{-2\beta J}\).) Read the two terms as a bond variable \(b_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\): “no bond” with weight \(1-p\), or “bond” with weight \(p\), allowed only between parallel spins. Multiplying over all bonds gives a joint distribution of spins and bonds whose sum over bonds is exactly \(e^{-\beta H}\) (Fortuin and Kasteleyn’s random-cluster representation). The algorithm samples the two variables alternately.

bonds given spins: between every pair of parallel neighbours, place a bond with probability \(p\), independently;
spins given bonds: the only constraint is that bonded spins are equal, so every connected cluster of bonds carries one common sign, chosen independently with probability \(1/2\) for each cluster.

Each step samples exactly from a conditional distribution of the joint distribution, so the pair of steps leaves \(e^{-\beta H}\) invariant. Near \(T_c\) the clusters have all sizes, and one update can turn around a domain as large as the lattice. The method works for ferromagnetic couplings (a bond requires parallel spins to lower the energy); for the frustrated \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model we keep Metropolis.
Finding connected clusters is usually a sequential graph search. In array form, as JAX needs it, every site starts with a label (its own index) and we repeat two operations until nothing changes: each site takes the smallest label among itself and its bonded neighbours, and then the label of its label (pointer jumping). Each iteration is a few jnp.roll and jnp.minimum operations on the whole lattice, inside a lax.while_loop.
References: R. H. Swendsen, J.-S. Wang, Phys. Rev. Lett. 58, 86 (1987), doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86; C. M. Fortuin, P. W. Kasteleyn, Physica 57, 536 (1972), doi:10.1016/0031-8914(72)90045-6; the single-cluster variant: U. Wolff, Phys. Rev. Lett. 62, 361 (1989), doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.62.361; textbook: Newman and Barkema (references at the end).


Code
def cluster_labels(bond_r, bond_d):
    # bond_r[x, y]: (x, y) bonded to (x, y+1);  bond_d[x, y]: (x, y) bonded to (x+1, y);  periodic lattice
    L = bond_r.shape[0]
    big = L * L
    bond_l, bond_u = jnp.roll(bond_r, 1, 1), jnp.roll(bond_d, 1, 0)       # bonds to the left / upper neighbour
    def body(carry):
        lab, _ = carry
        m = lab
        m = jnp.minimum(m, jnp.where(bond_r, jnp.roll(lab, -1, 1), big))
        m = jnp.minimum(m, jnp.where(bond_l, jnp.roll(lab, 1, 1), big))
        m = jnp.minimum(m, jnp.where(bond_d, jnp.roll(lab, -1, 0), big))
        m = jnp.minimum(m, jnp.where(bond_u, jnp.roll(lab, 1, 0), big))
        m = m.ravel()[m]                                                  # pointer jumping
        return m, jnp.any(m != lab)
    lab, _ = lax.while_loop(lambda c: c[1], body, (jnp.arange(L * L).reshape(L, L), True))
    return lab

def sw_step(s, key, beta):
    k1, k2, k3 = jax.random.split(key, 3)
    p = 1.0 - jnp.exp(-2.0 * beta)
    bond_r = (s == jnp.roll(s, -1, 1)) & (jax.random.uniform(k1, s.shape) < p)
    bond_d = (s == jnp.roll(s, -1, 0)) & (jax.random.uniform(k2, s.shape) < p)
    lab = cluster_labels(bond_r, bond_d)
    flip = jax.random.bernoulli(k3, 0.5, (s.size,))                       # one coin per cluster label
    return jnp.where(flip[lab], -s, s)

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_samples", "n_between"))
def sw_chains(s0, keys, Ts, n_equil, n_samples, n_between):
    def one_chain(s, key):
        def at_T(carry, T):
            def step(c, _):
                s, key = c
                key, k = jax.random.split(key)
                return (sw_step(s, k, 1.0 / T), key), None
            carry, _ = lax.scan(step, carry, None, length=n_equil)
            def store(c, _):
                c, _ = lax.scan(step, c, None, length=n_between)
                return c, c[0].astype(jnp.int8)
            return lax.scan(store, carry, None, length=n_samples)
        return lax.scan(at_T, (s, key), Ts)[1]
    return jax.vmap(one_chain)(s0, keys)

def run_sw(L, Ts, n_chains, n_equil, n_samples, n_between, seed):
    k_init, k_run = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed))
    s0 = jnp.where(jax.random.bernoulli(k_init, 0.5, (n_chains, L, L)), 1.0, -1.0)
    out = np.asarray(sw_chains(s0, jax.random.split(k_run, n_chains), jnp.asarray(Ts, jnp.float32), n_equil, n_samples, n_between))
    return out.transpose(1, 0, 2, 3, 4).reshape(len(Ts), n_chains * n_samples, L, L)     # (nT, samples, L, L)

# check against exact enumeration of the 4x4 lattice at g = 0; error bars from the spread between independent chains
for T in (1.5, 2.27, 3.0):
    n_ch = 32768
    smp = run_sw(4, [T], n_chains=n_ch, n_equil=50, n_samples=8, n_between=10, seed=41)[0].reshape(n_ch, 8, 4, 4).astype(np.float32)
    e_c = np.asarray(energy_per_spin(jnp.asarray(smp), 0.0)).mean(1); m_c = np.abs(smp.mean((-1, -2))).mean(1)
    e_ex, m_ex, _ = exact_4x4(0.0, T)
    err_e, err_m = e_c.std() / np.sqrt(n_ch), m_c.std() / np.sqrt(n_ch)
    print(f"T = {T}:  <e> {e_c.mean():+.4f} +- {err_e:.4f} (exact {e_ex:+.4f}, {(e_c.mean() - e_ex) / err_e:+.1f} sigma)   "
          f"<|m|> {m_c.mean():.4f} +- {err_m:.4f} (exact {m_ex:.4f}, {(m_c.mean() - m_ex) / err_m:+.1f} sigma)")


T = 1.5:  <e> -1.9510 +- 0.0003 (exact -1.9506, -1.0 sigma)   <|m|> 0.9862 +- 0.0001 (exact 0.9862, +0.7 sigma)


T = 2.27:  <e> -1.5662 +- 0.0010 (exact -1.5650, -1.2 sigma)   <|m|> 0.8441 +- 0.0004 (exact 0.8436, +1.0 sigma)


T = 3.0:  <e> -1.0166 +- 0.0011 (exact -1.0171, +0.4 sigma)   <|m|> 0.6010 +- 0.0006 (exact 0.6013, -0.5 sigma)


To see what the clusters look like, we take one configuration of \(L=50\) at \(T_c\), draw its Swendsen–Wang clusters (each cluster in its own colour), and show the configuration after one update.


Code
L_pic = 50
s_pic = jnp.asarray(run_sw(L_pic, [TC_ISING], n_chains=1, n_equil=100, n_samples=1, n_between=1, seed=31)[0, 0], jnp.float32)
k1, k2, k3 = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(32), 3)
p_pic = 1.0 - np.exp(-2.0 / TC_ISING)
b_r = (s_pic == jnp.roll(s_pic, -1, 1)) & (jax.random.uniform(k1, s_pic.shape) < p_pic)
b_d = (s_pic == jnp.roll(s_pic, -1, 0)) & (jax.random.uniform(k2, s_pic.shape) < p_pic)
lab = np.asarray(jax.jit(cluster_labels)(b_r, b_d))
flip = np.asarray(jax.random.bernoulli(k3, 0.5, (L_pic * L_pic,)))
s_new = np.where(flip[lab], -np.asarray(s_pic), np.asarray(s_pic))
ids, sizes = np.unique(lab, return_counts=True)
colour = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(ids))[np.searchsorted(ids, lab)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.6))
ax[0].imshow(np.asarray(s_pic), cmap=SPIN_CMAP, vmin=-1, vmax=1); ax[0].set_title("configuration at $T_c$", fontsize=10)
ax[1].imshow(colour, cmap="tab20", interpolation="nearest"); ax[1].set_title(f"{len(ids)} clusters, largest {sizes.max()} spins", fontsize=10)
ax[2].imshow(s_new, cmap=SPIN_CMAP, vmin=-1, vmax=1); ax[2].set_title("after one update", fontsize=10)
for a in ax: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_ising_sw_clusters.png"); plt.show()
NUMBERS.update(sw_pic_n_clusters=int(len(ids)), sw_pic_largest=int(sizes.max()))





To measure the gain, we compare the autocorrelation of \(|m|\) along one chain at \(T_c\) for \(L=50\), for Metropolis with one sweep per step and for Swendsen–Wang with one cluster update per step, \[
A(t) = \frac{\langle |m|_{s}\,|m|_{s+t}\rangle - \langle|m|\rangle^2}{\langle |m|^2\rangle - \langle|m|\rangle^2}.
\] The faster \(A(t)\) decays, the more independent the stored samples are.


Code
def autocorr(x, t_max):
    x = x - x.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    v = (x * x).mean(-1)
    return np.array([np.mean((x[:, : x.shape[1] - t] * x[:, t:]).mean(-1) / v) for t in range(t_max)])

L_ac, T_ac, n_steps, n_ch = 50, TC_ISING, 400, 16
t0 = time.time()
met = run(L_ac, [0.0], [T_ac], n_chains=n_ch, n_equil=1000, n_samples=n_steps, n_between=1, seed=21)[0, 0]
t_met = time.time() - t0; t0 = time.time()
sw = run_sw(L_ac, [T_ac], n_chains=n_ch, n_equil=100, n_samples=n_steps, n_between=1, seed=22)[0]
t_sw = time.time() - t0
m_met = np.abs(met.reshape(n_ch, n_steps, -1).mean(-1)); m_sw = np.abs(sw.reshape(n_ch, n_steps, -1).mean(-1))
A_met, A_sw = autocorr(m_met, 150), autocorr(m_sw, 150)
tau = lambda A: 0.5 + A[1:np.argmax(A < 0.05) if (A < 0.05).any() else len(A)].sum()   # integrated autocorrelation time
print(f"L = {L_ac}, T = T_c:  integrated autocorrelation time  Metropolis {tau(A_met):.1f} sweeps,  Swendsen-Wang {tau(A_sw):.1f} updates")
print(f"wall time for {n_steps} steps of {n_ch} chains:  Metropolis {t_met:.1f} s,  Swendsen-Wang {t_sw:.1f} s")
NUMBERS.update(tau_metropolis=round(float(tau(A_met)), 1), tau_sw=round(float(tau(A_sw)), 1))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2))
ax[0].plot(m_met[0], color=UJBlue, lw=1, label="Metropolis (1 sweep / step)"); ax[0].plot(m_sw[0], color=DSOrange, lw=1, label="Swendsen-Wang (1 update / step)")
ax[0].set_xlabel("Monte Carlo step"); ax[0].set_ylabel(r"$|m|$"); ax[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax[1].plot(A_met, color=UJBlue, label="Metropolis"); ax[1].plot(A_sw, color=DSOrange, label="Swendsen-Wang")
ax[1].axhline(0, color=UJGray, lw=0.8); ax[1].set_xlabel("lag $t$"); ax[1].set_ylabel("$A(t)$"); ax[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle(f"$L={L_ac}$ at $T_c$", fontsize=10); fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_ising_autocorr.png"); plt.show()


L = 50, T = T_c:  integrated autocorrelation time  Metropolis 26.4 sweeps,  Swendsen-Wang 3.4 updates
wall time for 400 steps of 16 chains:  Metropolis 2.7 s,  Swendsen-Wang 29.5 s





Per step, Swendsen–Wang decorrelates \(|m|\) faster, with an integrated autocorrelation time of \(3.4\) cluster updates against \(26.4\) Metropolis sweeps. One cluster update, however, costs more computing time in this implementation. The printed wall times for 400 steps of 16 chains, which may include compilation, are \(29.5\) s for Swendsen–Wang and \(2.7\) s for Metropolis. The time per autocorrelation time, \(\tau\) times the time per step, is then about \(0.25\) s for Swendsen–Wang and \(0.18\) s for Metropolis, so at \(L=50\) this run shows fewer correlated steps for the cluster algorithm but no saving in computing time.

section: 3. Ising data set for several lattice sizes
text:
3. Ising data set for several lattice sizes
For finite-size scaling (Lab 019) we need the same temperature grid for several \(L\), and nearly independent samples close to \(T_c\). We use the Swendsen–Wang sampler: 32 chains per size, each cooled through the temperature grid, 8 samples per temperature separated by 4 cluster updates. We store configurations as bits (np.packbits), eight spins per byte.


Code
def pack(configs):
    return np.packbits(configs > 0, axis=-1)

def unpack(packed, L):
    return np.unpackbits(packed, axis=-1, count=L).astype(np.int8) * 2 - 1

ISING_L = [20, 30, 50]
# cooling order; dense steps of 0.02 around T_c, coarse steps of 0.1 elsewhere
ISING_T = np.round(np.concatenate([np.arange(3.5, 2.55, -0.1), np.arange(2.5, 2.095, -0.02), np.arange(2.0, 1.45, -0.1)]), 4)
t_total = time.time()
for L in ISING_L:
    t0 = time.time()
    c = run_sw(L, ISING_T, n_chains=32, n_equil=40, n_samples=8, n_between=4, seed=100 + L)
    np.savez_compressed(f"{DATA}/ising_L{L}.npz", configs=pack(c), T=ISING_T, L=L)
    print(f"L = {L:3d}: {c.shape[0]} temperatures x {c.shape[1]} samples   {time.time() - t0:6.1f} s")
print(f"total {time.time() - t_total:.0f} s")
NUMBERS["ising_L"] = ISING_L; NUMBERS["ising_nT"] = len(ISING_T); NUMBERS["ising_samples_per_T"] = 32 * 8

4. \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) data set in the \((g,T)\) plane
One call simulates all values of \(g\) at once (vmap over chains), each chain cooled from \(T=4\) to \(T=0.1\).

J_G = np.round(np.arange(0.0, 1.0001, 0.0125), 4)                # 81 couplings
J_T = np.round(np.arange(4.0, 0.0999, -0.05), 4)                 # 79 temperatures, cooling order

title: Lab 018: Classical spin models in JAX, the 2D Ising and the J1–J2 model
text:
5. Choice of observable
Suppose we know nothing about stripes and do what is natural for a magnet, measuring \(\langle|m|\rangle\) at every point of the grid. Then we measure \(\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle\), which requires knowing the stripe pattern. Finally we measure the specific heat \[
c = \frac{N}{T^2}\left(\langle e^2\rangle-\langle e\rangle^2\right),
\] which needs no order parameter and has a peak at a transition whatever the order is.


Code
@jax.jit
def observables(s, g):
    # s: (nT, n, L, L) float, g scalar -> per-temperature averages
    o = order_parameters(s)
    e = energy_per_spin(s, g)
    return o["m"].mean(1), o["m_str"].mean(1), e.mean(1), e.var(1)

N = J_L**2
# one coupling at a time keeps the memory small (the whole dataset as float32 would need ~0.7 GB)
res = [observables(jnp.asarray(cj[i], jnp.float32), J_G[i]) for i in range(len(J_G))]
M_map, Ms_map, E_map, varE = (np.stack([np.asarray(r[k]) for r in res]) for k in range(4))
C_map = N * varE / J_T[None, :] ** 2

def show_map(ax, Z, title, cmap="viridis", vmax=None):
    im = ax.pcolormesh(J_G, J_T, Z.T, shading="nearest", cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=vmax, rasterized=True)
    ax.set_xlabel("$g=J_2/J_1$", labelpad=1); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xticks([0, 0.5, 1]); ax.set_yticks([1, 2, 3, 4])
    cb = plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.08, pad=0.04)
    cb.set_ticks([0, 0.5, 1] if vmax == 1 else [0, 1, 2])

with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_STYLE):
    # physical size on the slide (full text width)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 1.75), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
    show_map(ax[0], M_map, r"magnetisation $\langle|m|\rangle$", vmax=1)
    show_map(ax[1], Ms_map, r"stripe order $\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle$", vmax=1)
    show_map(ax[2], C_map, r"specific heat $c$", cmap="magma", vmax=np.percentile(C_map, 99))
    ax[0].set_ylabel("$T$")
    gg = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
    for a in ax:
        a.plot(gg[gg <= 0.5], 4 * (1 - gg[gg <= 0.5]), "--", color="w", lw=1)
        a.plot(gg[gg >= 0.5], 4 * gg[gg >= 0.5], "--", color="w", lw=1)
        a.set_ylim(J_T.min(), J_T.max())
    fig.get_layout_engine().set(w_pad=0.01, h_pad=0.01, wspace=0.03)
    fig.savefig(f"{FIG}/gen_j1j2_physicist_maps.png", dpi=200); plt.show()





The dashed white lines are the mean-field predictions \(T^{\rm MF}=4(1-g)\) and \(4g\); they overshoot everywhere and miss the dip to \(T_c=0\) at \(g=1/2\).
The magnetisation map shows one ordered region, \(g<1/2\); the whole stripe phase looks like a paramagnet. The stripe map shows the other ordered region, but only because we told it what pattern to look for. The specific-heat map shows both boundaries without any order parameter. Its price is noise, because \(c\) is a variance, and variances need many more samples than means.

5.1 Cost of a dense scan
A boundary from the specific heat needs a peak position, so it needs \(c\) on a fine grid with small error bars. To see how many samples per grid point this takes, we estimate \(c(T)\) at \(g=0.25\) from five random subsets of \(n=10\) and five of \(n=30\) of the 100 stored samples per temperature, and compare with the estimate from all 100 samples. In the subsets the variance of the energy is the unbiased one.


Code
ig = np.argmin(abs(J_G - 0.25))
e_line = np.asarray(energy_per_spin(jnp.asarray(cj[ig], jnp.float32), J_G[ig]))           # (nT, samples)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE_STYLE):
    # physical size on the slide (full text width)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 1.9), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
    for a, n in zip(ax, [10, 30, cj.shape[2]]):
        for rep in range(5 if n < cj.shape[2] else 1):
            idx = rng.choice(cj.shape[2], n, replace=False)
            a.plot(J_T, N * e_line[:, idx].var(1, ddof=1) / J_T**2, "-", lw=1, alpha=0.8, color=UJBlue if n < cj.shape[2] else UJNavy)
        a.set_title(f"{n} samples" if n < cj.shape[2] else f"all {n} samples", fontsize=11)
        a.set_xlabel("$T$", labelpad=1); a.set_xticks([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
    ax[0].set_ylabel("$c$ at $g=0.25$")
    fig.savefig(f"{FIG}/gen_j1j2_cost.png", dpi=200); plt.show()

n_points = len(J_G) * len(J_T)
NUMBERS.update(j1j2_grid_points=n_points, j1j2_total_configs=int(n_points * cj.shape[2]))
print(f"{n_points} grid points x {cj.shape[2]} samples = {n_points * cj.shape[2]} configurations")





6399 grid points x 100 samples = 639900 configurations


With 10 samples per point the five estimates of \(c\) differ strongly near the peak, in height and in shape. With 30 samples they scatter less, and the curve from all 100 samples is still visibly noisy. Near a transition the stored samples are also correlated (critical slowing down), so that more of them are needed. In a laboratory, every grid point is a separate preparation of the sample at a given pressure, field or temperature.
This is the motivation for Labs 019 and 020, which test whether an algorithm that has never been told about magnetisation or stripes finds the ordered phases from raw snapshots, and whether it can do so from a coarse scan and point to the region where a dense scan is worth its cost.

title: Lab 018: Classical spin models in JAX, the 2D Ising and the J1–J2 model
text:
Summary
The \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) Ising model has a ferromagnetic phase (\(g<1/2\)) and a stripe phase (\(g>1/2\)). At \(g=1/2\) the competition makes the ground state highly degenerate and the transition temperature vanishes, a point that mean-field theory gets qualitatively wrong. The natural “magnet” observable, \(\langle|m|\rangle\), is blind to the stripe phase, so choosing the right observable requires prior knowledge, and fluctuation observables such as \(c\), which show both transitions here, are expensive because they need many samples per grid point.
On the computational side, the whole simulation is built from one pure sweep function, with lax.scan for the loops over time, vmap over chains and couplings, and jit for the whole program. Near \(T_c\) local updates slow down. The Swendsen–Wang cluster algorithm (ferromagnetic couplings only) gives nearly independent samples after a few updates, and its cluster search is a lax.while_loop of array operations.

Exercises

Add a \(J_3\) coupling (third neighbours, two sites apart along the axes) to local_field. Find the sub-lattice decomposition that is now needed.
Replace annealing by independent random starts at every temperature. Compare the stripe phase at low \(T\) near \(g=0.55\) with the annealed data.
Compute the full structure factor \(S(\boldsymbol k)\) with jnp.fft.fft2 for snapshots at \(g=0.25\) and \(g=0.75\), \(T=0.5\). Locate the peaks.

title: Lab 019: The 2D Ising transition without labels
text:
1. Exact results and finite-size scaling
For the infinite lattice (\(J=k_B=1\)) three results are known exactly. * Onsager (1944) found \(T_c = 2/\ln(1+\sqrt2) = 2.2692\ldots\) and a logarithmic divergence of the specific heat. * Yang (1952) found the spontaneous magnetisation \(M(T)=\left(1-\sinh^{-4}(2/T)\right)^{1/8}\) below \(T_c\), so \(M\sim (T_c-T)^{1/8}\). * The correlation length diverges as \(\xi\sim|T-T_c|^{-\nu}\) with \(\nu=1\), and the susceptibility as \(\chi\sim|T-T_c|^{-7/4}\).
On a finite lattice nothing diverges, since the growth of \(\xi\) stops when it reaches \(L\). Finite-size scaling turns this limitation into a tool. Near \(T_c\) every observable depends on \(T\) and \(L\) only through \(L/\xi\), that is through the scaling variable \(t\,L^{1/\nu}\) with \(t=(T-T_c)/T_c\), \[
\langle|m|\rangle = L^{-1/(8\nu)}\,\tilde m\!\left(tL^{1/\nu}\right),\qquad
\chi = L^{7/(4\nu)}\,\tilde\chi\!\left(tL^{1/\nu}\right),\qquad
U_4 = \tilde U\!\left(tL^{1/\nu}\right).
\] The Binder cumulant \(U_4 = 1-\dfrac{\langle m^4\rangle}{3\langle m^2\rangle^2}\) is dimensionless, so at \(t=0\) it takes the same value for every \(L\), and the curves for different \(L\) cross at \(T_c\). Its limits are \(U_4\to 2/3\) in the ordered phase (\(m=\pm M\) sharp) and \(U_4\to0\) in the paramagnet (\(m\) Gaussian, \(\langle m^4\rangle = 3\langle m^2\rangle^2\)). The susceptibility peak sits at \(T_c(L)\) with \(T_c(L)-T_c\propto L^{-1/\nu}\), and extrapolating to \(L\to\infty\) gives \(T_c\).
All these quantities are thermal averages over the Boltzmann distribution, \(\langle O\rangle=\frac1Z\sum_{\mathbf s}O(\mathbf s)\,e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}\) with \(Z=\sum_{\mathbf s}e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}\) and \(\beta=1/T\). The data of Lab 018 contain, for every lattice size and temperature, \(n=256\) configurations \(\mathbf s^{(k)}\) sampled from this distribution, and every average is estimated by a sample mean over them. With \(m_k=\frac1N\sum_is^{(k)}_i\) the magnetisation of sample \(k\) and \(\overline{x}=\frac1n\sum_kx_k\), the code below (functions moments and blocked) computes the estimators of the table.








observable
definition through \(Z\)
estimator from \(n\) samples (as in the code)




magnetisation
\(\langle\lvert m\rvert\rangle=\frac1Z\sum_{\mathbf s}\lvert m(\mathbf s)\rvert e^{-\beta H}\)
\(\overline{\lvert m\rvert}=\frac1n\sum_k\lvert m_k\rvert\)


susceptibility
\(\chi=N\beta\big(\langle m^2\rangle-\langle\lvert m\rvert\rangle^2\big)\)
\(N\beta\big(\overline{m^2}-\overline{\lvert m\rvert}^{\,2}\big)\)


Binder cumulant
\(U_4=1-\dfrac{\langle m^4\rangle}{3\langle m^2\rangle^2}\)
\(1-\dfrac{\overline{m^4}}{3\,\overline{m^2}^{\,2}}\)



On a finite lattice \(\langle m\rangle=0\) by the symmetry \(\mathbf s\to-\mathbf s\), so the susceptibility is built from \(|m|\). The variance in \(\chi\) is a population variance (division by \(n\)). The error bar of an observable comes from \(B=8\) blocks of consecutive columns of the data (groups of chains). The observable \(O_b\) is computed on each block, and the error is \(\sigma_B/\sqrt{B-1}\), with \(\sigma_B\) the population standard deviation of the \(O_b\).
Both observables were constructed, since we had to know that \(m\) is the order parameter. The figure shows, from left to right, the magnetisation \(\overline{|m|}\), the Binder cumulant \(U_4\) and the susceptibility \(\chi\) against \(T\) for the three sizes, with the exact \(T_c\) dotted. The Binder curves cross near \(T_c\), and the susceptibility peak drifts towards \(T_c\) as \(L\) grows.


Code
def moments(x):
    # x: (nT, n) samples of a scalar order parameter -> U4, chi-like variance, mean |x|
    x2, x4 = (x**2).mean(1), (x**4).mean(1)
    return 1 - x4 / (3 * x2**2), x2 - np.abs(x).mean(1) ** 2, np.abs(x).mean(1)

def blocked(f, x, n_blocks=8):
    # mean and error of f(x) from n_blocks independent groups of samples (columns are grouped by chain in Lab 018)
    vals = np.stack([f(b) for b in np.array_split(x, n_blocks, axis=1)])
    return f(x), vals.std(0) / np.sqrt(n_blocks - 1)

M = {L: s.mean((-2, -1)).astype(np.float64) for L, (T, s) in DATA_SETS.items()}

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 2.1))
    chi_peak = {}
    for L in L_LIST:
        T = DATA_SETS[L][0]; N = L * L
        (U, U_err) = blocked(lambda x: moments(x)[0], M[L])
        (chi, chi_err) = blocked(lambda x: N * moments(x)[1], M[L])
        chi = chi / T; chi_err = chi_err / T
        ax[0].plot(T, np.abs(M[L]).mean(1), ".-", color=size_colors[L], label=f"$L={L}$")
        ax[1].errorbar(T, U, U_err, fmt=".-", color=size_colors[L], label=f"$L={L}$", ms=3, capsize=1)
        ax[2].errorbar(T, chi, chi_err, fmt=".-", color=size_colors[L], ms=3, capsize=1)
        chi_peak[L] = T[np.argmax(chi)]
    for a, lab in zip(ax, [r"$\langle|m|\rangle$", r"$U_4$", r"$\chi$"]):
        a.axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":"); a.set_xlabel("$T$"); a.set_ylabel(lab)
    ax[1].set_xlim(2.1, 2.5); ax[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="lower left"); ax[2].set_xlim(1.9, 3.0)
    fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_ising_fss_observables.png"); plt.show()
print("chi peak positions:", chi_peak)





chi peak positions: {20: np.float64(2.38), 30: np.float64(2.36), 50: np.float64(2.3)}



1.1 Binder crossings and susceptibility peaks
To turn the figure into numbers, we find for each pair of consecutive sizes where \(U_4(L)\) and \(U_4(L')\) cross (linear interpolation between grid points). For the susceptibility we fit \(T_c(L) = T_c + a\,L^{-1/\nu}\) with the exact \(\nu=1\), and the peak position is refined by a parabola through the three highest points.


Code
def crossing(T, y1, y2, lo=2.1, hi=2.5):
    d = y1 - y2; sel = (T >= lo) & (T <= hi)
    T, d = T[sel], d[sel]
    idx = np.where(np.sign(d[:-1]) != np.sign(d[1:]))[0]
    if len(idx) == 0: return np.nan
    i = idx[np.argmin(abs(T[idx] - TC))] if len(idx) > 1 else idx[0]
    return T[i] - d[i] * (T[i + 1] - T[i]) / (d[i + 1] - d[i])

def peak(T, y):
    i = int(np.clip(np.argmax(y), 1, len(y) - 2))
    c = np.polyfit(T[i - 1:i + 2], y[i - 1:i + 2], 2)
    return -c[1] / (2 * c[0])

U4 = {L: moments(M[L])[0] for L in L_LIST}
cross = {(L1, L2): crossing(T_GRID, U4[L1], U4[L2]) for L1, L2 in zip(L_LIST[:-1], L_LIST[1:])}
for k, v in cross.items(): print(f"U4 crossing {k}: T = {v:.4f}")
chi_T = np.array([peak(T_GRID, L * L * moments(M[L])[1] / T_GRID) for L in L_LIST])
A = np.vstack([np.ones(len(L_LIST)), 1.0 / np.array(L_LIST)]).T
tc_chi, a_chi = np.linalg.lstsq(A, chi_T, rcond=None)[0]
print("chi peaks T_c(L):", np.round(chi_T, 4), f"-> extrapolated T_c = {tc_chi:.4f}  (exact {TC:.4f})")
NUMBERS.update(fss_U4_crossings={f"{a}-{b}": round(float(v), 4) for (a, b), v in cross.items()},
               fss_chi_peaks=[round(float(x), 4) for x in chi_T], fss_tc_chi=round(float(tc_chi), 4))
