title: Lab 019: The 2D Ising transition without labels
text:
2. PCA on raw spins
PCA (Lab 016) diagonalises the covariance matrix of the data. Here a data point is one configuration, a vector of \(N=L^2\) spins. The data set contains all temperatures, and no temperature or label is given to PCA.

2.1 PCA implementation in JAX
We compute the decomposition with a singular value decomposition in JAX, for \(L=30\), and look at how much variance the first component carries, what its weights, the entries of the principal direction \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1\), look like on the lattice, and how the projection \(w^{(1)}=\boldsymbol\lambda_1^{\top}(\mathbf s-\bar{\mathbf s})\) of a configuration \(\mathbf s\) compares with the magnetisation.


Code
@jax.jit
def pca(X):
    mu = X.mean(0)
    _, S, Vt = jnp.linalg.svd(X - mu, full_matrices=False)
    return mu, S**2 / jnp.sum(S**2), Vt

L = 30
T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
X = jnp.asarray(s.reshape(-1, L * L), jnp.float32)
mu, var_ratio, Vt = pca(X)
z = np.asarray((X - mu) @ Vt[:2].T).reshape(len(T), -1, 2)
v1 = np.asarray(Vt[0]) * np.sign(np.asarray(Vt[0]).sum())
print("fraction of the variance sigma_l^2 / sum sigma^2 of the first 5 components:", np.round(np.asarray(var_ratio[:5]), 4))
corr = np.corrcoef(np.abs(z[..., 0]).ravel(), np.abs(M[L]).ravel())[0, 1]
print(f"correlation between |w^(1)| and |m| over all configurations: {corr:.6f}")
print(f"entries of sqrt(N) lambda_1: mean {np.mean(v1 * L):.4f}, std {np.std(v1 * L):.4f}")
NUMBERS.update(pca_L=L, pca_var1=round(float(var_ratio[0]), 4), pca_var2=round(float(var_ratio[1]), 4),
               pca_corr_pc1_m=round(float(corr), 6), pca_v1_std=round(float(np.std(v1 * L)), 4))

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(4.7, 2.1), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.2, 1]))
    sc = ax[0].scatter(z[..., 0].ravel(), z[..., 1].ravel(), c=np.repeat(T, z.shape[1]), cmap="coolwarm", s=2)
    plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax[0], label="$T$"); ax[0].set_xlabel("$w^{(1)}$"); ax[0].set_ylabel("$w^{(2)}$")
    ax[1].plot(T, np.abs(z[..., 0]).mean(1) / L, "o", ms=3, color=UJBlue, label=r"$\langle|w^{(1)}|\rangle/\sqrt{N}$")
    ax[1].plot(T, np.abs(M[L]).mean(1), "-", color=DSOrange, label=r"$\langle|m|\rangle$")
    ax[1].axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":"); ax[1].set_xlabel("$T$"); ax[1].set_ylim(0, 1.75); ax[1].set_yticks([0, 0.5, 1.0])
    ax[1].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", handlelength=1.2, borderaxespad=0.1)
    fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_ising_pca.png"); plt.show()

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(2.1, 1.9))
    im = ax.imshow((v1 * L).reshape(L, L), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=0.9, vmax=1.1); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(r"$\sqrt{N}\,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_1$"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_ising_v1.png"); plt.show()


fraction of the variance sigma_l^2 / sum sigma^2 of the first 5 components: [0.373  0.0141 0.0133 0.013  0.0124]
correlation between |w^(1)| and |m| over all configurations: 0.999960
entries of sqrt(N) lambda_1: mean 1.0000, std 0.0096








The first figure shows the coordinates \((w^{(1)},w^{(2)})\) of every configuration coloured by its temperature (left) and, against \(T\), the average \(\langle|w^{(1)}|\rangle/\sqrt N\) over the configurations of each temperature next to \(\langle|m|\rangle\) (right). The second figure shows the entries of \(\sqrt N\,\boldsymbol\lambda_1\) on the lattice.
The first component carries far more variance than all others, its weights are uniform over the lattice, and its projection is almost perfectly correlated with \(|m|\). Below \(T_c\) the spins are strongly correlated, \(\langle s_is_j\rangle\approx M^2\) for all pairs, so the covariance matrix has a large uniform block and its leading eigenvector is the uniform vector \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1\approx(1,\dots,1)/\sqrt N\). The projection is then \(w^{(1)}=\boldsymbol\lambda_1^{\top}(\mathbf s-\bar{\mathbf s})\approx\sqrt N\,(m-\bar m)\), where \(\bar m\) is the magnetisation averaged over the whole data set. The correlation of 0.99996 between \(|w^{(1)}|\) and \(|m|\) shows that \(\bar m\) is negligible here, so \(w^{(1)}\approx\sqrt N\,m\).
PCA has therefore found what we could have guessed. The Ising order parameter is linear in the spins, and a linear method finds linear structure. The result is still useful, because the first principal component is an order-parameter candidate produced without prior knowledge, and its weights \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1\) show which pattern orders. Lab 020 tests the same idea on a model with two different ordering patterns, and Lab 021 on a model where the relevant variables are not linear in the spins.
Because \(w^{(1)}\propto m\), every finite-size analysis of Section 1 can be repeated with \(w^{(1)}\) in place of \(m\), and the Binder crossings come out nearly the same.


Code
z1 = {}
for L in L_LIST:
    T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
    Xl = jnp.asarray(s.reshape(-1, L * L), jnp.float32)
    mu_l, _, Vt_l = pca(Xl)
    z1[L] = np.asarray((Xl - mu_l) @ Vt_l[0]).reshape(len(T), -1) / L      # = m up to a sign
U4_pca = {L: moments(z1[L])[0] for L in L_LIST}
cross_pca = {(L1, L2): crossing(T_GRID, U4_pca[L1], U4_pca[L2]) for L1, L2 in zip(L_LIST[:-1], L_LIST[1:])}
for k in cross: print(f"crossing {k}:  U4(m) {cross[k]:.4f}   U4(w^(1)) {cross_pca[k]:.4f}")


crossing (20, 30):  U4(m) 2.2495   U4(w^(1)) 2.2495
crossing (30, 50):  U4(m) 2.2784   U4(w^(1)) 2.2773


The crossings from the first principal component reproduce those from \(m\), for the first pair of sizes to all printed digits and for the second within \(0.0011\).


2.2 PCA with scikit-learn
In scikit-learn the same decomposition is done by the estimator PCA(n_components=5, svd_solver="full"), fitted to the same \(L=30\) configurations with fit(X). It stores the mean configuration in mean_, the components as the rows of components_ and their fractions of the variance in explained_variance_ratio_, and transform(X) returns the projections. With svd_solver="full" it performs a complete singular value decomposition (SVD) of the centred data, the same computation as our pca, so the fractions of variance must agree to float32 precision (32-bit floating point). The sign of a component is arbitrary in both programs, so components are compared through the absolute cosine of the angle between them. The first component is well separated from the rest of the spectrum and must agree. Components 2–5 have almost equal variances, and a nearly degenerate eigenvalue leaves its eigenvector poorly defined, so for them only the variances are compared. The cell asserts the agreement and prints the correlation of the two projections on the first component.


Code
L = 30
X30 = np.asarray(DATA_SETS[L][1].reshape(-1, L * L), np.float32)
sk_pca = PCA(n_components=5, svd_solver="full").fit(X30)
mu30, ratio30, Vt30 = pca(jnp.asarray(X30))
ratio30, Vt30 = np.asarray(ratio30), np.asarray(Vt30)
cos1 = abs(float(sk_pca.components_[0] @ Vt30[0]))
z1_sk = sk_pca.transform(X30)[:, 0]
corr_sk = abs(np.corrcoef(z1_sk, np.asarray((jnp.asarray(X30) - mu30) @ Vt30[0]))[0, 1])
print("fraction of variance, first 5 components:")
print("  JAX         ", np.round(ratio30[:5], 5))
print("  scikit-learn", np.round(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_, 5))
print(f"|cos| between the first components: {cos1:.8f} | correlation of the projections on PC 1: {corr_sk:.8f}")
assert np.allclose(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_, ratio30[:5], rtol=1e-3)
assert cos1 > 0.99999 and corr_sk > 0.99999
NUMBERS["pca_sklearn_var1"] = round(float(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]), 4)

title: Lab 019: The 2D Ising transition without labels
text:
3. Autoencoder anomaly detection
PCA found the order parameter because it is linear in the spins. A different unsupervised approach does not look for an order parameter at all (Kottmann, Huembeli, Lewenstein, Acín, Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 170603 (2020)). An autoencoder is trained only on configurations from a region we understand, and its reconstruction error serves as an anomaly score everywhere else. Inside the training region the error is small, and where the data stop looking like the training data it rises.
The architecture is the same for every \(L\). The \(N\) spins enter a dense layer of 128 units with the rectified linear activation \(\mathrm{ReLU}(u)=\max(0,u)\), then a latent layer of 8 numbers, and the decoder mirrors this and ends with \(\tanh\), so \(\tilde s_i\in[-1,1]\). The loss is \(\frac1N\lVert\mathbf s-\tilde{\mathbf s}\rVert^2\), minimised with Adam (adaptive moment estimation), a gradient descent in which the step of every parameter is set by running averages of its gradient and of its squared gradient.
The model is built with Flax NNX, the current interface (flax.nnx) of the neural-network library Flax for JAX. A model is a Python object (nnx.Module) whose layers hold their parameters. nnx.Optimizer holds the optax state, nnx.value_and_grad differentiates a loss with respect to the model’s parameters, and nnx.jit compiles the whole training step.


Code
class DenseAE(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in, latent=8, hidden=128, *, rngs):
        self.e1 = nnx.Linear(n_in, hidden, rngs=rngs); self.e2 = nnx.Linear(hidden, latent, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1 = nnx.Linear(latent, hidden, rngs=rngs); self.d2 = nnx.Linear(hidden, n_in, rngs=rngs)
    def encode(self, x):
        return self.e2(nnx.relu(self.e1(x)))
    def __call__(self, x):
        return jnp.tanh(self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(self.encode(x)))))

@nnx.jit
def train_step(model, opt, x):
    loss, grads = nnx.value_and_grad(lambda m: jnp.mean((m(x) - x) ** 2))(model)
    opt.update(model, grads)
    return loss

@nnx.jit
def recon_error(model, x):
    return jnp.mean((model(x) - x) ** 2, axis=-1)

def train_ae(X_train, epochs=200, batch=64, seed=0, lr=1e-3):
    model = DenseAE(X_train.shape[1], rngs=nnx.Rngs(seed))
    opt = nnx.Optimizer(model, optax.adam(lr), wrt=nnx.Param)
    X_train = jnp.asarray(X_train, jnp.float32); n = X_train.shape[0]
    key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed); hist = []
    for ep in range(epochs):
        key, k = jax.random.split(key)
        perm = jax.random.permutation(k, n)
        for i in range(0, n - batch + 1, batch):
            loss = train_step(model, opt, X_train[perm[i:i + batch]])
        hist.append(float(loss))
    return model, hist

def error_vs_T(model, L):
    T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
    e = recon_error(model, jnp.asarray(s.reshape(-1, L * L), jnp.float32))
    return np.asarray(e).reshape(len(T), -1)



3.1 Training on the ordered phase
The well-understood region is the deep ordered phase, \(T\le1.7\), where Yang’s formula gives \(M>0.97\) (the cell prints the value). We train one autoencoder per lattice size and three random seeds per size, and record the reconstruction error at every temperature.
The rise of the error has to be located in a way that is robust to noise. The mean reconstruction error \(\bar\varepsilon(T)=\langle\varepsilon(\mathbf s)\rangle_T\), with \(\varepsilon(\mathbf s)=\frac1N\sum_i(s_i-\tilde s_i)^2\) averaged over the configurations sampled at temperature \(T\), rises like a smoothed step, and we fit \[
\bar\varepsilon(T) = a + b\,\tanh\!\left(\frac{T-T_{\mathrm{AE}}}{\delta}\right)
\] on \(1.9\le T\le 3.0\). The centre of the step \(T_{\mathrm{AE}}(L)\) and its width \(\delta(L)\) are the result. A fit uses all temperatures at once and is less sensitive to noise than the position of the steepest slope between two grid points.
The susceptibility peak has a known finite-size law, \(T_c(L)-T_c\propto L^{-1/\nu}\), so it can be extrapolated. The autoencoder signal is not a thermodynamic observable and has no derived law. We therefore watch how \(T_{\mathrm{AE}}(L)\) and \(\delta(L)\) change with \(L\), and compare the width with the finite-size rounding of the transition, \(\propto L^{-1/\nu}=L^{-1}\).


Code
T_TRAIN_MAX = 1.7
print(f"Yang: M(T = {T_TRAIN_MAX}) = {(1 - np.sinh(2 / T_TRAIN_MAX) ** -4) ** 0.125:.4f}")

from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

def step_fit(T, err, lo=1.9, hi=3.0):
    sel = (T >= lo) & (T <= hi)
    f = lambda t, a, b, t0, w: a + b * np.tanh((t - t0) / w)
    p0 = [0.5 * (err[sel].max() + err[sel].min()), 0.5 * (err[sel].max() - err[sel].min()), TC, 0.1]
    (a, b, t0, w), _ = curve_fit(f, T[sel], err[sel], p0=p0, maxfev=20000)
    return t0, abs(w)

SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]
ae_curves, T_star, W_star = {}, {}, {}
t0 = time.time()
for L in L_LIST:
    T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
    X_tr = s[T <= T_TRAIN_MAX].reshape(-1, L * L)
    curves = []
    for seed in SEEDS:
        model, hist = train_ae(X_tr, seed=seed)
        curves.append(error_vs_T(model, L).mean(1))
    ae_curves[L] = np.array(curves)
    fits = np.array([step_fit(T, c) for c in curves])
    T_star[L], W_star[L] = fits[:, 0], fits[:, 1]
    print(f"L = {L:2d}: train on {X_tr.shape[0]} configs, final loss {hist[-1]:.4f};  T* = {T_star[L].mean():.4f} +- {T_star[L].std():.1e},"
          f"  width Delta = {W_star[L].mean():.4f} +- {W_star[L].std():.1e} (mean +- std over {len(SEEDS)} seeds)   ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")
    if L == 30:                                                  # one example for the slides: input and reconstruction
        x_ex = jnp.asarray(s[np.argmin(abs(T - 2.0)), 0].reshape(1, -1), jnp.float32)
        for name, img in [("gen_ising_ae_in.png", x_ex), ("gen_ising_ae_out.png", model(x_ex))]:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(1.6, 1.6))
            ax.imshow(np.asarray(img).reshape(L, L), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1); ax.axis("off")
            fig.savefig(f"{FIG}/{name}", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight", pad_inches=0); plt.close(fig)

In the figure the centre carries the label \(T^\ast\) and the width the label \(\Delta\).

REGIMES = {"ordered, $T\\leq1.7$": lambda T: T <= 1.7,
           "paramagnet, $T\\geq3.0$": lambda T: T >= 3.0,

regime_curves, regime_T = {}, {}
t0 = time.time()
for name, rule in REGIMES.items():
    for L in L_LIST:
        T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
        model, _ = train_ae(s[rule(T)].reshape(-1, L * L), seed=0)
        e = error_vs_T(model, L).mean(1)
        regime_curves[(name, L)] = e
        regime_T[(name, L)] = step_fit(T, e)[0]
    print(f"{name:32s}: T* = " + ", ".join(f"L={L}: {regime_T[(name, L)]:.3f}" for L in L_LIST) + f"   ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    # top row: the error curves of the three training regimes; bottom row: the step centre T* against 1/L
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, len(REGIMES), figsize=(5.5, 2.7), gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.3, 1]))
    for r, (name, rule) in enumerate(REGIMES.items()):
        a = axes[0, r]
        for L in L_LIST:
            T = DATA_SETS[L][0]; e = regime_curves[(name, L)]
            a.plot(T, e, ".-", color=size_colors[L], label=f"$L={L}$")
        T = DATA_SETS[L_LIST[0]][0]
        a.fill_between(T, 0, 1, where=rule(T), transform=a.get_xaxis_transform(), color=UJBlue, alpha=0.1)
        a.axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":"); a.set_title(name, fontsize=10); a.set_xlabel("$T$")

        b.plot(1.0 / np.array(L_LIST), [regime_T[(name, L)] for L in L_LIST], "o", color=DSOrange)
        b.axhline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":"); b.set_ylim(2.1, 2.45); b.set_xlabel("$1/L$")
    axes[0, 0].set_ylabel(r"$\bar\varepsilon(T)$"); axes[1, 0].set_ylabel(r"$T_{\rm AE}$")
    fig.legend(*axes[0, 0].get_legend_handles_labels(), frameon=False, loc="upper center", ncol=3, borderaxespad=0.1)   # legend above the panels
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.93), h_pad=0.3, w_pad=1.2); savefig(fig, "gen_ising_ae_regimes.png"); plt.show()

                          for name in REGIMES}

The answer depends on the training region. Trained on the ordered phase, the centres \(T_{\mathrm{AE}}=2.308\), \(2.278\), \(2.264\) for \(L=20\), 30, 50 move towards \(T_c\). Trained on the paramagnet, the centres \(2.279\), \(2.253\), \(2.197\) drift below \(T_c\) as \(L\) grows. Trained around \(T_c\), the jump of the error sits close to the upper edge of the training window, \(T=2.34\), at \(2.389\), \(2.363\), \(2.328\). The detector tells whether a configuration resembles its training data, so its answer depends on that data, and the region to train on is a well-structured, well-understood phase.


3.3 Latent space and the magnetisation
The error tells us where the data change, but not what the autoencoder has learned. The 8 latent numbers of an autoencoder trained on all temperatures are compressed descriptions of a configuration, and a linear regression from the latent vector to \(m\) measures how much of the order parameter is stored there. A coefficient of determination \(R^2\) close to 1 means that \(m\) is a linear function of the latent numbers.


Code
L = 30
T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
X_all = s.reshape(-1, L * L)
model_all, _ = train_ae(X_all, epochs=60, seed=0)
Z = np.asarray(model_all.encode(jnp.asarray(X_all, jnp.float32)))
m_abs = np.abs(M[L]).ravel(); m_sgn = M[L].ravel()
A_lat = np.hstack([Z, np.ones((len(Z), 1))])
coef = np.linalg.lstsq(A_lat, m_sgn, rcond=None)[0]
r2 = 1 - np.var(m_sgn - A_lat @ coef) / np.var(m_sgn)
print(f"linear readout of m from the 8 latent numbers: R^2 = {r2:.4f}")
NUMBERS["ae_latent_R2_m"] = round(float(r2), 4)


linear readout of m from the 8 latent numbers: R^2 = 0.9942

4. Summary

Binder cumulant, \(\chi\)

PCA

autoencoder, anomaly score
spins from one window of \(T\)
the centre \(T_{\mathrm{AE}}(L)\) and width \(\delta(L)\) of the step in the error

PCA gives an order parameter, after which the full finite-size analysis applies, and the Binder crossings from \(w^{(1)}\) agree with those from \(m\) within \(0.002\). The autoencoder gives a signal, the place where the data stop resembling the training data. Trained on the ordered phase, its centre approaches \(T_c\) with \(L\) and its width shrinks with \(L\), the properties we expect from a detector of the transition. Trained on the paramagnet or around \(T_c\), the centre moves elsewhere, so the signal depends on the training data. The latent vector of an autoencoder trained on all temperatures stores the magnetisation, with \(R^2=0.9942\) for a linear readout. With three lattice sizes the power law of the width is only indicative, and the signal has no derived finite-size law. Its use is exploration, as a pointer to the region where a careful conventional analysis is worth doing.

Exercises

Replace the mean reconstruction error by its variance over configurations at each \(T\) and compare the position of its peak with \(T_c\).
Train with latent dimension 1 and correlate the single latent number with \(m\) and with the energy.
Move the upper edge of the ordered training window from \(T=1.7\) to \(T=2.1\) and follow how \(T_{\mathrm{AE}}(L)\) changes.

title: Lab 020: The J1–J2 phase diagram without labels
text:
1. Reference maps from known observables
Every unsupervised result needs something to be judged against. We recompute the three maps of Lab 018 from the same snapshots, the magnetisation \(\langle|m|\rangle\), stripe order parameter \(\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle\), and specific heat \(c\). Each is a thermal average over the Boltzmann distribution, \(\langle O\rangle=\frac1Z\sum_{\mathbf s}O(\mathbf s)\,e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}\) with \(Z=\sum_{\mathbf s}e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}\) and \(\beta=1/T\), and is estimated from the \(n=100\) snapshots \(\mathbf s^{(k)}\) of each grid point by sample means. With \(e_k=H(\mathbf s^{(k)})/N\) (computed from the local field of every spin, function local_field), \(m_k=\frac1N\sum_is^{(k)}_i\) and \(\overline{x}=\frac1n\sum_kx_k\), the function observables computes the estimators of the table.








observable
definition through \(Z\)
estimator from \(n\) samples (as in the code)




magnetisation
\(\langle\lvert m\rvert\rangle=\frac1Z\sum_{\mathbf s}\lvert m(\mathbf s)\rvert e^{-\beta H}\)
\(\overline{\lvert m\rvert}=\frac1n\sum_k\lvert m_k\rvert\)


stripe order
\(\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle\), \(m_{\rm str}=\sqrt{m_{(\pi,0)}^2+m_{(0,\pi)}^2}\), \(m_{(\pi,0)}=\frac1N\sum_{\mathbf r}(-1)^{x}s_{\mathbf r}\), \(m_{(0,\pi)}=\frac1N\sum_{\mathbf r}(-1)^{y}s_{\mathbf r}\)
\(\overline{m_{\rm str}}=\frac1n\sum_km_{{\rm str},k}\)


specific heat
\(c=\frac{\beta^2}{N}\partial^2_\beta\ln Z=N\beta^2\big(\langle e^2\rangle-\langle e\rangle^2\big)\)
\(N\beta^2\big(\overline{e^2}-\overline{e}^{\,2}\big)\) (population variance, division by \(n\))



From the specific heat we extract the reference boundary, for every \(g\) the temperature of the maximum of \(c\). The figure shows the three maps over the \((g,T)\) plane, with the reference boundary as white dots. These are the known properties against which every unsupervised result is judged.


Code
def local_field(s, g):
    nn = jnp.roll(s, 1, -2) + jnp.roll(s, -1, -2) + jnp.roll(s, 1, -1) + jnp.roll(s, -1, -1)
    nnn = (jnp.roll(s, (1, 1), (-2, -1)) + jnp.roll(s, (1, -1), (-2, -1))
           + jnp.roll(s, (-1, 1), (-2, -1)) + jnp.roll(s, (-1, -1), (-2, -1)))
    return nn - g * nnn

@jax.jit
def observables(s, g):
    ph = jnp.where(jnp.arange(L) % 2 == 0, 1.0, -1.0)
    m = jnp.abs(s.mean((-2, -1)))
    ms = jnp.sqrt((s * ph[:, None]).mean((-2, -1)) ** 2 + (s * ph[None, :]).mean((-2, -1)) ** 2)
    e = -0.5 * jnp.mean(s * local_field(s, g), axis=(-2, -1))
    return m.mean(-1), ms.mean(-1), e.var(-1)

obs = [observables(jnp.asarray(S[i], jnp.float32), G[i]) for i in range(nG)]
M_map, Ms_map, varE = (np.stack([np.asarray(o[k]) for o in obs]) for k in range(3))
C_map = L * L * varE / T[None, :] ** 2
T_c_ref = T[np.argmax(C_map, axis=1)]                     # specific-heat peak for every g

def draw_reference(ax, color="w", label=True):
    ax.plot(G, T_c_ref, "o", ms=2.5, color=color, label="specific-heat peak" if label else None)

def show_map(ax, Z, title, cmap="viridis", vmin=None, vmax=None, cbar_label=None):
    im = ax.pcolormesh(G, T, Z.T, shading="nearest", cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax)
    ax.set_xlabel("$g=J_2/J_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("$T$"); ax.set_title(title)
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, label=cbar_label)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6))
show_map(ax[0], M_map, r"$\langle|m|\rangle$", vmin=0, vmax=1)
show_map(ax[1], Ms_map, r"$\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle$", vmin=0, vmax=1)
show_map(ax[2], C_map, r"specific heat $c$", cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=np.percentile(C_map, 99))
for a in ax: draw_reference(a, label=False)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The specific-heat peak traces both boundaries, \(T_c(g)\) falling towards \(g=1/2\) from both sides. Near \(g=1/2\) at low temperature the peak position is not reliable, because there the system does not order down to our lowest temperature and \(c\) shows only a broad maximum.

title: Lab 020: The J1–J2 phase diagram without labels
text:
2. PCA on all snapshots

2.1 PCA implementation in JAX
All snapshots from the whole grid (a subset of 20 per grid point) go into one PCA, with no information about \(g\) or \(T\). We look at the leading principal directions \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1,\boldsymbol\lambda_2,\dots\) (unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, also called PC 1, PC 2, …) as images on the lattice, and we measure their overlap with the three candidate ordering patterns of Lab 018, uniform \((0,0)\) and stripes \((\pi,0)\) and \((0,\pi)\). With \(\mathbf p\) a pattern of entries \(\pm1\), the overlap is \(|\boldsymbol\lambda_l^{\top}\mathbf p|/\sqrt N\), the absolute cosine of the angle between the two vectors, and an overlap of 1 means that a component is that pattern.


Code
n_pca = 20
Xp = jnp.asarray(S[:, :, :n_pca].reshape(-1, L * L), jnp.float32)

@jax.jit
def pca(X):
    mu = X.mean(0)
    _, sv, Vt = jnp.linalg.svd(X - mu, full_matrices=False)
    return mu, sv**2 / jnp.sum(sv**2), Vt

mu, var_ratio, Vt = pca(Xp)
var_ratio, Vt = np.asarray(var_ratio), np.asarray(Vt)
x = np.arange(L)
patterns = {"uniform (0,0)": np.ones((L, L)), "stripes (pi,0)": np.outer((-1.0) ** x, np.ones(L)),
            "stripes (0,pi)": np.outer(np.ones(L), (-1.0) ** x)}
overlaps = np.array([[abs((Vt[k].reshape(L, L) * p).sum()) / L for p in patterns.values()] for k in range(6)])
print("explained variance ratio:", np.round(var_ratio[:6], 4))
for k in range(6):
    print(f"PC{k + 1}: " + "  ".join(f"{n} {o:.3f}" for n, o in zip(patterns, overlaps[k])))
NUMBERS.update(pca_var=[round(float(v), 4) for v in var_ratio[:6]],
               pca_overlaps=[[round(float(o), 3) for o in row] for row in overlaps[:4]])


explained variance ratio: [0.1659 0.0839 0.0822 0.0031 0.003  0.0028]
PC1: uniform (0,0) 1.000  stripes (pi,0) 0.001  stripes (0,pi) 0.001
PC2: uniform (0,0) 0.001  stripes (pi,0) 1.000  stripes (0,pi) 0.024
PC3: uniform (0,0) 0.001  stripes (pi,0) 0.024  stripes (0,pi) 1.000
PC4: uniform (0,0) 0.001  stripes (pi,0) 0.000  stripes (0,pi) 0.000
PC5: uniform (0,0) 0.002  stripes (pi,0) 0.000  stripes (0,pi) 0.000
PC6: uniform (0,0) 0.001  stripes (pi,0) 0.000  stripes (0,pi) 0.000


Projecting every snapshot \(\mathbf s\) on the first three directions, \(w^{(l)}=\boldsymbol\lambda_l^{\top}(\mathbf s-\bar{\mathbf s})\), gives two order-parameter candidates, \(|w^{(1)}|\) from the uniform direction and \(\sqrt{(w^{(2)})^2+(w^{(3)})^2}\) from the two stripe directions. We map their averages over the \((g,T)\) plane and correlate them with the known order parameters of Section 1. In the figure the top row shows the first three principal directions on a \(12\times12\) corner of the lattice with their fractions of the variance, and the fractions \(\sigma_l^2/\sum\sigma^2\) of the first ten components. The bottom row shows the maps of \(\langle|w^{(1)}|\rangle/\sqrt N\) and \(\langle\sqrt{(w^{(2)})^2+(w^{(3)})^2}\rangle/\sqrt N\), with the specific-heat peaks as white dots.


Code
z = np.asarray((jnp.asarray(S.reshape(-1, L * L), jnp.float32) - mu) @ Vt[:3].T).reshape(nG, nT, nS, 3) / L
pc_uniform = np.abs(z[..., 0]).mean(-1)
pc_stripe = np.sqrt(z[..., 1] ** 2 + z[..., 2] ** 2).mean(-1)

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    # drawn at its size on the slide (5.5 x 2.6 in, full text width); top: the first three components on a 12 x 12 corner
    # of the lattice and the variance spectrum, bottom: the two order-parameter maps built from them
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.6))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 4, height_ratios=[1.0, 1.15])
    for k in range(3):
        a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, k])
        a.imshow(Vt[k].reshape(L, L)[:12, :12] * L, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1.5, vmax=1.5)
        a.set_title(rf"$\boldsymbol{{\lambda}}_{k + 1}$: {100 * var_ratio[k]:.1f}%", fontsize=11); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 3])
    a.bar(np.arange(1, 11), 100 * var_ratio[:10], color=UJBlue); a.set_title(r"$\sigma_l^2/\sum\sigma^2$ (%)", fontsize=11)
    a.set_xticks([1, 5, 10])
    a2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0:2]); show_map(a2, pc_uniform, r"$\langle|w^{(1)}|\rangle/\sqrt{N}$", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    a3 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2:4]); show_map(a3, pc_stripe, r"$\langle\sqrt{(w^{(2)})^2+(w^{(3)})^2}\rangle/\sqrt{N}$", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    for a in (a2, a3): draw_reference(a, label=False); a.title.set_fontsize(11)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.3, w_pad=0.6); savefig(fig, "gen_j1j2_pca.png"); plt.show()
corr_u = np.corrcoef(pc_uniform.ravel(), M_map.ravel())[0, 1]; corr_s = np.corrcoef(pc_stripe.ravel(), Ms_map.ravel())[0, 1]
print(f"correlation of the PC maps with the known order parameters:  <|w^(1)|> vs <|m|> {corr_u:.4f},  <sqrt(w^(2)^2 + w^(3)^2)> vs <m_str> {corr_s:.4f}")
NUMBERS.update(pca_corr_m=round(float(corr_u), 4), pca_corr_mstr=round(float(corr_s), 4))





correlation of the PC maps with the known order parameters:  <|w^(1)|> vs <|m|> 1.0000,  <sqrt(w^(2)^2 + w^(3)^2)> vs <m_str> 0.9999


The first three principal components are the uniform pattern and the two stripe patterns (overlaps close to 1), and the rest of the spectrum is flat. Projecting on them reproduces both order-parameter maps, with correlations 1.0000 and 0.9999. PCA has found the stripe order parameter, the quantity the magnetisation scan missed, without being told it exists.
It works here because both order parameters are linear functions of the spins, \(m=\frac1N\sum_r s_r\) and \(m_{(\pi,0)}=\frac1N\sum_r(-1)^{x}s_r\), and patterns that are linear in the data are what PCA is built to find. Order that is not linear in the spins (vortices in the XY model of planar spins, Wilson loops in gauge theories, the overlap of a spin glass) cannot appear as a single principal direction of the raw spins. Labs 021–023 test this.
One detail of the spectrum is a property of our data and not of the model. PC 2 and PC 3 carry slightly different variances, 0.0839 and 0.0822, although vertical and horizontal stripes are equivalent by symmetry. Each annealed chain picks one orientation when it orders and keeps it, so with a finite number of chains the two orientations are not sampled equally.


2.2 PCA with scikit-learn
The same analysis with scikit-learn uses the estimator PCA(n_components=6, svd_solver="full"). Its fit(X) centres the snapshots, performs a complete singular value decomposition (SVD) and stores the components as the rows of components_ and their fractions of the variance in explained_variance_ratio_, and transform(X) would return the projections \(w^{(l)}\). The computation is the one our pca performs, so the fractions of variance must agree to float32 precision (32-bit floating point). Single components are defined only up to sign, and PC 2 and PC 3 carry similar variances, so a small rounding difference could rotate them into each other. We therefore compare the three-dimensional subspace spanned by PC 1–3. Its principal angles with our subspace are the arccosines of the singular values of \(V_{\rm sk}V^{\top}\), where the rows of \(V_{\rm sk}\) and \(V\) are the two sets of principal directions \(\boldsymbol\lambda_l^{\top}\), and all three singular values must be 1. The cell asserts both statements.


Code
t0 = time.time()
sk_pca = PCA(n_components=6, svd_solver="full").fit(np.asarray(Xp))
print(f"scikit-learn PCA of {Xp.shape[0]} x {Xp.shape[1]} snapshots: {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")
print("fraction of variance: JAX         ", np.round(var_ratio[:6], 5))
print("                      scikit-learn", np.round(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_, 5))
cos_sub = np.linalg.svd(sk_pca.components_[:3] @ Vt[:3].T, compute_uv=False)
print("cosines of the principal angles between the two PC 1-3 subspaces:", np.round(cos_sub, 7))
print("overlaps of the scikit-learn components with the patterns:")
for k in range(3):
    print(f"  PC{k + 1}: " + "  ".join(f"{n} {abs((sk_pca.components_[k].reshape(L, L) * q).sum()) / L:.3f}" for n, q in patterns.items()))
assert np.allclose(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_, var_ratio[:6], rtol=1e-3)
assert cos_sub.min() > 0.9999


scikit-learn PCA of 127980 x 1024 snapshots: 14.9 s
fraction of variance: JAX          [0.1659  0.0839  0.08216 0.00306 0.003   0.00281]
                      scikit-learn [0.1659  0.0839  0.08216 0.00306 0.003   0.00281]
cosines of the principal angles between the two PC 1-3 subspaces: [1.0000007 1.0000006 1.0000002]
overlaps of the scikit-learn components with the patterns:
  PC1: uniform (0,0) 1.000  stripes (pi,0) 0.001  stripes (0,pi) 0.001
  PC2: uniform (0,0) 0.001  stripes (pi,0) 1.000  stripes (0,pi) 0.024

title: Lab 020: The J1–J2 phase diagram without labels
text:
3. Autoencoder anomaly maps
PCA needed the order to be linear in the spins. Anomaly detection with an autoencoder makes no such assumption and locates the places where the snapshots stop looking like those of a region we understand. The procedure has four parts. 1. Choose a training region, a small rectangle in the \((g,T)\) plane where we trust our understanding. 2. Train an autoencoder on snapshots from that rectangle only. 3. Evaluate the reconstruction error \(\varepsilon(\boldsymbol s)=\frac1N\lVert\boldsymbol s-\tilde{\boldsymbol s}\rVert^2\) on snapshots from every grid point, and plot its mean \(\bar\varepsilon\) as a map. 4. Read off a boundary, for every \(g\) the temperature where \(\bar\varepsilon\) changes fastest.
We repeat this for three training regions, all in corners of the plane.








regime
region
what we know there




A, ferromagnet
\(g\le0.2\), \(T\le1.0\)
nearly saturated ferromagnet (weak \(J_2\), low \(T\))


B, paramagnet
\(g\le0.2\), \(T\ge3.5\)
high temperature, weakly correlated spins


C, stripes
\(g\ge0.8\), \(T\le1.0\)
strong \(J_2\), low \(T\), stripe order



The autoencoder is a small convolutional network. Two stride-2 convolutions with periodic boundaries, like the lattice, reduce \(32\times32\) to \(16\times16\) and \(8\times8\), a dense bottleneck holds 4 numbers, and the mirror image leads back, ending with \(\tanh\).
One known symmetry is built into the training data. The energy is unchanged when all spins flip, \(H(\boldsymbol s)=H(-\boldsymbol s)\), so \(\boldsymbol s\) and \(-\boldsymbol s\) are equally likely. A finite training set need not contain both signs equally often (an annealed chain orders into one of them and stays there), so we add every training snapshot also with all spins flipped.


Code
class ConvAE(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent=4, *, rngs):
        self.c1 = nnx.Conv(1, 16, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="CIRCULAR", rngs=rngs)      # 32 -> 16
        self.c2 = nnx.Conv(16, 32, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="CIRCULAR", rngs=rngs)     # 16 -> 8
        self.fe = nnx.Linear(8 * 8 * 32, latent, rngs=rngs)
        self.fd = nnx.Linear(latent, 8 * 8 * 32, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1 = nnx.ConvTranspose(32, 16, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2), padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)
        self.d2 = nnx.ConvTranspose(16, 1, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2), padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)
    def encode(self, x):
        h = nnx.relu(self.c1(x[..., None])); h = nnx.relu(self.c2(h))
        return self.fe(h.reshape(h.shape[0], -1))
    def __call__(self, x):
        h = nnx.relu(self.fd(self.encode(x))).reshape(-1, 8, 8, 32)
        return jnp.tanh(self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(h)))[..., 0])

@nnx.jit
def train_step(model, opt, x):
    loss, grads = nnx.value_and_grad(lambda m: jnp.mean((m(x) - x) ** 2))(model)
    opt.update(model, grads)
    return loss

@nnx.jit
def recon_error(model, x):
    return jnp.mean((model(x) - x) ** 2, axis=(-2, -1))

def train_ae(X, epochs=15, batch=64, seed=0):
    model = ConvAE(rngs=nnx.Rngs(seed))
    opt = nnx.Optimizer(model, optax.adam(1e-3), wrt=nnx.Param)
    X = jnp.asarray(np.concatenate([X, -X]), jnp.float32)  # H(s) = H(-s): every snapshot also with all spins flipped
    key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        key, k = jax.random.split(key); perm = jax.random.permutation(k, X.shape[0])
        for i in range(0, X.shape[0] - batch + 1, batch):
            loss = train_step(model, opt, X[perm[i:i + batch]])
    return model, float(loss)

N_EVAL = 20                                                # snapshots per grid point used for the maps
def spread(n_total, n):                                    # n snapshot indices spread over all chains
    return np.linspace(0, n_total - 1, n).round().astype(int)

def error_map(model, data=S, n=N_EVAL):
    idx = spread(data.shape[2], n)
    out = np.zeros(data.shape[:2])
    for i in range(data.shape[0]):
        e = recon_error(model, jnp.asarray(data[i][:, idx].reshape(-1, L, L), jnp.float32))
        out[i] = np.asarray(e).reshape(data.shape[1], n).mean(1)
    return out

def boundary_from_map(err, T_axis=T):
    # for every g: temperature of the fastest change of the error along T (midpoint between grid temperatures),
    # and the size of that change relative to the full range of the map
    d = np.abs(np.diff(err, axis=1))
    i = np.argmax(d, axis=1)
    return 0.5 * (T_axis[i] + T_axis[i + 1]), d[np.arange(len(i)), i] / (err.max() - err.min())

REGIMES = {"A: ferromagnet": dict(g=(0.0, 0.2), T=(0.0, 1.0), color=UJBlue),
           "B: paramagnet": dict(g=(0.0, 0.2), T=(3.5, 9.9), color=DSOrange),
           "C: stripes": dict(g=(0.8, 1.0), T=(0.0, 1.0), color="#2E8B57")}
N_TRAIN = 40                                               # snapshots per grid point used for training
JUMP_MIN = 0.15                                            # a boundary point needs a jump of >= 15% of the map's range




Code
results = {}
for name, r in REGIMES.items():
    gi = (G >= r["g"][0] - 1e-9) & (G <= r["g"][1] + 1e-9); ti = (T >= r["T"][0] - 1e-9) & (T <= r["T"][1] + 1e-9)
    X_tr = S[gi][:, ti][:, :, spread(nS, N_TRAIN)].reshape(-1, L, L)
    t0 = time.time()
    model, loss = train_ae(X_tr)
    err = error_map(model)
    Tb, jump = boundary_from_map(err)
    results[name] = dict(model=model, err=err, Tb=Tb, jump=jump, gi=gi, ti=ti, n_train=X_tr.shape[0])
    in_err = err[np.ix_(gi, ti)].mean()
    print(f"{name:16s}: {X_tr.shape[0]:5d} training snapshots, final loss {loss:.4f}, mean error inside region {in_err:.4f}, "
          f"min/max over map {err.min():.4f}/{err.max():.4f}   ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")

B: paramagnet   :  7480 training snapshots, final loss 0.9863, mean error inside region 0.9859, min/max over map 0.1785/1.0018   (85 s)


C: stripes      : 12920 training snapshots, final loss 0.0005, mean error inside region 0.0006, min/max over map 0.0000/2.0057   (103 s)




Code
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 2.2))
    for a, (name, r) in zip(axes, REGIMES.items()):
        res = results[name]
        show_map(a, res["err"], name, cmap="cividis")
        a.add_patch(Rectangle((r["g"][0] - 0.0125, max(r["T"][0], T.min()) - 0.05), r["g"][1] - r["g"][0] + 0.025,
                              min(r["T"][1], T.max()) - max(r["T"][0], T.min()) + 0.1, fill=False, ec=r["color"], lw=1.5))
        strong = res["jump"] > JUMP_MIN
        a.plot(G[strong], res["Tb"][strong], "o", ms=2.5, color=r["color"], mec="w", mew=0.5, label="detected boundary")
        a.set_ylim(T.min() - 0.05, T.max() + 0.05)
    fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_j1j2_ae_maps.png"); plt.show()





For every \(g\) the boundary point is the temperature where the mean error changes fastest between neighbouring grid temperatures, and it is drawn only if that change is at least 15% of the full range of the map. In each map the colour is the mean reconstruction error \(\bar\varepsilon\) of that regime’s autoencoder, the rectangle marks its training region, and the dots are the detected boundary points.
The autoencoder of regime A, trained on the ferromagnet, reconstructs the ferromagnetic region almost perfectly, and its boundary \(T_c(g)\) for \(g<1/2\) is a sharp edge that falls towards \(g=1/2\). Everything else, paramagnet and stripes, is “not ferromagnet” with similar large errors, so this regime cannot separate the stripe phase from the paramagnet.
Regime B, trained on nearly uncorrelated spins, learns little more than the average, and its error is large everywhere. Ferromagnetic snapshots are reconstructed better than the training data, so the ferromagnetic boundary is visible as a drop of the error. The stripe phase is invisible, with the same error as the paramagnet.
Regime C, trained on the stripes, reconstructs the stripe region well, and its boundary \(T_c(g)\) for \(g>1/2\) appears. The ferromagnet and the paramagnet are both anomalous.
One training region tests only whether a snapshot resembles its training data, and it cannot tell two different anomalies apart. The next figure puts the detected boundaries of all three regimes (open circles) on the specific-heat map (grey scale) with its maxima (black dots) and the mean-field transition lines (dotted), \(T_{\rm MF}=4J_1(1-g)\) for the ferromagnet and \(T_{\rm MF}=4J_1g\) for the stripes. Mean-field theory replaces the neighbours of every spin by their average magnetisation, which neglects fluctuations and overestimates transition temperatures.

Where an autoencoder detects a boundary, it lies on the specific-heat ridge to within the grid spacing in temperature (\(\Delta T=0.05\)), with a median deviation of \(0.025\) for each regime (printed above). Each regime sees only the boundaries of its own phase. A and B find the ferromagnetic line, and C finds the stripe line. None of them is reliable close to \(g=1/2\), where the transition temperature goes to zero and no phase is fully developed within our temperature range. The mean-field lines lie far above the specific-heat ridge for every \(g\).

title: Lab 020: The J1–J2 phase diagram without labels
text:
4. Combined map
Each regime recognises only its own phase, so we combine them. Each trained autoencoder defines a normal level of its reconstruction error, measured on its own training region. For grid point \((g,T)\) and regime \(k\) the anomaly score measures how far the mean error lies from that level, in units of its spread, \[
a_k(g,T) = \frac{\left|\,\bar\varepsilon_k(g,T) - \mu_k\right|}{\sigma_k},
\] where \(\mu_k\) and \(\sigma_k\) are the mean and standard deviation of \(\bar\varepsilon_k\) over the grid points of the training region. The absolute value matters, because regime B reconstructs ferromagnetic snapshots better than its training data, which is also an anomaly. A grid point is assigned to the regime with the smallest score if that score is below 3. Otherwise it is unassigned, since it looks like none of the three references. In the figure every grid point is coloured by its regime, or grey if unassigned, and the black dots mark the specific-heat maxima.


Code
names = list(REGIMES)
scores = []
for name in names:
    res = results[name]
    inside = res["err"][np.ix_(res["gi"], res["ti"])]
    scores.append(np.abs(res["err"] - inside.mean()) / (inside.std() + 1e-3))   # small floor: the ordered regions are almost exact
scores = np.stack(scores)                                    # (3, nG, nT)
assign = np.argmin(scores, axis=0)
assign = np.where(scores.min(0) < 3.0, assign, len(names))
colors = [REGIMES[n]["color"] for n in names] + ["#D9D9D9"]
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.0, 2.8))
    ax.pcolormesh(G, T, assign.T, shading="nearest", cmap=ListedColormap(colors), vmin=-0.5, vmax=len(names) + 0.5)
    ax.plot(G, T_c_ref, "k.", ms=3, label="$c$ peak")
    for k, n in enumerate(names + ["unassigned"]):
        ax.plot([], [], "s", color=colors[k], ms=7, label=n)
    ax.set_xlabel("$g=J_2/J_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("$T$")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.45, 1.0), ncol=2, columnspacing=0.8,
              handletextpad=0.3, borderaxespad=0.2, labelspacing=0.25)
    fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_j1j2_ae_combined.png"); plt.show()
frac = {n: round(float((assign == k).mean()), 3) for k, n in enumerate(names + ["unassigned"])}
print("fraction of grid points:", frac)
un = assign == len(names)
print("unassigned points: g in", np.unique(G[np.where(un)[0]]).round(3), "\n                   T in", np.unique(T[np.where(un)[1]]).round(2))

The three colours reproduce the three known phases, and two further features need the physics to be understood. The unassigned band lies mainly on the ordered side of each transition line. There the system is ordered, but thermal fluctuations (flipped islands, domain walls) make the snapshots atypical for a model trained deep in the phase at \(T\le1\). The band marks where the references stop being representative, the critical region and its surroundings. Around \(g=1/2\) at the lowest temperatures the points are assigned to the paramagnet, in agreement with the physics, since at the frustrated point the transition temperature goes to zero and the system does not order within our temperature range.
None of this used an order parameter. It used a choice of reference regions, and the result depends on that choice (regime B alone would have missed the stripe phase entirely). Choosing the reference regions requires physical knowledge.

title: Lab 020: The J1–J2 phase diagram without labels
text:
5. Coarse scan and refinement
The maps above used the full grid. Suppose instead we can afford only a coarse scan, with every eighth value of \(g\) (\(\Delta g = 0.1\)), every eighth temperature (\(\Delta T = 0.4\)), and 10 snapshots per point. We train regimes A and C on the coarse data only, and look for intervals where the error jumps. Those intervals are where a dense measurement is worth paying for, and the cell compares the total number of snapshots of this strategy with that of the dense scan.


Code
gi_c = np.arange(0, nG, 8); ti_c = np.arange(0, nT, 8)
Gc, Tc_ax = G[gi_c], T[ti_c]
S_coarse = S[np.ix_(gi_c, ti_c)][:, :, spread(nS, 10)]
print(f"coarse grid: {len(Gc)} x {len(Tc_ax)} points x 10 snapshots = {S_coarse.shape[0] * S_coarse.shape[1] * 10} snapshots")

coarse = {}
for name in ["A: ferromagnet", "C: stripes"]:
    r = REGIMES[name]
    gsel = (Gc >= r["g"][0] - 1e-9) & (Gc <= r["g"][1] + 1e-9); tsel = (Tc_ax >= r["T"][0] - 1e-9) & (Tc_ax <= r["T"][1] + 1e-9)
    X_tr = S_coarse[gsel][:, tsel].reshape(-1, L, L)
    model, _ = train_ae(X_tr, epochs=40)
    err_c = error_map(model, S_coarse, n=10)
    Tb_c, jump_c = boundary_from_map(err_c, Tc_ax)
    i = np.argmax(np.abs(np.diff(err_c, axis=1)), axis=1)
    coarse[name] = dict(model=model, err=err_c, lo=Tc_ax[i], hi=Tc_ax[i + 1], jump=jump_c, n_train=X_tr.shape[0])
    print(f"{name}: trained on {X_tr.shape[0]} snapshots")

# refinement: for every coarse g with a clear jump, measure densely (all grid temperatures in the bracket, all snapshots)
refine_cost, refined = 0, {}
for name, c in coarse.items():
    model_c = c["model"]                                   # the model trained on the coarse data only
    pts = []
    for k, gval in enumerate(Gc):
        if c["jump"][k] < JUMP_MIN: continue
        g_idx = gi_c[k]; t_idx = np.where((T >= c["lo"][k] - 1e-9) & (T <= c["hi"][k] + 1e-9))[0]
        refine_cost += len(t_idx) * N_EVAL
        e = np.array([np.asarray(recon_error(model_c, jnp.asarray(S[g_idx, j, spread(nS, N_EVAL)], jnp.float32))).mean() for j in t_idx])
        j = np.argmax(np.abs(np.diff(e)))
        pts.append((gval, 0.5 * (T[t_idx[j]] + T[t_idx[j + 1]])))
    refined[name] = np.array(pts)

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.0, 3.0))
    ax.plot(G, T_c_ref, "k.", ms=3, label="$c$ peak (dense scan)")
    gg_, tt_ = np.meshgrid(Gc, Tc_ax, indexing="ij"); ax.plot(gg_.ravel(), tt_.ravel(), "+", color=UJGray, ms=3, label="coarse grid")
    for name, c in coarse.items():
        col = REGIMES[name]["color"]; ok = c["jump"] >= JUMP_MIN
        for k in np.where(ok)[0]:
            ax.plot([Gc[k], Gc[k]], [c["lo"][k], c["hi"][k]], "-", color=col, lw=3, alpha=0.35)
        if len(refined[name]): ax.plot(refined[name][:, 0], refined[name][:, 1], "o", color=col, ms=3.5, label=f"refined, regime {name[0]}")
    ax.set_xlabel("$g=J_2/J_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("$T$"); fig.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower center", ncol=2, columnspacing=0.8, handletextpad=0.3)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.2, 1, 1)); savefig(fig, "gen_j1j2_coarse.png"); plt.show()

dense_cost = nG * nT * nS
coarse_cost = S_coarse.shape[0] * S_coarse.shape[1] * 10
print(f"dense scan (specific heat): {dense_cost} snapshots")
print(f"coarse scan {coarse_cost} + refinement {refine_cost} = {coarse_cost + refine_cost} snapshots "
      f"({100 * (coarse_cost + refine_cost) / dense_cost:.1f}% of the dense scan)")
NUMBERS.update(cost_dense=int(dense_cost), cost_coarse=int(coarse_cost), cost_refine=int(refine_cost),
               cost_fraction=round(float((coarse_cost + refine_cost) / dense_cost), 3))

The shaded bars are the temperature brackets in which the coarse scan saw the error jump, the crosses mark the coarse grid, and the dots are the boundary points after measuring densely only inside those brackets. They land on the specific-heat ridge of the dense scan (black dots) at 0.5% of its cost in snapshots (printed above).
In an experiment this is the useful mode. A cheap survey with raw snapshots comes first, then dense, careful measurements only where the survey says something changes, analysed with the physicist’s tools (order parameters, finite-size scaling) once we know what to look for.

title: Lab 021: The 2D XY model without labels
section: 1. Reference values from the data set
text:
1. Reference values from the data set
Every file contains, besides the snapshots theta of shape (19, 192, L, L), the per-chain averages chain_moments of shape (19, 24, 9) accumulated over all 1000 measurement steps of each Monte Carlo chain. From them we recompute, as in Lab 030, the quantities against which the unsupervised results will be judged. These are the mean modulus of the magnetisation \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) with \(\boldsymbol m=\frac1N\sum_i(\cos\theta_i,\sin\theta_i)\) and \(N=L^2\), the energy per spin \(u=\langle H\rangle/N\), the specific heat \(c=(\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2)/(NT^2)\), the vortex density \(\langle n_v\rangle\) (plaquettes with non-zero winding number per site), and the helicity modulus (spin stiffness), the resistance of the spin system to a twist of the angles, \[
\Upsilon=\frac{1}{2N}\Big[\langle C_x+C_y\rangle-\beta\,\langle S_x^2+S_y^2\rangle\Big],\qquad
C_\mu=\sum_r\cos\phi^\mu_r,\quad S_\mu=\sum_r\sin\phi^\mu_r,\quad \phi^\mu_r=\theta_{r+\hat\mu}-\theta_r ,
\] with \(J=1\) and \(\beta=1/T\).
Each of these quantities has a definition and an estimator. The definition is an average over the Boltzmann distribution, \(\langle O\rangle=Z^{-1}\int d\boldsymbol\theta\,O(\boldsymbol\theta)\,e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol\theta)}\) with the partition function \(Z=\int d\boldsymbol\theta\,e^{-\beta H}\). The energy and the specific heat are derivatives of \(\ln Z\), \(u=-\frac1N\partial_\beta\ln Z\) and \(c=\frac{\beta^2}{N}\partial_\beta^2\ln Z=\frac{\beta^2}{N}(\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2)\). The helicity modulus is the curvature of the free energy \(F(\Delta)=-T\ln Z(\Delta)\) when every horizontal bond angle is shifted by \(\Delta/L\), a total twist \(\Delta\) across the sample, \(\Upsilon=\partial_\Delta^2F|_{\Delta=0}\), which gives the expression above (with \(\langle S_\mu\rangle=0\) by symmetry, and averaged over the two directions). The estimator is what the code computes from the \(n=24\times1000\) Monte Carlo measurements per temperature. Every \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) is replaced by the sample mean \(\overline{x}=\frac1n\sum_kx_k\), pooled over all chains and steps, so that \(u=\overline E/N\), \(c=\beta^2(\overline{E^2}-\overline E^{\,2})/N\) (a variance that divides by \(n\)), \(\Upsilon=[\overline{C_x+C_y}-\beta\,\overline{S_x^2+S_y^2}]/(2N)\), \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\to\overline{|\boldsymbol m|}\) and \(\langle n_v\rangle\to\overline{n_v}\). The quantities of the later sections follow the same pattern. The PCA coordinate is \(\overline{|\mathbf w|}/\sqrt N\) (defined in Section 3) over the 192 snapshots of a temperature, and the anomaly score \(\bar\varepsilon(T)\) is the sample mean of the reconstruction error over the 96 held-out snapshots (and over the two training seeds).
Two reference temperatures follow for each \(L\). The first is the crossing \(T^*(L)\) of \(\Upsilon_L(T)\) with the line \(2T/\pi\), the finite-size image of the universal jump, which approaches \(T_{\rm BKT}\) from above as \(L\) grows. The second is the position of the specific-heat maximum, from a parabola through the five grid points around it. Both are computed with the same code as in Lab 030, so the printed values must agree with the numbers quoted in the introduction.


Code
MOM = [str(s) for s in DS[16]["moment_names"]]                 # E, E2, C, S2, absm, m2, m4, nv, acc

def reference(d):
    # pooled averages over the 24 chains of every temperature -> dict of arrays of shape (nT,)
    L = int(d["L"]); N = L * L; beta = 1.0 / T_GRID
    v = d["chain_moments"].mean(1)                              # (nT, 9)
    col = lambda name: v[:, MOM.index(name)]
    return dict(absm=col("absm"), m2=col("m2"), u=col("E") / N, nv=col("nv"),
                c=beta**2 * (col("E2") - col("E") ** 2) / N,
                ups=(col("C") - beta * col("S2")) / (2 * N))

def crossing(T, ups):
    # temperature where ups(T) - 2T/pi changes sign, linear interpolation between grid points
    f = ups - 2 * T / np.pi
    i = np.nonzero((f[:-1] > 0) & (f[1:] <= 0))[0][0]
    return T[i] - f[i] * (T[i + 1] - T[i]) / (f[i + 1] - f[i])

def peak_parabola(T, y):
    # position of the maximum of y(T) from a parabola through the five grid points around the largest value
    i = int(np.argmax(y)); p = np.polyfit(T[i - 2:i + 3], y[i - 2:i + 3], 2)
    return -p[1] / (2 * p[0])

REF = {L: reference(DS[L]) for L in L_LIST}
T_UPS = {L: crossing(T_GRID, REF[L]["ups"]) for L in L_LIST}
T_CMAX = {L: peak_parabola(T_GRID, REF[L]["c"]) for L in L_LIST}
print(f"literature: T_BKT = {T_BKT_LIT:.4f}")
for L in L_LIST:
    print(f"L = {L}:  stiffness crossing T*(L) = {T_UPS[L]:.4f}   specific-heat maximum at T = {T_CMAX[L]:.3f}")
NUMBERS.update(T_BKT_literature=round(T_BKT_LIT, 4), **{f"T_ups_L{L}": round(float(T_UPS[L]), 4) for L in L_LIST},
               **{f"T_cmax_L{L}": round(float(T_CMAX[L]), 3) for L in L_LIST})

L = 48:  stiffness crossing T*(L) = 0.9170   specific-heat maximum at T = 1.060

title: Lab 021: The 2D XY model without labels
text:
2. Three representations of a snapshot
A snapshot is the array of angles \(\theta_r\in[0,2\pi)\) on the \(L\times L\) torus. The angle itself is a poor input for a neural network, since \(\theta=0.01\) and \(\theta=6.27\) describe almost the same spin but are far apart as numbers. We therefore never feed angles directly, and use three representations, each an array of shape (..., L, L, channels) with the channel axis last, as Flax convolutions expect.
The spin vectors keep all information, two channels per site, \[
\boldsymbol s_r=(\cos\theta_r,\ \sin\theta_r)\qquad\text{shape }(\dots,L,L,2).
\] Under the global rotation \(\theta_r\to\theta_r+\alpha\), the symmetry of \(H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j)\), every \(\boldsymbol s_r\) is multiplied by the same \(2\times2\) rotation matrix. The representation is therefore not invariant, and two snapshots that differ only by a rotation are physically identical but numerically different.
The vortex map is the winding number of every plaquette (Lab 030, Section 4.1), \[
\begin{aligned}
w_r=\frac{1}{2\pi}\Big(&[\theta_{r+\hat x}-\theta_r]+[\theta_{r+\hat x+\hat y}-\theta_{r+\hat x}]\\
&+[\theta_{r+\hat y}-\theta_{r+\hat x+\hat y}]+[\theta_r-\theta_{r+\hat y}]\Big)\in\{-1,0,1\},\qquad\text{shape }(\dots,L,L,1),
\end{aligned}
\] where \([x]\) is \(x\) mapped to \([-\pi,\pi)\) (the sum of four brackets lies in \([-4\pi,4\pi)\), and \(w_r=-2\) would need all four to equal \(-\pi\)). It depends only on angle differences, so it is invariant under global rotations, and it contains the topological defects that drive the transition. It discards the spin waves.
The bond-energy map keeps the two bonds leaving every site, \[
b_r=\big(\cos(\theta_{r+\hat x}-\theta_r),\ \cos(\theta_{r+\hat y}-\theta_r)\big)\qquad\text{shape }(\dots,L,L,2),
\] so that \(H=-J\sum_r(b_r^x+b_r^y)\). It is rotation invariant and is the local energy density of the snapshot.
The cell below implements the three maps and checks their symmetry properties on 16 snapshots of the \(L=32\) data set. The vortex and bond maps must not change under a global rotation, the spin vectors must rotate rigidly, and the winding numbers of every snapshot must sum to zero on the torus (every bond enters two plaquettes with opposite signs). It also compares the vortex density counted in the stored snapshots with the density \(\langle n_v\rangle\) that Lab 030 accumulated over all Monte Carlo steps.


Code
def wrap(a):
    # map angles to [-pi, pi)
    return (a + jnp.pi) % TWO_PI - jnp.pi

def to_spins(theta):
    # (..., L, L) -> (..., L, L, 2): channels cos(theta), sin(theta)
    return jnp.stack([jnp.cos(theta), jnp.sin(theta)], -1)

def to_vortices(theta):
    # (..., L, L) -> (..., L, L, 1): winding number of the plaquette with lower-left corner r, counter-clockwise
    t01 = jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1); t11 = jnp.roll(t01, -1, -2); t10 = jnp.roll(theta, -1, -2)
    circ = wrap(t01 - theta) + wrap(t11 - t01) + wrap(t10 - t11) + wrap(theta - t10)
    return jnp.round(circ / TWO_PI)[..., None]

def to_bonds(theta):
    # (..., L, L) -> (..., L, L, 2): cos of the angle difference on the bond to the right (x) and to the upper (y) neighbour
    return jnp.stack([jnp.cos(jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1) - theta), jnp.cos(jnp.roll(theta, -1, -2) - theta)], -1)

REPS = {"spins": to_spins, "vortices": to_vortices, "bonds": to_bonds}
CHANNELS = {"spins": 2, "vortices": 1, "bonds": 2}

th = jnp.asarray(DS[32]["theta"][8, :16])                       # 16 snapshots at T = 1.00, shape (16, 32, 32)
alpha = 1.234
R = jnp.array([[np.cos(alpha), -np.sin(alpha)], [np.sin(alpha), np.cos(alpha)]])
assert jnp.allclose(to_spins(th + alpha), to_spins(th) @ R.T, atol=1e-5)           # spins rotate rigidly
assert jnp.array_equal(to_vortices(th + alpha), to_vortices(th))                   # vortex map invariant
assert jnp.allclose(to_bonds(th + alpha), to_bonds(th), atol=1e-5)                 # bond map invariant
assert jnp.all(to_vortices(th).sum((1, 2, 3)) == 0)                                # total winding zero on the torus
energy = -(to_bonds(th).sum((1, 2, 3))) / 32**2
print("shapes:", {k: f(th).shape for k, f in REPS.items()})
print(f"energy per spin of the 16 snapshots from the bond map: {float(energy.mean()):+.4f}   "
      f"chain average u(T=1.00) = {REF[32]['u'][8]:+.4f}")
for L in L_LIST:
    w = np.asarray(to_vortices(jnp.asarray(DS[L]["theta"])))
    print(f"L = {L}: vortex density in the stored snapshots at T = 0.90 / 1.50: {(w[6] != 0).mean():.4f} / {(w[-1] != 0).mean():.4f}"
          f"   (Lab 030, all MC steps: {REF[L]['nv'][6]:.4f} / {REF[L]['nv'][-1]:.4f})")

From left to right the panels show the angle \(\theta_r\) in a cyclic colour scale, the vortex map \(w_r\) and the mean bond energy \((b^x_r+b^y_r)/2\) of every site. The three maps of one snapshot look very different, and what an algorithm learns depends on which of them we show it.


Code
L = 32
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(3.3, 2.45))
for row, T in enumerate([0.80, 1.20]):
    i = int(np.argmin(abs(T_GRID - T)))
    th = jnp.asarray(DS[L]["theta"][i, 0])
    w = np.asarray(to_vortices(th))[..., 0]; b = np.asarray(to_bonds(th)).mean(-1)
    panels = [(np.asarray(th), "twilight", 0, TWO_PI, r"$\theta_r$"), (w, "RdBu_r", -1.5, 1.5, r"$w_r$"),
              (b, "viridis", -1, 1, r"$(b^x_r+b^y_r)/2$")]
    for ax, (img, cmap, lo, hi, title) in zip(axes[row], panels):
        ax.imshow(img, cmap=cmap, vmin=lo, vmax=hi, origin="lower")
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
        if row == 0: ax.set_title(title)
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(f"$T={T_GRID[i]:.2f}$")
    print(f"T = {T_GRID[i]:.2f}: {int((w > 0).sum())} vortices, {int((w < 0).sum())} antivortices in the shown snapshot")

title: Lab 021: The 2D XY model without labels
text:
3. Principal component analysis

3.1 Spectra of the three representations
PCA (Lab 016) receives a data matrix \(X\) of shape (n, D), one flattened snapshot per row, subtracts the mean row \(\bar{\boldsymbol x}\), and diagonalises the covariance matrix through the singular value decomposition \(X-\bar{\boldsymbol x}=USV^{\mathsf T}\), with singular values \(s_l\) on the diagonal of \(S\). The rows \(\boldsymbol\lambda_l^{\mathsf T}\) of \(V^{\mathsf T}\) are the principal directions, the variance along \(\boldsymbol\lambda_l\) is the eigenvalue \(\sigma_l^2=s_l^2/n\) of the covariance matrix, the fraction of the variance carried by direction \(l\) is \(\sigma_l^2/\sum_{l'}\sigma_{l'}^2\), and the projections \(w^{(l)}=\boldsymbol\lambda_l^{\mathsf T}(\boldsymbol x-\bar{\boldsymbol x})\) are the coordinates of a snapshot (the superscript in parentheses distinguishes them from the winding numbers \(w_r\) of the vortex map). We pool all \(19\times192=3648\) snapshots of one lattice size, with no temperature attached. For the spin vectors \(D=2N\), with the \(\cos\theta_r\) in the first \(N\) entries of a row and the \(\sin\theta_r\) in the next \(N\). For the bond map also \(D=2N\), and for the vortex map \(D=N\).
The Monte Carlo chains of Lab 030 started from the ordered state \(\theta_r=0\), and at low temperature a large lattice turns its global direction only slowly, so the stored snapshots of \(L=48\) at \(T=0.60\) still point mostly near \(\theta=0\). The mean row \(\bar{\boldsymbol x}\) would then contain a spurious magnetisation along \(x\). The physics does not prefer any direction, so we rotate every snapshot by its own random angle \(\alpha\in[0,2\pi)\) before the analysis, which uses the symmetry of \(H\). The rotation does not change the vortex and bond maps.
We check the PCA implementation in JAX against sklearn.decomposition.PCA on the spin vectors of \(L=32\). The explained-variance fractions must agree, and so must the principal directions up to sign. The first two directions turn out to carry equal variance (the reason follows below), so any rotation of the two inside their common plane is an equally valid answer. We therefore compare the plane instead of the individual vectors, through the cosines of the principal angles between the two planes (the singular values of \(V_{\rm JAX}V_{\rm sklearn}^{\mathsf T}\) restricted to the two directions), which are \(1\) for identical planes.


Code
@jax.jit
def pca_fit(X):
    # X: (n, D) data matrix -> mean (D,), explained-variance fractions (min(n, D),), principal directions as rows (min(n, D), D)
    mu = X.mean(0)
    _, sv, Vt = jnp.linalg.svd(X - mu, full_matrices=False)
    return mu, sv**2 / jnp.sum(sv**2), Vt

def design_matrix(L, rep, seed=0):
    # all snapshots of size L, each rotated by a random global angle, in representation rep -> (19 * 192, D), channel-major
    theta = jnp.asarray(DS[L]["theta"].reshape(-1, L, L))
    alpha = jax.random.uniform(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed), (theta.shape[0], 1, 1), maxval=TWO_PI)
    x = REPS[rep](theta + alpha)                                 # (n, L, L, c)
    return jnp.moveaxis(x, -1, 1).reshape(theta.shape[0], -1)    # (n, c * L * L)

X32 = design_matrix(32, "spins")
mu32, var32, Vt32 = pca_fit(X32)
sk = SklearnPCA(n_components=10, svd_solver="full").fit(np.asarray(X32))
print("explained variance, JAX    :", np.round(np.asarray(var32[:6]), 5))
print("explained variance, sklearn:", np.round(sk.explained_variance_ratio_[:6], 5))
assert np.allclose(np.asarray(var32[:10]), sk.explained_variance_ratio_, atol=1e-5)
cos_angles = np.linalg.svd(np.asarray(Vt32[:2]) @ sk.components_[:2].T, compute_uv=False)
print("cosines of the principal angles between the leading planes (JAX vs sklearn):", np.round(cos_angles, 6))
assert np.all(cos_angles > 1 - 1e-4)
k3 = abs(float(np.asarray(Vt32[2]) @ sk.components_[2]))
print(f"|lambda_3(JAX) . lambda_3(sklearn)| = {k3:.6f}   (1 means equal up to sign; below 1 the third direction is degenerate with the fourth)")

With the implementation checked, we compute the spectrum of each representation for \(L=32\), and the overlap of the leading directions with the two uniform patterns of the spin vectors, \[
\boldsymbol u_c=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt N}(\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{\cos\ \text{part}},\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{\sin\ \text{part}}),\qquad
\boldsymbol u_s=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt N}(0,\dots,0,1,\dots,1),
\] measured as the length of the projection of \(\boldsymbol u_c\) and \(\boldsymbol u_s\) onto the plane of \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1,\boldsymbol\lambda_2\) (1 if the plane contains the vector). For the bond map the analogous check is the overlap of \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1\) with the uniform vector \((1,\dots,1)/\sqrt{2N}\), whose projection is proportional to the energy of the snapshot.


Code
SPEC = {}
for rep in REPS:
    X = X32 if rep == "spins" else design_matrix(32, rep)
    mu, var, Vt = pca_fit(X)
    SPEC[rep] = (np.asarray(var), np.asarray(Vt[:4]))
    print(f"{rep:9s}: explained variance of the first 6 directions (%):", np.round(100 * np.asarray(var[:6]), 2))
N32 = 32 * 32
u_c = np.r_[np.ones(N32), np.zeros(N32)] / np.sqrt(N32); u_s = np.r_[np.zeros(N32), np.ones(N32)] / np.sqrt(N32)
P = SPEC["spins"][1][:2]
ov = [float(np.linalg.norm(P @ u)) for u in (u_c, u_s)]
ov_b = abs(float(SPEC["bonds"][1][0] @ np.ones(2 * N32) / np.sqrt(2 * N32)))
print(f"spins: projection of u_c, u_s onto the plane (lambda_1, lambda_2): {ov[0]:.4f}, {ov[1]:.4f}")
print(f"bonds: overlap of lambda_1 with the uniform vector: {ov_b:.4f}")
NUMBERS.update(pca_var_spins_L32=[round(100 * float(v), 2) for v in SPEC["spins"][0][:4]],
               pca_var_bonds_L32=[round(100 * float(v), 2) for v in SPEC["bonds"][0][:4]],
               pca_var_vortices_L32=[round(100 * float(v), 3) for v in SPEC["vortices"][0][:4]],
               pca_overlap_uniform=round(min(ov), 4), pca_overlap_bonds=round(ov_b, 4))

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(3.2, 2.55))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2, height_ratios=[1.25, 1])
a0 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :])
for rep, col, lab in zip(REPS, [UJBlue, DSOrange, Green], ["spins", "vortices", "bonds"]):
    a0.plot(np.arange(1, 21), 100 * SPEC[rep][0][:20], "o-", ms=3, color=col, label=lab)
a0.set_yscale("log"); a0.set_xlabel("$l$", labelpad=0); a0.set_ylabel(r"$\sigma_l^2/\sum\sigma^2$ (%)")
a0.set_xticks([1, 5, 10, 15, 20]); a0.legend(frameon=False, ncol=3, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.3),
                                             handlelength=1.0, columnspacing=0.8, handletextpad=0.3)
for j, k in enumerate([0, 1]):
    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, j])
    v = SPEC["spins"][1][k].reshape(2, 32, 32) * np.sqrt(N32)
    a.imshow(np.concatenate([v[0], np.full((32, 3), np.nan), v[1]], 1), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1.6, vmax=1.6, origin="lower")
    a.set_xticks([16, 51]); a.set_xticklabels([r"$\cos$", r"$\sin$"]); a.set_yticks([])
    a.set_ylabel(rf"$\boldsymbol{{\lambda}}_{k + 1}$")
fig.tight_layout(pad=0.2, h_pad=0.4); savefig(fig, "gen_xy_ml_pca_spectra.png"); plt.show()

The top panel of the figure shows the fraction of the variance \(\sigma_l^2/\sum\sigma^2\) in per cent against the index \(l\), on a logarithmic scale, for the three representations. The bottom panels show the first two principal directions of the spin vectors, each as its \(\cos\) part and its \(\sin\) part on the lattice.
The three spectra are very different. For the spin vectors two directions stand far above the rest and carry equal variance, and the images show that the \(\cos\) part and the \(\sin\) part are each uniform, so \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1,\boldsymbol\lambda_2\) span the plane of \(\boldsymbol u_c,\boldsymbol u_s\) (projections printed above, close to 1). The equal variance reflects the rotation symmetry. After the random rotations \(m_x\) and \(m_y\) fluctuate identically, and PCA has found the two components of the magnetisation as an \(O(2)\) pair. The next directions carry nearly equal variances, as expected for long-wavelength spin waves. For the bond map one direction dominates and is the uniform pattern, the energy of the snapshot. For the vortex map the spectrum is flat, and no linear combination of the winding numbers varies much more than any other. The uniform combination, the total vorticity, is zero on the torus, and the physics of the transition, whether vortices are bound in pairs, is a statement about correlations between defects, which no single linear pattern expresses. PCA has nothing to find there.


3.2 The magnetisation pair and its finite-size drift
The projections onto the leading plane give a two-component coordinate \(\mathbf w=(w^{(1)},w^{(2)})\) per snapshot. Because the plane is spanned by \(\boldsymbol u_c\) and \(\boldsymbol u_s\), and \(\boldsymbol u_c\cdot\boldsymbol x=\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_r\cos\theta_r=\sqrt N\,m_x\), \[
\frac{|\mathbf w|}{\sqrt N}=\frac{\sqrt{(w^{(1)})^2+(w^{(2)})^2}}{\sqrt N}\simeq|\boldsymbol m| ,
\] so the PCA order parameter is the modulus of the finite-lattice magnetisation. We compute it for all three sizes and locate the temperature \(T_{\rm PCA}(L)\) where it falls fastest, the maximum of \(-d\langle|\mathbf w|\rangle/dT\), estimated by central differences on the grid and refined with a parabola through the three largest slopes. The error bar comes from a bootstrap over the 24 independent Monte Carlo chains (we resample chains with replacement, 200 times, and take the standard deviation of the estimate).
Lab 030 tells us what to expect. Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the magnetisation decays as \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\propto L^{-\eta(T)/2}\) with \(\eta(T)=T/(2\pi\Upsilon)\), a power law in \(L\) with a small exponent, so it is never an order parameter. Above \(T_{\rm BKT}\) it decays faster, as \(\xi/L\) once the correlation length \(\xi\) is smaller than \(L\). The upper panel of the figure shows \(\langle|\mathbf w|\rangle/\sqrt N\) against \(T\) for the three sizes, with the steepest falls \(T_{\rm PCA}(L)\) as dashed lines and \(T_{\rm BKT}\) in orange. The lower panel tests the decay law with the effective exponent \(x_{\rm eff}(T)\) from a fit \(\langle|\mathbf w|\rangle/\sqrt N\propto L^{-x_{\rm eff}}\) to the three sizes, compared with \(\eta/2=T/(4\pi\Upsilon_{48})\) computed from the measured helicity modulus of \(L=48\). The dotted horizontal line marks \(\eta/2=1/8\), the value at \(T_{\rm BKT}\), where \(\eta=1/4\).


Code
def steepest(T, y, sign=+1):
    # temperature of the steepest rise (sign=+1) or fall (sign=-1) of y(T): central differences, parabola through the 3 largest slopes
    d = sign * np.gradient(y, T)
    i = int(np.clip(np.argmax(d), 1, len(T) - 2))
    p = np.polyfit(T[i - 1:i + 2], d[i - 1:i + 2], 2)
    return float(np.clip(-p[1] / (2 * p[0]), T[i - 1], T[i + 1]))

def bootstrap_steepest(per_sample, chain, sign=+1, n_boot=200, seed=0):
    # per_sample: (nT, n) values for n snapshots per temperature; chain: (n,) chain index of each snapshot.
    # Returns the estimate from all snapshots and its bootstrap standard deviation over chains.
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    chains = np.unique(chain)
    per_chain = np.stack([per_sample[:, chain == c].mean(1) for c in chains], 1)      # (nT, n_chains)
    boot = [steepest(T_GRID, per_chain[:, rng.integers(0, len(chains), len(chains))].mean(1), sign) for _ in range(n_boot)]
    return steepest(T_GRID, per_chain.mean(1), sign), float(np.std(boot))

ZABS, T_PCA = {}, {}
for L in L_LIST:
    N = L * L
    X = design_matrix(L, "spins")

The upper panel looks like the plot of an order parameter, with \(\langle|\mathbf w|\rangle/\sqrt N\) large at low \(T\) and falling around \(T\approx1\). It agrees with \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) of the same snapshots to within \(0.0021\) at every temperature, so PCA has rediscovered the magnetisation, as for the Ising model in Lab 019. Two observations show that this is not an order parameter of the XY model. First, the low-temperature plateau decreases with \(L\), and up to \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the effective exponent in the lower panel follows the prediction \(\eta/2\) computed from the measured stiffness (for example \(0.064\) against \(0.058\) at \(T=0.60\), \(0.128\) against \(0.117\) at \(T=0.90\)). This is a power law in \(L\), so \(\langle|\mathbf w|\rangle\to0\) as \(L\to\infty\) at every temperature. Second, the steepest-fall temperatures \(T_{\rm PCA}(L)\) lie above \(T_{\rm BKT}\) and drift to lower \(T\) as \(L\) grows. What PCA locates is roughly the temperature at which the correlation length becomes comparable with the lattice, a finite-size crossover that approaches \(T_{\rm BKT}\) only logarithmically slowly (the same mechanism as for the stiffness crossings, Lab 030 Section 5.3). At high temperature the exponent approaches \(1\), the value for \(\xi\ll L\).
This agrees with Hu, Singh and Scalettar (2017), who applied PCA to the XY model, found the magnetisation, and noted that PCA does not capture the vorticity. Wang and Zhai (2017) applied PCA to frustrated XY models with the same \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) input.

title: Lab 021: The 2D XY model without labels
text:
4. Autoencoder anomaly detection

4.1 A convolutional autoencoder on the torus
The autoencoder (Lab 017) compresses a snapshot \(\boldsymbol x\) to a few latent numbers and reconstructs it, \(\tilde{\boldsymbol x}=D_\phi(E_\psi(\boldsymbol x))\), with an encoder \(E_\psi\) and a decoder \(D_\phi\) of parameters \(\psi\) and \(\phi\). Trained only on snapshots from one region of temperature, it reconstructs snapshots that resemble the training data well and the others badly. The reconstruction error of one snapshot is \[
\varepsilon(\boldsymbol x)=\frac{1}{N\,C}\sum_{r}\sum_{c=1}^{C}\big(x_{r,c}-\tilde x_{r,c}\big)^2 ,
\] with \(C\) the number of channels, and its average over the snapshots at temperature \(T\), \(\bar\varepsilon(T)\), is the anomaly score (Kottmann, Huembeli, Lewenstein, Acín 2020). The same network is used for all three representations, and only the number of input channels changes. The table gives the output shapes for a batch of \(B\) snapshots of size \(L\) (divisible by 4).







layer
output shape




input
\((B, L, L, C)\)


convolution \(3\times3\), stride 2, periodic padding, 16 filters, ReLU
\((B, L/2, L/2, 16)\)


convolution \(3\times3\), stride 2, periodic padding, 32 filters, ReLU
\((B, L/4, L/4, 32)\)


dense \(\to\) latent
\((B, 4)\)


dense, ReLU, reshape
\((B, L/4, L/4, 32)\)


transposed convolution, stride 2, ReLU
\((B, L/2, L/2, 16)\)


transposed convolution, stride 2, linear
\((B, L, L, C)\)



ReLU is the rectified linear unit, \(\mathrm{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x)\), applied to every entry, and a stride of 2 halves each spatial dimension. The convolutions use periodic (“circular”) padding, the boundary condition of the lattice, and the latent space has 4 numbers as in Lab 020. The output is linear because the targets differ between representations (\(\cos\theta,\sin\theta\in[-1,1]\), \(w\in\{-1,0,1\}\), \(b\in[-1,1]\)).
The training protocol uses what we know about the model. Every training batch is rotated by fresh random angles \(\alpha\), one per snapshot, before being converted to the representation, so the network sees every global direction and never has to learn a direction-specific reconstruction (for vortices and bonds the rotation changes nothing). The 24 Monte Carlo chains of each temperature are split, chains 0–11 providing the training snapshots and chains 12–23 the evaluation snapshots, so that the error at the training temperatures is measured on snapshots the network has not seen. The training region is the low-temperature end \(T\in\{0.60,0.65,0.70\}\), well below \(T_{\rm BKT}\), where spin-wave theory describes the physics (Lab 030). For the raw spins we also train on the high-temperature end \(T\in\{1.40,1.45,1.50\}\). Each region gives \(3\times96=288\) training snapshots, and we train with the Adam optimiser (adaptive moment estimation, Lab 017) with learning rate \(10^{-3}\), batches of 32 and 40 epochs. Every low-temperature training is repeated with two random seeds, and the high-temperature control is trained once. A temperature estimate \(T_{\rm AE}(L)\) is the position of the steepest rise of \(\bar\varepsilon(T)\), with the same estimator and chain bootstrap as for PCA, applied to the seed-averaged curve.
The cell defines the model and checks the shapes for all three sizes and representations.


Code
class ConvAE(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels, L, latent=4, width=1, *, rngs):
        # width multiplies the number of filters (16 and 32 for width = 1)
        self.l4, f1, f2 = L // 4, 16 * width, 32 * width
        self.f2 = f2
        self.c1 = nnx.Conv(channels, f1, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="CIRCULAR", rngs=rngs)       # L   -> L/2
        self.c2 = nnx.Conv(f1, f2, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="CIRCULAR", rngs=rngs)             # L/2 -> L/4
        self.fe = nnx.Linear(self.l4 * self.l4 * f2, latent, rngs=rngs)
        self.fd = nnx.Linear(latent, self.l4 * self.l4 * f2, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1 = nnx.ConvTranspose(f2, f1, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2), padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)   # L/4 -> L/2
        self.d2 = nnx.ConvTranspose(f1, channels, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2), padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)  # L/2 -> L

    def encode(self, x):                                     # (B, L, L, C) -> (B, latent)
        h = nnx.relu(self.c2(nnx.relu(self.c1(x))))
        return self.fe(h.reshape(h.shape[0], -1))

    def __call__(self, x):                                   # (B, L, L, C) -> (B, L, L, C)
        h = nnx.relu(self.fd(self.encode(x))).reshape(-1, self.l4, self.l4, self.f2)
        return self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(h)))

for L in L_LIST:
    for rep, C in CHANNELS.items():
        m = ConvAE(C, L, rngs=nnx.Rngs(0))
        x = REPS[rep](jnp.asarray(DS[L]["theta"][0, :3]))
        assert m(x).shape == x.shape == (3, L, L, C) and m.encode(x).shape == (3, 4)
n_par = sum(p.size for p in jax.tree.leaves(nnx.state(ConvAE(2, 32, rngs=nnx.Rngs(0)), nnx.Param)))
print(f"shapes correct; number of parameters for L = 32, two channels: {n_par}")
