title: Lab 023: The SK spin glass without labels
text:
2. Single snapshots

2.1 Consequences of the gauge symmetry
Lab 032 (Section 8.1) showed that the gauge transformation \(s_i\to\gamma_is_i\), \(J_{ij}\to\gamma_i\gamma_jJ_{ij}\) with \(\gamma_i=\pm1\) leaves the distribution of the couplings unchanged, so that the distribution of a single snapshot, pooled over disorder samples, is \([p_J(\boldsymbol s)]=2^{-N}\) at every temperature. This has two consequences for a data set. First, snapshots from different samples are independent, so a data set with one snapshot per sample is a set of independent, uniformly random strings of signs, in the paramagnet and in the spin glass alike, and every statistic computed from it has the same distribution at every temperature. Second, snapshots of the same sample are not independent. Below \(T_c\) two snapshots of one sample are frozen in the same or related valleys, and their overlap is large. A data set with many snapshots per sample therefore contains replica pairs in disguise, and a method can pick up the low-temperature structure from them. We test both statements with PCA.


2.2 PCA of single snapshots
PCA diagonalises the covariance matrix of the data. For a data matrix \(X\) of shape (M, N) (one snapshot per row) with column means \(\bar{\boldsymbol x}\), \[
C=\frac{1}{M-1}(X-\bar{\boldsymbol x})^T(X-\bar{\boldsymbol x}),\qquad C\,\boldsymbol\lambda_l=\sigma_l^2\boldsymbol\lambda_l,\qquad \sigma_1^2\ge\sigma_2^2\ge\dots,
\] where the unit eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol\lambda_l\) are the principal directions and the eigenvalues \(\sigma_l^2\) the variances along them. The projection of a data vector \(\boldsymbol x\) on the \(l\)-th direction is \(w^{(l)}=\boldsymbol\lambda_l^T(\boldsymbol x-\bar{\boldsymbol x})\). These variances carry a component index \(l\) and are unrelated to the Mattis spins \(\sigma_i\) of Section 4 and to the spread \(\sigma_{\rm train}\) of the anomaly score. Since \(N\le128\) is small, we diagonalise the \(N\times N\) matrix \(C\) directly with jnp.linalg.eigh, which avoids a singular value decomposition of the long data matrix. The largest eigenvalue \(\sigma_1^2\) is the variance of the data along the most important direction. For independent uniform strings \(C\) is the identity plus sampling noise, and \(\sigma_1^2\) fluctuates around the upper edge of the Marchenko–Pastur distribution, \((1+\sqrt{N/M})^2\). Instead of relying on this asymptotic formula we compare with the same computation on uniformly random strings of the same shape (40 draws, mean and two standard deviations).
At every temperature we compute \(\sigma_1^2\) for two data sets of the \(N=128\) samples, one with one snapshot per sample (\(M=D\)) and one with all \(2\times32\) snapshots of every sample (\(M=64D\)).


Code
@jax.jit
def pca_jax(X):
    """PCA by diagonalising the covariance matrix. X: (M, N).
    Returns the mean (N,), variances sigma_l^2 in decreasing order (N,), principal directions (N, N) with rows lambda_l."""
    mu = X.mean(0)
    Xc = X - mu
    C = Xc.T @ Xc / (X.shape[0] - 1)                     # (N, N) covariance matrix
    lam, V = jnp.linalg.eigh(C)                          # ascending eigenvalues, eigenvectors in columns
    return mu, lam[::-1], V[:, ::-1].T

def top_variance(X):
    return float(pca_jax(jnp.asarray(X, jnp.float32))[1][0])

def random_null(M, N, n_draw=40, seed=0):
    """Mean and standard deviation of sigma_1^2 for uniformly random +-1 strings of shape (M, N)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    v = [top_variance(rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(M, N))) for _ in range(n_draw)]
    return np.mean(v), np.std(v)

N = 128; c = sk[N]["configs"]; D = sk[N]["D"]
lam_one = np.array([top_variance(c[:, 0, k, 0]) for k in range(K_T)])                    # one snapshot per sample, (D, N)
lam_all = np.array([top_variance(c[:, :, k].reshape(-1, N)) for k in range(K_T)])        # all snapshots, (64 D, N)
null_one, null_all = random_null(D, N), random_null(64 * D, N)
print(f"N = {N}, D = {D}")
print(f"one snapshot per sample: sigma_1^2 from {lam_one.min():.2f} to {lam_one.max():.2f};  random strings {null_one[0]:.2f} ± {null_one[1]:.2f}"
      f"  (Marchenko-Pastur edge {(1 + np.sqrt(N / D))**2:.2f})")
print(f"all snapshots          : sigma_1^2 = {lam_all[0]:.2f} at T = {T_GRID[0]},  {lam_all[-1]:.2f} at T = {T_GRID[-1]};"
      f"  random strings {null_all[0]:.2f} ± {null_all[1]:.2f}")
NUMBERS["single_pca"] = dict(N=N, lam_one_range=[round(float(lam_one.min()), 2), round(float(lam_one.max()), 2)],
                             null_one=[round(null_one[0], 2), round(null_one[1], 2)],
                             lam_all_lowT=round(float(lam_all[0]), 2), lam_all_highT=round(float(lam_all[-1]), 2),
                             null_all=[round(null_all[0], 2), round(null_all[1], 2)])


N = 128, D = 96
one snapshot per sample: sigma_1^2 from 4.23 to 4.72;  random strings 4.46 ± 0.15  (Marchenko-Pastur edge 4.64)
all snapshots          : sigma_1^2 = 3.35 at T = 0.4,  1.37 at T = 1.6;  random strings 1.30 ± 0.01


With one snapshot per sample, \(\sigma_1^2\) stays inside the band of random strings at every temperature, as the gauge argument requires. With all snapshots of each sample, \(\sigma_1^2\) grows below \(T\approx1\) and reaches about two and a half times its high-temperature value at \(T=0.4\). This growth is not a property of single snapshots. It comes from the fact that the data set contains 64 strongly correlated snapshots of each of only 96 samples. The leading directions are the frozen spin patterns of individual samples, and their weight should decrease as the number of samples grows. PCA is in effect measuring the overlap between snapshots of the same sample, which is a replica overlap.


2.3 An autoencoder on single snapshots
The anomaly-detection protocol of the previous labs trains an autoencoder on one region and maps its reconstruction error. We use a dense autoencoder, because the SK model has no lattice. The label \(i\) of a spin carries no geometry, so convolutions have nothing to exploit. The encoder maps \(\boldsymbol s\in\{-1,1\}^N\) through a hidden layer of 64 rectified linear units (ReLU, \(\mathrm{ReLU}(u)=\max(0,u)\)) to a latent vector \(\boldsymbol z\), and the decoder maps \(\boldsymbol z\) back through 64 ReLU units to \(\tilde{\boldsymbol s}\in[-1,1]^N\) with a final \(\tanh\). The reconstruction error of one input is \[
\varepsilon(\boldsymbol x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(x_i-\tilde x_i)^2 ,
\] and the loss is its mean over a mini-batch of inputs, the mean squared error between input and reconstruction. It is minimised with Adam (adaptive moment estimation), a gradient-descent method that scales the step of every parameter by running averages of its past gradients and their squares, with learning rate \(10^{-3}\). For speed the whole training epoch is compiled into one function with jax.lax.scan over mini-batches. Every training set is augmented by the global flip \(\boldsymbol x\to-\boldsymbol x\), a symmetry of the Hamiltonian.
A memorising network could reconstruct the snapshots of the samples it was trained on without learning anything general. We therefore split the disorder samples into two halves (even and odd sample index) and evaluate on samples that the network has never seen. Two single-snapshot autoencoders are trained on the even samples, one on the paramagnet (\(T\ge1.3\), latent dimension 8) and one on the frozen phase (\(T\le0.6\), latent dimension 16, enough to store frozen patterns).


Code
class DenseAE(nnx.Module):
    """Dense autoencoder n_in -> hidden -> latent -> hidden -> n_in; output tanh (spins) or linear."""
    def __init__(self, n_in, latent, hidden=64, out="tanh", *, rngs):
        self.e1 = nnx.Linear(n_in, hidden, rngs=rngs); self.e2 = nnx.Linear(hidden, latent, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1 = nnx.Linear(latent, hidden, rngs=rngs); self.d2 = nnx.Linear(hidden, n_in, rngs=rngs)
        self.out = out
    def encode(self, x):
        return self.e2(nnx.relu(self.e1(x)))
    def __call__(self, x):
        y = self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(self.encode(x))))
        return jnp.tanh(y) if self.out == "tanh" else y

def train_ae(X, latent, epochs, hidden=64, out="tanh", batch=256, lr=1e-3, seed=0):
    """Train a DenseAE on X (M, n_in) with Adam; one compiled lax.scan per epoch. Returns the model and the loss per epoch."""
    X = jnp.asarray(X, jnp.float32)
    model = DenseAE(X.shape[1], latent, hidden, out, rngs=nnx.Rngs(seed))
    graph, params = nnx.split(model, nnx.Param)
    tx = optax.adam(lr); opt_state = tx.init(params)
    n_b = X.shape[0] // batch
    loss_fn = lambda p, x: jnp.mean((nnx.merge(graph, p)(x) - x) ** 2)

    @jax.jit
    def epoch(p, o, key):
        perm = jax.random.permutation(key, X.shape[0])[: n_b * batch].reshape(n_b, batch)   # (n_b, batch) indices
        def body(carry, idx):
            p, o = carry
            l, g = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn)(p, X[idx])
            u, o = tx.update(g, o, p)
            return (optax.apply_updates(p, u), o), l
        (p, o), ls = jax.lax.scan(body, (p, o), perm)
        return p, o, ls.mean()

    key, hist = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed), []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        key, k = jax.random.split(key)
        params, opt_state, l = epoch(params, opt_state, k)
        hist.append(float(l))
    return nnx.merge(graph, params), np.array(hist)

@nnx.jit
def recon_error(model, x):
    """Reconstruction error per input, x: (M, n_in) -> (M,)."""
    return jnp.mean((model(x) - x) ** 2, axis=-1)

@nnx.jit
def encode(model, x):
    return model.encode(x)

def flip_augment(X):
    return np.concatenate([X, -X])

HIGH_T, LOW_T = T_GRID >= 1.3, T_GRID <= 0.6
def folds(D):
    """Two-fold split of the disorder samples: (train, test) index arrays by even / odd sample index."""
    i = np.arange(D)
    return [(i[i % 2 == f], i[i % 2 != f]) for f in (0, 1)]




Code
t0 = time.time()
single_ae = {}
for N in SIZES:
    c = sk[N]["configs"]; tr, te = folds(sk[N]["D"])[0]
    m_hi, h_hi = train_ae(flip_augment(c[tr][:, :, HIGH_T].reshape(-1, N)), latent=8, epochs=30)
    m_lo, h_lo = train_ae(flip_augment(c[tr][:, :, LOW_T].reshape(-1, N)), latent=16, epochs=60)
    err = lambda m, idx: np.array([float(recon_error(m, jnp.asarray(c[idx][:, :, k].reshape(-1, N))).mean()) for k in range(K_T)])
    single_ae[N] = dict(hi_test=err(m_hi, te), lo_train=err(m_lo, tr), lo_test=err(m_lo, te))
    r = single_ae[N]
    print(f"N = {N:3d}: trained on T >= 1.3, held-out samples: error {r['hi_test'].min():.3f} .. {r['hi_test'].max():.3f};"
          f"  trained on T <= 0.6: training samples {r['lo_train'][0]:.3f} (T = 0.4) .. {r['lo_train'][-1]:.3f} (T = 1.6),"
          f" held-out samples {r['lo_test'].min():.3f} .. {r['lo_test'].max():.3f}")
print(f"training time {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
NUMBERS["single_ae"] = {N: dict(hi_test=[round(float(single_ae[N]["hi_test"].min()), 3), round(float(single_ae[N]["hi_test"].max()), 3)],
                                lo_train_T04=round(float(single_ae[N]["lo_train"][0]), 3),
                                lo_test=[round(float(single_ae[N]["lo_test"].min()), 3), round(float(single_ae[N]["lo_test"].max()), 3)])
                        for N in SIZES}

The left panel of the figure shows \(\sigma_1^2\) against \(T/J\) for one snapshot per sample and for all 64 snapshots per sample of \(N=128\), with the bands of random strings (mean and two standard deviations) shaded. The right panel shows the mean reconstruction error \(\bar\varepsilon\) of the single-snapshot autoencoders, trained on \(T\ge1.3\) and on \(T\le0.6\) and evaluated on new samples, and of the \(T\le0.6\) autoencoder on its own training samples.
The autoencoder trained on the paramagnet has an error that does not depend on temperature on held-out samples, since there is nothing in single snapshots that distinguishes the phases. (For \(N=32\) the error is well below \(1\), because a latent vector of 8 numbers can store a good part of a random string of 32 signs. The value is the same at every temperature.) The autoencoder trained on the frozen phase is more informative. On its own training samples its error grows strongly with temperature (for \(N=128\) from \(0.343\) at \(T=0.4\) to \(0.975\) at \(T=1.6\)), because it has stored the frozen patterns of those particular samples. On held-out samples its error hardly depends on temperature, with printed ranges at most \(0.016\) wide. The structure of a frozen snapshot is specific to its sample, and nothing of it transfers to a new sample. A network that seems to detect the transition on the training samples is detecting its own memory.

title: Lab 023: The SK spin glass without labels
text:
3. Overlap fields

3.1 The gauge-invariant input
For two replicas \(a,b\) of the same sample the overlap field is \[
q_i=s_i^a s_i^b\in\{-1,1\},\qquad i=1,\dots,N,\qquad q=\frac1N\sum_iq_i .
\] It is invariant under the gauge transformation (\(\gamma_i^2=1\)), and Lab 032 showed that the pooled distribution of pairs depends on the configurations only through \(\boldsymbol q\), and, because the SK ensemble is also symmetric under permutations of the spin labels, only on the number of \(+1\) entries, that is on \(q\). Every \((\boldsymbol s^a,\boldsymbol s^b)\) pair of the data set gives one overlap field. Pairing snapshot \(t\) of replica \(a\) with snapshot \(t'\) of replica \(b\) for all \(t,t'\) gives \(32\times32=1024\) fields per sample and temperature. The 32 simultaneous pairs \(t=t'\) are used for training, and all 1024 pairs for measurements. A field is a vector of length \(N\), so the data matrices have shape (pairs, N). The flip of one replica, \(\boldsymbol q\to-\boldsymbol q\), is an exact symmetry and is used for augmentation.
The permutation symmetry has a consequence for every method. A function of one overlap field that does not depend on the order of the spins can depend only on the number of \(+1\) entries, that is, on \(q\). A permutation-invariant network would therefore be forced to learn some function of \(q\), and we will see that the unconstrained dense networks arrive there too.


Code
def overlap_fields(c, idx, k, all_pairs=False):
    """Overlap fields of samples idx at temperature slot k. c: (D, 2, K, S, N).
    Simultaneous pairs: (len(idx) * S, N); all pairs (t, t'): (len(idx) * S * S, N)."""
    a, b = c[idx, 0, k], c[idx, 1, k]                                   # (n, S, N) each
    if all_pairs:
        return (a[:, :, None, :] * b[:, None, :, :]).reshape(-1, a.shape[-1])
    return (a * b).reshape(-1, a.shape[-1])

N = 128; c = sk[N]["configs"]

3.2 PCA of overlap fields
We pool the simultaneous-pair overlap fields of all samples and all 25 temperatures, add their mirror images \(-\boldsymbol q\), and run PCA. The method receives neither the temperature nor the sample index. Before looking at the result we can predict it. Because the pooled distribution is symmetric under permutations of the labels and under \(\boldsymbol q\to-\boldsymbol q\), the covariance matrix has the form \(C_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+(1-\delta_{ij})\,c\) with one number \(c\). Its eigenvectors are the uniform vector \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1=(1,\dots,1)/\sqrt N\) and the \(N-1\) vectors orthogonal to it. The projection on the uniform vector is the overlap itself, \[
w^{(1)}=\boldsymbol\lambda_1^T\boldsymbol q=\sqrt N\,q,\qquad \sigma_{\rm uniform}^2=\boldsymbol\lambda_1^TC\,\boldsymbol\lambda_1=N\,\overline{q^2},
\] where \(\overline{q^2}\) is the mean of \(q^2\) over the pooled data. Evaluated at a single temperature, \(N[\langle q^2\rangle]\) is the spin-glass susceptibility \(\chi_{\rm SG}\) of Lab 032. The PCA implementation in JAX from Section 2 is checked against sklearn.decomposition.PCA on the same data, and the explained-variance ratios and the principal directions must agree, the directions up to a sign.


Code
pca_q = {}
for N in SIZES:
    c = sk[N]["configs"]; D = sk[N]["D"]
    Xq = np.concatenate([overlap_fields(c, np.arange(D), k) for k in range(K_T)])     # (D * K * S, N)
    Xq = flip_augment(Xq)
    mu, lam, Vt = (np.asarray(a) for a in pca_jax(jnp.asarray(Xq)))
    v1 = Vt[0] * np.sign(Vt[0].sum())                                                  # fix the sign: positive sum
    pca_q[N] = dict(mu=mu, lam=lam, v1=v1, ratio=lam / lam.sum(), q2_pooled=float((Xq.mean(1) ** 2).mean()))
    print(f"N = {N:3d}: {Xq.shape[0]} fields;  sigma_1^2 = {lam[0]:.3f},  N * mean(q^2) = {N * pca_q[N]['q2_pooled']:.3f};"
          f"  explained variance PC1 {100 * lam[0] / lam.sum():.1f}%, PC2 {100 * lam[1] / lam.sum():.2f}%;"
          f"  sqrt(N) lambda_1: mean {np.sqrt(N) * v1.mean():.4f}, spread {np.sqrt(N) * v1.std():.4f}")

The first principal component is the uniform vector. The entries of \(\sqrt N\,\boldsymbol\lambda_1\) are \(1\) up to a spread of a few percent, and \(\sigma_1^2\) equals \(N\overline{q^2}\). The second component carries a variance comparable to all the others, and the remaining spectrum is noise around the value fixed by the trace, \(\sum_l\sigma_l^2=N\). The higher components show some spread because a finite number of samples is not exactly permutation symmetric, the same finite-sample effect as in Section 2.2, now much weaker. JAX and scikit-learn agree to the printed precision.
PCA has found the order parameter of the spin glass, the overlap, as it found the magnetisation of the Ising model in Lab 019. There the uniform vector projected the spins onto \(\sqrt N m\), and here it projects the overlap field onto \(\sqrt N q\). The spins themselves gave PCA nothing, and the gauge-invariant pair input made the order linear again.
We now measure the projection \(w^{(1)}=\boldsymbol\lambda_1^T(\boldsymbol q-\bar{\boldsymbol q})\) on all 1024 pairs of every sample and temperature, and compute from it the same Binder cumulant as in Section 1, with \(w^{(1)}\) in place of \(q\). The figure shows the percentage of the variance carried by the first ten principal directions for \(N=128\) (left) and the Binder cumulant of the projection, \(g_{\rm B}[w^{(1)}]\) (axis label \(g\,[w^{(1)}]\)), against \(T/J\) for the three sizes with \(T_c\) dotted (right).

Because \(w^{(1)}\) is \(\sqrt N q\) up to the small spread of \(\boldsymbol\lambda_1\) and a negligible shift \(\bar{\boldsymbol q}\), the projection reproduces the overlap \([\langle|q|\rangle]\) (printed values) and the Binder cumulant of Lab 032, and the crossings agree with the reference table of Section 1 within the bootstrap intervals (the small differences come from using the 1024 snapshot pairs instead of the 512 overlaps measured during the run). The linear method, given the right input, reproduces the full finite-size-scaling analysis. It does not do better than the physicist’s analysis, because it computes the same quantity.


3.3 An autoencoder on overlap fields
The anomaly-detection protocol of Lab 019 trains on a well-structured phase. Here that is the frozen phase, \(T\le0.6\), where the fields are mostly \(+1\) or mostly \(-1\) with scattered exceptions. The autoencoder has a latent dimension of one, so it must compress each field into a single number, and everything else is as in Section 2.3. We use two folds, and the network trained on the even samples is evaluated on the odd ones and vice versa, so every sample is evaluated by a network that never saw it.
The best result such a network can reach can be predicted before training. If it encodes the overlap \(q\) and outputs the constant vector \(\tilde q_i=q\), the error is \[
\varepsilon=\frac1N\sum_i(q_i-q)^2=1-q^2,
\] because \(q_i^2=1\) and \(\frac1N\sum_iq_i=q\). Positions of the exceptional spins are sample-specific and, as Section 2.3 showed, do not transfer to new samples. We therefore expect a mean error \(\bar\varepsilon(T)\approx1-[\langle q^2\rangle]\), an anomaly signal that is a known physical observable.


Code
t0 = time.time()
ae_q = {}
for N in SIZES:
    c = sk[N]["configs"]; D = sk[N]["D"]
    E1, E2, Q2, Zq = np.zeros((D, K_T)), np.zeros((D, K_T)), np.zeros((D, K_T)), []
    for f, (tr, te) in enumerate(folds(D)):
        X_tr = np.concatenate([overlap_fields(c, tr, k) for k in np.where(LOW_T)[0]])
        model, hist = train_ae(flip_augment(X_tr), latent=1, epochs=60, seed=f)

            q = X.mean(1).reshape(len(te), -1)

The printed numbers confirm the prediction. The left panel of the figure shows the error \(\varepsilon\) of individual pairs against their overlap \(q\) at three temperatures for \(N=128\), with the parabola \(1-q^2\) dashed, and the right panel the mean error \(\bar\varepsilon\) against \(T/J\) for the three sizes. For each pair the error lies on the parabola \(1-q^2\), and the mean error follows \(1-[\langle q^2\rangle]\) at every temperature, with a largest deviation below \(0.005\) for every size. The latent variable is strongly correlated with \(q\), close to \(1\) at low temperature and somewhat less at \(T=1.6\), where all overlaps are small and the error hardly depends on them. Without being told, the network has learned the overlap, and its reconstruction error is one minus the square of the overlap.
This fixes where the anomaly signal can sit. In the thermodynamic limit the Edwards–Anderson order parameter grows linearly below \(T_c\), \(q_{\rm EA}\approx1-T/J\) (Lab 032, Section 4.6), so \(q^2\) starts quadratically and the error has no kink at \(T_c\). The steepest change of the mean error lies between \(T=0.42\) and \(0.48\) for all three sizes (printed above), far below \(T_c=J\), and it does not move towards \(T_c\) as \(N\) grows. In the Ising model (Lab 019), by contrast, the magnetisation rises steeply below \(T_c\) and the centre of the step in the error approached \(T_c\) as \(L\) grew. Locating \(T_c\) from the learned overlap requires finite-size scaling, which we did in Section 3.2 with the PCA projection.

3.4 Anomalies at the level of the overlap distribution
The single-field autoencoder can only learn \(q\). The physics of the spin glass is richer. Below \(T_c\) the overlap distribution \(P_J(q)\) of each sample is broad, with weight between its peaks, and it differs from sample to sample. To let a network see this, we give it one input vector per sample and temperature, the histogram of \(|q|\) over the 1024 pairs, in 16 bins of width \(1/16\) on \([0,1]\). The histogram is invariant under permutations of the spins and of the snapshots, and it is a suitable input when the object of interest is a distribution. The input has shape (16,), the data set has (D, K, 16).
The anomaly detector is trained on the paramagnet, \(T\ge1.3\), where every \(P_J(q)\) is a narrow Gaussian around \(0\) and the hypothesis “nothing happens here” is safe. The autoencoder has a hidden layer of 32 units, a latent dimension of 2, and a linear output. As anomaly score we use the error in units of its spread on the training data, \[
a(\text{sample},T)=\frac{\varepsilon-\mu_{\rm train}}{\sigma_{\rm train}},
\] evaluated, as before, on held-out samples with two folds. A score above \(3\) means that the histogram is unlike any typical paramagnetic histogram.


Code
def abs_q_histograms(c, n_bins=16):
    """Histogram of |q| over all S*S pairs, for every sample and temperature: (D, K, n_bins)."""
    D, _, K, S, N = c.shape
    H = np.zeros((D, K, n_bins))
    for k in range(K):
        q = np.einsum("dsi,dti->dst", c[:, 0, k], c[:, 1, k]).reshape(D, -1) / N         # (D, S*S)
        idx = np.minimum((np.abs(q) * n_bins).astype(int), n_bins - 1)
        H[:, k] = np.stack([(idx == b).mean(1) for b in range(n_bins)], axis=1)
    return H

def histogram_anomaly(H, seed=0):
    """Two-fold anomaly score of per-sample histograms H (D, K, n_bins); detector trained on T >= 1.3. Returns (D, K)."""
    D, K, n_b = H.shape
    score = np.zeros((D, K))
    for f, (tr, te) in enumerate(folds(D)):
        X_tr = H[tr][:, HIGH_T].reshape(-1, n_b)
        model, _ = train_ae(X_tr, latent=2, epochs=400, hidden=32, out="linear", batch=64, seed=seed + f)
        e_tr = np.asarray(recon_error(model, jnp.asarray(X_tr)))
        e = np.asarray(recon_error(model, jnp.asarray(H[te].reshape(-1, n_b)))).reshape(len(te), K)
        score[te] = (e - e_tr.mean()) / e_tr.std()
    return score

def onset(T, s, level):
    """Highest temperature at which the mean score s(T) reaches `level`, scanning down from high T (linear interpolation)."""
    above = np.where(s >= level)[0]
    if len(above) == 0:
        return np.nan
    i = above.max()
    if i == len(T) - 1:
        return T[-1]
    return T[i] + (level - s[i]) * (T[i + 1] - T[i]) / (s[i + 1] - s[i])

t0 = time.time()
hist_sk, score_sk = {}, {}
for N in SIZES:
    hist_sk[N] = abs_q_histograms(sk[N]["configs"])
    score_sk[N] = histogram_anomaly(hist_sk[N])
    s = score_sk[N].mean(0)
    print(f"N = {N:3d}: mean score at T = 1.6: {s[-1]:+.2f}, T = 1.2: {s[16]:.1f}, T = 1.0: {s[12]:.1f}, T = 0.4: {s[0]:.0f};"
          f"  score reaches 3 at T = {onset(T_GRID, s, 3):.3f}, 10 at T = {onset(T_GRID, s, 10):.3f}")
print(f"time {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
NUMBERS["hist_onset"] = {N: dict(score3=round(float(onset(T_GRID, score_sk[N].mean(0), 3)), 3),
                                 score10=round(float(onset(T_GRID, score_sk[N].mean(0), 10)), 3)) for N in SIZES}

N =  64: mean score at T = 1.6: +0.02, T = 1.2: 0.7, T = 1.0: 12.2, T = 0.4: 471;  score reaches 3 at T = 1.094, 10 at T = 1.017


N = 128: mean score at T = 1.6: +0.02, T = 1.2: 1.1, T = 1.0: 48.7, T = 0.4: 424;  score reaches 3 at T = 1.167, 10 at T = 1.103
time 5 s


The score rises from zero well above \(T_c\), and the temperature at which it reaches a given level increases with \(N\) (printed above), so for the largest size the detector signals an anomaly at the highest temperature. This behaviour follows from the physics. Above \(T_c\) the width of \(P_J(q)\) is set by the spin-glass susceptibility, \([\langle q^2\rangle]=\chi_{\rm SG}/N\) with \(\chi_{\rm SG}=1/(1-\beta^2J^2)\), which grows continuously as \(T\) decreases towards \(J\). The detector notices this growth as soon as it is larger than the sample-to-sample noise of the training histograms, and that noise decreases as the histograms become more precise. An anomaly onset is therefore not a transition temperature, since it depends on the threshold, on the training window, and on the statistical resolution of the data. A mean-field transition, approached by a smooth growth of fluctuations on both sides, gives an autoencoder no sharp edge to find.

title: Lab 023: The SK spin glass without labels
section: 4. The Mattis model as a control
text:
4. The Mattis model as a control
Mattis couplings \(J_{ij}=\frac JN\xi_i\xi_j\) with random fixed signs \(\xi_i=\pm1\) look as random as SK couplings, but Lab 032 (Section 7) showed that the gauge transformation \(\sigma_i=\xi_is_i\) turns the model into the Curie–Weiss ferromagnet. This gives an exact sampler. In the Curie–Weiss model the energy depends only on the magnetisation \(M=\sum_i\sigma_i\), so the probability of \(M\) is \[
P(M)\propto\binom{N}{(N+M)/2}\exp\!\left[\frac{\beta J}{2N}\left(M^2-N\right)\right],
\] and given \(M\) all configurations with that magnetisation are equally likely. We draw \(M\) from \(P(M)\), place its \((N+M)/2\) up-spins at random positions, and multiply by \(\xi\) to obtain an exact equilibrium Mattis snapshot, with no Monte Carlo and no equilibration question. The overlap field of two replicas is \(s_i^as_i^b=\sigma_i^a\sigma_i^b\), independent of \(\xi\), so the hidden pattern drops out, as the couplings drop out for the SK overlap field. We generate a data set with the same shape as the SK data and check the sampler against the exact moment \(\langle\sigma_i\sigma_j\rangle=(\langle M^2\rangle-N)/(N(N-1))\) for \(i\neq j\).


Code
def cw_probabilities(N, T):
    """Exact P(M) of the Curie-Weiss model, M = 2 n_up - N, for J = 1: array (N + 1,) over n_up = 0..N."""
    n = np.arange(N + 1); M = 2 * n - N
    logw = gammaln(N + 1) - gammaln(n + 1) - gammaln(N - n + 1) + (M**2 - N) / (2 * N * T)
    p = np.exp(logw - logw.max())
    return p / p.sum()

def mattis_dataset(N, D, S=32, seed=0):
    """Exact equilibrium Mattis snapshots with the layout of the SK data: (D, 2, K, S, N) float32."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    xi = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(D, 1, 1, 1, N))                              # hidden pattern of every sample
    out = np.empty((D, 2, K_T, S, N), np.float32)
    for k, T in enumerate(T_GRID):
        n_up = rng.choice(N + 1, size=(D, 2, S), p=cw_probabilities(N, T))             # magnetisations
        rank = np.argsort(rng.random((D, 2, S, N)), axis=-1).argsort(axis=-1)          # a random permutation per configuration
        out[:, :, k] = np.where(rank < n_up[..., None], 1.0, -1.0)                     # n_up up-spins at random positions
    return out * xi, xi[:, 0, 0, 0]                                                    # s_i = xi_i sigma_i;  xi: (D, N)

mattis, mattis_xi = {}, {}
for N in SIZES:
    mattis[N], mattis_xi[N] = mattis_dataset(N, sk[N]["D"], seed=N)
    m_xi = np.abs((mattis[N][:, :, 0] * mattis_xi[N][:, None, None, :]).mean(-1)).mean()
    print(f"N = {N:3d}: Mattis data {mattis[N].shape};  mean |m| of single snapshots: T = 0.4 {np.abs(mattis[N][:, :, 0].mean(-1)).mean():.3f},"
          f" T = 1.6 {np.abs(mattis[N][:, :, -1].mean(-1)).mean():.3f};  mean |m_xi| at T = 0.4: {m_xi:.3f}")

# check of the sampler: <sigma_i sigma_j> (i != j) from the snapshots against the exact value, N = 64
N = 64
for k in (0, 12, 24):
    p = cw_probabilities(N, T_GRID[k]); M = 2 * np.arange(N + 1) - N
    exact = ((p * M**2).sum() - N) / (N * (N - 1))
    Ms = (mattis[N][:, :, k] * mattis_xi[N][:, None, None, :]).sum(-1)              # M = sum_i xi_i s_i of every snapshot
    est = ((Ms**2 - N) / (N * (N - 1))).mean()
    print(f"N = {N}, T = {T_GRID[k]}: <sigma_i sigma_j> from the snapshots {est:.4f}, exact {exact:.4f}")

The first figure compares the two models. Its left panel shows \(P(q)\) at \(T=0.4\) and \(N=128\) for the SK model (solid) and the Mattis model (dashed), and its right panel the Binder cumulant \(g_{\rm B}\) (axis label \(g\)) of the PCA projection against \(T/J\), for the Mattis model at the three sizes (dashed, open squares) and the SK model at \(N=128\) (solid). The second figure shows the mean reconstruction error \(\bar\varepsilon\) of the overlap-field autoencoder (left) and the mean anomaly score \(\bar a\) of the histogram detector (right, logarithmic axis, threshold 3 as a horizontal line) against \(T/J\), for the SK model (solid) and the Mattis model (dashed).
The control behaves like a ferromagnet in the first two detectors. The Binder cumulant of the PCA projection rises to \(1\) below \(T_c\) (two sharp peaks of \(P(q)\) at \(\pm m^2\), nothing in between), and the curves for different sizes cross at a well-defined point, with bootstrap intervals more than ten times narrower than for the SK model. The crossing moves towards \(T_c=J\) as \(N\) grows. The autoencoder error falls from about \(1\) near \(T_c\) to about \(0.06\) at \(T=0.4\), which is \(1-m^4\) with \(m\) the Curie–Weiss magnetisation. In the SK model the Binder cumulant stays between \(0.81\) and \(0.85\) at the lowest temperature (the weight between the peaks of \(P(q)\)), and the error decreases slowly and smoothly, only to \(0.51\)–\(0.56\).
The histogram detector behaves alike in both models. In the Mattis model, too, the score passes 3 above \(T_c\), at a temperature that increases with \(N\). The Curie–Weiss transition is also a mean-field transition, with a susceptibility \(1/(1-\beta J)\) that grows continuously as \(T\) approaches \(J\) from above. The onset of an anomaly score measures where fluctuations become noticeable at the given resolution, and it does not locate the critical temperature.
Both data sets have uniformly random single snapshots and both have random-sign couplings. The difference that the overlap-based detectors see, a broad \(P(q)\) that stays broad, is the signature of frustration.

The order of the spin glass is invisible in single snapshots, and no learning method can change this, because the gauge symmetry makes the data uniform. The right input, the overlap of two replicas, was found by physicists through the replica theory. Given it, PCA finds the overlap as its first component and the autoencoder learns \(q^2\). Neither locates \(T_c\) by itself. The PCA projection becomes a measurement of \(T_c\) only through the finite-size scaling of its Binder cumulant, with the same wide intervals as the physicist’s analysis, and the anomaly onsets reflect the smooth growth of fluctuations of a mean-field transition. Supervised work on the three-dimensional Edwards–Anderson spin glass reached the same conclusion about the input. Munoz-Bauza, Hamze and Katzgraber fed a convolutional network with replica overlap configurations.

Exercises

Exercise 1
Assume the pooled overlap fields have a distribution symmetric under permutations of the labels and under \(\boldsymbol q\to-\boldsymbol q\) (an exchangeable distribution). (a) Show that the covariance matrix is \(C=(1-c)\,\mathbb 1+c\,\boldsymbol 1\boldsymbol 1^T\) with \(c=(N\overline{q^2}-1)/(N-1)\). (b) Find all eigenvalues. (c) Compare with the PCA of Section 3.2 for \(N=128\), the value of \(\sigma_1^2\) and the mean of the other eigenvalues.

Solution

The diagonal entries are \(\overline{q_i^2}=1\), and by symmetry all off-diagonal entries are equal to \(c\). Summing all entries, \(\sum_{ij}\overline{q_iq_j}=N^2\overline{q^2}=N+N(N-1)c\), which gives \(c\). (b) \(C\boldsymbol 1=(1-c+Nc)\boldsymbol 1\), so \(\sigma_{\rm uniform}^2=1+(N-1)c=N\overline{q^2}\). Every vector orthogonal to \(\boldsymbol 1\) has eigenvalue \(1-c=N(1-\overline{q^2})/(N-1)\), \(N-1\) times. (c) The code compares these with the measured spectrum. Small differences in \(\sigma_1^2\) come from the centring of PCA and the factor \(M/(M-1)\). The other eigenvalues of the data scatter around their mean, which is fixed by the trace, because the finite set of samples is only approximately exchangeable.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
1. Statistical mechanics and frustration
We begin with the five objects of statistical mechanics that the notebook uses, energy, Boltzmann weight, partition function, free energy and order parameter, and then introduce the one new idea of the model, frustration. Lab 012 develops the same material at length for the ordinary Ising model.
A configuration is a vector \(\mathbf s=(s_1,\dots,s_N)\in\{-1,+1\}^N\) of \(N\) spins, and a Hamiltonian \(H(\mathbf s)\) assigns it an energy. For pair interactions \[
H(\mathbf s) = -\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\,s_is_j ,
\] a bond with \(J_{ij}>0\) is ferromagnetic (energy \(-J_{ij}\) if \(s_i=s_j\), \(+J_{ij}\) otherwise) and a bond with \(J_{ij}<0\) is antiferromagnetic. We call a bond satisfied when it has its lower energy.
In thermal equilibrium at temperature \(T\) a configuration occurs with the Boltzmann probability \[
p(\mathbf s) = \frac{e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}}{Z},\qquad \beta=\frac1T,\qquad Z(T) = \sum_{\mathbf s}e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)} .
\] Here the normalisation \(Z\) is the partition function. At low \(T\) the low-energy configurations dominate, and at high \(T\) all \(2^N\) configurations become equally likely.
All thermal averages follow from the free energy per spin \(f = -\frac{T}{N}\ln Z\). The energy per spin is \(u = \partial(\beta f)/\partial\beta = \langle H\rangle/N\), the specific heat per spin is \(c = \partial u/\partial T = (\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2)/(NT^2)\), and the entropy per spin is \(s_{\rm ent}=(u-f)/T\). A phase transition is a temperature at which \(f\), in the limit \(N\to\infty\), is not an analytic function of \(T\).
An ordered phase is recognised by an order parameter, a quantity that is non-zero in it and zero in the disordered (paramagnetic) phase. For a ferromagnet this is the magnetisation \(m = \frac1N\sum_is_i\). Since the Hamiltonian is invariant under \(\mathbf s\to-\mathbf s\), \(\langle m\rangle=0\) on any finite lattice, and one therefore uses \(\langle|m|\rangle\) or \(\langle m^2\rangle\). Choosing the order parameter requires knowing what pattern the spins form, which for our model is the subject of Sections 2 and 3.

1.1 Frustration on a triangle of bonds
On the square lattice with only ferromagnetic bonds all bonds can be satisfied at once, by setting all spins up. A diagonal antiferromagnetic bond changes this. It closes a triangle of two nearest-neighbour bonds and one diagonal bond, and the three bonds of this triangle cannot all be satisfied. Take sites \(1,2,3\) with \(1\)–\(2\) and \(2\)–\(3\) nearest neighbours and \(1\)–\(3\) diagonal neighbours, \[
H_\triangle = -J_1(s_1s_2+s_2s_3) + J_2\,s_1s_3 .
\] Satisfying both \(J_1\) bonds requires \(s_1=s_2=s_3\), and then \(s_1s_3=+1\) breaks the \(J_2\) bond. Satisfying the \(J_2\) bond requires \(s_1=-s_3\), and then \(s_2\) agrees with only one of them.
The sketch below shows three of the eight states of the triangle, with the \(J_1\) bonds \(1\)–\(2\) and \(2\)–\(3\) between nearest neighbours and the \(J_2\) bond \(1\)–\(3\) on the diagonal. A solid line is a satisfied bond, a dashed purple line with a cross a broken one, a navy disc is \(s=+1\) and a white disc with an orange rim \(s=-1\), the convention of all sketches in this course. One bond always stays broken. Aligning all three spins breaks the diagonal, and turning one end spin to satisfy the diagonal breaks a nearest-neighbour bond.

def draw_spin(ax, x, y, s, r=0.26, sign=False, alpha=1.0, fs=10, lw=1.3):
    # one Ising spin at (x, y): navy disc for s = +1, white disc with orange rim for s = -1 (optionally with "+" / "-")
    face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if s > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
    ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x, y), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=lw, alpha=alpha, zorder=4))
    if sign:
        ax.text(x, y, "+" if s > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", alpha=alpha,
                fontsize=fs, fontweight="bold", zorder=5)

def draw_bond(ax, p, q, broken=False, lw=1.5, alpha=1.0, color=None, cross=True):
    # bond between points p and q: solid blue if satisfied, dashed purple with a cross if broken
    c = color or (PURPLE if broken else BLUE)
    ax.plot([p[0], q[0]], [p[1], q[1]], color=c, lw=lw, ls=(0, (2.5, 1.5)) if broken else "-",
            alpha=alpha, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=2)
    if broken and cross:
        ax.plot((p[0] + q[0]) / 2, (p[1] + q[1]) / 2, marker="x", ms=3.5 * lw, mew=lw * 0.9, color=c, alpha=alpha, zorder=3)

def sketch_j1j2_triangle():
    # sites 1 = (0, 0), 2 = (1, 0), 3 = (1, 1): bonds 1-2 and 2-3 are J1 (nearest neighbours), 1-3 is J2 (diagonal)
    pos = {1: (0, 0), 2: (1, 0), 3: (1, 1)}
    bonds = [(1, 2, "J1"), (2, 3, "J1"), (1, 3, "J2")]
    states = [(+1, +1, +1), (+1, +1, -1), (+1, -1, -1)]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 2.2))
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, bottom=0.12, top=0.86, wspace=0.05)
    for ax, st in zip(axes, states):
        s = dict(zip((1, 2, 3), st))
        for a, b, kind in bonds:
            # J1 is satisfied by parallel spins, J2 (antiferromagnetic) by antiparallel spins
            satisfied = s[a] * s[b] > 0 if kind == "J1" else s[a] * s[b] < 0
            draw_bond(ax, pos[a], pos[b], broken=not satisfied, lw=1.8)
            mx, my = (pos[a][0] + pos[b][0]) / 2, (pos[a][1] + pos[b][1]) / 2
            off = {(1, 2): (0, -0.24), (2, 3): (0.24, 0), (1, 3): (-0.22, 0.16)}[(a, b)]
            ax.text(mx + off[0], my + off[1], "$J_1$" if kind == "J1" else "$J_2$", fontsize=10, ha="center", va="center",
                    color=GRAY)
        for k, (x, y) in pos.items():
            draw_spin(ax, x, y, s[k], r=0.16, sign=True, fs=10)
            ax.text(x + (-0.24 if k == 1 else 0.24), y + (0.0 if k != 3 else 0.12), f"{k}", fontsize=10, color=GRAY, ha="center", va="center")
        E = -(st[0] * st[1] + st[1] * st[2])                            # J1 part, in units of J1 ...
        E2 = st[0] * st[2]                                               # ... plus J2 part
        e_txt = rf"$E={'-' if E < 0 else '+'}{abs(E)}J_1{'+' if E2 > 0 else '-'}J_2$" if E != 0 else rf"$E={'+' if E2 > 0 else '-'}J_2$"
        ax.set_title(e_txt, fontsize=11, color=NAVY)
        ax.set_xlim(-0.45, 1.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.45, 1.35); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    fig.text(0.5, 0.02, "every state breaks at least one bond (dashed)", ha="center", fontsize=10, color=GRAY)
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_j1j2_triangle()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_j1j2_triangle.png")
plt.show()





The same reasoning gives a general criterion. Going around a closed loop of bonds, multiply the signs of the couplings (ferromagnetic \(+\), antiferromagnetic \(-\)). If the product is negative, at least one bond on the loop is broken in every configuration. The product of the bond variables \(s_is_j\) around a loop is \(\prod_i s_i^2=+1\), and a satisfied bond has \(s_is_j=\operatorname{sign}J_{ij}\), so if all bonds were satisfied the product of signs would be \(+1\). Our triangle has signs \((+,+,-)\), so it is frustrated.
The next cell writes the energies of the triangle as symbolic functions of \(J_1,J_2\) with SymPy and counts the broken bonds. It prints the four states with \(s_1=+1\) (the other four follow by the global flip) and the minimum number of broken bonds over all eight states, which the criterion says cannot be zero.


Code
J1s, J2s, gs_ = sp.symbols("J_1 J_2 g", positive=True)

def H_triangle(s1, s2, s3):
    # energy of the triangle: two nearest-neighbour bonds (1-2, 2-3) and one diagonal bond (1-3)
    return -J1s * (s1 * s2 + s2 * s3) + J2s * s1 * s3

print("  s1 s2 s3   energy              broken bonds")
for s in itertools.product([1, -1], repeat=3):
    if s[0] == -1:                       # the global flip gives the same energy: list one state of each pair
        continue
    broken = int(s[0] * s[1] < 0) + int(s[1] * s[2] < 0) + int(s[0] * s[2] > 0)
    print(f"  {s[0]:+d} {s[1]:+d} {s[2]:+d}   {str(H_triangle(*s)):18s}  {broken}")

# the product of coupling signs around the loop (+J1, +J1, -J2) is negative: at least one broken bond in every state
min_broken = min(int(s[0]*s[1] < 0) + int(s[1]*s[2] < 0) + int(s[0]*s[2] > 0) for s in itertools.product([1, -1], repeat=3))
assert min_broken == 1
print(f"minimum number of broken bonds over all 8 states: {min_broken}")


  s1 s2 s3   energy              broken bonds
  +1 +1 +1   -2*J_1 + J_2        1
  +1 +1 -1   -J_2                1
  +1 -1 +1   2*J_1 + J_2         3
  +1 -1 -1   -J_2                1
minimum number of broken bonds over all 8 states: 1


Every state of the triangle breaks at least one bond, and two kinds of state compete, \((+,+,+)\) with energy \(-2J_1+J_2\) (the diagonal bond broken) and \((+,+,-)\), \((+,-,-)\) with energy \(-J_2\) (one nearest-neighbour bond broken). For an isolated triangle the first wins when \(-2J_1+J_2<-J_2\), that is for \(J_2<J_1\). On the lattice every nearest-neighbour bond is shared by several triangles, so the balance point moves, and Section 3 shows that it lies at \(J_2=J_1/2\). Frustration alone does not decide which state wins. It says that some bonds must be broken, and the remaining task is to find the compromise of lowest energy and the number of compromises of equal energy.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
2. Hamiltonian, symmetries and order parameters
Before computing anything we need the symmetries of the model. They decide which ordered states are degenerate, which order parameter measures them and, through the symmetry group of the order parameter, which universality class a continuous transition can belong to. A universality class is a set of models that share the critical exponents, the powers that describe how quantities such as the order parameter or the correlation length behave near a continuous transition. We establish the symmetries once here and use them in every later section.
The spins \(s_{x,y}=\pm1\) live on an \(L\times L\) square lattice with periodic boundaries (a torus), \(x,y\in\{0,\dots,L-1\}\), \(N=L^2\), and the Hamiltonian is \[
\begin{aligned}
H(\mathbf s) &= -J_1\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}s_is_j + J_2\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}s_is_j\\
&= -J_1\,B_1(\mathbf s) + J_2\,B_2(\mathbf s),\qquad g=\frac{J_2}{J_1}\ge0 ,
\end{aligned}
\] which is the convention of Lab 018. Here \(\langle i,j\rangle\) runs over the \(2N\) nearest-neighbour bonds (horizontal \((x,y)\)–\((x+1,y)\) and vertical \((x,y)\)–\((x,y+1)\)), \(\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle\) over the \(2N\) diagonal bonds (\((x,y)\)–\((x+1,y+1)\) and \((x,y)\)–\((x+1,y-1)\)), and \(B_1=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j\), \(B_2=\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}s_is_j\) are integers in \([-2N,2N]\). With \(J_1=1\) the energy is \(H=-B_1+gB_2\), so computing \(B_1,B_2\) once gives the energy for every \(g\). We also split \(B_1=B_1^{x}+B_1^{y}\) into horizontal and vertical bonds.
The figure below shows the lattice and its two kinds of bonds. Every site \(i\) has four nearest neighbours, coupled by \(J_1\) (solid blue), and four diagonal neighbours, coupled by \(J_2\) (dashed green). The ferromagnetic \(J_1\) favours parallel nearest neighbours, the antiferromagnetic \(J_2\) favours antiparallel diagonal neighbours, and no configuration satisfies both. The ratio \(g=J_2/J_1\) decides which compromise has the lowest energy.


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.

A symmetry is a map of configurations that leaves \(H\) unchanged, and the model has two kinds of them. The global spin flip \(\mathbf s\to-\mathbf s\) leaves every product \(s_is_j\) unchanged, the \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry of every Ising model. The lattice symmetries, translations by one site, rotation by \(90^\circ\) and reflections, map nearest-neighbour bonds onto nearest-neighbour bonds and diagonal bonds onto diagonal bonds.
Two further transformations change the signs of a subset of spins. They map \(H\) onto another Hamiltonian, so they are gauge transformations, and both will be useful later. The checkerboard gauge \(s_{x,y}\to(-1)^{x+y}s_{x,y}\) changes the sign of every nearest-neighbour product, because nearest neighbours have opposite parity of \(x+y\), while diagonal neighbours have equal parity and their products are unchanged, so \(B_1\to-B_1\) and \(B_2\to B_2\). Consequently the model with antiferromagnetic \(J_1\) has the same thermodynamics as ours, with Néel order (the chessboard pattern \(\pm(-1)^{x+y}\)) mapped onto ferromagnetic order. Several papers in Section 10 use \(J_1<0\) (nearest-neighbour antiferromagnet) or write \(J_1<0\) for the ferromagnet, and their phase diagrams apply here without change. The column gauge \(s_{x,y}\to(-1)^{x}s_{x,y}\) acts differently. Horizontal and diagonal bonds join different \(x\) parities and change sign, vertical bonds do not, so \(B_1^x\to-B_1^x\), \(B_1^y\to B_1^y\) and \(B_2\to-B_2\). Section 5 uses it for the limit \(g\to\infty\).
The cell below verifies all of these statements on random configurations, and every line of its output should read True.


Code
def bond_sums(s):
    # s: (..., L, L) array of +-1; axis -2 is x, axis -1 is y; periodic boundaries.
    # Returns (B1x, B1y, B2): sums of s_i s_j over horizontal, vertical and diagonal bonds (each bond counted once), integer arrays of shape (...).
    s = np.asarray(s, dtype=np.int64)
    ax = (-2, -1)
    b1x = (s * np.roll(s, -1, -2)).sum(ax)                                    # (x,y)-(x+1,y)
    b1y = (s * np.roll(s, -1, -1)).sum(ax)                                    # (x,y)-(x,y+1)
    b2 = (s * np.roll(s, (-1, -1), ax)).sum(ax) + (s * np.roll(s, (-1, 1), ax)).sum(ax)   # (x,y)-(x+1,y+1) and (x,y)-(x+1,y-1)
    return b1x, b1y, b2

def energy(s, g, J1=1.0):
    # H = -J1 B1 + J2 B2 with J2 = g J1; shape (...)
    b1x, b1y, b2 = bond_sums(s)
    return -J1 * (b1x + b1y) + g * J1 * b2

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
L = 8
S_rand = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=(1000, L, L))                               # 1000 random configurations, shape (1000, 8, 8)

b1x, b1y, b2 = bond_sums(S_rand)
ops = {"global flip": -S_rand,
       "translation x -> x+1": np.roll(S_rand, 1, -2),
       "rotation by 90 degrees": np.rot90(S_rand, 1, axes=(-2, -1)),
       "reflection x -> -x": np.roll(S_rand[..., ::-1, :], 1, -2)}
for name, S2 in ops.items():
    c = bond_sums(S2)
    print(f"{name:24s}: B1 unchanged {np.array_equal(c[0] + c[1], b1x + b1y)},  B2 unchanged {np.array_equal(c[2], b2)}")
c = bond_sums(S_rand * (-1) ** (x + y))
print(f"checkerboard gauge      : B1 -> -B1 {np.array_equal(c[0] + c[1], -(b1x + b1y))},  B2 unchanged {np.array_equal(c[2], b2)}")
c = bond_sums(S_rand * (-1) ** x)

2.1 Stripe order parameter and its symmetry group
Periodic patterns of spins are described by their Fourier components \[
\begin{aligned}
m_{\boldsymbol k}(\mathbf s) &= \frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol r}s_{\boldsymbol r}\,e^{i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r},\\
\boldsymbol r&=(x,y),\quad \boldsymbol k\in\Big\{\tfrac{2\pi}{L}(n_x,n_y)\Big\}.
\end{aligned}
\] Section 3 compares three candidate orders, listed in the table with their patterns, wave vectors and order parameters.









order
pattern \(s_{x,y}\)
wave vector
order parameter




ferromagnet
\(\pm1\)
\((0,0)\)
\(m = m_{(0,0)}\)


stripes
\(\pm(-1)^x\) (vertical) or \(\pm(-1)^y\) (horizontal)
\((\pi,0)\), \((0,\pi)\)
\(m_{\rm str}=\sqrt{m_x^2+m_y^2}\), \(\ m_x\equiv m_{(\pi,0)},\ m_y\equiv m_{(0,\pi)}\)


Néel

\((\pi,\pi)\)
\(m_{(\pi,\pi)}\)



For \(\boldsymbol k\) with components \(0\) or \(\pi\), \(e^{i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r}=\pm1\) and \(m_{\boldsymbol k}\) is real.
The stripe phase has four ground states, two orientations times the global flip. In the plane \((m_x,m_y)\) they sit at \((\pm1,0)\) (vertical stripes) and \((0,\pm1)\) (horizontal stripes), whereas the ferromagnet has only two states, \(m=\pm1\), on a line.
The lattice symmetries act on the stripe order parameter in a simple way. A translation \(x\to x+1\) changes the sign of \((-1)^{x}\), so \((m_x,m_y)\to(-m_x,m_y)\), and a translation in \(y\) gives \((m_x,-m_y)\). A rotation by \(90^\circ\), \((x,y)\to(-y,x)\), turns the factor \((-1)^x\) into \((-1)^y\), so \((m_x,m_y)\to(m_y,m_x)\). The global flip sends \((m_x,m_y)\to(-m_x,-m_y)\). A sign change of one component together with the exchange of the two components generate the eight symmetries of a square, the dihedral group \(D_4\), while the ferromagnetic order parameter sees only \(\mathbb Z_2\) (\(m\to-m\)).
An order parameter with two components and the symmetry of a square is that of the Ashkin–Teller model [Ashkin & Teller 1943], two Ising spins \(\sigma_i,\tau_i\) per site coupled by \(-K_2(\sigma_i\sigma_j+\tau_i\tau_j)-K_4\,\sigma_i\sigma_j\tau_i\tau_j\). The four stripe states correspond to the four values of \((\sigma,\tau)\), and one possible identification is \(\sigma=\operatorname{sign}(m_x+m_y)\), \(\tau=\operatorname{sign}(m_x-m_y)\). For this reason the stripe transition, unlike the ferromagnetic one, can belong to the Ashkin–Teller class, whose critical exponents vary continuously along a line [Jin, Sen, Sandvik 2012]. Section 5 shows the same structure from the \(g\to\infty\) limit, where \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\) become the magnetisations of two decoupled sublattices.
The cell below applies the lattice operations to the four stripe states (labelled V\(\pm\) and H\(\pm\) for vertical and horizontal stripes of either sign), prints where each state is sent, and generates the group from two of its elements. The first line also confirms that the four states have the same energy.


Code
def order_params(s):
    # s: (..., L, L) -> dict of m, m_x = m_(pi,0), m_y = m_(0,pi), m_(pi,pi), each of shape (...)
    L = s.shape[-1]
    ph = (-1.0) ** np.arange(L)
    s = np.asarray(s, dtype=float)
    return {"m": s.mean((-2, -1)),
            "mx": (s * ph[:, None]).mean((-2, -1)),
            "my": (s * ph[None, :]).mean((-2, -1)),
            "mpp": (s * ph[:, None] * ph[None, :]).mean((-2, -1))}

L = 8
x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(L), np.arange(L), indexing="ij")
stripes = {"V+": (-1) ** x, "V-": -(-1) ** x, "H+": (-1) ** y, "H-": -(-1) ** y}
lattice_ops = {"translate x": lambda s: np.roll(s, 1, 0), "translate y": lambda s: np.roll(s, 1, 1),
               "rotate 90":   lambda s: np.rot90(s),    "global flip": lambda s: -s}

def label(s):
    # name of the stripe state with the same (m_x, m_y)
    o = order_params(s)
    for k, v in stripes.items():
        ov = order_params(v)
        if np.isclose(o["mx"], ov["mx"]) and np.isclose(o["my"], ov["my"]):
            return k

print("energy per spin of the four stripe states at g = 0.7:", [float(energy(v, 0.7)) / L**2 for v in stripes.values()])
print("\n operation     " + "   ".join(f"{k}->" for k in stripes))
for name, op in lattice_ops.items():
    print(f" {name:12s}  " + "   ".join(f"{label(op(v)):>4s}" for v in stripes.values()))

# the action on (m_x, m_y) as 2x2 matrices, and the group they generate
R = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])        # rotation: exchange m_x and m_y
Tx = np.array([[-1, 0], [0, 1]])      # translation in x: m_x -> -m_x
group = {R.tobytes(): R, Tx.tobytes(): Tx}
while True:
    new = {(a @ b).tobytes(): a @ b for a in group.values() for b in group.values()}
    if new.keys() <= group.keys():
        break
    group.update(new)
print(f"\nnumber of distinct 2x2 matrices generated by 'rotate' and 'translate x': {len(group)} (the symmetry group of a square, D4, has 8)")

The table reproduces the action derived above, and the two generators produce eight distinct matrices. The Hamiltonian therefore has the global \(\mathbb Z_2\) flip and the lattice symmetries. Ferromagnetic order breaks only \(\mathbb Z_2\) (two states), whereas stripe order breaks \(\mathbb Z_2\) and the \(90^\circ\) rotation (four states), and its two-component order parameter transforms under the eight-element group \(D_4\), as in the Ashkin–Teller model. The checkerboard gauge shows that the sign of \(J_1\) is irrelevant for thermodynamics.
The schematic below shows idealised configurations of the phases on an \(8\times8\) lattice, with both order parameters printed above each panel. In the ferromagnet nearly all spins point the same way and \(m\) is close to \(1\), while \(m_{\rm str}\) is close to zero. In the two stripe states whole columns or whole rows alternate in sign. Their magnetisation is close to zero, but \(m_{\rm str}\) is close to \(1\), carried by the component \(m_x\) for vertical and \(m_y\) for horizontal stripes. A few thermally flipped spins reduce the order parameters slightly below \(1\). In the paramagnet, the disordered phase at high temperature, both order parameters are small and vanish for \(N\to\infty\), although on \(64\) random spins \(m_{\rm str}\) is not zero. The Néel pattern, the antiferromagnetic order of nearest neighbours, does not occur as a phase of our model, since it breaks every \(J_1\) bond.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
3. Ground states
We now turn to the lowest temperatures. At \(T=0\) the Boltzmann weight selects the configurations of minimum energy. They tell us which orders can appear at low temperature, and their number, the degeneracy, tells us how strongly thermal fluctuations will compete with them. For this model the answer changes qualitatively at one value of \(g\).

3.1 Bond counting
We start by comparing the energies of the three simple periodic patterns. Every spin has 4 nearest neighbours and 4 diagonal neighbours, and each bond is shared by two spins, so there are 2 nearest-neighbour bonds and 2 diagonal bonds per spin. For a periodic pattern the energy per spin is therefore the average over one unit cell of \(-J_1(s_{x,y}s_{x+1,y}+s_{x,y}s_{x,y+1})+J_2(s_{x,y}s_{x+1,y+1}+s_{x,y}s_{x+1,y-1})\).
For the ferromagnet (all \(+1\)) both nearest-neighbour products and both diagonal products are \(+1\), so both diagonal bonds are broken and \(E/N=-2J_1+2J_2\). For the stripes \((-1)^x\) the horizontal product is \(-1\) and the vertical one \(+1\), which cancel, while both diagonal products are \(-1\), so \(E/N=-2J_2\). For the Néel state \((-1)^{x+y}\) both nearest-neighbour products are \(-1\) and both diagonal products \(+1\), so \(E/N=+2J_1+2J_2\).
The figure below draws the four patterns on a \(4\times4\) patch with every bond marked. Thick lines are \(J_1\) bonds, thin lines \(J_2\) bonds, solid when satisfied and dashed purple when broken. In the ferromagnet every \(J_1\) bond is satisfied and every diagonal broken. In the stripes half of the \(J_1\) bonds are broken but every diagonal is satisfied. The Néel state, drawn for contrast, breaks every bond and is never a ground state for \(J_1>0\). It is the ground state of the antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbour model, which the checkerboard gauge of Section 2 maps onto our ferromagnet.

The ferromagnet and the stripes cross where \(-2J_1+2J_2=-2J_2\), that is at \(g=1/2\). SymPy reproduces the counting on the \(2\times2\) unit cell and solves for the crossing, and the last lines compare the symbolic energies with a direct numerical evaluation at three values of \(g\).

def energy_per_spin_pattern(P):
    # symbolic energy per spin of a pattern of period 2 in x and y; P(x, y) returns +-1
    e = 0
    for x0, y0 in itertools.product(range(2), repeat=2):
        s = P(x0, y0)
        e += -J1s * (s * P((x0 + 1) % 2, y0) + s * P(x0, (y0 + 1) % 2)) \
             + J2s * (s * P((x0 + 1) % 2, (y0 + 1) % 2) + s * P((x0 + 1) % 2, (y0 - 1) % 2))
    return sp.simplify(e / 4)

patterns_sym = {"ferromagnet": lambda x, y: 1, "stripes": lambda x, y: (-1) ** x, "Neel": lambda x, y: (-1) ** (x + y)}
E_sym = {k: energy_per_spin_pattern(P) for k, P in patterns_sym.items()}
for k, v in E_sym.items():
    print(f"E/N ({k:11s}) = {v}")
g_cross = sp.solve(sp.Eq(E_sym["ferromagnet"], E_sym["stripes"]), J2s)
print("ferromagnet = stripes at J_2 =", g_cross, "   i.e. g =", sp.simplify(g_cross[0] / J1s))
print("Neel - min(ferromagnet, stripes) =", sp.simplify(E_sym["Neel"] - E_sym["ferromagnet"]), "and",
      sp.simplify(E_sym["Neel"] - E_sym["stripes"]), "(both > 0 for J_1 > 0)")

3.2 Plaquette bound
Section 3.1 compared three guesses, and a proof must exclude every other configuration. We obtain one by writing \(H\) as a sum over the \(N\) elementary squares (plaquettes) and bounding each term from below.
Label the corners of the plaquette with lower-left corner \((x,y)\) as \(a=(x,y)\), \(b=(x+1,y)\), \(c=(x+1,y+1)\), \(d=(x,y+1)\). Every nearest-neighbour bond is an edge of two plaquettes, and every diagonal bond is a diagonal of one plaquette. Therefore \[
H = \sum_{P}h_P,\qquad h_P = -\frac{J_1}{2}\big(s_as_b+s_bs_c+s_cs_d+s_ds_a\big) + J_2\big(s_as_c+s_bs_d\big).
\] It follows that \(H\ge N\min h_P\), where the minimum runs over the 16 states of one plaquette. If a configuration reaches the minimum on every plaquette simultaneously, it is a ground state and the bound is the ground-state energy.
The cell lists \(h_P\) for all 16 plaquette states with SymPy (with \(J_1=1\), \(J_2=g\)), groups them by energy, finds the lower envelope, and checks numerically that the plaquette energies indeed add up to \(H\).


Code
def h_plaquette(a, b, c, d, J1=1, J2=gs_):
    # energy of one plaquette, corners a, b, c, d in cyclic order
    return -sp.Rational(1, 2) * J1 * (a * b + b * c + c * d + d * a) + J2 * (a * c + b * d)

plaq = {}
for st in itertools.product([1, -1], repeat=4):
    plaq.setdefault(sp.expand(h_plaquette(*st)), []).append(st)
print("distinct plaquette energies h_P(g) and the number of plaquette states with that energy:")
for h, sts in sorted(plaq.items(), key=lambda kv: float(kv[0].subs(gs_, 0.3))):
    print(f"   h_P = {str(h):10s}  ({len(sts):2d} states), e.g. corners a,b,c,d = {sts[0]}")

# lower envelope of the distinct linear functions on a grid of g, compared with min(-2 + 2g, -2g)
g_grid = np.linspace(0, 2, 2001)
env = np.min([sp.lambdify(gs_, h)(g_grid) * np.ones_like(g_grid) for h in plaq], axis=0)
print("max |lower envelope - min(-2+2g, -2g)| on g in [0, 2]:", np.abs(env - np.minimum(-2 + 2 * g_grid, -2 * g_grid)).max())

# numerical check of the decomposition H = sum_P h_P on random configurations
def plaquette_energies(s, g):
    a, b = s, np.roll(s, -1, 0); c, d = np.roll(s, (-1, -1), (0, 1)), np.roll(s, -1, 1)
    return -0.5 * (a * b + b * c + c * d + d * a) + g * (a * c + b * d)      # shape (L, L): one value per plaquette
S8 = np.random.default_rng(1).choice([-1, 1], size=(200, 8, 8))
dev = max(abs(plaquette_energies(s, 0.37).sum() - energy(s, 0.37)) for s in S8)
print(f"max |sum_P h_P - H| over 200 random 8x8 configurations at g = 0.37: {dev:.1e}")

   h_P = -2*g        ( 4 states), e.g. corners a,b,c,d = (1, 1, -1, -1)

Only four distinct plaquette energies occur, and the lowest is \(\min(-2J_1+2J_2,\,-2J_2)\), reached by the uniform plaquettes (\(g<1/2\)) or by the plaquettes with one edge up and the opposite edge down (\(g>1/2\)). The ferromagnet and the stripes reach the minimum on every plaquette, so they are exact ground states, \[
\frac{E_0}{N} = \begin{cases}-2J_1+2J_2, & g<\tfrac12 \quad\text{(ferromagnet, 2 states)},\\[2pt] -2J_2, & g>\tfrac12\quad\text{(stripes, 4 states)}.\end{cases}
\] The Néel plaquette is the most expensive one for every \(g\ge0\). At \(g=1/2\) both kinds of plaquette, 2 uniform and 4 half-up/half-down, 6 of the 16, have the minimal energy \(-J_1\), and every configuration built from these six plaquettes is a ground state. Section 3.5 counts them.


3.3 Enumeration on the \(4\times4\) torus
The bound can also be tested by brute force on a small lattice. A \(4\times4\) torus has \(2^{16}=65\,536\) configurations. We compute \((B_1,B_2)\) for all of them once (arrays of shape \((65536,)\)) and obtain \(E_0(g)\) and the degeneracy \(n_0(g)\) for 401 values of \(g\) by broadcasting. The degeneracy column matters as much as the energy.


Code
def all_configs(n):
    # all 2^n configurations of n spins as rows of +-1 (bit k of the row index -> spin k, s = 1 - 2 bit); shape (2^n, n)
    bits = (np.arange(2**n)[:, None] >> np.arange(n)) & 1
    return (1 - 2 * bits).astype(np.int8)

S44 = all_configs(16).reshape(-1, 4, 4)                         # (65536, 4, 4)
b1x, b1y, b2 = bond_sums(S44)
B1_44, B2_44 = b1x + b1y, b2
g_scan = np.linspace(0, 2, 401)
E_44 = -B1_44[None, :] + g_scan[:, None] * B2_44[None, :]      # (401, 65536)
E0_44 = E_44.min(1)
n0_44 = (E_44 <= E0_44[:, None] + 1e-9).sum(1)
exact_E0 = np.minimum(-2 + 2 * g_scan, -2 * g_scan)
print(f"max |E0/N (enumeration) - min(-2+2g, -2g)| over 401 values of g: {np.abs(E0_44 / 16 - exact_E0).max():.1e}")
for gv in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 2.0):
    i = np.argmin(abs(g_scan - gv))
    print(f"g = {gv:4.2f}:  E0/N = {E0_44[i]/16:+.4f}   degeneracy n0 = {n0_44[i]}")

3.4 Zero-temperature transfer matrix
The degeneracy \(n_0=30\) at \(g=1/2\) is the first sign of something special, and understanding it requires larger lattices. Enumeration stops at about \(5\times5\) (\(2^{25}\) states). A transfer matrix performs the sum over configurations row by row, at a cost exponential only in the width, and at \(T\to0\) it turns into a shortest-path calculation that also counts the shortest paths.
Group the spins of an \(L\times M\) torus into rows \(\sigma_y=(s_{0,y},\dots,s_{L-1,y})\), super-spins with \(2^L\) states each. The energy splits into terms within a row and terms between neighbouring rows, \[
\begin{aligned}
H &= \sum_{y=0}^{M-1}W(\sigma_y,\sigma_{y+1}),\\
W(\sigma,\sigma') &= -J_1\sum_x s_xs'_x + J_2\sum_x s_x\big(s'_{x+1}+s'_{x-1}\big)\\
&\quad - \frac{J_1}{2}\sum_x\big(s_xs_{x+1}+s'_xs'_{x+1}\big),
\end{aligned}
\] where the bonds inside a row are split half–half between the two neighbouring factors. Then \(Z = \operatorname{Tr}\mathsf V^M\) with \(\mathsf V_{\sigma\sigma'}=e^{-\beta W(\sigma,\sigma')}\) (Lab 012, Section 3).
In the limit \(\beta\to\infty\) the ordinary algebra of Boltzmann weights turns into the (min, +) algebra, \(e^{-\beta a}+e^{-\beta b}\simeq n\,e^{-\beta\min(a,b)}\) with \(n\) the number of terms attaining the minimum, and \(e^{-\beta a}e^{-\beta b}=e^{-\beta(a+b)}\). The matrix product \(\sum_{\sigma'}\mathsf V_{\sigma\sigma'}\mathsf V_{\sigma'\sigma''}\) therefore becomes \[
\begin{aligned}
(W\otimes W)_{\sigma\sigma''} &= \min_{\sigma'}\big[W_{\sigma\sigma'}+W_{\sigma'\sigma''}\big],\\
n_{\sigma\sigma''} &= \sum_{\sigma'\,\text{attaining the min}} n_{\sigma\sigma'}n_{\sigma'\sigma''} ,
\end{aligned}
\] and \(Z\simeq n_0e^{-\beta E_0}\) with \(E_0=\min_\sigma(W^{\otimes M})_{\sigma\sigma}\) and \(n_0\) the sum of the counts on the diagonal entries attaining \(E_0\). This is a shortest-path problem with path counting, solved by repeated (min, +) matrix products. The function minplus_torus below implements it with arrays of shape \((2^L,2^L)\). We first make sure that it reproduces the enumeration on the \(4\times4\) torus, and then go to tori up to \(8\times8\).


Code
def row_terms(L):
    # for all 2^L rows of width L (periodic): intra[sigma] = sum_x s_x s_{x+1};  nn[sigma, sigma'] = sum_x s_x s'_x;
    # dd[sigma, sigma'] = sum_x s_x (s'_{x+1} + s'_{x-1}).  Shapes (2^L,), (2^L, 2^L), (2^L, 2^L).
    R = all_configs(L).astype(np.float64)
    intra = (R * np.roll(R, -1, 1)).sum(1)
    nn = R @ R.T
    dd = R @ np.roll(R, -1, 1).T + R @ np.roll(R, 1, 1).T
    return intra, nn, dd

def W_matrix(L, J1, J2):
    # row-pair energy W(sigma, sigma') of the text; shape (2^L, 2^L)
    intra, nn, dd = row_terms(L)
    return -J1 * nn + J2 * dd - 0.5 * J1 * (intra[:, None] + intra[None, :])

def minplus_mult(Ea, Ca, Eb, Cb, tol=1e-9, block=64):
    # (min,+) product with path counting; E: energies, C: counts, all (n, n)
    n = Ea.shape[0]
    E = np.empty((n, n)); C = np.empty((n, n))
    for i0 in range(0, n, block):                                     # blocks of rows keep the (block, n, n) temporary small
        tot = Ea[i0:i0 + block, :, None] + Eb[None, :, :]
        m = tot.min(1)
        hit = tot <= m[:, None, :] + tol
        E[i0:i0 + block] = m
        C[i0:i0 + block] = (hit * Ca[i0:i0 + block, :, None] * Cb[None, :, :]).sum(1)
    return E, C

def minplus_torus(L, M, g):
    # ground-state energy per spin and degeneracy of the L x M torus (J1 = 1, J2 = g)
    W = W_matrix(L, 1.0, g); C1 = np.ones_like(W)
    E, C = W.copy(), C1.copy()
    for _ in range(M - 1):
        E, C = minplus_mult(E, C, W, C1)
    d = np.diag(E); E0 = d.min()
    return E0 / (L * M), int(round(np.diag(C)[d <= E0 + 1e-9].sum()))

3.5 Ground-state degeneracy at \(g=1/2\)
At \(g=1/2\) the plaquette bound of Section 3.2 is reached by six of the sixteen plaquette states at once, shown in the first six panels below together with two higher plaquettes for comparison (bonds marked as in the figure of Section 3.1, and \(h_P\) is the plaquette energy of Section 3.2 with \(J_2=J_1/2\)). The two uniform plaquettes and the four with one edge up and the opposite edge down all have \(h_P=-J_1\). The energy the uniform plaquettes lose on their two broken diagonals equals the energy the others lose on their two broken nearest-neighbour edges. A ground state must be built from these six plaquettes only, and counting such configurations gives the degeneracy.

This growth can be derived. At \(g=1/2\) a configuration is a ground state if and only if every plaquette is one of the six minimal ones of Section 3.2, the two uniform plaquettes and the four with one edge up and the opposite edge down. Describe a configuration by its bond variables \(b^{\rm h}_{x,y}=s_{x,y}s_{x+1,y}\) (horizontal) and \(b^{\rm v}_{x,y}=s_{x,y}s_{x,y+1}\) (vertical). Two properties characterise the six minimal plaquettes.

The product of the four corner spins is \(+1\). For the plaquette at \((x,y)\) this says \(s_{x,y}s_{x+1,y}=s_{x,y+1}s_{x+1,y+1}\), that is \(b^{\rm h}_{x,y}=b^{\rm h}_{x,y+1}\). The horizontal bond variables do not depend on \(y\), \(b^{\rm h}_{x,y}\equiv b^{\rm h}_x\). Likewise \(b^{\rm v}_{x,y}\equiv b^{\rm v}_y\) does not depend on \(x\).
It is not a Néel plaquette. A Néel plaquette is the only one with product \(+1\) that has a broken horizontal and a broken vertical edge. So \(b^{\rm h}_x=-1\) and \(b^{\rm v}_y=-1\) never occur together.

By property 2, either all \(b^{\rm h}_x=+1\), so that every row is uniform and the \(M\) row signs are free (\(2^M\) configurations), or all \(b^{\rm v}_y=+1\), so that every column is uniform (\(2^L\) configurations). The two sets share the two uniform states. Hence, on the \(L\times M\) torus, \[
\boxed{\,n_0\big(g=\tfrac12\big) = 2^{L}+2^{M}-2\,}.
\] The degeneracy grows exponentially with the linear size, and the entropy per spin \(\ln n_0/N\approx\ln 2/L\) vanishes for large lattices. The ground state at \(g=1/2\) is therefore a sub-extensively degenerate manifold, a set of ground states whose number grows more slowly than exponentially in the number of spins, made of independently flippable rows (or columns).
The same count follows from a transfer matrix, which gives an independent check. In the row language, two rows \(\sigma,\sigma'\) may follow each other if all \(L\) plaquettes between them are minimal. We define the \(0/1\) matrix \(A_{\sigma\sigma'}\) accordingly, so that \(n_0=\operatorname{Tr}A^M\). The derivation predicts the structure of \(A\). A uniform row may be followed by either uniform row (a \(2\times2\) block of ones, eigenvalues \(2\) and \(0\)), and a non-uniform row only by itself (an identity block of size \(2^L-2\)). So \(\operatorname{Tr}A^M = 2^M+(2^L-2)\), and the largest eigenvalue of \(A\) is \(2\) for every width \(L\). The cell builds \(A\) from the plaquette energies, checks its structure through its largest eigenvalue, and counts \(\operatorname{Tr}A^M\) for \(L,M\le10\). For \(L\le6\) it also checks against the full (min, +) calculation.

def good_row_pairs(L):
    # A[sigma, sigma'] = 1 if all L plaquettes between rows sigma (bottom) and sigma' (top) have the minimal energy -1 at g = 1/2; shape (2^L, 2^L)
    R = all_configs(L).astype(np.int64)
    a, b = R[:, None, :], np.roll(R, -1, 1)[:, None, :]           # bottom corners: (x, y), (x+1, y)
    d, c = R[None, :, :], np.roll(R, -1, 1)[None, :, :]           # top corners:    (x, y+1), (x+1, y+1)
    hP = -0.5 * (a * b + b * c + c * d + d * a) + 0.5 * (a * c + b * d)     # (2^L, 2^L, L)
    return np.all(hP == -1, axis=2).astype(np.float64)

Every entry of the table equals \(2^L+2^M-2\) and the largest eigenvalue of \(A\) is \(2\) for every width, as derived. The figures show several of these ground states, rows or columns of independent sign, all with the same energy. For \(g\neq1/2\) the ground state is therefore the ferromagnet (2 states) or the stripes (4 states). At \(g=1/2\) the ground-state energy is \(-J_1\) per spin and the degeneracy on an \(L\times M\) torus is \(2^L+2^M-2\), since any row (or column) can be flipped at no cost. This is the microscopic form of frustration in this model, and it has two consequences developed below. Domain walls along rows cost nothing at \(g=1/2\) (Section 4), and the strip free energy keeps a residual entropy \(\ln2/L\) per spin at \(T\to0\) (Section 8).

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
4. Domain walls
The ground states tell us what orders, but not up to which temperature the order survives. An ordered phase survives at \(T>0\) only if large regions of the other ordered state are rare. Such a region is bounded by a domain wall, and the competition between the energy of the wall and the number of ways to draw it decides whether order survives (Lab 012, Section 3.3). We therefore compute the energy per unit length \(\sigma\) of straight walls as a function of \(g\). There are four kinds of straight wall along a lattice axis (a vertical line between columns \(x_0\) and \(x_0+1\), or a horizontal one).

Ferromagnet, \(+|-\). Across the wall, per unit length, one horizontal nearest-neighbour bond turns from satisfied to broken (\(+2J_1\)), and the two diagonal bonds crossing the wall turn from broken (\(s_is_j=+1\)) to satisfied (\(-2J_2\) each), so \(\sigma_{\rm FM} = 2J_1-4J_2 = 2J_1(1-2g)\).
Stripes, wall parallel to the stripes (a phase slip, \(\dots{+}{-}{+}\,|\,{+}{-}{+}\dots\)). The horizontal bond across the wall turns from broken to satisfied (\(-2J_1\)) and the two diagonals from satisfied to broken (\(+4J_2\)), so \(\sigma_{\parallel} = 4J_2-2J_1 = 2J_1(2g-1)\).
Stripes, wall perpendicular to the stripes (all spins flipped on one side). The vertical bond turns from satisfied to broken (\(+2J_1\)) and the two diagonals from satisfied to broken (\(+4J_2\)), so \(\sigma_{\perp} = 2J_1+4J_2\).
Stripes, a \(90^\circ\) wall between vertical and horizontal stripes. Here a bond-by-bond count near the wall is misleading, because a finite domain of horizontal stripes has a different share of satisfied horizontal and vertical bonds than a domain of vertical stripes, so we count the totals. In both stripe orientations half of the nearest-neighbour bonds are satisfied, \(B_1=0\), and the horizontal bonds crossing the wall have products that alternate along it and sum to zero, so \(\Delta B_1=0\). The two diagonal bonds per unit length that cross the wall change from \(s_is_j=-1\) to products that alternate along the wall, that is from energy \(-J_2\) to \(0\) on average, so \(\sigma_{90^\circ} = 2J_2\).

The four walls are drawn below on \(8\times6\) patches. The purple line marks the wall, and each panel gives its energy per unit length \(\sigma\). In the ferromagnet and for the stripe wall parallel to the stripes, crossing the wall exchanges broken nearest-neighbour bonds for satisfied diagonal bonds or the reverse, which is why their cost is proportional to \(1-2g\) or \(2g-1\).
