numerical wall energies agree with the symbolic formulas for all 151 values of g


SymPy recovers all four wall energies from the constructed configurations, and the plot shows them as functions of \(g\), with two lines crossing zero at \(g=1/2\).
The wall energies can be turned into a temperature scale by a Peierls-type argument. Consider a closed wall of length \(\ell\) (in lattice units) enclosing a region of the other ordered state. Its energy is \(\sigma\ell\). The number of closed walls of length \(\ell\) through a given bond grows at most like \(\mu^\ell\) with some constant \(\mu\) (for walls drawn along lattice bonds \(\mu\le3\), since each step can go in at most three directions without stepping back). The free energy of such walls is therefore \[
\Delta F(\ell) \gtrsim \ell\,\big(\sigma - T\ln\mu\big).
\] While \(\sigma>T\ln\mu\), long walls are exponentially suppressed and the order survives. This is Peierls’ argument for the ferromagnet [Peierls 1936, rigorous form Griffiths 1964], which gives the estimate \(T_c\gtrsim 2J_1/\ln3\approx1.82\,J_1\) at \(g=0\) (Lab 012), consistent with the exact \(2.269\,J_1\). For our model the argument is a heuristic, since other wall shapes, corners and the extra stripe walls would have to be counted, but two of its conclusions do not depend on these details. First, the temperature scale below which walls are suppressed is proportional to the cheapest wall energy, \(\sigma_{\min}(g) = 2J_1(1-2g)\) on the ferromagnetic side and \(\sigma_{\min}=\min(2J_1(2g-1),\,2J_2)\) on the stripe side, which is the parallel wall for \(1/2<g<1\) and the \(90^\circ\) wall for \(g>1\). Second, at \(g=1/2\) this energy vanishes. Walls along rows cost nothing, as the free row flips of Section 3.5 showed, and nothing prevents thermal fluctuations from destroying the order at any \(T>0\). Near \(g=1/2\) the ordering temperature must therefore go to zero.
Section 9 plots the estimate \(T_{\rm wall}(g)=\sigma_{\min}(g)/\ln3\) together with the computed \(T_c(g)\). It is an order-of-magnitude estimate of the temperature scale and makes no prediction of \(T_c\) itself.
Straight domain walls thus cost \(2J_1(1-2g)\) per unit length in the ferromagnet. In the stripe phase the parallel wall costs \(2J_1(2g-1)\), the \(90^\circ\) wall \(2J_2\) and the perpendicular wall \(2J_1+4J_2\). The cheapest wall on each side vanishes linearly at \(g=1/2\), which is the physical reason why the transition temperature drops to zero there.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
5. Exact limits
Before computing \(T_c(g)\) numerically we fix its two ends, where the model can be solved exactly. These limits anchor the phase diagram and test every numerical method below, and the large-\(g\) limit explains the Ashkin–Teller structure of Section 2.

5.1 Onsager limit
At \(J_2=0\) the model is the square-lattice Ising ferromagnet, solved by Onsager [1944]. Its \(T_c\) is fixed by \(\sinh(2J_1/T_c)=1\), the self-dual point of the Kramers–Wannier duality between high and low temperatures (Lab 012), so \(T_c = 2J_1/\ln(1+\sqrt2)\).


5.2 Decoupled sublattices at large \(g\)
Dividing by \(J_2\) gives \(H/J_2 = B_2 - B_1/g\), so for \(g\to\infty\) only the diagonal bonds remain. A diagonal bond joins \((x,y)\) to \((x\pm1,y\pm1)\), which has the same parity of \(x+y\). The lattice splits into two sublattices, \(\mathcal A\) (\(x+y\) even) and \(\mathcal B\) (\(x+y\) odd), with no bond between them. Each is itself a square lattice, rotated by \(45^\circ\) and with lattice constant \(\sqrt2\) (primitive vectors \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\)), on which the diagonal bonds are nearest-neighbour bonds with antiferromagnetic coupling \(J_2\).
The antiferromagnetic sign is removed by the column gauge \(s_{x,y}\to(-1)^xs_{x,y}\), which changes the sign of every diagonal product (Section 2), \[
\begin{aligned}
Z(J_1=0,J_2) &= \sum_{\mathbf s}e^{-\beta J_2B_2(\mathbf s)} = \sum_{\mathbf s}e^{+\beta J_2B_2(\mathbf s)}\\
&= Z^{\rm Ising}_{\mathcal A}(J_2)\;Z^{\rm Ising}_{\mathcal B}(J_2),
\end{aligned}
\] because the gauge is a bijection of the configuration space. Each factor is a square-lattice Ising ferromagnet with coupling \(J_2\), so \[
\begin{aligned}
T_c &\xrightarrow{g\to\infty} \frac{2J_2}{\ln(1+\sqrt2)} = g\cdot\frac{2J_1}{\ln(1+\sqrt2)},\\
\frac{T_c}{J_2}&\to2.269 .
\end{aligned}
\]
The gauge also exposes the Ashkin–Teller variables. After it, vertical stripes \((-1)^x\) become all \(+1\), and horizontal stripes \((-1)^y\) become \((-1)^{x+y}\), which is \(+1\) on \(\mathcal A\) and \(-1\) on \(\mathcal B\). The four stripe states are therefore the four combinations of the two sublattice magnetisations \((\sigma_{\mathcal A},\sigma_{\mathcal B})=(\pm1,\pm1)\), two Ising order parameters as in the Ashkin–Teller model. A finite \(J_1\) couples the two sublattices. In the gauged frame the nearest-neighbour bonds are ferromagnetic vertically and antiferromagnetic horizontally, so a spin of \(\mathcal A\) in a uniformly magnetised \(\mathcal B\) feels \(J_1(\sigma_{\mathcal B}+\sigma_{\mathcal B}-\sigma_{\mathcal B}-\sigma_{\mathcal B})=0\). The coupling \(J_1\) does not couple the magnetisations linearly and cannot prefer either orientation, which is the fourfold degeneracy again. Kalz, Honecker and Moliner [2011] derived, by perturbation in \(J_1\) around the two decoupled critical Ising models, that the effective theory is the Ashkin–Teller model.
The next two cells check these statements. The first solves \(\sinh2K=1\) with SymPy and applies the gauge to the Hamiltonian symbolically. The second verifies the factorisation \(Z=Z_{\mathcal A}Z_{\mathcal B}\) by complete enumeration on the \(4\times4\) torus at three temperatures, and confirms that \(J_1\) gives the same energy to all four stripe states while the gauge maps them onto the four sign combinations \((\sigma_{\mathcal A},\sigma_{\mathcal B})\).

Both ends of the phase diagram are now fixed, \(T_c(0)=2.269\,J_1\) and \(T_c/J_2\to2.269\) for \(g\to\infty\), and the transfer matrices (Section 8) and Monte Carlo (Section 9) must reproduce both. title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
6. Mean-field theory
Mean-field theory is the first approximation one tries for any interacting system. It reduces the many-body problem to one spin in an effective field. For this model it gets the ordered phases right, the transition temperatures wrong, and misses the vanishing of \(T_c\) at \(g=1/2\) entirely, and each of these outcomes says something about the physics.
Write \(H=-\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}s_is_j\) with \(J_{ij}=J_1\) for nearest neighbours and \(J_{ij}=-J_2\) for diagonal neighbours. Spin \(i\) interacts with its neighbours through the local field \(h_i=\sum_jJ_{ij}s_j\). Mean-field theory replaces the neighbours by their averages \(m_j=\langle s_j\rangle\), which neglects the correlations between \(s_i\) and its neighbours. Since a single spin in a field \(h_i\) has \(\langle s_i\rangle = \frac{e^{\beta h_i}-e^{-\beta h_i}}{e^{\beta h_i}+e^{-\beta h_i}}=\tanh\beta h_i\), we obtain \[
m_i = \tanh\Big(\beta\sum_jJ_{ij}m_j\Big)\qquad\text{(self-consistency).}
\]
To solve these equations we try modulated solutions \(m_{\boldsymbol r}=m\,e^{i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r}\) with \(\boldsymbol k\in\{(0,0),(\pi,0),(0,\pi),(\pi,\pi)\}\) (then \(e^{i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r}=\pm1\)). The local field becomes \(\sum_jJ_{ij}m_j = \mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\,m_i\) with the Fourier transform of the couplings \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k) &= \sum_{\boldsymbol\delta}J_{\boldsymbol\delta}e^{i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol\delta}\\
&= 2J_1(\cos k_x+\cos k_y) - 4J_2\cos k_x\cos k_y ,
\end{aligned}
\] (\(\boldsymbol\delta\) runs over the 4 nearest and 4 diagonal neighbour vectors), and the self-consistency reduces to the single equation \(m=\tanh(\beta\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)m)\).
The transition temperature follows from the expansion for small \(m\), \(\tanh z = z - z^3/3+O(z^5)\), \[
\begin{aligned}
m &= \beta\mathcal J m - \tfrac13(\beta\mathcal J)^3m^3\\
\Rightarrow\quad m&=0\ \ \text{or}\ \ m^2 = \frac{3T^2(T_{\rm MF}-T)}{T_{\rm MF}^3}\approx 3\Big(1-\frac{T}{T_{\rm MF}}\Big),\\
T_{\rm MF}&=\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k).
\end{aligned}
\] A non-zero solution exists below \(T_{\rm MF}\), with \(m\propto(T_{\rm MF}-T)^{1/2}\). The power \(1/2\) is the mean-field value of the order-parameter exponent, whose exact two-dimensional Ising value is \(1/8\). For general \(m_i\), the linearised equation \(m_i=\beta\sum_jJ_{ij}m_j\) first has a non-zero solution when \(T\) equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix \(J_{ij}\), which is \(\max_{\boldsymbol k}\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\) because plane waves diagonalise the matrix. The maximum runs over the Brillouin zone, the square \(-\pi<k_x,k_y\le\pi\) that contains every distinct wave vector of the lattice. Evaluating at the candidate wave vectors gives \[
\begin{aligned}
T^{\rm FM}_{\rm MF}&=\mathcal J(0,0)=4(J_1-J_2),\\
T^{\rm str}_{\rm MF}&=\mathcal J(\pi,0)=4J_2,\\
\mathcal J(\pi,\pi)&=-4(J_1+J_2)<0 .
\end{aligned}
\] The cell derives these results with SymPy and also shows that at \(g=1/2\) the maximum of \(\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\) is reached on whole lines of the Brillouin zone.


Code
kx, ky, Ts_, Tmf, m_ = sp.symbols("k_x k_y T T_MF m", real=True)
Jk = 2 * J1s * (sp.cos(kx) + sp.cos(ky)) - 4 * J2s * sp.cos(kx) * sp.cos(ky)
for name, (a, b) in {"(0,0)": (0, 0), "(pi,0)": (sp.pi, 0), "(0,pi)": (0, sp.pi), "(pi,pi)": (sp.pi, sp.pi)}.items():
    print(f"J(k = {name:7s}) = {sp.simplify(Jk.subs({kx: a, ky: b}))}")
print("ferromagnet and stripes have equal T_MF at J_2 =", sp.solve(sp.Eq(4 * J1s - 4 * J2s, 4 * J2s), J2s))

# expansion of the self-consistency m = tanh(T_MF m / T) for small m
eq = sp.series(sp.tanh(Tmf * m_ / Ts_), m_, 0, 5).removeO() - m_
m2 = sp.solve(sp.expand(eq / m_), m_**2)[0]
print("non-zero solution: m^2 =", sp.factor(m2))
t_ = sp.symbols("t", positive=True)
print("with T = T_MF (1 - t):  m^2 =", sp.series(m2.subs(Ts_, Tmf * (1 - t_)), t_, 0, 2), "  -> m ~ sqrt(3 t), exponent 1/2")

# at g = 1/2 the maximum of J(k) is degenerate on the lines k_x = 0 and k_y = 0
J_half = sp.expand(Jk.subs({J1s: 1, J2s: sp.Rational(1, 2)}))
print("J(k) at g = 1/2:", J_half, "  =  2 - 2(1 - cos k_x)(1 - cos k_y):",
      sp.simplify(J_half - (2 - 2 * (1 - sp.cos(kx)) * (1 - sp.cos(ky)))) == 0)

Three numerical experiments test these statements. First, we solve the self-consistency \(m=\tanh(T_{\rm MF}m/T)\) by iteration and compare the result with the expansion \(m\approx\sqrt{3(1-T/T_{\rm MF})}\). Second, we compute the largest eigenvalue of the \(N\times N\) coupling matrix \(J_{ij}\) of a \(12\times12\) torus and compare it with \(\max(4(1-g),4g)\), together with its multiplicity, which matters at \(g=1/2\). Third, we iterate the site-dependent self-consistency \(m_i=\tanh(\beta\sum_jJ_{ij}m_j)\) from a random start on the \(12\times12\) torus just below \(T_{\rm MF}\) and record the pattern it converges to.


Code
# (i) uniform self-consistency by fixed-point iteration
for tau in (0.99, 0.95, 0.8, 0.5):                         # tau = T / T_MF
    m = 1.0
    for _ in range(20000):
        m = np.tanh(m / tau)
    print(f"T/T_MF = {tau:4.2f}:  m (iteration) = {m:.5f}   sqrt(3(1 - T/T_MF)) = {np.sqrt(3 * (1 - tau)):.5f}")

# (ii) coupling matrix of an L x L torus: J_ij = J1 (nearest), -J2 (diagonal); shape (N, N)
def coupling_matrix(L, g):
    N = L * L; Jm = np.zeros((N, N)); idx = lambda x, y: (x % L) * L + (y % L)
    for x0, y0 in itertools.product(range(L), repeat=2):
        for dx, dy in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
            Jm[idx(x0, y0), idx(x0 + dx, y0 + dy)] = 1.0
        for dx, dy in ((1, 1), (1, -1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1)):
            Jm[idx(x0, y0), idx(x0 + dx, y0 + dy)] = -g
    return Jm

L_mf = 12
for gv in (0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0):
    lam = np.linalg.eigvalsh(coupling_matrix(L_mf, gv))
    print(f"g = {gv:3.1f}:  largest eigenvalue of J_ij = {lam[-1]:.6f}   max(4(1-g), 4g) = {max(4 * (1 - gv), 4 * gv):.6f}"
          f"   its multiplicity = {np.sum(np.isclose(lam, lam[-1]))}")

Code
# (iii) site-dependent mean field on the 12 x 12 torus, damped iteration from a random start at T = 0.9 T_MF
def m_uniform(tau, n_iter=20000):
    # solution of m = tanh(m / tau) by fixed-point iteration, tau = T / T_MF
    m = 1.0
    for _ in range(n_iter):
        m = np.tanh(m / tau)
    return m

L_mf = 12; rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
for gv in (0.25, 0.75):
    Jm = coupling_matrix(L_mf, gv); T_mf = max(4 * (1 - gv), 4 * gv); T = 0.9 * T_mf
    m = 0.1 * rng.standard_normal(L_mf * L_mf)
    for _ in range(3000):
        m = 0.5 * m + 0.5 * np.tanh(Jm @ m / T)
    o = order_params(m.reshape(L_mf, L_mf))
    print(f"g = {gv}: T = 0.9 T_MF = {T:.2f}:  |m| = {abs(o['m']):.3f},  m_str = {np.hypot(o['mx'], o['my']):.3f},"
          f"   uniform solution at T/T_MF = 0.9: m = {m_uniform(0.9):.3f}")


g = 0.25: T = 0.9 T_MF = 2.70:  |m| = 0.525,  m_str = 0.000,   uniform solution at T/T_MF = 0.9: m = 0.525


g = 0.75: T = 0.9 T_MF = 2.70:  |m| = 0.000,  m_str = 0.525,   uniform solution at T/T_MF = 0.9: m = 0.525


The expansion \(m\approx\sqrt{3(1-T/T_{\rm MF})}\) is accurate only close to \(T_{\rm MF}\). Far below, \(m\to1\) and the expansion overshoots. The site-dependent iteration lands, without being told, in the ferromagnet for \(g=0.25\) and in a stripe state for \(g=0.75\), with the amplitude of the uniform solution at \(T/T_{\rm MF}=0.9\). The figure below shows \(\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\) over the Brillouin zone at \(g=0.25\), \(0.5\) and \(0.75\), and the mean-field phase diagram \(T_{\rm MF}(g)\).


Code
k = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 201); KX, KY = np.meshgrid(k, k, indexing="ij")
Jk_num = lambda g: 2 * (np.cos(KX) + np.cos(KY)) - 4 * g * np.cos(KX) * np.cos(KY)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.2))
for a, gv in zip(ax[:3], (0.25, 0.5, 0.75)):
    Z = Jk_num(gv)
    im = a.pcolormesh(KX, KY, Z, cmap="viridis", shading="auto")
    a.contour(KX, KY, Z, levels=[Z.max() - 1e-3], colors="w", linewidths=1.5)
    a.set_title(f"$\\mathcal{{J}}(\\mathbf{{k}})$, g = {gv}; max = {Z.max():.2f}", fontsize=10)
    a.set_xlabel("$k_x$"); a.set_ylabel("$k_y$"); a.set_aspect("equal"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=a, fraction=0.046)
gl = np.linspace(0, 1.5, 301)
ax[3].plot(gl[gl <= 0.5], 4 * (1 - gl[gl <= 0.5]), color=UJBlue, lw=2, label="ferromagnet: $4(J_1-J_2)$")
ax[3].plot(gl[gl >= 0.5], 4 * gl[gl >= 0.5], color=DSOrange, lw=2, label="stripes: $4J_2$")
ax[3].plot([0, 1.5], [TC_ISING, 1.5 * TC_ISING], ":", color=UJGray, label="exact limits: $2.269$ and $2.269\\,g$")
ax[3].set_xlabel("$g$"); ax[3].set_ylabel("$T_{\\rm MF}$"); ax[3].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); ax[3].set_title("mean-field phase diagram")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The figure shows the V-shaped mean-field transition line, and the theory fails in three respects. The first is an overestimate of \(T_c\). At \(g=0\) mean field predicts \(4J_1\) instead of \(2.269J_1\) (a factor \(1.76\)), and for \(g\to\infty\) it predicts \(4J_2\) instead of \(2.269J_2\). Mean field neglects the correlations between a spin and its neighbours. In reality the neighbours fluctuate together with the spin, ordered patches form and disappear, and these fluctuations lower \(T_c\). In two dimensions they are strong.
The second failure is the point \(g=1/2\). Mean field predicts \(T_{\rm MF}=2J_1\) there, the lowest point of the V but still a finite temperature, while the domain-wall argument and the numerics of Sections 4, 8 and 9 point to \(T_c\to0\). The white contour shows the reason. At \(g=1/2\) the maximum of \(\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\) is reached on the two lines \(k_x=0\) and \(k_y=0\), \(2L-1\) wave vectors on an \(L\times L\) torus (the multiplicity \(23=2\cdot12-1\) printed above). A mode \((0,k_y)\) is a pattern uniform along \(x\) with an arbitrary profile along \(y\), the row-flip degeneracy of Section 3.5. Mean field picks one mode and orders it, while the real system fluctuates between all of them, and no order survives at \(T>0\).
The third failure concerns the nature of the transition. Mean field always gives a continuous transition with order-parameter exponent \(1/2\). The true ferromagnetic transition has the two-dimensional Ising exponents, and the stripe transition is weakly first order or Ashkin–Teller-like (Section 10).
Mean field thus identifies the two ordered phases and the special role of \(g=1/2\), the degenerate maximum of \(\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\), but turns it into a wrong prediction, because fluctuations dominate the physics of this model.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
section: 7. Monte Carlo and the static structure factor
text:
7. Monte Carlo and the static structure factor
The exact methods so far either work at \(T=0\) (Section 3) or neglect fluctuations (Section 6). To see the phases at finite temperature on a large lattice we sample the Boltzmann distribution with Monte Carlo. The snapshots also give the static structure factor, the quantity measured by neutron or X-ray scattering, which identifies the ordering pattern without knowing it in advance.

7.1 Four-sublattice Metropolis sampler
We use the Metropolis algorithm of Lab 010. It proposes flipping spin \(i\) and accepts the flip with probability \(\min(1,e^{-\beta\Delta E_i})\), where \[
\Delta E_i = 2s_ih_i,\qquad h_i = J_1\sum_{j\in\rm nn(i)}s_j - J_2\sum_{j\in\rm diag(i)}s_j .
\] This choice satisfies detailed balance, \(p(\mathbf s)P(\mathbf s\to\mathbf s')=p(\mathbf s')P(\mathbf s'\to\mathbf s)\), so the Boltzmann distribution is stationary.
Spins that are not coupled to each other can be updated simultaneously. The chessboard decomposition used for the Ising model fails here, because diagonal neighbours have the same chessboard colour. The four sublattices \((x\bmod2,\,y\bmod2)\) work instead. Nearest neighbours differ in one parity and diagonal neighbours in both, so no two spins of one sublattice interact (for \(L\) even and \(L\ge4\)). One sweep updates the four sublattices in turn, which amounts to one attempted flip per spin.
We therefore store a configuration directly as its four sublattices, a tuple S of four arrays S[2a+b] = s[a::2, b::2], each of shape \((C, L/2, L/2)\) for \(C\) chains. The neighbours of a spin of sublattice \((a,b)\) lie on the other three sublattices, its two horizontal neighbours on \((1-a,b)\), its two vertical neighbours on \((a,1-b)\) and its four diagonal neighbours on \((1-a,1-b)\). With nsum(X, a, axis) \(=X+\) roll\((X,\pm1)\) (sign \(+\) for \(a=0\), \(-\) for \(a=1\)) the local field is h = nsum(S[1-a,b], a, x) + nsum(S[a,1-b], b, y) - g * nsum(nsum(S[1-a,1-b], a, x), b, y). No work is wasted on spins that are not being updated, and all chains are processed by the same array operations.
In JAX the sampler is a pure function sweep(S, key, g, beta). lax.scan repeats sweeps inside one compiled program, and jax.jit compiles the whole simulation. The chains form the leading axis of every array (equivalent to jax.vmap over chains, written out explicitly). Each chain has its own \(g\) and its own temperature schedule. T_sched has shape \((n_{\rm steps}, C)\), and at step \(k\) chain \(c\) runs n_equil sweeps of equilibration at temperature T_sched[k, c] followed by n_meas measurements separated by n_between sweeps. A decreasing schedule anneals the chains, and a schedule with one row runs every chain at its own fixed temperature. Each measurement is the vector \((m,m_x,m_y,e)\), with \(e=H/N\) the energy per spin, and with keep=True the configurations are stored as well. The input S0 consists of four arrays of shape \((C,L/2,L/2)\), g has shape \((C,)\) and T_sched shape \((n_{\rm steps},C)\). The output measurements have shape \((n_{\rm steps}, n_{\rm meas}, C, 4)\) and, with keep=True, the configurations shape \((n_{\rm steps}, n_{\rm meas}, C, L, L)\), stored as int8. The cell ends by checking the sublattice layout against a plain NumPy implementation.


Code
def nsum(X, a, axis):
    # X plus its copy shifted by one site along axis; for a = 0 the partner sites are i and i-1, for a = 1 they are i and i+1
    return X + jnp.roll(X, 1 if a == 0 else -1, axis)

def sublattice_field(S, a, b, g):
    # local field h on sublattice (a, b): nearest neighbours minus g times diagonal neighbours; shape (C, L/2, L/2)
    return (nsum(S[2 * (1 - a) + b], a, 1) + nsum(S[2 * a + 1 - b], b, 2)
            - g * nsum(nsum(S[2 * (1 - a) + 1 - b], a, 1), b, 2))

def sweep(S, key, g, beta):
    # one Metropolis sweep of all chains; g, beta: (C, 1, 1)
    S = list(S)
    for a, b in ((0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)):
        key, sub = jax.random.split(key)
        si = S[2 * a + b]
        dE = 2.0 * si * sublattice_field(S, a, b, g)
        accept = jax.random.uniform(sub, si.shape) < jnp.exp(-beta * dE)
        S[2 * a + b] = jnp.where(accept, -si, si)
    return tuple(S), key

def measure(S, g):
    # (m, m_x, m_y, e) per chain, shape (C, 4); g: (C,); the sign of (-1)^x on sublattice (a, b) is (-1)^a
    s00, s01, s10, s11 = S
    g = jnp.reshape(g, (-1, 1, 1))
    mean = lambda X: X.mean((1, 2)) / 4
    m, mx, my = mean(s00 + s01 + s10 + s11), mean(s00 + s01 - s10 - s11), mean(s00 - s01 + s10 - s11)
    e = -0.5 * sum(mean(S[2 * a + b] * sublattice_field(S, a, b, g)) for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1))   # each bond twice
    return jnp.stack([m, mx, my, e], 1)

def assemble(S):
    # four sublattices (C, L/2, L/2) -> full configurations (C, L, L), s[c, 2i+a, 2j+b] = S[2a+b][c, i, j]
    X = jnp.stack(S)                                         # (4, C, h, h)
    C, h = X.shape[1], X.shape[2]
    return X.reshape(2, 2, C, h, h).transpose(2, 3, 0, 4, 1).reshape(C, 2 * h, 2 * h)

def split(s):
    # full configurations (C, L, L) -> tuple of four sublattices
    return tuple(jnp.asarray(s[:, a::2, b::2], jnp.float32) for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1))

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_meas", "n_between", "keep"))
def simulate(S0, key, g, T_sched, n_equil, n_meas, n_between, keep=False):
    g = g[:, None, None]
    def at_step(carry, T):
        beta = (1.0 / T)[:, None, None]
        step = lambda c, _: (sweep(c[0], c[1], g, beta), None)
        carry, _ = lax.scan(step, carry, None, length=n_equil)
        def record(c, _):
            c, _ = lax.scan(step, c, None, length=n_between)
            obs = measure(c[0], g[:, 0, 0])
            return c, ((obs, assemble(c[0]).astype(jnp.int8)) if keep else (obs,))
        return lax.scan(record, carry, None, length=n_meas)
    return lax.scan(at_step, (S0, key), T_sched)[1]

def run_mc(s0, g, T_sched, n_equil, n_meas, n_between, seed, keep=False):
    # s0: (C, L, L) initial configurations; g: (C,); T_sched: (n_steps, C). Returns numpy arrays (see shapes above).
    out = simulate(split(np.asarray(s0)), jax.random.PRNGKey(seed), jnp.asarray(g, jnp.float32),
                   jnp.asarray(T_sched, jnp.float32), n_equil, n_meas, n_between, keep)
    return tuple(np.asarray(o) for o in out) if keep else np.asarray(out[0])

def random_configs(C, L, seed):
    return np.random.default_rng(seed).choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(C, L, L))

# consistency of the sublattice layout: assemble(split(s)) = s, and measure() agrees with the numpy functions of Sections 2-3
s_test = random_configs(6, 8, 0)
assert np.array_equal(np.asarray(assemble(split(s_test))), s_test)
obs = np.asarray(measure(split(s_test), jnp.full(6, 0.37)))
o_np = order_params(s_test)
assert np.allclose(obs[:, 0], o_np["m"]) and np.allclose(obs[:, 1], o_np["mx"]) and np.allclose(obs[:, 2], o_np["my"])
assert np.allclose(obs[:, 3], energy(s_test, 0.37) / 64, atol=1e-5)
print("sublattice layout: assemble/split round trip and (m, m_x, m_y, e) agree with the numpy reference")


sublattice layout: assemble/split round trip and (m, m_x, m_y, e) agree with the numpy reference


Before using the sampler for physics we compare it with exact enumeration. On the \(4\times4\) torus the exact averages of \(e\), \(|m|\) and \(m_{\rm str}=\sqrt{m_x^2+m_y^2}\) follow from the \(2^{16}\) configurations of Section 3.3, \(\langle A\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf s}A(\mathbf s)e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}/Z\). The Monte Carlo averages use 512 chains per point (all five points in one batch of \(C=2560\) chains), and the error bar is the standard error over chains. The Monte Carlo value and the exact value should agree within a few error bars at every point.


Code
o44 = order_params(S44)
m_abs_44, mstr_44 = np.abs(o44["m"]), np.hypot(o44["mx"], o44["my"])
def exact_4x4(g, T):
    E = -B1_44 + g * B2_44
    w = np.exp(-(E - E.min()) / T); w /= w.sum()
    return (w * E / 16).sum(), (w * m_abs_44).sum(), (w * mstr_44).sum()

checks = [(0.0, 2.0), (0.3, 1.2), (0.5, 0.6), (0.75, 1.0), (1.5, 3.0)]

(6.8 s)




7.2 Static structure factor
The Monte Carlo averages agree with the exact values within two error bars at all five points, so the sampler can be used on larger lattices. For a configuration \(\mathbf s\) define the Fourier amplitude \(\tilde s(\boldsymbol k)=\sum_{\boldsymbol r}s_{\boldsymbol r}e^{-i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r}\) on the \(L^2\) wave vectors \(\boldsymbol k=\frac{2\pi}{L}(n_x,n_y)\). The static structure factor is \[
\begin{aligned}
S(\boldsymbol k) &= \frac1N\big\langle|\tilde s(\boldsymbol k)|^2\big\rangle = N\big\langle|m_{\boldsymbol k}|^2\big\rangle\\
&= \sum_{\boldsymbol r}e^{-i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r}\,\frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol r'}\langle s_{\boldsymbol r'}s_{\boldsymbol r'+\boldsymbol r}\rangle ,
\end{aligned}
\] the Fourier transform of the spin–spin correlation function and the quantity a scattering experiment measures.
In a phase with long-range order at wave vector \(\boldsymbol Q\), \(\langle|m_{\boldsymbol Q}|^2\rangle\) stays finite as \(N\to\infty\), so \(S(\boldsymbol Q)\propto N\), a Bragg peak. In the paramagnet correlations decay over a finite length and \(S(\boldsymbol k)\) is a broad, \(N\)-independent function. Parseval’s theorem adds a sum rule, \(\sum_{\boldsymbol k}|\tilde s(\boldsymbol k)|^2=N\sum_{\boldsymbol r}s_{\boldsymbol r}^2=N^2\), so the average of \(S(\boldsymbol k)\) over the Brillouin zone is \(1\), and ordering only redistributes the weight.
We compute \(S(\boldsymbol k)\) with np.fft.fft2 from Monte Carlo snapshots (\(L=32\), 16 annealed chains \(\times\) 20 snapshots per point, all four points in one batch) in four situations, the ferromagnet, the paramagnet, the frustrated point \(g=1/2\) at low \(T\), and the stripe phase. The figure shows one snapshot of each case (top) and \(\log_{10}S(\boldsymbol k)\) over the Brillouin zone (bottom).


Code
L_sk = 32
cases = [(0.25, 1.0, "ferromagnet"), (0.25, 3.0, "paramagnet"), (0.5, 0.3, "g = 1/2, low T"), (0.75, 0.8, "stripes")]
n_ch, n_steps = 16, 12
# every chain is cooled linearly from T = 4 to its target temperature in n_steps steps; snapshots are kept at the last step
g_sk = np.repeat([c[0] for c in cases], n_ch)                                          # (64,)
lam_sk = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_steps)[:, None]                                       # interpolation parameter, (12, 1)
T_sk = (1 - lam_sk) * 4.0 + lam_sk * np.repeat([c[1] for c in cases], n_ch)[None, :]   # (12, 64): from T = 4 to the target
t0 = time.perf_counter()
meas, conf = run_mc(random_configs(len(g_sk), L_sk, 2), g_sk, T_sk, n_equil=200, n_meas=20, n_between=10, seed=21, keep=True)
Sk, snaps = {}, {}
for k, (gv, T, name) in enumerate(cases):
    c = conf[-1, :, k * n_ch:(k + 1) * n_ch].reshape(-1, L_sk, L_sk).astype(np.float64)   # (320, 32, 32) snapshots at the target T
    Sk[name] = (np.abs(np.fft.fft2(c)) ** 2).mean(0) / L_sk**2                          # S(k) on the 32 x 32 grid of wave vectors
    snaps[name] = c[-1]

The sum rule holds to all printed digits, and the four maps agree with the predictions. The ferromagnet shows one Bragg peak at \(\boldsymbol k=(0,0)\) of height comparable to \(N\) (\(S(0,0)\approx1005\) for \(N=1024\)). The paramagnet has a broad maximum around \((0,0)\) of height of order one (\(3.5\)), the signature of short-range ferromagnetic correlations without order. In the stripe phase the peaks sit at \((\pi,0)\) and \((0,\pi)\). The map averages over chains, which may have chosen different orientations, so both peaks appear. At \(g=1/2\) and low \(T\) the weight concentrates on the lines \(k_x=0\) and \(k_y=0\). These are the modes of the degenerate ground-state manifold (rows or columns with independent signs, Section 3.5) and the lines on which \(\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\) is maximal (Section 6). The snapshot shows domains of rows or columns instead of a single ordered pattern.
The structure factor thus identifies the ordering wave vector without prior knowledge, with a point peak for long-range order and a line of weight at the frustrated point. Lab 020 asks an algorithm to make the same distinction from raw snapshots.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
8. Transfer matrices of infinite strips
Monte Carlo has statistical errors and needs equilibration. For a strip of finite width \(L\) and infinite length the free energy can be computed exactly from the largest eigenvalue of the row transfer matrix, the method of Lab 012 extended by diagonal bonds. The results are exact for each \(L\), and the limit \(L\to\infty\) is approached through a sequence of widths.
With the row-pair energy \(W(\sigma,\sigma')\) of Section 3.4 the transfer matrix is \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf V_{\sigma\sigma'} &= e^{-\beta W(\sigma,\sigma')}\\
&= \exp\Big\{\beta\Big[J_1\sum_xs_xs'_x - J_2\sum_xs_x\big(s'_{x+1}+s'_{x-1}\big) + \frac{J_1}{2}\sum_x\big(s_xs_{x+1}+s'_xs'_{x+1}\big)\Big]\Big\},
\end{aligned}
\] a \(2^L\times2^L\) matrix. It is symmetric (\(\sum_xs_x(s'_{x+1}+s'_{x-1})=\sum_xs'_x(s_{x-1}+s_{x+1})\)) and has positive entries. For a strip of length \(M\to\infty\), \(Z=\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf V^M\simeq\lambda_0^M\), so \[
f_L(T) = -\frac{T}{L}\ln\lambda_0,\qquad \xi_L = \frac{1}{\ln(\lambda_0/|\lambda_1|)},
\] where \(\lambda_0\) is the largest eigenvalue (positive and non-degenerate by the Perron–Frobenius theorem) and \(\lambda_1\) the eigenvalue of largest modulus among the eigenvectors odd under the global spin flip, the ones that carry the spin–spin correlation along the strip, \(\langle s_0s_r\rangle\sim(|\lambda_1|/\lambda_0)^r\). The modulus matters here, because horizontal stripes (rows alternately \(+\) and \(-\)) appear as a negative eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\approx-\lambda_0\).
The spin-flip symmetry halves the work. The flip \(\sigma\to-\sigma\) maps the index \(n\to2^L-1-n\) and commutes with \(\mathsf V\). With \(\mathsf V^{\pm}_{ab}=\mathsf V_{ab}\pm\mathsf V_{a,\bar b}\) for \(a,b<2^{L-1}\) (Lab 012), the even and odd sectors are two symmetric matrices of half the size.
As a first test, \(Z\) of the \(4\times4\) torus is \(\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf V^4\) and must equal the enumeration of Section 3.3 at any \((g,T)\).


Code
_row_cache = {}
def log_V(L, J1, J2, T):
    # ln V[sigma, sigma'] = -W(sigma, sigma') / T, shape (2^L, 2^L)
    if L not in _row_cache:
        _row_cache[L] = row_terms(L)
    intra, nn, dd = _row_cache[L]
    return (J1 * nn - J2 * dd + 0.5 * J1 * (intra[:, None] + intra[None, :])) / T

def top_eig(A, which):
    # largest algebraic ("LA") or largest-modulus ("LM") eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix
    n = A.shape[0]
    if n <= 512:
        w = eigh(A, eigvals_only=True)
        return w[-1] if which == "LA" else w[np.argmax(np.abs(w))]
    return eigsh(A, k=1, which=which, tol=0)[0][0]

def strip_eigs(L, J1, J2, T, odd=True):
    # ln(lambda_0) and ln|lambda_1| of the strip of width L (lambda_1 only if odd=True)
    lv = log_V(L, J1, J2, T)
    shift = lv.max()
    V = np.exp(lv - shift)                                 # rescaled to avoid overflow; ln lambda = ln(eig) + shift
    n = V.shape[0] // 2
    Vf = V[:n, ::-1][:, :n]                                # V[a, flip(b)] for a, b < 2^(L-1)
    l0 = np.log(top_eig(V[:n, :n] + Vf, "LA")) + shift
    l1 = np.log(abs(top_eig(V[:n, :n] - Vf, "LM"))) + shift if odd else np.nan
    return l0, l1

# check against enumeration: Z(4x4 torus) = Tr V^4
for gv, T in [(0.0, 2.0), (0.4, 1.0), (0.5, 0.5), (0.8, 1.5)]:
    V = np.exp(log_V(4, 1.0, gv, T))
    lnZ_tm = np.log(np.trace(np.linalg.matrix_power(V, 4)))
    E = -B1_44 + gv * B2_44
    lnZ_ex = -E.min() / T + np.log(np.exp(-(E - E.min()) / T).sum())
    print(f"g = {gv}, T = {T}:  ln Z (Tr V^4) = {lnZ_tm:.12f}   ln Z (enumeration) = {lnZ_ex:.12f}")

8.1 Free energy, specific heat and residual entropy
The two values of \(\ln Z\) agree to twelve digits. For widths \(L=4,6,8,10\) and several \(g\) we compute \(f_L(T)\) on a fine grid and the specific heat \(c_L=-T\,\partial^2f_L/\partial T^2\) by finite differences (the eigenvalues are accurate to machine precision, so second differences are reliable). The results are stored in strip_f[(g, L)] and strip_c[(g, L)], each of shape \((n_T,)\). The figure shows \(c_L\) against \(T\) for the four widths, one panel per value of \(g\), and the maximum moves to lower temperature as \(g\) approaches \(1/2\).

for gv in g_curves:

        l0 = np.array([strip_eigs(L, 1.0, gv, T, odd=False)[0] for T in T_fine])
        strip_f[(gv, L)] = -T_fine * l0 / L
        strip_c[(gv, L)] = -T_fine * np.gradient(np.gradient(strip_f[(gv, L)], dT), dT)

The strip free energy also reveals a residual entropy at \(g=1/2\). For \(T\to0\) only the ground states contribute, \(\lambda_0^M\simeq n_0\,e^{-\beta E_0}\) with \(E_0=-J_1LM\) at \(g=1/2\). Section 3.5 gives \(n_0\simeq2^M\) for a long strip (each row uniform with a free sign), so \[
\lambda_0\,e^{-\beta J_1 L}\xrightarrow{T\to0}2,\qquad s_{{\rm ent},L}(T\to0) = \frac{\ln2}{L}\ \text{per spin}.
\] For \(g\neq1/2\) the ground states are a fixed finite number and the same ratio (with the corresponding \(E_0\)) tends to \(1\), which means zero entropy. The entropy per spin follows from the free energy as \(s_{\rm ent}=(u-f)/T\) with \(u=\partial(\beta f)/\partial\beta = f - T\,\partial f/\partial T\), so \(s_{\rm ent}=-\partial f/\partial T\). The cell evaluates the ratio and the entropy (printed as s) at low temperature for \(g=0.3\), \(0.5\) and \(0.7\).

At \(g=1/2\) the strip keeps an entropy \(\ln2/L\) per spin down to \(T=0\), the transfer-matrix version of the degeneracy \(2^M\), while away from \(g=1/2\) the entropy vanishes. For \(g\) near \(1/2\) the maximum of \(c_L\) moves to lower temperature (\(T=0.700\), \(0.600\) and \(0.775\) for \(L=10\) at \(g=0.45\), \(0.5\) and \(0.55\)), but at \(g=1/2\) it does not disappear, although there is no transition there. The strip specific heat also counts local excitations (a single flipped spin costs \(4J_1\) at \(g=1/2\), Exercise 1), so a peak of \(c_L\) alone does not prove a phase transition.


8.2 Transition temperature from the strips
For each \(g\) the position \(T_{\max}(g)\) of the maximum of \(c_L\) is a finite-size indicator of the transition, which for the Ising model approaches \(T_c\) slowly (Lab 012). The correlation length gives a sharper indicator. Above \(T_c\), \(\xi_L\) saturates as \(L\) grows, so \(\xi_L/L\) decreases with \(L\). Below \(T_c\) the ordered states become degenerate, \(|\lambda_1|\to\lambda_0\), and \(\xi_L/L\) increases with \(L\). The temperature \(T^*(L,L+2)\) where \(\xi_L/L=\xi_{L+2}/(L+2)\) therefore estimates \(T_c\), and for the Ising model it converges fast (Lab 012). We solve for the crossing with brentq, a bracketing root finder of SciPy, in a bracket found on a coarse grid, for the pairs \((6,8)\) and \((8,10)\) at every \(g\). The most expensive pair, \((10,12)\) with \(2^{12}\times2^{12}\) matrices, is computed only for \(g=0\), \(0.3\), \(0.7\), \(1\) and \(2\), and the table prints none where a crossing was not computed.


Code
def xi_over_L(L, J1, J2, T):
    l0, l1 = strip_eigs(L, J1, J2, T)
    return 1.0 / (l0 - l1) / L

def crossing(L, J1, J2, T_lo, T_hi, n_grid=12):
    # temperature where xi_L/L = xi_{L+2}/(L+2), searched in [T_lo, T_hi]; None if no sign change
    F = lambda T: xi_over_L(L, J1, J2, T) - xi_over_L(L + 2, J1, J2, T)
    Tg = np.linspace(T_lo, T_hi, n_grid)
    Fg = np.array([F(T) for T in Tg])
    Fg = np.where(np.isfinite(Fg), Fg, 0.0)
    idx = np.where(Fg[:-1] * Fg[1:] < 0)[0]
    if len(idx) == 0:
        return None
    i = idx[-1]                                                       # the highest-temperature sign change
    return brentq(F, Tg[i], Tg[i + 1], xtol=1e-6)

def T_guess(g):
    # bracket centre from the mean-field shape, used only to place the search window
    return TC_ISING * max(1 - 2 * g, 2 * g - 1, 0.15) if g < 1 else TC_ISING * g

For large \(g\), \(T^*/g\) grows towards \(2.269\) (\(2.0798\), \(2.1830\), \(2.2205\) and \(2.2508\) at \(g=1\), \(1.5\), \(2\) and \(4\)), and the decoupled limit \(J_1=0\) gives \(T^*/J_2\) close to \(2.269\) directly. In between, the crossings trace a line far below mean field that dips towards \(g=1/2\). At these widths the dip stops at \(T^*\approx0.7\) for \(g=0.45\) and \(0.55\). Close to \(g=1/2\) the relevant length scales exceed \(L\le12\), and Kalz et al. [2008] find from much larger Monte Carlo lattices that the data are consistent with \(T_c\to0\) at \(g=1/2\), as the domain-wall argument of Section 4 suggests.

The specific-heat maximum lies close to the crossings away from \(g=1/2\) but stays at a finite temperature at \(g=1/2\) itself, where there is no transition.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
9. Binder cumulants
The strips of Section 8 are exact but narrow (\(L\le12\)). Monte Carlo reaches larger lattices at the price of statistical errors. A finite lattice has no sharp transition (Lab 012, Section 1), so we need a quantity whose size dependence changes sign at \(T_c\), and the Binder cumulant [Binder 1981] is such a quantity. For a scalar order parameter, here the ferromagnetic \(m\), it is defined as \[
U_m = 1-\frac{\langle m^4\rangle}{3\langle m^2\rangle^2}.
\] In the disordered phase, \(L\gg\xi\), \(m\) is a sum of many weakly correlated contributions, hence Gaussian by the central limit theorem, so \(\langle m^4\rangle=3\langle m^2\rangle^2\) and \(U_m\to0\). In the ordered phase \(m\approx\pm m_0\), \(\langle m^4\rangle=\langle m^2\rangle^2\) and \(U_m\to2/3\). At \(T_c\) the distribution of \(m/\sqrt{\langle m^2\rangle}\) has an \(L\)-independent shape (scale invariance), so \(U_m\) takes the same value for all large \(L\), and the curves \(U_m(T)\) for different \(L\) cross at \(T_c\).
The stripe order parameter has two components \((m_x,m_y)\), and the normalisation must be adapted. For a two-dimensional Gaussian vector \(\langle r^4\rangle=2\langle r^2\rangle^2\), and for a vector of fixed length \(\langle r^4\rangle=\langle r^2\rangle^2\), so \[
U_{\rm str} = 2-\frac{\langle m_{\rm str}^4\rangle}{\langle m_{\rm str}^2\rangle^2}
\] goes from \(0\) (disordered) to \(1\) (ordered). SymPy verifies the Gaussian moments.


Code
xg, yg, sg = sp.symbols("x y sigma", positive=True)
gauss1 = sp.exp(-xg**2 / (2 * sg**2)) / sp.sqrt(2 * sp.pi * sg**2)

print("1D Gaussian:  <x^4> / <x^2>^2 =", sp.simplify(mom(4) / mom(2)**2), "  ->  U_m = 1 - 3/3 =", 1 - sp.simplify(mom(4) / mom(2)**2) / 3)

For the simulations we choose, for each \(g\), a temperature window from \(0.9\) to \(1.12\) times the transfer-matrix estimate \(T^*\) of Section 8.2 and simulate three sizes, \(L=16,24,32\), at 8 temperatures with 16 independent chains per \((g,T,L)\). All \(5\times8\times16=640\) chains of one size run in a single batch. Each chain starts in the ordered state and runs at fixed temperature, n_equil sweeps of equilibration followed by n_meas measurements separated by n_between sweeps. Error bars come from a jackknife over chains. The jackknife recomputes the cumulant with one block of 2 chains left out, for each of the 8 blocks, and the spread of these 8 values gives the error. The ferromagnetic side uses \(U_m\) and the stripe side \(U_{\rm str}\), and at \(g=2\) the comparison with \(2.269\,g\) tests the large-\(g\) limit of Section 5.


Code
def binder(meas, stripe):
    # meas: (chains, nT, n_meas, 4) -> U(T) and its jackknife error over blocks of chains; shapes (nT,), (nT,)
    q = np.hypot(meas[..., 1], meas[..., 2]) if stripe else meas[..., 0]
    q2, q4 = (q**2).mean(2), (q**4).mean(2)                         # per chain and temperature: (chains, nT)
    U = (lambda a2, a4: 2 - a4 / a2**2) if stripe else (lambda a2, a4: 1 - a4 / (3 * a2**2))
    full = U(q2.mean(0), q4.mean(0))
    blocks = np.array_split(np.arange(q2.shape[0]), 8)
    jk = np.array([U(np.delete(q2, b, 0).mean(0), np.delete(q4, b, 0).mean(0)) for b in blocks])
    err = np.sqrt((len(blocks) - 1) * ((jk - jk.mean(0))**2).mean(0))
    return full, err

def crossing_T(T, Ua, Ub, T_ref):
    # temperature where the interpolated curves Ua(T), Ub(T) cross, the crossing closest to T_ref; None if none
    d = Ua - Ub
    idx = np.where(d[:-1] * d[1:] < 0)[0]
    if len(idx) == 0:
        return None
    Tx = [T[i] - d[i] * (T[i + 1] - T[i]) / (d[i + 1] - d[i]) for i in idx]
    return min(Tx, key=lambda t: abs(t - T_ref))

The curves cross, and the table lists the crossing temperatures next to the other estimates. The \((24,32)\) crossings agree with the transfer-matrix crossings to within \(3.5\%\). They lie \(2.6\%\) below at \(g=0\) and \(3.4\%\) below at \(g=0.3\), and within \(0.6\%\) at \(g=0.7\), \(1\) and \(2\). These deviations, and the spread between the \((16,24)\) and \((24,32)\) crossings, show the statistical and equilibration limits of local Metropolis updates with 16 chains per point (Lab 018 discusses critical slowing down). At \(g=2\) the crossing gives \(T_c/g=2.232\), \(1.6\%\) below the large-\(g\) limit \(2.269\). Mean field overestimates \(T_c\) by factors between \(1.8\) and \(2.3\).
The second figure assembles the phase diagram from all methods of this notebook, the transfer-matrix crossings of the widest available pair (orange dots), the Binder crossings \((24,32)\) (blue squares), the exact limits \(2.269\) and \(2.269\,g\) (dotted), mean field (dashed) and the domain-wall estimate \(\sigma_{\min}/\ln3\) (dash-dotted). The domain-wall estimate lies below the computed line and vanishes at \(g=1/2\), where the true transition temperature drops. Locating \(T_c(g)\) very close to \(g=1/2\), and deciding the order of the stripe transition, requires larger lattices and specialised methods, which Section 10 reviews.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
10. First-order and continuous transitions
Our calculations locate the transition line but cannot decide its nature close to \(g=1/2\), which needs lattices far larger than ours, histogram analysis and dedicated methods. The model has a long history of conflicting answers, which makes it a demanding benchmark and shows that small-lattice data can mislead. Each statement below is attributed to the paper that makes it. Some papers take the nearest-neighbour coupling antiferromagnetic, others write the ferromagnetic one as \(J_1<0\), and by the checkerboard gauge of Section 2 all these results apply to our model with \(g=|J_2/J_1|\) (an antiferromagnetic \(J_1\) turns our ferromagnet into a Néel state).
On the ferromagnetic side, \(g<1/2\), the order parameter is a scalar with \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry. Kalz, Honecker, Fuchs and Pruschke [2008] find a transition in the two-dimensional Ising universality class (for example the correlation-length exponent \(\nu=0.99(1)\) at \(g=0.3\), against the Ising value \(\nu=1\)), and a transition temperature consistent with \(T_c\to0\) at \(g=1/2\).
On the stripe side, \(g>1/2\), the literature records a long debate. Early Monte Carlo work [Landau & Binder 1985, among others] was interpreted as a continuous transition with non-universal, continuously varying exponents (as summarised by Kalz et al. [2008]). Kalz et al. [2008] then observed a double-peaked energy histogram at \(g=0.6\), the signature of a first-order transition (coexistence of the ordered and disordered phases), and concluded that the transition is weakly first order for moderate \(g>1/2\). Kalz, Honecker and Moliner [2011] found doubly peaked histograms for \(1/2<g\lesssim1\) and, by perturbation theory around the two decoupled critical Ising models at \(J_1=0\) (Section 5.2), derived the Ashkin–Teller model as the effective theory.
Jin, Sen and Sandvik [2012] reached a different picture. They found that for \(g\ge g^*\) the transition is continuous with Ashkin–Teller exponents that vary continuously from those of the 4-state Potts model (a generalisation of the Ising model in which each spin takes four values) at \(g=g^*\) to those of the Ising model for \(g\to\infty\), with \(g^*=0.67(1)\). In their picture the transition is first order for \(1/2<g<g^*\) and pseudo-first-order for \(g^*<g<1\), meaning that on finite lattices a continuous transition near the Potts point shows first-order-like features such as double-peaked histograms. Jin, Sen, Guo and Sandvik [2013] extended this with cluster mean-field theory, Monte Carlo and transfer matrices, finding a line of very weak first-order transitions for \(1/2<g<g^*\) and continuous transitions above \(g^*\) that map onto the critical line of the Ashkin–Teller model from its 4-state Potts point to the decoupled-Ising limit. Li and Yang [2021] used tensor networks and found that if a first-order region exists, it is smaller than in the earlier studies. Their analysis suggests that the model evolves continuously from two decoupled Ising models (central charge \(1\), a number that labels the universality class of a two-dimensional critical point) to a point in the tricritical Ising class (central charge \(0.7\)) at \(g^*\simeq0.54\).
These results connect directly with this notebook. The Ashkin–Teller structure is the \(D_4\) symmetry of the stripe order parameter (Section 2.1) and the two sublattice magnetisations of the \(g\to\infty\) limit (Section 5.2). The difficulty of the problem near \(g=1/2\), with tiny energy scales (Section 4), a degenerate manifold (Section 3.5) and first-order or pseudo-first-order behaviour, makes the model a demanding test for the unsupervised methods of Lab 020.
The results of this notebook and the literature above combine into the phase diagram drawn below. A phase diagram is a map of the control parameters, here the coupling ratio \(g=J_2/J_1\) and the temperature \(T/J_1\), divided into regions with qualitatively different behaviour, the phases, and the lines between them, the phase transitions. The type of a transition is read off from the free energy per spin \(f\) and its derivatives. At a first-order transition a first derivative of \(f\), such as the energy or the order parameter, jumps, and the two phases coexist at the transition temperature. On a finite lattice this shows up as an energy histogram with two peaks, the observation of Kalz et al. [2008]. At a continuous transition the first derivatives are continuous, the order parameter goes to zero continuously, and the correlation length diverges as a power of \(|T-T_c|\) with critical exponents shared by a whole universality class.
The orange dots are the transfer-matrix crossings of Section 8.2 for the strip widths \(L=8\) and \(10\), and the blue squares the Monte Carlo Binder crossings of Section 9. The solid lines through them are only a guide to the eye. Three limits are drawn at their exact positions, \(T_c=2/\ln(1+\sqrt2)=2.269\,J_1\) at \(g=0\) (Onsager), the asymptote \(T_c\to2.269\,g\,J_1\) for \(g\to\infty\) (two decoupled Ising lattices, Section 5.2), and \(T_c\to0\) at \(g=1/2\), where domain walls cost nothing (Section 4) and where Kalz et al. [2008] find their data consistent with a vanishing transition temperature. The dashed segments connect the computed points to this limit. Below the line on the left the ferromagnet has \(m\neq0\), below the line on the right the stripe phase has \(m_{\rm str}\neq0\), and above both lies the paramagnet. On the ferromagnetic side the transition is continuous and in the two-dimensional Ising universality class [Kalz et al. 2008]. On the stripe side, for \(g\) well above \(1/2\), it is continuous with exponents that vary along the line, those of the Ashkin–Teller model introduced in Section 2.1 [Jin, Sen & Sandvik 2012]. Close to \(g=1/2\) (hatched band, \(1/2<g\lesssim0.7\)) its nature is debated. It is first order according to Kalz et al. [2008, 2011] and Jin et al. [2012, 2013], who place the end of the first-order region at \(g^*=0.67(1)\), while Li and Yang [2021] find at most a much smaller first-order region.

Exercises

Exercise 1 — single spin flips and mean field
Compute, symbolically and numerically, the energy cost \(\Delta E\) of flipping a single spin in the ferromagnetic ground state and in the stripe ground state as a function of \(J_1,J_2\). Compare with \(T_{\rm MF}\) of Section 6 and explain the relation using \(\Delta E_i=2s_ih_i\).

Solution


Code
L = 8; x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(L), np.arange(L), indexing="ij")
for name, s0 in {"ferromagnet": np.ones((L, L), int), "stripes": (-1) ** x}.items():
    s1 = s0.copy(); s1[3, 3] *= -1                                        # flip one spin
    b0, b1 = bond_sums(s0), bond_sums(s1)
    dE = sp.expand(-J1s * (b1[0] + b1[1] - b0[0] - b0[1]) + J2s * (b1[2] - b0[2]))
    print(f"{name:11s}: Delta E = {dE}   (numerical at g = 0.3: {energy(s1, 0.3) - energy(s0, 0.3):+.2f})")


ferromagnet: Delta E = 8*J_1 - 8*J_2   (numerical at g = 0.3: +5.60)
stripes    : Delta E = 8*J_2   (numerical at g = 0.3: +2.40)


\(\Delta E_{\rm FM}=8J_1-8J_2=2\cdot4(J_1-J_2)\) and \(\Delta E_{\rm str}=8J_2=2\cdot4J_2\), so in both cases \(\Delta E=2T_{\rm MF}\). The reason is that \(\Delta E_i=2s_ih_i\), and in the perfectly ordered state the local field is \(|h_i|=\mathcal J(\boldsymbol Q)\), with \(\boldsymbol Q\) the ordering wave vector, which is also \(T_{\rm MF}\). Mean field treats the ordered state as a collection of independent spins in this field. A single flip costs \(8|J_1-J_2|\) or \(8J_2\), which stays finite at \(g=1/2\) (\(4J_1\)). The soft excitations at \(g=1/2\) are extended domain walls (Section 4).



Exercise 2 — odd lattice sizes
Use minplus_torus to compute \(E_0/N\) and the degeneracy on \(4\times5\) and \(5\times5\) tori at \(g=0.75\) and \(g=0.5\). Explain the results.

Solution


Code
for L, M in [(4, 5), (5, 5)]:
    for gv in (0.75, 0.5):
        e0, n0 = minplus_torus(L, M, gv)
        print(f"{L} x {M}, g = {gv}:  E0/N = {e0:+.4f}  (bulk value {min(-2 + 2*gv, -2*gv):+.4f}),  n0 = {n0}  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = {2**L + 2**M - 2})")


4 x 5, g = 0.75:  E0/N = -1.5000  (bulk value -1.5000),  n0 = 2  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = 46)
4 x 5, g = 0.5:  E0/N = -1.0000  (bulk value -1.0000),  n0 = 46  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = 46)
5 x 5, g = 0.75:  E0/N = -1.3000  (bulk value -1.5000),  n0 = 20  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = 62)
5 x 5, g = 0.5:  E0/N = -1.0000  (bulk value -1.0000),  n0 = 62  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = 62)


At \(g=0.75\) stripes need an even period. On \(4\times5\) only the stripes that alternate along the even direction fit, so the degeneracy drops from 4 to 2 while the energy is unchanged. On \(5\times5\) no stripe state fits, and the ground state must contain a domain wall. The cheapest is one parallel (phase-slip) wall of length 5, with energy \(5\,\sigma_\parallel=5\cdot2(2g-1)=5\) at \(g=0.75\), that is \(0.2\) per spin above \(-2g\), the printed difference. Its degeneracy is \(2\) orientations \(\times\) \(5\) positions \(\times\) \(2\) signs \(=20\). At \(g=1/2\) the derivation of Section 3.5 never used the parity of \(L\) or \(M\), and the count \(2^L+2^M-2\) holds for odd sizes as well. Simulations of this model therefore use even \(L\).



Exercise 3 — Binder cumulant limits by sampling
Draw \(10^6\) samples of (a) a Gaussian scalar, (b) a scalar \(\pm1\), (c) a two-dimensional Gaussian vector, (d) a two-dimensional vector of length 1 pointing to one of the four directions \((\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)\). Evaluate \(U_m\) for (a), (b) and \(U_{\rm str}\) for (c), (d), and compare with the limits of Section 9.

Solution


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(7); n = 10**6
U1 = lambda q: 1 - (q**4).mean() / (3 * (q**2).mean()**2)
U2 = lambda q: 2 - (q**4).mean() / (q**2).mean()**2
a = rng.standard_normal(n); b = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], n)
c = np.hypot(rng.standard_normal(n), rng.standard_normal(n))
d = np.ones(n)                                                         # |(+-1, 0)| = |(0, +-1)| = 1
print(f"(a) Gaussian scalar: U_m = {U1(a):+.4f} (expected 0);   (b) +-1: U_m = {U1(b):.4f} (expected 2/3 = {2/3:.4f})")
print(f"(c) 2D Gaussian: U_str = {U2(c):+.4f} (expected 0);   (d) four stripe states: U_str = {U2(d):.4f} (expected 1)")


(a) Gaussian scalar: U_m = +0.0002 (expected 0);   (b) +-1: U_m = 0.6667 (expected 2/3 = 0.6667)
(c) 2D Gaussian: U_str = +0.0006 (expected 0);   (d) four stripe states: U_str = 1.0000 (expected 1)


The finite-sample values deviate from the limits by \(O(n^{-1/2})\). In a simulation the distribution at \(T_c\) is neither Gaussian nor two delta peaks, and the cumulant takes an intermediate, universal value that depends on the universality class and on the boundary conditions.

title: Lab 030: Physics of the 2D XY model and the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
text:
1. Continuous symmetry in two dimensions
We begin by recalling equilibrium statistical mechanics. A configuration \(\boldsymbol\theta\) of a classical system with energy \(H(\boldsymbol\theta)\) occurs at temperature \(T\) with the Boltzmann probability \[
\begin{aligned}
p(\boldsymbol\theta)&=\frac{e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol\theta)}}{Z},\qquad \beta=\frac1T,\\
Z&=\int\! d\boldsymbol\theta\; e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol\theta)},
\end{aligned}
\] with \(k_B=1\). The free energy \(F=-T\ln Z\) balances energy against entropy, \(F=E-TS\). At low \(T\) the energy wins and the system orders, and at high \(T\) the entropy wins and it disorders. A phase transition is a temperature at which \(F/N\) (with \(N\) the number of spins, \(N\to\infty\)) is not an analytic function of \(T\).
In the 2D Ising model (\(s_i=\pm1\)) the energy is invariant under the global flip \(s_i\to-s_i\), yet below \(T_c\) the system picks one of the two ordered states and the magnetisation \(\langle m\rangle\) is non-zero. The symmetry is spontaneously broken. To destroy the order one has to create a domain wall, whose energy grows with its length, and at low \(T\) such walls are too expensive.
The situation changes when the symmetry is continuous. If the spins are planar unit vectors \(\boldsymbol s_i=(\cos\theta_i,\sin\theta_i)\) and the energy, with coupling \(J\) between neighbours, depends only on relative angles, the direction can rotate gradually over a long distance and no sharp domain wall is needed. Turning the spins by \(2\pi\) gradually across a region of linear size \(\ell\) costs \(\frac J2(2\pi/\ell)^2\) per bond, which gives an energy \(\propto\ell^{d-2}\) for the whole region in \(d\) dimensions. This is independent of \(\ell\) in two dimensions, whereas an Ising domain wall costs \(\propto\ell^{d-1}\) (Section 3 gives the full spin-wave argument). These long-wavelength twists, the spin waves, are the Goldstone modes of the broken continuous symmetry, excitations whose energy goes to zero at long wavelength, and they are so cheap in \(d\le2\) that thermal fluctuations destroy the long-range order at every \(T>0\). Mermin and Wagner (1966) proved this rigorously for the isotropic Heisenberg model, and Berezinskii (1971) analysed systems with a continuous symmetry group in one and two dimensions. We derive the effect for the XY model in the spin-wave approximation and check it with Monte Carlo.
The sketch below compares the two cases on a strip of twelve columns. In the Ising model (top) the spins change from up to down across a single column of bonds. Every bond on that column is broken and costs \(2J\), so a wall across a region of linear size \(\ell\) costs an energy proportional to \(\ell^{d-1}\). In the XY model (bottom) the angle can turn by \(2\pi\) gradually, by \(2\pi/\ell\) from one column to the next. Each bond then costs only about \(\frac J2(2\pi/\ell)^2\), and the twist of a whole region costs an energy proportional to \(\ell^{d-2}\), which in two dimensions does not grow with \(\ell\).


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;
#   satisfied bond: solid blue line, broken (frustrated) bond: dashed purple line marked with a cross.
# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (3.19 in = 0.58 text width) with 10-12 pt text,
# and shown here at a higher screen resolution.
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

NAVY, ORANGE, BLUE, GRAY, PURPLE, GREEN = "#002B5C", "#D35A05", "#005CA7", "#5A6270", "#AA3377", "#228833"
SKETCH_STYLE = {"font.size": 11, "axes.titlesize": 12, "axes.labelsize": 11, "xtick.labelsize": 10,
                "ytick.labelsize": 10, "legend.fontsize": 10, "figure.dpi": 130, "lines.linewidth": 1.5,
                "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}

def save_sketch(fig, name, extra_dirs=()):
    # PNG copy for the lecture slides: white background, 300 dpi, included at its physical width
    os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
    for d in ("figures",) + tuple(d for d in extra_dirs if os.path.isdir(d)):
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, name), dpi=300, facecolor="white")

def draw_spin(ax, x, y, s, r=0.26, sign=False, alpha=1.0, fs=10, lw=1.3):
    # one Ising spin at (x, y): navy disc for s = +1, white disc with orange rim for s = -1 (optionally with "+" / "-")
    face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if s > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
    ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x, y), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=lw, alpha=alpha, zorder=4))
    if sign:
        ax.text(x, y, "+" if s > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", alpha=alpha,
                fontsize=fs, fontweight="bold", zorder=5)

def draw_bond(ax, p, q, broken=False, lw=1.5, alpha=1.0, color=None, cross=True):
    # bond between points p and q: solid blue if satisfied, dashed purple with a cross if broken
    c = color or (PURPLE if broken else BLUE)
    ax.plot([p[0], q[0]], [p[1], q[1]], color=c, lw=lw, ls=(0, (2.5, 1.5)) if broken else "-",
            alpha=alpha, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=2)
    if broken and cross:
        ax.plot((p[0] + q[0]) / 2, (p[1] + q[1]) / 2, marker="x", ms=3.5 * lw, mew=lw * 0.9, color=c, alpha=alpha, zorder=3)

def draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.75, color=NAVY, lw=1.3, head=7, dot=True):
    # planar spins: an arrow of fixed length centred on every lattice site (x, y), angle theta[y, x]
    for (y, x), t in np.ndenumerate(theta):
        dx, dy = 0.5 * length * np.cos(t), 0.5 * length * np.sin(t)
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x + dx, y + dy), xytext=(x - dx, y - dy),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=lw, mutation_scale=head, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
        if dot:
            ax.plot(x, y, "o", color=GRAY, ms=1.5, zorder=1)

def plaquette_winding(theta):
    # winding number of every plaquette (lower-left corner (x, y)), corners traversed counter-clockwise
    wrap = lambda a: (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi           # angle difference mapped to [-pi, pi)
    t1, t2 = theta[:-1, :-1], theta[:-1, 1:]                       # (x, y), (x+1, y)
    t3, t4 = theta[1:, 1:], theta[1:, :-1]                         # (x+1, y+1), (x, y+1)
    return np.rint((wrap(t2 - t1) + wrap(t3 - t2) + wrap(t4 - t3) + wrap(t1 - t4)) / (2 * np.pi)).astype(int)

def draw_vortex_marks(ax, w, r=0.3):
    # vortex (w = +1): navy disc with "+";  antivortex (w = -1): white disc with orange rim and "-"
    for (y, x), v in np.ndenumerate(w):
        if v != 0:
            face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if v > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
            ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x + 0.5, y + 0.5), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=1.3, zorder=6, alpha=0.9))
            ax.text(x + 0.5, y + 0.5, "+" if v > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=7)

def sketch_wall_versus_spin_wave():
    nx, ny = 12, 3
    W, H, h = 3.19, 2.14, 0.76                       # figure width and height, panel height (in)
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(W, H))
    ax1 = fig.add_axes([0.01, (h + 0.34) / H, 0.98, h / H]); ax2 = fig.add_axes([0.01, 0.02 / H, 0.98, h / H])
    # (a) Ising: the spins flip abruptly across one column of bonds
    for yy in range(ny):
        for xx in range(nx):
            draw_spin(ax1, xx, yy, 1 if xx < nx // 2 else -1, r=0.3, lw=0.8)
    ax1.plot([nx / 2 - 0.5] * 2, [-0.5, ny - 0.5], color=PURPLE, lw=2.0)
    ax1.set_title(r"(a) Ising: sharp wall, $2J$ per broken bond", fontsize=11, color=NAVY, loc="left")
    # (b) XY: the angle turns by 2 pi gradually over ell = nx columns, i.e. by 2 pi / ell per bond
    theta = np.tile(2 * np.pi * np.arange(nx) / nx + np.pi / 2, (ny, 1))
    draw_xy_spins(ax2, theta, length=0.75, lw=1.1, head=6)
    ax2.set_title(r"(b) XY: $2\pi$ over $\ell$ sites, $\frac{J}{2}(2\pi/\ell)^2$ per bond", fontsize=11, color=NAVY, loc="left")
    for ax in (ax1, ax2):
        ax.set_xlim(-0.6, nx - 0.4); ax.set_ylim(-0.45, ny - 0.55); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_wall_versus_spin_wave()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_xy_spin_wave.png")
plt.show()





Berezinskii (1971, 1972) and Kosterlitz and Thouless (1973) showed that the 2D XY model nevertheless has two distinct phases, and hence a transition without an order parameter. At low \(T\) correlations decay as a power law of distance, a behaviour called quasi-long-range order, and the system resists a twist with a non-zero spin stiffness. At high \(T\) correlations decay exponentially and the stiffness vanishes. The transition between them is caused by vortices, points around which the angle winds by \(2\pi\). Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) vortices exist only in tightly bound vortex–antivortex pairs, and above it free vortices proliferate. Kosterlitz (1974) worked out the critical behaviour with the renormalisation group, a method that follows how the effective couplings change when the system is viewed on longer length scales, and Nelson and Kosterlitz (1977) predicted that the stiffness drops discontinuously at \(T_{\rm BKT}\) by a universal amount.
The same physics describes any 2D system whose state is described by a phase angle, such as thin films of superfluid \(^4\)He (the phase of the condensate wave function), thin superconducting films and planar magnets. The Nelson–Kosterlitz prediction refers directly to superfluid films (their paper is titled Universal jump in the superfluid density of two-dimensional superfluids), and Bishop and Reppy (1978) studied the superfluid transition in two-dimensional \(^4\)He films experimentally.
The 2016 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded “with one half to David J. Thouless, and the other half to F. Duncan M. Haldane and J. Michael Kosterlitz for theoretical discoveries of topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter” (nobelprize.org), and the BKT transition is the topological phase transition of that citation.
For the notebooks that follow, a learning algorithm looking at snapshots will find whatever varies most between them. For the XY model the most visible candidate, the magnetisation, is a finite-size effect, and the relevant objects, the vortices, are invisible in the value of a single spin. They are a property of the angles around a plaquette, an elementary square of four sites. Judging what an algorithm has found requires this physics.

title: Lab 030: Physics of the 2D XY model and the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
section: 2. Model, symmetries and Monte Carlo sampling
text:
2. Model, symmetries and Monte Carlo sampling

2.1 Definition
On an \(L\times L\) square lattice with periodic boundaries (a torus), \(N=L^2\) planar unit vectors \(\boldsymbol s_i=(\cos\theta_i,\sin\theta_i)\), \(\theta_i\in[0,2\pi)\), interact with their nearest neighbours, \[
\begin{aligned}
H(\boldsymbol\theta)&=-J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\boldsymbol s_i\cdot\boldsymbol s_j\\
&=-J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j),\qquad J>0,
\end{aligned}
\] where \(\langle i,j\rangle\) runs over the \(2N\) nearest-neighbour bonds. We set \(J=1\) and \(k_B=1\), and the lattice spacing is \(a=1\).
The figure below shows the model on a small patch. The energy is invariant under several transformations. The global rotation \(\theta_i\to\theta_i+\alpha\) for all \(i\), with any \(\alpha\), is a continuous symmetry, the rotation group \(U(1)\cong SO(2)\), and together with the global reflection \(\theta_i\to-\theta_i\) it forms the group \(O(2)\). The periodicity \(\theta_i\to\theta_i+2\pi\) on any single site looks harmless, but it is what allows vortices (Section 4). Finally there are the lattice symmetries, translations, rotations by \(90^\circ\) and mirror reflections.
Every term of \(H\) is at least \(-J\), so the minimum energy \(E_0=-2JN\) is reached when all spins are parallel, \(\theta_i=\theta_0\). The ground state is a continuous family labelled by \(\theta_0\in[0,2\pi)\), in contrast to the two ground states of the Ising model.
The basic observables are the magnetisation vector and the energy per spin, \[
\boldsymbol m=\frac1N\sum_i\boldsymbol s_i,\qquad |\boldsymbol m|=\sqrt{m_x^2+m_y^2},\qquad e=\frac{H}{N}.
\] Because of the rotation symmetry \(\langle\boldsymbol m\rangle=0\) on any finite lattice, and the useful quantities are \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) and \(\langle\boldsymbol m^2\rangle\).
In the code, angles are stored as an array theta of shape (..., L, L), axis -1 is the \(x\) direction (columns) and axis -2 the \(y\) direction (rows). jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1) is the right neighbour of every site, so jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1) - theta lists the angle differences on all \(N\) horizontal bonds at once (and similarly for the \(N\) vertical bonds). The cell below checks the ground-state energy, the energy of a random state, and the invariance of \(H\) under the global rotation, the reflection and a shift by \(2\pi\) on one site. For a random state with independent angles uniform in \([0,2\pi)\) each bond term \(\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j)\) has mean \(0\) and variance \(1/2\), and the \(2N\) bond terms are uncorrelated, so \(e=-(J/N)\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j)\) has mean \(0\) and variance \((J/N)^2\cdot 2N\cdot\frac12=J^2/N\), which gives a standard deviation \(J/\sqrt N=0.0625\,J\) for \(N=16^2\).

TWO_PI = 2 * np.pi

def wrap(a):
    # map angles to the interval [-pi, pi)
    return (a + jnp.pi) % TWO_PI - jnp.pi

def bond_differences(theta):
    # theta: (..., L, L).  Returns dx = theta_{r+x} - theta_r and dy = theta_{r+y} - theta_r, each (..., L, L): one entry per bond
    return jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1) - theta, jnp.roll(theta, -1, -2) - theta

def energy_per_spin(theta):
    # e = H / N = -(J/N) sum over the 2N bonds of cos(theta_i - theta_j);  output shape (...)
    dx, dy = bond_differences(theta)
    return -J * (jnp.cos(dx) + jnp.cos(dy)).mean((-2, -1))

def magnetisation(theta):
    # m = (1/N) sum_i (cos theta_i, sin theta_i);  returns (m_x, m_y), each of shape (...)
    return jnp.cos(theta).mean((-2, -1)), jnp.sin(theta).mean((-2, -1))
