2.2 Checkerboard Metropolis updates
To sample the Boltzmann distribution we start from the Metropolis algorithm, which Lab 010 derived for Ising spins and which works for any energy. We propose a new angle for spin \(i\), \(\theta_i'=\theta_i+\delta\,(2u-1)\) with \(u\) uniform in \([0,1)\) and a step width \(\delta\), and accept with probability \(\min\!\left(1,e^{-\beta\Delta E_i}\right)\). The proposal is symmetric, so detailed balance holds. The energy change only involves the four neighbours \(j\) of \(i\) and is expressed through the local field \[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol h_i&=\sum_{j\in{\rm nn}(i)}\boldsymbol s_j=\Big(\sum_j\cos\theta_j,\ \sum_j\sin\theta_j\Big),\\
\Delta E_i&=-J\,\boldsymbol h_i\cdot(\boldsymbol s_i'-\boldsymbol s_i).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since nearest neighbours always have different colours on a chessboard (\((x+y)\bmod 2\)), all spins of one colour can be updated simultaneously, because none of them appears in another’s local field. One sweep updates all black sites and then all white sites, which amounts to one attempted move per spin. In code we propose new angles for all sites and accept only on the current colour (a mask). This wastes half of the random numbers but keeps the code short.


2.3 Wolff cluster updates
Local moves are slow near and below the transition. Near \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the correlation length is comparable with \(L\), and below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) it is infinite. Rotating a large correlated region one spin at a time takes many steps, and the autocorrelation time of Metropolis, the number of steps after which configurations become nearly independent (defined in Section 2.6), grows with \(L\), as we measure below.
Wolff (1989) turns the XY model into an Ising model for one update. Choose a random direction \(\hat{\boldsymbol n}=(\cos\psi,\sin\psi)\) and consider only reflections of spins across the line perpendicular to \(\hat{\boldsymbol n}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
&\boldsymbol s_i\to\boldsymbol s_i-2(\boldsymbol s_i\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol n})\,\hat{\boldsymbol n}\\
\Longleftrightarrow\quad &\theta_i\to\pi+2\psi-\theta_i .
\end{aligned}
\] Write \(\sigma_i=\boldsymbol s_i\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol n}=\cos(\theta_i-\psi)\). If a spin is reflected and its neighbour is not, the bond energy changes by \(2J\sigma_i\sigma_j\), and reflecting both leaves it unchanged. With respect to reflections the XY model is therefore an Ising model with bond-dependent couplings \(J\sigma_i\sigma_j\), and the Swendsen–Wang/Wolff construction of Lab 018 applies. 1. Pick a random seed site. 2. Activate each bond \(\langle i,j\rangle\) with probability \(p_{ij}=1-\exp\!\big(\min(0,\,-2\beta J\sigma_i\sigma_j)\big)\) (only bonds with \(\sigma_i\sigma_j>0\) can be active). 3. Reflect the whole cluster of sites connected to the seed by active bonds.
The update satisfies detailed balance and needs no acceptance step (Wolff 1989). Combined with a random \(\psi\) and with the Metropolis moves it is ergodic.
The cluster search needs some care in JAX, because a sequential loop that grows the cluster is awkward to vectorise over many chains. The bond variables are independent, so drawing all bonds of the lattice first and then taking the connected component of the seed gives the same cluster distribution as growing it bond by bond. The connected components are found as in Lab 018 by label propagation. Every site starts with its own index as label and repeatedly takes the smallest label among itself and its bonded neighbours, followed by pointer jumping (a site adopts the label of its label), until no label changes. Under vmap every chain then waits until the slowest chain has converged, and at low \(T\) the clusters span the lattice and need many iterations. On a CPU this makes one Wolff update much more expensive than one Metropolis sweep (measured in Section 2.6).


2.4 Over-relaxation
A cheap alternative for speeding up the sampling (Creutz 1987, Brown and Woch 1987) is to reflect each spin about its local field. With \(\omega_i\) the direction of \(\boldsymbol h_i\), \[
\begin{aligned}
&\theta_i\to2\omega_i-\theta_i\\
\Longrightarrow\quad &\boldsymbol h_i\cdot\boldsymbol s_i\ \text{unchanged},\quad\Delta E_i=0 .
\end{aligned}
\] The move is deterministic, its own inverse, and conserves the energy, so it is accepted with probability \(1\) and leaves the Boltzmann distribution invariant. Because it keeps the energy fixed, on its own it is not ergodic, and combined with Metropolis sweeps it is. It moves spins by large angles at no energy cost, and Section 2.6 measures how much this shortens the autocorrelation times. The checkerboard decomposition applies as for Metropolis.


Code
def checkerboard(L):
    # (L, L) array with values 0 / 1 = colour (x + y) mod 2
    return (jnp.arange(L)[:, None] + jnp.arange(L)[None, :]) % 2

def local_field(theta):
    # h_i = sum of the 4 neighbour vectors;  returns (h_x, h_y), each of the same shape as theta (..., L, L)
    c, s = jnp.cos(theta), jnp.sin(theta)
    nbrs = ((1, -2), (-1, -2), (1, -1), (-1, -1))          # (shift, axis) for the up / down / left / right neighbours
    return sum(jnp.roll(c, d, ax) for d, ax in nbrs), sum(jnp.roll(s, d, ax) for d, ax in nbrs)

def metropolis_sweep(theta, key, beta, delta):
    # theta: (L, L);  one sweep = black sites, then white sites.  Returns new theta and the acceptance rate.
    colour = checkerboard(theta.shape[-1])
    k_prop, k_acc = jax.random.split(key)
    # every site is updated exactly once per sweep, so one proposal and one acceptance number per site suffice
    new = theta + delta * (2.0 * jax.random.uniform(k_prop, theta.shape) - 1.0)
    u_acc = jax.random.uniform(k_acc, theta.shape)
    n_acc = 0.0
    for c in (0, 1):                                          # Python loop, unrolled by jit
        hx, hy = local_field(theta)
        dE = -J * (hx * (jnp.cos(new) - jnp.cos(theta)) + hy * (jnp.sin(new) - jnp.sin(theta)))
        accept = (u_acc < jnp.exp(-beta * dE)) & (colour == c)
        theta = jnp.where(accept, jnp.mod(new, TWO_PI), theta)
        n_acc = n_acc + accept.sum()
    return theta, n_acc / theta.size

def overrelaxation_sweep(theta):
    # reflect every spin about its local field, black sites then white sites: theta_i -> 2 phi_i - theta_i,
    # with phi_i = atan2(h_y, h_x) the direction of the local field.  The energy is unchanged; no random numbers.
    colour = checkerboard(theta.shape[-1])
    for c in (0, 1):
        hx, hy = local_field(theta)
        theta = jnp.where(colour == c, jnp.mod(2.0 * jnp.arctan2(hy, hx) - theta, TWO_PI), theta)
    return theta

def connected_labels(bond_x, bond_y):
    # bond_x[y, x]: site (y, x) bonded to (y, x+1);  bond_y[y, x]: site (y, x) bonded to (y+1, x);  periodic lattice.
    # Returns (L, L) int labels: two sites have the same label iff they are connected by active bonds.
    L = bond_x.shape[0]
    big = L * L
    bond_xm, bond_ym = jnp.roll(bond_x, 1, 1), jnp.roll(bond_y, 1, 0)        # bonds to the left / lower neighbour
    def body(carry):
        lab, _ = carry
        new = lab
        new = jnp.minimum(new, jnp.where(bond_x, jnp.roll(lab, -1, 1), big))
        new = jnp.minimum(new, jnp.where(bond_xm, jnp.roll(lab, 1, 1), big))
        new = jnp.minimum(new, jnp.where(bond_y, jnp.roll(lab, -1, 0), big))
        new = jnp.minimum(new, jnp.where(bond_ym, jnp.roll(lab, 1, 0), big))
        new = new.ravel()[new]                                                  # pointer jumping
        return new, jnp.any(new != lab)
    lab, _ = lax.while_loop(lambda c: c[1], body, (jnp.arange(big).reshape(L, L), True))
    return lab

def wolff_update(theta, key, beta):
    # one Wolff single-cluster update of theta (L, L).  Returns new theta and the cluster size / N.
    L = theta.shape[-1]
    k_phi, k_x, k_y, k_seed = jax.random.split(key, 4)
    phi = jax.random.uniform(k_phi, (), maxval=TWO_PI)                         # reflection direction r = (cos phi, sin phi)
    sigma = jnp.cos(theta - phi)                                               # sigma_i = s_i . r
    p_x = 1.0 - jnp.exp(jnp.minimum(0.0, -2.0 * beta * J * sigma * jnp.roll(sigma, -1, 1)))
    p_y = 1.0 - jnp.exp(jnp.minimum(0.0, -2.0 * beta * J * sigma * jnp.roll(sigma, -1, 0)))
    bond_x = jax.random.uniform(k_x, theta.shape) < p_x
    bond_y = jax.random.uniform(k_y, theta.shape) < p_y
    lab = connected_labels(bond_x, bond_y)
    seed = jax.random.randint(k_seed, (), 0, L * L)
    in_cluster = lab == lab.ravel()[seed]
    theta = jnp.where(in_cluster, jnp.mod(jnp.pi + 2.0 * phi - theta, TWO_PI), theta)
    return theta, in_cluster.mean()


After every Monte Carlo step (one Metropolis sweep followed by n_or over-relaxation sweeps and n_wolff Wolff updates) we record ten numbers per chain. With \(\Delta^x_r=\theta_{r+\hat x}-\theta_r\) and \(\Delta^y_r=\theta_{r+\hat y}-\theta_r\) the bond angles, these are the bond sums \[
\begin{aligned}
C_x&=\sum_r\cos\Delta^x_r,\quad C_y=\sum_r\cos\Delta^y_r,\\
S_x&=\sum_r\sin\Delta^x_r,\quad S_y=\sum_r\sin\Delta^y_r,\\
E&=-J(C_x+C_y),
\end{aligned}
\] together with the magnetisation \((m_x,m_y)\), the vortex density \(n_v\) (number of plaquettes with non-zero winding number per site, defined in Section 4), the Metropolis acceptance rate and the Wolff cluster size. The sums \(S_x,S_y\) enter the helicity modulus (Section 5).
The function simulate runs many independent chains at once, with jax.vmap over chains (each with its own \(\beta\) and random key), lax.scan over Monte Carlo steps and everything compiled by jax.jit. The input theta0 has shape (C, L, L), keys (C, 2), betas (C,), and the output time series has shape (C, n_meas, 10) and the stored snapshots (C, n_store, L, L), taken every n_meas // n_store steps.


Code
def vorticity(theta):
    # winding number of every plaquette (Section 4).  Plaquette (y, x) has corners (y,x) -> (y,x+1) -> (y+1,x+1) -> (y+1,x),
    # traversed counter-clockwise (x to the right, y upwards).  Output: int32 array (..., L, L) with values in {-1, 0, +1} (rarely +-2).
    t00 = theta
    t01 = jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1)                    # (y, x+1)
    t11 = jnp.roll(t01, -1, -2)                      # (y+1, x+1)
    t10 = jnp.roll(theta, -1, -2)                    # (y+1, x)
    circ = wrap(t01 - t00) + wrap(t11 - t01) + wrap(t10 - t11) + wrap(t00 - t10)
    return jnp.round(circ / TWO_PI).astype(jnp.int32)

OBS = ["E", "Cx", "Cy", "Sx", "Sy", "mx", "my", "nv", "acc", "cluster"]       # the ten recorded numbers

def measure(theta):
    dx, dy = bond_differences(theta)
    cx, cy = jnp.cos(dx).sum(), jnp.cos(dy).sum()
    sx, sy = jnp.sin(dx).sum(), jnp.sin(dy).sum()
    mx, my = magnetisation(theta)
    nv = (vorticity(theta) != 0).mean()
    return jnp.stack([-J * (cx + cy), cx, cy, sx, sy, mx, my, nv])

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_meas", "n_store", "n_wolff", "n_or"))
def simulate(theta0, keys, betas, delta, n_equil, n_meas, n_store, n_wolff, n_or):
    gap = n_meas // n_store
    def one_chain(theta, key, beta):
        def mc_step(carry, _):
            theta, key = carry
            key, k_m, k_w = jax.random.split(key, 3)
            theta, acc = metropolis_sweep(theta, k_m, beta, delta)
            for _ in range(n_or):                                           # n_or over-relaxation sweeps
                theta = overrelaxation_sweep(theta)
            size = 0.0
            for k in jax.random.split(k_w, max(n_wolff, 1))[:n_wolff]:     # n_wolff cluster updates (0 = Metropolis only)
                theta, size = wolff_update(theta, k, beta)
            return (theta, key), jnp.concatenate([measure(theta), jnp.stack([acc, size])])
        carry, _ = lax.scan(mc_step, (theta, key), None, length=n_equil)    # equilibration, measurements discarded
        def block(carry, _):
            carry, series = lax.scan(mc_step, carry, None, length=gap)
            return carry, (series, carry[0])
        carry, (series, snaps) = lax.scan(block, carry, None, length=n_store)
        return series.reshape(n_store * gap, len(OBS)), snaps, carry[0]
    return jax.vmap(one_chain)(theta0, keys, betas)

def run_chains(L, T_list, n_chains, n_equil, n_meas, n_store, n_wolff=0, n_or=0, delta=1.0, seed=0, start="ordered"):
    # n_chains independent chains for every temperature in T_list.
    # Returns series (nT, n_chains, n_meas, 10) and snapshots (nT, n_chains, n_store, L, L), as numpy arrays.
    T_list = np.asarray(T_list, np.float32)
    C = len(T_list) * n_chains
    betas = jnp.asarray(np.repeat(1.0 / T_list, n_chains))
    k_init, k_run = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed))
    if start == "ordered":
        theta0 = jnp.zeros((C, L, L))
    else:
        theta0 = jax.random.uniform(k_init, (C, L, L), maxval=TWO_PI)
    series, snaps, _ = simulate(theta0, jax.random.split(k_run, C), betas, delta, n_equil, n_meas, n_store, n_wolff, n_or)
    series = np.asarray(series).reshape(len(T_list), n_chains, n_meas, len(OBS))
    snaps = np.asarray(snaps).reshape(len(T_list), n_chains, n_store, L, L)
    return series, snaps




2.5 Low- and high-temperature limits
Before trusting the sampler we test it. There is no exact solution of the 2D XY model, but two limits are known well enough to test the code, and the three update schemes must agree with each other.
At low temperature, expanding \(\cos x\approx1-x^2/2\) (Section 3) gives a quadratic energy with \(N-1\) non-zero modes, each carrying \(T/2\) by equipartition, so \(e\approx-2J+\tfrac{T}{2}\,\tfrac{N-1}{N}\), with corrections of order \(T^2\). At high temperature the bonds become nearly independent, and for independent bonds \(\langle\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j)\rangle=\dfrac{\int_0^{2\pi}\cos x\,e^{\beta J\cos x}dx}{\int_0^{2\pi}e^{\beta J\cos x}dx}=\dfrac{I_1(\beta J)}{I_0(\beta J)}\), with \(I_n\) the modified Bessel functions. This is exact on a lattice without closed loops (for instance an open chain), and on the square lattice closed loops of bonds give corrections that become small at high \(T\). So \(e\approx-2J\,I_1(\beta J)/I_0(\beta J)\). Finally, Metropolis alone, Metropolis with over-relaxation and Metropolis with Wolff updates all sample the Boltzmann distribution, so at \(T=0.9\) they must give the same averages within errors.
The SymPy cell checks the Bessel-function ratio symbolically, as an expansion in \(\beta J\).

def jackknife(f, chain_means):
    # chain_means: (n_chains, k) per-chain averages;  f maps a (k,) vector of averages to an estimate.
    # Returns (estimate, jackknife error) using leave-one-chain-out averages.
    n = chain_means.shape[0]
    full = f(chain_means.mean(0))
    loo = (chain_means.sum(0)[None, :] - chain_means) / (n - 1)
    vals = np.array([f(v) for v in loo])
    return full, np.sqrt((n - 1) / n * ((vals - vals.mean(0)) ** 2).sum(0))

def helicity_from_means(v, beta, N):
    # v = per-chain or pooled averages of (C_x + C_y, S_x^2 + S_y^2);  Section 5 derives Upsilon = [<C> - beta <S^2>] / (2N)
    return (v[0] - beta * v[1]) / (2 * N)

def chain_moments(series):
    # series: (n_chains, n_meas, 10)  ->  per-chain means (n_chains, 9) of the quantities needed below
    E, Cx, Cy, Sx, Sy, mx, my, nv, acc = (series[..., k] for k in range(9))
    m2 = mx**2 + my**2
    cols = [E, E**2, Cx + Cy, Sx**2 + Sy**2, np.sqrt(m2), m2, m2**2, nv, acc]
    return np.stack([c.mean(-1) for c in cols], -1)

2.6 Autocorrelation times and cost
The three schemes agree within the errors in \(e\), \(\Upsilon\) and \(\langle\boldsymbol m^2\rangle\), so they differ only in efficiency, which we measure next. Consecutive Monte Carlo configurations are correlated. For an observable \(A\) with time series \(A_t\), the normalised autocorrelation function and the integrated autocorrelation time are \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho(t)&=\frac{\langle A_sA_{s+t}\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2}{\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2},\\
\tau_{\rm int}&=\frac12+\sum_{t=1}^{W}\rho(t),
\end{aligned}
\] where the window \(W\) is the first \(t\) with \(t\ge6\,\tau_{\rm int}(t)\), a self-consistent cut-off that stops the sum before it collects mostly noise. A run of \(n\) steps contains about \(n/(2\tau_{\rm int})\) independent measurements. We measure \(\tau_{\rm int}\) of \(|\boldsymbol m|^2\), a slowly varying observable, at \(T=0.9\approx T_{\rm BKT}\) for \(L=16\) and \(L=32\), and compare it with the CPU time of one step. The figure of merit is the CPU time per independent sample, \(2\tau_{\rm int}\times\)(time per step).


Code
def tau_int(series):
    # series: (n_chains, n_t).  Autocorrelation averaged over chains, then the self-consistent window.
    a = series - series.mean()
    n_t = a.shape[1]
    f = np.fft.rfft(a, 2 * n_t, axis=1)
    acf = np.fft.irfft(f * np.conj(f), axis=1)[:, :n_t].mean(0)
    rho = acf / acf[0]
    tau = 0.5
    for t in range(1, n_t):
        tau += rho[t]
        if t >= 6 * tau:
            break
    return tau, rho

With Metropolis alone \(\tau_{\rm int}\) grows from \(38.5\) to \(113\) steps when \(L\) doubles from 16 to 32, a factor of \(2.9\) and an example of critical slowing down. def thermodynamics(d):
    L = int(d["L"]); N = L * L
    out = {k: np.zeros((len(d["T"]), 2)) for k in ["u", "c", "ups", "absm", "m2", "nv"]}
    for i, T in enumerate(d["T"]):
        cm = d["chain_moments"][i]
        beta = 1.0 / T
        out["u"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: v[0] / N, cm)
        out["c"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: beta**2 * (v[1] - v[0] ** 2) / N, cm)
        out["ups"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: helicity_from_means(v[[2, 3]], beta, N), cm)
        out["absm"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: v[4], cm)
        out["m2"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: v[5], cm)
        out["nv"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: v[7], cm)
    return out

title: Lab 030: Physics of the 2D XY model and the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
section: 3. Spin waves and the Mermin–Wagner theorem
text:
3. Spin waves and the Mermin–Wagner theorem
With the data in hand we turn to theory, starting at low temperature, where neighbouring spins are almost parallel and the cosine can be expanded. The result is a Gaussian (quadratic) theory that can be solved exactly, and it already shows the central fact of two dimensions. The angle fluctuations grow logarithmically with the system size, and the magnetisation goes to zero as a power of \(L\).

3.1 Gaussian approximation
Expand each bond to second order, \(\cos x=1-\tfrac{x^2}{2}+O(x^4)\), and treat \(\theta_i\) as a real variable, ignoring its \(2\pi\) periodicity and therefore the vortices of Section 4, \[
H\approx E_0+\frac J2\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}(\theta_i-\theta_j)^2 .
\] On the torus we use Fourier modes \(\theta_{\boldsymbol r}=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{\boldsymbol k}\tilde\theta_{\boldsymbol k}\,e^{i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r}\) with \(\boldsymbol k=\frac{2\pi}{L}(n_x,n_y)\), \(n_{x,y}=0,\dots,L-1\). A difference along \(x\) becomes multiplication by \(e^{ik_x}-1\), and \(|e^{ik_x}-1|^2=2-2\cos k_x\), so \[
\begin{aligned}
H&\approx E_0+\frac J2\sum_{\boldsymbol k}\lambda_{\boldsymbol k}\,|\tilde\theta_{\boldsymbol k}|^2,\\
\lambda_{\boldsymbol k}&=4-2\cos k_x-2\cos k_y\;\xrightarrow{\;k\to0\;}\;k^2 .
\end{aligned}
\] The modes decouple, each is a Gaussian variable, and equipartition gives \[
\langle|\tilde\theta_{\boldsymbol k}|^2\rangle=\frac{T}{J\lambda_{\boldsymbol k}}\qquad(\boldsymbol k\neq0).
\] The mode \(\boldsymbol k=0\) is the global rotation. It costs no energy and does not affect \(|\boldsymbol m|\).
SymPy confirms the three ingredients used here, the expansion of the cosine, the small-\(k\) form of \(\lambda_{\boldsymbol k}\), and the identity \(|e^{ik}-1|^2=2-2\cos k\).


Code
xs, kx, ky = sp.symbols("x k_x k_y", real=True)
print("cos x            =", sp.series(sp.cos(xs), xs, 0, 6))
lam = 4 - 2 * sp.cos(kx) - 2 * sp.cos(ky)
print("lambda_k         =", sp.series(sp.series(lam, kx, 0, 5).removeO(), ky, 0, 5).removeO(), "+ O(k^6)")
print("|e^{ik} - 1|^2   =", sp.simplify(sp.expand_complex((sp.exp(sp.I * kx) - 1) * (sp.exp(-sp.I * kx) - 1))))


cos x            = 1 - x**2/2 + x**4/24 + O(x**6)
lambda_k         = -k_x**4/12 + k_x**2 - k_y**4/12 + k_y**2 + O(k^6)


|e^{ik} - 1|^2   = 2 - 2*cos(k_x)




3.2 Angle fluctuations
Let \(\phi_i=\theta_i-\bar\theta\) be the angle measured from the mean direction (\(\bar\theta\) is the \(\boldsymbol k=0\) part). Then \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle\phi_i^2\rangle&=\frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol k\neq0}\langle|\tilde\theta_{\boldsymbol k}|^2\rangle=\frac TJ\,G_L,\\
G_L&=\frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol k\ne0}\frac1{\lambda_{\boldsymbol k}} .
\end{aligned}
\] For large \(L\) the sum becomes an integral, \(\frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol k}\to\int\frac{d^2k}{(2\pi)^2}\), cut off at small \(k\) by the system size, \(k_{\min}\approx2\pi/L\), and at large \(k\) by the lattice, \(k_{\max}\approx\pi/a\). In two dimensions \(d^2k=2\pi k\,dk\), and \[
\begin{aligned}
G_L&\approx\int_{2\pi/L}^{\pi}\frac{2\pi k\,dk}{(2\pi)^2\,k^2}=\frac1{2\pi}\ln\frac{L}{2a}\\
\Longrightarrow\quad\langle\phi^2\rangle&\simeq\frac{T}{2\pi J}\ln L+\text{const}.
\end{aligned}
\] The fluctuations diverge with the system size, however small \(T\) is. In three dimensions \(d^3k=4\pi k^2dk\) cancels the \(1/k^2\), the integral converges, and \(\langle\phi^2\rangle\) stays finite (Exercise 2).
The cell below evaluates the continuum integral with SymPy and then computes the exact lattice sum \(G_L\) for \(L=8,\dots,512\). If the continuum argument holds, the slope of \(G_L\) against \(\ln L\) approaches \(1/(2\pi)\).


Code
k, Lsym, a = sp.symbols("k L a", positive=True)
G_cont = sp.integrate(2 * sp.pi * k / ((2 * sp.pi) ** 2 * k**2), (k, 2 * sp.pi / Lsym, sp.pi / a))
print("continuum G_L      =", sp.expand_log(G_cont, force=True))
print("d G_L / d ln L     =", sp.simplify(sp.diff(G_cont, Lsym) * Lsym), " = ", float(1 / (2 * sp.pi)))

def lattice_G(L, d=2):
    # G_L = (1/N) sum_{k != 0} 1 / lambda_k on an L^d torus, lambda_k = sum_mu (2 - 2 cos k_mu)
    kk = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(L) / L
    grids = np.meshgrid(*([kk] * d), indexing="ij")
    lam = sum(2 - 2 * np.cos(g) for g in grids)
    lam.flat[0] = np.inf                                   # drop the k = 0 mode
    return (1 / lam).sum() / L**d

Ls = np.array([8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512])
GL = np.array([lattice_G(L) for L in Ls])
print("\n   L      G_L      slope dG_L/d ln L between consecutive sizes")
for i, L in enumerate(Ls):
    sl = "" if i == 0 else f"{(GL[i] - GL[i-1]) / np.log(Ls[i] / Ls[i-1]):.5f}"
    print(f"{L:5d}  {GL[i]:.5f}   {sl}")
print(f"1/(2 pi) = {1 / (2 * np.pi):.5f}")


continuum G_L      = (-log(a) + log(pi))/(2*pi) - (-log(L) + log(2) + log(pi))/(2*pi)
d G_L / d ln L     = 1/(2*pi)  =  0.15915494309189535

3.3 Finite-size magnetisation
The slope converges to \(1/(2\pi)\) to five digits, which confirms the logarithmic growth. Its consequence for the magnetisation follows quickly.
For a Gaussian variable \(\phi\) with variance \(\sigma^2\), \(\langle\cos\phi\rangle=e^{-\sigma^2/2}\) (symbolic check below). To leading order \(|\boldsymbol m|\approx\frac1N\sum_i\cos\phi_i\), so \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle&\approx\exp\!\Big(-\frac{T}{2J}\,G_L\Big)\\
&\propto\;L^{-T/(4\pi J)}\;\xrightarrow{\;L\to\infty\;}\;0 .
\end{aligned}
\] This is the spin-wave version of the

Mermin–Wagner theorem (Mermin and Wagner, 1966). At any \(T>0\), a one- or two-dimensional isotropic Heisenberg model with finite-range interactions has no spontaneous (anti)ferromagnetic order.

The rigorous proof uses the Bogoliubov inequality, and its physical content is the logarithmic divergence of \(\int d^2k/k^2\) that we just computed. The decay is a power law with a small exponent (\(T/(4\pi J)=0.024\) at \(T=0.3\)), so on any lattice that fits into a computer, or a laboratory sample, \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) is large at low \(T\). It is a finite-size effect nevertheless.


Code
phi, sig = sp.symbols("phi sigma", positive=True)
gauss = sp.exp(-phi**2 / (2 * sig**2)) / sp.sqrt(2 * sp.pi * sig**2)
print("<cos phi> for a Gaussian of variance sigma^2 =", sp.simplify(sp.integrate(sp.cos(phi) * gauss, (phi, -sp.oo, sp.oo))))


<cos phi> for a Gaussian of variance sigma^2 = exp(-sigma**2/2)


We test this prediction with Monte Carlo. At \(T=0.3\) we simulate \(L=8,16,32,64,128\) and compare \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) with the parameter-free spin-wave prediction \(\exp(-\tfrac{T}{2J}G_L)\) computed from the exact lattice sum. We then fit \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\propto L^{-x}\) and compare the exponent with \(T/(4\pi J)\).
The leading anharmonic correction is a renormalisation of the stiffness, \(J\to J_{\rm eff}\approx J-T/4\) at low \(T\) (Section 5.2 derives this for the helicity modulus), which predicts a slightly larger exponent \(T/(4\pi J_{\rm eff})\), and the cell prints both predictions.


Code
T_MW = 0.3
L_MW = [8, 16, 32, 64, 128]
t0 = time.time()
mw = []
for L in L_MW:
    ser, _ = run_chains(L, [T_MW], n_chains=16, n_equil=1000, n_meas=1000, n_store=1, n_or=1, seed=10 + L)
    absm = np.hypot(ser[0, :, :, 5], ser[0, :, :, 6]).mean(1)              # per-chain <|m|>
    mw.append((absm.mean(), absm.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(absm))))
mw = np.array(mw)
print(f"(Monte Carlo at T = {T_MW}: {time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")
sw = np.exp(-T_MW / (2 * J) * np.array([lattice_G(L) for L in L_MW]))
for L, (m, dm), s in zip(L_MW, mw, sw):
    print(f"L = {L:3d}:  <|m|>_MC = {m:.5f} +- {dm:.5f}   spin waves exp(-T G_L / 2J) = {s:.5f}   ratio = {m / s:.4f}")
x_fit, _ = np.polyfit(np.log(L_MW), np.log(mw[:, 0]), 1)
print(f"fitted exponent  x = {-x_fit:.4f}   spin waves T/(4 pi J) = {T_MW / (4 * np.pi * J):.4f}   "
      f"with J_eff = J - T/4: {T_MW / (4 * np.pi * (J - T_MW / 4)):.4f}")
print(f"factor in L that halves <|m|>:  2^(1/x) = {2 ** (1 / -x_fit):.1e}")
NUMBERS.update(mw_T=T_MW, mw_exponent_fit=round(-x_fit, 4), mw_exponent_sw=round(T_MW / (4 * np.pi), 4))

The figure compares the Monte Carlo values of \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) with the spin-wave prediction as functions of \(L\). The ratios in the printout lie between \(0.988\) and \(0.995\), so the Gaussian theory predicts the magnetisation of the finite lattice to about 1% with no free parameter at \(T=0.3\). The small deviation grows slowly with \(L\), and the fitted exponent \(x=0.0261\) is close to \(T/(4\pi J_{\rm eff})=0.0258\). The magnetisation decreases with \(L\) as a power law, so it is zero for \(L\to\infty\) (Mermin–Wagner), but so slowly that halving \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) requires multiplying \(L\) by \(2^{1/x}\approx3.5\times10^{11}\).


3.4 Spin-wave correlation function
The same calculation gives the spin–spin correlation function at distance \(r\), \[
\begin{aligned}
G(r)&=\langle\cos(\theta_0-\theta_{\boldsymbol r})\rangle=\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12\langle(\theta_0-\theta_{\boldsymbol r})^2\rangle\Big),\\
\langle(\theta_0-\theta_{\boldsymbol r})^2\rangle&=\frac TJ\,D(\boldsymbol r),\\
D(\boldsymbol r)&=\frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol k}\frac{2-2\cos(\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r)}{\lambda_{\boldsymbol k}} .
\end{aligned}
\] For \(1\ll r\ll L\), \(D(r)\approx\frac1\pi\ln r+\text{const}\) (the lattice sum below shows this), hence \[
G(r)\propto r^{-\eta},\qquad \eta=\frac{T}{2\pi J}.
\] A power law decays more slowly than any exponential and still goes to zero, and this behaviour is called quasi-long-range order. The exponent \(\eta\) depends continuously on \(T\), so the whole low-temperature phase is a line of critical points.


Code
L_big = 1024
kk = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(L_big) / L_big
KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kk, kk, indexing="ij")
lam_big = 4 - 2 * np.cos(KX) - 2 * np.cos(KY); lam_big[0, 0] = np.inf
r_list = np.array([2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
D = np.array([((2 - 2 * np.cos(KX * r)) / lam_big).sum() / L_big**2 for r in r_list])     # separation r along x
print(f"lattice sum D(r) on a {L_big} x {L_big} torus")
for i in range(1, len(r_list)):
    print(f"r = {r_list[i-1]:2d} -> {r_list[i]:2d}:  slope dD/d ln r = {(D[i] - D[i-1]) / np.log(2):.5f}")
print(f"1/pi = {1 / np.pi:.5f}")

title: Lab 030: Physics of the 2D XY model and the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
text:
4. Vortices
The slopes of the lattice sum come close to \(1/\pi\approx0.318\), which completes the spin-wave picture. The Gaussian theory has treated \(\theta\) as a real number. Since \(\theta\) is an angle, going around a closed loop it may return to its starting value plus a multiple of \(2\pi\). Such configurations cannot be removed by any small deformation. They are topological defects, the Gaussian theory misses them entirely, and they drive the BKT transition.

4.1 Winding number
For a closed loop \(\mathcal C\) around a point, the winding number (vorticity) is \[
w=\frac1{2\pi}\oint_{\mathcal C}\nabla\theta\cdot d\boldsymbol l\;\in\;\mathbb Z .
\] A vortex is \(\theta(\boldsymbol r)=\arctan(y/x)\) (the polar angle, atan2(y, x)), with \(w=+1\), and an antivortex \(\theta=-\arctan(y/x)\) has \(w=-1\). On the lattice the smallest loop is a plaquette. We label each plaquette by the site \(r\) at its lower-left corner and map the bond angle differences to \([-\pi,\pi)\) (the shortest rotation between two neighbours), \[
\begin{aligned}
w_r&=\frac1{2\pi}\Big([\theta_2-\theta_1]+[\theta_3-\theta_2]+[\theta_4-\theta_3]+[\theta_1-\theta_4]\Big),\\
[x]&=x \text{ mapped to }[-\pi,\pi),
\end{aligned}
\] for the corners \(1\to2\to3\to4\) traversed counter-clockwise. Without the brackets the sum would be \(0\), and with them it is \(2\pi\) times an integer. Each bracket lies in \([-\pi,\pi)\), so the sum lies in \([-4\pi,4\pi)\) and \(w_r\in\{-2,-1,0,1\}\). The value \(-2\) requires all four brackets to equal \(-\pi\), which has probability zero, so in practice \(w_r\in\{-1,0,1\}\).
The sketch below draws the two elementary defects on a \(6\times6\) patch, with the core at the centre of a plaquette. Following the spins once counter-clockwise around the dashed contour \(\mathcal C\), the arrow turns once counter-clockwise around a vortex (\(w=+1\)) and once clockwise around an antivortex (\(w=-1\)). No smooth deformation of the angles can change these integers, and a vortex disappears only by meeting an antivortex.


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;
#   satisfied bond: solid blue line, broken (frustrated) bond: dashed purple line marked with a cross.
# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (5.5 in = full text width) with 10-12 pt text,
# and shown here at a higher screen resolution.
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

NAVY, ORANGE, BLUE, GRAY, PURPLE, GREEN = "#002B5C", "#D35A05", "#005CA7", "#5A6270", "#AA3377", "#228833"
SKETCH_STYLE = {"font.size": 11, "axes.titlesize": 12, "axes.labelsize": 11, "xtick.labelsize": 10,
                "ytick.labelsize": 10, "legend.fontsize": 10, "figure.dpi": 130, "lines.linewidth": 1.5,
                "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}

def save_sketch(fig, name, extra_dirs=()):
    # PNG copy for the lecture slides: white background, 300 dpi, included at its physical width
    os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
    for d in ("figures",) + tuple(d for d in extra_dirs if os.path.isdir(d)):
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, name), dpi=300, facecolor="white")

def draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.75, color=NAVY, lw=1.3, head=7, dot=True):
    # planar spins: an arrow of fixed length centred on every lattice site (x, y), angle theta[y, x]
    for (y, x), t in np.ndenumerate(theta):
        dx, dy = 0.5 * length * np.cos(t), 0.5 * length * np.sin(t)
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x + dx, y + dy), xytext=(x - dx, y - dy),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=lw, mutation_scale=head, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
        if dot:
            ax.plot(x, y, "o", color=GRAY, ms=1.5, zorder=1)

def plaquette_winding(theta):
    # winding number of every plaquette (lower-left corner (x, y)), corners traversed counter-clockwise
    wrap = lambda a: (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi           # angle difference mapped to [-pi, pi)
    t1, t2 = theta[:-1, :-1], theta[:-1, 1:]                       # (x, y), (x+1, y)
    t3, t4 = theta[1:, 1:], theta[1:, :-1]                         # (x+1, y+1), (x, y+1)
    return np.rint((wrap(t2 - t1) + wrap(t3 - t2) + wrap(t4 - t3) + wrap(t1 - t4)) / (2 * np.pi)).astype(int)

def draw_vortex_marks(ax, w, r=0.3):
    # vortex (w = +1): navy disc with "+";  antivortex (w = -1): white disc with orange rim and "-"
    for (y, x), v in np.ndenumerate(w):
        if v != 0:
            face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if v > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
            ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x + 0.5, y + 0.5), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=1.3, zorder=6, alpha=0.9))
            ax.text(x + 0.5, y + 0.5, "+" if v > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=7)

def sketch_vortex_antivortex():
    L = 6
    y, x = np.indices((L, L)).astype(float)
    core = (2.5, 2.5)                                               # the core sits at the centre of a plaquette
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 2.9))
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, bottom=0.13, top=0.9, wspace=0.08)
    for ax, n, name in [(axes[0], +1, "vortex"), (axes[1], -1, "antivortex")]:
        theta = n * np.arctan2(y - core[1], x - core[0])            # theta = +-(polar angle around the core)
        for k in range(L):
            ax.plot([0, L - 1], [k, k], color=GRAY, lw=0.6, alpha=0.3); ax.plot([k, k], [0, L - 1], color=GRAY, lw=0.6, alpha=0.3)
        draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.62, lw=1.3, head=7)
        # the closed contour C around the core, traversed counter-clockwise
        phi = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200); R = 1.95
        ax.plot(core[0] + R * np.cos(phi), core[1] + R * np.sin(phi), color=ORANGE, lw=1.4, ls="--")
        ax.annotate("", xy=(core[0] + R * np.cos(1.85), core[1] + R * np.sin(1.85)),
                    xytext=(core[0] + R * np.cos(1.5), core[1] + R * np.sin(1.5)),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=ORANGE, lw=1.4, mutation_scale=12))
        ax.text(core[0] + R * 0.72 + 0.1, core[1] + R * 0.72 + 0.1, r"$\mathcal{C}$", fontsize=12, color=ORANGE)
        ax.plot(*core, "o", ms=6, color=NAVY if n > 0 else "white", mec=NAVY if n > 0 else ORANGE, mew=1.4, zorder=6)
        ax.set_title(f"{name}: $w={n:+d}$", fontsize=12, color=NAVY)
        ax.set_xlim(-0.5, L - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.5, L - 0.5); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    fig.text(0.5, 0.04, r"$w=\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint_{\mathcal{C}}\nabla\theta\cdot d\mathbf{l}$ = number of turns of the spins along $\mathcal{C}$",
             ha="center", fontsize=10, color=GRAY)
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_vortex_antivortex()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_xy_vortices.png")
plt.show()





SymPy evaluates the contour integral for \(\theta=n\,\mathrm{atan2}(y,x)\) on a circle of radius \(R\), and also gives \(|\nabla\theta|^2\), which we need for the vortex energy.


Code
X, Y, R, t = sp.symbols("x y R t", real=True)
n = sp.symbols("n", integer=True)
theta_v = n * sp.atan2(Y, X)
grad = [sp.simplify(sp.diff(theta_v, X)), sp.simplify(sp.diff(theta_v, Y))]
print("grad theta =", grad)
on_circle = {X: R * sp.cos(t), Y: R * sp.sin(t)}
integrand = sp.simplify((grad[0] * sp.diff(R * sp.cos(t), t) + grad[1] * sp.diff(R * sp.sin(t), t)).subs(on_circle))
print("grad theta . dl/dt on the circle =", integrand)
print("winding number w = (1/2 pi) * contour integral =", sp.integrate(integrand, (t, 0, 2 * sp.pi)) / (2 * sp.pi))
print("|grad theta|^2 =", sp.simplify(grad[0] ** 2 + grad[1] ** 2), "  (= n^2 / r^2)")


grad theta = [-n*y/(x**2 + y**2), n*x/(x**2 + y**2)]
grad theta . dl/dt on the circle = n
winding number w = (1/2 pi) * contour integral = n
|grad theta|^2 = n**2/(x**2 + y**2)   (= n^2 / r^2)


On the lattice we compute the winding numbers of a vortex, an antivortex and a vortex–antivortex pair. Two general properties of vorticity are tested as well. On a torus the total winding number of any configuration is \(0\), because every bond is shared by two plaquettes and enters them with opposite signs, and a smooth configuration (here a spin wave) has no vortices.


Code
Lv = 12
yy, xx = np.meshgrid(np.arange(Lv), np.arange(Lv), indexing="ij")          # yy = row index (y), xx = column index (x)
def vortex_field(x0, y0, w=1):
    # angle of a vortex (w = +1) or antivortex (w = -1) centred at the plaquette centre (x0, y0)
    return w * np.arctan2(yy - y0, xx - x0)
configs = {"vortex": vortex_field(5.5, 5.5, +1),
           "antivortex": vortex_field(5.5, 5.5, -1),

for name, th in configs.items():

4.2 Vortex energy
Far from its core a vortex is a smooth configuration, so the Gaussian (continuum) energy \(E-E_0=\frac J2\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2\) applies. With \(|\nabla\theta|^2=1/r^2\) (SymPy above, \(n=1\)) and the integral running from the core radius \(a\) (the lattice spacing) to the system size \(R\approx L\), \[
E_v=\frac J2\int_a^{R}\frac{1}{r^2}\,2\pi r\,dr+E_{\rm core}=\pi J\ln\frac{R}{a}+E_{\rm core}.
\] A single vortex costs an energy that diverges logarithmically with the system size. A vortex–antivortex pair at distance \(d\) behaves differently. Far away (\(r\gg d\)) the two windings cancel, \(\nabla\theta\) decays as \(d/r^2\), the integral converges, and \[
E_{\rm pair}(d)\approx2\pi J\ln\frac da+2E_{\rm core},
\] independent of \(L\). Pairs are cheap, and single vortices are expensive.


Code
r_, a_, R_, Jsym, Tsym = sp.symbols("r a R J T", positive=True)
E_vortex = sp.integrate(Jsym / 2 * (1 / r_**2) * 2 * sp.pi * r_, (r_, a_, R_))
print("E_vortex - E_core =", sp.expand_log(E_vortex, force=True), "  = pi J ln(R/a)")


E_vortex - E_core = pi*J*log(R) - pi*J*log(a)   = pi J ln(R/a)


We check both results on the lattice. We build the vortex atan2 on an \(L\times L\) lattice with open boundaries (only the bonds inside the square count), centred in the middle plaquette, and compute \(E_v(L)-E_0(L)\) for \(L=8,\dots,512\). The slope against \(\ln L\) should approach \(\pi J\). The atan2 field is the continuum solution, and to get the true lattice minimum we also relax the interior with gradient descent (jax.grad of the lattice energy) while keeping the boundary spins fixed, so that the vortex cannot leave. For the pair we place a vortex and an antivortex at distance \(d\) in the middle of a \(512\times512\) lattice and check the slope \(2\pi J\).


Code
def open_energy(theta):
    # energy of an L x L patch with open boundaries: only bonds inside the patch
    return -J * (jnp.cos(theta[:, 1:] - theta[:, :-1]).sum() + jnp.cos(theta[1:, :] - theta[:-1, :]).sum())

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_steps",))
def relax_interior(theta, n_steps, lr=0.2):
    # gradient descent on the interior spins; boundary spins stay fixed
    mask = jnp.zeros_like(theta).at[1:-1, 1:-1].set(1.0)
    g = jax.grad(open_energy)
    return lax.fori_loop(0, n_steps, lambda i, th: th - lr * mask * g(th), theta)

Lv_list = [8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]
Ev, Ev_relax = [], []
for L in Lv_list:
    yy_, xx_ = np.meshgrid(np.arange(L), np.arange(L), indexing="ij")
    th = jnp.asarray(np.arctan2(yy_ - (L - 1) / 2, xx_ - (L - 1) / 2))
    E0 = -J * 2 * L * (L - 1)                                               # all spins parallel, 2L(L-1) bonds
    Ev.append(float(open_energy(th)) - E0)
    Ev_relax.append(float(open_energy(relax_interior(th, 3000))) - E0)
Ev, Ev_relax = np.array(Ev), np.array(Ev_relax)
print("   L    E_v - E_0 (atan2)   relaxed     slope vs ln L (atan2, relaxed)")
for i, L in enumerate(Lv_list):
    s = "" if i == 0 else f"{(Ev[i] - Ev[i-1]) / np.log(2):.4f}, {(Ev_relax[i] - Ev_relax[i-1]) / np.log(2):.4f}"
    print(f"{L:4d}   {Ev[i]:10.4f}        {Ev_relax[i]:10.4f}    {s}")
print(f"pi J = {np.pi * J:.4f}")

Lp = 512
yy_, xx_ = np.meshgrid(np.arange(Lp), np.arange(Lp), indexing="ij")
c0 = (Lp - 1) / 2
d_list = np.array([2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
Epair = np.array([float(open_energy(jnp.asarray(np.arctan2(yy_ - c0, xx_ - (c0 - d / 2)) - np.arctan2(yy_ - c0, xx_ - (c0 + d / 2)))))
                  + J * 2 * Lp * (Lp - 1) for d in d_list])
for i in range(1, len(d_list)):
    print(f"pair distance d = {d_list[i-1]:2d} -> {d_list[i]:2d}:  slope dE_pair/d ln d = {(Epair[i] - Epair[i-1]) / np.log(2):.4f}")
print(f"2 pi J = {2 * np.pi * J:.4f}")
NUMBERS.update(vortex_slope_relaxed=round((Ev_relax[-1] - Ev_relax[-2]) / np.log(2), 4))

The single-vortex slope stays between \(3.13\) and \(3.19\), close to \(\pi J=3.14\), for both the atan2 field and the relaxed lattice configuration. The pair slope is close to \(2\pi J\) for intermediate distances (\(6.40\) to \(6.31\) for \(d\) from 8 to 32). At the smallest \(d\) the cores overlap, and at the largest \(d\) the finite \(512\times512\) patch lowers the slope.


4.3 Kosterlitz–Thouless free-energy argument
The energy alone would forbid single vortices, but the entropy also grows with the system size. The vortex core can sit on any of the \(\approx(L/a)^2\) plaquettes, so its entropy is \(S_v=\ln(L/a)^2=2\ln(L/a)\), and the free energy of one free vortex is (Kosterlitz and Thouless, 1973) \[
F_v=E_v-TS_v=(\pi J-2T)\ln\frac La+\dots
\] For \(T<\pi J/2\) the coefficient is positive and \(F_v\to+\infty\) as \(L\to\infty\), so free vortices are suppressed and only bound pairs (finite energy) appear. For \(T>\pi J/2\), \(F_v\to-\infty\) and free vortices proliferate. The estimate of the transition temperature is \[
T_{\rm KT}^{\rm (estimate)}=\frac{\pi J}{2}\approx1.571\,J .
\]


Code
F_v = (sp.pi * Jsym - 2 * Tsym) * sp.log(sp.Symbol("L", positive=True) / a_)
print("F_v =", F_v)
T_est = sp.solve(sp.Eq(sp.pi * Jsym - 2 * Tsym, 0), Tsym)[0]
print("coefficient of ln(L/a) vanishes at T =", T_est, "=", float(T_est.subs(Jsym, 1)), "J")
print(f"literature value T_BKT = {T_BKT_LIT:.4f} J;  ratio estimate / literature = {np.pi / 2 / T_BKT_LIT:.3f}")


F_v = (pi*J - 2*T)*log(L/a)
coefficient of ln(L/a) vanishes at T = pi*J/2 = 1.5707963267948966 J
literature value T_BKT = 0.8929 J;  ratio estimate / literature = 1.759


The estimate is too high by about 76% (the ratio \(1.759\) printed above). Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the system is full of thermally excited bound pairs, which act like a polarisable medium (an analogy with dipoles in a dielectric) and screen the interaction, so that a free vortex costs \(\pi\Upsilon\ln(L/a)\) with a reduced, renormalised stiffness \(\Upsilon<J\) (defined in Section 5) in place of \(\pi J\ln(L/a)\). Replacing \(J\) by \(\Upsilon\) in the argument gives the self-consistency condition \(\Upsilon(T_{\rm BKT})=2T_{\rm BKT}/\pi\), the Nelson–Kosterlitz universal jump of Section 5, derived with the renormalisation group by Kosterlitz (1974) and Nelson and Kosterlitz (1977).
The sketch below contrasts the two situations of the argument. On the left, a vortex and an antivortex sit two lattice spacings apart. Far from the pair their windings cancel and the spins are almost parallel, so the pair costs a finite energy and occurs at low temperature. On the right, vortices and antivortices are far apart from each other. Each twists the spins over a large region, and such free vortices appear only above the transition, where their entropy wins. The discs mark the plaquettes with winding number \(w_r=+1\) (navy, “+”) and \(w_r=-1\) (white with an orange rim, “−”), computed from the arrows with the formula of Section 4.1. The sketches follow the course convention, and the snapshot figure below uses its own markers.


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;
#   satisfied bond: solid blue line, broken (frustrated) bond: dashed purple line marked with a cross.

# and shown here at a higher screen resolution.
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

NAVY, ORANGE, BLUE, GRAY, PURPLE, GREEN = "#002B5C", "#D35A05", "#005CA7", "#5A6270", "#AA3377", "#228833"
SKETCH_STYLE = {"font.size": 11, "axes.titlesize": 12, "axes.labelsize": 11, "xtick.labelsize": 10,
                "ytick.labelsize": 10, "legend.fontsize": 10, "figure.dpi": 130, "lines.linewidth": 1.5,
                "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}

def save_sketch(fig, name, extra_dirs=()):
    # PNG copy for the lecture slides: white background, 300 dpi, included at its physical width
    os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
    for d in ("figures",) + tuple(d for d in extra_dirs if os.path.isdir(d)):
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, name), dpi=300, facecolor="white")

def draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.75, color=NAVY, lw=1.3, head=7, dot=True):
    # planar spins: an arrow of fixed length centred on every lattice site (x, y), angle theta[y, x]
    for (y, x), t in np.ndenumerate(theta):
        dx, dy = 0.5 * length * np.cos(t), 0.5 * length * np.sin(t)
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x + dx, y + dy), xytext=(x - dx, y - dy),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=lw, mutation_scale=head, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
        if dot:
            ax.plot(x, y, "o", color=GRAY, ms=1.5, zorder=1)

def plaquette_winding(theta):
    # winding number of every plaquette (lower-left corner (x, y)), corners traversed counter-clockwise
    wrap = lambda a: (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi           # angle difference mapped to [-pi, pi)
    t1, t2 = theta[:-1, :-1], theta[:-1, 1:]                       # (x, y), (x+1, y)
    t3, t4 = theta[1:, 1:], theta[1:, :-1]                         # (x+1, y+1), (x, y+1)
    return np.rint((wrap(t2 - t1) + wrap(t3 - t2) + wrap(t4 - t3) + wrap(t1 - t4)) / (2 * np.pi)).astype(int)

def draw_vortex_marks(ax, w, r=0.3):
    # vortex (w = +1): navy disc with "+";  antivortex (w = -1): white disc with orange rim and "-"
    for (y, x), v in np.ndenumerate(w):
        if v != 0:
            face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if v > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
            ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x + 0.5, y + 0.5), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=1.3, zorder=6, alpha=0.9))
            ax.text(x + 0.5, y + 0.5, "+" if v > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=7)

def sketch_bound_and_free_vortices():
    L = 8
    y, x = np.indices((L, L)).astype(float)
    def field(defects):
        # superposition of vortices (q = +1) and antivortices (q = -1) at plaquette centres (cx, cy)
        return sum(q * np.arctan2(y - cy, x - cx) for (cx, cy, q) in defects)
    panels = [([(2.5, 3.5, +1), (4.5, 3.5, -1)], "bound pair\nlow $T$"),
              ([(1.5, 5.5, +1), (4.5, 6.5, -1), (6.5, 4.5, +1), (3.5, 3.5, -1), (1.5, 1.5, +1), (5.5, 1.5, -1)],
               "free vortices\nhigh $T$")]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(2.585, 1.66))           # physical size on the slide (0.47 text width)
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, bottom=0.006, top=0.76, wspace=0.08)
    for ax, (defects, title) in zip(axes, panels):
        theta = field(defects)
        draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.66, lw=0.8, head=4, dot=False)
        draw_vortex_marks(ax, plaquette_winding(theta), r=0.45)      # winding numbers computed on every plaquette
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11, color=NAVY)
        ax.set_xlim(-0.5, L - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.5, L - 0.5); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_bound_and_free_vortices()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_xy_vortex_pairs.png")
plt.show()







4.4 Vortices in Monte Carlo snapshots
To see the defects we look at snapshots from the data set (\(L=48\)) at three temperatures, below, near and above \(T_{\rm BKT}\). In the figure the colour is the angle \(\theta\) (cyclic colour map), orange circles are vortices and navy squares antivortices.


Code
L = 48
T_show = [0.80, 0.90, 1.20]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4.2))
for ax, T in zip(axes, T_show):

At \(T=0.80\) each of the three vortices sits on a plaquette next to an antivortex. At \(T=0.90\approx T_{\rm BKT}\) there are more defects, still in tightly bound vortex–antivortex pairs. At \(T=1.20\) the defects are numerous, many of them have no partner on a neighbouring plaquette, and the angle field is disordered.
To quantify this we measure the vortex density \(n_v\), the number of plaquettes with \(w_r\neq0\) per site, averaged over all measurement steps. At low \(T\) bound pairs are thermally activated, \(n_v\propto e^{-E_a/T}\), with an activation energy \(E_a\) that we fit on the low-temperature part (\(T\le0.75\), \(L=48\)). The figure shows \(\langle n_v\rangle\) against \(T\) (left) and on a logarithmic scale against \(1/T\) with the fit (right), for the three sizes.

The vortex density is essentially independent of \(L\) (\(0.0083\), \(0.0091\) and \(0.0090\) at \(T=0.90\) for \(L=16\), 32 and 48) and smooth in \(T\). It rises steeply around and above \(T_{\rm BKT}\) but shows no feature at \(T_{\rm BKT}\) itself. The density counts bound pairs and free vortices alike, while the transition concerns whether they are bound, which a density cannot tell. This matters for Section 8. title: Lab 030: Physics of the 2D XY model and the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
text:
5. Helicity modulus (spin stiffness)
Neither \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) (zero for \(L\to\infty\)) nor the vortex density (smooth) distinguishes the two phases. The quantity that does is the response to a twist. In the low-temperature phase the spins resist being twisted, as a solid resists shear or a superfluid resists a phase gradient (an analogy, with the superfluid density in the role of the stiffness). In the high-temperature phase free vortices relax any twist and the resistance vanishes.

5.1 Definition and estimator
Impose a total twist \(\Delta\) of the angle across the system in the \(x\) direction, spread evenly over the \(L\) columns, by replacing every horizontal bond angle \(\theta_{r+\hat x}-\theta_r\) by \(\theta_{r+\hat x}-\theta_r-\alpha\) with \(\alpha=\Delta/L\). The helicity modulus \(\Upsilon\) is defined by the increase of the free energy, \[
\begin{aligned}
F(\Delta)-F(0)&=\frac{\Upsilon}{2}\,\Delta^2+O(\Delta^4)\quad\text{(in two dimensions)},\quad\text{so}\\
\Upsilon&=\frac{\partial^2F}{\partial\Delta^2}\Big|_0=\frac1{L^2}\frac{\partial^2F}{\partial\alpha^2}\Big|_0 .
\end{aligned}
\]
The sketch below shows the twist at low temperature. A total twist \(\Delta\) means that the right neighbour of the last column is the first column turned by \(\Delta\) (orange arrows). The spins respond by turning gradually, by \(\alpha=\Delta/L\) from one column to the next, so each horizontal bond costs about \(\frac J2\alpha^2\). At \(T=0\) the \(L^2\) horizontal bonds give \(F(\Delta)-F(0)=\frac J2\Delta^2\), so \(\Upsilon=J\). At high temperature free vortices can unwind the twist, and then \(\Upsilon=0\).


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;
#   satisfied bond: solid blue line, broken (frustrated) bond: dashed purple line marked with a cross.
# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (5.5 in = full text width) with 10-12 pt text,

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

def save_sketch(fig, name, extra_dirs=()):

    for d in ("figures",) + tuple(d for d in extra_dirs if os.path.isdir(d)):
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, name), dpi=300, facecolor="white")

def draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.75, color=NAVY, lw=1.3, head=7, dot=True):
    # planar spins: an arrow of fixed length centred on every lattice site (x, y), angle theta[y, x]
    for (y, x), t in np.ndenumerate(theta):
        dx, dy = 0.5 * length * np.cos(t), 0.5 * length * np.sin(t)
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x + dx, y + dy), xytext=(x - dx, y - dy),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=lw, mutation_scale=head, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
        if dot:
            ax.plot(x, y, "o", color=GRAY, ms=1.5, zorder=1)

def plaquette_winding(theta):
    # winding number of every plaquette (lower-left corner (x, y)), corners traversed counter-clockwise
    wrap = lambda a: (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi           # angle difference mapped to [-pi, pi)
    t1, t2 = theta[:-1, :-1], theta[:-1, 1:]                       # (x, y), (x+1, y)
    t3, t4 = theta[1:, 1:], theta[1:, :-1]                         # (x+1, y+1), (x, y+1)
    return np.rint((wrap(t2 - t1) + wrap(t3 - t2) + wrap(t4 - t3) + wrap(t1 - t4)) / (2 * np.pi)).astype(int)

def draw_vortex_marks(ax, w, r=0.3):
    # vortex (w = +1): navy disc with "+";  antivortex (w = -1): white disc with orange rim and "-"
    for (y, x), v in np.ndenumerate(w):

            ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x + 0.5, y + 0.5), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=1.3, zorder=6, alpha=0.9))
            ax.text(x + 0.5, y + 0.5, "+" if v > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=7)

def sketch_twisted_boundary():

    Delta = np.pi / 2                                               # total twist imposed across the system
    alpha = Delta / L                                               # twist per horizontal bond
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.4))
    ax = fig.add_axes([0.02, 0.0, 0.96, 0.86])

    # so that the right neighbour of the last column is column 1 turned by Delta
    theta = np.tile(np.pi / 2 - alpha * np.arange(L + 1), (ny, 1))
    draw_xy_spins(ax, theta[:, :L], length=0.62, lw=1.4, head=8)

        t = theta[yy, L]

    ax.text(L + 0.5, 1.0, "column 1\nturned by $\\Delta$", fontsize=10, color=ORANGE, va="center")
    ax.text(3.5, -0.85, r"twist per bond: $\alpha=\Delta/L$,  energy $\approx\frac{J}{2}\alpha^2$ per bond", ha="center", fontsize=11, color=NAVY)
    ax.set_title(r"twisted boundary:  $F(\Delta)-F(0)=\frac{\Upsilon}{2}\Delta^2$", fontsize=12, color=NAVY, loc="left")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.6, L + 2.0); ax.set_ylim(-1.2, ny - 0.3); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_twisted_boundary()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_xy_twist.png")
plt.show()





(In the continuum, \(F=\frac\Upsilon2\int d^2r\,(\nabla\theta)^2\) with \(\nabla\theta=\Delta/L\) gives the same \(\frac\Upsilon2\Delta^2\), so \(\Upsilon\) is the renormalised, effective \(J\) at long wavelengths.) With \(F=-T\ln Z(\alpha)\) and \(H(\alpha)=-J\sum_{\rm x\ bonds}\cos(\Delta^x_r-\alpha)-J\sum_{\rm y\ bonds}\cos\Delta^y_r\), two derivatives give \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2F}{\partial\alpha^2}\Big|_0&=\Big\langle\frac{\partial^2H}{\partial\alpha^2}\Big\rangle-\beta\Big(\Big\langle\Big(\frac{\partial H}{\partial\alpha}\Big)^2\Big\rangle-\Big\langle\frac{\partial H}{\partial\alpha}\Big\rangle^2\Big)\\
&=J\langle C_x\rangle-\beta J^2\big(\langle S_x^2\rangle-\langle S_x\rangle^2\big),
\end{aligned}
\] with \(C_x=\sum\cos\Delta^x_r\) and \(S_x=\sum\sin\Delta^x_r\) as measured in Section 2. By symmetry \(\langle S_x\rangle=0\), and averaging the \(x\) and \(y\) directions gives \[
\boxed{\;\Upsilon=\frac{1}{2N}\Big[J\langle C_x+C_y\rangle-\beta J^2\langle S_x^2+S_y^2\rangle\Big]\;}
\] The first term is (minus) the energy per bond, and the second is the fluctuation of the sums of bond sines \(S_x\), \(S_y\), called the spin current.
The derivative identity can be checked symbolically on a toy system with three configurations and two twisted bonds each. SymPy computes \(\partial_\alpha^2(-T\ln Z)\) and compares it with the right-hand side.


Code
al, bt, Js = sp.symbols("alpha beta J", positive=True)
d = sp.symbols("d0:6", real=True)                        # bond angles: configuration c has bonds d[2c], d[2c+1]
Hc = [-Js * (sp.cos(d[2 * c] - al) + sp.cos(d[2 * c + 1] - al)) for c in range(3)]
Z = sum(sp.exp(-bt * h) for h in Hc)
F2 = sp.diff(-sp.log(Z) / bt, al, 2).subs(al, 0)
w_ = [sp.exp(-bt * h.subs(al, 0)) / Z.subs(al, 0) for h in Hc]
Cc = [sp.cos(d[2 * c]) + sp.cos(d[2 * c + 1]) for c in range(3)]
Sc = [sp.sin(d[2 * c]) + sp.sin(d[2 * c + 1]) for c in range(3)]
avg = lambda q: sum(wi * qi for wi, qi in zip(w_, q))
estimator = Js * avg(Cc) - bt * Js**2 * (avg([s**2 for s in Sc]) - avg(Sc) ** 2)
print("d^2F/d alpha^2 - [J<C> - beta J^2 (<S^2> - <S>^2)] simplifies to:", sp.simplify(F2 - estimator))

5.2 Low-temperature stiffness
In the Gaussian theory each bond angle has \(\langle(\Delta^x)^2\rangle=T/(2J)\) (equipartition gives \(N\) modes \(\times\,T/2\) shared by \(2N\) bonds, each with energy \(\frac J2(\Delta^x)^2\)), so \(\langle\cos\Delta^x\rangle\approx1-\frac T{4J}\). The current term vanishes at this order. With periodic boundaries the sum of \(\Delta^x\) along each row is zero in the Gaussian theory, so \(S_x=\sum\sin\Delta^x\approx\sum\Delta^x=0\). Therefore \[
\Upsilon\approx J-\frac T4+O(T^2).
\] This is the anharmonic stiffness used in Section 3.3. Below we compare with the Monte Carlo data at the lowest temperatures, and run two extra temperatures, \(T=0.1\) and \(0.3\), for \(L=32\).

5.3 Universal jump
Nelson and Kosterlitz (1977) showed with the renormalisation group that in the thermodynamic limit the stiffness jumps from a universal value to zero, \[
\lim_{T\to T_{\rm BKT}^-}\Upsilon(T)=\frac{2}{\pi}\,T_{\rm BKT},\qquad \Upsilon(T)=0\ \text{ for }T>T_{\rm BKT}.
\] This is the self-consistent version of the free-energy argument of Section 4.3 (a free vortex costs \(\pi\Upsilon\ln L\) and gains \(2T\ln L\)). For superfluid films \(\Upsilon\) is proportional to the superfluid density, hence the title of their paper.
On a finite lattice \(\Upsilon_L(T)\) is smooth and positive at all \(T\). It decreases with \(L\) above \(T_{\rm BKT}\), and the drop sharpens as \(L\) grows. This suggests the crossing method. We define \(T^*(L)\) as the temperature where \(\Upsilon_L(T)\) crosses the line \(2T/\pi\), and as \(L\to\infty\), \(T^*(L)\to T_{\rm BKT}\).
The approach to the limit is slow. Above \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the correlation length diverges as (Kosterlitz 1974) \(\xi\propto\exp\!\big(b/\sqrt{T-T_{\rm BKT}}\big)\), with a non-universal constant \(b\). The finite lattice looks critical as long as \(\xi\gtrsim L\), and setting \(\xi=L\) gives \[
T^*(L)\simeq T_\infty+\frac{b^2}{(\ln L)^2},\qquad T_\infty=T_{\rm BKT},
\] a very slow, logarithmic approach. We fit this form to our three sizes with \(T_\infty\) and \(b^2\) as free parameters (the printout and the legend of the figure write the fitted intercept as \(T_{\rm BKT}\)). With only \(L=16,32,48\) the extrapolation is rough.


Code

print("solve exp(b / sqrt(t)) = L for t:", sp.solve(sp.Eq(sp.exp(bb / sp.sqrt(tt)), Ls_), tt))

def crossing(T, ups):
    # temperature where ups(T) - 2T/pi changes sign, by linear interpolation between grid points
    f = ups - 2 * T / np.pi
    i = np.nonzero((f[:-1] > 0) & (f[1:] <= 0))[0][0]
    return T[i] - f[i] * (T[i + 1] - T[i]) / (f[i + 1] - f[i])

def ups_curve(cm_all, L):
    # cm_all: (nT, k) pooled moments -> Upsilon(T) on the grid
    return np.array([helicity_from_means(cm_all[i, [2, 3]], 1 / T_GRID[i], L * L) for i in range(len(T_GRID))])

T_cross = {}

title: Lab 030: Physics of the 2D XY model and the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
text:
6. Correlation function
The spin-wave theory (Section 3.4) predicts \(G(r)\propto r^{-\eta(T)}\) with \(\eta=T/(2\pi J)\) at low \(T\). Vortices modify this in two ways. Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) bound pairs renormalise \(J\to\Upsilon\), so \(\eta(T)=T/(2\pi\Upsilon(T))\), and at \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the universal jump gives \[
\eta(T_{\rm BKT})=\frac{T_{\rm BKT}}{2\pi\cdot2T_{\rm BKT}/\pi}=\frac14
\] (Kosterlitz 1974). Above \(T_{\rm BKT}\) free vortices randomise the angle beyond a distance \(\xi\), and \(G(r)\propto e^{-r/\xi}\).
To measure the correlation function we use, for each snapshot, \(G(\boldsymbol r)=\frac1N\sum_i\cos(\theta_i-\theta_{i+\boldsymbol r})\), the real part of the circular autocorrelation of \(z_i=e^{i\theta_i}\), computed with fast Fourier transforms (FFT), \(G=\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{IFFT}(|\mathrm{FFT}(z)|^2)/N\). We average over snapshots and over the two lattice directions, \(r=0,\dots,L/2\).
Two tests follow. Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) we test renormalised spin waves. On the same \(48\times48\) torus the Gaussian theory with \(J\) replaced by the measured stiffness \(\Upsilon\) predicts, with no free parameter, \[
\begin{aligned}
G_{\rm SW}(r)&=\exp\!\Big(-\frac{T}{2\Upsilon}\,D_L(r)\Big),\\
D_L(r)&=\frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol k\neq0}\frac{2-2\cos k_xr}{\lambda_{\boldsymbol k}},
\end{aligned}
\] which contains the periodic images automatically. A direct power-law fit \(G\propto r^{-\eta}\) is unreliable on a lattice this small, because the image at distance \(L-r\) and the short-distance corrections bend the curve on the log–log plot over the whole range \(r\le L/2\). Above \(T_{\rm BKT}\) we test exponential decay and fit \(G(r)=A\big[e^{-r/\xi}+e^{-(L-r)/\xi}\big]\) (with the periodic image) for \(r\ge2\).


Code
print("eta at the universal jump:", sp.simplify(Tsym / (2 * sp.pi * (2 * Tsym / sp.pi))))

def correlation(theta):
    # theta: (n, L, L) -> G(r), r = 0..L/2, averaged over samples and the x and y directions
    L = theta.shape[-1]
    z = np.exp(1j * theta.astype(np.float64))
    Fz = np.fft.fft2(z)
    G2d = np.fft.ifft2(np.abs(Fz) ** 2).real.mean(0) / (L * L)          # (L, L), G2d[dy, dx]
    return 0.5 * (G2d[0, : L // 2 + 1] + G2d[: L // 2 + 1, 0])

def D_torus(L):
    # D_L(r) = (1/N) sum_{k != 0} (2 - 2 cos k_x r) / lambda_k on the L x L torus, r = 0..L/2
    kk = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(L) / L
    KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kk, kk, indexing="ij")
    lam = 4 - 2 * np.cos(KX) - 2 * np.cos(KY); lam[0, 0] = np.inf
    return np.array([((2 - 2 * np.cos(KX * r)) / lam).sum() / L**2 for r in range(L // 2 + 1)])

GR = {L: np.array([correlation(DS[L]["theta"][i]) for i in range(len(T_GRID))]) for L in L_LIST}
L = 48
r = np.arange(L // 2 + 1)
D48 = D_torus(L)

print("test 1: G_MC(r) vs renormalised spin waves exp(-T D_L(r) / 2 Upsilon_48), L = 48")
for T in [0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90]:
    i = int(np.argmin(abs(T_GRID - T)))
    g_sw = np.exp(-T_GRID[i] / (2 * TH[48]["ups"][i, 0]) * D48)
    dev = np.abs(GR[48][i, 1:] / g_sw[1:] - 1).max()
    print(f"  T = {T_GRID[i]:.2f}:  G_MC(24) = {GR[48][i, 24]:.4f},  G_SW(24) = {g_sw[24]:.4f},  max over r of |G_MC/G_SW - 1| = {dev:.3f}")

print("test 2: correlation length from exponential fits, L = 48")
xi_fit = {}

The figure shows \(G(r)\) of \(L=48\) for five temperatures on log–log axes (left, with the renormalised spin-wave prediction dashed), where a power law is a straight line, and on semi-log axes (right), where an exponential is a straight line. Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) Monte Carlo and renormalised spin waves agree to within 1% for \(T\le0.8\) and 4% at \(T=0.9\), and above \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the correlation length falls from \(9.3\) lattice spacings at \(T=1.05\) to \(1.5\) at \(T=1.5\).
The exponent \(\eta\) can also be extracted from the system-size dependence. Summing the power law over the lattice gives \(\langle\boldsymbol m^2\rangle=\frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol r}G(\boldsymbol r)\propto L^{-\eta}\), so the effective exponent between two sizes is \[
\eta_{\rm eff}(T)=-\frac{\ln\big(\langle\boldsymbol m^2\rangle_{L_2}/\langle\boldsymbol m^2\rangle_{L_1}\big)}{\ln(L_2/L_1)} .
\] Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) it should follow \(T/(2\pi\Upsilon)\) and reach \(1/4\) at \(T_{\rm BKT}\). Above \(T_{\rm BKT}\), \(\langle\boldsymbol m^2\rangle\propto\xi^2/L^2\) once \(L\gg\xi\), so \(\eta_{\rm eff}\) grows towards \(2\). The figure below shows \(\eta_{\rm eff}\) from \(L=16\) and \(48\), the renormalised value \(T/(2\pi\Upsilon_{48})\) with the stiffness of \(L=48\), the bare spin-wave value \(T/(2\pi J)\) and the line \(\eta=1/4\), against \(T\).

title: Lab 030: Physics of the 2D XY model and the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
text:
7. Specific heat
At an ordinary continuous transition (2D Ising) the specific heat diverges at \(T_c\). At the BKT transition the free energy is infinitely differentiable. The singular part of the free energy per site scales like \(\xi^{-2}\) (one unit of \(k_BT\) per correlated area \(\xi^2\)), and with \(\xi\propto e^{b/\sqrt{t}}\), \(t=T-T_{\rm BKT}\), \[
f_{\rm sing}\propto e^{-2b/\sqrt t},
\] a function all of whose derivatives vanish as \(t\to0^+\) (an essential singularity). Every thermodynamic derivative, including \(c=-T\,\partial^2f/\partial T^2\), is continuous at \(T_{\rm BKT}\), and the transition is called “of infinite order”. The Monte Carlo data below show where the specific heat has its maximum.
We compute \(c=\beta^2(\langle E^2\rangle-\langle E\rangle^2)/N\) from the energy fluctuations and, as a check, the numerical derivative \(du/dT\) of the measured energy for \(L=48\). The figure shows both against \(T\), with \(T_{\rm BKT}\) as a dotted line. The SymPy cell verifies the essential singularity, the limit of every derivative of \(e^{-2b/\sqrt t}\) at \(t\to0^+\) being zero (shown for the first three).

The maximum of \(c\) lies above \(T_{\rm BKT}\), at \(T\approx1.06\) for \(L=48\) from a parabola through the largest values. Next to \(T_{\rm BKT}\) (\(T=0.90\)) the specific heat is the same for all three sizes within the errors, as expected for an infinitely differentiable free energy. The height of the maximum still grows slightly between \(L=16\) and \(L=48\) (\(1.40\), \(1.46\) and \(1.55\), with errors of \(0.03\) to \(0.06\)), and larger lattices would be needed to follow it further. In the figure the two estimates of \(c\), from the energy fluctuations and from \(du/dT\), agree. A measurement of \(c\) alone would place the “transition” at the maximum, well above \(T_{\rm BKT}\).
We can now put the two phases side by side. The schematic below shows idealised configurations on a \(10\times10\) lattice, with vortices marked as in Section 4. Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the arrows are nearly parallel and vary slowly as spin waves, and the only vortices are tightly bound vortex–antivortex pairs. The correlation function \(G(r)\) decays as a power law, \(G\sim r^{-\eta}\), and the helicity modulus \(\Upsilon\) is positive. This phase has quasi-long-range order, zero magnetisation but correlations that decay more slowly than any exponential. Above \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the arrows are disordered and free vortices of both signs are scattered over the lattice, \(G(r)\) decays exponentially, \(G\sim e^{-r/\xi}\), and \(\Upsilon=0\). Neither phase has a magnetisation in the thermodynamic limit. The two phases differ in how the spins are correlated and in whether the vortices are bound.

def save_sketch(fig, name, extra_dirs=()):

def draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.75, color=NAVY, lw=1.3, head=7, dot=True):
    # planar spins: an arrow of fixed length centred on every lattice site (x, y), angle theta[y, x]
    for (y, x), t in np.ndenumerate(theta):
        dx, dy = 0.5 * length * np.cos(t), 0.5 * length * np.sin(t)
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x + dx, y + dy), xytext=(x - dx, y - dy),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=lw, mutation_scale=head, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
        if dot:
            ax.plot(x, y, "o", color=GRAY, ms=1.5, zorder=1)

def plaquette_winding(theta):
    # winding number of every plaquette (lower-left corner (x, y)), corners traversed counter-clockwise
    wrap = lambda a: (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi           # angle difference mapped to [-pi, pi)
    t1, t2 = theta[:-1, :-1], theta[:-1, 1:]                       # (x, y), (x+1, y)
    t3, t4 = theta[1:, 1:], theta[1:, :-1]                         # (x+1, y+1), (x, y+1)
    return np.rint((wrap(t2 - t1) + wrap(t3 - t2) + wrap(t4 - t3) + wrap(t1 - t4)) / (2 * np.pi)).astype(int)

def draw_vortex_marks(ax, w, r=0.3):
    # vortex (w = +1): navy disc with "+";  antivortex (w = -1): white disc with orange rim and "-"
    for (y, x), v in np.ndenumerate(w):
        if v != 0:
            face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if v > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
            ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x + 0.5, y + 0.5), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=1.3, zorder=6, alpha=0.9))
            ax.text(x + 0.5, y + 0.5, "+" if v > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=7)

def sketch_xy_phases_configs():
    L = 10
    y, x = np.indices((L, L)).astype(float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(11)                                 # fixed seed: the same schematic every time
    # low T: nearly aligned spins with a slow spin-wave twist and one tightly bound vortex-antivortex pair
    low = (0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * x / L) + 0.3 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * y / L)
           + np.arctan2(y - 5.5, x - 3.5) - np.arctan2(y - 5.5, x - 5.5))
    # high T: independent random angles; the vortices are found by computing the winding of every plaquette
    high = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, (L, L))
    panels = [(low, r"$T<T_{\rm BKT}$: bound pair", r"$\Upsilon>0$, $G(r)\sim r^{-\eta}$"),
              (high, r"$T>T_{\rm BKT}$: free vortices", r"$\Upsilon=0$, $G(r)\sim e^{-r/\xi}$")]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 3.1))
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, bottom=0.01, top=0.86, wspace=0.06)
    for ax, (theta, title, sub) in zip(axes, panels):
        draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.62, lw=1.0, head=5, dot=False)
        draw_vortex_marks(ax, plaquette_winding(theta), r=0.33)
        ax.set_title(f"{title}\n{sub}", fontsize=10, color=NAVY)
        ax.set_xlim(-0.5, L - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.5, L - 0.5); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):

The phase diagram of the 2D XY model has a single control parameter, the temperature, and the figure below draws it as a temperature axis together with the quantity that distinguishes the two phases, the helicity modulus. Its leading low-temperature behaviour \(\Upsilon\approx J-T/4\) (Section 5.2) and its universal value \(2T_{\rm BKT}/\pi\) at the transition (Section 5.3, dashed line) are drawn to scale, and the curve between them is schematic. Above \(T_{\rm BKT}=1/1.1199=0.8929\,J\) [Hasenbusch 2005], \(\Upsilon=0\).
The BKT transition differs from the Ising transitions of Labs 010–012 and 029. At a first-order transition a first derivative of the free energy jumps. At a continuous transition the first derivatives are continuous but the correlation length diverges as a power law, \(\xi\sim|T-T_c|^{-\nu}\), and the specific heat or other second derivatives diverge. At the BKT transition no symmetry is broken on either side, the correlation length diverges faster than any power, \(\xi\propto\exp\big(b/\sqrt{T-T_{\rm BKT}}\big)\), and the singular part of the free energy, \(f_{\rm sing}\propto e^{-2b/\sqrt t}\) (Section 7), has derivatives of all orders that vanish at \(T_{\rm BKT}\), so every thermodynamic derivative is continuous. Such a transition is called a transition of infinite order. It is visible in the jump of the helicity modulus from \(2T_{\rm BKT}/\pi\) to zero and in the change from power-law to exponential decay of \(G(r)\). The dashed orange marker at \(T\approx1.06\) is the maximum of the specific heat for \(L=48\) (Section 7), a smooth maximum above \(T_{\rm BKT}\) with no transition.

Vortices are the relevant objects, but their density is not an order parameter either. The transition is the unbinding of pairs. Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) every vortex has an antivortex partner nearby, and above it free vortices exist. This is a statement about the spatial arrangement of defects, which their number does not capture.
These facts have direct consequences for the anomaly-detection study of Lab 021. An algorithm fed with raw angles (or with \((\cos\theta_i,\sin\theta_i)\)) will most easily pick up the magnetisation, the dominant variation between low- and high-temperature snapshots of a finite lattice. A “transition” found from that signal is a finite-size crossover that drifts with \(L\) (\(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) is closest to \(0.5\) at \(T=1.10\), \(1.00\) and \(1.00\) for \(L=16\), 32 and 48), distinct from \(T_{\rm BKT}\). The global rotation symmetry adds a second difficulty. Two snapshots differing by \(\theta_i\to\theta_i+\alpha\) are physically identical, and a representation that is not invariant (raw angles) spends capacity on this difference. A physics-informed input is the vortex map \(w_r\in\{-1,0,1\}\) per plaquette, which is rotation invariant and consists directly of the topological objects. Even then, a detector must be sensitive to how vortices are arranged (paired or free), since their density is smooth through \(T_{\rm BKT}\). Finally, any temperature an algorithm singles out should be compared with the reference values of this notebook, the stiffness crossings \(T^*(L)\), the specific-heat maximum (above \(T_{\rm BKT}\)) and the literature value \(T_{\rm BKT}=0.8929\).

text:
Exercises

Exercise 1 — the helicity modulus from a real twist
The estimator of Section 5.1 is a second derivative. Check it with a finite twist. Simulate \(L=16\) at \(T=0.7\) with every horizontal bond twisted by \(\alpha\), that is with energy \(-J\sum\cos(\Delta^x_r-\alpha)-J\sum\cos\Delta^y_r\), for \(\alpha=\pm0.03\), measure the “current” \(I(\alpha)=\langle\partial H/\partial\alpha\rangle=-J\langle\sum\sin(\Delta^x_r-\alpha)\rangle\), and compare \(\big(I(\alpha)-I(-\alpha)\big)/(2\alpha N)\) with \(\Upsilon\) from the estimator. (Hint: \(\partial F/\partial\alpha=\langle\partial H/\partial\alpha\rangle\).)

Solution
A twist by \(\alpha\) on every horizontal bond is the same as the substitution \(\theta_{x,y}\to\theta_{x,y}-\alpha x\) inside the bulk, but it cannot be removed on the torus because \(\alpha L\) is not a multiple of \(2\pi\). We write a twisted Metropolis sweep, in which only the horizontal neighbours carry the extra phase (the right neighbour is seen at angle \(\theta_{r+\hat x}-\alpha\), the left one at \(\theta_{r-\hat x}+\alpha\)), and use Metropolis only.


Code
def twisted_field(theta, alpha):
    c = lambda a: jnp.cos(a); s = lambda a: jnp.sin(a)
    right, left = jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1) - alpha, jnp.roll(theta, 1, -1) + alpha
    up, down = jnp.roll(theta, -1, -2), jnp.roll(theta, 1, -2)
    return (c(right) + c(left) + c(up) + c(down), s(right) + s(left) + s(up) + s(down))

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_meas"))
def twisted_run(theta0, keys, beta, alpha, n_equil, n_meas):
    colour = checkerboard(theta0.shape[-1])
    def sweep(carry, _):
        theta, key = carry
        for c in (0, 1):
            key, k1, k2 = jax.random.split(key, 3)
            new = theta + (2.0 * jax.random.uniform(k1, theta.shape) - 1.0)
            hx, hy = twisted_field(theta, alpha)
            dE = -J * (hx * (jnp.cos(new) - jnp.cos(theta)) + hy * (jnp.sin(new) - jnp.sin(theta)))
            acc = (jax.random.uniform(k2, theta.shape) < jnp.exp(-beta * dE)) & (colour == c)
            theta = jnp.where(acc, jnp.mod(new, TWO_PI), theta)
        dx = jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1) - theta - alpha
        return (theta, key), -J * jnp.sin(dx).sum()                        # dH/dalpha
    def chain(theta, key):
        carry, _ = lax.scan(sweep, (theta, key), None, length=n_equil)
        _, I = lax.scan(sweep, carry, None, length=n_meas)
        return I.mean()
    return jax.vmap(chain)(theta0, keys)

I_p = np.asarray(twisted_run(jnp.zeros((128, Lx, Lx)), keys, 1 / Tx, ax_, 500, 2500))
I_m = np.asarray(twisted_run(jnp.zeros((128, Lx, Lx)), keys, 1 / Tx, -ax_, 500, 2500))
