title: Lab 031: Physics of the Ising lattice gauge theory
section: 1. Order without a local order parameter
text:
1. Order without a local order parameter
The standard description of phases, due to Landau, rests on symmetry breaking. The Ising Hamiltonian \(H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j\) does not change under the global flip \(s_i\to-s_i\) of all spins. Below \(T_c\) the system picks one of the two ordered states, and the magnetisation \(m\), a quantity that changes sign under the symmetry, becomes non-zero. One local measurement (a spin, or the average over a small region) tells the phase.
Suppose instead that the energy were unchanged by flipping a small group of variables around one point, at any point, independently. Such a symmetry is called local or gauge symmetry. It is not a symmetry of the physics in the usual sense. Two configurations related by it describe the same physical state, expressed in different variables. We will see that a local symmetry can never be broken (Elitzur 1975), so no local quantity that changes under it can ever become non-zero. Yet the 3D model has a sharp phase transition. The phases are distinguished by non-local observables, products of variables around closed loops, the Wilson loops [Wilson 1974], which decay with the area enclosed by the loop in one phase and with its perimeter in the other.
This has a direct consequence for learning from data. A model trained on raw configurations sees the variables as they are given, redundancy included. Section 6 shows that, in the Ising gauge theory, every single variable and every pair of variables is pure noise at every temperature. The physics sits in products of four or more variables arranged in closed loops. This is the situation Carrasquilla and Melko met. Their fully connected network, which has no built-in notion of neighbouring links, failed, while a network with \(2\times2\) convolutions, which can read off one plaquette at a time, succeeded.

title: Lab 031: Physics of the Ising lattice gauge theory
text:
2. The model
Take a \(d\)-dimensional hypercubic lattice of linear size \(L\) with periodic boundaries (a torus), \(N=L^d\) sites \(x\), and unit vectors \(\hat e_\mu\), \(\mu=0,\dots,d-1\). A link \((x,\mu)\) joins \(x\) to \(x+\hat e_\mu\), and there are \(dN\) links. An Ising variable \(\sigma_\mu(x)=\pm1\) lives on every link, not on the sites. An elementary square of the lattice, a plaquette \(p=(x;\mu\nu)\) with \(\mu<\nu\), has four links on its boundary, and we define the plaquette variable as their product, \[
U_p = U_{\mu\nu}(x) = \sigma_\mu(x)\,\sigma_\nu(x+\hat e_\mu)\,\sigma_\mu(x+\hat e_\nu)\,\sigma_\nu(x) = \pm1 .
\] There are \(\binom d2N\) plaquettes, \(N\) in 2D and \(3N\) in 3D.
The energy is a sum over plaquettes, and configurations are weighted by the Boltzmann factor, \[
H(\sigma) = -J\sum_p U_p ,\qquad p(\sigma)=\frac{e^{-H(\sigma)/k_BT}}{Z},\qquad Z=\sum_{\sigma}e^{-H(\sigma)/k_BT}.
\] A plaquette with \(U_p=+1\) costs \(-J\), a frustrated plaquette (\(U_p=-1\), an odd number of negative links on its boundary) costs \(+J\).
The figure below shows these objects on a small two-dimensional patch. The Ising variables sit on the links (thin navy segments for \(\sigma=+1\) and thick orange segments for \(\sigma=-1\), as in the configuration plots of this notebook), the sites carry no variable, and each plaquette is the product of its four boundary links, labelled here for the plaquette with lower-left corner \(x\). The single flipped link frustrates the two plaquettes that contain it (orange), each of which costs \(+J\) instead of \(-J\).


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;
#   satisfied bond: solid blue line, broken (frustrated) bond: dashed purple line marked with a cross.
# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (5.5 in = full text width) with 10-12 pt text,
# and shown here at a higher screen resolution.
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

NAVY, ORANGE, BLUE, GRAY, PURPLE, GREEN = "#002B5C", "#D35A05", "#005CA7", "#5A6270", "#AA3377", "#228833"
SKETCH_STYLE = {"font.size": 11, "axes.titlesize": 12, "axes.labelsize": 11, "xtick.labelsize": 10,
                "ytick.labelsize": 10, "legend.fontsize": 10, "figure.dpi": 130, "lines.linewidth": 1.5,
                "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}

def save_sketch(fig, name, extra_dirs=()):
    # PNG copy for the lecture slides: white background, 300 dpi, included at its physical width
    os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
    for d in ("figures",) + tuple(d for d in extra_dirs if os.path.isdir(d)):
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, name), dpi=300, facecolor="white")

# links: sigma = +1 thin navy segment, sigma = -1 thick orange segment (as in the configuration plots of this notebook);
# plaquettes: light grey if U_p = +1, light orange if frustrated (U_p = -1)
def draw_links_2d(ax, U, lw=1.6, shade=True, sites=True):
    # U[mu, x, y]: U[0] horizontal link from (x, y) to (x+1, y), U[1] vertical link from (x, y) to (x, y+1); open patch
    n = U.shape[1]
    if shade:
        for x in range(n - 1):

We set \(J=k_B=1\) and use the single dimensionless coupling \[
\beta \equiv \frac{J}{k_BT}.
\] Large \(\beta\) is low temperature. In the lattice-gauge-theory literature this coupling is usually written \(\beta\) (or \(\beta_g\)), and we follow that convention. It is the analogue of \(K=J/k_BT\) of the Ising model (Lab 012). The average of an observable \(A\) is \(\langle A\rangle=\sum_\sigma A(\sigma)p(\sigma)\).
Throughout the notebook, and in the saved data, a configuration is an array U of shape (d, L, ..., L) with \(d\) spatial axes, where U[mu][x_0, ..., x_{d-1}] \(=\sigma_\mu(x)\) is the link from site \(x\) to \(x+\hat e_\mu\). The lattice axis \(\mu\) of U[mu] is array axis \(\mu\), so “the field at \(x+\hat e_\mu\)” is jnp.roll(a, -1, axis=mu). Plaquettes are returned with shape (P, L, ..., L), \(P=d(d-1)/2\), planes ordered \((0,1)\) in 2D and \((0,1),(0,2),(1,2)\) in 3D, and plaq[k][x] is the plaquette whose lower-left corner is \(x\).


Code
def shift(a, mu, n=1):
    # the field a (spatial axes only) evaluated at x + n e_mu, periodic boundaries
    return jnp.roll(a, -n, axis=mu)

def plaquettes(U):
    # U: (d, L, ..., L) links  ->  (P, L, ..., L) plaquettes, planes (mu, nu) with mu < nu in lexicographic order
    d = U.shape[0]
    return jnp.stack([U[mu] * shift(U[nu], mu) * shift(U[mu], nu) * U[nu]
                      for mu in range(d) for nu in range(mu + 1, d)])

def energy(U):
    # H = -J sum_p U_p with J = 1
    return -jnp.sum(plaquettes(U))

def energy_2d_loops(U):
    # the same energy for d = 2 with explicit loops over sites: an independent implementation used as a check
    U = np.asarray(U); L = U.shape[1]; E = 0
    for x in range(L):
        for y in range(L):
            E -= U[0, x, y] * U[1, (x + 1) % L, y] * U[0, x, (y + 1) % L] * U[1, x, y]
    return E

2.1 Heat-bath Monte Carlo
To sample the Boltzmann distribution with a heat-bath Monte Carlo (MC) algorithm we need the local field of a link. The link \(l=(x,\mu)\) belongs to \(2(d-1)\) plaquettes, one “above” (\((x;\mu\nu)\)) and one “below” (\((x-\hat e_\nu;\mu\nu)\)) for every direction \(\nu\neq\mu\). Each of these plaquettes equals \(\sigma_l\) times the product of its three other links, a staple. Collecting all terms of \(H\) that contain \(\sigma_l\) gives \[
\begin{aligned}
H &= -\sigma_l\,h_l + (\text{terms without }\sigma_l),\\
h_l &= \sum_{\nu\neq\mu}\Big[\sigma_\nu(x+\hat e_\mu)\sigma_\mu(x+\hat e_\nu)\sigma_\nu(x)\\
&\qquad\quad + \sigma_\nu(x+\hat e_\mu-\hat e_\nu)\sigma_\mu(x-\hat e_\nu)\sigma_\nu(x-\hat e_\nu)\Big].
\end{aligned}
\] The staple sum \(h_l\in\{-2(d-1),\dots,2(d-1)\}\) plays the role of the local field of the Ising model (Lab 010).
The sketch below shows the staples of a horizontal link \(l\) in two dimensions, the three other links of the plaquette above (green) and of the plaquette below (dashed blue). The product of the links of a staple is the value that its plaquette takes when \(\sigma_l=+1\), so \(h_l\) measures how strongly the surrounding links favour \(\sigma_l=+1\). In \(d\) dimensions every link has \(2(d-1)\) staples, four in 3D.

Instead of proposing a flip and accepting it with some probability (Metropolis), the heat-bath algorithm draws the new value of \(\sigma_l\) directly from its conditional distribution given all other links, \[
\begin{aligned}
P(\sigma_l=+1\mid\text{rest}) &= \frac{e^{\beta h_l}}{e^{\beta h_l}+e^{-\beta h_l}}\\
&= \frac{1}{1+e^{-2\beta h_l}}.
\end{aligned}
\] Sampling exactly from a conditional distribution of \(p(\sigma)\) leaves \(p(\sigma)\) invariant, so the chain converges to the Boltzmann distribution.
Updating links one at a time would be slow, so we look for links that can be updated simultaneously. Two links interact only if they lie on a common plaquette. Links of different directions can share plaquettes, so the directions are updated one after the other. Two links of the same direction \(\mu\) share a plaquette only if they are displaced by \(\pm\hat e_\nu\) with \(\nu\neq\mu\). If we colour the links of direction \(\mu\) by the parity of \(\sum_{\nu\neq\mu}x_\nu\), such a displacement changes the parity, so all links of one colour are independent given the rest and can be updated together (this needs even \(L\)). One sweep consists of \(2d\) such half-updates, that is, one update of every link.
The implementation follows the JAX idioms of Lab 018. A pure function sweep(U, key, beta) takes explicit random keys, lax.scan repeats sweeps inside one compiled program, jax.vmap runs many independent chains (different \(\beta\) and replicas) at once, and jax.jit compiles everything. The function run_gauge returns int8 links of shape (n_beta, n_rep * n_samples, d, L, ..., L). For each coupling, n_rep independent chains each store n_samples configurations separated by n_between sweeps after n_equil equilibration sweeps. Chains start from the cold configuration \(\sigma\equiv+1\) (Sections 4.3 and 5.4 discuss this choice).


Code
def staple_sum(U, mu):
    # h_l for all links of direction mu: shape (L, ..., L)
    h = jnp.zeros_like(U[mu])
    for nu in range(U.shape[0]):
        if nu != mu:
            h = h + shift(U[nu], mu) * shift(U[mu], nu) * U[nu]                                   # plaquette (x; mu nu)
            h = h + shift(shift(U[nu], mu), nu, -1) * shift(U[mu], nu, -1) * shift(U[nu], nu, -1)  # plaquette (x - e_nu; mu nu)
    return h

def parity_masks(d, L):
    # masks[mu, c]: links of direction mu whose parity of sum_{nu != mu} x_nu equals c;  shape (d, 2, L, ..., L)
    X = np.indices((L,) * d)
    return jnp.asarray(np.stack([[(X.sum(0) - X[mu]) % 2 == c for c in (0, 1)] for mu in range(d)]))

def sweep(U, key, beta, masks):
    for mu in range(U.shape[0]):
        for c in (0, 1):
            key, sub = jax.random.split(key)
            p_up = jax.nn.sigmoid(2.0 * beta * staple_sum(U, mu))           # heat-bath probability of sigma = +1
            new = jnp.where(jax.random.uniform(sub, p_up.shape) < p_up, 1.0, -1.0)
            U = U.at[mu].set(jnp.where(masks[mu, c], new, U[mu]))
    return U, key

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_samples", "n_between"))
def gauge_chains(U0, keys, betas, masks, n_equil, n_samples, n_between):
    # U0: (chains, d, L..), keys: (chains, 2), betas: (chains,) -> int8 samples (chains, n_samples, d, L..)
    def one_chain(U, key, beta):
        step = lambda c, _: (sweep(c[0], c[1], beta, masks), None)
        carry, _ = lax.scan(step, (U, key), None, length=n_equil)
        def store(c, _):
            c, _ = lax.scan(step, c, None, length=n_between)
            return c, c[0].astype(jnp.int8)
        return lax.scan(store, carry, None, length=n_samples)[1]
    return jax.vmap(one_chain)(U0, keys, betas)

def run_gauge(d, L, betas, n_rep, n_equil, n_samples, n_between, seed):
    # every beta gets n_rep independent chains, all started from sigma = +1;  returns (n_beta, n_rep * n_samples, d, L..) int8
    B = jnp.repeat(jnp.asarray(betas, jnp.float32), n_rep)
    U0 = jnp.ones((B.size, d) + (L,) * d, jnp.float32)
    out = gauge_chains(U0, jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed), B.size), B, parity_masks(d, L),
                       n_equil, n_samples, n_between)
    return np.asarray(out).reshape((len(betas), n_rep * n_samples, d) + (L,) * d)

3. Gauge symmetry
Choose a site \(x_0\) and flip all \(2d\) links that touch it. More generally, choose \(\gamma(x)=\pm1\) on every site and set \[
\sigma_\mu(x)\;\longrightarrow\;\sigma'_\mu(x) = \gamma(x)\,\sigma_\mu(x)\,\gamma(x+\hat e_\mu).
\] This transformation leaves every plaquette unchanged. Going around a plaquette, every corner \(y\) is the end of exactly two of its four links, so \(\gamma(y)\) appears twice and \(\gamma(y)^2=1\), \[
\begin{aligned}
U'_{\mu\nu}(x) &= \big[\gamma_1\sigma_\mu(x)\gamma_2\big]\big[\gamma_2\sigma_\nu(x+\hat e_\mu)\gamma_3\big]\big[\gamma_4\sigma_\mu(x+\hat e_\nu)\gamma_3\big]\big[\gamma_1\sigma_\nu(x)\gamma_4\big]\\
&= U_{\mu\nu}(x),
\end{aligned}
\] with \(\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_4\) the values at the four corners. Every plaquette, hence \(H\) and the Boltzmann weight, is unchanged. There are \(2^N\) choices of \(\gamma\), one independent \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry per site, and this is what makes the symmetry local. The global choice \(\gamma\equiv-1\) changes no link at all, so \(2^{N-1}\) distinct transformations act on the links.
The sketch below shows a gauge transformation at a single site \(x_0\), with \(\gamma(x_0)=-1\) and \(\gamma=+1\) everywhere else. The four links that touch \(x_0\) change sign, but every plaquette contains either none or exactly two of them, so no plaquette changes. The frustrated plaquettes (orange) are the same before and after, and so is the energy.

                    ax.plot([x, x + dx], [y, y + dy], color=NAVY if s > 0 else ORANGE, lw=lw if s > 0 else 2.2 * lw,
                            solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=2 if s > 0 else 3)
    if sites:
        for x in range(n):
            for y in range(n):
                ax.plot(x, y, "o", color=GRAY, ms=2.5, zorder=4)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.3, n - 0.7); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, n - 0.7); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

def sketch_gauge_transformation():

    V[1, x0[0], x0[1]] *= -1; V[1, x0[0], x0[1] - 1] *= -1           # the upper and lower links of x0

Configurations related by a gauge transformation form a gauge orbit and describe the same physical state. Only gauge-invariant quantities (the same on the whole orbit) are physical. The first cell below lets SymPy carry out the cancellation of the corner variables (called \(g_1,\dots,g_4\) in the code), and the second applies a random gauge transformation to random configurations in 2D and 3D and compares links, plaquettes and energies before and after.

# symbolic check: the plaquette is gauge invariant because every corner variable appears squared

def gauge_transform(U, g):
    # U: (d, L..) links, g: (L..) site variables +-1;  sigma'_mu(x) = g(x) sigma_mu(x) g(x + e_mu)
    return jnp.stack([g * U[mu] * shift(g, mu) for mu in range(U.shape[0])])

for U in (U_test, U3_test):
    d, L = U.shape[0], U.shape[1]

3.1 Counting gauge orbits
On a \(3\times3\) torus there are \(2\cdot9=18\) links and \(2^{18}=262\,144\) configurations, few enough to enumerate. We store each as an 18-bit integer. Flipping a link is an exclusive or (XOR) with its bit, and the gauge transformation at site \(x\) is an XOR with the 4-bit mask of the links touching \(x\). The group of all transformations is generated by these 9 masks, and the counting above predicts \(2^{N-1}=2^8\) distinct elements and therefore \(2^{18}/2^{8}=2^{10}\) orbits. We find the orbit of every configuration by taking the smallest integer in it as a label.


Code
def link_index(d, L):
    # integer index of link (mu, x): array of shape (d, L, ..., L) with values 0 .. d L^d - 1
    return np.arange(d * L**d).reshape((d,) + (L,) * d)

def site_masks(d, L):
    # bitmask (Python int) of the 2d links touching each site
    idx, masks = link_index(d, L), []
    for x in itertools.product(range(L), repeat=d):
        m = 0
        for mu in range(d):
            xm = list(x); xm[mu] = (xm[mu] - 1) % L
            m |= 1 << int(idx[(mu,) + x]) | 1 << int(idx[(mu,) + tuple(xm)])   # outgoing and incoming link of direction mu
        masks.append(m)
    return masks

def plaquette_masks(d, L):
    # bitmask of the 4 links of every plaquette, in the order of plaquettes(U).ravel()
    idx, masks = link_index(d, L), []
    for mu in range(d):
        for nu in range(mu + 1, d):
            for x in itertools.product(range(L), repeat=d):
                xm, xn = list(x), list(x); xm[mu] = (x[mu] + 1) % L; xn[nu] = (x[nu] + 1) % L
                masks.append(sum(1 << int(i) for i in {idx[(mu,) + x], idx[(nu,) + tuple(xm)], idx[(mu,) + tuple(xn)], idx[(nu,) + x]}))
    return masks

L2, d2 = 3, 2
n_links = d2 * L2**d2
configs = np.arange(2**n_links, dtype=np.int64)                         # all configurations; bit = 1 means sigma = -1
gm = site_masks(d2, L2)
group = {0}
for m in gm:                                                             # all products of site transformations
    group |= {h ^ m for h in group}
group = np.array(sorted(group), dtype=np.int64)
orbit_label = np.full(configs.shape, np.iinfo(np.int64).max)
for h in group:
    orbit_label = np.minimum(orbit_label, configs ^ h)
print(f"3x3 torus: {n_links} links, {configs.size} configurations")
print(f"distinct gauge transformations: {group.size}   (2^(N-1) = {2**(L2*L2-1)})")
print(f"gauge orbits: {np.unique(orbit_label).size}   (2^18 / 2^8 = {2**18 // 2**8})")

The enumeration confirms the counting. The 9 site masks generate 256 distinct transformations, and the \(2^{18}\) configurations fall into 1024 gauge orbits.


3.2 Elitzur’s theorem
Elitzur’s theorem states that the thermal average of any quantity that is not gauge invariant vanishes. For a single link the proof takes one line. Pick the gauge transformation \(\gamma\) that is \(-1\) only at the starting site of \(l\). It flips \(\sigma_l\), it maps the set of all configurations one-to-one onto itself, and it does not change the weight. Hence \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle\sigma_l\rangle &= \frac1Z\sum_\sigma\sigma_l\,e^{-\beta H(\sigma)} = \frac1Z\sum_{\sigma}(-\sigma_l)\,e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}\\
&= -\langle\sigma_l\rangle = 0 .
\end{aligned}
\] For the Ising ferromagnet the same argument with the global flip gives \(\langle m\rangle=0\) in every finite system, yet the magnetisation is spontaneously non-zero below \(T_c\). In an infinite system an infinitesimal field picks one of the two ordered states, and turning the whole lattice around would require a domain wall whose energy grows with the system size. Elitzur showed that for a local symmetry this never happens [Elitzur 1975]. The transformation that flips \(\sigma_l\) changes only the \(2d\) links at one site. If a small symmetry-breaking field \(h\) coupled to the links, \(-h\sum_l\sigma_l\), is added to \(H\), this transformation changes the weight by at most a factor \(e^{\pm2d\beta h}\), independently of \(L\). The bound survives the infinite-volume limit, so \(\langle\sigma_l\rangle\to0\) when \(h\to0\) afterwards. Equivalently, the barrier between \(\sigma_l=+1\) and \(\sigma_l=-1\) stays finite in the infinite system.
The difference between the two kinds of symmetry is visible in the dynamics. We start Monte Carlo from the perfectly “ordered” configuration \(\sigma\equiv+1\) and follow the link average \(\bar\sigma=\frac1{dN}\sum_l\sigma_l\) and the plaquette average \(\bar U=\frac1{N_p}\sum_pU_p\) (\(N_p\) = number of plaquettes) along the chain, for a 3D lattice at \(\beta=0.9\). Section 5 shows that this coupling lies in the ordered (deconfined) phase of the 3D model, where the plaquettes stay strongly ordered. For comparison we do the same with the 3D Ising ferromagnet, \(H_I=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j\), at \(K=J/k_BT=0.3\), which is in its ordered phase (\(K>K_{c}^{I}\), Section 5), starting from \(s\equiv+1\), and follow its magnetisation \(m\).


Code
# 3D Ising ferromagnet: heat bath on the two chessboard sublattices; spins s: (L, L, L)
def ising_field(s):
    return sum(jnp.roll(s, k, a) for a in range(3) for k in (1, -1))

def ising_sweep(s, key, K, chess):
    for c in (0, 1):
        key, sub = jax.random.split(key)
        p_up = jax.nn.sigmoid(2.0 * K * ising_field(s))
        new = jnp.where(jax.random.uniform(sub, s.shape) < p_up, 1.0, -1.0)
        s = jnp.where(chess == c, new, s)
    return s, key

def chessboard(L):
    return jnp.asarray(np.indices((L, L, L)).sum(0) % 2)

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_sweeps",))
def trace_gauge(U0, key, beta, masks, n_sweeps):
    # links from a cold start: per-sweep link average and plaquette average, shapes (n_sweeps,)
    def step(c, _):
        U, key = sweep(c[0], c[1], beta, masks)
        return (U, key), (jnp.mean(U), jnp.mean(plaquettes(U)))
    return lax.scan(step, (U0, key), None, length=n_sweeps)[1]

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_sweeps",))
def trace_ising(s0, key, K, chess, n_sweeps):
    def step(c, _):
        s, key = ising_sweep(c[0], c[1], K, chess)
        return (s, key), jnp.mean(s)
    return lax.scan(step, (s0, key), None, length=n_sweeps)[1]

n_sw, n_tr = 10000, 4                                         # sweeps, independent chains per lattice size
t0 = time.perf_counter()
traces = {}
for L in (6, 8, 10):
    keys = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(100 + L), n_tr)
    U0 = jnp.ones((3, L, L, L)); s0 = jnp.ones((L, L, L))
    g_tr = jax.vmap(lambda k: trace_gauge(U0, k, 0.9, parity_masks(3, L), n_sw))(keys)
    i_tr = jax.vmap(lambda k: trace_ising(s0, k, 0.3, chessboard(L), n_sw))(keys)
    traces[L] = [np.asarray(a).mean(0) for a in (*g_tr, i_tr)]          # chain averages: link, plaquette, Ising m
print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
tt = np.arange(1, n_sw + 1)
for i, L in enumerate((6, 8, 10)):
    col = blues(i / 2)
    ax[0].plot(tt, traces[L][0], color=col, lw=1.5, label=fr"link average $\bar\sigma$, $L={L}$")
    ax[0].plot(tt, traces[L][1], color=col, lw=1.5, ls="--", label=fr"plaquette average $\bar U$, $L={L}$")
    ax[1].plot(tt, traces[L][2], color=col, lw=1.5, label=f"3D Ising $m$, $L={L}$")
    print(f"L = {L:2d}: link average over the last 200 of {n_sw} sweeps = {traces[L][0][-200:].mean():+.3f}   plaquette average = {traces[L][1][-200:].mean():.3f}"
          f"   |   Ising m = {traces[L][2][-200:].mean():.3f}")
ax[0].set_xscale("log"); ax[1].set_xscale("log")
ax[0].set_title(r"Ising gauge theory, $\beta=0.9$, cold start"); ax[1].set_title(r"3D Ising ferromagnet, $K=0.3$, cold start")
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlabel("Monte Carlo sweeps"); a.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7); a.axhline(0, color=UJGray, lw=0.8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


72.1 s
L =  6: link average over the last 200 of 10000 sweeps = -0.037   plaquette average = 0.991   |   Ising m = 0.911
L =  8: link average over the last 200 of 10000 sweeps = -0.024   plaquette average = 0.991   |   Ising m = 0.910
L = 10: link average over the last 200 of 10000 sweeps = +0.013   plaquette average = 0.991   |   Ising m = 0.908





The link average starts at \(1\) and decays to zero on a time scale that does not depend on \(L\). Over the last 200 of 10 000 sweeps it lies between \(-0.037\) and \(+0.013\) for \(L=6,8,10\). The “order” of the links is not stable, because it can be undone site by site, through local moves with a finite barrier. The plaquette average, which is gauge invariant, relaxes quickly to a large equilibrium value (\(0.991\)) and stays there. The magnetisation of the Ising ferromagnet does not decay (it stays near \(0.91\) for all three sizes), because undoing it would require a domain wall across the whole lattice. Raw link variables therefore never carry an order parameter, and the physics of the gauge theory has to be read from gauge-invariant quantities.

title: Lab 031: Physics of the Ising lattice gauge theory
text:
4. Exact solution in two dimensions
In 2D every plaquette is a “face” of the lattice, and it turns out that the plaquettes behave as independent Ising variables. This makes the model solvable in a few lines. We derive the solution in three steps (gauge fixing, partition function, observables) and check every step.

4.1 Gauge fixing
We start with an open lattice of \(L\times L\) plaquettes, with \((L+1)^2\) sites, \(2L(L+1)\) links and no periodic wrap-around. A gauge transformation can set to \(+1\) every link of a maximal tree, a set of links that connects all sites without forming a loop. We walk from a root site along the tree and choose \(\gamma\) site by site so that each tree link becomes \(+1\). A tree on \((L+1)^2\) sites has \((L+1)^2-1\) links, so the number of links left free is \[
2L(L+1)-(L+1)^2+1 = L^2 = \text{number of plaquettes}.
\] Adding the free links one at a time in a suitable order, each one closes exactly one new plaquette, so the free links and the plaquettes determine each other one-to-one. Every gauge orbit contains exactly one tree-fixed configuration, and every orbit has \(2^{(L+1)^2-1}\) elements (all transformations except the global one act freely). Therefore \[
Z_{\rm open} = 2^{(L+1)^2-1}\sum_{\{U_p=\pm1\}}\prod_p e^{\beta U_p} = 2^{(L+1)^2-1}\,(2\cosh\beta)^{L^2}.
\] With periodic boundaries the torus has \(N\) sites, \(2N\) links and \(N\) plaquettes, and the counting changes in two places. First, every link lies on exactly two plaquettes, so \(\prod_pU_p=\prod_l\sigma_l^2=1\) and only \(N-1\) plaquettes are independent. Second, a maximal tree has \(N-1\) links, leaving \(2N-(N-1)=N+1\) free links, \(N-1\) fixed by the plaquettes and two more, the products of links along a horizontal and a vertical loop that winds around the torus (holonomies \(W_x\), \(W_y\)), which the plaquettes do not determine. The configurations are counted correctly, \(2^{N-1}\) (gauge) \(\times\,2^{N-1}\) (plaquettes) \(\times\,2^2\) (holonomies) \(=2^{2N}\). The sum over plaquettes with the constraint \(\prod_pU_p=1\) is done with the projector \(\frac12\big(1+\prod_pU_p\big)\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\{U_p\}}\tfrac12\Big(1+\prod_pU_p\Big)\prod_pe^{\beta U_p} &= \tfrac12\Big[(2\cosh\beta)^N + (2\sinh\beta)^N\Big]\\
\Longrightarrow\quad Z_{\rm torus} &= 2^{N-1}\cdot 4\cdot\tfrac12\Big[(2\cosh\beta)^N+(2\sinh\beta)^N\Big]\\
&= 2^N\Big[(2\cosh\beta)^N+(2\sinh\beta)^N\Big].
\end{aligned}
\] The cell below performs the maximal-tree gauge fixing on a random torus configuration and checks the counting. The next cell checks both formulas for \(Z\) against exact enumeration, symbolically.


Code
def tree_gauge_2d(U):
    # gauge transformation that sets all horizontal links with x < L-1 and the vertical links at x = 0 with y < L-1 to +1
    # (a maximal tree: N - 1 links).  g is built by walking from the root (0, 0) up the column x = 0, then along each row.
    U = np.asarray(U); L = U.shape[1]; g = np.ones((L, L))
    for y in range(1, L):
        g[0, y] = g[0, y - 1] * U[1, 0, y - 1]               # makes sigma'_1(0, y-1) = g(0,y-1) sigma g(0,y) = +1
    for x in range(1, L):
        g[x, :] = g[x - 1, :] * U[0, x - 1, :]               # makes sigma'_0(x-1, y) = +1
    return np.asarray(gauge_transform(U, g.astype(np.float32)))

Uf = tree_gauge_2d(U_test)
L = U_test.shape[1]; N = L * L
tree = np.zeros_like(Uf, bool); tree[0, :L - 1, :] = True; tree[1, 0, :L - 1] = True
print(f"tree links: {tree.sum()} (N - 1 = {N - 1}); all equal to +1 after gauge fixing: {bool(np.all(Uf[tree] == 1))}")
print(f"free links: {(~tree).sum()} = (N - 1) plaquettes + 2 holonomies = {N + 1}")
print(f"plaquettes unchanged by the gauge fixing: {bool(np.array_equal(np.asarray(plaquettes(Uf)), np.asarray(plaquettes(U_test))))}")
print(f"product of all plaquettes on the torus: {float(np.prod(np.asarray(plaquettes(U_test)))):+.0f}")
Wx = lambda U, y: np.prod(np.asarray(U)[0, :, y])            # horizontal non-contractible loop at height y
Wy = lambda U, x: np.prod(np.asarray(U)[1, x, :])            # vertical non-contractible loop at column x
print(f"holonomies W_x(y=0) = {Wx(U_test, 0):+.0f} -> {Wx(Uf, 0):+.0f} after gauge fixing,   W_y(x=0) = {Wy(U_test, 0):+.0f} -> {Wy(Uf, 0):+.0f}")

free links: 37 = (N - 1) plaquettes + 2 holonomies = 37
plaquettes unchanged by the gauge fixing: True
product of all plaquettes on the torus: +1
holonomies W_x(y=0) = +1 -> +1 after gauge fixing,   W_y(x=0) = +1 -> +1




Code
# exact enumeration: histogram of the number of satisfied minus frustrated plaquettes, then Z(beta) as a SymPy expression
def plaquette_sum_histogram(n_links, pmasks, chunk=2**20):
    # for all 2^n_links configurations (bit = 1: sigma = -1) count n_S = number of configurations with sum_p U_p = S
    pm = np.array(pmasks, dtype=np.int64); n_p = len(pm)
    hist = np.zeros(2 * n_p + 1, dtype=np.int64)
    for start in range(0, 2**n_links, chunk):
        c = np.arange(start, min(start + chunk, 2**n_links), dtype=np.int64)
        frustrated = np.zeros(c.shape, np.int64)
        for m in pm:
            frustrated += np.bitwise_count(c & m) & 1          # U_p = -1 iff an odd number of its links are -1
        hist += np.bincount(n_p - 2 * frustrated + n_p, minlength=2 * n_p + 1)   # index S + n_p
    return hist

def open_lattice_masks(Lp):
    # open lattice of Lp x Lp plaquettes: horizontal links (x, y) x < Lp, y <= Lp and vertical links x <= Lp, y < Lp
    h = {(x, y): i for i, (x, y) in enumerate((x, y) for x in range(Lp) for y in range(Lp + 1))}
    v = {(x, y): len(h) + i for i, (x, y) in enumerate((x, y) for x in range(Lp + 1) for y in range(Lp))}
    masks = [(1 << h[(x, y)]) | (1 << v[(x + 1, y)]) | (1 << h[(x, y + 1)]) | (1 << v[(x, y)]) for x in range(Lp) for y in range(Lp)]
    return len(h) + len(v), masks

b = sp.symbols("beta", positive=True)
def Z_from_hist(hist):
    n_p = (len(hist) - 1) // 2
    return sum(int(n) * sp.exp(b * (S - n_p)) for S, n in enumerate(hist) if n)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
nl, pm = open_lattice_masks(2)
h_open = plaquette_sum_histogram(nl, pm)
Z_open_enum = Z_from_hist(h_open)
Z_open_formula = 2**(9 - 1) * (2 * sp.cosh(b))**4
print(f"open 2x2-plaquette lattice: {nl} links, 9 sites;  Z_enum - 2^8 (2 cosh b)^4 =",
      sp.simplify((Z_open_enum - Z_open_formula).rewrite(sp.exp)))
for L in (2, 3):
    N = L * L
    h_tor = plaquette_sum_histogram(2 * N, plaquette_masks(2, L))
    Z_tor_formula = 2**N * ((2 * sp.cosh(b))**N + (2 * sp.sinh(b))**N)
    print(f"{L}x{L} torus: {2 * N} links;  Z_enum - 2^N[(2cosh b)^N + (2sinh b)^N] =",
          sp.simplify((Z_from_hist(h_tor) - Z_tor_formula).rewrite(sp.exp)))
print(f"({time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")

2x2 torus: 8 links;  Z_enum - 2^N[(2cosh b)^N + (2sinh b)^N] = 0


3x3 torus: 18 links;  Z_enum - 2^N[(2cosh b)^N + (2sinh b)^N] = 0
(0.5 s)


Both differences simplify to zero identically in \(\beta\), so the gauge-fixing argument gives the exact partition function on both geometries.


4.2 Thermodynamics
In the thermodynamic limit the term \((2\sinh\beta)^N\) is negligible (\(\tanh\beta<1\)), and \(Z\simeq 2^N(2\cosh\beta)^N\) is the partition function of \(N\) independent two-state variables with energy \(-U_p\). All thermodynamics therefore follows from a single plaquette, \[
\begin{aligned}
z_1 &= \sum_{U=\pm1}e^{\beta U} = 2\cosh\beta,\\
\langle U_p\rangle &= \frac{\partial\ln z_1}{\partial\beta} = \tanh\beta,\\
c &= \beta^2\frac{\partial^2\ln z_1}{\partial\beta^2} = \frac{\beta^2}{\cosh^2\beta},
\end{aligned}
\] where \(c=\beta^2N_p^{-1}\big(\langle E^2\rangle-\langle E\rangle^2\big)\) is the specific heat per plaquette (as in Lab 012, \(c=\partial u/\partial T\) with \(u\) the energy per plaquette). The free energy per plaquette, \(f=-T[\ln2+\ln(2\cosh\beta)]\), is an analytic function of \(T\) for every \(T>0\), so there is no phase transition. These are exactly the formulas of the 1D Ising chain (Lab 012, Section 2.1) with \(K\to\beta\). The 2D gauge theory is equivalent to a 1D Ising chain, the plaquettes playing the role of the bond variables \(s_is_{i+1}\).
On a finite torus we keep the second term and obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle U_p\rangle_{L} &= \frac1N\frac{\partial\ln Z_{\rm torus}}{\partial\beta} = \frac{t + t^{N-1}}{1+t^N},\\
t &= \tanh\beta ,
\end{aligned}

4.3 Monte Carlo and the 2D data set
We now generate (or load) the 2D Monte Carlo data set and compare the measured \(\langle U_p\rangle\) and \(c\) with the exact results. First we check the sampler itself on the \(4\times4\) torus, against the exact finite-size formula \(\langle U_p\rangle_L\).
One detail concerns the stored configurations. Local Monte Carlo moves randomise the gauge only slowly at large \(\beta\) (Section 3.2), so a chain started from \(\sigma\equiv+1\) would keep an artificial excess of positive links. Since the Boltzmann weight is gauge invariant, applying an independent uniformly random gauge transformation \(\gamma\) to every stored configuration produces an exact sample of the same distribution with the gauge degrees of freedom fully equilibrated. All saved configurations are gauge-randomised in this way.


Code
def gauge_randomise(U, d, seed):
    # U: (batch..., d, L, ..., L) int8 links;  sigma'_mu(x) = g(x) sigma_mu(x) g(x + e_mu) with random g per configuration
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    lat = U.shape[-d:]
    g = r.choice(np.array([-1, 1], np.int8), size=U.shape[:-d - 1] + lat)
    out = np.empty_like(U)
    for mu in range(d):
        idx = (Ellipsis, mu) + (slice(None),) * d                      # selects sigma_mu for every configuration
        out[idx] = g * U[idx] * np.roll(g, -1, axis=g.ndim - d + mu)
    return out

def per_chain(values, chain):
    # values: (n_samples,), chain: (n_samples,) -> per-chain means (n_rep,)
    return np.array([values[chain == k].mean() for k in np.unique(chain)])

def plaquette_stats(ds):
    # <U_p> and c with errors from the spread over chains;  returns arrays of shape (n_beta,)
    d, L = int(ds["d"]), int(ds["L"]); n_p = d * (d - 1) // 2 * L**d
    out = {k: [] for k in ("U", "dU", "c", "dc")}
    for i, bv in enumerate(ds["beta"]):
        ub = np.asarray(mean_plaq(jnp.asarray(ds["links"][i], jnp.float32)))
        cu = per_chain(ub, ds["chain"])
        cc = np.array([bv**2 * n_p * ub[ds["chain"] == k].var() for k in np.unique(ds["chain"])])
        out["U"].append(ub.mean()); out["dU"].append(cu.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(cu)))
        out["c"].append(bv**2 * n_p * ub.var()); out["dc"].append(cc.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(cc)))
    return {k: np.array(v) for k, v in out.items()}

4.4 Wilson loops
For a closed path \(C\) on the lattice the Wilson loop is the product of the links along it, \(W(C)=\big\langle\prod_{l\in C}\sigma_l\big\rangle\). It is gauge invariant, since every site of a closed path is the end of exactly two of its links. (A product along an open path is not invariant, since its end points appear once, and by the argument of Section 3.2 its average is zero, see Exercise 1.) For an \(R\times S\) rectangle we write \(W(R,S)\).
Wilson loops are related to plaquettes by a lattice version of Stokes’ theorem. For a contractible loop, the product of links along \(C\) equals the product of the plaquettes of any surface \(A\) bounded by \(C\), \[
\prod_{l\in C}\sigma_l = \prod_{p\in A}U_p .
\] In the product of plaquettes, every link inside \(A\) belongs to two plaquettes of \(A\) and appears squared, so only the boundary links remain.
The sketch below shows a rectangular loop \(\mathcal C\) of \(R=4\) by \(S=2\) lattice spacings. The product of the links along it equals the product of the eight plaquettes \(U_p\) of the enclosed area \(A\), because each interior link belongs to two of these plaquettes and drops out. How the average of this product decreases with the size of the loop, with its area or only with its perimeter, distinguishes the two phases of the gauge theory.

With independent plaquettes (open lattice, or the torus for \(N\to\infty\)) the Wilson loop therefore obeys an area law, \[
W(R,S) = \prod_{p\in A}\langle U_p\rangle = (\tanh\beta)^{RS} = e^{-\sigma_s\,RS},\qquad \sigma_s = -\ln\tanh\beta>0 .
\] On the finite torus the same projector trick as in Section 4.1 gives, with \(|A|\) plaquettes inside the loop, \[
\begin{aligned}
W_L(A) &= \frac{(2\sinh\beta)^{|A|}(2\cosh\beta)^{N-|A|} + (2\cosh\beta)^{|A|}(2\sinh\beta)^{N-|A|}}{(2\cosh\beta)^N+(2\sinh\beta)^N}\\
&= \frac{t^{|A|}+t^{N-|A|}}{1+t^N}.
\end{aligned}
\] The physical meaning of the area law comes from lattice gauge theory, where one lattice direction is (imaginary) time. A rectangle of spatial extent \(R\) and temporal extent \(S\) describes a pair of static external charges created at distance \(R\), held for a time \(S\) and annihilated. For large \(S\), \(W(R,S)\sim e^{-V(R)S}\) with \(V(R)\) the energy of the pair [Wilson 1974; Kogut 1979]. The area law gives \(V(R)=\sigma_sR\), so the energy grows linearly with the separation, and the charges can never be pulled apart. This is confinement, and the coefficient \(\sigma_s\) is the string tension. In 2D, \(\sigma_s>0\) at every finite \(\beta\), and the theory confines at every temperature.

# Stokes theorem on random configurations, and the torus Wilson-loop formula symbolically and by exact enumeration
def rect_loop(U, x, y, R, T):
    # product of links around the R x T rectangle with lower-left corner (x, y) in the plane (0, 1); U: (2, L, L) numpy
    L = U.shape[1]; p = 1
    for k in range(R): p *= U[0, (x + k) % L, y] * U[0, (x + k) % L, (y + T) % L]
    for k in range(T): p *= U[1, x, (y + k) % L] * U[1, (x + R) % L, (y + k) % L]
    return p

w = np.exp(bv * np.asarray(jax.vmap(lambda U: jnp.sum(plaquettes(U)))(jnp.asarray(Uall, jnp.float32)), dtype=np.float64))
for R, T in ((1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 2)):
    loop = np.prod(np.concatenate([Uall[:, 0, :R, 0], Uall[:, 0, :R, T], Uall[:, 1, 0, :T], Uall[:, 1, R, :T]], axis=1), axis=1)
    tv = np.tanh(bv)
    print(f"3x3 torus, beta = {bv}: W({R},{T}) enumeration = {(w * loop).sum() / w.sum():.12f}   "
          f"(t^A + t^(N-A))/(1+t^N) = {(tv**(R*T) + tv**(N - R*T)) / (1 + tv**N):.12f}")

We now measure Wilson loops in the Monte Carlo data. For square loops \(R\times R\) we average the loop product over all positions and both orientations of every configuration. The plot shows \(W(R,R)\) against the area \(A=R^2\) on a logarithmic axis, and the lines are \((\tanh\beta)^{A}\).


Code
def line_prod(a, mu, n):
    # product of n consecutive links of direction mu starting at x:  a = U[mu], shape (L..)
    out = jnp.ones_like(a)
    for k in range(n):
        out = out * shift(a, mu, k)
    return out

def wilson_loop(U, R, T):
    # average of the R x T loop product over positions and all ordered planes (mu, nu): R along mu, T along nu
    d, vals = U.shape[0], []
    for mu in range(d):
        for nu in range(d):
            if mu != nu:
                a, c = line_prod(U[mu], mu, R), line_prod(U[nu], nu, T)
                vals.append(jnp.mean(a * shift(c, mu, R) * shift(a, nu, T) * c))
    return jnp.mean(jnp.stack(vals))

_wilson_fns = {}
def wilson_table(links, Rmax, batch=256):
    # links: (n_samples, d, L..) int8 -> W[R-1, T-1] per sample, shape (n_samples, Rmax, Rmax); one compiled function per Rmax
    if Rmax not in _wilson_fns:
        _wilson_fns[Rmax] = jax.jit(jax.vmap(lambda U: jnp.stack([jnp.stack([wilson_loop(U, R, T) for T in range(1, Rmax + 1)])
                                                                  for R in range(1, Rmax + 1)])))
    f = _wilson_fns[Rmax]
    return np.concatenate([np.asarray(f(jnp.asarray(links[k:k + batch], jnp.float32))) for k in range(0, len(links), batch)])

L = 32

In 2D the Wilson loop decays exponentially with the area at every coupling, with string tension \(\sigma_s=-\ln\tanh\beta\) that is small at low \(T\) but never zero. A straight line on this logarithmic plot is the area law. At \(\beta=2.0\), for example, the measured \(W(6,6)=0.272\) compares with \((\tanh\beta)^{36}=0.267\), while at small \(\beta\) the large loops fall below the statistical noise of the data.


4.5 Topological sectors
The energy is minimal, \(E_0=-N_p\), when every plaquette is satisfied, \(U_p=+1\). On an open lattice this fixes the configuration up to a gauge transformation, so the ground states form one gauge orbit. On the torus the plaquettes do not fix the two holonomies \(W_x=\prod_{x}\sigma_0(x,y)\) and \(W_y=\prod_y\sigma_1(x,y)\) (Section 4.1). In a ground state, \(W_x\) does not depend on the row \(y\) where it is measured (two rows bound a strip of plaquettes, and by the Stokes argument their ratio is the product of these plaquettes, \(=+1\)), and it is gauge invariant. Hence the ground states split into \(2^2=4\) gauge-inequivalent topological sectors \((W_x,W_y)\in\{\pm1\}^2\), each a gauge orbit of \(2^{N-1}\) configurations, \[
\begin{aligned}
\#\{\text{ground states}\} &= 4\cdot 2^{N-1} = 2^{N+1}\ \text{configurations},\\
&\phantom{=}\ 4\ \text{physically distinct ground states}.
\end{aligned}
\] The number 4 does not depend on \(L\). It counts the independent non-contractible loops of the torus (\(2\) in 2D, \(d\) on a \(d\)-dimensional torus, giving \(2^d\) sectors). No local measurement distinguishes the sectors, since every plaquette is \(+1\) in all of them. This degeneracy is the classical counterpart of the topological ground-state degeneracy of Kitaev’s toric code [Kitaev 2003], whose ground states are built from the same closed-loop configurations.
We check the counting by exact enumeration on the \(3\times3\) torus in 2D (\(2^{18}\) configurations) and the \(2\times2\times2\) torus in 3D (\(24\) links, \(2^{24}\approx1.7\times10^{7}\) configurations).


Code
# 2D, 3x3 torus: ground states, their holonomies, and their gauge orbits
pm2 = np.array(plaquette_masks(2, 3), np.int64)
frustr = sum((np.bitwise_count(configs & m) & 1) for m in pm2)
gs = configs[frustr == 0]
Ugs = (1 - 2 * ((gs[:, None] >> np.arange(18)) & 1)).reshape(-1, 2, 3, 3)
sectors = np.stack([Ugs[:, 0, :, 0].prod(1), Ugs[:, 1, 0, :].prod(1)], 1)          # (W_x at y = 0, W_y at x = 0)
print(f"2D 3x3 torus: {gs.size} ground states (2^(N+1) = {2**10}),  gauge orbits among them: {np.unique(orbit_label[gs]).size}")
print("W_x independent of the row in every ground state:", bool(np.all(Ugs[:, 0].prod(1) == Ugs[:, 0, :, :1].prod(1))))
for s_ in itertools.product((1, -1), repeat=2):
    print(f"   sector (W_x, W_y) = ({s_[0]:+d}, {s_[1]:+d}): {int(np.all(sectors == s_, axis=1).sum())} configurations")

# 3D, 2x2x2 torus: 24 links, 24 plaquettes, expected 2^(N-1) * 2^3 = 1024 ground states

for start in range(0, 2**24, 2**21):

for k, (fx, fy) in enumerate(itertools.product((False, True), repeat=2)):

    if fx: Ur[0, 2, :] = -1          # horizontal links crossing the vertical line x = 2.5: flips W_x, keeps all plaquettes
    if fy: Ur[1, :, 3] = -1          # vertical links crossing the horizontal line y = 3.5: flips W_y

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





All four panels have every plaquette satisfied (no orange squares), the links look random because of the random gauge, and the only difference between them is the product of links along a loop that winds around the torus.
At nonzero temperature, however, the sectors are not protected in 2D. Frustrated plaquettes cost only \(2J\) each and are independent. Flipping one horizontal link of the row \(y\) creates (or removes) the two frustrated plaquettes above and below it and changes the sign of \(W_x\) measured on that row. A pair created in this way can separate and wander around the torus, so the value of \(W_x\) is not conserved. To see this we follow \(W_x\) on row \(y=0\) along Monte Carlo chains on an \(8\times8\) torus (raw chains without gauge randomisation, which \(W_x\) does not need because it is gauge invariant) and count how often it changes sign.


Code
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_sweeps",))
def trace_holonomy(U0, key, beta, masks, n_sweeps):
    # 2D: W_x measured on row y = 0 after every sweep, shape (n_sweeps,)
    def step(c, _):
        U, key = sweep(c[0], c[1], beta, masks)
        return (U, key), jnp.prod(U[0, :, 0])
    return lax.scan(step, (U0, key), None, length=n_sweeps)[1]

L, n_sw = 8, 20000
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for bv in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5):
    keys = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(int(bv * 10)), 4)
    tr = np.asarray(jax.vmap(lambda k: trace_holonomy(jnp.ones((2, L, L)), k, bv, parity_masks(2, L), n_sw))(keys))
    flips = (np.diff(tr, axis=1) != 0).sum(1)
    print(f"beta = {bv}: sign changes of W_x in {n_sw} sweeps (4 chains): {flips.tolist()}   <W_x> = {tr.mean():+.3f}")
print(f"({time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")

(9.7 s)


The sign changes become rarer as \(\beta\) grows (each needs a pair of frustrated plaquettes, of energy \(4J\) above the ground state), but they never stop, and \(\langle W_x\rangle\) stays close to zero. In 2D at \(T>0\) the sectors are mixed. The four-fold degeneracy is a property of the ground states.
In the two-dimensional model the plaquettes are independent, \(\langle U_p\rangle=\tanh\beta\) and \(c=\beta^2/\cosh^2\beta\) with no transition, Wilson loops obey the area law at all \(T\) (confinement), and the ground states form \(4\) topological sectors on the torus. In 3D the plaquettes are no longer independent, and this is what makes a phase transition possible.

title: Lab 031: Physics of the Ising lattice gauge theory
section: 5. The deconfinement transition in three dimensions
text:
5. The deconfinement transition in three dimensions

5.1 Flux loops
A three-dimensional lattice has elementary cubes, and they constrain the plaquettes. Each link of a cube lies on exactly two of its six faces. Therefore the product of the six face plaquettes is \(\prod\sigma_l^2=1\), so every cube has an even number of frustrated faces. In 3D the dual of a plaquette is a link of the dual lattice (the lattice of cube centres) piercing it, so the frustrated plaquettes form closed loops on the dual lattice, called flux loops. The smallest one is created by flipping a single link, which frustrates the \(4\) plaquettes around that link, a dual loop of length \(4\).
The competition between the energy and the entropy of flux loops drives a transition. A flux loop of length \(\ell\) costs \(2J\ell\), and the number of such loops grows exponentially with \(\ell\), as for the domain walls of the 2D Ising model (Lab 012, Section 3.3). At small \(T\) (large \(\beta\)) only small loops occur. At high \(T\) arbitrarily long loops proliferate, and between the two regimes there is a transition. In 2D there is no such constraint (a 2D lattice has no cubes), plaquettes are independent point defects, and no transition occurs.
The sketch below shows the smallest flux loop in three dimensions. One flipped link (orange) frustrates the four plaquettes around it, and the dual links that pierce these plaquettes (purple) form a closed square on the dual lattice.


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.

On a random configuration every cube product equals \(+1\), and a single flipped link frustrates exactly \(4\) plaquettes, the shortest flux loop.


5.2 Wegner duality
The derivation parallels Kramers–Wannier duality (Lab 012, Sections 4–5). Two expansions count the same geometric objects.
On the Ising side we use the high-temperature expansion. For \(H_I=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j\) on the cubic lattice at coupling \(K\), with \(e^{Kss'}=\cosh K(1+ss'\tanh K)\) (Lab 012, Section 4.1), \[
Z_I(K) = 2^N(\cosh K)^{3N}\sum_{G\ \text{closed}}(\tanh K)^{|G|},
\] the sum running over closed graphs \(G\) on the cubic lattice (every site touched by an even number of bonds of \(G\)), with \(|G|\) the number of bonds.
On the gauge side we use the low-temperature expansion. Start from all \(U_p=+1\), energy \(-3N\). A configuration whose frustrated plaquettes form the set \(F\) has weight \(e^{3N\beta}e^{-2\beta|F|}\). By Section 5.1, \(F\) is a set of closed loops on the dual lattice, which is again a simple cubic lattice. Every allowed \(F\) is realised by the same number of link configurations (one gauge orbit of size \(2^{N-1}\) times the \(2^3\) holonomy sectors), so \[
Z_g(\beta) = 2^{N-1}\,2^3\,e^{3N\beta}\sum_{F\ \text{closed on the dual lattice}}\big(e^{-2\beta}\big)^{|F|},
\] up to loops that wind around the torus, whose weight per site vanishes for \(N\to\infty\).
Both sums are the same function \(g(y)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\ln\sum_{G\ \rm closed}y^{|G|}\) of the cubic lattice. Hence, per site, \[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi_g(\beta) &\equiv \lim\frac{\ln Z_g}{N} = \ln2 + 3\beta + g\big(e^{-2\beta}\big),\\
\varphi_I(K) &= \ln2 + 3\ln\cosh K + g(\tanh K),
\end{aligned}
\] \[
\boxed{\ \tanh K = e^{-2\beta}\ }\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \varphi_g(\beta) - 3\beta = \varphi_I(K) - 3\ln\cosh K .
\] [F. J. Wegner, J. Math. Phys. 12, 2259 (1971); J. B. Kogut, Rev. Mod. Phys. 51, 659 (1979)] The map is decreasing. Weak gauge coupling (large \(\beta\), low \(T\)) corresponds to small \(K\), the disordered Ising phase, and vice versa. The 3D model is not self-dual (unlike the 2D Ising model). It is dual to a different model, and the free energies are equal up to analytic terms. So the gauge theory has a singularity exactly where the Ising model has one, of the same type.
The duality therefore maps the critical point of one model onto the critical point of the other. With the 3D Ising critical coupling from high-precision Monte Carlo, \(K_c^{I}=0.221654626(5)\) [Ferrenberg, Xu, Landau, Phys. Rev. E 97, 043301 (2018)], the critical coupling of the gauge theory is \[
\beta_c = -\tfrac12\ln\tanh K_c^{I},
\] which the cell below evaluates to \(\beta_c=0.761413\). Differentiating the boxed identity with respect to \(\beta\) (\(3N\) plaquettes and \(3N\) bonds per \(N\) sites) also gives a relation between quantities that can be measured in the two models, \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle U_p\rangle_g(\beta) &= 1 + \frac{dK}{d\beta}\Big(\langle s_is_j\rangle_I(K)-\tanh K\Big),\\
\frac{dK}{d\beta} &= -\frac{1}{\sinh2\beta},
\end{aligned}
\] where \(\langle s_is_j\rangle_I\) is the nearest-neighbour correlation of the Ising model. We derive it in SymPy and test it with two independent Monte Carlo simulations.

5.3 The duality energy relation
The energy relation connects two different models, so it can be tested with two independent simulations. We simulate the 3D Ising model at the dual couplings \(K(\beta)\), measure \(\langle s_is_j\rangle_I\), predict \(\langle U_p\rangle_g\) from the energy relation, and compare with direct gauge-theory Monte Carlo, both on \(L=8\) lattices. We stay away from \(\beta_c\), where finite-size effects differ between the two models.


Code
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_samples", "n_between"))
def ising_chains(s0, keys, Ks, chess, n_equil, n_samples, n_between):
    # per chain: nearest-neighbour correlation (1/3N) sum_<ij> s_i s_j of n_samples stored configurations, shape (chains, n_samples)
    def one(s, key, K):
        step = lambda c, _: (ising_sweep(c[0], c[1], K, chess), None)
        carry, _ = lax.scan(step, (s, key), None, length=n_equil)
        def store(c, _):
            c, _ = lax.scan(step, c, None, length=n_between)
            s = c[0]
            return c, sum(jnp.mean(s * jnp.roll(s, 1, a)) for a in range(3)) / 3
        return lax.scan(store, carry, None, length=n_samples)[1]
    return jax.vmap(one)(s0, keys, Ks)

5.5 Area law and perimeter law
The plaquette average shows that something happens at \(\beta_c\), and the Wilson loops show what. In the confined phase (\(\beta<\beta_c\), high \(T\)) flux loops proliferate, and every loop of the lattice is pierced by many of them at random. The Wilson loop then decays with the area, \(W(R,S)\sim e^{-\sigma_sRS}\), as in 2D. To leading order at small \(\beta\), \(W\approx(\tanh\beta)^{RS}\) (tile the minimal surface with plaquettes). In the deconfined phase (\(\beta>\beta_c\), low \(T\)) flux loops are small and rare. Only the small loops that pierce the surface close to its boundary contribute (a small loop deep inside pierces the surface twice and contributes \((-1)^2\)), so \(W(R,S)\sim e^{-2\kappa(R+S)}\), a perimeter law with a constant \(\kappa>0\).
Area and perimeter terms can be separated without fitting by the ratio proposed by Creutz [Creutz 1980], \[
\chi_{\rm C}(R,S) = -\ln\frac{W(R,S)\,W(R-1,S-1)}{W(R,S-1)\,W(R-1,S)} .
\] For \(W=e^{-\sigma_sRS-2\kappa(R+S)-c_0}\) the perimeter terms and the constant \(c_0\) cancel and \(\chi_{\rm C}=\sigma_s\) exactly. With a pure perimeter law \(\chi_{\rm C}=0\). With \(W(0,S)=W(R,0)=1\), \(\chi_{\rm C}(1,1)=-\ln W(1,1)=-\ln\langle U_p\rangle\). The figure and the printed table write the Creutz ratio as \(\chi(R,R)\).

The ratio \(\chi_{\rm C}(1,1)=-\ln\langle U_p\rangle\) contains the perimeter term and stays positive on both sides, so only the larger ratios measure the string tension. The ratios for larger loops are noisy, especially on the confined side, where \(W(R,R)\) is exponentially small.
This is a phase transition without a local order parameter. The two phases are told apart by how a non-local, gauge-invariant observable scales with the size of the loop.
The schematic below contrasts the two phases of the 3D model on a two-dimensional slice of links. In the confined phase (small \(\beta\), high temperature) the links are nearly random and about half of the plaquettes are frustrated. In the deconfined phase (large \(\beta\), low temperature) almost every plaquette is satisfied. The links nevertheless look random, because a random gauge transformation (Section 3) has been applied, and it leaves every plaquette unchanged. The difference between the phases is invisible in single links and appears only in plaquettes and Wilson loops.

                            solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=2 if s > 0 else 3)

def sketch_gauge_phases_configs():
    n = 7
    rng = np.random.default_rng(4)                                  # fixed seed: the same schematic every time
    # confined phase (small beta): links nearly independent, about half of the plaquettes frustrated
    U_conf = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=(2, n, n))
    # deconfined phase (large beta, 3D): all U_p = +1 except around one flipped link, seen through a random gauge

    g = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=(n, n))                            # random gauge transformation g(x) on every site
    U_dec[0, :-1, :] *= g[:-1, :] * g[1:, :]                        # horizontal link (x, y) -> (x+1, y)
    U_dec[1, :, :-1] *= g[:, :-1] * g[:, 1:]                        # vertical link (x, y) -> (x, y+1)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5.6))
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, bottom=0.02, top=0.8, wspace=0.1)

        draw_links_2d(ax, U, lw=2.0)
        P = U[0, :-1, :-1] * U[1, 1:, :-1] * U[0, :-1, 1:] * U[1, :-1, :-1]
        ax.set_title(f"{title}\nfraction of $U_p=-1$: {np.mean(P < 0):.2f}", fontsize=14, color=NAVY)
    return fig

with plt.rc_context({**SKETCH_STYLE, "figure.dpi": 100}):
    fig = sketch_gauge_phases_configs()
plt.show()





The phase diagram has a single control parameter, the coupling \(\beta=J/k_BT\), and is drawn below for two and three dimensions. In two dimensions the plaquettes are independent (Section 4), the Wilson loop obeys the area law with the string tension \(\sigma_s=-\ln\tanh\beta>0\) at every finite \(\beta\), and there is no phase transition, so the theory confines at all temperatures. In three dimensions the cube constraint of Section 5.1 makes the frustrated plaquettes form closed flux loops. Long loops proliferate at small \(\beta\), where the Wilson loop obeys the area law (confined phase), and are suppressed at large \(\beta\), where it obeys the perimeter law (deconfined phase). The two phases are separated at \(\beta_c=-\frac12\ln\tanh K_c^I=0.7614\), with \(K_c^I\) the critical coupling of the 3D Ising model (Section 5.2).
The transition is continuous. At a first-order transition a first derivative of the free energy would jump. At a continuous transition the first derivatives are continuous, and the correlation length diverges as a power of \(|\beta-\beta_c|\) with exponents shared by a whole universality class. Wegner duality equates the free energy of the gauge theory with that of the 3D Ising model up to analytic terms, so the singularity at \(\beta_c\) is exactly the 3D Ising singularity. The transition is therefore continuous and belongs to the 3D Ising universality class, although the gauge theory has no local order parameter.

title: Lab 031: Physics of the Ising lattice gauge theory
text:
6. Gauge redundancy
Elitzur’s argument extends to any product of links. Let \(S\) be a set of links and \(\sigma_S=\prod_{l\in S}\sigma_l\). A gauge transformation at site \(x\) multiplies \(\sigma_S\) by \(\gamma(x)^{n_x(S)}\), where \(n_x(S)\) is the number of links of \(S\) touching \(x\). So \(\sigma_S\) is gauge invariant only if every \(n_x(S)\) is even, that is, if \(S\) is a closed set of loops. Otherwise the argument of Section 3.2 gives \(\langle\sigma_S\rangle=0\). This has two consequences for data analysis.
The first is that every single link averages to zero and every pair of distinct links is uncorrelated, \(\langle\sigma_l\rangle=0\) and \(\langle\sigma_l\sigma_{l'}\rangle=\delta_{ll'}\), because two distinct links never form a closed loop. The covariance matrix of the raw links is the identity matrix at every temperature. Any method that uses only means and covariances of the raw variables (a linear classifier, principal component analysis (PCA), a Gaussian model) sees the same featureless data at every \(\beta\).
The second is that the smallest non-trivial correlations involve four links around a plaquette. A model on raw links has to discover four-point products, and a model that is not built to look at neighbouring links together (a fully connected network has no notion of which links are neighbours) faces a search over a huge number of possible combinations. A convolution with a small kernel sees one plaquette at a time, which is consistent with the CNN result of Carrasquilla and Melko.
Gauge-invariant features avoid the problem. Plaquettes \(U_p\) (local, gauge invariant) and Wilson loops (non-local, gauge invariant) carry all the physical information, and feeding plaquettes instead of links removes the redundancy by construction.
We check the first statement on the 3D data, comparing the covariance of raw links with the covariance of plaquettes, pooled over all couplings.


Code
L = 8
links = ds3[L]["links"]                                            # (n_beta, n_samples, 3, L, L, L)

X_links = links.reshape(n_b * n_s, -1).astype(np.float32)          # (n_beta * n_samples, 3 L^3)  raw features
X_plaq = np.asarray(jax.vmap(plaquettes)(jnp.asarray(links.reshape((-1, 3) + (L,) * 3), jnp.float32))).reshape(n_b * n_s, -1)
beta_of_row = np.repeat(BETAS_3D, n_s)
print("raw links:", X_links.shape, "  plaquettes:", X_plaq.shape, "  (rows = configurations, columns = features)")

X_noise = rng.choice(np.array([-1.0, 1.0], np.float32), size=X_links.shape)   # independent random +-1 entries, same shape
for name, X in (("raw links", X_links), ("plaquettes", X_plaq), ("pure noise", X_noise)):
    C = np.cov(X, rowvar=False)
    off = C - np.diag(np.diag(C))
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(C)[::-1]
    print(f"{name:10s}: mean = {X.mean():+.4f}   diag(C) in [{np.diag(C).min():.3f}, {np.diag(C).max():.3f}]   max |off-diagonal| = {np.abs(off).max():.3f}"
          f"   top eigenvalues = {np.round(ev[:3], 2)}   median eigenvalue = {np.median(ev):.3f}")

# per coupling: link correlations of neighbouring links stay zero, plaquette mean carries beta
print("\n beta   <sigma_l>    <sigma_l sigma_l'> (two links of one plaquette)    <U_p>")
for bv in (0.4, 0.76, 1.1):

    pair = (Ul[:, 0] * np.roll(Ul[:, 1], -1, axis=1)).mean()        # sigma_0(x) sigma_1(x + e_0): two sides of plaquette (x; 01)

# projection on the leading principal component of the pooled data, against beta
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.5))
for a, (name, X) in zip(ax, (("raw links", X_links), ("plaquettes", X_plaq))):
    Xc = X - X.mean(0)
    v1 = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(X, rowvar=False))[1][:, -1]           # leading eigenvector of the covariance
    pc1 = Xc @ v1 / np.sqrt(X.shape[1])
    a.plot(beta_of_row + rng.normal(0, 0.004, beta_of_row.size), pc1, ".", ms=1, alpha=0.3, color=UJBlue)
    a.axvline(BETA_C, color=DSOrange, ls=":", lw=1.5)
    a.set_xlabel(r"$\beta$"); a.set_ylabel(r"$\mathrm{PC1}=v_1\cdot(x-\bar x)/\sqrt{D}$"); a.set_title(f"{name}, $L={L}$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The covariance of the raw links is the identity matrix up to sampling noise. Its diagonal, its largest off-diagonal entry (\(0.032\)) and its eigenvalue range coincide with those of a matrix of independent random \(\pm1\) entries of the same shape (\(0.028\) for the largest off-diagonal entry). The spread of the eigenvalues around \(1\) is a finite-sample effect of estimating a \(D\times D\) covariance, with \(D=3L^3=1536\) features, from a finite number of rows. For plaquettes one eigenvalue (\(78.5\)) stands out. Every plaquette has the same mean, so its eigenvector is expected to lie close to the uniform vector, and the projection on it then measures the plaquette average.
The figure shows, for every configuration, the first principal coordinate \(w^{(1)}/\sqrt D\), labelled PC1, against \(\beta\), for raw links (left) and plaquettes (right). Here \(w^{(1)}=v_1\cdot(x-\bar x)\) is the projection of the centred feature vector \(x\) on the leading eigenvector \(v_1\) of the pooled covariance. For raw links it is a random direction whose coordinate has the same distribution at every \(\beta\). For plaquettes it tracks \(\beta\) and changes fastest around \(\beta_c\).
This is the starting point of the anomaly-detection study of Lab 022, which uses the data sets saved here and compares representations (raw links, plaquettes, Wilson loops) by whether an unsupervised model detects that something changes at \(\beta_c\).

Exercises

Exercise 1 — Open strings
Take the product of links along an open straight path of length \(n\) (a “string”), \(S_n(x)=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\sigma_0(x+k\hat e_0)\). Show that it is not gauge invariant and that \(\langle S_n\rangle=0\), then check it on the 2D data at large \(\beta\). Compare with the closed loop \(W(n,1)\), which contains the same string as one of its sides.

Solution


Code
# the gauge transformation at the starting site x flips only the first link of the string: S_n -> -S_n, hence <S_n> = 0
L = 32; i = int(np.argmin(np.abs(BETAS_2D - 2.0)))
Ul = jnp.asarray(ds2[L]["links"][i], jnp.float32)
for n in (1, 2, 3):
    Sn = float(jnp.mean(jax.vmap(lambda U: line_prod(U[0], 0, n))(Ul)))
    W1n = float(jnp.mean(jax.vmap(lambda U: wilson_loop(U, n, 1))(Ul)))
    print(f"beta = {BETAS_2D[i]}: open string of length {n}: <S_n> = {Sn:+.4f};   closed loop W({n},1) = {W1n:.4f}  (tanh^{n} = {np.tanh(BETAS_2D[i])**n:.4f})")

In \(S_n\) the starting site \(x\) and the end site \(x+n\hat e_0\) each touch one link of the path, the inner sites two. A gauge transformation with \(\gamma=-1\) only at \(x\) multiplies \(S_n\) by \(-1\) and leaves the weight unchanged, so \(\langle S_n\rangle=-\langle S_n\rangle=0\). Closing the path into a loop makes every site touch an even number of its links, and the average becomes \((\tanh\beta)^{\rm area}\).



Exercise 2 — Partition function of a strip
Using the maximal-tree argument, predict \(Z\) for an open lattice of \(2\times3\) plaquettes and verify it with plaquette_sum_histogram and SymPy.

Solution


Code
# open lattice of Lx x Ly plaquettes: (Lx+1)(Ly+1) sites, Lx(Ly+1) + (Lx+1)Ly links;  Z = 2^(sites-1) (2 cosh beta)^(Lx Ly)

h = {(x, y): k for k, (x, y) in enumerate((x, y) for x in range(Lx) for y in range(Ly + 1))}

n_l, n_sites = len(h) + len(v), (Lx + 1) * (Ly + 1)
print(f"links = {n_l}, sites = {n_sites}, free links after tree gauge = {n_l - (n_sites - 1)} = plaquettes = {Lx * Ly}")

Exercise 4 — Strong-coupling expansion in 3D
For small \(\beta\) write \(e^{\beta U_p}=\cosh\beta\,(1+tU_p)\), \(t=\tanh\beta\), for every plaquette and expand the product. Summing over links, only sets of plaquettes in which every link appears an even number of times survive, and these form closed surfaces. In 2D on the infinite lattice there are none, which gives \(\langle U_p\rangle=t\) exactly. In 3D the smallest closed surface is the boundary of a cube (6 plaquettes, with \(N\) such cubes on the lattice). Show that \[
\langle U_p\rangle = t + 2t^5 + O(t^7)
\] and compare with the Monte Carlo data at small \(\beta\).

Solution


Code
# Z = (cosh b)^(3N) 2^(3N) [1 + N t^6 + ...];  <U_p> = (1/3N) d ln Z / d b = t + (1/3N) (1 - t^2) d/dt ln(1 + N t^6) = t + 2 t^5 (1 - t^2) + ...
# ln Z per site to this order: 3 ln(2 cosh b) (3 plaquettes, 3 links per site) + tanh(b)^6 (one cube per site)
lnZ_site = 3 * sp.log(2 * sp.cosh(b)) + sp.tanh(b)**6
U_sc = sp.simplify(sp.diff(lnZ_site, b) / 3)                      # <U_p> = (1/3) d(ln Z / N)/d beta
U_sc_t = sp.simplify(U_sc.subs(b, sp.atanh(t)))
print("<U_p> =", U_sc_t, "=", sp.expand(U_sc_t), "  -> series:", sp.series(U_sc_t, t, 0, 7))
L = 10
for bv in (0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50):
    i = int(np.argmin(np.abs(BETAS_3D - bv))); tv = np.tanh(BETAS_3D[i])
    print(f"beta = {BETAS_3D[i]:.2f}:  MC {st3[L]['U'][i]:.5f} +- {st3[L]['dU'][i]:.5f}   t = {tv:.5f}   t + 2t^5 = {tv + 2 * tv**5:.5f}")


<U_p> = -2*t**7 + 2*t**5 + t = -2*t**7 + 2*t**5 + t   -> series: t + 2*t**5 + O(t**7)
beta = 0.30:  MC 0.29470 +- 0.00066   t = 0.29131   t + 2t^5 = 0.29551
beta = 0.35:  MC 0.34399 +- 0.00062   t = 0.33638   t + 2t^5 = 0.34499
beta = 0.40:  MC 0.39474 +- 0.00046   t = 0.37995   t + 2t^5 = 0.39579
beta = 0.45:  MC 0.44650 +- 0.00051   t = 0.42190   t + 2t^5 = 0.44863
beta = 0.50:  MC 0.50192 +- 0.00063   t = 0.46212   t + 2t^5 = 0.50427


Expanding the product gives \(Z=(\cosh\beta)^{3N}2^{3N}\sum_{\text{closed surfaces}}t^{|S|}=(\cosh\beta)^{3N}2^{3N}(1+Nt^6+\dots)\), with \(3N\) links giving the factor \(2^{3N}\). Then \(\langle U_p\rangle=\frac1{3N}\frac{\partial\ln Z}{\partial\beta}=t+\frac{1-t^2}{3N}\frac{6Nt^5}{1+Nt^6}+\dots=t+2t^5+O(t^7)\) (the \(N^2\) terms of pairs of cubes cancel in \(\ln Z\), as in Lab 012, Section 4). At \(\beta\le0.4\) the Monte Carlo data follow \(t+2t^5\) better than \(t\) alone. The deviation grows as \(\beta\) approaches the transition, where the expansion fails.



Exercise 5 (open) — Wilson loops in the dual Ising model
The duality maps the Wilson loop \(W(C)\) of the gauge theory to an Ising quantity, the ratio \(Z_I^{(C)}/Z_I\), where \(Z_I^{(C)}\) is the Ising partition function with the couplings of all bonds piercing a surface bounded by \(C\) reversed in sign (a frustrated “seam”). Argue why the area law of the gauge theory corresponds to the ordered Ising phase (the seam costs an energy proportional to its area) and the perimeter law to the disordered phase.
