title: Lab 032: Physics of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glass
text:
1. Disorder and frustration

1.1 Glassy magnets
The name spin glass was coined for metallic alloys of a non-magnetic metal with a few percent of randomly substituted magnetic atoms, such as iron in gold [Cannella & Mydosh 1972] or manganese in copper. Experiments found a low-temperature phase in which the magnetic moments freeze in non-periodic directions, with a very slow, strongly history-dependent response to external perturbations [Binder & Young 1986; Billoire 2007].
The moments interact through the conduction electrons. A standard model of this interaction is the RKKY (Ruderman–Kittel–Kasuya–Yosida) coupling \[
J(r)\propto\frac{\cos(2k_F r)}{r^3},
\] with \(k_F\) the Fermi wave number. Its sign oscillates with the distance \(r\). Combined with random positions of the magnetic atoms, any such coupling produces couplings of random sign. Some pairs prefer to be parallel (ferromagnetic, \(J>0\)), others antiparallel (antiferromagnetic, \(J<0\)). The positions are fixed when the alloy is made, so the couplings are random but frozen, or quenched. The cell below shows the random signs. \(n\) moments are placed uniformly at random in a cube, and we histogram the factor that carries the sign, \(\cos(2k_Fr_{ij})\), for the strongest couplings (pairs at distances \(1<r_{ij}<3\) in units of the lattice constant, with \(k_F=3\), although any value of order a few gives the same picture).


Code
def rkky(r, kF=3.0):
    # RKKY-like coupling: magnitude 1/r^3, sign oscillating with the distance r
    return np.cos(2 * kF * r) / r**3

n_moments, box = 400, 20.0
pos = rng.uniform(0, box, size=(n_moments, 3))                      # (n_moments, 3) random positions of the magnetic atoms
diff = pos[:, None, :] - pos[None, :, :]                            # (n_moments, n_moments, 3) pair separations
r_pairs = np.sqrt((diff**2).sum(-1))[np.triu_indices(n_moments, 1)] # all pair distances, each pair once
near = (r_pairs > 1) & (r_pairs < 3)                                 # the strongest couplings

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2))
rr = np.linspace(1, 6, 1000)
ax[0].plot(rr, rkky(rr), color=UJBlue, lw=2); ax[0].axhline(0, color=UJGray, lw=0.8)
ax[0].set_ylim(-0.12, 0.12); ax[0].set_xlabel("distance $r$"); ax[0].set_ylabel("$J(r)$"); ax[0].set_title("oscillating coupling")
ax[1].hist(np.cos(6.0 * r_pairs[near]), bins=40, color=UJBlue, alpha=0.85); ax[1].axvline(0, color=DSOrange, ls=":")
ax[1].set_xlabel(r"sign-carrying factor $\cos(2k_F r_{ij})$"); ax[1].set_ylabel("number of pairs")
ax[1].set_title("couplings between random positions, $1<r_{ij}<3$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"pairs with 1 < r < 3: {near.sum()};  fraction with J > 0 (ferromagnetic): {np.mean(rkky(r_pairs[near]) > 0):.3f},"
      f"  fraction with J < 0 (antiferromagnetic): {np.mean(rkky(r_pairs[near]) < 0):.3f}")





pairs with 1 < r < 3: 945;  fraction with J > 0 (ferromagnetic): 0.433,  fraction with J < 0 (antiferromagnetic): 0.567


Both signs occur in comparable numbers (43% ferromagnetic and 57% antiferromagnetic pairs in this example). The SK model keeps this ingredient, random signs, and drops the geometry. Every spin is coupled to every other spin, with a Gaussian random coupling.


1.2 Hard optimisation problems
Finding the lowest-energy configuration of \(E(\boldsymbol s)=-\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}s_is_j\) for given couplings is a combinatorial optimisation problem over \(2^N\) configurations. With the couplings chosen appropriately, many classic hard problems of computer science (graph partitioning, maximum cut, satisfiability, all of Karp’s 21 NP-complete problems, where NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time) can be expressed in this form [Lucas 2014]. The computational complexity of finding spin-glass ground states was analysed early by Barahona [Barahona 1982]. Conversely, spin-glass physics produced general-purpose algorithms. Simulated annealing [Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi 1983] was proposed by one of the two authors of the SK model, and the parallel-tempering method used in Section 5 was designed for spin glasses [Hukushima & Nemoto 1996].


1.3 Energy landscapes in machine learning
A network of binary units with symmetric weights \(W_{ij}\) and energy \(E(\boldsymbol s)=-\frac12\sum_{ij}W_{ij}s_is_j\) is the Hopfield network [Hopfield 1982], which has the same Hamiltonian with couplings constructed from data instead of drawn at random. The loss function of a neural network is likewise a function on a very high-dimensional space with many local minima. The SK model is the solvable prototype of such a rugged landscape, with exponentially many minima, barriers between them and slow dynamics. The vocabulary developed for it (metastable states, overlaps between minima, replicas) is used throughout the theory of learning [Mézard & Montanari 2009; Charbonneau et al. 2023].
In this notebook the spins have no positions at all. The SK model has no lattice, so there is no spatial pattern to look at. We will see that the low-temperature phase is nevertheless sharply defined, and that the right tool to see it is a comparison of two independent copies of the system with the same couplings.

title: Lab 032: Physics of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glass
text:
2. The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model

2.1 The Hamiltonian
The model consists of \(N\) Ising spins \(s_i=\pm1\), \(i=1,\dots,N\), and every pair \((i,j)\) is coupled, \[
\begin{aligned}
H(\boldsymbol s) &= -\sum_{i<j} J_{ij}\, s_i s_j = -\frac12\,\boldsymbol s^{T} J\, \boldsymbol s ,\\
J_{ij}&=J_{ji}\sim\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{J^2}{N}\right)\ \text{independent for } i<j,\qquad J_{ii}=0 .
\end{aligned}
\] Here \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is the Gaussian distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). The mean is zero, so ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic couplings are equally likely. A fixed matrix \(J\) is called a disorder realisation or sample.
The figure below draws one sample with \(N=8\) spins placed on a circle. The positions carry no meaning, since the model has no lattice. Every pair is connected. A solid blue line is a ferromagnetic coupling \(J_{ij}>0\), a dashed green line an antiferromagnetic coupling \(J_{ij}<0\), and the line width is proportional to \(|J_{ij}|\). The spins follow the convention of all sketches in this course (navy disc \(s_i=+1\), white disc with an orange rim \(s_i=-1\)).


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;
#   satisfied bond: solid blue line, broken (frustrated) bond: dashed purple line marked with a cross.
# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (5.5 in = full text width) with 10-12 pt text,
# and shown here at a higher screen resolution.
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

NAVY, ORANGE, BLUE, GRAY, PURPLE, GREEN = "#002B5C", "#D35A05", "#005CA7", "#5A6270", "#AA3377", "#228833"
SKETCH_STYLE = {"font.size": 11, "axes.titlesize": 12, "axes.labelsize": 11, "xtick.labelsize": 10,
                "ytick.labelsize": 10, "legend.fontsize": 10, "figure.dpi": 130, "lines.linewidth": 1.5,
                "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}

def save_sketch(fig, name, extra_dirs=()):
    # PNG copy for the lecture slides: white background, 300 dpi, included at its physical width
    os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
    for d in ("figures",) + tuple(d for d in extra_dirs if os.path.isdir(d)):
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, name), dpi=300, facecolor="white")

def draw_spin(ax, x, y, s, r=0.26, sign=False, alpha=1.0, fs=10, lw=1.3):
    # one Ising spin at (x, y): navy disc for s = +1, white disc with orange rim for s = -1 (optionally with "+" / "-")
    face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if s > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
    ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x, y), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=lw, alpha=alpha, zorder=4))
    if sign:
        ax.text(x, y, "+" if s > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", alpha=alpha,
                fontsize=fs, fontweight="bold", zorder=5)

def draw_bond(ax, p, q, broken=False, lw=1.5, alpha=1.0, color=None, cross=True):
    # bond between points p and q: solid blue if satisfied, dashed purple with a cross if broken
    c = color or (PURPLE if broken else BLUE)
    ax.plot([p[0], q[0]], [p[1], q[1]], color=c, lw=lw, ls=(0, (2.5, 1.5)) if broken else "-",
            alpha=alpha, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=2)
    if broken and cross:
        ax.plot((p[0] + q[0]) / 2, (p[1] + q[1]) / 2, marker="x", ms=3.5 * lw, mew=lw * 0.9, color=c, alpha=alpha, zorder=3)

def sketch_sk_model():
    N = 8
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)                                  # one fixed disorder sample and spin configuration
    Jm = np.triu(rng.normal(0.0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(N), (N, N)), 1)      # J_ij ~ N(0, J^2/N) for i < j, with J = 1
    s = rng.choice([-1, 1], N)
    phi = np.pi / 2 - 2 * np.pi * np.arange(N) / N
    X, Y = np.cos(phi), np.sin(phi)
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.9))
    ax = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.0, 0.45, 1.0]); tx = fig.add_axes([0.46, 0.0, 0.54, 1.0]); tx.axis("off")
    # every pair is coupled: blue solid for J_ij > 0 (ferromagnetic), green dashed for J_ij < 0; width proportional to |J_ij|
    scale = 4.0 / np.abs(Jm).max()
    for i in range(N):
        for j in range(i + 1, N):
            ax.plot([X[i], X[j]], [Y[i], Y[j]], color=BLUE if Jm[i, j] > 0 else GREEN, lw=0.3 + scale * abs(Jm[i, j]),
                    ls="-" if Jm[i, j] > 0 else (0, (3, 1.5)), alpha=0.85, zorder=1)
    for i in range(N):
        draw_spin(ax, X[i], Y[i], s[i], r=0.11, lw=1.2)
        ax.text(1.25 * X[i], 1.25 * Y[i], f"$s_{i + 1}$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, color=NAVY)
    ax.set_xlim(-1.4, 1.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.4, 1.4); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

    tx.set_xlim(0, 1); tx.set_ylim(0, 1)
    tx.text(0.0, 0.88, r"$H=-\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\,s_i\,s_j$", fontsize=12, color=NAVY, va="center")
    tx.text(0.0, 0.72, r"$J_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\,J^2/N)$, independent", fontsize=12, color=NAVY, va="center")
    tx.text(0.0, 0.6, r"every pair of the $N$ spins is coupled", fontsize=10, color=GRAY, va="center")
    tx.plot([0.0, 0.12], [0.44, 0.44], color=BLUE, lw=2.5)
    tx.text(0.16, 0.44, r"$J_{ij}>0$: prefers $s_i=s_j$", fontsize=11, va="center")
    tx.plot([0.0, 0.12], [0.31, 0.31], color=GREEN, lw=2.5, ls=(0, (3, 1.5)))
    tx.text(0.16, 0.31, r"$J_{ij}<0$: prefers $s_i=-s_j$", fontsize=11, va="center")
    tx.text(0.0, 0.15, r"line width $\propto|J_{ij}|$,  spins $s_i=\pm1$", fontsize=10, color=GRAY, va="center")
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_sk_model()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_sk_card.png")
plt.show()





Two quantities are used throughout. The local field on spin \(i\) is \(h_i=\sum_{j\neq i}J_{ij}s_j\), so that \(H=-\frac12\sum_i s_ih_i\). A flip \(s_i\to-s_i\) changes the sign of only the \(N-1\) terms containing \(s_i\), so the energy change of one flip is \(\Delta E_i = 2s_ih_i\). A configuration is therefore stable against every single flip if and only if \(s_ih_i>0\) for all \(i\), that is, if every spin is aligned with its local field.


2.2 Scaling of the couplings
The variance is chosen as \(J^2/N\), not \(J^2\), and the reason is the size of the local field. Take any fixed configuration \(\boldsymbol s\). Then \(J_{ij}s_j\) has the same Gaussian distribution as \(J_{ij}\) (the distribution is symmetric under \(J\to-J\)), so the local field is a sum of \(N-1\) independent Gaussians, \[
\operatorname{Var}(h_i) = (N-1)\,\sigma^2,\qquad \sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(J_{ij}).
\] With \(\sigma^2=J^2/N\) we get \(\operatorname{Var}(h_i)=J^2(N-1)/N\to J^2\). The field on a spin stays of order one as \(N\) grows, temperatures of order \(J\) compete with it, and the transition temperature has a finite limit. Without the scaling, \(\sigma^2=J^2\), the field would grow like \(\sqrt N\,J\), and so would every characteristic temperature, leaving no thermodynamic limit. A ferromagnet with all-to-all couplings needs \(J_{ij}=J_0/N\) (the Curie–Weiss model), because there the \(N\) terms add coherently, \(h_i=J_0m\). Random signs add incoherently, like a random walk, so the coupling is scaled by \(1/\sqrt N\) in magnitude, i.e. \(1/N\) in variance.
The energy of a configuration is \(H=-\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}s_is_j\), a sum of \(N(N-1)/2\) independent terms. For a random configuration it has mean \(0\) and variance \(\frac{N(N-1)}2\,\sigma^2 = \frac{(N-1)J^2}{2}\), so a typical configuration has energy of order \(\sqrt N\). The low-energy configurations, which dominate at low temperature, have energies of order \(-N\) (Section 6). The energy is extensive.
We check these statements symbolically with SymPy (the Gaussian moments by direct integration, then the sums by independence) and then numerically.


Code
x = sp.symbols("x", real=True)
sigma, Jc, N_s, alpha = sp.symbols("sigma J N alpha", positive=True)

gauss = sp.exp(-x**2 / (2 * sigma**2)) / sp.sqrt(2 * sp.pi * sigma**2)    # density of N(0, sigma^2)
moment = lambda k: sp.simplify(sp.integrate(x**k * gauss, (x, -sp.oo, sp.oo)))
print("normalisation   :", moment(0))
print("E[J_ij]         :", moment(1))
print("E[J_ij^2]       :", moment(2))
print("E[J_ij^4]       :", moment(4))

# independent terms: the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances
var_h = (N_s - 1) * moment(2)                       # local field: N-1 couplings
var_H = N_s * (N_s - 1) / 2 * moment(2)             # energy of a random configuration: N(N-1)/2 couplings
print("\nVar(h_i)               =", var_h)
print("Var(H), random config  =", var_H)

var_h_SK = sp.simplify(var_h.subs(sigma**2, Jc**2 / N_s))
print("\nwith sigma^2 = J^2/N:  Var(h_i) =", var_h_SK, "  ->  N -> oo:", sp.limit(var_h_SK, N_s, sp.oo))
print("with sigma^2 = J^2/N:  Var(H)   =", sp.simplify(var_H.subs(sigma**2, Jc**2 / N_s)))

# general scaling sigma^2 = J^2 / N^alpha: the field has a finite, non-zero limit only for alpha = 1
var_h_alpha = var_h.subs(sigma**2, Jc**2 / N_s**alpha)
for a in (sp.Rational(1, 2), 1, 2):
    print(f"alpha = {a}:  Var(h_i) = {sp.simplify(var_h_alpha.subs(alpha, a))}  ->  N -> oo: {sp.limit(var_h_alpha.subs(alpha, a), N_s, sp.oo)}")


normalisation   : 1
E[J_ij]         : 0


E[J_ij^2]       : sigma**2
E[J_ij^4]       : 3*sigma**4

Var(h_i)               = sigma**2*(N - 1)
Var(H), random config  = N*sigma**2*(N - 1)/2

with sigma^2 = J^2/N:  Var(h_i) = J**2*(N - 1)/N   ->  N -> oo: J**2
with sigma^2 = J^2/N:  Var(H)   = J**2*(N - 1)/2
alpha = 1/2:  Var(h_i) = J**2*(N - 1)/sqrt(N)  ->  N -> oo: oo

def sk_couplings(key, n_dis, N, J=1.0):
    """n_dis independent SK coupling matrices, shape (n_dis, N, N): symmetric, zero diagonal, J_ij ~ N(0, J^2/N)."""
    A = jax.random.normal(key, (n_dis, N, N)) * (J / jnp.sqrt(N))
    upper = jnp.triu(A, 1)                                   # keep i < j only
    return upper + jnp.swapaxes(upper, 1, 2)                 # J_ji = J_ij, J_ii = 0

def random_spins(key, shape):
    """Uniformly random configurations s_i = +-1 (float32)."""
    return jnp.where(jax.random.bernoulli(key, 0.5, shape), 1.0, -1.0)

2.3 Global flip and gauge symmetry
The Hamiltonian has two symmetries. The first is the global flip, \(H(-\boldsymbol s)=H(\boldsymbol s)\) for every sample, hence \(\langle s_i\rangle=0\) exactly at any finite \(N\). The second is a gauge transformation. Choose any signs \(\gamma_i=\pm1\) and transform \[
s_i\to\gamma_is_i,\qquad J_{ij}\to\gamma_i\gamma_jJ_{ij}.
\] Each term \(J_{ij}s_is_j\to\gamma_i^2\gamma_j^2J_{ij}s_is_j=J_{ij}s_is_j\) is unchanged, so the energy of every configuration is unchanged. Because the Gaussian distribution of \(J_{ij}\) is symmetric, the transformed couplings \(\gamma_i\gamma_jJ_{ij}\) moreover have the same distribution as the original ones.
The gauge symmetry constrains disorder averages. Every quantity averaged over the disorder must be invariant under the transformation. The magnetisation of a sample, \(\frac1N\sum_i\langle s_i\rangle\), is not invariant (\(s_i\to\gamma_is_i\) flips arbitrary spins), so it carries no information about the ordering after averaging over samples. The invariant combinations are products in which every spin index appears twice, such as \(\langle s_is_j\rangle^2\) or, for two copies \(a,b\) of the system, \(s_i^as_i^b\). These are the building blocks of the spin-glass order parameter (Section 4). The cell below verifies the invariance symbolically for \(N=4\) and numerically for one sample of \(N=200\) spins, where the energy is unchanged and the magnetisation is not.

2.4 Quenched disorder
A spin glass has two sources of randomness, on two very different time scales. The first is thermal noise. At fixed couplings \(J\) the spins fluctuate, and thermal averages are Boltzmann averages at fixed \(J\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle A\rangle_J&=\frac{1}{Z_J}\sum_{\boldsymbol s}A(\boldsymbol s)\,e^{-\beta H_J(\boldsymbol s)},\\
Z_J&=\sum_{\boldsymbol s}e^{-\beta H_J(\boldsymbol s)} .
\end{aligned}
\] The second is the disorder itself. The couplings are random but frozen (quenched). In the alloy the atoms do not move on the time scale of the spin dynamics. The average over realisations, \([X]=\int\!\prod_{i<j}dJ_{ij}\,P(J_{ij})\;X(J)\), is therefore taken after the thermal average, sample by sample.
The physically relevant free energy is the quenched average \[
f=-\frac{T}{N}\,[\ln Z_J],
\] not the annealed one, \(f_{\rm ann}=-\frac{T}{N}\ln[Z_J]\), which would describe couplings that fluctuate and equilibrate together with the spins. The reason the quenched average is the meaningful one is self-averaging. As \(N\to\infty\), the free energy per spin of a single large sample, \(-\frac{T}{N}\ln Z_J\), converges to its disorder average. One large sample is representative. \(Z_J\) itself is not self-averaging. It is exponential in \(N\) and its average is dominated by rare samples.
The logarithm is concave, so Jensen’s inequality gives \([\ln Z_J]\le\ln[Z_J]\), that is, \(f\ge f_{\rm ann}\).
The annealed free energy, unlike the quenched one, can be computed exactly. The average of \(Z\) is easy, because the couplings are independent and appear in the exponent, \[
\begin{aligned}
[Z_J] &= \sum_{\boldsymbol s}\prod_{i<j}\big[e^{\beta J_{ij}s_is_j}\big],\\
\big[e^{\beta J_{ij}s_is_j}\big]&=e^{\beta^2\sigma^2/2}\quad(\text{Gaussian integral; independent of } s_is_j=\pm1).
\end{aligned}
\] Every configuration contributes the same factor, so \([Z_J]=2^N\exp\!\big(\frac{N(N-1)}2\frac{\beta^2J^2}{2N}\big)\) and, for \(N\to\infty\), \[
\begin{aligned}
-\beta f_{\rm ann}&=\ln2+\frac{\beta^2J^2}{4},\\
u_{\rm ann}&=-\frac{\beta J^2}2,\\
s_{\rm ann}&=\ln2-\frac{\beta^2J^2}{4}.
\end{aligned}
\] The annealed entropy becomes negative below \(T^*=J/(2\sqrt{\ln2})\). The entropy of a system with a finite number of discrete states is \(-\sum p\ln p\ge0\), so the annealed result must fail at low temperature. Aizenman, Lebowitz and Ruelle proved that for \(T>J\) the quenched free energy equals the annealed one in the limit \(N\to\infty\) [Aizenman, Lebowitz & Ruelle 1987]. The high-temperature phase is therefore simple, and the annealed description breaks down at \(T=J\). We derive the annealed results with SymPy and then compare them with exact enumeration of small systems.

def half_configs(N):
    """All 2^(N-1) configurations with s_N = +1, shape (2^(N-1), N), float32."""
    k = jnp.arange(2 ** (N - 1), dtype=jnp.int32)
    bits = (k[:, None] >> jnp.arange(N - 1)) & 1
    return jnp.concatenate([2.0 * bits - 1.0, jnp.ones((k.size, 1))], axis=1)

@jax.jit
def enumerate_sample(J, betas, betas_chi):
    """Exact thermodynamics of one sample J (N, N).
    Returns ln Z (n_T,), U (n_T,), E0, number of single-flip-stable configurations, chi_SG (n_chi,)."""
    N = J.shape[0]
    S = half_configs(N)                                        # (M, N)
    Hf = S @ J                                                 # (M, N) local fields
    E = -0.5 * jnp.sum(S * Hf, axis=1)                         # (M,) energies
    n_stable = 2 * jnp.sum(jnp.all(S * Hf > 0, axis=1))        # x2 for the mirror images
    logw = -betas[:, None] * E[None, :]                        # (n_T, M)
    lse = jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(logw, axis=1)
    p = jnp.exp(logw - lse[:, None])                           # Boltzmann probabilities on the half space
    logZ = jnp.log(2.0) + lse
    U = p @ E
    # spin-glass susceptibility chi_SG = (1/N) sum_ij <s_i s_j>^2 at the temperatures betas_chi
    pc = jnp.exp(-betas_chi[:, None] * E[None, :] - jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(-betas_chi[:, None] * E[None, :], axis=1)[:, None])
    C = jnp.einsum("bm,mi,mj->bij", pc, S, S)                  # (n_chi, N, N) correlation matrices
    chi = jnp.sum(C**2, axis=(1, 2)) / N
    return logZ, U, jnp.min(E), n_stable, chi

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_chunk",))
def ground_state_chunked(J, n_chunk):
    """E0 and the number of single-flip-stable configurations, enumerating in n_chunk chunks (for N = 22, 24)."""
    N = J.shape[0]
    M = 2 ** (N - 1); m = M // n_chunk
    def body(carry, c):
        k = c * m + jnp.arange(m, dtype=jnp.int32)
        bits = (k[:, None] >> jnp.arange(N - 1)) & 1
        S = jnp.concatenate([2.0 * bits - 1.0, jnp.ones((m, 1))], axis=1)
        Hf = S @ J
        E = -0.5 * jnp.sum(S * Hf, axis=1)
        return (jnp.minimum(carry[0], E.min()), carry[1] + jnp.sum(jnp.all(S * Hf > 0, axis=1))), None
    (E0, n), _ = lax.scan(body, (jnp.inf, 0), jnp.arange(n_chunk))
    return E0, 2 * n

Below \(T\approx J\) the difference grows and is positive, as Jensen’s inequality requires. The middle panel shows why the annealed calculation cannot be trusted there. The quenched entropy stays positive at all temperatures (\(0.102\) per spin at \(T=0.2\) for \(N=20\)), while the annealed entropy becomes negative below \(T^*\approx0.60\,J\). The annealed calculation misses the physics of the low-temperature phase. Finally, the right panel shows that the sample-to-sample spread of \(\ln Z_J/N\) decreases with \(N\) at both temperatures, \(T=0.5\) and \(T=2\), so the free energy per spin is self-averaging.

title: Lab 032: Physics of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glass
text:
3. Frustration

3.1 One triangle
The simplest situation in which random signs matter is a triangle, three spins with couplings \(J_{12}=J_{13}=+1\) (ferromagnetic) and \(J_{23}=-1\) (antiferromagnetic). A bond \((ij)\) is satisfied if \(J_{ij}s_is_j>0\), i.e. if its contribution \(-J_{ij}s_is_j\) to the energy is negative.
The sketch below shows three configurations of this triangle with the coupling written next to each bond. In each of them two bonds are satisfied and one is broken (dashed). The minimum energy is \(E=-1\), and no configuration reaches \(-3\).

    broken = [f"{i + 1}{j + 1}" for (i, j), Jij in J_tri.items() if Jij * s[i] * s[j] < 0]

The minimum energy is \(E=-1\). Every configuration breaks at least one bond, and the minimum is six-fold degenerate (any one of the three bonds can be the broken one, times the global flip). The triangle is frustrated, since no configuration satisfies all its couplings.


3.2 Loop products
The triangle suggests a general criterion, and it can be found without enumerating anything. Multiply the three bond terms around the triangle, \[
(J_{12}s_1s_2)(J_{23}s_2s_3)(J_{31}s_3s_1)=J_{12}J_{23}J_{31}\,s_1^2s_2^2s_3^2=J_{12}J_{23}J_{31}.
\] The product of the bond terms does not depend on the spins. A satisfied bond has a positive term, so if all three bonds were satisfied the product would be positive. Hence if \(J_{12}J_{23}J_{31}<0\), at least one bond is broken in every configuration (in fact an odd number). The argument works for any closed loop of bonds, since every spin on a loop appears in exactly two bond terms. The product around a loop is also gauge invariant, since the replacement \(J_{ij}\to\gamma_i\gamma_jJ_{ij}\) multiplies it by \(\prod\gamma^2=1\). Frustration is a property of the couplings that no relabelling of spins can remove, while the signs of individual couplings change under such a relabelling.
For couplings of arbitrary magnitudes \(a,b,c>0\) and signs with a negative product, the ground-state energy is \(-(a+b+c)+2\min(a,b,c)\), because the weakest bond is the one that breaks. SymPy confirms both statements.


Code
s1, s2, s3 = sp.symbols("s1 s2 s3")
J12, J23, J31 = sp.symbols("J12 J23 J31", real=True)
loop = sp.expand((J12 * s1 * s2) * (J23 * s2 * s3) * (J31 * s3 * s1))
print("product of bond terms             :", loop)
print("with s_i^2 = 1                    :", loop.subs({s1**2: 1, s2**2: 1, s3**2: 1}))

# ground-state energy of a frustrated triangle: J12 = a, J31 = b, J23 = -c with a, b, c > 0
a, b, c = sp.symbols("a b c", positive=True)
Jv = {(0, 1): a, (1, 2): -c, (2, 0): b}
energies = sorted({sp.simplify(-sum(Jij * s[i] * s[j] for (i, j), Jij in Jv.items())) for s in itertools.product([1, -1], repeat=3)},
                  key=lambda e: str(e))
print("distinct energies of the 8 states :", energies)
print("E0 for a = 3, b = 2, c = 1        :", min(e.subs({a: 3, b: 2, c: 1}) for e in energies),
      "   formula -(a+b+c) + 2 min(a,b,c):", -(3 + 2 + 1) + 2 * 1)
print("gauge transformation of the product:", sp.expand((sp.Symbol('t1') * sp.Symbol('t2') * J12) * (sp.Symbol('t2') * sp.Symbol('t3') * J23)
                                                  * (sp.Symbol('t3') * sp.Symbol('t1') * J31)), "  (every tau appears squared)")

3.3 Frustrated triangles
In the SK model every triple \((i,j,k)\) forms a triangle. The product of three independent couplings with symmetric distributions is negative with probability \(1/2\) (an odd number of negative factors), so half of the \(\binom N3\) triangles are frustrated. For a large \(N\) we count them without a triple loop. Let \(\sigma_{ij}=\operatorname{sign}J_{ij}\) (with \(\sigma_{ii}=0\)). Then \[
\operatorname{Tr}\sigma^3=\sum_{i,j,k}\sigma_{ij}\sigma_{jk}\sigma_{ki}
\] runs over ordered triples of distinct indices (the zero diagonal removes the others), and each triangle appears \(3!=6\) times. Hence \[
\begin{aligned}
n_{\rm unfrustrated}-n_{\rm frustrated}&=\tfrac16\operatorname{Tr}\sigma^3,\\
n_{\rm unfrustrated}+n_{\rm frustrated}&=\binom N3 .
\end{aligned}
\] We compare three coupling matrices, the SK couplings, the ferromagnet \(J_{ij}=J/N\), and the Mattis couplings \(J_{ij}=J\xi_i\xi_j/N\) with random \(\xi_i=\pm1\) (Section 7), which have random signs too. For \(N=30\) the trace formula is first compared with an explicit loop over triangles.


Code
def frustrated_fraction(J):
    """Fraction of frustrated triangles from Tr(sign(J)^3), J of shape (N, N) with zero diagonal."""
    N = J.shape[0]
    sg = np.sign(np.asarray(J, dtype=np.float64))
    diff = np.trace(sg @ sg @ sg) / 6                         # n_unfrustrated - n_frustrated
    total = N * (N - 1) * (N - 2) / 6
    return (total - diff) / 2 / total

def frustrated_fraction_loop(J):
    """The same by an explicit loop over all triples (for checking)."""
    J = np.asarray(J); N = J.shape[0]
    f = [J[i, j] * J[j, k] * J[k, i] < 0 for i, j, k in itertools.combinations(range(N), 3)]
    return np.mean(f)

def mattis_couplings(xi, J=1.0):
    """Mattis couplings J xi_i xi_j / N, zero diagonal; xi of shape (N,)."""
    N = xi.shape[0]
    return J * (np.outer(xi, xi) - np.eye(N)) / N

N = 30
J_sk = np.asarray(sk_couplings(jax.random.PRNGKey(7), 1, N)[0])
xi = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=N)

N = 512
J_sk = np.asarray(sk_couplings(jax.random.PRNGKey(8), 1, N)[0])
xi = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=N)
J_ferro = (np.ones((N, N)) - np.eye(N)) / N
J_mattis = mattis_couplings(xi)
print(f"\nN = {N}, {N * (N - 1) * (N - 2) // 6} triangles")
for name, Jm in (("SK", J_sk), ("ferromagnet", J_ferro), ("Mattis", J_mattis)):
    print(f"  {name:12s} fraction of negative couplings {np.mean(Jm[np.triu_indices(N, 1)] < 0):.3f},   fraction of frustrated triangles {frustrated_fraction(Jm):.4f}")

N = 512, 22238720 triangles

The trace formula agrees with the explicit count, and for \(N=512\) the SK couplings have a fraction \(0.4999\) of frustrated triangles. The Mattis couplings have as many negative signs as the SK couplings, yet not a single frustrated triangle, because their loop products are \(\xi_i^2\xi_j^2\xi_k^2/N^3>0\). Random signs alone do not make a spin glass. Random signs with frustration do. Section 7 shows what this means physically.

title: Lab 032: Physics of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glass
text:
4. Order without a pattern

4.1 Frozen spins with zero magnetisation
In a ferromagnet below \(T_c\) the thermal averages \(\langle s_i\rangle\) are all equal, and the magnetisation \(m=\frac1N\sum_i\langle s_i\rangle\) measures the order. In a spin glass below its freezing temperature each spin also has a non-zero average \(\langle s_i\rangle\) inside the valley the system is trapped in, but the signs of the \(\langle s_i\rangle\) follow the random couplings, not a common direction. Their sum is a sum of \(N\) terms of random sign, so \(m\) is of order \(1/\sqrt N\) and vanishes for large \(N\). (After averaging over the disorder, \([\langle s_i\rangle]=0\) exactly by the gauge symmetry of Section 2.3.) The SK model has no lattice either, so a snapshot cannot show domains or stripes, because the labels \(i\) carry no geometry, and any permutation of the labels (with the couplings permuted accordingly) describes the same system. A snapshot of the frozen phase looks like noise.


4.2 The Edwards–Anderson order parameter
Edwards and Anderson proposed to measure the freezing itself, regardless of the directions [Edwards & Anderson 1975], \[
q_{\rm EA}=\frac1N\sum_i\langle s_i\rangle^2 .
\] It is zero in the paramagnet (\(\langle s_i\rangle=0\)) and positive when the spins are frozen. It is invariant under the gauge transformation. In a finite system, however, \(\langle s_i\rangle=0\) exactly (global flip symmetry), and \(\langle s_i\rangle\) restricted to “the valley we are in” cannot be defined directly in a simulation or an experiment.


4.3 Two replicas and the overlap
The way out is to simulate two independent copies \(a\) and \(b\) of the system, called replicas, with the same couplings \(J\) and independent thermal noise. Their joint distribution is the product \(p_J(\boldsymbol s^a)\,p_J(\boldsymbol s^b)\). The overlap \[
q_{ab}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Ns_i^as_i^b\ \in[-1,1]
\] is \(+1\) for identical configurations, \(-1\) for mirror images, and close to \(0\) for unrelated ones. The fraction of spins on which the two replicas differ is \((1-q_{ab})/2\).
The schematic below summarises the last three subsections on a row of \(N=12\) spins. A paramagnet looks different at every time (top pair of rows). A spin glass is frozen into one pattern, which does not change in time but has no net magnetisation (middle pair). Two replicas of the same sample (bottom) freeze into similar patterns. The overlap field \(q_i=s_i^as_i^b\) is \(+1\) (filled green square) where they agree, and the overlap \(q_{ab}=\frac1N\sum_iq_i\), here \(0.667\), measures how similar they are. Neither \(m\) nor a single snapshot reveals the frozen order, while the overlap of two replicas does.


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;
#   satisfied bond: solid blue line, broken (frustrated) bond: dashed purple line marked with a cross.
# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (5.5 in = full text width) with 10-12 pt text,

def draw_spin(ax, x, y, s, r=0.26, sign=False, alpha=1.0, fs=10, lw=1.3):

def draw_bond(ax, p, q, broken=False, lw=1.5, alpha=1.0, color=None, cross=True):

def sketch_sk_phases_configs():
    N = 12
    rng = np.random.default_rng(8)                                  # fixed seed: the same schematic every time
    para_t1, para_t2 = rng.choice([-1, 1], N), rng.choice([-1, 1], N)      # paramagnet: a new random pattern at every time
    frozen = rng.permutation(np.repeat([1, -1], N // 2))           # spin glass: a frozen random-looking pattern, m = 0
    rep_a = frozen.copy()
    rep_b = frozen.copy(); rep_b[[2, 9]] *= -1                      # second replica: same valley, two spins differ
    q_field = rep_a * rep_b                                         # overlap field q_i = s_i^a s_i^b
    rows = [(para_t1, "paramagnet, time $t$", f"$m={para_t1.mean():+.2f}$"),
            (para_t2, "paramagnet, time $t'$", f"$m={para_t2.mean():+.2f}$"),
            (frozen, "spin glass, time $t$", f"$m={frozen.mean():+.2f}$"),
            (frozen, "spin glass, time $t'$", "frozen"),
            (rep_a, "replica $a$", ""), (rep_b, "replica $b$", ""),
            (q_field, r"$q_i=s_i^a s_i^b$", rf"$q_{{ab}}={q_field.mean():.3f}$")]

    ax = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0])
    x0, dy = 7.2, 1.0
    for r, (spins, label, note) in enumerate(rows):
        yy = -r * dy - (0.5 if r >= 2 else 0) - (0.5 if r >= 4 else 0)       # small gaps between the three groups
        for i, s in enumerate(spins):
            if r == 6:                                              # overlap field: +1 where the replicas agree
                ax.add_patch(mpatches.Rectangle((x0 + i - 0.35, yy - 0.35), 0.7, 0.7, fc=GREEN if s > 0 else "white",
                                                ec=GREEN, lw=1.0))
            else:
                draw_spin(ax, x0 + i, yy, s, r=0.36, lw=0.9)
        ax.text(x0 - 0.7, yy, label, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=10, color=NAVY)
        ax.text(x0 + N - 0.2, yy, note, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=10, color=GRAY)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.2, x0 + N + 3.3); ax.set_ylim(-8.0, 0.7); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_sk_phases_configs()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_sk_phase_configs.png")
plt.show()





Because the replicas are independent at fixed \(J\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle q_{ab}^2\rangle&=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}\langle s_i^as_j^a\rangle\langle s_i^bs_j^b\rangle\\
&=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}\langle s_is_j\rangle^2 .
\end{aligned}
\] The global flip makes \(\langle q_{ab}\rangle=0\) at finite \(N\), but \(\langle q_{ab}^2\rangle\) is not affected. It measures the frozen correlations. If the system sits in one of two mirror valleys with averages \(\pm\langle s_i\rangle\), then \(q_{ab}=\pm q_{\rm EA}\) and \(\langle q^2_{ab}\rangle=q_{\rm EA}^2\).
The full information is in the overlap distribution of a sample and its disorder average, \[
P_J(q)=\big\langle\delta(q-q_{ab})\big\rangle_J,\qquad P(q)=\big[P_J(q)\big].
\] In the paramagnet \(q_{ab}\) is a sum of \(N\) weakly correlated terms \(\pm1/N\), so \(P(q)\) is a single Gaussian peak at \(q=0\) of width of order \(1/\sqrt N\). In the spin glass, by contrast, \(P(q)\) has weight at \(q\neq0\) that does not shrink as \(N\) grows (Sections 4.5 and 5).
The spin-glass susceptibility collects the frozen correlations, \[
\chi_{\rm SG}=\frac1N\sum_{i,j}\big[\langle s_is_j\rangle^2\big]=N\,\big[\langle q_{ab}^2\rangle\big],
\] and in the paramagnet it sets the width of \(P(q)\), \([\langle q^2\rangle]=\chi_{\rm SG}/N\).


4.4 Spin-glass susceptibility
At high temperature \(\chi_{\rm SG}\) can be computed by an expansion in powers of \(\beta\), and the result tells us where the paramagnet ends. Write each Boltzmann factor as \(e^{\beta J_{ij}s_is_j}=\cosh(\beta J_{ij})\,(1+t_{ij}s_is_j)\) with \(t_{ij}=\tanh(\beta J_{ij})\approx\beta J_{ij}\) (small, of order \(1/\sqrt N\)). Expanding the product, \(\langle s_is_j\rangle\) is a sum over paths of bonds from \(i\) to \(j\), each path contributing the product of its \(t\)’s. Now square and average over the disorder. Cross terms between two different paths contain some coupling an odd number of times, and \([J_{kl}]=0\) removes them, so only the squares of single paths survive. A path of length \(\ell\) contributes \(\prod[t^2]\approx(\beta^2J^2/N)^\ell\), and the number of paths of length \(\ell\) from \(i\) to \(j\) through distinct intermediate sites is \((N-2)(N-3)\cdots(N-\ell)\approx N^{\ell-1}\). Summing over the end point \(j\) gives another factor \(N\). Therefore, to leading order in \(1/N\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\chi_{\rm SG}&=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}N^{\ell}\Big(\frac{\beta^2J^2}{N}\Big)^{\ell}=\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty(\beta J)^{2\ell}\\
&=\frac{1}{1-\beta^2J^2}\qquad(T>J).
\end{aligned}
\] The series diverges at \(\beta J=1\), so the paramagnet becomes unstable at \(T_c=J\). This is the value of the SK critical temperature (the replica solution below uses the same convention, \(T_c=J\), as e.g. [Crisanti & Rizzo 2002]). SymPy checks the two ingredients, the path count and the geometric sum, and we then compare with exact enumeration.

def exact_Pq(J, betas, S, O):
    """Exact P_J(q) for one sample, shape (n_T, 13). S: (4096, N) all configurations, O: (4096, 4096) values N q_ab."""
    N = S.shape[1]

4.6 Replica-symmetric solution
Sherrington and Kirkpatrick computed \([\ln Z]\) with the replica trick [Sherrington & Kirkpatrick 1975]. The identity \(\ln Z=\lim_{n\to0}(Z^n-1)/n\) replaces the hard average of a logarithm by averages of \(Z^n\), the partition function of \(n\) replicas with the same couplings, which are Gaussian integrals as in Section 2.4. Averaging couples the replicas through the overlaps \(q_{ab}\). The simplest assumption, replica symmetry (RS), is that all overlaps are equal, \(q_{ab}=q\). We quote its result without repeating the calculation.
The central result is a self-consistency equation for \(q\), which can be understood directly. In a frozen state, spin \(i\) feels the field of the other spins with \(i\) itself removed (the cavity field), \(h_i=\sum_jJ_{ij}\langle s_j\rangle\). It is a sum of \(N\) terms with random signs, hence Gaussian, with variance \(\sum_jJ_{ij}^2\langle s_j\rangle^2\approx J^2q\). The spin then has \(\langle s_i\rangle=\tanh(\beta h_i)\), and averaging \(\langle s_i\rangle^2\) over the Gaussian field gives \[
q=\int\!Dz\;\tanh^2\!\big(\beta J\sqrt q\,z\big),\qquad Dz=\frac{dz}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2},
\] \[
\begin{aligned}
-\beta f_{\rm RS}&=\frac{\beta^2J^2}{4}(1-q)^2+\int\!Dz\,\ln\!\big(2\cosh\beta J\sqrt q\,z\big),\\
u_{\rm RS}&=-\frac{\beta J^2}{2}\big(1-q^2\big).
\end{aligned}
\] At \(q=0\) this is exactly the annealed result of Section 2.4. (The same expression is the constant-\(q\) case of Parisi’s free energy given in [Crisanti & Rizzo 2002].)
Linearising the equation gives the critical temperature. For small \(q\), \(\tanh^2x\approx x^2\) and \(\int Dz\,z^2=1\), so \(q\approx\beta^2J^2q\), and a non-zero solution appears only for \(\beta J>1\). Expanding one order further gives \(q\approx\tau\) with \(\tau=1-T/J\), so the Edwards–Anderson order parameter grows linearly below \(T_c\). SymPy does the expansion.

We evaluate them with scipy.integrate.quad on \(z>0\) (the integrands are even), and find \(q(T)\) as the root of \(q-\int Dz\tanh^2(\beta\sqrt q z)\) with brentq. From \(q\) we get \(f_{\rm RS}\), \(u_{\rm RS}\) and the entropy \(s_{\rm RS}=\beta(u_{\rm RS}-f_{\rm RS})\).

from scipy.integrate import quad
from scipy.optimize import brentq

phi = lambda z: np.exp(-z**2 / 2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)
gauss_avg = lambda g: 2 * quad(lambda z: phi(z) * g(z), 0, 12, limit=400)[0]          # int Dz g(z) for an even g

def rs_solution(T):
    """Replica-symmetric q, f, u, s at temperature T (J = 1)."""
    b = 1 / T
    F = lambda q: q - gauss_avg(lambda z: np.tanh(b * np.sqrt(q) * z) ** 2)
    q = brentq(F, 1e-10, 1.0) if T < 1 else 0.0
    log2cosh = lambda x: np.abs(x) + np.log1p(np.exp(-2 * np.abs(x)))               # ln(2 cosh x) without overflow
    mbf = b**2 * (1 - q) ** 2 / 4 + gauss_avg(lambda z: log2cosh(b * np.sqrt(q) * z))
    u = -b * (1 - q**2) / 2
    return q, -T * mbf, u, mbf + b * u

4.7 Parisi’s solution
Parisi found the correct solution by breaking the replica symmetry in infinitely many steps [Parisi 1979; Parisi 1980], and his free energy was later proved rigorously to be exact [Talagrand 2006]. We state its main results without derivation, and the rest of the notebook tests them.
The order parameter becomes a function. Instead of one number \(q\), the solution is a non-decreasing function \(q(x)\), \(0\le x\le1\), whose inverse defines the overlap distribution, \(P(q)=dx/dq\) [Parisi 1983; Crisanti & Rizzo 2002]. Its physical content is that below \(T_c\) the Boltzmann distribution of a large sample splits into many “pure states” (valleys) \(\alpha\) with weights \(w_\alpha\). Two replicas fall into states \(\alpha,\alpha'\) independently, and \(P_J(q)=\sum_{\alpha\alpha'}w_\alpha w_{\alpha'}\,\delta(q-q_{\alpha\alpha'})\), with \(q_{\alpha\alpha'}\) the overlap of the two states. Pairs in the same state give the self-overlap \(q_{\rm EA}\). Pairs in different states give smaller overlaps. Hence \(P(q)\) has peaks at \(\pm q_{\rm EA}\) and a continuous part in between [Mézard, Parisi & Virasoro 1986], whereas a ferromagnet has only a pair of delta functions. The weights \(w_\alpha\) differ from sample to sample, so \(P_J(q)\) differs between samples even for large \(N\).
The cartoons below compare the overlap distributions met so far, for \(N\to\infty\). They are schematic shapes drawn without computation. In the paramagnet two replicas are unrelated and \(P(q)\) is a single delta function at \(q=0\). A ferromagnet, and the Mattis model of Section 7, has two mirror states and two delta peaks at \(\pm m^2\). The replica-symmetric ansatz of Section 4.6 predicts the same shape, two delta peaks at \(\pm q\). Parisi’s solution adds a continuous part between the peaks at \(\pm q_{\rm EA}\), the Edwards–Anderson order parameter of Section 4.2. Replicas that fall into different valleys have overlaps smaller than \(q_{\rm EA}\). Section 5.6 measures \(P(q)\) at finite \(N\).

5. The spin-glass transition

5.1 Parallel tempering
Testing these predictions requires equilibrium samples at low temperature, and this is where spin glasses are hard. Below \(T_c\) the free-energy landscape has many valleys separated by barriers that grow with \(N\). A Metropolis chain at a fixed low temperature (single spin flips, accepted with probability \(\min(1,e^{-\beta\Delta E})\)) stays in one valley for a very long time. The samples it produces are correct locally but do not represent the relative weights of the valleys, and the estimate of \(P(q)\), which is all about different valleys, is wrong. Section 6.3 shows this directly.
The cartoon below illustrates the difficulty on a one-dimensional caricature of configuration space. The energy has many local minima, the metastable states of Section 6.2, separated by barriers. At low temperature a chain of single spin flips stays in one valley. At high temperature it crosses the barriers easily, but it does not settle in the deep valleys.

Parallel tempering (also called replica exchange or exchange Monte Carlo) [Swendsen & Wang 1986; Hukushima & Nemoto 1996; Earl & Deem 2005] runs \(K\) copies of the same sample at temperatures \(T_1<T_2<\dots<T_K\). The joint distribution of the copies is the product of their Boltzmann distributions, \[
\Pi(\boldsymbol s_1,\dots,\boldsymbol s_K)=\prod_{k=1}^K\frac{e^{-\beta_kE(\boldsymbol s_k)}}{Z(\beta_k)} .
\] Two kinds of moves alternate. In a local move every copy performs one Metropolis sweep at its own temperature. Each copy is updated with a move that preserves its own Boltzmann distribution, so \(\Pi\) is preserved. In an exchange move we propose, for neighbouring temperatures \(k,k+1\), to swap the two configurations, and accept with probability \[
\min\Big(1,\ \exp\big[(\beta_k-\beta_{k+1})(E_k-E_{k+1})\big]\Big),
\] where \(E_k\) is the energy of the configuration currently at temperature \(T_k\). This is the Metropolis rule for the swap, because the ratio \(\Pi(\text{after})/\Pi(\text{before})\) equals the exponential (SymPy below), so detailed balance holds and \(\Pi\) is preserved.
The exchanges let a configuration do a random walk in temperature. At high temperature it crosses barriers easily. When it comes back down it can land in a different valley. The swap is accepted often when the energy histograms of neighbouring temperatures overlap, which sets how dense the temperature grid must be. For the replica overlap we need two independent parallel-tempering simulations of the same sample (replicas \(a\) and \(b\)), each with its own \(K\) copies.
The sketch below shows the scheme for \(K=4\) temperatures. Every copy is updated by Metropolis sweeps at its own temperature, and copies at neighbouring temperatures propose to exchange their configurations with the acceptance probability above.

5.2 Implementation
One simulation handles \(D\) disorder samples, \(2\) replicas and \(K\) temperatures at once. For one sample the \(C=2K\) chains (replica \(r\), temperature slot \(k\), column \(c=rK+k\)) are the columns of a matrix, and jax.vmap maps the per-sample code over the \(D\) samples. The table lists the arrays.

All spins of the SK model are coupled to each other, so the energy change of one flip depends on all other spins and two spins cannot be flipped simultaneously. A sweep therefore visits the spins one after another. After a flip of spin \(i\) by \(\Delta s_i=-2s_i\) every local field changes, \(h_j\to h_j+J_{ji}\Delta s_i\), which is \(O(N)\) work per flip and \(O(N^2)\) per sweep. Done literally, spin by spin, this reads and writes the whole field array \(N\) times per sweep. We organise the same sequential sweep in blocks of \(b=16\) spins. Inside a block the spins are visited one by one, and each flip updates only the fields of the \(b\) spins of the block (a small (b, C) array, couplings J_bb of shape (b, b)). After the block, the fields of all \(N\) spins are updated at once by one matrix product, \(h\leftarrow h+J_{:,\text{block}}\,\Delta s_{\text{block}}\), with shapes (N, b) @ (b, C). Every spin still sees the exact current field when it is visited, so this is the same sequential Metropolis sweep, with the expensive part done as matrix products.
In the exchange step, for one sample and one replica, the \(K\) configurations are permuted. Slot \(k\) receives the configuration from slot \(k+1\) and vice versa if the swap is accepted. Even pairs \((0,1),(2,3),\dots\) and odd pairs \((1,2),(3,4),\dots\) alternate between sweeps, so the attempted swaps never overlap.

from math import gcd

def sweep_sample(s, h, J, beta_c, u, block):
    """One sequential Metropolis sweep of all chains of one sample.
    s, h: (N, C) spins and local fields, one chain per column; J: (N, N); beta_c: (C,) inverse temperature of each chain;
    u: (N, C) uniform random numbers. Spins are visited in the order i = 0, ..., N-1, in blocks of `block` spins."""
    N, C = s.shape
    thr = -jnp.log(u) / (2.0 * beta_c)                             # (N, C): flip spin i iff s_i h_i < thr_i, i.e. u < exp(-2 beta s_i h_i)
    def do_block(kb, carry):
        s, h = carry
        i0 = kb * block
        s_old = lax.dynamic_slice_in_dim(s, i0, block, 0)          # (b, C) spins of the block
        hb = lax.dynamic_slice_in_dim(h, i0, block, 0)             # (b, C) their fields at the start of the block
        tb = lax.dynamic_slice_in_dim(thr, i0, block, 0)           # (b, C) acceptance thresholds
        J_cols = lax.dynamic_slice_in_dim(J, i0, block, 1)         # (N, b) couplings of every spin to the block
        J_bb = lax.dynamic_slice_in_dim(J_cols, i0, block, 0)      # (b, b) couplings inside the block
        rows = []
        for j in range(block):                                     # sequential inside the block (unrolled by jit)
            sj = s_old[j]
            accept = sj * hb[j] < tb[j]                            # Metropolis rule, Delta E = 2 s_j h_j
            d = jnp.where(accept, -2.0 * sj, 0.0)                  # (C,) change of s_j, 0 if rejected
            hb = hb + J_bb[:, j:j + 1] * d[None, :]                # fields of the block spins after this flip
            rows.append(sj + d)
        s_new = jnp.stack(rows)                                    # (b, C)
        s = lax.dynamic_update_slice_in_dim(s, s_new, i0, 0)
        h = h + J_cols @ (s_new - s_old)                           # all N fields, one matrix product per block
        return s, h
    return lax.fori_loop(0, N // block, do_block, (s, h))

def swap_moves(s, h, lab, E, beta, u, parity):
    """Exchange moves for all samples and replicas. s, h: (D, N, 2, K); lab, E: (D, 2, K); beta: (K,); u: (D, 2, K-1).
    Pairs (k, k+1) with k % 2 == parity are attempted; returns the permuted arrays and the accepted swaps (D, 2, K-1)."""
    K = beta.shape[0]
    log_ratio = (beta[:-1] - beta[1:]) * (E[..., :-1] - E[..., 1:])            # (D, 2, K-1)
    acc = (jnp.log(u) < log_ratio) & (jnp.arange(K - 1) % 2 == parity)
    pad = jnp.zeros(acc.shape[:-1] + (1,), bool)
    up = jnp.concatenate([acc, pad], -1).astype(jnp.int32)                     # slot k takes from k+1
    down = jnp.concatenate([pad, acc], -1).astype(jnp.int32)                   # slot k+1 takes from k
    perm = jnp.arange(K) + up - down                                           # (D, 2, K)
    take = lambda a: jnp.take_along_axis(a, perm[:, None], axis=3)             # permute the K axis of (D, N, 2, K)
    return take(s), take(h), jnp.take_along_axis(lab, perm, 2), jnp.take_along_axis(E, perm, 2), acc

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_save", "n_meas", "meas_every", "use_swaps"))
def parallel_tempering(J, s0, beta, key, n_equil, n_save, n_meas, meas_every, use_swaps=True):
    """Parallel tempering for D samples x 2 replicas x K temperatures; s0: (D, 2, K, N) initial spins.
    Equilibration: n_equil sweeps. Production: n_save blocks of n_meas measurements, one every meas_every sweeps;
    one configuration per slot is stored at the end of every block. Returns a dict of arrays (shapes in the comments)."""
    D, R, K, N = s0.shape
    C = R * K
    sweep_all = jax.vmap(partial(sweep_sample, block=gcd(N, 16)), in_axes=(0, 0, 0, None, 0))   # over the D samples
    beta_c = jnp.tile(beta, R)                                                  # (C,) column c = r K + k
    s_init = jnp.transpose(s0, (0, 3, 1, 2))                                   # (D, N, 2, K)
    h_init = jnp.einsum("dij,djrk->dirk", J, s_init)
    carry0 = dict(s=s_init, h=h_init, lab=jnp.broadcast_to(jnp.arange(K), (D, R, K)),
                  emin=jnp.full((D, R), jnp.inf), smin=s0[:, :, 0], acc=jnp.zeros(K - 1), t=0, key=key)

    def one_sweep(c, _):
        key, k1, k2 = jax.random.split(c["key"], 3)
        s, h = sweep_all(c["s"].reshape(D, N, C), c["h"].reshape(D, N, C), J, beta_c, jax.random.uniform(k1, (D, N, C)))
        s, h = s.reshape(D, N, R, K), h.reshape(D, N, R, K)
        E = -0.5 * jnp.sum(s * h, axis=1)                                      # (D, 2, K) energies
        lab, acc = c["lab"], jnp.zeros((D, R, K - 1), bool)
        if use_swaps:
            s, h, lab, E, acc = swap_moves(s, h, lab, E, beta, jax.random.uniform(k2, (D, R, K - 1)), c["t"] % 2)
        k_low = jnp.argmin(E, -1)                                              # (D, 2) lowest-energy slot
        s_low = jnp.take_along_axis(s, k_low[:, None, :, None], axis=3)[..., 0]   # (D, N, 2)
        better = E.min(-1) < c["emin"]
        q = jnp.mean(s[:, :, 0] * s[:, :, 1], axis=1)                          # (D, K) overlaps of the two replicas
        new = dict(s=s, h=h, lab=lab, emin=jnp.where(better, E.min(-1), c["emin"]),
                   smin=jnp.where(better[..., None], jnp.swapaxes(s_low, 1, 2), c["smin"]),
                   acc=c["acc"] + acc.sum((0, 1)), t=c["t"] + 1, key=key)
        trace = (E.mean((0, 1)) / N, (q**2).mean(0), lab[0, 0].astype(jnp.int8))   # [E]/N (K,), [q^2] (K,), labels (K,)
        return new, trace

    def measure(c, _):
        c, tr = lax.scan(one_sweep, c, None, length=meas_every)
        q_int = jnp.sum(c["s"][:, :, 0] * c["s"][:, :, 1], axis=1).astype(jnp.int16)   # (D, K): N q
        return c, (tr, q_int)

    def block(c, _):
        c, (tr, q_int) = lax.scan(measure, c, None, length=n_meas)
        return c, (tr, q_int, jnp.transpose(c["s"], (0, 2, 3, 1)).astype(jnp.int8))   # snapshot (D, 2, K, N)

    c, tr_eq = lax.scan(one_sweep, carry0, None, length=n_equil)
    c, (tr_pr, q_int, conf) = lax.scan(block, c, None, length=n_save)
    flat = lambda a: a.reshape((-1,) + a.shape[3:])                             # (n_save, n_meas, meas_every, K) -> (sweeps, K)
    traces = [jnp.concatenate([tr_eq[i], flat(tr_pr[i])]) for i in range(3)]
    return dict(e_trace=traces[0], q2_trace=traces[1], label_trace=traces[2],
                q_int=jnp.transpose(q_int.reshape(-1, D, K), (1, 2, 0)),        # (D, K, n_save * n_meas)
                configs=jnp.transpose(conf, (1, 2, 3, 0, 4)),                   # (D, 2, K, n_save, N)

5.3 Accuracy of the sampler
Before using the sampler where no exact answer exists, we test it where one does. For \(N=12\) we know the exact thermal averages of every sample. We run the sampler for \(D=32\) samples on a few temperatures and compare the disorder averages \([e]=[\langle E\rangle]/N\) and \([\langle q^2\rangle]\) with the exact values for the same samples. The exact \(\langle q^2\rangle=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{ij}\langle s_is_j\rangle^2\) comes from the correlation matrix (Section 2.4). def block_error(x, n_blocks=16):
    """Mean and standard error of a time series x (n_time,) from n_blocks consecutive block means."""
    b = x[: len(x) // n_blocks * n_blocks].reshape(n_blocks, -1).mean(1)
    return b.mean(), b.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n_blocks)

5.4 An exact energy–overlap identity
For \(N=128\) no exact answer is available, so equilibration has to be checked in another way. For Gaussian couplings there is an exact identity between the energy and the overlap [Katzgraber, Palassini & Young 2001], and it rests on two ingredients. The first is Gaussian integration by parts (Stein’s lemma), which states that for \(x\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\) and a smooth function \(g\), \(\ [x\,g(x)]=\sigma^2\,[g'(x)]\). It follows from \(\frac{d}{dx}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}=-\frac{x}{\sigma^2}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}\) and one integration by parts. The second is the derivative of a correlation with respect to its own coupling. Since \(J_{ij}\) enters \(Z\) through \(e^{\beta J_{ij}s_is_j}\), \(\partial\langle s_is_j\rangle/\partial J_{ij}=\beta\big(\langle(s_is_j)^2\rangle-\langle s_is_j\rangle^2\big)=\beta\big(1-\langle s_is_j\rangle^2\big)\).
Apply both to the disorder-averaged energy, \([U]=-\sum_{i<j}[J_{ij}\langle s_is_j\rangle]=-\sum_{i<j}\sigma^2\beta\big(1-[\langle s_is_j\rangle^2]\big)\), and use \(\sum_{i<j}\langle s_is_j\rangle^2=\frac12\big(N^2\langle q^2\rangle-N\big)\) (Section 4.3). With \(\sigma^2=J^2/N\) everything combines into \[
\boxed{\;\frac{[U]}{N}=-\frac{\beta J^2}{2}\Big(1-\big[\langle q^2\rangle\big]\Big)\;}
\] exactly, for every \(N\) and every temperature. In a simulation that starts from random configurations the two sides approach the equilibrium value from opposite directions. The energy decreases from \(0\), while the right-hand side starts near \(-\beta J^2/2\) (no overlap yet) and increases. Equality of the two sides (within errors) is a necessary condition for equilibrium. At high temperature \([\langle q^2\rangle]\to0\) and the identity reduces to the annealed \(u=-\beta J^2/2\).
We check Stein’s lemma and the sum identity with SymPy, and the boxed identity with the exact enumeration data of Section 2.4.

5.5 The Monte Carlo data set
The production simulation uses \(K=25\) temperatures \(T=0.40,0.45,\dots,1.60\) (in units of \(J\)), symmetric around \(T_c=1\) in the sense that the grid reaches \(0.6\,J\) above and below. The lowest temperature is limited by the equilibration time, which grows quickly as \(T\to0\).

def generate_sk_dataset(N, D, n_equil, n_save, n_meas, meas_every, seed_couplings, seed_run, couplings=None):
    """Run parallel tempering for D SK samples of N spins and return the data set as a dict of NumPy arrays."""
    J = sk_couplings(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed_couplings), D, N) if couplings is None else jnp.asarray(couplings, jnp.float32)
    k_init, k_run = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed_run))
    s0 = random_spins(k_init, (D, 2, K_T, N))
    out = parallel_tempering(J, s0, jnp.asarray(1 / T_GRID, jnp.float32), k_run, n_equil=n_equil, n_save=n_save,
                             n_meas=n_meas, meas_every=meas_every)
    out = {k: np.asarray(v) for k, v in out.items()}
    n_tot = int(out["n_sweeps"])
    attempts = np.array([np.sum(np.arange(n_tot) % 2 == k % 2) for k in range(K_T - 1)]) * D * 2   # attempts per pair
    return dict(configs=out["configs"], T=T_GRID, J=np.asarray(J, np.float32), seed_couplings=seed_couplings, seed_run=seed_run,
                q_int=out["q_int"], e_trace=out["e_trace"].astype(np.float32), q2_trace=out["q2_trace"].astype(np.float32),
                label_trace=out["label_trace"], swap_acceptance=out["acc_count"] / attempts,
                E_min=out["E_min"].astype(np.float32), s_min=out["s_min"], N=N, D=D,
                n_equil=n_equil, n_save=n_save, n_meas=n_meas, meas_every=meas_every)

def load_or_generate(N, **settings):
    path = f"{DATA}/sk_N{N}.npz"
    if os.path.exists(path):
        f = dict(np.load(path))
        same = (np.allclose(f["T"], T_GRID) and all(int(f[k]) == v for k, v in settings.items()))
        if same:
            print(f"N = {N:3d}: loaded")
            return f
    t0 = time.time()
    ds = generate_sk_dataset(N, seed_couplings=1000 + N, seed_run=2000 + N, **settings)
    np.savez_compressed(path, **ds)
    print(f"N = {N:3d}: generated in {time.time() - t0:6.1f} s and saved ({os.path.getsize(path) / 2**20:.1f} MB)")
    return ds

5.6 The overlap distribution
We can now measure the central object of the theory. From the measured overlaps we build \(P_J(q)\) for every sample (a histogram over the \(N+1\) possible values \(q=-1,-1+2/N,\dots,1\)) and average over samples. We plot the density \(P(q)\), i.e. the probability of each value divided by the spacing \(2/N\), so that curves for different \(N\) can be compared. The panels show \(P(q)\) at \(T=0.4\), \(0.7\), \(1.0\) and \(1.5\), and four single samples of \(N=128\) at \(T=0.4\). The global flip symmetry makes every \(P_J(q)\) exactly symmetric, \(P_J(q)=P_J(-q)\). A finite run visits the mirror valleys only a limited number of times, so we symmetrise the histogram of each sample, which uses this exact symmetry to reduce the noise.


Code
def overlap_hist(d):
    """P_J(q) for every sample and temperature: array (D, K, N+1) of probabilities of q = -1, -1+2/N, ..., 1,
    symmetrised, P_J(q) -> [P_J(q) + P_J(-q)]/2 (an exact symmetry; it halves the statistical noise of a finite run)."""
    N = int(d["N"])
    idx = (d["q_int"].astype(np.int64) + N) // 2                               # 0 .. N
    D, K, n = idx.shape
    P = np.zeros((D, K, N + 1))
    np.add.at(P, (np.arange(D)[:, None, None], np.arange(K)[None, :, None], idx), 1.0)
    return 0.5 * (P + P[..., ::-1]) / n

At \(T=1.5\) the distribution is a single Gaussian peak at \(q=0\) that narrows as \(N\) grows, and \([\langle|q|\rangle]\) falls from \(0.181\) to \(0.131\) to \(0.094\) for \(N=32,64,128\), roughly as \(1/\sqrt N\). This is the paramagnet. At \(T=1.0\) the distribution is a broad single bump that still narrows with \(N\), but more slowly than at \(T=1.5\), as expected near the critical point. At \(T=0.7\) and \(0.4\) the picture changes. The distribution has two peaks at \(\pm q_{\max}\), the positions of the maxima, that sharpen with \(N\), and non-zero weight between them, including at \(q=0\). The weight near \(q=0\) at \(T=0.4\) shows no systematic decrease from \(N=32\) to \(N=128\) (\(P(|q|<0.1)=0.042\), \(0.053\), \(0.040\)). A ferromagnet would show two sharp peaks only (compare the Mattis model in Section 7). The right panel shows single samples at \(T=0.4\). They look very different from each other and from the average. Their peaks sit at different values of \(|q|\), and some have most of their weight at intermediate overlaps. This is the sample-to-sample fluctuation of \(P_J(q)\) described by Parisi’s solution.


5.7 Susceptibility and Binder cumulant
The overlap distribution also gives the two standard quantities for locating the transition. The spin-glass susceptibility \(\chi_{\rm SG}=N[\langle q^2\rangle]\) should approach \(1/(1-\beta^2J^2)\) above \(T_c\) (Section 4.4). Below \(T_c\), where \([\langle q^2\rangle]\) stays finite, it grows proportionally to \(N\).
A sharper tool is the Binder cumulant, the dimensionless ratio \[
g_{\rm B}(T,N)=\frac12\left(3-\frac{[\langle q^4\rangle]}{[\langle q^2\rangle]^2}\right),
\] which is \(0\) for a Gaussian \(P(q)\) (because \(\langle q^4\rangle=3\langle q^2\rangle^2\)) and \(1\) for two delta peaks at \(\pm q_0\). Near a continuous transition, finite-size scaling says that \(g_{\rm B}\) depends on \(T\) and \(N\) only through one combination. For the SK model this combination is \((T-T_c)N^{1/3}\) (mean-field exponents with the upper critical dimension \(d=6\) and \(\nu=1/2\), so \(N^{1/(\nu d)}=N^{1/3}\)) [Billoire 2007]. Consequently \(g_{\rm B}(T_c,N)\) does not depend on \(N\), so the curves for different \(N\) cross at \(T_c\).
The figure axes label \(g_{\rm B}\) as \(g\). We compute both quantities from the per-sample moments \(\langle q^2\rangle\), \(\langle q^4\rangle\), and estimate errors with a bootstrap over the disorder samples (200 resamplings of the \(D\) samples with replacement).


Code
def overlap_moments(d):
    """Per-sample thermal moments <q^2>, <q^4>: arrays (D, K)."""
    q = d["q_int"].astype(np.float64) / int(d["N"])
    return (q**2).mean(-1), (q**4).mean(-1)

def binder(q2, q4):
    return 0.5 * (3 - q4.mean(0) / q2.mean(0) ** 2)

def crossing(T, g1, g2, window=(0.6, 1.4)):
    """Temperature in the window where g1 - g2 changes sign (linear interpolation); NaN if it does not."""
    sel = (T >= window[0]) & (T <= window[1])
    T, dlt = T[sel], (g1 - g2)[sel]
    i = np.where(np.sign(dlt[:-1]) != np.sign(dlt[1:]))[0]
    if len(i) == 0:
        return np.nan
    i = i[0]
    return T[i] - dlt[i] * (T[i + 1] - T[i]) / (dlt[i + 1] - dlt[i])

mom = {N: overlap_moments(sk[N]) for N in SIZES}
n_boot = 200
boot_rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
def bootstrap_binder(q2, q4, n_boot, rng):
    """Binder cumulant of n_boot resamplings of the D samples; q2 and q4 of a sample stay together."""
    out = []
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        idx = rng.integers(0, len(q2), len(q2))           # one index array per bootstrap resampling, used for both moments
        out.append(binder(q2[idx], q4[idx]))
    return np.array(out)

g_boot = {N: bootstrap_binder(*mom[N], n_boot, boot_rng) for N in SIZES}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.8))
TT = np.linspace(1.02, 1.62, 200)
ax[0].plot(TT, 1 / (1 - 1 / TT**2), color=DSOrange, lw=2, label=r"$1/(1-\beta^2J^2)$")

    g = binder(*mom[N]); g_err = g_boot[N].std(0)
    ax[1].errorbar(T_GRID, g, yerr=g_err, fmt="o-", ms=3, color=SIZE_COLORS[N], label=f"$N={N}$")
    ax[2].errorbar((T_GRID - T_C) * N ** (1 / 3), g, yerr=g_err, fmt="o", ms=3, color=SIZE_COLORS[N], label=f"$N={N}$")
ax[0].set_yscale("log"); ax[0].axvline(T_C, color=UJGray, ls=":"); ax[0].set_xlabel("$T/J$"); ax[0].set_ylabel(r"$\chi_{\rm SG}=N[\langle q^2\rangle]$")
ax[0].set_title("spin-glass susceptibility"); ax[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax[1].axvline(T_C, color=UJGray, ls=":"); ax[1].set_xlabel("$T/J$"); ax[1].set_ylabel("$g$"); ax[1].set_title("Binder cumulant of $q$"); ax[1].legend(frameon=False)
ax[2].axvline(0, color=UJGray, ls=":"); ax[2].set_xlabel(r"$(T-T_c)\,N^{1/3}$  with $T_c=J$"); ax[2].set_ylabel("$g$")
ax[2].set_title("finite-size scaling"); ax[2].legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_sk_binder.png"); plt.show()

print("Binder crossings (bootstrap median and 68% interval over disorder resamplings):")
for N1, N2 in ((32, 64), (64, 128), (32, 128)):
    c0 = crossing(T_GRID, binder(*mom[N1]), binder(*mom[N2]))
    cb = np.array([crossing(T_GRID, g_boot[N1][i], g_boot[N2][i]) for i in range(n_boot)])
    lo, med, hi = np.nanpercentile(cb, [16, 50, 84])
    print(f"  N = {N1:3d} and {N2:3d}:  T_cross = {c0:.3f};  bootstrap median {med:.3f}, 68% interval [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}],"
          f" no crossing in {np.isnan(cb).sum()} of {n_boot} resamplings;   exact T_c = {T_C} J")
for T in (1.2, 1.4, 1.6):
    k = np.argmin(abs(T_GRID - T))
    print(f"  T = {T}: chi_SG = " + ", ".join(f"{N * mom[N][0][:, k].mean():.3f} (N={N})" for N in SIZES) + f";  1/(1-beta^2) = {1 / (1 - 1 / T**2):.3f}")





Binder crossings (bootstrap median and 68% interval over disorder resamplings):
  N =  32 and  64:  T_cross = 0.870;  bootstrap median 0.867, 68% interval [0.765, 0.933], no crossing in 6 of 200 resamplings;   exact T_c = 1.0 J
  N =  64 and 128:  T_cross = 0.920;  bootstrap median 0.914, 68% interval [0.816, 0.999], no crossing in 4 of 200 resamplings;   exact T_c = 1.0 J
  N =  32 and 128:  T_cross = 0.894;  bootstrap median 0.885, 68% interval [0.848, 0.938], no crossing in 0 of 200 resamplings;   exact T_c = 1.0 J
  T = 1.2: chi_SG = 2.296 (N=32), 2.564 (N=64), 2.819 (N=128);  1/(1-beta^2) = 3.273
  T = 1.4: chi_SG = 1.797 (N=32), 1.900 (N=64), 1.967 (N=128);  1/(1-beta^2) = 2.042
  T = 1.6: chi_SG = 1.553 (N=32), 1.591 (N=64), 1.614 (N=128);  1/(1-beta^2) = 1.641


The figure shows \(\chi_{\rm SG}\) against \(T/J\) on a logarithmic axis with \(1/(1-\beta^2J^2)\) (left), the Binder cumulant \(g_{\rm B}\) against \(T/J\) (middle), and \(g_{\rm B}\) against \((T-T_c)N^{1/3}\) with \(T_c=J\) (right). Above \(T_c\) the spin-glass susceptibility approaches \(1/(1-\beta^2J^2)\) from below as \(N\) grows, most closely at \(T=1.6\) (\(1.553\), \(1.591\), \(1.614\) against \(1.641\)). Near \(T_c\) the finite systems cannot follow the divergence. Below \(T_c\), \(\chi_{\rm SG}\) grows roughly proportionally to \(N\), because \([\langle q^2\rangle]\) stays finite in the frozen phase.
Above \(T_c\) the Binder cumulant \(g_{\rm B}\) is largest for \(N=32\) and smallest for \(N=128\), and the curves come together below \(T_c\). The pairwise crossings printed above lie at \(0.870\) for \(N=32\) and \(64\), \(0.920\) for \(64\) and \(128\), and \(0.894\) for \(32\) and \(128\), with 68% bootstrap intervals \([0.765,0.933]\), \([0.816,0.999]\) and \([0.848,0.938]\). Two of the three intervals lie entirely below \(T=J\) and the third reaches it only at its upper end, so at these sizes the crossings lie below \(T_c\). They move up as the sizes grow, from \(0.870\) for the smaller pair to \(0.920\) for the larger one, which is how finite-size corrections to the crossing point behave. With \(N\le128\) this drift cannot be extrapolated reliably. The curves meet at a small angle, so a few resamplings (6 and 4 of 200 for the pairs \(32/64\) and \(64/128\)) have no crossing in the window at all. Plotted against \((T-T_c)N^{1/3}\) with the exact \(T_c=J\), the three sizes fall on one curve within the error bars. The size dependence of the data is consistent with the mean-field finite-size scaling of the SK model and with \(T_c=J\), up to finite-size corrections that shift the crossings of the smallest sizes downwards.

title: Lab 032: Physics of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glass
text:
6. The energy landscape

6.1 Ground-state energy
Finding the ground state of one SK sample is a hard optimisation problem (Section 1.2). For \(N\le24\) exact enumeration gives it (Section 2.4). For \(N=32,64,128\) we use the parallel-tempering runs. The lowest energy visited by each replica during the run (E_min) is improved by a zero-temperature descent, which flips, one at a time, every spin anti-aligned with its local field (\(s_ih_i<0\), so \(\Delta E_i<0\)) until no such spin is left. The descent is also applied to all snapshots stored at the lowest temperature. The result is an upper bound on the true ground-state energy of each sample. A useful indicator of its quality is that the two replicas search independently, so if both find the same lowest energy, it is very likely the ground state.
For the extrapolation to \(N\to\infty\) we use the form \([E_0]/N=e_\infty+a\,N^{-2/3}\). The exponent \(2/3\) of the finite-size correction is supported by extensive ground-state computations for the SK model [Boettcher 2005].


Code
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("block",))
def descent_columns(s, J, block):
    """Zero-temperature descent of C chains of one sample, s: (N, C), J: (N, N). The sweep of Section 5.2 at beta -> infinity
    (beta = infinity, u = 1/2, so the threshold is 0): a spin flips if and only if s_i h_i < 0. Sweeps are repeated until no spin flips."""
    big = jnp.full(s.shape[1], jnp.inf)
    half = jnp.full(s.shape, 0.5)
    def body(c):
        s, h, _ = c
        s2, h2 = sweep_sample(s, h, J, big, half, block)
        return s2, h2, jnp.any(s2 != s)
    s, _, _ = lax.while_loop(lambda c: c[2], body, (s, J @ s, True))
    return s

descent_many = lambda s, J: descent_columns(s.T, J, gcd(s.shape[-1], 16)).T                  # s: (B, N), one sample
descent_samples = jax.jit(jax.vmap(lambda s, J: descent_columns(s.T, J, 16).T))              # s: (D, B, N), J: (D, N, N)

def energies(s, J):
    """Energies of configurations s (D, B, N) for couplings J (D, N, N): array (D, B)."""
    return -0.5 * jnp.einsum("dbi,dij,dbj->db", s, J, s)

gs = {}
for N in SIZES:
    d = sk[N]; D = int(d["D"])
    J = jnp.asarray(d["J"])
    # candidates: the lowest configuration of each replica and all snapshots at the lowest temperature, both replicas
    cand = np.concatenate([d["s_min"][:, :, None, :], d["configs"][:, :, 0]], axis=2).astype(np.float32)   # (D, 2, 1 + n_save, N)
    cand = jnp.asarray(cand.reshape(D, -1, N))
    s_loc = descent_samples(cand, J)
    E_loc = np.asarray(energies(s_loc, J)).reshape(D, 2, -1)                          # (D, 2, 1 + n_save)
    best_rep = np.minimum(E_loc.min(-1), d["E_min"])                                 # (D, 2) best of each replica
    gs[N] = dict(best=best_rep.min(1) / N, agree=np.mean(np.abs(best_rep[:, 0] - best_rep[:, 1]) < 1e-4))
    print(f"N = {N:3d}: [E0]/N <= {gs[N]['best'].mean():.4f} ± {gs[N]['best'].std() / np.sqrt(D):.4f};"
          f"  both replicas found the same lowest energy in {100 * gs[N]['agree']:.0f}% of the {D} samples")


N =  32: [E0]/N <= -0.6911 ± 0.0027;  both replicas found the same lowest energy in 100% of the 256 samples


N =  64: [E0]/N <= -0.7183 ± 0.0019;  both replicas found the same lowest energy in 100% of the 160 samples


N = 128: [E0]/N <= -0.7345 ± 0.0016;  both replicas found the same lowest energy in 97% of the 96 samples




Code
N_all = np.array(sorted(list(N_ENUM) + list(N_GS_ONLY) + SIZES))
e_mean = np.array([(enum[N]["E0"] / N).mean() if N in enum else gs[N]["best"].mean() for N in N_all])
e_err = np.array([(enum[N]["E0"] / N).std() / np.sqrt(len(enum[N]["E0"])) if N in enum
                  else gs[N]["best"].std() / np.sqrt(len(gs[N]["best"])) for N in N_all])

x_fit = N_all ** (-2 / 3)

def fit_e0(mask):
    """Weighted least squares of e(N) = e_inf + a N^(-2/3) over the sizes selected by mask: (e_inf, a), error of e_inf, chi^2."""
    A = np.stack([np.ones(mask.sum()), x_fit[mask]], 1) / e_err[mask, None]
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, e_mean[mask] / e_err[mask], rcond=None)
    cov = np.linalg.inv(A.T @ A)
    chi2 = np.sum(((e_mean[mask] - (coef[0] + coef[1] * x_fit[mask])) / e_err[mask]) ** 2)
    return coef, np.sqrt(cov[0, 0]), chi2

coef, e_inf_err, chi2 = fit_e0(np.ones(len(N_all), bool))
e_inf = coef[0]
coef16, e_inf16_err, chi2_16 = fit_e0(N_all >= 16)
E0_RS = -np.sqrt(2 / np.pi)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
is_enum = np.isin(N_all, list(N_ENUM) + list(N_GS_ONLY))
ax.errorbar(x_fit[is_enum], e_mean[is_enum], yerr=e_err[is_enum], fmt="o", color=UJBlue, ms=5, label="exact enumeration, $N\\leq24$")
ax.errorbar(x_fit[~is_enum], e_mean[~is_enum], yerr=e_err[~is_enum], fmt="s", color=DSOrange, ms=5, label="parallel tempering + descent, $N=32,64,128$")
xx = np.linspace(0, x_fit.max(), 100)
ax.plot(xx, coef[0] + coef[1] * xx, color=UJGray, lw=1.2, label=r"fit $e_\infty+aN^{-2/3}$")
ax.plot(0, E0_PARISI, "*", ms=14, color=UJNavy, label=f"Parisi: {E0_PARISI}")
ax.plot(0, E0_RS, "v", ms=9, color=UJGray, label=f"replica symmetric: {E0_RS:.4f}")
ax.set_xlabel("$N^{-2/3}$"); ax.set_ylabel("$[E_0]/N$"); ax.set_title("SK ground-state energy per spin"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_sk_ground_state.png"); plt.show()
print(f"fit over N = {N_all.min()}..{N_all.max()}: e_inf = {e_inf:.4f} ± {e_inf_err:.4f},  a = {coef[1]:.3f},  chi^2 = {chi2:.1f} for {len(N_all) - 2} degrees of freedom")
print(f"fit over N = 16..{N_all.max()}: e_inf = {coef16[0]:.4f} ± {e_inf16_err:.4f},  a = {coef16[1]:.3f},  chi^2 = {chi2_16:.1f} for {(N_all >= 16).sum() - 2} degrees of freedom")
print(f"relative difference of the full fit from Parisi's value: {100 * (e_inf - E0_PARISI) / abs(E0_PARISI):+.2f}%")
print(f"Parisi (Crisanti & Rizzo 2002): {E0_PARISI},   replica-symmetric value -sqrt(2/pi) = {E0_RS:.4f}")





fit over N = 8..128: e_inf = -0.7674 ± 0.0016,  a = 0.796,  chi^2 = 14.3 for 10 degrees of freedom
fit over N = 16..128: e_inf = -0.7643 ± 0.0023,  a = 0.746,  chi^2 = 9.5 for 6 degrees of freedom
relative difference of the full fit from Parisi's value: -0.55%
Parisi (Crisanti & Rizzo 2002): -0.76321,   replica-symmetric value -sqrt(2/pi) = -0.7979


The data for \(N\le24\) are exact (up to the statistical error of the disorder average). For \(N\ge32\) they are upper bounds, but the two independent replicas found the same lowest energy in almost all samples (all samples for \(N=32\) and \(64\), 97% for \(N=128\)), so the bound is very likely reached. All sizes lie close to one straight line in \(N^{-2/3}\), and the extrapolation lands within about one percent of Parisi’s value (\(e_\infty=-0.7674\) from the fit over all sizes, \(-0.7643\) without the smallest ones, against \(-0.76321\), and the two fits show how much the result depends on the range of sizes). With sizes up to \(N=128\) this is a modest test, but it clearly separates Parisi’s value from the replica-symmetric value \(-\sqrt{2/\pi}\), which lies well below the data, so the RS solution overestimates how deep the landscape goes.


6.2 Metastable states
A configuration is metastable (a local minimum for single flips) if every spin is aligned with its local field, \(s_ih_i>0\) for all \(i\). The ferromagnet has exactly two such configurations (all up, all down) for any \(N\). The exact enumeration of Section 2.4 counted them for the SK model.


Code
Ns_ms = np.array(sorted(list(N_ENUM) + list(N_GS_ONLY)))
n_ms = np.array([enum[N]["n_stable"].mean() for N in Ns_ms])
n_ms_err = np.array([enum[N]["n_stable"].std() / np.sqrt(len(enum[N]["n_stable"])) for N in Ns_ms])
sel = Ns_ms >= 12
alpha_fit, c_fit = np.polyfit(Ns_ms[sel], np.log(n_ms[sel]), 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.errorbar(Ns_ms, n_ms, yerr=n_ms_err, fmt="o", color=UJBlue, ms=5, label="SK, exact enumeration")
ax.plot(Ns_ms, np.exp(c_fit + alpha_fit * Ns_ms), color=DSOrange, lw=1.2, label=fr"$\exp({alpha_fit:.3f}\,N{c_fit:+.2f})$")
ax.axhline(2, color=UJGray, ls="--", lw=1, label="ferromagnet: 2")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("$N$"); ax.set_ylabel("mean number of single-flip-stable states")
ax.set_title("metastable states"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for N, m in zip(Ns_ms, n_ms):
    print(f"N = {N:2d}: [number of metastable states] = {m:9.1f}")
print(f"growth rate from a fit over N >= 12: ln[n] = {alpha_fit:.4f} N {c_fit:+.3f}  ->  at N = 128 this extrapolates to about {np.exp(c_fit + alpha_fit * 128):.1e}")





N =  8: [number of metastable states] =       5.3
N = 10: [number of metastable states] =       7.8
N = 12: [number of metastable states] =      11.4
N = 14: [number of metastable states] =      17.4
N = 16: [number of metastable states] =      25.3
N = 18: [number of metastable states] =      38.5
N = 20: [number of metastable states] =      54.3
N = 22: [number of metastable states] =      92.1

growth rate from a fit over N >= 12: ln[n] = 0.2004 N +0.036  ->  at N = 128 this extrapolates to about 1.4e+11


The number of metastable states grows exponentially with \(N\), roughly as \(e^{0.20N}\) according to the fit. A local search started from a random configuration therefore ends in one of exponentially many traps, most of them well above the ground state. We see this directly at \(N=128\) in zero-temperature descents from \(2000\) random starts for one sample of the data set.


Code
d128 = sk[128]; J0 = jnp.asarray(d128["J"][0])
n_starts = 2000
s_start = random_spins(jax.random.PRNGKey(31), (n_starts, 128))
s_desc = descent_many(s_start, J0)
e_desc = np.asarray(-0.5 * jnp.einsum("bi,ij,bj->b", s_desc, J0, s_desc)) / 128
canon = np.asarray(s_desc * s_desc[:, :1]).astype(np.int8)                      # identify s and -s (fix the first spin to +1)
n_distinct = len({c.tobytes() for c in canon})
q_desc = np.asarray(s_desc @ s_desc.T / 128)[np.triu_indices(n_starts, 1)]

k04 = 0
conf04 = d128["configs"][0, :, k04].reshape(-1, 128).astype(np.float32)        # equilibrium snapshots at T = 0.4, both replicas
q_eq = (conf04 @ conf04.T / 128)[np.triu_indices(len(conf04), 1)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4))
ax[0].hist(e_desc, bins=40, color=UJBlue, alpha=0.85, label="local minima from descent")

Almost every descent ends in a different local minimum (\(1974\) distinct minima from \(2000\) starts). The typical minimum, with mean energy \(-0.654\) per spin, lies well above the lowest energy found by parallel tempering, \(-0.728\), and only the best of the \(2000\) descents reaches it. The minima reached by descent are also less similar to each other than equilibrium configurations at \(T=0.4\) (mean \(|q|\) of \(0.18\) against \(0.63\)). 6.3 Slow dynamics
