 1.00     0.6118 /   0.6118                         0.0588 /   0.0588
 4.00     0.5200 /   0.5200                         0.2000 /   0.2000


16.00     0.3250 /   0.3250                         0.5000 /   0.5000


The minimiser agrees with the tempered posterior to all printed digits. As \(\beta\) grows the optimal code moves towards the prior. Its mean shrinks towards 0 and its variance grows towards 1, and at \(\beta=16\) the code has almost forgotten the observation.


2.4 Decomposition of the rate
The rate \(R\) is an average over images of a KL divergence between each image’s cloud and the prior. One part of it pushes the latent coordinates to be independent, and it appears when we look at all codes together. For a data set of \(N\) images \(\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_N\), put the index \(n\) of an image on equal footing with \(\mathbf z\) and define two joint distributions over pairs \((n,\mathbf z)\), \[q(n,\mathbf z)=\tfrac1N\,q(\mathbf z|\mathbf x_n),\qquad p(n,\mathbf z)=\tfrac1N\,p(\mathbf z).\] Their marginals over \(n\) are both uniform, \(1/N\). The marginal of \(q\) over \(n\) is the aggregate posterior \[q(\mathbf z)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N q(\mathbf z|\mathbf x_n),\] the distribution of codes over the whole data set, a mixture of \(N\) Gaussian clouds. Its one-dimensional marginals are \(q(z_j)\). The derivation needs only the definition of KL and the splitting of a logarithm.
The first step follows M. D. Hoffman and M. J. Johnson [ELBO surgery: yet another way to carve up the variational evidence lower bound, NIPS 2016 Workshop on Advances in Approximate Bayesian Inference, PDF]. The rate is \[\begin{aligned}R&=\frac1N\sum_n\mathbb E_{q(\mathbf z|\mathbf x_n)}\Big[\log\frac{q(\mathbf z|\mathbf x_n)}{p(\mathbf z)}\Big]\\&=\mathbb E_{q(n,\mathbf z)}\Big[\log\frac{q(\mathbf z|n)}{p(\mathbf z)}\Big].\end{aligned}\] Multiplying and dividing by \(q(\mathbf z)\) inside the logarithm gives \[R=\mathbb E_{q(n,\mathbf z)}\Big[\log\frac{q(\mathbf z|n)}{q(\mathbf z)}\Big]+\mathbb E_{q(n,\mathbf z)}\Big[\log\frac{q(\mathbf z)}{p(\mathbf z)}\Big].\] In the first term \(q(\mathbf z|n)/q(\mathbf z)=q(n,\mathbf z)/\big(q(n)q(\mathbf z)\big)\) with \(q(n)=1/N\), so this term is the mutual information (MI) \(I_q(n;\mathbf z)\) between the index of an image and its code. The mutual information of two random variables \(a\) and \(b\) with joint distribution \(P(a,b)\) and marginals \(P(a)\), \(P(b)\) is the KL divergence of the joint distribution from the product of the marginals, \(I(a;b)=\mathrm{KL}\big(P(a,b)\,\|\,P(a)P(b)\big)=\mathbb E\big[\log\frac{P(a,b)}{P(a)P(b)}\big]\ge0\). It is zero if and only if \(a\) and \(b\) are independent, and it equals the reduction of uncertainty about \(a\) obtained by learning \(b\), \(I(a;b)=H(a)-H(a|b)\), where \(H(a)=-\mathbb E\log P(a)\) is the entropy (both in nats). In the second term the integrand does not depend on \(n\), the average over \(n\) leaves \(\mathbb E_{q(\mathbf z)}\), and the term is \(\mathrm{KL}\big(q(\mathbf z)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big)\), which gives \[R=I_q(n;\mathbf z)+\mathrm{KL}\big(q(\mathbf z)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big).\]
The second step follows R. T. Q. Chen, X. Li, R. Grosse and D. Duvenaud [Isolating Sources of Disentanglement in Variational Autoencoders, NeurIPS 2018, arXiv:1802.04942]. The prior factorises, \(p(\mathbf z)=\prod_jp(z_j)\). Multiplying and dividing by \(\prod_jq(z_j)\) inside the second logarithm gives \[\begin{aligned}\mathrm{KL}\big(q(\mathbf z)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big)=\;&\mathbb E_{q(\mathbf z)}\Big[\log\frac{q(\mathbf z)}{\prod_jq(z_j)}\Big]\\&+\mathbb E_{q(\mathbf z)}\Big[\sum_j\log\frac{q(z_j)}{p(z_j)}\Big].\end{aligned}\] The first term is the total correlation \(\mathrm{TC}(\mathbf z)=\mathrm{KL}\big(q(\mathbf z)\,\|\,\prod_jq(z_j)\big)\). In the second, each summand depends only on \(z_j\), so its average over \(q(\mathbf z)\) is an average over the marginal \(q(z_j)\). Altogether, \[\begin{aligned}R=\;&\underbrace{I_q(n;\mathbf z)}_{\text{index-code mutual information}}+\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\Big(q(\mathbf z)\,\Big\|\,\prod_jq(z_j)\Big)}_{\text{total correlation (TC)}}\\&+\underbrace{\sum_j\mathrm{KL}\big(q(z_j)\,\|\,p(z_j)\big)}_{\text{dimension-wise KL}}\end{aligned}\]
The index-code mutual information says how well the code identifies the image it came from. It is what the decoder needs, because if the clouds of different images overlap completely, \(I_q=0\) and no reconstruction is possible. It cannot exceed \(\log N\), since \(I_q(n;\mathbf z)=H(n)-H(n|\mathbf z)\le H(n)=\log N\). Penalising it, as \(\beta>1\) does, directly harms the reconstruction. The total correlation is the KL divergence between the distribution of codes and the product of its marginals, so it is zero if and only if the coordinates \(z_1,\dots,z_d\) are statistically independent over the data set, and positive otherwise. For a two-dimensional Gaussian with correlation coefficient \(\rho\) it equals \(-\frac12\log(1-\rho^2)\) (Exercise 3). The dimension-wise KL says how far each coordinate’s distribution is from \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).
The total correlation is the term that connects to disentangling. If the factors that generate the data are independent, as in dSprites, then a code in which each coordinate carries one factor has independent coordinates, \(\mathrm{TC}=0\), whereas a code in which coordinates carry mixtures of factors generally has \(\mathrm{TC}>0\) (a rotation of two independent non-Gaussian coordinates makes them dependent). A loss that penalises TC therefore favours codes aligned with independent factors. The β-VAE penalises TC, but only together with the other two terms, and its penalty on \(I_q\) costs reconstruction quality. The β-TCVAE of Chen et al. keeps the weight 1 on \(I_q\) and on the dimension-wise KL and puts the weight \(\beta\) on TC alone, \[\mathcal L_{\beta\text{-TC}}=D+I_q(n;\mathbf z)+\beta\,\mathrm{TC}(\mathbf z)+\sum_j\mathrm{KL}\big(q(z_j)\,\|\,p(z_j)\big).\] The FactorVAE [H. Kim, A. Mnih, Disentangling by Factorising, ICML 2018, PMLR 80, 2649] penalises the same TC term, estimated with an auxiliary classifier. We train a β-TCVAE on dSprites in Section 4.
Computing these terms requires \(\log q(\mathbf z)\), a mixture over all \(N\) images. For a set of \(M\) images we can compute it exactly, \(\log q(\mathbf z)=\operatorname{logsumexp}_m\log q(\mathbf z|\mathbf x_m)-\log M\), and the same for each \(q(z_j)\). This is the aggregate posterior of those \(M\) images. We draw one \(\mathbf z\) from every cloud, average the logarithms, and obtain Monte Carlo estimates of the three terms. Their sum is then an estimate of \(R\) for these \(M\) images, which we can compare with the closed-form KL of each cloud averaged over the same images. The function below implements this, and Section 3 applies it to trained models. During training, the β-TCVAE uses the minibatch instead of a fixed set of images, with the “minibatch weighted sampling” estimate of Chen et al., \(\log q(\mathbf z_i)\approx\operatorname{logsumexp}_{j\le B}\log q(\mathbf z_i|\mathbf x_j)-\log(NB)\) for a minibatch of \(B\) images.


Code
@jax.jit
def _decomposition_rows(z, mu, lv):
    '''For samples z (C, d) and all clouds (mu, lv) (M, d): log q(z|x_m) summed and per coordinate.'''
    lq = log_normal(z[:, None, :], mu[None], lv[None])                     # (C, M, d)
    M = mu.shape[0]
    log_qz = jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(lq.sum(-1), axis=1) - jnp.log(M)  # (C,)   log q(z)
    log_qzj = jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(lq, axis=1) - jnp.log(M)         # (C, d) log q(z_j)
    return log_qz, log_qzj

def kl_decomposition(mu, lv, key, n_samples=4, chunk=250):
    '''Rate of M images split into index-code MI, total correlation and dimension-wise KL (nats per image).
    mu, lv: (M, d) encoder outputs. q(z) is the aggregate posterior of these M images.'''
    mu, lv = jnp.asarray(mu), jnp.asarray(lv)
    M, d = mu.shape
    acc = {"mi": 0.0, "tc": 0.0, "dimkl": np.zeros(d)}
    for s in range(n_samples):
        z = reparametrise(mu, lv, jax.random.fold_in(key, s))               # one z per cloud, (M, d)
        for i in range(0, M, chunk):
            zi = z[i:i + chunk]
            log_qz, log_qzj = _decomposition_rows(zi, mu, lv)
            log_qz_x = log_normal(zi, mu[i:i + chunk], lv[i:i + chunk]).sum(-1)   # log q(z | x_n), own cloud
            log_pzj = log_normal(zi, 0.0, 0.0)
            acc["mi"] += float((log_qz_x - log_qz).sum())
            acc["tc"] += float((log_qz - log_qzj.sum(-1)).sum())
            acc["dimkl"] += np.asarray((log_qzj - log_pzj).sum(0))
    n = M * n_samples
    out = {"mi": acc["mi"] / n, "tc": acc["tc"] / n, "dimkl_per_dim": acc["dimkl"] / n}
    out["dimkl"] = float(out["dimkl_per_dim"].sum())
    out["sum"] = out["mi"] + out["tc"] + out["dimkl"]
    out["rate_closed_form"] = float(kl_per_dim(mu, lv).sum(-1).mean())
    out["log_M"] = float(np.log(M))
    return out

# check on clouds with a known answer: M identical clouds N(0, 1) in d = 3 -> every term is 0
_o = kl_decomposition(jnp.zeros((500, 3)), jnp.zeros((500, 3)), jax.random.key(0))
print({k: np.round(v, 4) for k, v in _o.items()})
assert abs(_o["mi"]) < 1e-5 and abs(_o["tc"]) < 1e-5 and abs(_o["rate_closed_form"]) < 1e-6

For clouds that all equal the prior, every term vanishes, as it must. The codes carry no information about the image (\(I_q=0\)), the aggregate is \(\mathcal N(0,I)\) with independent coordinates (\(\mathrm{TC}=0\)), and each marginal is the prior.


2.5 Limits of unsupervised disentangling
Nothing in \(\mathcal L_\beta\) refers to the factors we would like to find, and without further assumptions minimising it cannot find them, as F. Locatello et al. proved [Challenging Common Assumptions in the Unsupervised Learning of Disentangled Representations, ICML 2019, PMLR 97, 4114]. The simplest case of their argument is already in Lab 024. If \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), then for any rotation matrix \(R\) also \(R\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\). A model with decoder \(G(\mathbf z)\) and a model with decoder \(G(R^\top\mathbf z)\) generate exactly the same distribution of images, have the same prior and the same total correlation of the prior, yet if the coordinates of the first model are disentangled, those of the second are mixtures of factors. Locatello et al. show that for any factorised prior there are infinitely many such reparametrisations, so the data alone cannot prefer the disentangled one.
In practice β-VAEs do often find meaningful axes, and the reason lies in the assumptions built into the model. The most important is the diagonal encoder covariance \(\mathrm{diag}\,\boldsymbol\sigma^2\). A rotation of the latent space turns a diagonal covariance into a non-diagonal one, which the encoder cannot represent, so the model is not rotation invariant and prefers some axes. The data set, the architecture, \(\beta\) and even the random seed decide which axes. In the large study of Locatello et al. the random seed and the hyperparameters mattered more than the choice of the model, and good disentanglement scores could not be selected without access to the true factors.
The contrast with the cVAE is now clear. A cVAE receives the factor as a label, which is supervision. The condition \(\mathbf c\) is guaranteed to control the requested property, and the latent \(\mathbf z\) is pushed to carry the rest. A β-VAE receives no labels, and whatever factors it finds have to be identified afterwards, by looking (traversals) or by measuring against known quantities (Sections 4 and 6). The two approaches serve different purposes. The cVAE generates a requested factor, and the β-VAE explores what varies in the data.

title: Lab 026: Disentangled representations and the β-VAE
section: 3. The loss at work on MNIST
text:
3. The loss at work on MNIST
MNIST is familiar ground, so we can concentrate on what \(\beta\) changes. We train the dense VAE of Section 1 with \(d=10\) five times, with \(\beta\in\{0.5,1,2,4,8\}\), and look at the rate and the distortion, at reconstructions and samples, at the distribution of the codes, at how many coordinates stay in use, at the three parts of the rate, and finally at traversals.

3.1 A sweep over β
Each model is trained for 8 epochs with Adam (learning rate \(10^{-3}\), minibatches of 128) from the same initialisation and the same seed, so that the five models differ only in \(\beta\). The \(\beta=1\) model is the one of Section 1.4 and is loaded from its checkpoint. The printed numbers are per image, in nats, and give the loss \(\mathcal L_\beta=D+\beta R\), the distortion \(D\) (the BCE) and the rate \(R\) (the KL term). On 8 CPU cores one model takes about 17 s. After training, \(D\) and \(R\) are measured on the 10 000 test images, with one sample \(\mathbf z\sim q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)\) per image for \(D\) and the closed form for \(R\), together with the average KL of each coordinate, \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k\), and the number of active coordinates, those with \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k>0.1\) nats (Section 3.4).


Code
BETAS = [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0]
EPOCHS_MNIST = 8
mnist = {}
for beta in BETAS:
    model, hist = fit(f"mnist_beta{beta:g}", DenseVAE(784, D_LATENT, rngs=nnx.Rngs(1)), bvae_loss(beta),
                      (Xtr_m,), epochs=EPOCHS_MNIST, seed=1)
    mnist[beta] = {"model": model, "hist": hist}
nums["mnist_train_seconds_per_model"] = float(np.mean([mnist[b]["hist"]["seconds"] for b in BETAS]))

for beta in BETAS:
    D, R, kl = in_chunks(lambda x: rate_distortion(mnist[beta]["model"], x, jax.random.key(0)), Xte_m)
    mnist[beta].update(D=float(D.mean()), R=float(R.mean()), kl_dims=kl.mean(0))
    mnist[beta]["active"] = int((mnist[beta]["kl_dims"] > 0.1).sum())
    print(f"beta = {beta:3g}:  test D = {mnist[beta]['D']:6.1f}  R = {mnist[beta]['R']:5.1f}  "
          f"-ELBO = D + R = {mnist[beta]['D'] + mnist[beta]['R']:6.1f} nats;  active coordinates: {mnist[beta]['active']}")
nums["mnist"] = {f"{b:g}": {"D": mnist[b]["D"], "R": mnist[b]["R"], "neg_elbo": mnist[b]["D"] + mnist[b]["R"],
                            "active": mnist[b]["active"], "kl_dims_sorted": sorted(mnist[b]["kl_dims"].tolist(), reverse=True)}
                 for b in BETAS}

3.2 The rate–distortion curve
The five models are five points in the \((R,D)\) plane. Through each point we draw the line \(D+\beta R=\text{const}\), the set of points with the same β-loss. According to Section 2.2 the model of a given \(\beta\) should sit where such a line of slope \(-\beta\) touches the curve of achievable points from below. The right panel shows the per-image \(-\mathrm{ELBO}=D+R\) of each model, the quantity that a plain VAE minimises.


Code
Rs = np.array([mnist[b]["R"] for b in BETAS]); Ds = np.array([mnist[b]["D"] for b in BETAS])
cols = plt.get_cmap("viridis")(np.linspace(0.05, 0.85, len(BETAS)))
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(FULL, 1.9), layout="constrained", gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.6, 1]))
    ax = axs[0]
    ax.plot(Rs, Ds, "-", color="0.7", lw=1, zorder=1)
    rr = np.linspace(0, Rs.max() * 1.15, 50)
    for b, R_, D_, c in zip(BETAS, Rs, Ds, cols):
        ax.plot(rr, D_ - b * (rr - R_), "--", color=c, lw=0.8)          # the line D + beta R = const through the point
        ax.scatter([R_], [D_], color=c, s=30, zorder=3, edgecolor="k", lw=0.5, label=f"{b:g}")
    ax.set_ylim(Ds.min() - 10, Ds.max() + 20); ax.set_xlim(0, Rs.max() * 1.15)
    ax.set_xlabel("rate $R$ (nats)"); ax.set_ylabel("distortion $D$ (nats)")
    ax.legend(title="$\\beta$", loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 1.0), handletextpad=0.1, borderaxespad=0.1)
    axs[1].bar(range(len(BETAS)), Ds + Rs, color=cols, edgecolor="k", lw=0.5)
    axs[1].set_xticks(range(len(BETAS))); axs[1].set_xticklabels([f"{b:g}" for b in BETAS])
    axs[1].set_xlabel("$\\beta$"); axs[1].set_ylabel("$D + R$ (nats)")
    axs[1].set_ylim((Ds + Rs).min() - 15, (Ds + Rs).max() + 5)
    save(fig, "mnist_rd"); plt.show()





Increasing \(\beta\) from 0.5 to 8 lowers the rate from 22.9 to 4.5 nats and raises the distortion from 85.2 to 138.5 nats. The five models lie on a decreasing, convex curve, and each dashed line passes close to the curve near its own model, as the slope argument of Section 2.2 predicts. The ELBO is best for \(\beta=1\), with \(-\mathrm{ELBO}=107.1\) nats, as it must be, since \(\beta=1\) is the model trained on the ELBO itself. Yet the models with \(\beta=0.5\) and \(\beta=2\) are within 1.1 and 2.3 nats of it, although their codes carry 4.5 nats more and 4.9 nats less. The ELBO alone barely distinguishes models whose latent codes differ substantially, which is the point made by Alemi et al.


3.3 How β changes reconstructions, samples and the distribution of codes
The rate is the amount of information about the image that survives in the code, so a lower rate must show up in the pictures, both in reconstructions and in generated samples. In the next figure the left block shows eight test digits (top row) and their reconstructions \(\mathrm{sigm}(G_\theta(\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x)))\) by each model, and the right block shows, for each model, the decoder means of eight samples decoded from the same eight random vectors \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\).


Code
x8 = to_unit(Xte_m[:8])
z8 = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(5), (8, D_LATENT))
rec_rows = [np.asarray(x8)] + [np.asarray(dec_fn(mnist[b]["model"], enc_fn(mnist[b]["model"], x8)[0])) for b in BETAS]
smp_rows = [np.zeros((8, 784))] + [np.asarray(dec_fn(mnist[b]["model"], z8)) for b in BETAS]
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(FULL, 2.1), layout="constrained")
    show_rows(rec_rows, ["data"] + [f"$\\beta={b:g}$" for b in BETAS], axs[0]); axs[0].set_title("reconstructions")
    show_rows(smp_rows, [""] * 6, axs[1]); axs[1].set_title("samples, $\\mathbf{z}\\sim\\mathcal{N}(0,I)$")
    save(fig, "mnist_recon_samples"); plt.show()





The reconstructions lose detail as \(\beta\) grows. For \(\beta=8\) the 4 of the seventh column is reconstructed as a 9 and the 2 becomes a thick, blurred shape. The samples change in two ways. They become blurrier, because the decoder of a low-rate model has to produce an average of all images whose codes overlap. They also change identity. The same \(\mathbf z\) decodes to different digits for different \(\beta\), because each model has organised its latent space differently. Samples from \(\beta=0.5\) and \(\beta=1\) include malformed or faint shapes (third and sixth columns). With \(\beta=2\) and \(\beta=4\) most samples are clean digits, and with \(\beta=8\) they are blurred again.
Samples are good when the decoder has learned to produce digits wherever the prior puts its probability, that is, when the codes of the training images fill \(\mathcal N(0,I)\). The distribution of codes over the whole data set is the aggregate posterior \(q(\mathbf z)=\frac1N\sum_nq_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x_n)\) of Section 2.4. Lab 024 described the latent space with the analogy of a map. An autoencoder sticks one pin per image into the map and leaves an empty sea between the pins, a VAE replaces each pin by a cloud and the KL term pulls all clouds onto one standard disc, \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), so that a dart thrown at the disc (a sample of the prior) lands on land. The β-VAE version of the picture is that a larger \(\beta\) pushes the clouds harder onto the disc. Each cloud becomes wider and closer to the prior, and only the directions that carry the most information keep clouds that are narrow and well separated. To see this, we plot the encoder means \(\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x)\) of the test digits in the plane of the two most active coordinates, coloured by digit, for \(\beta=1\), \(4\) and \(8\), together with the circles of radius 1, 2 and 3 of the prior. For 40 of the digits we also draw the cloud itself as an ellipse with half-axes \(\sigma_k\), i.e. the region \(\boldsymbol\mu\pm\boldsymbol\sigma\) of \(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)\) in that plane.


Code
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(FULL, 1.9), layout="constrained", sharey=True)
    t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
    for ax, b in zip(axs, [1.0, 4.0, 8.0]):
        mu = in_chunks(lambda x: enc_fn(mnist[b]["model"], to_unit(x))[0], Xte_m)
        k1_, k2_ = np.argsort(mnist[b]["kl_dims"])[::-1][:2]
        for dgt in range(10):
            m = yte == dgt
            ax.scatter(mu[m, k1_], mu[m, k2_], s=0.3, color=cmap10(dgt), rasterized=True)
        for r in (1, 2, 3): ax.plot(r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t), "k:", lw=0.8)
        lv = in_chunks(lambda x: enc_fn(mnist[b]["model"], to_unit(x))[1], Xte_m[:40])
        for i in range(40):                                              # clouds: ellipses mu +- sigma in this plane
            sx, sy = np.exp(0.5 * lv[i, k1_]), np.exp(0.5 * lv[i, k2_])
            ax.plot(mu[i, k1_] + sx * np.cos(t), mu[i, k2_] + sy * np.sin(t), color=cmap10(yte[i]), lw=0.6)
        ax.set_xlim(-4, 4); ax.set_ylim(-4, 4); ax.set_aspect("equal")
        ax.set_title(f"$\\beta={b:g}$"); ax.set_xlabel(f"$\\mu_{{{k1_ + 1}}}$", labelpad=0)
        ax.set_ylabel(f"$\\mu_{{{k2_ + 1}}}$", labelpad=0)
        nums.setdefault("mnist_mu_std_top2", {})[f"{b:g}"] = mu[:, [k1_, k2_]].std(0).tolist()
    save(fig, "mnist_aggregate"); plt.show()
print("standard deviation of the two plotted mean coordinates:", {k: np.round(v, 2).tolist() for k, v in nums["mnist_mu_std_top2"].items()})





standard deviation of the two plotted mean coordinates: {'1': [1.05, 1.09], '4': [0.98, 1.01], '8': [0.93, 0.93]}


For \(\beta=1\) the clouds are tiny compared with the disc. Each image occupies a small, well-separated region, and the codes of different digits fill the disc like a mosaic. For \(\beta=8\) the clouds are much wider and overlap, the means are squeezed towards the centre (standard deviation 0.93 in both plotted coordinates, against 1.05 and 1.09 for \(\beta=1\)), and the details that distinguished nearby images are lost, which is the blur of the previous figure. In the map picture, a larger \(\beta\) pushes the clouds harder onto the disc.


3.4 Latent coordinates switching off
The rate is a sum over latent coordinates, \(R=\sum_k\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k\), with \[\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k=\Big\langle\tfrac12\big(\mu_k^2+\sigma_k^2-\ln\sigma_k^2-1\big)\Big\rangle_{\mathbf x}\] averaged over the test images, so we can see where the information sits. As in Lab 024, a coordinate with \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k<0.1\) nats is called inactive. Its cloud is the prior for every image, so it carries no information and the decoder ignores it. For each \(\beta\) the figure shows the ten values of \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k\) sorted in decreasing order, on a logarithmic scale.


Code
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(HALF, 2.0), layout="constrained")
    for b, c in zip(BETAS, cols):
        ax.plot(np.arange(1, D_LATENT + 1), np.sort(mnist[b]["kl_dims"])[::-1], "o-", color=c, ms=3, lw=1.2, label=f"{b:g}")
    ax.axhline(0.1, color="k", ls=":", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("coordinate (sorted)"); ax.set_ylabel("$\\overline{\\mathrm{KL}}_k$ (nats)", labelpad=0)
    ax.set_xticks([1, 4, 7, 10]); ax.legend(title="$\\beta$", ncol=2, loc="lower left", columnspacing=0.6, handlelength=1.2)
    save(fig, "mnist_kl_dims"); plt.show()





For \(\beta\le2\) all ten coordinates are active, with \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k\) decreasing smoothly. For \(\beta=4\) two coordinates switch off and for \(\beta=8\) five, with a drop of more than two orders of magnitude, to about \(10^{-3}\) nats, so these coordinates are practically the prior for every image. The β-weight does not shrink all coordinates equally. It removes the least useful ones and keeps a few informative ones, which is the first ingredient of a disentangled code.


3.5 The three parts of the rate
Section 2.4 split the rate into the index-code mutual information \(I_q(n;\mathbf z)\), the total correlation and the dimension-wise KL. We now estimate the three parts for each model on \(M=2000\) test images, with the aggregate posterior of these images and four samples of \(\mathbf z\) per image. The sum of the three Monte Carlo estimates must reproduce the closed-form rate of the same images, which tests the implementation, and the mutual information cannot exceed \(\log M=7.60\) nats.


Code
M_DEC = 2000
decomp = {}
for b in BETAS:
    mu, lv = enc_fn(mnist[b]["model"], to_unit(Xte_m[:M_DEC]))
    decomp[b] = kl_decomposition(mu, lv, jax.random.key(7))
    o = decomp[b]
    print(f"beta = {b:3g}:  I = {o['mi']:5.2f}  TC = {o['tc']:5.2f}  dim-KL = {o['dimkl']:5.2f}  "
          f"sum = {o['sum']:6.2f}   closed-form rate = {o['rate_closed_form']:6.2f}   (log M = {o['log_M']:.2f})")
    assert abs(o["sum"] - o["rate_closed_form"]) < 0.02 * o["rate_closed_form"] + 0.05
    assert o["mi"] <= o["log_M"] + 1e-6
nums["mnist_decomposition"] = {f"{b:g}": {k: decomp[b][k] for k in ["mi", "tc", "dimkl", "rate_closed_form"]} for b in BETAS}

with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(HALF, 2.0), layout="constrained")
    bottom = np.zeros(len(BETAS))
    for key, lab, c in [("mi", "$I_q(n;\\mathbf{z})$", UJBlue), ("tc", "TC", DSOrange), ("dimkl", "dim. KL", UJGray)]:
        v = np.array([decomp[b][key] for b in BETAS])
        ax.bar(range(len(BETAS)), v, bottom=bottom, color=c, label=lab, width=0.65); bottom += v
    ax.axhline(np.log(M_DEC), color="k", ls=":", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(BETAS))); ax.set_xticklabels([f"{b:g}" for b in BETAS]); ax.set_xlabel("$\\beta$")
    ax.set_ylabel("nats per image"); ax.legend(loc="upper right", handlelength=1.0)
    save(fig, "mnist_decomposition"); plt.show()


beta = 0.5:  I =  7.59  TC = 14.50  dim-KL =  0.38  sum =  22.48   closed-form rate =  22.47   (log M = 7.60)


beta =   1:  I =  7.55  TC = 10.22  dim-KL =  0.26  sum =  18.03   closed-form rate =  18.02   (log M = 7.60)


beta =   2:  I =  7.38  TC =  5.66  dim-KL =  0.17  sum =  13.20   closed-form rate =  13.19   (log M = 7.60)


beta =   4:  I =  6.53  TC =  1.69  dim-KL =  0.19  sum =   8.40   closed-form rate =   8.39   (log M = 7.60)


beta =   8:  I =  3.86  TC =  0.26  dim-KL =  0.11  sum =   4.23   closed-form rate =   4.22   (log M = 7.60)





In all five models the three Monte Carlo estimates add up to the closed-form rate within 0.01 nats. The parts behave differently. The index-code mutual information stays close to its maximum \(\log M=7.60\) for \(\beta\le2\) (7.59, 7.55, 7.38 nats) and only then decreases (6.53 for \(\beta=4\), 3.86 for \(\beta=8\)). The codes of different images overlap only when \(\beta\) is large, which is when reconstructions deteriorate. The total correlation falls fastest, from 14.50 nats at \(\beta=0.5\) and 10.22 at \(\beta=1\) to 1.69 at \(\beta=4\) and 0.26 at \(\beta=8\), so the coordinates of the code become nearly independent. The dimension-wise KL is small throughout (below 0.4 nats), so each coordinate on its own is close to \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) in every model. What distinguishes the models is the dependence between coordinates.


3.6 Traversals of the MNIST codes
We return to the question of Section 1.5 and compare the traversals of the model with \(\beta=1\) (the one shown there) with those of the model with \(\beta=4\). Each row again varies one coordinate from \(-3\) to \(3\) around the code of the same test digit, for the active coordinates with the largest \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k\) (at most five).


Code
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(FULL, 1.75), layout="constrained")
    for ax, b in zip(axs, [1.0, 4.0]):
        m = mnist[b]["model"]
        dims = [k for k in np.argsort(mnist[b]["kl_dims"])[::-1][:5] if mnist[b]["kl_dims"][k] > 0.1]
        mu0 = enc_fn(m, to_unit(Xte_m[i_seed:i_seed + 1]))[0][0]
        show_rows(traversal_rows(m, mu0, dims), [f"$z_{{{k + 1}}}$" for k in dims], ax)
        ax.set_title(f"$\\beta={b:g}$")
    save(fig, "mnist_traversal"); plt.show()





Both models change the digit continuously along every axis, and both change its identity. For \(\beta=4\), \(z_2\) turns a 6 into a 3 and then a 1, \(z_8\) turns the 3 into a 7, and \(z_5\) a 6 into a 3, while \(z_4\) mainly changes the width and the thickness of the stroke. The coordinates of the \(\beta=4\) model are fewer and individually somewhat cleaner, but none of them is “the digit”, and slant, width and thickness still appear together with identity changes.
The reason why identity does not separate is structural. The identity of a digit is a discrete factor with ten values, and the latent space is a continuous Gaussian. There is no single coordinate along which “3” turns into “8” without passing through shapes in between, so identity ends up spread over several coordinates and regions of the latent space. This is the situation in which the cVAE helps, because it receives the digit as a one-hot label and leaves only the continuous style to \(\mathbf z\). Whether the remaining coordinates are disentangled we cannot tell on MNIST, because nobody has listed the true factors of handwriting. The next data set has them.

title: Lab 026: Disentangled representations and the β-VAE
text:
4. Measuring disentanglement on dSprites

4.1 Data with known factors
dSprites [L. Matthey, I. Higgins, D. Hassabis, A. Lerchner, dSprites: Disentanglement testing Sprites dataset (2017), github.com/deepmind/dsprites-dataset] contains \(64\times64\) binary images of a single white sprite, generated from five independent factors, namely shape (square, ellipse, heart; 3 values), scale (6 values in \([0.5,1]\)), orientation (40 values in \([0,2\pi]\)), and position \(x\) and \(y\) (32 values each in \([0,1]\)). Every combination occurs exactly once, \(3\cdot6\cdot40\cdot32\cdot32=737\,280\) images, and the file stores the factor values of every image. This makes dSprites a test bed, because we know the right answer.
To fit the CPU budget we use a random subset of \(75\,000\) images for training and \(10\,000\) other images for evaluation, and average each \(2\times2\) block of pixels, which gives \(32\times32\) images with grey values at the edges of the sprite. The positions remain resolved because a half-pixel shift changes the grey values. A square looks the same after a quarter turn and an ellipse after a half turn, so the orientation factor is ambiguous for these shapes, and no code can carry it perfectly.


Code
DS_DIR = f"{DATA}/dsprites"
DS_FILE = f"{DS_DIR}/dsprites_ndarray_co1sh3sc6or40x32y32_64x64.npz"
if not os.path.exists(DS_FILE):
    os.makedirs(DS_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://github.com/deepmind/dsprites-dataset/raw/master/" + os.path.basename(DS_FILE), DS_FILE)
ds = np.load(DS_FILE, allow_pickle=False)                     # the pickled 'metadata' entry is not needed
imgs64, fclass = ds["imgs"], ds["latents_classes"][:, 1:]    # (737280, 64, 64) uint8 in {0, 1}; (737280, 5) factor indices
FACTORS = ["shape", "scale", "orientation", "x", "y"]
print("dSprites:", imgs64.shape, "| values per factor:", [int(fclass[:, k].max()) + 1 for k in range(5)])

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = rng.permutation(len(imgs64))
idx_tr, idx_ev = np.sort(idx[:75_000]), np.sort(idx[75_000:85_000])
def to32(ims):
    '''(n, 64, 64) {0,1} -> (n, 32, 32) uint8: mean of each 2x2 block, scaled to 0..255.'''
    return (ims.reshape(-1, 32, 2, 32, 2).mean((2, 4)) * 255).round().astype(np.uint8)
Xds_tr, Xds_ev = jnp.asarray(to32(imgs64[idx_tr]).reshape(-1, 1024)), jnp.asarray(to32(imgs64[idx_ev]).reshape(-1, 1024))
F_ev = fclass[idx_ev]                                         # (10000, 5) true factors of the evaluation images
print("training", Xds_tr.shape, "evaluation", Xds_ev.shape)

# one row per factor: change that factor only, starting from the same sprite
base_cls = np.array([0, 1, 5, 0, 16, 16])                     # color, shape, scale, orientation, x, y (class indices)
strides = np.array([3 * 6 * 40 * 32 * 32, 6 * 40 * 32 * 32, 40 * 32 * 32, 32 * 32, 32, 1])   # row-major order of the file
rows = []
for k, n_val in zip(range(1, 6), [3, 6, 40, 32, 32]):
    vals = np.linspace(0, n_val - 1, 8).round().astype(int)
    cls = np.repeat(base_cls[None], 8, 0); cls[:, k] = vals
    rows.append(to32(imgs64[cls @ strides]) / 255.0)
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(HALF, 1.7), layout="constrained")
    show_rows(rows, FACTORS, ax, shape=(32, 32), cmap="gray")
    save(fig, "dsprites_data"); plt.show()
assert np.all(fclass[base_cls @ strides] == base_cls[1:])


dSprites: (737280, 64, 64) | values per factor: [3, 6, 40, 32, 32]


training (75000, 1024) evaluation (10000, 1024)







4.2 The mutual information gap (MIG)
To measure how disentangled a code is, we ask, for every true factor \(v_k\), how much information about it each latent coordinate carries, and whether one coordinate carries much more than all others. The mutual information gap (MIG) of Chen et al. (Section 2.4) turns this into one number. With the mutual information \(I(z_j;v_k)\) between latent coordinate \(j\) and factor \(k\), and the entropy \(H(v_k)\) of the factor, \[\mathrm{MIG}=\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\frac{I(z_{j^{(k)}_1};v_k)-I(z_{j^{(k)}_2};v_k)}{H(v_k)},\] where \(j^{(k)}_1\) and \(j^{(k)}_2\) are the coordinates with the largest and second-largest mutual information with \(v_k\). Each term lies between 0 and 1. It is 1 when one coordinate determines the factor completely and no other coordinate knows anything about it. It is small when the information about the factor is shared by two coordinates, as for a rotated code, or when no coordinate carries it. Dividing by \(H(v_k)\) makes factors with different numbers of values comparable.
Mutual information of continuous variables is hard to estimate, so we discretise. The latent coordinate is the encoder mean \(\mu_j(\mathbf x)\) of each evaluation image, cut into 20 equal-width bins between its minimum and maximum, while the factors are already discrete. Then \[I(a;b)=\sum_{a,b}P(a,b)\log\frac{P(a,b)}{P(a)P(b)},\qquad H(b)=-\sum_bP(b)\log P(b),\] with the probabilities \(P\) given by the counts in the joint histogram. Two checks on codes whose answer we know come first. A code made of the five true factors themselves, padded with five coordinates of pure noise to \(d=10\), should give MIG \(=1\) when the bins resolve every value. With 20 bins, positions and orientations that share a bin lower it. A code made of random numbers gives MIG close to 0, and a code in which the \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates are rotated by 45°, \(z_x=(x+y)/\sqrt2\), \(z_y=(x-y)/\sqrt2\), loses the contribution of both position factors.


Code
def discretise(Z, bins=20):
    '''Each column of Z (n, d) cut into `bins` equal-width bins between its min and max -> integer codes (n, d).'''
    lo, hi = Z.min(0), Z.max(0)
    return np.clip(((Z - lo) / np.where(hi > lo, hi - lo, 1) * bins).astype(int), 0, bins - 1)

def mutual_info(a, b):
    '''Mutual information (nats) of two integer arrays of equal length, from their joint histogram.'''
    joint = np.zeros((a.max() + 1, b.max() + 1))
    np.add.at(joint, (a, b), 1)
    P = joint / joint.sum()
    Pa, Pb = P.sum(1, keepdims=True), P.sum(0, keepdims=True)
    nz = P > 0
    return float((P[nz] * np.log(P[nz] / (Pa @ Pb)[nz])).sum())

def entropy(b):
    p = np.bincount(b) / len(b); p = p[p > 0]
    return float(-(p * np.log(p)).sum())

def mig(Z, F, bins=20):
    '''MIG of a code Z (n, d) for discrete factors F (n, K); returns (MIG, gap per factor (K,), normalised MI matrix (d, K)).'''
    Zd = discretise(np.asarray(Z, float), bins)
    H = np.array([entropy(F[:, k]) for k in range(F.shape[1])])
    MI = np.array([[mutual_info(Zd[:, j], F[:, k]) for k in range(F.shape[1])] for j in range(Z.shape[1])]) / H
    top = np.sort(MI, axis=0)[::-1]
    gaps = top[0] - top[1]
    return float(gaps.mean()), gaps, MI

Ftrue = F_ev.astype(float)
noise = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=(len(F_ev), 5))
rot = Ftrue.copy(); rot[:, 3], rot[:, 4] = (Ftrue[:, 3] + Ftrue[:, 4]) / np.sqrt(2), (Ftrue[:, 3] - Ftrue[:, 4]) / np.sqrt(2)
checks = {"true factors, 40 bins": mig(np.c_[Ftrue, noise], F_ev, bins=40)[0],
          "true factors, 20 bins": mig(np.c_[Ftrue, noise], F_ev)[0],
          "random code": mig(np.random.default_rng(2).normal(size=(len(F_ev), 10)), F_ev)[0],
          "x, y rotated by 45 degrees": mig(np.c_[rot, noise], F_ev)[0]}
for k, v in checks.items():
    print(f"MIG of a code made of {k:28s}: {v:.3f}")
assert checks["true factors, 40 bins"] > 0.95 and checks["random code"] < 0.05
nums["mig_checks"] = checks


MIG of a code made of true factors, 40 bins       : 0.987
MIG of a code made of true factors, 20 bins       : 0.896
MIG of a code made of random code                 : 0.000
MIG of a code made of x, y rotated by 45 degrees  : 0.559


The true factors give MIG \(=0.987\) with 40 bins, which resolve every value. The small deficit from 1 is a property of the estimator. A mutual information computed from a histogram of 10 000 samples is biased upwards, so the noise coordinates appear to know a few hundredths of a nat about each factor, and this is subtracted in the gap. With 20 bins the value drops to 0.896, because neighbouring positions and orientations now share a bin. A random code gives 0.000, and rotating \(x\) and \(y\) by 45° lowers the MIG to 0.559, because the two position factors, two of five, no longer have a coordinate of their own. This is the effect of the rotation discussed in Section 2.5.


4.3 Four models on dSprites
We train four models with the dense network of Section 1 adapted to \(32\times32=1024\) inputs (\(1024\to256\to128\to d=10\) and back), namely a VAE (\(\beta=1\)), two β-VAEs (\(\beta=4\) and \(\beta=16\)), and a β-TCVAE with weight \(\beta_{\rm TC}=6\) on the total correlation alone, estimated on each minibatch as described in Section 2.4. Each model is trained for 15 epochs, about 35 to 55 s on 8 CPU cores. The β-TCVAE loss needs, for every sample \(\mathbf z_i\) of the minibatch, the density of all \(B\) clouds of the minibatch at \(\mathbf z_i\), an array of shape \((B,B,d)\).


Code
N_DS = Xds_tr.shape[0]

def tcvae_loss(beta_tc, N=N_DS):
    '''beta-TCVAE: D + I + beta_tc * TC + dim-KL, with minibatch weighted sampling for log q(z) and log q(z_j).'''
    def loss_fn(model, batch, key):
        x = to_unit(batch[0]); B = x.shape[0]
        mu, lv = model.encode(x)
        z = reparametrise(mu, lv, key)                                        # (B, d)
        D = optax.sigmoid_binary_cross_entropy(model.decode(z), x).sum(-1).mean()
        lq = log_normal(z[:, None, :], mu[None], lv[None])                    # (B, B, d): log q(z_i,j | x_m)
        log_qz_x = log_normal(z, mu, lv).sum(-1)                              # (B,)   log q(z_i | x_i)
        log_qz = jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(lq.sum(-1), axis=1) - jnp.log(N * B)            # (B,)
        log_qz_prod = (jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(lq, axis=1) - jnp.log(N * B)).sum(-1)    # (B,)
        log_pz = log_normal(z, 0.0, 0.0).sum(-1)
        mi, tc, dkl = (log_qz_x - log_qz).mean(), (log_qz - log_qz_prod).mean(), (log_qz_prod - log_pz).mean()
        loss = D + mi + beta_tc * tc + dkl
        return loss, {"loss": loss, "D": D, "R": kl_per_dim(mu, lv).sum(-1).mean(), "TC": tc}
    return loss_fn

EPOCHS_DS = 15
DS_MODELS = {"VAE, $\\beta=1$": ("ds_beta1", bvae_loss(1.0)), "$\\beta=4$": ("ds_beta4", bvae_loss(4.0)),
             "$\\beta=16$": ("ds_beta16", bvae_loss(16.0)), "$\\beta$-TCVAE": ("ds_tcvae6", tcvae_loss(6.0))}
dsm = {}
for label, (name, loss) in DS_MODELS.items():
    model, hist = fit(name, DenseVAE(1024, 10, hidden=(256, 128), rngs=nnx.Rngs(3)), loss, (Xds_tr,), epochs=EPOCHS_DS, seed=3)
    D, R, kl = in_chunks(lambda x: rate_distortion(model, x, jax.random.key(0)), Xds_ev)
    mu_ev = in_chunks(lambda x: enc_fn(model, to_unit(x))[0], Xds_ev)
    m_, gaps, MI = mig(mu_ev, F_ev)
    dsm[label] = dict(name=name, model=model, hist=hist, D=float(D.mean()), R=float(R.mean()), kl_dims=kl.mean(0),
                      mu=mu_ev, mig=m_, gaps=gaps, MI=MI)
    print(f"{label:18s} D = {D.mean():6.1f}  R = {R.mean():5.1f} nats   active = {(kl.mean(0) > 0.1).sum():2d}   MIG = {m_:.3f}   "
          "gap per factor: " + ", ".join(f"{f} {g:.2f}" for f, g in zip(FACTORS, gaps)))
nums["dsprites"] = {v["name"]: {"D": v["D"], "R": v["R"], "active": int((v["kl_dims"] > 0.1).sum()), "MIG": v["mig"],
                                "gaps": dict(zip(FACTORS, map(float, v["gaps"]))), "train_seconds": v["hist"]["seconds"]}
                    for v in dsm.values()}

4.4 Mutual information between coordinates and factors
The MIG compresses a whole matrix into one number. The matrix itself is more instructive. For each model, the figure shows the normalised mutual information \(I(z_j;v_k)/H(v_k)\) for every latent coordinate \(j\) (rows, sorted by \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_j\), inactive coordinates greyed) and every factor \(k\) (columns). A disentangled code has one bright entry per column, in different rows.


Code
for label, v in dsm.items():                                   # the full matrices, printed
    print(label, "| rows: coordinates sorted by KL; columns:", FACTORS)

The VAE (\(\beta=1\), MIG 0.036) spreads every factor over several coordinates. Its six active coordinates each carry a little information about \(x\), \(y\) or scale and none dominates. Increasing \(\beta\) helps. The value \(\beta=4\) gives MIG 0.097, mainly through one coordinate that carries the scale (normalised MI 0.40), and \(\beta=16\) gives the highest value, 0.222, with three active coordinates, one for \(x\) and one for \(y\) (0.56 each, with gaps 0.48 and 0.46) and one for the scale (0.39). The β-TCVAE (MIG 0.164) isolates the scale best (gap 0.51) and partly the shape (gap 0.22), with a much smaller distortion than \(\beta=16\) (36.1 against 64.5 nats), but it keeps \(x\) and \(y\) mixed over three coordinates. No model learns the orientation, which, as noted above, is ambiguous for two of the three shapes, and no model separates the shape cleanly. These values are lower than those reported in the literature for long training runs. Our models see each image 15 times, about \(9\times10^3\) updates, on a CPU budget of under a minute per model.


4.5 Traversals on dSprites
Traversals now have a known answer. For the VAE and for the model with the largest MIG, each row varies one active coordinate from \(-2.5\) to \(2.5\) around the code of one sprite, and the row label gives the factor with which that coordinate shares the most information.


Code
best = max(dsm, key=lambda k: dsm[k]["mig"])
nums["dsprites_best"] = dsm[best]["name"]
seed_img = Xds_ev[3:4]
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(FULL, 1.9), layout="constrained")
    for ax, label in zip(axs, ["VAE, $\\beta=1$", best]):
        v = dsm[label]
        dims = list(np.argsort(v["kl_dims"])[::-1][:max(2, int((v["kl_dims"] > 0.1).sum()))][:6])
        mu0 = enc_fn(v["model"], to_unit(seed_img))[0][0]
        rows = traversal_rows(v["model"], mu0, dims, vals=np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, 9))
        labs = [f"{FACTORS[int(np.argmax(v['MI'][j]))].replace('orientation', 'orient.')} {v['MI'][j].max():.2f}" for j in dims]
        show_rows(rows, labs, ax, shape=(32, 32), cmap="gray")
        ax.set_title(f"{label}, MIG {v['mig']:.2f}")
    save(fig, "dsprites_traversal"); plt.show()





The traversals of the \(\beta=16\) model show what a disentangled coordinate looks like. One row moves the sprite horizontally, one vertically, one changes its size, and nothing else changes. The rows of the VAE mix effects. The sprite moves and changes size along the same axis, a row labelled “scale” also deforms the shape, and some rows produce two faint sprites at once, a decoding that belongs to no image of the data set.

title: Lab 026: Disentangled representations and the β-VAE
text:
5. Faces: CelebA

5.1 Published results
Faces are the classic showcase of disentangling, for two reasons. We recognise immediately whether a change of the image is “one thing” (the head turns) or several (the head turns and the person becomes someone else), and there is a large labelled data set, CelebA (CelebFaces Attributes) [Z. Liu, P. Luo, X. Wang, X. Tang, Deep Learning Face Attributes in the Wild, ICCV 2015, doi:10.1109/ICCV.2015.425], with 202 599 aligned photographs of 10 177 celebrities, each annotated with 40 binary attributes such as Eyeglasses, Male, Smiling, Wearing_Hat.
Two published figures set the standard. Figure 1 of Higgins et al. (ICLR 2017) compares latent traversals of a β-VAE with \(\beta=250\), of a VAE and of InfoGAN on CelebA at \(64\times64\) pixels. In the β-VAE single coordinates turn the head (azimuth), change the smile, or change the hair, while in the VAE the azimuth coordinate also changes the expression, the glasses and the gender. The paper also notes that the β-VAE did not isolate the presence of sunglasses. The second figure, with the famous arithmetic “man with glasses − man without glasses + woman without glasses = woman with glasses” and a “turn” vector that rotates faces from looking left to looking right, comes from a different kind of generative model, a generative adversarial network (GAN), the deep convolutional GAN of A. Radford, L. Metz, S. Chintala [Unsupervised Representation Learning with Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks, arXiv:1511.06434], trained on faces collected by the authors from the web, not on CelebA. GANs are not part of this course. The figure is shown because it introduced latent arithmetic, which works in any model with a well-organised latent space, and we repeat it with our β-VAE below.


5.2 A small CelebA
The official CelebA download is a Google-Drive archive that torchvision can fetch only with an extra package (gdown). We therefore use a public mirror on the Hugging Face hub, flwrlabs/celeba, which stores the original aligned images together with the 40 attributes and the identity of each celebrity in the official training/validation/test split. We take the first four of its 19 training files, 34 268 images. Within these files the images are ordered by identity, so the subset contains about a fifth of the celebrities of the training split. Every image (\(178\times218\) pixels) is cropped to the central \(140\times140\) square, shifted 15 pixels down onto the face, and reduced to \(32\times32\) pixels. The result (100 MB) is computed once and stored. Faces at \(32\times32\) are small, and a VAE trained on them on a CPU will produce blurry images. Blur is the expected price of a Gaussian latent code with a limited rate, and it grows with \(\beta\), as Section 3.3 showed.


Code
CELEBA_FILE = f"{DATA}/celeba/celeba32.npz"
CELEBA_MIRROR = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/flwrlabs/celeba/resolve/main/img_align%2Bidentity%2Battr"

def build_celeba32(out, n_files=4):
    '''Download n_files training files of the CelebA mirror (parquet: PNG image + 40 attributes per row),
    crop the central 140 x 140 square (15 px below the centre), resize to 32 x 32, store images and attributes.'''
    import pyarrow.parquet as pq
    from PIL import Image
    raw = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(out), "raw")
    os.makedirs(raw, exist_ok=True)
    imgs, attrs, names = [], [], None
    for i in range(n_files):
        f = f"{raw}/train-{i:05d}-of-00019.parquet"
        if not os.path.exists(f):
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{CELEBA_MIRROR}/train-{i:05d}-of-00019.parquet", f)
        t = pq.read_table(f)
        names = names or [c for c in t.column_names if c not in ("image", "celeb_id")]
        for d in t.column("image").to_pylist():
            im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(d["bytes"])).convert("RGB")
            w, h = im.size; l, tp = (w - 140) // 2, (h - 140) // 2 + 15
            imgs.append(np.asarray(im.crop((l, tp, l + 140, tp + 140)).resize((32, 32), Image.LANCZOS), np.uint8))
        attrs.append(np.stack([np.asarray(t.column(n).to_pylist(), bool) for n in names], 1))
    np.savez_compressed(out, images=np.stack(imgs), attrs=np.concatenate(attrs), attr_names=np.array(names))

if not os.path.exists(CELEBA_FILE):
    build_celeba32(CELEBA_FILE)
cz = np.load(CELEBA_FILE)
X_cel, A_cel, ATTR = cz["images"], cz["attrs"], [str(a) for a in cz["attr_names"]]   # (34268, 32, 32, 3) uint8, (34268, 40) bool
perm = np.random.default_rng(4).permutation(len(X_cel))

Xc_tr, Xc_te = jnp.asarray(X_cel[i_ctr]), jnp.asarray(X_cel[i_cte])
Ac_tr, Ac_te = A_cel[i_ctr], A_cel[i_cte]
print("CelebA subset: training", Xc_tr.shape, "test", Xc_te.shape)
for a in ["Eyeglasses", "Male", "Smiling", "Wearing_Hat", "Blond_Hair"]:
    print(f"  fraction with {a:12s}: {A_cel[:, ATTR.index(a)].mean():.3f}")

sel = [np.flatnonzero(Ac_te[:, ATTR.index(a)])[:3] for a in ["Eyeglasses", "Male", "Smiling"]]
sel = np.r_[np.arange(5), np.concatenate(sel)]                 # five random test faces, then three each with the attributes
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FULL, 0.6), layout="constrained")
    show_rows([np.asarray(Xc_te[sel]) / 255.0], [""], ax, shape=(32, 32, 3))
    save(fig, "celeba_data"); plt.show()


CelebA subset: training (20000, 32, 32, 3) test (2000, 32, 32, 3)
  fraction with Eyeglasses  : 0.058
  fraction with Male        : 0.390
  fraction with Smiling     : 0.481
  fraction with Wearing_Hat : 0.053
  fraction with Blond_Hair  : 0.166







5.3 A convolutional β-VAE
Dense layers would treat the \(32\times32\times3=3072\) numbers of a colour image as an unordered list. A convolutional network uses the fact that neighbouring pixels belong together (Lab 024 used one as a classifier). The encoder applies three \(4\times4\) convolutions with stride 2, each halving the image size, \(32\to16\to8\to4\), with 32, 64 and 64 channels, then a dense layer of 256 units and the two heads \(\boldsymbol\mu,\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2\in\mathbb R^{32}\). The decoder mirrors it. A dense layer maps \(\mathbf z\) to \(4\times4\times64\) numbers, and three blocks of “double the image size by repeating each pixel, then a \(3\times3\) convolution” return to \(32\times32\times3\) logits, one Bernoulli probability per colour value. For a minibatch of \(B\) images the shapes are \((B,32,32,3)\to(B,16,16,32)\to(B,8,8,64)\to(B,4,4,64)\to(B,1024)\to(B,256)\to(B,32)\) for \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2\), and \((B,32)\to(B,256)\to(B,1024)\to(B,4,4,64)\to(B,8,8,64)\to(B,16,16,32)\to(B,32,32,3)\) in the decoder.


Code
def upsample2(h):
    '''(B, H, W, C) -> (B, 2H, 2W, C): every pixel repeated in a 2 x 2 block.'''
    return jnp.repeat(jnp.repeat(h, 2, axis=1), 2, axis=2)

class ConvVAE(nnx.Module):
    '''Convolutional VAE for 32 x 32 x 3 images, Bernoulli pixels.
    encoder: conv 4x4/2 (32) -> conv 4x4/2 (64) -> conv 4x4/2 (64) -> dense 256 -> mu, logvar (d each)
    decoder: dense 256 -> dense 4*4*64 -> [upsample x2, conv 3x3] x 3 -> logits (B, 32, 32, 3)'''
    def __init__(self, d, *, rngs):
        self.c1 = nnx.Conv(3, 32, (4, 4), strides=2, rngs=rngs)
        self.c2 = nnx.Conv(32, 64, (4, 4), strides=2, rngs=rngs)
        self.c3 = nnx.Conv(64, 64, (4, 4), strides=2, rngs=rngs)
        self.fc = nnx.Linear(4 * 4 * 64, 256, rngs=rngs)
        self.mu, self.logvar = nnx.Linear(256, d, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(256, d, rngs=rngs)
        self.g1, self.g2 = nnx.Linear(d, 256, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(256, 4 * 4 * 64, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1 = nnx.Conv(64, 64, (3, 3), rngs=rngs)
        self.d2 = nnx.Conv(64, 32, (3, 3), rngs=rngs)
        self.d3 = nnx.Conv(32, 3, (3, 3), rngs=rngs)
    def encode(self, x):                                             # x: (B, 32, 32, 3) in [0, 1]
        h = nnx.relu(self.c1(x))                                     # (B, 16, 16, 32)
        h = nnx.relu(self.c2(h))                                     # (B, 8, 8, 64)
        h = nnx.relu(self.c3(h))                                     # (B, 4, 4, 64)
        h = nnx.relu(self.fc(h.reshape(h.shape[0], -1)))            # (B, 256)
        return self.mu(h), self.logvar(h)                            # (B, d) each
    def decode(self, z):                                             # z: (B, d)
        h = nnx.relu(self.g2(nnx.relu(self.g1(z)))).reshape(-1, 4, 4, 64)
        h = nnx.relu(self.d1(upsample2(h)))                          # (B, 8, 8, 64)
        h = nnx.relu(self.d2(upsample2(h)))                          # (B, 16, 16, 32)
        return self.d3(upsample2(h))                                 # (B, 32, 32, 3) logits

D_CEL = 32
_c = ConvVAE(D_CEL, rngs=nnx.Rngs(0))
_mu, _ = _c.encode(to_unit(Xc_tr[:4]))
assert _mu.shape == (4, D_CEL) and _c.decode(_mu).shape == (4, 32, 32, 3)
print("parameters of the convolutional VAE:", n_params(_c))
print(nnx.tabulate(_c, to_unit(Xc_tr[:2]), method="encode", depth=1))

with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FULL, 1.8), layout="constrained")
    draw_conv_vae([(32, 3, ""), (16, 32, "conv\n4×4/2"), (8, 64, "conv\n4×4/2"), (4, 64, "conv\n4×4/2")], D_CEL,
                  [(4, 64, "dense"), (8, 64, "×2,\n3×3"), (16, 32, "×2,\n3×3"), (32, 3, "×2,\n3×3")], ax)

We train one model with \(\beta=3\) for 10 epochs on 20 000 training faces, which takes about 37 minutes on 8 CPU cores. The architecture follows the one Higgins et al. used for CelebA (their Table 1 lists \(4\times4\) convolutions with stride 2 and 32 or 64 channels, a dense layer of 256 units and \(d=32\)), scaled down to \(32\times32\) images. Their model, for \(64\times64\times3\) images, used \(\beta=250\) with a Gaussian decoder, whose reconstruction term is measured on a different scale than our BCE, so the two values of \(\beta\) cannot be compared directly. We chose \(\beta\) such that the faces remain recognisable while several coordinates switch off.


Code

cel, hist_cel = fit(f"celeba_beta{BETA_CEL:g}", ConvVAE(D_CEL, rngs=nnx.Rngs(5)), bvae_loss(BETA_CEL), (Xc_tr,),

                  "train_minutes": hist_cel["seconds"] / 60, "kl_dims_sorted": kl_cel[order_cel].tolist()}

The model uses 18 of its 32 coordinates (\(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k>0.1\) nats) and has a rate of 15.8 nats per face. The reconstructions keep the pose, the skin and hair colour, the background and the overall shape of the face, while eyes, mouths and glasses are smeared. A rate of 15.8 nats is a small budget for a \(32\times32\) colour image, and blur is the visible consequence (Section 3.3).


5.4 Latent traversals of faces
To find out what each coordinate does, we use two tools together. The first is the traversal, which decodes the code of a test face with one coordinate moved from \(-3\) to \(3\). The second is a label we did not use in training. For each coordinate \(k\) we compute the Pearson correlation coefficient between \(\mu_k(\mathbf x)\) and each of the 40 binary attributes \(a(\mathbf x)\in\{0,1\}\) over the training faces, \(\rho(\mu_k,a)=\frac{\langle\mu_ka\rangle-\langle\mu_k\rangle\langle a\rangle}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}\,\mu_k\,\mathrm{Var}\,a}}\in[-1,1]\) (\(\langle\cdot\rangle\) is the average over the faces), which is \(\pm1\) for an exact linear relation and 0 when there is no linear relation at all, and write the attribute with the largest \(|\rho|\) next to the row. A large correlation says that the coordinate tracks the attribute. It does not say that it tracks nothing else.


Code
Ac_f = Ac_tr.astype(float)
rho_attr = np.corrcoef(np.c_[mu_ctr, Ac_f].T)[:D_CEL, D_CEL:]                          # (d, 40)
active_cel = [k for k in order_cel if kl_cel[k] > 0.1]
for k in active_cel[:12]:
    a = int(np.argmax(np.abs(rho_attr[k])))
    print(f"z_{k + 1:2d}: KL = {kl_cel[k]:5.2f} nats   strongest attribute {ATTR[a]:20s} rho = {rho_attr[k, a]:+.2f}")
nums["celeba_top_attr"] = {f"z{k + 1}": [ATTR[int(np.argmax(np.abs(rho_attr[k])))], float(rho_attr[k, np.argmax(np.abs(rho_attr[k]))]),
                                         float(kl_cel[k])] for k in active_cel[:12]}

dims = (active_cel + [k for k in order_cel if k not in active_cel])[:8]   # active coordinates first
seeds = [3, 11]
# each row: 9 steps of z_k for the first face, a white gap, 9 steps for the second face
both = [traversal_rows(cel, mu_cte[s], dims, vals=np.linspace(-3, 3, 9)) for s in seeds]
rows = [np.concatenate([a.reshape(-1, 32, 32, 3), np.ones((1, 32, 32, 3)), b.reshape(-1, 32, 32, 3)]) for a, b in zip(*both)]
labs = [f"$z_{{{k + 1}}}$ {ATTR[int(np.argmax(np.abs(rho_attr[k])))].replace('_', ' ')} {rho_attr[k, np.argmax(np.abs(rho_attr[k]))]:+.2f}" for k in dims]
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FULL, 2.1), layout="constrained")
    show_rows(rows, labs, ax, shape=(32, 32, 3))
    save(fig, "celeba_traversal"); plt.show()

The coordinates with the largest KL change global properties of the image, each continuously and mostly one at a time. \(z_{10}\) darkens the background, \(z_{32}\) moves the illumination from one side of the face to the other, \(z_{25}\) changes skin and hair from dark to light, \(z_{23}\) turns a short-haired male face into a female face with long hair, \(z_{19}\) goes from a bright, smiling face to a darker, neutral one, and \(z_2\) changes the length of the hair and the fringe. None of the eight coordinates turns the head cleanly to the left or right as in the published figure, and the correlations with the attributes are weak (the largest \(|\rho|\) is 0.35, Wearing_Lipstick for \(z_{19}\)). The labels of CelebA describe local details, while the coordinates of a low-rate model describe global appearance. The attribute names next to the rows are therefore the best match among 40 labels and do not name the coordinates.


5.5 Arithmetic with attributes
The attribute labels allow a second, more direct way to move a face in a chosen direction. For a binary attribute \(a\) we average the codes of all training faces that have it and of all that do not, and take the difference, \[\mathbf v_a=\big\langle\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x)\big\rangle_{a=1}-\big\langle\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x)\big\rangle_{a=0}.\] Adding \(\alpha\,\mathbf v_a\) to the code of a face without the attribute and decoding should add the attribute, more strongly for larger \(\alpha\). The labels are used only after training, to find the direction, and the model itself never saw them. We do this for three attributes, Eyeglasses, Male and Smiling. Each block of the figure shows five test faces without the attribute (rows) for \(\alpha=0,0.5,1,1.5,2\) (columns), and \(\alpha=0\) gives the plain reconstruction.


Code
def attr_vector(a):
    j = ATTR.index(a)
    return mu_ctr[Ac_tr[:, j]].mean(0) - mu_ctr[~Ac_tr[:, j]].mean(0)

alphas = np.array([0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0])
vecs = {}
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(FULL, 1.7), layout="constrained")
    for ax, a in zip(axs, ["Eyeglasses", "Male", "Smiling"]):
        vecs[a] = attr_vector(a)
        without = np.flatnonzero(~Ac_te[:, ATTR.index(a)])[:5]
        rows = [np.asarray(dec_fn(cel, jnp.asarray(mu_cte[i][None] + alphas[:, None] * vecs[a][None]))) for i in without]
        show_rows([r.reshape(-1, 32, 32, 3) for r in rows], [""] * 5, ax, shape=(32, 32, 3))
        ax.set_title(f"$+\\alpha\\,\\mathbf{{v}}$, {a}")
        nums[f"celeba_vec_norm_{a}"] = float(np.linalg.norm(vecs[a]))
    save(fig, "celeba_attribute_arithmetic"); plt.show()
print({a: round(float(np.linalg.norm(v)), 2) for a, v in vecs.items()}, "(lengths of the attribute vectors)")





{'Eyeglasses': 0.97, 'Male': 0.97, 'Smiling': 0.79} (lengths of the attribute vectors)


The directions exist but are weak. With increasing \(\alpha\) the Eyeglasses vector darkens the region around the eyes (most visible in the fourth and fifth rows, where a dark band appears at \(\alpha=2\)), the Male vector darkens and broadens the faces and shortens the hair, and the Smiling vector brightens the lower half of the face. None of them adds a sharp pair of glasses or a clear smile. The vectors have lengths 0.97, 0.97 and 0.79, comparable to one standard deviation of a single coordinate, and at \(32\times32\) pixels a pair of glasses is a detail that a code of 15.8 nats largely cannot afford.
The same vectors reproduce the published equation. We average the codes of three groups of training faces, men with glasses, men without glasses and women without glasses, decode each average, and decode the combination \(\bar{\boldsymbol\mu}_{\text{man, glasses}}-\bar{\boldsymbol\mu}_{\text{man}}+\bar{\boldsymbol\mu}_{\text{woman}}\). The second row does the same arithmetic with the average images instead of codes.


Code
jm, jg = ATTR.index("Male"), ATTR.index("Eyeglasses")
groups = {"man with glasses": Ac_tr[:, jm] & Ac_tr[:, jg], "man without glasses": Ac_tr[:, jm] & ~Ac_tr[:, jg],
          "woman without glasses": ~Ac_tr[:, jm] & ~Ac_tr[:, jg]}
mbar = {k: mu_ctr[v].mean(0) for k, v in groups.items()}
xbar = {k: np.asarray(Xc_tr)[v].mean(0) / 255.0 for k, v in groups.items()}
z_eq = mbar["man with glasses"] - mbar["man without glasses"] + mbar["woman without glasses"]
lat = np.asarray(dec_fn(cel, jnp.asarray(np.stack(list(mbar.values()) + [z_eq]))))
pix = list(xbar.values()); pix.append(np.clip(pix[0] - pix[1] + pix[2], 0, 1))
with plt.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(HALF, 1.45), layout="constrained")
    show_rows([lat.reshape(-1, 32, 32, 3), np.stack(pix)], ["codes", "pixels"], ax, shape=(32, 32, 3))
    ax.set_xticks([16 + 33 * i for i in range(4)])
    ax.set_xticklabels(["man,\nglasses", "$-$ man", "+\nwoman", "="])
    save(fig, "celeba_glasses_equation"); plt.show()
print("group sizes:", {k: int(v.sum()) for k, v in groups.items()})
nums["celeba_group_sizes"] = {k: int(v.sum()) for k, v in groups.items()}





group sizes: {'man with glasses': 871, 'man without glasses': 6977, 'woman without glasses': 11899}


The decoded average codes are very blurred average faces, because the average of thousands of codes lies near the centre of the latent space, where the decoder produces the “mean face”. Their combination is again a mean face, now with a faint dark band at the eyes. The pixel arithmetic, in contrast, produces a recognisable woman with glasses. This is the opposite of what Radford et al. found. The reason is that CelebA images are aligned, so the eyes of all faces are at the same pixels and averaging pixels is meaningful, whereas the faces of Radford et al. were not aligned and pixel averages overlapped incoherently. Latent arithmetic pays off when the data vary in ways that pixels cannot average, and when the latent code is rich enough to carry the attribute. Our small, blurred model is at the edge of both.

title: Lab 026: Disentangled representations and the β-VAE
section: 6. Interpreting the latent space of spin models
text:
6. Interpreting the latent space of spin models

6.1 From generating to understanding
In Labs 024 and 025 the VAE was a generator, judged by the quality of what it draws. Here we use the β-VAE to learn about the physical system from which the data come. The network receives only spin snapshots, no temperature, no phase, no Hamiltonian, and compresses each snapshot into a few latent numbers that the β-term pushes to be independent. If the compression is good, these numbers must describe the most important ways in which snapshots differ from each other, and for a system in thermal equilibrium those are the macroscopic quantities. The question is whether we can read them.
Class activation maps show where in an image a classifier looks, one way to interpret a trained network. The first principal component of Ising snapshots is the magnetisation, \(z_1\propto m\) [L. Wang, Phys. Rev. B 94, 195105 (2016), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.94.195105], and S. J. Wetzel found that the latent variable of a VAE trained on Ising snapshots correlates with the magnetisation [Phys. Rev. E 96, 022140 (2017), doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.96.022140]. R. Iten, T. Metger, H. Wilming, L. del Rio and R. Renner used a related architecture with a β-weighted latent layer (the β-VAE cost function of this lab) to recover the spring constant and the damping factor of a damped pendulum from time series of its position alone [Discovering Physical Concepts with Neural Networks, Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 010508 (2020), doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.124.010508].
The procedure we follow has four steps, and the definitions are the same for both models.

train a β-VAE on snapshots only, with a small latent dimension \(d=8\);
keep the active coordinates, those whose average KL over held-out snapshots exceeds \(0.1\) nats, \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k>0.1\), since the others carry no information;
probe each active coordinate by computing the encoder mean \(\mu_k(\mathbf s)\) for every held-out snapshot \(\mathbf s\), and its Pearson correlation coefficient with each observable \(O(\mathbf s)\) computed from the spins, \[\rho_{kO}=\frac{\langle\mu_kO\rangle-\langle\mu_k\rangle\langle O\rangle}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}\,\mu_k\;\mathrm{Var}\,O}}\in[-1,1],\] where \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) is the average over held-out snapshots of all temperatures;
collect the coefficients in a table (coordinates × observables) and look at scatter plots of \(\mu_k\) against the observable with the largest \(|\rho_{kO}|\).

The observables, as in Lab 025, are the magnetisation \(m=\frac1N\sum_is_i\) and its modulus \(|m|\), the energy per spin \(e=H/N\), the temperature \(T\) at which the snapshot was simulated, and, for the \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model, the two stripe order parameters \(m_x=\frac1N\sum_{x,y}(-1)^xs_{x,y}\) and \(m_y=\frac1N\sum_{x,y}(-1)^ys_{x,y}\) (spins alternating along \(x\) or along \(y\)), their moduli, \(m_{\rm str}=\sqrt{m_x^2+m_y^2}\) and the coupling ratio \(g=J_2/J_1\). Pearson’s coefficient detects linear relations. A coordinate that encodes \(m\) gives \(|\rho|\approx1\) with \(m\), while a coordinate that is a symmetric function of \(m\) (for example \(\mu_k\approx m^2\)) gives \(\rho\approx0\) with \(m\) and must be found with \(|m|\).


6.2 The 2D Ising model
We use the 9472 snapshots of Lab 025, \(L=30\), 256 Swendsen–Wang configurations at each of 37 temperatures in \([1.5,3.5]\). A random 80% of them train the network (bits \(b_i=(s_i+1)/2\), Bernoulli decoder, dense \(900\to512\to256\to d=8\) and back), and the remaining 20% are held out for probing. We train two models, \(\beta=1\) and \(\beta=4\), for 40 epochs each.


Code
def unpack_spins(packed, L):
    '''Packed bits (..., L, ceil(L/8)) uint8 -> spins (..., L, L) int8 with values -1, +1.'''
    return np.unpackbits(packed, axis=-1, count=L).astype(np.int8) * 2 - 1

di = np.load(f"{DATA}/ising_L30.npz")
L_I = int(di["L"]); o = np.argsort(di["T"]); T_I = di["T"][o]
S_I = unpack_spins(di["configs"], L_I)[o]                                   # (37, 256, 30, 30)
nT, nS = S_I.shape[:2]
s = S_I.reshape(-1, L_I, L_I).astype(np.float32)                            # (9472, 30, 30)
obs_I = {"m": s.mean((1, 2)), "|m|": np.abs(s.mean((1, 2))),
         "e": -(s * np.roll(s, 1, 1) + s * np.roll(s, 1, 2)).mean((1, 2)),  # each bond once, J = 1
         "T": np.repeat(T_I, nS)}
X_I = ((S_I.reshape(-1, L_I * L_I) > 0) * 255).astype(np.uint8)        # bits as 0 / 255, read by to_unit
pI = np.random.default_rng(6).permutation(len(X_I)); itr_I, ite_I = pI[:int(0.8 * len(pI))], pI[int(0.8 * len(pI)):]
print("Ising:", S_I.shape, "| training", len(itr_I), "held out", len(ite_I))
assert np.isclose(obs_I["e"].min(), -2, atol=0.1)                           # the lowest-T snapshots are close to the ground state

def probe(model, X, O, thr=0.1):
    '''Encoder means of the held-out snapshots, KL per coordinate, active coordinates (sorted by KL), and the
    Pearson coefficient rho[k, l] of mu_k with observable l.'''
    mu, lv = in_chunks(lambda x: enc_fn(model, to_unit(x)), jnp.asarray(X))
    kl = np.asarray(kl_per_dim(mu, lv)).mean(0)
    act = [k for k in np.argsort(kl)[::-1] if kl[k] > thr]
    if len(act) < 2:                                                  # keep at least two coordinates for the plots
        act = list(np.argsort(kl)[::-1][:2])
    Om = np.stack(list(O.values()), 1)
    rho = np.corrcoef(np.c_[mu, Om].T)[:mu.shape[1], mu.shape[1]:]
    return {"mu": mu, "kl": kl, "active": act, "rho": rho, "names": list(O)}

ising = {}
for beta in [1.0, 4.0]:
    model, hist = fit(f"ising_beta{beta:g}", DenseVAE(L_I * L_I, 8, hidden=(512, 256), rngs=nnx.Rngs(7)),
                      bvae_loss(beta), (jnp.asarray(X_I[itr_I]),), epochs=40, seed=7, log_every=10)
    P = probe(model, X_I[ite_I], {k: v[ite_I] for k, v in obs_I.items()})
    ising[beta] = dict(model=model, hist=hist, **P)
    print(f"beta = {beta:g}: active coordinates {[k + 1 for k in P['active']]}, KL = {np.round(P['kl'][P['active']], 2)}")
    for k in P["active"]:
        print(f"   z_{k + 1}: " + "  ".join(f"rho(mu, {n}) = {r:+.2f}" for n, r in zip(P["names"], P["rho"][k])))

6.3 The \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model
The frustrated \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model of Lab 025, \(H=-J_1\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j+J_2\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}s_is_j\) with \(g=J_2/J_1\), has three phases, a ferromagnet for \(g<1/2\) at low \(T\), a stripe phase for \(g>1/2\) at low \(T\), and a paramagnet at high \(T\). The stripe phase has four ground states, with stripes along \(x\) or along \(y\), each with two signs. A disentangled code would need separate coordinates for the magnetisation and for each stripe direction. From the \(81\times79\) grid of \((g,T)\) points with 100 snapshots each we take 12 snapshots per point, 10 for training and 2 held out, which gives 63 990 training and 12 798 held-out snapshots of \(32\times32\) spins. Two models, \(\beta=1\) and \(\beta=4\), are trained for 8 epochs each.

def j1j2_obs(S, G, T):
    '''Per-snapshot observables of S (n, L, L) with couplings G (n,) and temperatures T (n,).'''
    s = S.astype(np.float32)
    px = np.where(np.arange(S.shape[-1]) % 2 == 0, 1.0, -1.0)
    nn = sum(np.roll(s, sh, ax) for sh in (1, -1) for ax in (1, 2))                              # 4 nearest neighbours
    nnn = sum(np.roll(np.roll(s, sy, 1), sx, 2) for sy in (1, -1) for sx in (1, -1))              # 4 diagonal neighbours
    m, mx, my = s.mean((1, 2)), (s * px[None, None, :]).mean((1, 2)), (s * px[None, :, None]).mean((1, 2))
    return {"m": m, "|m|": np.abs(m), "m_x": mx, "m_y": my, "|m_x|": np.abs(mx), "|m_y|": np.abs(my),
            "m_str": np.sqrt(mx**2 + my**2), "e": -0.5 * (s * (nn - G[:, None, None] * nnn)).mean((1, 2)),
            "c_nn": (s * nn).mean((1, 2)) / 4, "c_nnn": (s * nnn).mean((1, 2)) / 4, "g": G, "T": T}

6.4 The role of β
The β-pressure towards independent coordinates should make the probes cleaner. For each observable we take the largest \(|\rho_{kO}|\) over the active coordinates and the gap to the second largest, \(|\rho|_{(1)}-|\rho|_{(2)}\), the same idea as the MIG of Section 4 with correlations in place of mutual information. 6.5 From a check to a discovery tool
For the two models above we knew the order parameters in advance, so the probes serve as a check that the network, trained without any physical label, finds the quantities physicists use. For a model whose phases are not understood the same procedure becomes a discovery tool. A coordinate that is active, and whose average \(\langle|\mu_k|\rangle\) changes sharply across some range of a parameter, is a candidate order parameter. The next step is to express it in terms of the spins, for example by fitting \(\mu_k\) with a small library of simple functions of the configuration. We try this on the \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) coordinates as if we did not know the answer, with a least-squares fit of \(\mu_k\) by a linear combination of eight candidate features, the magnetisation \(m\), the two stripe amplitudes \(m_x,m_y\), their moduli \(|m|,|m_x|,|m_y|\) and the nearest- and next-nearest-neighbour correlations \(c_{\rm nn}=\frac1{4N}\sum_is_i\sum_{j\in\mathrm{nn}(i)}s_j\) and \(c_{\rm nnn}\) (all standardised to zero mean and unit variance), with the coefficient of determination \[R^2=1-\frac{\sum_{\mathbf s}\big(\mu_k(\mathbf s)-\tilde\mu_k(\mathbf s)\big)^2}{\sum_{\mathbf s}\big(\mu_k(\mathbf s)-\langle\mu_k\rangle\big)^2}\] measuring how much of the coordinate the features explain. The feature with the largest coefficient names the coordinate.

    y = P["mu"][:, k]
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A_, y, rcond=None)
    r2 = 1 - ((y - A_ @ coef) ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    top = np.argsort(np.abs(coef[1:]))[::-1][:2]
    fits[f"z{k + 1}"] = {"R2": float(r2), "top": [(FEATS[t], float(coef[1 + t])) for t in top]}
    print(f"z_{k + 1}: R^2 = {r2:.3f};  largest coefficients: " + ", ".join(f"{FEATS[t]} {coef[1 + t]:+.2f}" for t in top))
nums["j1j2_fits"] = fits


z_8: R^2 = 0.982;  largest coefficients: m +0.78, |m_x| -0.45
z_7: R^2 = 0.992;  largest coefficients: m_x -0.68, |m_x| -0.09
z_5: R^2 = 0.989;  largest coefficients: m_y +0.58, m_x -0.08


All three coordinates are explained almost completely by the eight features, with \(R^2=0.982\), 0.992 and 0.989. The largest coefficient names each of them, \(m\) for \(z_8\) (with a smaller negative contribution of \(|m_x|\), the mixing seen in the maps), \(m_x\) for \(z_7\) and \(m_y\) for \(z_5\). On a model whose phases were not known, this is the step that turns an unnamed latent coordinate into a candidate formula in terms of the spins.


6.6 Limits of probing
The probes deserve the same caution as any correlation. A large \(|\rho|\) with a known quantity confirms that a coordinate follows it but does not explain the coordinate, since it may follow a mixture of quantities that are themselves correlated, as the magnetisation and the energy are across the Ising transition. The sign and the scale of a coordinate are arbitrary, and a coordinate may be a nonlinear function of an observable that a linear probe misses. Which coordinates appear, and how cleanly they separate the quantities, depends on the model, the data, the architecture and \(\beta\), which is the practical face of the result of Locatello et al. (Section 2.5). Finally, a probe only finds what we probe for. A coordinate that matches none of our observables is either noise or a quantity we have not thought of, and only further work, such as the fits above, can tell which.
