section: 7. Discovering factors and conditioning on them
text:
7. Discovering factors and conditioning on them
We can now compare the two ways of controlling a generative model met so far.









conditional VAE (Labs 024, 025)
β-VAE (this lab)




training data
pairs \((\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\): images with labels
images \(\mathbf x\) only


loss
\(D+R\) with \(\mathbf c\) given to encoder and decoder
\(D+\beta R\)


the factor of interest
chosen by us, given as \(\mathbf c\)
found by the network, identified afterwards


guarantee
\(\mathbf c\) controls what it labels
none in general (Locatello et al.)


what \(\mathbf z\) carries
everything except \(\mathbf c\)
everything, ideally one factor per coordinate


typical use
generate on demand
explore the data, find factors, interpret



The difference is also a difference in how the models are sampled. A trained β-VAE is sampled in two steps, \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), then the decoder (Section 1.4). To control a property we must first find the coordinate or the direction that carries it (Sections 3.6, 5.4, 5.5). A trained cVAE is sampled with the condition chosen by us. Fixing \(\mathbf c\) and drawing \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) gives many variants of the requested digit, and decoding the same \(\mathbf z\) with different \(\mathbf c\) keeps the style and changes the digit. The figure from Lab 024 shows both at once. Each row is one condition \(\mathbf c=0,\dots,9\), and each column one random \(\mathbf z\), the same in every row.



cVAE of Lab 024: rows are the conditions c = 0, …, 9, columns are random z, the same in every row


The two complement each other. A cVAE is the right tool when the factor is known and labelled, such as the digit, the temperature of a Monte Carlo run or the point \((g,T)\) of a phase diagram. A β-VAE is the right tool when we do not yet know what varies in the data, and its findings can then be turned into labels for a conditional model. In physics, where the parameters of a simulation are always known, both appear naturally, conditioning on \((g,T)\) to generate and an unconditioned β-VAE to ask which collective variables the configurations contain.

title: Lab 026: Disentangled representations and the β-VAE
text:
8. Exercises
The exercises are graded by difficulty, with (★) for a short calculation or a few lines of code, (★★) for a derivation or a small experiment, and (★★★) for an experiment that needs a new training run. A solution follows each exercise in a separate cell. Try the exercise first.

Exercise 1 (★)
Show that the KL divergence between two one-dimensional Gaussians is \[\begin{aligned}\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)\,\|\,\mathcal N(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)\big)&=\log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}\\&\quad+\frac{\sigma_1^2+(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2}-\frac12 ,\end{aligned}\] check that it reduces to the formula of Lab 024 for \(\mu_2=0\), \(\sigma_2=1\), and verify it numerically by Monte Carlo for one choice of parameters.

Solution of Exercise 1
With \(\log\mathcal N(z;\mu,\sigma^2)=-\frac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{(z-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\), \[\begin{aligned}\mathrm{KL}=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mathcal N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)}\Big[&\log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}-\frac{(z-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}\\&+\frac{(z-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2}\Big].\end{aligned}\] Under \(q\), \(\mathbb E[(z-\mu_1)^2]=\sigma_1^2\) and \(\mathbb E[(z-\mu_2)^2]=\sigma_1^2+(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2\), which gives the formula. For \(\mu_2=0\), \(\sigma_2=1\) it becomes \(-\log\sigma_1+\frac12(\sigma_1^2+\mu_1^2)-\frac12=\frac12(\mu_1^2+\sigma_1^2-\ln\sigma_1^2-1)\), the expression used throughout. The cell compares the formula with a Monte Carlo average over \(10^6\) samples.


Code
def kl_gauss(m1, s1, m2, s2):
    return np.log(s2 / s1) + (s1**2 + (m1 - m2)**2) / (2 * s2**2) - 0.5
m1, s1, m2, s2 = 0.4, 0.7, -0.5, 1.6
zz = m1 + s1 * np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=1_000_000)
mc = np.mean(np.asarray(log_normal(zz, m1, np.log(s1**2)) - log_normal(zz, m2, np.log(s2**2))))
print(f"closed form {kl_gauss(m1, s1, m2, s2):.4f}   Monte Carlo {mc:.4f}")


closed form 0.5806   Monte Carlo 0.5803





Exercise 2 (★)
Show that the index-code mutual information obeys \(0\le I_q(n;\mathbf z)\le\log N\), and describe the encoders for which each bound is reached. Compare with the MNIST numbers of Section 3.5.

Solution of Exercise 2
Write \(I_q(n;\mathbf z)=H(n)-H(n|\mathbf z)\) with the entropies of the discrete index. \(H(n)=\log N\) because \(q(n)=1/N\), and \(0\le H(n|\mathbf z)\le H(n)\) because a conditional entropy of a discrete variable is non-negative and conditioning cannot increase entropy. The upper bound is reached when the code determines the index, \(H(n|\mathbf z)=0\), which happens when the clouds of different images do not overlap. The lower bound is reached when all clouds are the same, so that \(\mathbf z\) says nothing about \(n\). This is posterior collapse. In Section 3.5 the models with small \(\beta\) come close to \(\log M=7.60\), while the models with large \(\beta\) stay well below it.



Exercise 3 (★★)

Show that the total correlation of a two-dimensional Gaussian with unit variances and correlation coefficient \(\rho\) is \(-\frac12\log(1-\rho^2)\). (b) Take two independent coordinates uniformly distributed on \([-1,1]\) and rotate them by 45°. Show that the rotated coordinates are uncorrelated but have a positive total correlation, and estimate it with a two-dimensional histogram. (c) Explain why (b) matters for disentangling, in contrast with Section 2.5.


Solution of Exercise 3

For a Gaussian \(\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)\) with marginals \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(\mathrm{TC}=\mathbb E[\log q(\mathbf z)-\log q(z_1)-\log q(z_2)]=-\frac12\log\det\Sigma+\frac12\mathbb E[z_1^2+z_2^2-\mathbf z^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf z]=-\frac12\log(1-\rho^2)\), because \(\mathbb E[\mathbf z^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf z]=\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma)=2\) and \(\det\Sigma=1-\rho^2\). (b) Rotating independent coordinates with equal variances leaves the covariance matrix proportional to the identity, so the correlation is zero. The rotated square, however, is a diamond, and knowing \(z_1\) restricts the range of \(z_2\), so the coordinates are dependent and \(\mathrm{TC}>0\). The cell estimates it with a histogram as the mutual information of the two coordinates (for two variables TC is their mutual information). (c) For Gaussian coordinates a rotation keeps \(\mathrm{TC}=0\), which is why the Gaussian prior alone cannot fix the axes (Section 2.5). For non-Gaussian factors, like the uniform positions of dSprites, a rotated code has \(\mathrm{TC}>0\), so penalising TC prefers the unrotated, disentangled axes. This is one of the reasons why TC penalties help when the true factors are not Gaussian.



Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
u = rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=(400_000, 2))
w = u @ (np.array([[1, -1], [1, 1]]) / np.sqrt(2)).T                    # rotation by 45 degrees
def tc_hist(z, bins=40):
    return mutual_info(discretise(z[:, :1], bins)[:, 0], discretise(z[:, 1:], bins)[:, 0])
print(f"correlation after rotation: {np.corrcoef(w.T)[0, 1]:+.4f}")
print(f"TC (histogram, nats): independent {tc_hist(u):.3f}, rotated {tc_hist(w):.3f}")
for r_ in [0.5, 0.9]:
    g2 = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, r_], [r_, 1]], size=400_000)
    print(f"Gaussian, rho = {r_}: TC histogram {tc_hist(g2):.3f}, formula {-0.5 * np.log(1 - r_**2):.3f}")

Exercise 4 (★★)
Repeat the derivation of Section 2.4 for a conditional VAE, in which the encoder is \(q(\mathbf z|\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\) and the prior \(p(\mathbf z)\) does not depend on \(\mathbf c\). Identify the mutual information that appears now and explain what a penalty on it does to the information about \(\mathbf c\) in \(\mathbf z\).

Solution of Exercise 4
With \(q(n,\mathbf z)=\frac1Nq(\mathbf z|\mathbf x_n,\mathbf c_n)\) and the same steps, the rate splits into \(I_q(n;\mathbf z)+\mathrm{TC}+\sum_j\mathrm{KL}(q(z_j)\|p(z_j))\), where \(n\) now indexes pairs \((\mathbf x_n,\mathbf c_n)\). Since the decoder receives \(\mathbf c\) directly, information about \(\mathbf c\) in \(\mathbf z\) is useless for the reconstruction but still costs rate, through \(I_q(n;\mathbf z)\ge I_q(\mathbf c;\mathbf z)\) (the label is a function of the index). Minimising the rate therefore removes the label from the code, which is the separation of identity and style seen in the latent plane of the cVAE in Lab 024. A larger \(\beta\) strengthens this pressure.



Exercise 5 (★★)
The MIG depends on the discretisation. Recompute it for the four dSprites models with 10, 20 and 40 bins. Check whether the ranking of the models changes.

Solution of Exercise 5
The cell recomputes the MIG for the three bin numbers. The absolute values change, because coarse bins merge neighbouring positions and fine bins make the histogram estimate noisier, so a MIG value is meaningful only together with its estimator. The ranking is what we compare. It is the same for 10, 20 and 40 bins.

Exercise 6 (★★)
Pearson’s coefficient misses symmetric relations. For the Ising models, correlate \(|\mu_k|\) (instead of \(\mu_k\)) with \(|m|\), \(e\) and \(T\). Identify the coordinates that gain and explain why.

Solution of Exercise 6
A coordinate that follows the signed magnetisation has \(\mu_k\approx\pm\kappa|m|\) with a constant \(\kappa>0\) depending on the sign of \(m\), so \(\mu_k\) is uncorrelated with \(|m|\) while \(|\mu_k|\) is strongly correlated with it, and therefore also with \(e\) and \(T\), which are related to \(|m|\) through the phase transition. Coordinates that are already symmetric gain nothing.

Exercise 7 (★★★)
Train a β-TCVAE with \(\beta_{\rm TC}=6\) on MNIST (same network and epochs as Section 3) and compare its rate, distortion, total correlation and traversals with the β-VAE with \(\beta=4\). Determine which of the two costs less reconstruction quality.

Solution of Exercise 7
The cell trains the model (as long as one model of Section 3) and evaluates it as in Sections 3.2 and 3.5. The losses printed during training contain the minibatch estimate of the total correlation, around 100 nats. The minibatch-weighted estimate of \(\log q(\mathbf z)\) uses only \(B=128\) of the \(N=60\,000\) clouds and carries a large offset of order \((d-1)\log(NB)\), so its value is not the total correlation. The training uses only its gradient. The estimate on 2000 test digits with their full aggregate posterior is the meaningful number, 0.97 nats for the β-TCVAE against 1.69 nats for the β-VAE with \(\beta=4\), at a slightly smaller rate (7.7 against 8.7 nats) and a larger distortion (117.4 against 111.5 nats). In this short training run the β-TCVAE therefore does not buy its lower total correlation more cheaply than the β-VAE does. Whether its traversals are more disentangled can only be judged by eye on MNIST, which is the point of Section 3.6.

title: Lab 026: Disentangled representations and the β-VAE
Lab 027: Galaxy morphology with a β-VAE
text:
1. Galaxy10 DECaLS
One sample of the data set is a colour image of one galaxy, \(64\times64\) pixels in three channels, together with a morphology label \(y\in\{0,\dots,9\}\). The images come from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, the imaging surveys that prepared the target selection of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). These surveys mapped a large part of the sky outside the Milky Way through three filters called \(g\), \(r\) and \(z\). The \(g\) filter passes blue-green light, \(r\) red light and \(z\) near-infrared light just beyond the visible range, so the three images of one galaxy record how much light it emits in three colour ranges [Dey et al., AJ 157, 168 (2019), doi:10.3847/1538-3881/ab089d]. Most of the area used here was observed by DECaLS, the Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey, which gives the data set its name. The compilation code of the data set (github.com/henrysky/Galaxy10) requests from the Legacy Surveys viewer a \(512\times512\) colour cutout of data release 8 in the bands \(g, r, z\) at the native pixel scale of \(0.262''\) per pixel (the symbol \(''\) denotes an arcsecond, \(1/3600\) of a degree on the sky) and keeps the central \(256\times256\) pixels, a field of \(67''\). For the largest galaxies it keeps the whole cutout and resizes it to \(256\times256\), so that their pixels are \(0.524''\) wide. We average blocks of \(4\times4\) pixels once, which gives the \(64\times64\) images of this notebook with \(1.05''\) (or \(2.10''\)) per pixel.
A pixel value is therefore not a raw photon count. The viewer turns the three bands into the three colour channels, \(z\to\) red, \(r\to\) green and \(g\to\) blue, scales each band, applies an \(\operatorname{arcsinh}\) stretch that compresses bright regions and keeps faint ones visible, and stores 8-bit integers (function sdss_rgb in legacypipe/survey.py). After division by 255, a value \(x\in[0,1]\) is a monotonic but nonlinear function of the surface brightness in one band at one position on the sky. Empty sky is not black, and the ratio between the red and blue channels carries the colour of the light. Old stellar populations and dust make a galaxy redder, while young massive stars make it bluer.
The labels come from Galaxy Zoo DECaLS, in which volunteers answered a decision tree of questions for each image, about whether the galaxy is smooth or has features, whether it is seen edge-on, whether it has a bar or spiral arms, how tightly the arms are wound, and whether it is merging [Walmsley et al., MNRAS 509, 3966 (2022), doi:10.1093/mnras/stab2093]. H. W. Leung and J. Bovy selected the galaxies whose vote fractions pass thresholds and sorted them into ten classes. For example, the merging class requires a merger vote fraction above 0.7 with more than ten votes. The data set is Galaxy10 DECaLS, published on Zenodo under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence (CC BY 4.0) [H. W. Leung, J. Bovy, doi:10.5281/zenodo.10845026] and documented with the astroNN package (astronn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/galaxy10.html).

LOCAL_64 = f"{DATA_DIR}/galaxy10_decals_64.npz"

          "releases/download/data-v1/galaxy10_decals_64.npz")
URL_H5 = "https://zenodo.org/records/10845026/files/Galaxy10_DECals.h5?download=1"


def downsample_h5(h5_path, out_path, factor=4, chunk=1000):
    """Read Galaxy10_DECals.h5 in chunks, average factor x factor pixel blocks, save as npz."""
    import h5py
    with h5py.File(h5_path, "r") as f:
        n, H, W, C = f["images"].shape
        h, w = H // factor, W // factor
        small = np.empty((n, h, w, C), np.uint8)
        for i in range(0, n, chunk):
            b = f["images"][i:i + chunk].astype(np.float32)
            b = b.reshape(-1, h, factor, w, factor, C).mean(axis=(2, 4))
            small[i:i + chunk] = np.clip(np.round(b), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
        meta = {k: f[k][:] for k in f if k != "images"}
    np.savez_compressed(out_path, images=small, **meta)

title: Lab 027: Galaxy morphology with a β-VAE
text:
2. The β-VAE loss
A variational autoencoder (Lab 024) describes an image \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^D\), here \(D=3\cdot64\cdot64=12\,288\), through a latent vector \(\mathbf z\in\mathbb R^d\) with prior \(p(\mathbf z)=\mathcal N(0,I_d)\) and a decoder distribution \(p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)\) with parameters \(\theta\). The log-likelihood \(\log p_\theta(\mathbf x)=\log\int p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)\,p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z\) is an integral that cannot be computed. An encoder \(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)=\mathcal N\big(\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x),\operatorname{diag}\boldsymbol\sigma^2_\phi(\mathbf x)\big)\) with parameters \(\phi\) proposes the latent vectors that could have produced \(\mathbf x\). Multiplying and dividing by \(q_\phi\) under the integral and applying Jensen’s inequality \(\log\mathbb E[\cdot]\ge\mathbb E[\log\,\cdot\,]\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log p_\theta(\mathbf x)&=\log\mathbb E_{q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)}\!\left[\frac{p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)\,p(\mathbf z)}{q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)}\right]\\
&\ge\mathbb E_{q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)}\big[\log p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)\big]-\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big)\\
&\equiv\mathrm{ELBO}(\mathbf x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The ELBO, the evidence lower bound, is a computable lower bound on the log-likelihood \(\log p_\theta(\mathbf x)\) (the “evidence”). Here \(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)=\mathbb E_q[\log q-\log p]\ge0\) is the Kullback–Leibler divergence, and the gap of the bound equals \(\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)\,\|\,p_\theta(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)\big)\). The VAE minimises \(-\mathrm{ELBO}\). The β-VAE [Higgins et al., ICLR 2017, openreview.net/forum?id=Sy2fzU9gl] multiplies the KL term by a weight \(\beta\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_\beta(\mathbf x)&=\mathbb E_{q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)}\big[-\log p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)\big]\\
&\quad+\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,I_d)\big).
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(\beta=1\) this is the VAE loss \(-\mathrm{ELBO}\). For \(\beta>1\), since the KL term is non-negative, \(-\mathcal L_\beta\le\mathrm{ELBO}\) is still a lower bound on \(\log p_\theta(\mathbf x)\), only a looser one. The expectation over \(q_\phi\) is estimated, as in Lab 024, with one sample \(\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x)+\boldsymbol\sigma_\phi(\mathbf x)\odot\boldsymbol\varepsilon\), \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\) (reparametrisation trick).
For a diagonal Gaussian encoder and the standard normal prior the KL term splits into a sum over latent coordinates,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,I_d)\big)&=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mathrm{KL}_k(\mathbf x),\\
\mathrm{KL}_k(\mathbf x)&=\tfrac12\big(\mu_k^2+\sigma_k^2-\ln\sigma_k^2-1\big)\ge0,
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(\mu_k=\mu_{\phi,k}(\mathbf x)\) and \(\sigma_k=\sigma_{\phi,k}(\mathbf x)\). A term vanishes only when \(\mu_k=0\) and \(\sigma_k=1\), that is when coordinate \(k\) looks the same for every image and carries no information about \(\mathbf x\). Averaged over the data, the KL term is an upper bound on the mutual information between image and code, measured in nats (1 nat \(=1/\ln2\) bits). The β-VAE loss therefore charges a price \(\beta\) for each nat of information that the code carries about the image, and the price is paid coordinate by coordinate.
Three properties of this price favour disentangled codes when \(\beta>1\) [Burgess et al., arXiv:1804.03599]. Information is expensive, so the encoder buys only a few nats and spends them where they reduce the reconstruction error most, which means on the factors of variation that change many pixels. For galaxies we expect size, elongation, orientation, brightness and colour long before spiral arms. The prior \(\mathcal N(0,I_d)=\prod_k\mathcal N(0,1)\) is factorised, and the data-averaged KL contains the total correlation of the codes, a measure of the statistical dependence between coordinates (the rate decomposition of Lab 026 [Chen et al., arXiv:1802.04942]). A larger \(\beta\) pushes the coordinates towards independence, so independent factors tend to end up in different coordinates. Finally, the posterior is diagonal. A rotated code, in which every coordinate mixes two factors, would need correlated posteriors, which the diagonal family cannot represent, and this breaks the rotation symmetry of the prior in favour of particular axes [Rolinek et al., arXiv:1812.06775]. All three effects have the same price, since fewer nats in the code mean less detail in the reconstruction. Lab 026 measured this trade-off along the rate–distortion curve, and here we look at it on galaxies.
The remaining choice is the decoder distribution. Lab 024 treated every pixel of an MNIST digit as an independent coin with probability \(\tilde x_i\) of being black, a Bernoulli distribution, for which \(-\log p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)\) is the binary cross-entropy (BCE) \[
\mathrm{BCE}(\mathbf x,\tilde{\mathbf x})=-\sum_{i=1}^{D}\big[x_i\ln\tilde x_i+(1-x_i)\ln(1-\tilde x_i)\big],
\] with \(x_i\) the value of pixel \(i\) and \(\tilde x_i\) its decoded value. The BCE is the natural measure of mismatch when pixels are close to 0 or 1, as for digits. Galaxy pixels are continuous, and most of them belong to the sky at values near 0.13, where the BCE is a shallow function of \(\tilde x_i\). A small error in a faint galaxy then costs almost nothing, and the encoder finds it cheaper to store no information at all (Exercise 1). We therefore use a Gaussian decoder with a fixed width \(\sigma_x\), which penalises the squared difference between the image and its reconstruction,
\[
-\log p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)=\frac{\|\mathbf x-\tilde{\mathbf x}_\theta(\mathbf z)\|^2}{2\sigma_x^2}+\frac D2\ln\big(2\pi\sigma_x^2\big),
\]
where \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_\theta(\mathbf z)\in(0,1)^D\) is the mean image produced by the decoder network, \(\|\mathbf v\|^2=\sum_i v_i^2\), and \(\sigma_x\) is the typical size of the pixel deviations that the model treats as noise. The constant is dropped in the code. To compare models we also report the mean squared error (MSE) per pixel of the reconstruction from the posterior mean, \(\mathrm{MSE}=\frac1{ND}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\|\mathbf x_n-\tilde{\mathbf x}_\theta(\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x_n))\|^2\) over \(N\) test images, so that \(\sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}}\) is the typical error of one pixel value. The width \(\sigma_x\) sets the exchange rate between the two terms, because one nat in the code pays off when it lowers the summed squared error \(\|\mathbf x-\tilde{\mathbf x}\|^2\) by \(2\beta\sigma_x^2\). We use \(\sigma_x=0.15\).

title: Lab 027: Galaxy morphology with a β-VAE
text:
3. A convolutional β-VAE
The encoder applies four convolutions with \(4\times4\) kernels and stride 2, each followed by a rectified linear unit (ReLU), the elementwise function \(\mathrm{ReLU}(u)=\max(0,u)\), so that the image shrinks \(64\to32\to16\to8\to4\) pixels while the number of channels grows to 16, 32, 32 and 64. A dense layer of 256 units then produces \(2d=20\) numbers, the means \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and the log-variances \(\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2\) of a latent code of dimension \(d=10\). The decoder mirrors the encoder with transposed convolutions, which double the image size at each step, and the logistic function \(\mathrm{sigm}(u)=1/(1+e^{-u})\) at the end, which maps every output to the interval \((0,1)\) of pixel values, gives the mean image \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_\theta(\mathbf z)\). The layer-by-layer table below comes from torchinfo.summary, which runs one forward pass and records the shape of every intermediate tensor and the number of trainable parameters of every layer.


Code
D_LATENT = 10
SIGMA_X = 0.15      # standard deviation of the Gaussian decoder p(x|z), in pixel-value units


class BetaVAE(nn.Module):
    """Convolutional VAE for 3 x 64 x 64 images with a d-dimensional diagonal-Gaussian latent code."""

    def __init__(self, d=D_LATENT, ch=(16, 32, 32, 64), hidden=256):
        super().__init__()
        c = [3, *ch]
        enc = []
        for a, b in zip(c[:-1], c[1:]):          # each 4x4 convolution with stride 2 halves the image
            enc += [nn.Conv2d(a, b, 4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.ReLU()]
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(*enc, nn.Flatten(),
                                     nn.Linear(ch[-1] * 4 * 4, hidden), nn.ReLU(),
                                     nn.Linear(hidden, 2 * d))          # mu and log sigma^2
        dec = [nn.Linear(d, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, ch[-1] * 4 * 4), nn.ReLU(),
               nn.Unflatten(1, (ch[-1], 4, 4))]
        r = [*ch[::-1], 3]
        for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(r[:-1], r[1:])):   # each transposed convolution doubles the image
            dec += [nn.ConvTranspose2d(a, b, 4, stride=2, padding=1)]
            if i < len(r) - 2:
                dec += [nn.ReLU()]
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(*dec)

    def encode(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encoder(x).chunk(2, dim=1)
        return mu, logvar

    def decode(self, z):
        return torch.sigmoid(self.decoder(z))           # mean image x_hat(z), pixel values in (0, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x)
        z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)   # reparametrisation trick
        return self.decode(z), mu, logvar


def beta_vae_loss(x, x_hat, mu, logvar, beta, sigma_x=SIGMA_X):
    """Minibatch average of L_beta; also returns the reconstruction term and the KL of each coordinate."""
    rec = ((x - x_hat) ** 2).sum(dim=(1, 2, 3)) / (2 * sigma_x ** 2)   # -log p(x|z) up to a constant
    kl_k = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + logvar.exp() - logvar - 1)                # KL per latent coordinate
    return (rec + beta * kl_k.sum(1)).mean(), rec.mean(), kl_k.mean(0)


print(summary(BetaVAE(), input_size=(1, 3, 64, 64), depth=2,
              col_names=("input_size", "output_size", "num_params"), verbose=0))

A table is precise but hides the structure. The function draw_network below draws the same network as columns of nodes joined by edges. In a convolutional column a node stands for a whole channel (a feature map), not for a pixel, and edges join only nearby nodes as a reminder that a convolution looks at a small patch of its input. Dense columns are connected all-to-all. Columns with more units than max_nodes are cut, which the vertical ellipsis marks. The orange column is the latent code \(\mathbf z\), the only place where randomness enters.


Code
def draw_network(layers, ax=None, max_nodes=8, node_radius=0.17, x_gap=1.5, edge_alpha=0.25,
                 colors=None, title=None, fontsize=12):
    """Draw a feed-forward network as columns of nodes joined by edges.

    Parameters
    ----------
    layers : list of dict
        One dict per layer, in the order in which the data flow through the network. Keys:
          'name'  : str, label printed above the column (e.g. 'conv 4x4/2');
          'shape' : str, shape of the tensor the layer outputs, printed below the column
                    (e.g. '16x32x32' = channels x height x width);
          'n'     : int, number of units of the layer: channels for a convolution, neurons for
                    a dense layer; only min(n, max_nodes) nodes are drawn, and a vertical
                    ellipsis marks the ones left out;
          'kind'  : str, one of 'input', 'conv', 'dense', 'latent', 'output'; it sets the colour
                    of the nodes and the edges to the previous column: a 'conv' column is joined
                    only to the nearest nodes of the previous one (a picture of a local receptive
                    field), every other column to all nodes of the previous one.
    ax : matplotlib.axes.Axes or None
        Axes to draw into; when None a new figure of a suitable width is created.
    max_nodes : int
        Largest number of nodes drawn in one column.
    node_radius : float
        Radius of a node in data units; nodes in a column are 0.5 apart.
    x_gap : float
        Horizontal distance between consecutive columns, in data units.
    edge_alpha : float
        Opacity of the edges, between 0 and 1; small values keep fully connected layers readable.
    colors : dict or None
        Map from 'kind' to a matplotlib colour; kinds that are missing use the default colours.
    title : str or None
        Title written above the drawing.
    fontsize : float
        Font size of the layer names and shapes.

    Returns
    -------
    matplotlib.axes.Axes
        The axes with the drawing.
    """
    default = {"input": UJGray, "conv": UJBlue, "dense": UJNavy, "latent": DSOrange, "output": UJGray}
    colors = {**default, **(colors or {})}
    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(1.0 * x_gap * len(layers) + 1, 3.6))
    columns = []                                         # (x, y) positions of the drawn nodes
    for i, layer in enumerate(layers):
        m = min(layer["n"], max_nodes)
        ys = 0.5 * (np.arange(m) - (m - 1) / 2)          # centred column
        columns.append([(i * x_gap, y) for y in ys])
    for i in range(1, len(layers)):                      # edges first, so that nodes cover them
        prev, cur = columns[i - 1], columns[i]
        for j, (x1, y1) in enumerate(cur):
            for (x0, y0) in prev:
                if layers[i]["kind"] == "conv":
                    # local connectivity: join nodes at similar relative height only
                    rel0 = y0 / (abs(prev[0][1]) + 1e-9)
                    rel1 = y1 / (abs(cur[0][1]) + 1e-9)
                    if abs(rel0 - rel1) > 0.45:
                        continue
                ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=UJGray, lw=0.5, alpha=edge_alpha, zorder=1)
    top = max(abs(c[0][1]) for c in columns) + 0.6
    for i, layer in enumerate(layers):
        for (x, y) in columns[i]:
            ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((x, y), node_radius, color=colors[layer["kind"]], zorder=2))
        x = i * x_gap
        if layer["n"] > max_nodes:
            ax.text(x, columns[i][-1][1] + 0.38, "\u22ee", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fontsize + 2)
        ax.text(x, top, layer["name"], ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=fontsize, rotation=0)
        ax.text(x, -top, layer["shape"], ha="center", va="top", fontsize=fontsize, color=UJGray)
    ax.set_xlim(-x_gap / 2, (len(layers) - 0.5) * x_gap)
    ax.set_ylim(-top - 0.6, top + 0.6)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=fontsize + 2)
    return ax

]

             "  $\\longrightarrow$  $\\mathbf{z} = \\boldsymbol{\\mu} + \\boldsymbol{\\sigma}\\odot\\boldsymbol{\\varepsilon}$"

The same network can be drawn automatically. torchview.draw_graph traces one forward pass and draws the computation graph with the graphviz program dot. Every box is a module or a tensor operation, labelled with the shapes of its inputs and outputs. Both models are trained with Adam (adaptive moment estimation, the gradient method of Lab 024 that rescales each parameter’s step by running averages of its gradient and squared gradient) at learning rate \(10^{-3}\) on minibatches of 128 images for 10 epochs over the 15,000 training images. The seed fixes the initial weights, the noise \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\) and the order of the minibatches, so a second run gives the same model. The weights and the training history are saved, and when they exist the notebook loads them instead of training again.


Code
EPOCHS_VAE, BATCH, LR = 10, 128, 1e-3


def train_vae(beta, seed, epochs=EPOCHS_VAE, data=Xtr):
    """Train a beta-VAE with Adam, or load its stored weights if they exist; returns (model, history)."""
    path = f"{CKPT}/lab027_bvae_beta{beta:g}_seed{seed}.pt"
    torch.manual_seed(seed)                                   # fixes the initial weights and the noise
    model = BetaVAE().to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
    if os.path.exists(path):
        ck = torch.load(path, weights_only=False)
        model.load_state_dict(ck["state"])
        print(f"beta={beta:g}, seed={seed}: weights loaded "
              f"(trained {ck['train_time_s'] / 60:.1f} min)")
        return model.eval(), ck["history"]
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=LR)
    gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)                 # fixes the order of the minibatches
    n = data.shape[0]
    hist = {"rec": [], "kl": [], "kl_k": []}
    t0 = time.time()
    for ep in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        order = torch.randperm(n, generator=gen)
        rec_sum, kl_sum, klk_sum, nb = 0.0, 0.0, torch.zeros(D_LATENT), 0
        for i in range(0, n - BATCH + 1, BATCH):
            x = data[order[i:i + BATCH]]
            x_hat, mu, logvar = model(x)
            loss, rec, kl_k = beta_vae_loss(x, x_hat, mu, logvar, beta)
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
            rec_sum += rec.item(); kl_sum += kl_k.sum().item(); klk_sum += kl_k.detach(); nb += 1
        hist["rec"].append(rec_sum / nb); hist["kl"].append(kl_sum / nb); hist["kl_k"].append((klk_sum / nb).tolist())
        print(f"  beta={beta:g} seed={seed} epoch {ep + 1:2d}: reconstruction {hist['rec'][-1]:8.1f}"
              f"  KL {hist['kl'][-1]:6.2f} nats   ({time.time() - t0:5.0f} s)")
    torch.save({"state": model.state_dict(), "history": hist, "beta": beta, "seed": seed,
                "train_time_s": time.time() - t0}, path)
    return model.eval(), hist

@torch.no_grad()
def encode_all(model, X, chunk=1000):
    """Posterior means and log-variances of all images in X."""
    mus, lvs = [], []
    for i in range(0, X.shape[0], chunk):
        mu, lv = model.encode(X[i:i + chunk]); mus.append(mu); lvs.append(lv)
    return torch.cat(mus).numpy(), torch.cat(lvs).numpy()


@torch.no_grad()
def decode_all(model, Z, chunk=1000):
    """Decoded mean images x_hat(z), as a float tensor (n, 3, 64, 64)."""
    Z = torch.as_tensor(Z, dtype=torch.float32)
    return torch.cat([model.decode(Z[i:i + chunk]) for i in range(0, Z.shape[0], chunk)])

text:
4. Active coordinates and latent traversals
The KL term of the loss tells us which latent coordinates the model actually uses. For each coordinate \(k\) we average its KL contribution over the test images,
\[
\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^{N}\tfrac12\big(\mu_k(\mathbf x_n)^2+\sigma_k(\mathbf x_n)^2-\ln\sigma_k(\mathbf x_n)^2-1\big),
\]
and call the coordinate active when \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k>0.1\) nats, the threshold used in Labs 024 and 026. An inactive coordinate has \(\mu_k\approx0\) and \(\sigma_k\approx1\) for every image. The encoder writes nothing into it and the decoder has learned to ignore it, so moving along it changes nothing. The bar chart sorts the coordinates of each model by \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k\), and the dashed line marks the threshold.

    kl_dim[b] = (0.5 * (mu ** 2 + np.exp(lv) - lv - 1)).mean(0)
    active[b] = [int(k) for k in np.argsort(-kl_dim[b]) if kl_dim[b][k] > KL_ACTIVE]   # sorted by KL

nums["kl_per_dim"] = {b: kl_dim[b].tolist() for b in models}

At \(\beta=1\) all ten coordinates are active, with \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k\) between 1.73 and 3.48 nats. At \(\beta=4\) nine are active, between 0.18 and 2.63 nats, and the tenth carries 0.08 nats. Which properties of the galaxy these coordinates carry is the next question.
A latent traversal starts from the code \(\mathbf z_0=\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x_0)\) of one galaxy, changes one coordinate, \(z_k=z_{0,k}+v\) with \(v\in[-3,3]\) in units of the prior standard deviation, keeps all other coordinates fixed, and decodes. As base galaxy \(\mathbf x_0\) we take the test galaxy whose \(\beta=4\) code lies closest to the origin, a typical galaxy of the data set (it is a round smooth galaxy). The first figure, drawn for the slides, compares the four coordinates with the largest \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k\) of each model on seven values of \(v\), and the second shows all active coordinates of the \(\beta=4\) model. In each row, look for whether one property of the image changes or several at once.
In the \(\beta=4\) model the rows are easy to describe. Along \(z_5\) the galaxy grows from a faint point into a large bright blob, so size and brightness change together. Along \(z_2\) a round image is stretched along one diagonal for negative and along the other diagonal for positive values. Along \(z_7\) and \(z_9\) it is stretched along the horizontal or the vertical image axis, \(z_7\) horizontal for negative values, \(z_9\) vertical for negative values. The coordinates \(z_3\) and \(z_1\) add faint asymmetric light, and \(z_8\), \(z_4\) and \(z_0\) produce no change visible by eye. In the \(\beta=1\) model the leading rows mix properties. Along \(z_3\) the galaxy shrinks and turns at the same time, and \(z_9\) changes brightness and compactness together with the shape. No row of either model changes the colour.

def traversal(model, z0, coords, values):
    """Decoded images with one coordinate k set to z0[k] + v, for each k in coords and v in values."""
    Z = np.repeat(z0[None], len(coords) * len(values), 0).reshape(len(coords), len(values), -1).copy()
    for r, k in enumerate(coords):
        Z[r, :, k] = z0[k] + values
    return decode_all(model, Z.reshape(-1, Z.shape[-1])).reshape(len(coords), len(values), 3, 64, 64)

section: 5. Physical quantities measured from the images
text:
5. Physical quantities measured from the images
Traversals are judged by eye, and the eye is easily convinced. To name a coordinate we need numbers that describe each galaxy and that do not come from the labels. The function below measures, from the pixels of each test image alone, the quantities that astronomers use to describe the light distribution of a galaxy.
The intensity of a pixel is the mean of its three channels, \(I(x,y)\), with \(x\) the column and \(y\) the row index. The sky level \(s\) is the median of \(I\) over a frame of width 4 pixels along the image border, and the noise of the sky \(\sigma_s\) is \(1.4826\) times the median absolute deviation of the same pixels (for Gaussian noise this equals the standard deviation, while bright stars on the border do not inflate it). The galaxy mask is the connected region of pixels with \(I-s>3\sigma_s\) that contains the image centre, after a morphological opening that removes isolated noisy pixels. Foreground stars and neighbouring galaxies form separate regions and are left out. Inside the mask the pixel weights are \(w=I-s\), the total weight is \(F_{\rm g}=\sum w\), and the flux-weighted centroid \((\bar x,\bar y)\) and second moments are
\[
I_{xx}=\frac1{F_{\rm g}}\sum w\,(x-\bar x)^2,\qquad I_{yy}=\frac1{F_{\rm g}}\sum w\,(y-\bar y)^2,\qquad I_{xy}=\frac1{F_{\rm g}}\sum w\,(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y).
\]
From these we define seven quantities:

size \(R_{\rm g}=\sqrt{A/\pi}\), the radius in pixels of a disc with the same area \(A\) as the mask;
axis ratio \(q_{\rm ax}=\sqrt{\lambda_2/\lambda_1}\), where \(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\) are the eigenvalues of the second-moment matrix, with \(q_{\rm ax}\approx1\) for a round image and \(q_{\rm ax}\ll1\) for an elongated one. For a thin circular disk inclined by an angle \(i\) to the line of sight \(q_{\rm ax}\approx\cos i\), so for disk galaxies \(q_{\rm ax}\) measures the inclination;
ellipticity components \(\epsilon_1=(I_{xx}-I_{yy})/(I_{xx}+I_{yy})\) and \(\epsilon_2=2I_{xy}/(I_{xx}+I_{yy})\), which describe the orientation. The position angle \(\varphi=\tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2I_{xy},I_{xx}-I_{yy})\) is undefined for round galaxies and jumps by \(\pi\). The components \(\epsilon_1=|\boldsymbol\epsilon|\cos2\varphi\) and \(\epsilon_2=|\boldsymbol\epsilon|\sin2\varphi\), with \(|\boldsymbol\epsilon|=(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)=(1-q_{\rm ax}^2)/(1+q_{\rm ax}^2)\), are smooth functions of the image and are the same components used for galaxy shapes in weak gravitational lensing;
brightness \(F_{\rm g}\), the summed sky-subtracted intensity in the mask, in the stretched units of the image (not a calibrated magnitude);
colour \(c_{\rm col}=\frac1{F_{\rm g}}\sum w\,(x_{\rm red}-x_{\rm blue})\), the flux-weighted difference between the red (\(z\)-band) and blue (\(g\)-band) channels, so that a larger \(c_{\rm col}\) means a redder galaxy. It plays the role of the astronomical colour index \(g-z\), but in stretched units;
concentration \(C=r_{80}/r_{20}\), where \(r_{80}\) and \(r_{20}\) are the radii of circles around the centroid that contain 80% and 20% of \(F_{\rm g}\) (\(r_{20}\) is kept above half a pixel). A galaxy dominated by a bright central bulge has a large \(C\), a disk with a slowly falling profile a small one. At 64 pixels \(r_{20}\) is often about one pixel, and a circular aperture on an edge-on disk also gives a large \(C\), so this is the least reliable of the seven.

The figures and the printed tables write these quantities as R, q, e1, e2, F, c and C. The classes are used only as a check, and the cell prints the median of every quantity for each class.


Code
def measure_galaxy(img, k_sigma=3.0):
    """Morphological quantities of the central galaxy of one image.

    img : float array (64, 64, 3), pixel values in [0, 1], channels (z, r, g) as (R, G, B).
    Returns a dict with the size R, axis ratio q, ellipticity components e1, e2, position angle pa,
    brightness F, colour c, concentration C and the boolean mask of the galaxy.
    """
    I = img.mean(-1)                                            # intensity: mean of the three bands
    edge = np.concatenate([I[:4].ravel(), I[-4:].ravel(), I[4:-4, :4].ravel(), I[4:-4, -4:].ravel()])
    sky = np.median(edge)
    noise = 1.4826 * np.median(np.abs(edge - sky)) + 1e-3       # robust standard deviation of the sky
    J = I - sky
    above = ndimage.binary_opening(J > k_sigma * noise)        # drop isolated noisy pixels
    lab, n = ndimage.label(above)
    H, W = I.shape
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:H, :W]
    if n == 0:
        return None
    g = lab[H // 2, W // 2]
    if g == 0:                                                  # centre not above threshold: nearest region
        d2 = np.where(lab > 0, (yy - H / 2) ** 2 + (xx - W / 2) ** 2, np.inf)
        g = lab.ravel()[np.argmin(d2)]
    mask = lab == g
    w = np.where(mask, np.clip(J, 0, None), 0.0)
    Ftot = w.sum()
    yc, xc = (w * yy).sum() / Ftot, (w * xx).sum() / Ftot
    Ixx = (w * (xx - xc) ** 2).sum() / Ftot
    Iyy = (w * (yy - yc) ** 2).sum() / Ftot
    Ixy = (w * (xx - xc) * (yy - yc)).sum() / Ftot
    tr, det = Ixx + Iyy, Ixx * Iyy - Ixy ** 2
    disc = np.sqrt(max(tr ** 2 / 4 - det, 0.0))
    lam1, lam2 = tr / 2 + disc, max(tr / 2 - disc, 0.0)        # eigenvalues of the second-moment matrix
    r = np.hypot(yy - yc, xx - xc)[mask]
    f = w[mask]
    o = np.argsort(r)
    cum = np.cumsum(f[o]) / Ftot
    r20, r80 = np.interp(0.2, cum, r[o]), np.interp(0.8, cum, r[o])
    return dict(R=np.sqrt(mask.sum() / np.pi), q=np.sqrt(lam2 / lam1),
                e1=(Ixx - Iyy) / tr, e2=2 * Ixy / tr, pa=0.5 * np.arctan2(2 * Ixy, Ixx - Iyy),
                F=Ftot, c=(w * (img[..., 0] - img[..., 2])).sum() / Ftot, C=r80 / max(r20, 0.5),
                mask=mask, xc=xc, yc=yc, lam1=lam1, lam2=lam2)

We compare each latent coordinate with each measured quantity through the Spearman rank correlation \(\rho\), the Pearson correlation of the ranks of the two variables over the test galaxies. It equals \(\pm1\) for any monotonic relation, so it does not depend on the nonlinear stretch of the pixel values or on how a coordinate is scaled. The latent value of an image is its posterior mean \(\mu_k(\mathbf x)\). The matrix \(|\rho(\mu_k,\text{quantity})|\) has one row per active coordinate, sorted by \(\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k\), and one column per quantity.
A coordinate is named after a quantity only when the correlation is clear, meaning \(|\rho|\ge0.5\) and larger by at least \(0.15\) than the next-largest \(|\rho|\) in the same row. The measured quantities are themselves correlated, for example a large galaxy is usually also a bright one, so a coordinate may correlate with two quantities at once, and the margin rule then refuses to name it.


Code
def spearman_matrix(mu, Q, coords):
    """|Spearman rank correlation| between posterior means mu[:, k], k in coords, and the columns of Q."""
    if len(coords) == 0:
        return np.zeros((0, Q.shape[1]))
    rk_mu = stats.rankdata(mu[:, coords], axis=0)
    rk_q = stats.rankdata(Q, axis=0)
    a = (rk_mu - rk_mu.mean(0)) / rk_mu.std(0)
    c = (rk_q - rk_q.mean(0)) / rk_q.std(0)
    return a.T @ c / len(a)                                  # signed correlation, shape (len(coords), n_quantities)


RHO_NAME, MARGIN = 0.5, 0.15


def name_coordinates(rho, coords):
    """Name coordinate k after quantity j if |rho_kj| >= RHO_NAME and exceeds the next-largest |rho| in its row by MARGIN."""
    names = {}
    for r, k in enumerate(coords):
        s = np.sort(np.abs(rho[r]))[::-1]
        j = int(np.argmax(np.abs(rho[r])))
        if s[0] >= RHO_NAME and s[0] - s[1] >= MARGIN:
            names[k] = QUANT[j]
    return names

The matrices confirm the traversals. In the \(\beta=4\) model one coordinate, \(z_5\), carries both size (\(|\rho|=0.93\)) and brightness (\(|\rho|=0.97\)). The margin rule does not name it, since two correlated quantities share the coordinate, but no other coordinate correlates with \(R_{\rm g}\) or \(F_{\rm g}\) above 0.39. The orientation of the light distribution is stored in four named coordinates. The coordinates \(z_9\) (\(|\rho|=0.80\)) and \(z_7\) (0.60) follow \(\epsilon_1\), and \(z_2\) (0.78) and \(z_0\) (0.71) follow \(\epsilon_2\). In the \(\beta=1\) model size and brightness are spread over \(z_3\), \(z_9\), \(z_0\), \(z_4\) and \(z_6\), each with \(|\rho|\) between 0.47 and 0.94, and the four named coordinates again follow \(\epsilon_1\) and \(\epsilon_2\).
Two quantities have no coordinate in either model. The colour \(c_{\rm col}\) reaches at most \(|\rho|=0.27\), in agreement with the grey reconstructions. The axis ratio \(q_{\rm ax}\) reaches at most 0.22, although elongation is clearly encoded. The traversals show the reason. Moving \(z_7\) in either direction makes the galaxy more elongated, once horizontally and once vertically, so \(q_{\rm ax}\) is a symmetric, non-monotonic function of each orientation coordinate, and a rank correlation, which measures monotonic dependence, cannot see it. The β-VAE stores the shape as the two Cartesian components \((\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\) of the ellipticity, the same components astronomers use, and the inclination is the length of that vector.
The correlation gap summarises this for each model. For every quantity it is the largest minus the second-largest \(|\rho|\) over the coordinates. It is large when one coordinate alone carries the quantity, which is what disentangling means here. It plays the role of the mutual information gap (MIG) of Lab 026 [Chen et al., arXiv:1802.04942], with rank correlation in place of mutual information and measured quantities in place of known generative factors. Raising \(\beta\) from 1 to 4 raises the mean gap from 0.122 to 0.218, almost entirely through size and brightness (0.22 to 0.57 and 0.21 to 0.58), because at \(\beta=4\) they are concentrated in one coordinate and at \(\beta=1\) spread over five.


Code
def correlation_gap(rho):
    """For each quantity: largest minus second-largest |rho| over the latent coordinates."""
    s = np.sort(np.abs(rho), axis=0)[::-1]
    s = np.vstack([s, np.zeros((2, rho.shape[1]))])          # fewer than two active coordinates
    return s[0] - s[1]

text:
6. Latent coordinates across morphology classes
The β-VAE never saw a label. The violin plots show, for the six coordinates with the largest KL, the distribution of \(\mu_k\) over the test galaxies of each Galaxy Zoo class. The number \(R^2_{\rm cls}\), written \(\eta^2\) in each title, is the correlation ratio, the fraction of the variance of \(\mu_k\) explained by the class means,
\[
R^2_{\rm cls}=\frac{\sum_{c}N_c\,(\bar\mu_{k,c}-\bar\mu_k)^2}{\sum_n(\mu_k(\mathbf x_n)-\bar\mu_k)^2},
\]
where \(c\) labels the classes, \(N_c\) is the number of test galaxies in class \(c\), \(\bar\mu_{k,c}\) their mean value of \(\mu_k\) and \(\bar\mu_k\) the mean over all test galaxies. The ratio is \(R^2_{\rm cls}=0\) if all classes have the same mean, \(R^2_{\rm cls}=1\) if the class determines \(\mu_k\).

    lab = names[4].get(k)
    a.set_title(f"$\\mu_{{{k}}}$" + (f" ({QLABEL[lab]})" if lab else "") + f",  $\\eta^2$ = {eta2[k]:.2f}")
for a in axs[-1]:

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The size–brightness coordinate \(z_5\) separates the classes best (\(R^2_{\rm cls}=0.19\)). Barred and tightly wound spirals are the largest and brightest galaxies in the images (median \(R_{\rm g}\) 12.8 and 12.9 pixels in the measurement table of Section 5), in-between and cigar-shaped smooth galaxies and edge-on disks with a bulge the smallest. The orientation coordinates have \(R^2_{\rm cls}\le0.07\), as expected, because a galaxy’s orientation on the sky says nothing about its morphology. Their distributions nevertheless differ between classes in their width, while their means are similar. Edge-on disks spread over the whole range of \(z_2\) and \(z_9\), because they are strongly elongated and oriented in every direction on the sky, while round smooth galaxies stay near zero. The class information is in the length of the ellipticity vector, which \(R^2_{\rm cls}\) of a single coordinate does not measure.

title: Lab 027: Galaxy morphology with a β-VAE
section: 7. Counterfactual explanations of a morphology classifier
text:
7. Counterfactual explanations of a morphology classifier
The β-VAE is unsupervised. The second network of this notebook is a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) that predicts the Galaxy Zoo class from the image. Four blocks of a \(3\times3\) convolution, a ReLU and a \(2\times2\) max pooling reduce the image to \(64\times4\times4\) numbers, and two dense layers produce ten logits. The network is trained with the cross-entropy loss, Adam at learning rate \(10^{-3}\) and minibatches of 128, for 10 epochs. Each minibatch is rotated by a multiple of \(90^\circ\) and possibly mirrored, one of the eight symmetries of the square. The morphology of a galaxy does not depend on its orientation on the sky, and the augmentation builds this into the training. The weights are stored and reloaded like those of the β-VAE.


Code
class MorphologyCNN(nn.Module):
    """Four 3x3 convolution blocks with max pooling, then two dense layers; 10 class logits."""

    def __init__(self, ch=(16, 32, 64, 64), n_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        c = [3, *ch]
        blocks = []
        for a, b in zip(c[:-1], c[1:]):
            blocks += [nn.Conv2d(a, b, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2)]
        self.net = nn.Sequential(*blocks, nn.Flatten(), nn.Dropout(0.3),
                                 nn.Linear(ch[-1] * 4 * 4, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, n_classes))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)


def random_dihedral(x, gen):
    """Apply one of the 8 rotations/reflections of the square to the whole minibatch."""
    t = int(torch.randint(8, (1,), generator=gen))
    if t & 1:
        x = x.flip(3)
    if t & 2:
        x = x.flip(2)
    if t & 4:
        x = x.transpose(2, 3)
    return x


EPOCHS_CLF = 10


def train_classifier(seed=0, epochs=EPOCHS_CLF):
    path = f"{CKPT}/lab027_morphology_cnn_seed{seed}.pt"
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    clf = MorphologyCNN().to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
    if os.path.exists(path):
        ck = torch.load(path, weights_only=False)
        clf.load_state_dict(ck["state"])
        print(f"classifier loaded (trained {ck['train_time_s'] / 60:.1f} min)")
        return clf.eval(), ck["history"]
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(clf.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    hist, t0 = {"loss": [], "test_acc": []}, time.time()
    for ep in range(epochs):
        clf.train()
        order = torch.randperm(len(ytr), generator=gen)
        tot, nb = 0.0, 0
        for i in range(0, len(ytr) - BATCH + 1, BATCH):
            b = order[i:i + BATCH]
            loss = F.cross_entropy(clf(random_dihedral(Xtr[b], gen)), ytr[b])
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
            tot += loss.item(); nb += 1
        clf.eval()
        acc = (predict(clf, Xte).argmax(1) == yte.numpy()).mean()
        hist["loss"].append(tot / nb); hist["test_acc"].append(float(acc))
        print(f"  epoch {ep + 1:2d}: cross-entropy {tot / nb:.3f}  test accuracy {acc:.3f}  ({time.time() - t0:4.0f} s)")
    torch.save({"state": clf.state_dict(), "history": hist, "train_time_s": time.time() - t0}, path)
    return clf.eval(), hist


@torch.no_grad()
def predict(clf, X, chunk=1000):
    """Class probabilities, numpy array (n, 10)."""
    X = X.contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
    return torch.cat([F.softmax(clf(X[i:i + chunk]), 1) for i in range(0, X.shape[0], chunk)]).numpy()


clf, clf_hist = train_classifier()
P_real = predict(clf, Xte)
pred_real = P_real.argmax(1)
nums["clf_acc"] = float((pred_real == yte.numpy()).mean())
print(f"test accuracy on real images: {nums['clf_acc']:.3f} (largest class alone: {counts.max() / N_IMG:.3f})")


classifier loaded (trained 6.0 min)


test accuracy on real images: 0.640 (largest class alone: 0.149)


The confusion matrix below summarises the classifier. Its entry \(C_{ab}\) is the fraction of test galaxies of true class \(a\) that the network assigns to class \(b\), so the diagonal holds the recall of each class. After ten epochs the test accuracy is 0.640, while always predicting the largest class would give 0.149. Round smooth galaxies and edge-on disks are recognised best (recall 0.87, 0.86 and 0.85), disturbed galaxies worst (0.07), and cigar-shaped smooth galaxies (0.24, the class with only 334 images) and barred spirals (0.39) are often confused with their neighbours in the Galaxy Zoo decision tree. These classes are defined by thresholds on vote fractions, so their boundaries are fuzzy even for humans.
The last lines of the output matter for what follows. On the reconstructions \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_\theta(\boldsymbol\mu)\) of the \(\beta=4\) model the same classifier reaches only 0.315, and it gives the same answer as on the real image for 0.413 of the galaxies. The reconstructions lack the arms, bars and companions that define several classes. The counterfactual analysis therefore compares every modified image with the unmodified reconstruction, never with the real image.


Code
def confusion(y_true, y_pred, n=10):
    C = np.zeros((n, n))
    np.add.at(C, (y_true, y_pred), 1)
    return C / C.sum(1, keepdims=True)


Cm = confusion(yte.numpy(), pred_real)

ax.imshow(Cm, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)

            ax.text(j, i, f"{100 * Cm[i, j]:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12,
                    color="white" if Cm[i, j] > 0.5 else "black")

ax.set_yticks(range(10)); ax.set_yticklabels(SHORT)

      f"same prediction as on the real image: {nums['clf_agree_recon_real']:.3f}")

recall per class: {'disturbed': np.float64(0.07), 'merging': np.float64(0.57), 'round': np.float64(0.87), 'in-betw.': np.float64(0.8), 'cigar': np.float64(0.24), 'barred': np.float64(0.39), 'tight sp.': np.float64(0.59), 'loose sp.': np.float64(0.59), 'edge-on': np.float64(0.86), 'edge-on+b': np.float64(0.85)}

different prediction on x_hat(mu) and on the real image: 0.587


A counterfactual explanation states what the classifier would have said if this galaxy were more inclined, with everything else unchanged. The β-VAE supplies the “everything else unchanged”. We encode the galaxy, move one latent coordinate, decode, and show the new image to the classifier. For each of \(N_{\rm cf}=600\) test galaxies and each active coordinate \(k\) of the \(\beta=4\) model we set
\[
\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x)+\delta\,\mathbf e_k,\qquad\delta\in\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\},
\]
where \(\mathbf e_k\) is the \(k\)-th unit vector, and classify \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_\theta(\mathbf z)\). The reference decision is the class predicted for the unmodified reconstruction (\(\delta=0\)), not for the real image, so that a change of decision is caused by the moved coordinate and not by the blur of the reconstruction. The flip rate \(f_k(\delta)\) is the fraction of galaxies whose decision differs from the reference, and the sensitivity of the classifier to coordinate \(k\) is \(S_k=\tfrac12\big(f_k(-2)+f_k(2)\big)\).


Code
N_CF = 600
DELTAS = np.array([-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32)
cf_idx = np.arange(N_CF)                       # the first N_CF test galaxies (the split is random)
mu_cf = enc[4][0][cf_idx]
cf_pred = {}                                   # k -> (len(DELTAS), N_CF) predicted classes
t0 = time.time()
for k in active[4]:
    Z = np.repeat(mu_cf[None], len(DELTAS), 0).copy()
    Z[:, :, k] += DELTAS[:, None]
    ims = decode_all(models[4], Z.reshape(-1, D_LATENT))

base = cf_pred[active[4][0]][DELTAS == 0][0]     # prediction on the unmodified reconstruction
flip = {k: (cf_pred[k] != base[None]).mean(1) for k in active[4]}
sens = {k: float(flip[k][np.abs(DELTAS) == 2].mean()) for k in active[4]}
ranking = sorted(active[4], key=lambda k: -sens[k])
nums["flip_rate_delta2"] = {str(k): sens[k] for k in ranking}
nums["flip_rate_delta3"] = {str(k): float(flip[k][np.abs(DELTAS) == 3].mean()) for k in ranking}
print(f"{len(active[4])} coordinates x {len(DELTAS)} shifts x {N_CF} galaxies decoded and classified "
      f"in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
print("sensitivity ranking (flip rate at |delta| = 2):")
for k in ranking:
    print(f"  z_{k}: {sens[k]:.3f}" + (f"   [{names[4][k]}]" if k in names[4] else ""))

All nine active coordinates were moved for each of the 600 galaxies. The coordinates that change the image visibly move the decision most. At \(|\delta|=2\) the flip rate is 0.68 for \(z_2\) (\(\epsilon_2\)), 0.64 for \(z_9\) (\(\epsilon_1\)), 0.62 for \(z_5\) (size and brightness) and 0.56 for \(z_7\) (\(\epsilon_1\)), and at most 0.25 for \(z_1\), \(z_8\), \(z_4\) and \(z_0\). Inclination is the factor one expects to turn a face-on spiral into an edge-on disk. Since no single coordinate carries \(q_{\rm ax}\), the cell takes the coordinate most correlated with \(q_{\rm ax}\), \(z_7\) (an \(\epsilon_1\) coordinate), orients it so that positive \(\delta\) means smaller \(q_{\rm ax}\), and follows the galaxies whose reconstruction the classifier calls a face-on spiral (classes 5–7).


Code

sign_q = -1.0 if rho[4][active[4].index(k_q), QUANT.index("q")] > 0 else 1.0   # direction in which q decreases

                                                 for d in DELTAS]))
q_line = np.array([m["q"] if m is not None else np.nan for m in
                   (measure_galaxy(im) for im in ims_line.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).numpy())]).reshape(7, -1)
nums["q_decoded_median"] = np.nanmedian(q_line, 1).round(3).tolist()

      f"on the reconstruction")

Of the 249 galaxies with a face-on spiral decision, 12.4% are classified as edge-on (class 8 or 9) after a shift of \(\delta=3\) towards smaller \(q_{\rm ax}\), and 6.4% after a shift by 3 the other way. The measured axis ratio of the decoded images confirms that the shift does what its name says. Its median falls from 0.65 at \(\delta=0\) to 0.37 at \(\delta=3\). It also falls slightly, to 0.60, at \(\delta=-3\), because the opposite direction elongates the galaxy along the other axis, which is why the opposite shift also produces some edge-on decisions. The figure shows two galaxies that Galaxy Zoo labels as face-on spirals and whose reconstruction the classifier also calls a spiral. The most sensitive coordinate, \(z_2\), is an orientation (\(\epsilon_2\)) coordinate, and the most frequent flips at \(|\delta|=3\) show what it does to the classifier. Round smooth galaxies become loose spirals (213 cases out of 1,200 shifted images) or edge-on disks (168), and loose spirals become edge-on disks (136). Stretching a blob makes it look like a disk, and stretching it further makes it look like a disk seen from the side. The classifier responds to the elongation of the light distribution in a physically sensible way. That it calls a stretched, featureless blob a “loose spiral” shows how far these images are from the training data.

title: Lab 027: Galaxy morphology with a β-VAE
text:
8. Limits of unsupervised disentanglement
The analysis above rests on assumptions that the data cannot check. Locatello et al. proved that for a factorised prior there are infinitely many invertible maps of the latent space that leave the distribution of \(\mathbf z\), and therefore the distribution of generated images, unchanged, while mixing every factor into every coordinate [Locatello et al., ICML 2019, arXiv:1811.12359]. A loss that sees only images cannot prefer the disentangled member of this family, so unsupervised disentangling is not identifiable without inductive biases on the model and the data. In their large study of trained models, the random seed and the hyperparameters influenced the result more than the choice of the objective, and good models could not be selected without access to the true factors. Here the inductive biases are the diagonal posterior, the convolutional architecture and \(\beta\), and the “true factors” are replaced by quantities we chose to measure.
The cell below makes the dependence on the seed concrete. It trains the \(\beta=4\) model once more, with seed 1 instead of 0 and nothing else changed, and compares the number of active coordinates, the named coordinates, the largest \(|\rho|\) for each quantity and the correlation gap with those of the two models of Section 3.


Code
model_s1, hist_s1 = train_vae(4, seed=1)
mu_s1, lv_s1 = encode_all(model_s1, Xte)
kl_s1 = (0.5 * (mu_s1 ** 2 + np.exp(lv_s1) - lv_s1 - 1)).mean(0)
active_s1 = [int(k) for k in np.argsort(-kl_s1) if kl_s1[k] > KL_ACTIVE]
rho_s1 = spearman_matrix(mu_s1[ok], Q[ok], active_s1)
names_s1 = name_coordinates(rho_s1, active_s1)
gap_s1 = correlation_gap(rho_s1)
nums["seed1"] = {"n_active": len(active_s1), "named": {str(k): v for k, v in names_s1.items()},
                 "max_abs_rho": dict(zip(QUANT, np.abs(rho_s1).max(0, initial=0).round(3).tolist())),
                 "corr_gap_mean": float(gap_s1.mean())}
print(f"{'':22s}" + " ".join(f"{k:>6s}" for k in QUANT))
for lab, r_ in [("beta=1, seed 0", rho[1]), ("beta=4, seed 0", rho[4]), ("beta=4, seed 1", rho_s1)]:
    print(f"{lab + ' max |rho|':22s}" + " ".join(f"{v:6.2f}" for v in np.abs(r_).max(0, initial=0)))
for lab, g in [("beta=1, seed 0", gap[1]), ("beta=4, seed 0", gap[4]), ("beta=4, seed 1", gap_s1)]:
    print(f"{lab + ' gap':22s}" + " ".join(f"{v:6.2f}" for v in g) + f"   mean {g.mean():.3f}")
print("active coordinates:", {"beta=1": len(active[1]), "beta=4 seed 0": len(active[4]), "beta=4 seed 1": len(active_s1)})
print("named coordinates, beta=4 seed 0:", names[4], "| seed 1:", names_s1)
print(f"KL term of the seed-1 model in the last training epoch: {hist_s1['kl'][-1]:.1f} nats per image")

beta=4, seed 0 max |rho|  0.93   0.13   0.80   0.78   0.97   0.22   0.15
beta=4, seed 1 max |rho|  0.93   0.17   0.79   0.59   0.96   0.26   0.22

active coordinates: {'beta=1': 10, 'beta=4 seed 0': 9, 'beta=4 seed 1': 10}
named coordinates, beta=4 seed 0: {2: 'e2', 7: 'e1', 9: 'e1', 0: 'e2'} | seed 1: {4: 'e2', 6: 'e1'}
KL term of the seed-1 model in the last training epoch: 11.5 nats per image


The second seed reaches the same rate (11.5 nats per image in the last training epoch) and finds the same kind of factors. The largest \(|\rho|\) with size and brightness is 0.93 and 0.96, with \(\epsilon_1\) 0.79. The organisation differs. The seed-1 model keeps all 10 coordinates active instead of 9, spreads size and brightness over several coordinates (correlation gap 0.26 and 0.23 instead of 0.57 and 0.58) and names only two coordinates instead of four. Its mean gap, 0.141, is closer to the \(\beta=1\) model (0.122) than to the seed-0 \(\beta=4\) model (0.218). With two seeds we cannot tell whether \(\beta=4\) disentangles better than \(\beta=1\) on these images, only that the seed matters as much as \(\beta\), as Locatello et al. found on larger studies.
Three further limits concern the counterfactuals. A decoded image at \(\delta=\pm3\) is not a real galaxy. It is a blurred, grey blob that may lie outside the distribution of images the classifier was trained on, and the classifier’s answer to it may say more about the blur than about morphology (the classifier already gives a different answer on the plain reconstruction than on the real image for a fraction 0.587 of the test galaxies). The β-VAE at 64 pixels and ten nats per image does not represent arms, bars or companions, so it cannot produce counterfactuals that add or remove them, and the factors it can move are the coarse ones. And the names we gave rest on quantities we chose to measure, with a threshold, a mask and a margin rule that are choices too.

title: Lab 027: Galaxy morphology with a β-VAE
text:
Summary
A β-VAE trained without labels on 15,000 galaxy images of the Galaxy10 DECaLS set stores about 25 nats per image at \(\beta=1\) and 11 nats at \(\beta=4\), with nearly the same reconstruction error. What it stores is the coarse light distribution, namely size and brightness, which travel together in one coordinate at \(\beta=4\), and the shape as the two ellipticity components \((\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\), spread over two coordinates each. Colour, arms and bars are not stored. Rank correlations with quantities measured from the pixels, size, axis ratio, ellipticity, brightness, colour and concentration, turned the traversals into named coordinates, and showed that the axis ratio is the length of the ellipticity vector and has no coordinate of its own. A convolutional classifier reaches an accuracy of 0.640 on ten classes. Moving one latent coordinate and decoding changes its decision most often for the orientation and size coordinates, and turns 12% of the face-on spirals into edge-on disks when the galaxy is elongated. The analysis is not identifiable. A second seed found the same factors organised differently, the counterfactual images are far from real galaxies, and every name rests on measured quantities we chose.
Exercises:

Replace the Gaussian decoder by the binary cross-entropy of Lab 024 and count the active coordinates of a \(\beta=1\) model. Explain the result through the curvature of the binary cross-entropy at the sky value of the pixels.
Train models with \(\beta\in\{2,8\}\) and plot the mean correlation gap against \(\beta\), together with the test mean squared error. Locate the trade-off for these images.
Replace the posterior means \(\mu_k\) by the measured quantities themselves. Fit a linear map from the seven quantities to \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and decode galaxies with a chosen axis ratio. Describe which properties of the decoded image follow.
Train the classifier on the reconstructions \(\tilde{\mathbf x}_\theta(\boldsymbol\mu)\) instead of the real images and repeat the counterfactual analysis. Report which flips survive.
Move the two coordinates with the largest sensitivity \(S_k\) at once and describe the region of the latent plane in which the classifier answers “edge-on with bulge”.
