Because of the binning, the estimator gives 0.916 for the true factors, below the ideal value 1. It gives 0.462 when \(\omega\) and \(x_0\) are mixed by the rotation, so mixing two of four factors halves the score. All twelve models lie between 0.026 and 0.066, far below even the rotated code.


Code
SHOW_BETA = 4
show_seed = max(SEEDS, key=lambda s: migs[SHOW_BETA, s].mean())
key_show = (SHOW_BETA, show_seed)
act_show = active[key_show][np.argsort(kl_dims[key_show][active[key_show]])[::-1]]   # active, by decreasing KL
print(f"model shown: beta = {SHOW_BETA}, seed = {show_seed} (largest MIG of the three seeds)")
print("|corr|, rows: active coordinates by decreasing KL; columns: omega, ln gamma, x0, v0")
print(np.round(corr[key_show][act_show], 2))

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 1.9), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1, 1.15]))
    order = np.argsort(kl_dims[key_show])[::-1]
    axs[0].bar(np.arange(D_LATENT), kl_dims[key_show][order], color=[UJBlue if k in act_show else UJGray for k in order])
    axs[0].axhline(ACTIVE_NATS, color=DSOrange, lw=1, ls="--")
    axs[0].set_xticks(np.arange(D_LATENT)); axs[0].set_xticklabels([f"$z_{k}$" for k in order])
    axs[0].set_ylabel(r"$\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_k$ (nats)"); axs[0].set_title("coordinates, by KL")
    C_show = corr[key_show][act_show]
    im = axs[1].imshow(C_show, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1, aspect="auto")
    for (r, c), v in np.ndenumerate(C_show):
        axs[1].text(c, r, f"{v:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, color="white" if v > 0.6 else UJNavy)
    axs[1].set_xticks(range(4)); axs[1].set_xticklabels(FACTOR_NAMES)
    axs[1].set_yticks(range(len(act_show))); axs[1].set_yticklabels([f"$z_{k}$" for k in act_show])
    axs[1].set_title(r"$|\rho(\mu_k,\mathrm{factor})|$")
    axs[1].spines[:].set_visible(False); axs[1].tick_params(length=0)
    save(fig, "gen_traj_corr.png"); plt.show()

k_w = act_show[np.argmax(corr[key_show][act_show, 0])]      # coordinate most correlated with omega
k_g = act_show[np.argmax(corr[key_show][act_show, 1])]      # ... with ln gamma
k_x = act_show[np.argmax(corr[key_show][act_show, 2])]      # ... with x0
print(f"omega-coordinate z_{k_w}, gamma-coordinate z_{k_g}, x0-coordinate z_{k_x}")
nums["show"] = {"beta": SHOW_BETA, "seed": int(show_seed), "active": [int(k) for k in act_show],
                "corr": np.round(corr[key_show][act_show], 3).tolist(), "k_w": int(k_w), "k_g": int(k_g), "k_x": int(k_x)}


model shown: beta = 4, seed = 2 (largest MIG of the three seeds)
|corr|, rows: active coordinates by decreasing KL; columns: omega, ln gamma, x0, v0
[[0.27 0.87 0.19 0.18]
 [0.4  0.3  0.63 0.26]
 [0.62 0.11 0.46 0.11]
 [0.08 0.16 0.23 0.58]]





omega-coordinate z_3, gamma-coordinate z_5, x0-coordinate z_1


The figure shows the model with \(\beta=4\) whose MIG is the largest of its three seeds (seed 2). Choosing it requires the true factors, which an experiment without ground truth would not have. The other seeds and values of \(\beta\) are summarised in Section 4.3. Its four active coordinates read as follows. \(z_5\), the most informative (2.28 nats), follows \(\ln\gamma\) with \(|\rho|=0.87\) and nothing else above 0.27, so it is the damping coordinate. \(z_1\) follows \(x_0\) (0.63) but also \(\omega\) (0.40), and \(z_3\) follows \(\omega\) (0.62) and \(x_0\) (0.46). \(z_7\), the weakest active coordinate (0.22 nats), follows \(v_0\) (0.58). Every factor has one coordinate in which it is the largest entry, so the code is roughly one coordinate per factor, but only the damping sits in a coordinate of its own. Frequency and initial position are shared between \(z_1\) and \(z_3\). Only \(z_5\) can be named without hesitation.


4.3 Disentangling against β
The figure summarises all twelve models. The left panel shows, for each factor, the largest \(|\rho|\) over the active coordinates, averaged over the three seeds, with a band from the smallest to the largest seed. The right panel shows the gap of the MIG for each factor and their mean, the MIG.


Code
best_corr = {key: corr[key][active[key]].max(0) if len(active[key]) else np.zeros(4) for key in vaes}
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 1.8))
    cols = [UJBlue, DSOrange, UJNavy, UJGray]
    xb = np.arange(len(BETAS))
    for k in range(4):
        m = np.array([[best_corr[b, s][k] for s in SEEDS] for b in BETAS])
        axs[0].plot(xb, m.mean(1), "o-", color=cols[k], label=FACTOR_NAMES[k], ms=4)
        axs[0].fill_between(xb, m.min(1), m.max(1), color=cols[k], alpha=0.15, lw=0)
        g = np.array([[migs[b, s][k] for s in SEEDS] for b in BETAS])
        axs[1].plot(xb, g.mean(1), "o-", color=cols[k], ms=4)
        axs[1].fill_between(xb, g.min(1), g.max(1), color=cols[k], alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    m_all = np.array([[migs[b, s].mean() for s in SEEDS] for b in BETAS])
    axs[1].plot(xb, m_all.mean(1), "s--", color="k", ms=4, label="MIG")
    for a in axs:
        a.set_xticks(xb); a.set_xticklabels([f"{b:g}" for b in BETAS]); a.set_xlabel(r"$\beta$")
    axs[0].set_ylim(0, 1.25); axs[0].set_yticks([0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1]); axs[0].set_title(r"best $|\rho|$ per factor")
    axs[1].set_title("gap per factor, MIG"); axs[1].set_ylim(0, None)
    axs[0].legend(loc="upper center", ncol=4, handlelength=0.8, columnspacing=0.5, handletextpad=0.3, borderaxespad=0.0)
    axs[1].legend(loc="upper left", handlelength=1.4, borderaxespad=0.1)
    save(fig, "gen_traj_mig.png"); plt.show()
nums["best_corr_mean"] = {str(b): np.mean([best_corr[b, s] for s in SEEDS], 0).round(3).tolist() for b in BETAS}
print("largest |rho| per factor over the active coordinates: mean over seeds [smallest, largest seed]")
print("beta   " + "".join(f"{f:>20s}" for f in ("omega", "ln gamma", "x0", "v0")) + "   MIG (mean over seeds)")
for b in BETAS:
    m = np.array([best_corr[b, s] for s in SEEDS])
    print(f"{b:4g}   " + "".join(f"{m[:, k].mean():8.2f} [{m[:, k].min():.2f}, {m[:, k].max():.2f}]" for k in range(4))
          + f"   {np.mean([migs[b, s].mean() for s in SEEDS]):.3f}")





largest |rho| per factor over the active coordinates: mean over seeds [smallest, largest seed]
beta                  omega            ln gamma                  x0                  v0   MIG (mean over seeds)
 0.5       0.62 [0.59, 0.65]    0.74 [0.72, 0.78]    0.50 [0.44, 0.61]    0.58 [0.45, 0.71]   0.041
   1       0.63 [0.57, 0.67]    0.76 [0.72, 0.81]    0.57 [0.48, 0.62]    0.54 [0.29, 0.71]   0.054
   4       0.55 [0.48, 0.62]    0.82 [0.79, 0.87]    0.60 [0.56, 0.63]    0.56 [0.51, 0.60]   0.049
   8       0.48 [0.46, 0.50]    0.82 [0.80, 0.83]    0.57 [0.55, 0.58]    0.23 [0.21, 0.24]   0.040


Over all models the damping is the factor found best. Averaged over seeds, its largest \(|\rho|\) is 0.74 at \(\beta=0.5\) and 0.82 at \(\beta=4\) and \(\beta=8\), with a narrow band over the seeds. The frequency and the initial position stay between 0.48 and 0.63. The initial velocity keeps about 0.55 up to \(\beta=4\) and drops to 0.23 at \(\beta=8\), so it is the factor that the strongest pressure switches off. The MIG, averaged over seeds, is 0.041, 0.054, 0.049 and 0.040 for \(\beta=0.5,1,4,8\). No value of \(\beta\) gives a disentangled code, and increasing \(\beta\) beyond 1 does not help here, because it only removes the factor that is least visible in the data. The seed-to-seed spread of the MIG is as large as its change with \(\beta\), the observation of Locatello et al.


4.4 Latent traversals
Correlations are computed from the encoder. A traversal probes the decoder. We take the latent mean \(\boldsymbol\mu\) of one test trajectory (\(\omega\approx1.5\), \(\gamma\approx1\), \(x_0\approx1\), \(v_0\approx0\)), change one active coordinate \(z_k\) from \(-2.5\) to \(2.5\) while keeping the others fixed, and decode. The title of each panel names the factor with the largest \(|\rho|\) for that coordinate.


Code
ref = int(np.argmin(((Pte - np.array([1.5, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0])) / Pte.std(0)) ** 2 @ np.ones(4)))
mu_ref = ev[key_show][0][ref]
z_vals = np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, 7)
trav_coords = list(act_show[:4])
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    nr = int(np.ceil(len(trav_coords) / 2))
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(nr, 2, figsize=(5.5, 1.0 * nr + 0.15), sharex=True, sharey=True, squeeze=False)
    for a, k in zip(axs.ravel(), trav_coords):
        Z = np.repeat(mu_ref[None], len(z_vals), 0); Z[:, k] = z_vals
        curves = np.asarray(decode(vaes[key_show], jnp.asarray(Z, jnp.float32)))
        for v, cv in zip(z_vals, curves):
            a.plot(t_grid, cv, color=plt.cm.coolwarm((v + 2.5) / 5), lw=1.2)
        f = int(np.argmax(corr[key_show][k]));
        a.set_title(rf"$z_{k}$: {FACTOR_NAMES[f]}, $|\rho|={corr[key_show][k, f]:.2f}$")
    for a in axs.ravel()[len(trav_coords):]:
        a.axis("off")
    for a in axs[-1]: a.set_xlabel("$t$")
    for a in axs[:, 0]: a.set_ylabel(r"$G_\theta(\mathbf{z})$")
    cb = fig.colorbar(plt.cm.ScalarMappable(Normalize(-2.5, 2.5), "coolwarm"), ax=axs, pad=0.02, aspect=20)
    cb.set_label("$z_k$")
    save(fig, "gen_traj_traversal.png"); plt.show()
print("reference trajectory: omega = %.2f, gamma = %.2f, x0 = %.2f, v0 = %.2f" % tuple(Fte[ref]))





reference trajectory: omega = 1.48, gamma = 1.06, x0 = 1.01, v0 = -0.01


The traversals confirm the reading of the correlations and show what the numbers hide. Moving \(z_5\) turns a damped oscillation into an overdamped creep, which identifies it as the damping. Moving \(z_3\) changes the frequency of the decoded oscillation, shifting the position of the first minimum to later times, but the starting value \(x(0)\) moves as well. Moving \(z_1\) changes the initial position and with it the depth of the oscillation, together with its phase. \(z_7\) changes the trajectory only slightly, near \(t=0\), as befits a coordinate with 0.22 nats.


4.5 The frequency and the damping coordinate
A correlation coefficient compresses a cloud of points into one number. The scatter plots show the clouds for the coordinate most correlated with \(\omega\) against \(\omega\), coloured by \(x_0\), and for the coordinate most correlated with \(\ln\gamma\) against \(\ln\gamma\), coloured by the regime. The cell also measures how much of the variance of the \(\omega\)-coordinate is explained by least-squares fits with \(\omega\) alone and with \(\omega\) and \(x_0\) together, and it computes the correlations separately in the underdamped and the overdamped regime, where Section 1.1 predicts that only \(\omega^2/\gamma\) matters.


Code
mu_s = ev[key_show][0]
def r2(y, cols):
    """Fraction of the variance of y explained by a least-squares fit with the given columns (and a constant)."""
    A = np.c_[np.ones(len(y)), *cols]
    res = y - A @ np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)[0]
    return 1 - res.var() / y.var()
w_, lg_, x0_ = Pte[:, 0], Pte[:, 1], Pte[:, 2]
fits = {"omega": r2(mu_s[:, k_w], [w_]), "omega, x0": r2(mu_s[:, k_w], [w_, x0_]),
        "omega, x0, omega*x0": r2(mu_s[:, k_w], [w_, x0_, w_ * x0_]),
        "omega, ln gamma, x0, v0 (all, + squares and products)":
            r2(mu_s[:, k_w], [Pte[:, i] * Pte[:, j] for i in range(4) for j in range(i, 4)] + [Pte[:, i] for i in range(4)])}
print(f"R^2 of the omega-coordinate z_{k_w} explained by:")
for k, v in fits.items(): print(f"  {k:55s} {v:.3f}")
for name, m in [("underdamped", ~over_te), ("overdamped", over_te)]:
    print(f"{name:12s} ({m.sum()} test trajectories): |rho(z_{k_g}, ln gamma)| = {abs(np.corrcoef(mu_s[m, k_g], lg_[m])[0, 1]):.2f}, "
          f"|rho(z_{k_w}, omega)| = {abs(np.corrcoef(mu_s[m, k_w], w_[m])[0, 1]):.2f}, "
          f"|rho(z_{k_g}, ln(omega^2/gamma))| = {abs(np.corrcoef(mu_s[m, k_g], 2 * np.log(w_[m]) - lg_[m])[0, 1]):.2f}, "
          f"|rho(z_{k_w}, ln(omega^2/gamma))| = {abs(np.corrcoef(mu_s[m, k_w], 2 * np.log(w_[m]) - lg_[m])[0, 1]):.2f}")
nums["fits_w"] = {k: float(v) for k, v in fits.items()}
nums["regimes"] = {name: {"rho_g": float(abs(np.corrcoef(mu_s[m, k_g], lg_[m])[0, 1])), "rho_w": float(abs(np.corrcoef(mu_s[m, k_w], w_[m])[0, 1])),
                          "rho_g_slow": float(abs(np.corrcoef(mu_s[m, k_g], 2 * np.log(w_[m]) - lg_[m])[0, 1]))}
                   for name, m in [("under", ~over_te), ("over", over_te)]}

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 1.8))
    sc = axs[0].scatter(w_, mu_s[:, k_w], c=x0_, cmap="viridis", s=3, rasterized=True)
    cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=axs[0], pad=0.02, aspect=15); cb.set_label("$x_0$")
    axs[0].set_xlabel(r"$\omega$"); axs[0].set_ylabel(rf"$\mu_{k_w}$")
    axs[1].scatter(lg_[~over_te], mu_s[~over_te, k_g], s=3, color=UJBlue, label="underdamped", rasterized=True)
    axs[1].scatter(lg_[over_te], mu_s[over_te, k_g], s=3, color=DSOrange, label="overdamped", rasterized=True)
    axs[1].set_xlabel(r"$\ln\gamma$"); axs[1].set_ylabel(rf"$\mu_{k_g}$")
    axs[1].legend(loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0), ncol=2, markerscale=4, handletextpad=0.1,
                  columnspacing=0.8, borderaxespad=0.1)
    save(fig, "gen_traj_scatter.png"); plt.show()


R^2 of the omega-coordinate z_3 explained by:
  omega                                                   0.385
  omega, x0                                               0.598
  omega, x0, omega*x0                                     0.626
  omega, ln gamma, x0, v0 (all, + squares and products)   0.927
underdamped  (3932 test trajectories): |rho(z_5, ln gamma)| = 0.80, |rho(z_3, omega)| = 0.69, |rho(z_5, ln(omega^2/gamma))| = 0.84, |rho(z_3, ln(omega^2/gamma))| = 0.50
overdamped   (1068 test trajectories): |rho(z_5, ln gamma)| = 0.13, |rho(z_3, omega)| = 0.36, |rho(z_5, ln(omega^2/gamma))| = 0.69, |rho(z_3, ln(omega^2/gamma))| = 0.29





The damping coordinate \(\mu_5\) is close to a linear function of \(\ln\gamma\) over the whole range. In the overdamped regime (orange) the cloud widens, and the correlations computed separately in the two regimes explain why. Among the underdamped trajectories \(|\rho(\mu_5,\ln\gamma)|=0.80\), among the overdamped ones only 0.13, while there \(\mu_5\) follows \(\ln(\omega^2/\gamma)\) with \(|\rho|=0.69\). This agrees with the prediction of Section 1.1. Deep in the overdamped regime a trajectory is a slow decay with rate \(\approx\omega^2/\gamma\), and the damping coordinate follows that combination (\(|\rho|=0.69\)). In the underdamped regime the correlation with \(\ln(\omega^2/\gamma)\) is also high, 0.84, because \(\omega\) varies only by a factor of 2 while \(\gamma\) varies by a factor of 30, so that \(\ln(\omega^2/\gamma)\) is dominated by \(\ln\gamma\).
The frequency coordinate \(\mu_3\) decreases with \(\omega\), but the colours show that the slope depends on \(x_0\). For small initial positions (dark) \(\mu_3\) hardly changes with \(\omega\), while for large ones (yellow) it changes strongly. A least-squares fit with \(\omega\) alone explains \(R^2=0.385\) of its variance, with \(\omega\) and \(x_0\) 0.598, with the product \(\omega x_0\) in addition 0.626, and with all factors, their squares and products 0.927. The coordinate is therefore a nonlinear function of the factors, dominated by \(\omega\) and \(x_0\) together. Physically this is natural, because the encoder can measure the frequency only as accurately as the oscillation is visible, and the amplitude of the oscillation is set by \(x_0\). A code that stores \(\omega\) to a precision proportional to its visibility uses a scale that depends on \(x_0\).


4.6 Sensitivity of a trajectory to the parameters
The network can only separate what the data separate. Two properties of the data matter here, how strongly a trajectory responds to each factor and whether two factors change it in different ways. For the Gaussian likelihood with mean \(\langle\mathbf x\rangle(\mathbf p)\) and parameters \(\mathbf p=(\omega,\ln\gamma,x_0,v_0)\), both are measured by the Fisher information matrix \[F_{ab}=\frac{1}{\sigma_x^2}\sum_{i=1}^T\frac{\partial\langle x(t_i)\rangle}{\partial p_a}\,\frac{\partial\langle x(t_i)\rangle}{\partial p_b}.\] Its diagonal says how many \(\sigma_x\) the trajectory moves when one parameter changes. We report the visibility \(\sqrt{F_{aa}}\,\mathrm{std}(p_a)\), which is the change of the whole trajectory, in units of \(\sigma_x\), for a change of \(p_a\) by one standard deviation of its distribution in the data. The normalised off-diagonal element \(F_{ab}/\sqrt{F_{aa}F_{bb}}\) is the cosine of the angle between the two sensitivity vectors \(\partial\langle\mathbf x\rangle/\partial p_a\) and \(\partial\langle\mathbf x\rangle/\partial p_b\). If it is close to \(\pm1\), a small change of \(p_a\) can be compensated by a change of \(p_b\). The data then hardly distinguish the two directions, and a network has no reason to put them into different coordinates. The derivatives of the exact mean trajectory are obtained with jax.jacfwd, at 2000 test parameter points, and we report medians.


Code
def sensitivity_matrix(mean_fn, P, t):
    """Fisher information F_ab = (1/sigma_x^2) sum_i d<x(t_i)>/dp_a d<x(t_i)>/dp_b at every parameter point P (n, K)."""
    J = jax.vmap(jax.jacfwd(mean_fn), in_axes=(0, None))(jnp.asarray(P, jnp.float32), jnp.asarray(t))   # (n, T, K)
    return np.asarray(jnp.einsum("nta,ntb->nab", J, J)) / SIGMA_X**2

osc_mean = lambda p, t: mean_trajectory(p[0], jnp.exp(p[1]), p[2], p[3], t)     # p = (omega, ln gamma, x0, v0)
F_fish = sensitivity_matrix(osc_mean, Pte[:2000], t_grid)
diag = np.sqrt(np.einsum("naa->na", F_fish))
cosines = np.median(np.abs(F_fish / (diag[:, :, None] * diag[:, None, :])), 0)
visibility = np.median(diag, 0) * Pte.std(0)          # change of the trajectory, in units of sigma_x, for a 1-std change
print("median |cos| between the sensitivity vectors d<x>/dp (omega, ln gamma, x0, v0):")
print(np.round(cosines, 2))
print("median visibility  sqrt(F_aa) * std(p_a)  (omega, ln gamma, x0, v0):", np.round(visibility, 1))
nums["fisher_cos"] = np.round(cosines, 3).tolist(); nums["visibility"] = np.round(visibility, 2).tolist()


median |cos| between the sensitivity vectors d<x>/dp (omega, ln gamma, x0, v0):
[[1.   0.69 0.24 0.79]
 [0.69 1.   0.48 0.46]
 [0.24 0.48 1.   0.59]
 [0.79 0.46 0.59 1.  ]]
median visibility  sqrt(F_aa) * std(p_a)  (omega, ln gamma, x0, v0): [16.7 23.3 11.9  5.4]


The visibilities order the factors. A change of \(\ln\gamma\) by one standard deviation moves the trajectory by 23.3 \(\sigma_x\), of \(\omega\) by 16.7, of \(x_0\) by 11.9, and of \(v_0\) by only 5.4. The factor that the network drops first at large \(\beta\), \(v_0\), is the least visible one. For this factor the KL price of storage exceeds the reconstruction gain. The cosines show which directions the data confuse. The largest one, 0.79, belongs to \(\omega\) and \(v_0\). Within the window, a faster oscillation and a negative initial velocity both bring the particle down earlier, and the two changes look alike. \(\omega\) and \(\ln\gamma\) follow with 0.69, since stronger friction also lowers the damped frequency \(\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega^2-\gamma^2/4}\) and shifts the zero crossings. \(\omega\) and \(x_0\) have the smallest cosine, 0.24, so the local, linear picture does not explain why they share coordinates. The mixing is nonlinear, with the product structure seen in Section 4.5, because the sensitivity to \(\omega\) is itself proportional to the amplitude.
This also explains the choice of the parameter ranges. With many oscillation periods in the window, \(\partial\langle x(t)\rangle/\partial\omega\propto t\,\sin(\omega_dt)\) grows with time and oscillates. The trajectories for neighbouring \(\omega\) separate quickly, the map from \(\omega\) to the trajectory folds on itself, and a Gaussian code with a smooth decoder cannot follow it. With \(x_0\) of both signs, the trajectory of \((\omega,\gamma,x_0,v_0)\) and that of \((\omega,\gamma,-x_0,-v_0)\) differ only by a sign, and the code must fold again.
In summary, the \(\beta\)-VAE finds the number of independent factors and, robustly, the damping, while it finds the frequency and the initial conditions only as mixtures. The most visible and least confusable parameter is the one that ends up in its own coordinate.

title: Lab 028: Physical parameters from trajectories
text:
5. Question-and-answer networks

5.1 SciNet of Iten et al.
Iten, Metger, Wilming, del Rio and Renner [Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 010508 (2020)] proposed a network modelled on how a physicist works, in which observations are compressed into a few parameters and the answers to questions about the system are computed from these parameters alone. Their network, SciNet, has three parts (their Fig. 1). An encoder, a feed-forward network, maps an observation \(o\) to a small latent representation. A question \(q\), encoded as real numbers, is appended to the latent values. A decoder, again feed-forward, maps (representation, question) to an answer \(a\). Training uses triples \((o,q,a_{\rm corr}(o,q))\). Unlike an autoencoder, the latent representation need not describe the observation completely, only what is needed to answer the questions. To make the latent neurons statistically independent, they use the \(\beta\)-VAE cost. The encoder outputs means and standard deviations of independent Gaussians, and with a Gaussian decoder of fixed variance the cost becomes (their Eq. (D1), Supplemental Material) \[\begin{aligned}
C_\beta&=\lVert\tilde a-a\rVert_2^2-\frac\beta2\sum_i\big(\log\sigma_i^2-\mu_i^2-\sigma_i^2\big)+\text{const}\\
&=\lVert\tilde a-a\rVert_2^2+\beta\,\mathrm{KL}+\text{const},
\end{aligned}\] the same KL term as ours, with the reconstruction measured on the answer instead of on the input.
Their first example (Box 1 and Sec. E1 of the Supplemental Material, arXiv:1807.10300) is a damped pendulum, \(m\ddot x=-\kappa x-b\dot x\), without noise. The mass \(m=1\,\)kg, the amplitude \(A_0=1\,\)m and the phase \(\delta_0=0\) are fixed, so that \(x(t)=A_0e^{-bt/(2m)}\cos(\omega t+\delta_0)\) with \(\omega=\sqrt{\kappa/m}\sqrt{1-b^2/(4m\kappa)}\). The spring constant \(\kappa\in[5,10]\,\)kg/s\(^2\) and the damping factor \(b\in[0.5,1]\,\)kg/s vary between samples. The observation is the position at 50 equally spaced times in \([0,5]\,\)s, the question a prediction time \(t_{\rm pred}\in[0,10]\,\)s, the answer \(x(t_{\rm pred})\). The encoder has hidden layers of 500 and 100 neurons, the decoder two layers of 100, with exponential linear units (ELU, \(u\) for \(u>0\) and \(e^u-1\) otherwise), and three latent neurons (their Table I), and training used 95 000 samples, batch size 512, learning rate \(10^{-3}\), \(\beta=10^{-3}\) and 1000 epochs (their Table II). They report predictions with a root-mean-square error below 2% of the amplitude, and that the network stores \(\kappa\) and \(b\) in two latent neurons, the first depending nearly linearly on \(b\) and almost not on \(\kappa\), the second only on \(\kappa\), while the third neuron carries no information (their Fig. 6, with the main text speaking of “frequency and damping factor”).
Compared with our \(\beta\)-VAE, three things differ. The decoder answers one question at a time instead of reproducing the whole input, and the questions reach beyond the observed window, so the code must allow extrapolation. The data contain no noise and no nuisance factors, since with fixed amplitude and phase \(\kappa\) and \(b\) are the only things that vary. Finally, \(\beta=10^{-3}\) is small in their units, so the KL term only breaks the rotational symmetry of the latent space and hardly limits the information.


5.2 Data in the setting of the paper
We generate the pendulum data of the paper on the grid \(t=0,0.1,\dots,10\). The observation is the first 50 points, \(t\in[0,4.9]\) (the paper uses 50 points on \([0,5]\)), and the questions are the 101 grid times. The initial condition \(x(0)=1\), \(\dot x(0)=-b/2\) reproduces \(e^{-bt/2}\cos\omega t\), which the cell checks against the closed form. To see what noise and nuisance factors do, we build two more versions of the same data, one with the random force of strength \(D=0.002\) (Euler–Maruyama, \(\Delta t=0.01\)) and one with noise and random initial conditions \(x_0\in[0.5,1.5]\), \(v_0\in[-0.5,0.5]\) as in Section 2. Each version has 20 000 training and 5000 test trajectories. The cell also repeats the sensitivity analysis of Section 4.6 for \((\kappa,b)\) on the observation window.


Code
KAPPA_RANGE, B_RANGE = (5.0, 10.0), (0.5, 1.0)       # spring constant and damping factor of Iten et al. (m = 1)
t_q = 0.1 * np.arange(101)                             # question times 0, 0.1, ..., 10
N_OBS = 50                                             # observation: x at t = 0, 0.1, ..., 4.9

def make_paper_data(n, seed, noise=False, random_ic=False):
    """Trajectories on t_q (n, 101) and factors (kappa, b, x0, v0). Without random_ic: A0 = 1, delta0 = 0,
    i.e. x(0) = 1, x'(0) = -b/2, so that the noise-free solution is exp(-b t / 2) cos(omega t)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    kap, b = rng.uniform(*KAPPA_RANGE, n), rng.uniform(*B_RANGE, n)
    x0, v0 = (rng.uniform(*X0_RANGE, n), rng.uniform(-V0_MAX, V0_MAX, n)) if random_ic else (np.ones(n), -b / 2)
    args = [jnp.asarray(a, jnp.float32) for a in (np.sqrt(kap), b, x0, v0)]
    if noise:
        X, _ = simulate(*args, jax.random.key(seed), n_sub=10, n_rec=101)
    else:
        X = mean_trajectories(*args, jnp.asarray(t_q))
    return np.asarray(X, np.float32), np.stack([kap, b, x0, v0], 1)

# the closed form of the paper, x(t) = exp(-b t/2) cos(omega t) with omega = sqrt(kappa - b^2/4), is reproduced
Xp, Fp = make_paper_data(5, 0)
om_p = np.sqrt(Fp[:, 0] - Fp[:, 1]**2 / 4)
print("max |x - exp(-bt/2) cos(omega t)| =", np.abs(Xp - np.exp(-Fp[:, 1:2] * t_q / 2) * np.cos(om_p[:, None] * t_q)).max())

SETUPS = {"noise-free, fixed A0 and phase (paper)": dict(noise=False, random_ic=False),
          "with noise": dict(noise=True, random_ic=False),
          "with noise and random x0, v0": dict(noise=True, random_ic=True)}
paper_sets = {name: (make_paper_data(20_000, 21, **kw), make_paper_data(5_000, 22, **kw)) for name, kw in SETUPS.items()}

# the sensitivity (Fisher) analysis of Section 4.6 for the parameters (kappa, b) on the observation window
paper_mean = lambda p, t: mean_trajectory(jnp.sqrt(p[0]), p[1], 1.0, -p[1] / 2, t)
Fp_fish = sensitivity_matrix(paper_mean, paper_sets["noise-free, fixed A0 and phase (paper)"][1][1][:2000, :2], t_q[:N_OBS])
dp = np.sqrt(np.einsum("naa->na", Fp_fish))
print(f"median |cos(kappa, b)| = {np.median(np.abs(Fp_fish[:, 0, 1]) / (dp[:, 0] * dp[:, 1])):.2f}; "
      f"visibility (kappa, b) = {np.round(np.median(dp, 0) * np.array([5, 0.5]) / np.sqrt(12), 1)}")


max |x - exp(-bt/2) cos(omega t)| = 2.4576880644500143e-07


median |cos(kappa, b)| = 0.14; visibility (kappa, b) = [11.2  3. ]


The closed form of the paper is reproduced to the precision of single-precision arithmetic. The sensitivity analysis gives a median \(|\cos|\) of 0.14 between the directions of \(\kappa\) and \(b\) on the observation window, much smaller than the cosines between our factors in Section 4.6, and visibilities of 11.2 and 3.0 \(\sigma_x\) for one standard deviation of \(\kappa\) and of \(b\). In the setting of the paper the two parameters therefore change the trajectory in nearly orthogonal ways.


5.3 Network and cost
Our implementation follows Tables I and II of the paper for the layer sizes, the activation, the batch size, the learning rate and \(\beta=10^{-3}\). Each observation is paired with 8 random question times per training step, so one minibatch contains 4096 (observation, question, answer) triples that share 512 samples of \(\mathbf z\). The cost is the mean of \((\tilde x-x)^2\) over the triples plus \(\beta\) times the KL. We train for 100 epochs on 20 000 observations instead of 1000 epochs on 95 000, which amounts to about 4000 gradient steps instead of about 186 000, a difference to keep in mind when comparing results. For the setting of the paper we therefore also train SciNet for 1000 epochs, about 39 000 steps. With random initial conditions the representation needs two more numbers, so that version gets five latent neurons instead of three. For comparison, each data version also trains our \(\beta\)-VAE (\(\beta=4\), \(\sigma_x=0.1\), same latent size, 60 epochs) on the 50 observed points. The drawing shows both networks in the same style. The \(\beta\)-VAE reconstructs the observation, while SciNet receives the question \(t\) next to \(\mathbf z\) and returns one number.


Code
class SciNet(nnx.Module):
    """Question-and-answer network in the style of Iten et al.: ELU activations.
    encoder: observation o (B, 50) -> 500 -> 100 -> mu (B, d), logvar (B, d)
    decoder: [z, t] (B, Q, d + 1)  -> 100 -> 100 -> answer x(t) (B, Q)"""
    def __init__(self, n_obs=N_OBS, d=3, *, rngs):
        self.e1, self.e2 = nnx.Linear(n_obs, 500, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(500, 100, rngs=rngs)
        self.mu, self.logvar = nnx.Linear(100, d, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(100, d, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1, self.d2, self.d3 = nnx.Linear(d + 1, 100, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(100, 100, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(100, 1, rngs=rngs)

    def encode(self, o):
        h = nnx.elu(self.e2(nnx.elu(self.e1(o))))
        return self.mu(h), self.logvar(h)

    def answer(self, z, q):
        """z (B, d), question times q (B, Q) -> predicted positions (B, Q)."""
        zq = jnp.concatenate([jnp.repeat(z[:, None, :], q.shape[1], 1), q[..., None]], -1)
        return self.d3(nnx.elu(self.d2(nnx.elu(self.d1(zq)))))[..., 0]

def scinet_loss(model, batch, key, beta=1e-3, n_q=8):
    """Cost of Iten et al. per (observation, question, answer) triple: (x_hat - x)^2 + beta KL;
    here n_q random questions per observation share one sample z."""
    o, a = batch                                   # observation (B, 50), answers on all question times (B, 101)
    k1, k2 = jax.random.split(key)
    mu, logvar = model.encode(o)
    z = reparametrise(mu, logvar, k1)
    idx = jax.random.randint(k2, (o.shape[0], n_q), 0, a.shape[1])
    pred = model.answer(z, jnp.asarray(t_q, jnp.float32)[idx])
    rec = ((pred - jnp.take_along_axis(a, idx, 1)) ** 2).mean()
    kl = kl_per_dim(mu, logvar).sum(-1).mean()
    return rec + beta * kl, {"loss": rec + beta * kl, "rec": rec, "kl": kl}

_s = SciNet(rngs=nnx.Rngs(0))
print("SciNet parameters:", sum(p.size for p in jax.tree.leaves(nnx.state(_s, nnx.Param))))


SciNet parameters: 86907




Code
def scinet_columns(n_obs=N_OBS, d=3):
    """Columns of the question-and-answer network: o -> 500 -> 100 -> (mu, log sigma^2) -> [z, t] -> 100 -> 100 -> x(t)."""
    return [[dict(n=n_obs, color="white", label=r"$o$")], [dict(n=500, color=UJLight, label="500")],
            [dict(n=100, color=UJLight, label="100")],
            [dict(n=d, color=UJSky, label=r"$\boldsymbol{\mu}$", show=2), dict(n=d, color="#9CC3E6", label=r"$\log\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2$", show=2)],
            [dict(n=d, color=DSOrange, label=r"$\mathbf{z}$", show=2), dict(n=1, color="#F2C14E", label="$t$")],
            [dict(n=100, color=UJLight, label="100")], [dict(n=100, color=UJLight, label="100")],
            [dict(n=1, color="white", label=r"$\tilde x(t)$")]]

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.05), layout="none")
    axs = fig.subplots(2, 1)
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0, right=1, bottom=0, top=1, hspace=0)
    draw_network(axs[0], vae_columns(N_OBS, (256, 128), 3, in_label=r"$o$", out_label=r"$\tilde o$"), x_gap=0.95, max_nodes=4,
                 y_gap=0.2, node_r=0.085)
    axs[0].text(-0.8, 0, r"$\beta$-VAE", rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, color=UJNavy)
    draw_network(axs[1], scinet_columns(), x_gap=0.95, max_nodes=4, y_gap=0.2, node_r=0.085)
    axs[1].text(-0.8, 0, "SciNet", rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, color=UJNavy)
    for a in axs: a.set_xlim(-1.0, 7.3); a.set_ylim(-1.4, 1.25)
    save(fig, "gen_traj_scinet.png"); plt.show()







5.4 Training and probing
Both networks are probed in the same way as in Section 4, through the KL per latent neuron, the active neurons and \(|\rho|\) with \(\kappa\) and \(b\) on the test set. For each parameter we print the best and the second-best \(|\rho|\) over the active neurons. A large best value and a small second value mean that one neuron, and only one, follows the parameter.


Code
EPOCHS_QA = 100
probe = {}
t0 = time.time()
for j, (name, ((Xa, Fa), (Xb, Fb))) in enumerate(paper_sets.items()):
    d_lat = 5 if SETUPS[name]["random_ic"] else 3
    sn, _ = train(lambda s: SciNet(d=d_lat, rngs=nnx.Rngs(s)), scinet_loss, (Xa[:, :N_OBS], Xa), EPOCHS_QA, 0,
                  name=f"lab028_scinet_setup{j}", batch_size=512)
    bv, _ = train(lambda s: TrajVAE(N_OBS, d_lat, rngs=nnx.Rngs(s)), partial(beta_vae_loss, beta=4), (Xa[:, :N_OBS],), 60, 0,
                  name=f"lab028_paper_bvae_setup{j}")
    P_b = np.c_[Fb[:, :2], Fb[:, 2:]] if SETUPS[name]["random_ic"] else Fb[:, :2]
    nets = [("SciNet", sn), ("beta-VAE", bv)]
    if j == 0:                                     # the setting of the paper, also trained for 1000 epochs as there
        sn_long, _ = train(lambda s: SciNet(d=d_lat, rngs=nnx.Rngs(s)), scinet_loss, (Xa[:, :N_OBS], Xa), 1000, 0,
                           name="lab028_scinet_setup0_1000ep", batch_size=512, log_every=250)
        nets.append(("SciNet, 1000 epochs", sn_long))
    for net_name, net in nets:
        mu, lv = (np.asarray(a) for a in encode(net, jnp.asarray(Xb[:, :N_OBS])))
        kl_n = np.asarray(kl_per_dim(mu, lv)).mean(0)
        act_n = np.flatnonzero(kl_n > ACTIVE_NATS)
        probe[name, net_name] = dict(kl=kl_n, active=act_n, corr=abs_corr(mu, P_b), mu=mu)
    for net_name, net in nets:
        if net_name.startswith("SciNet"):
            pred = np.asarray(nnx.jit(lambda m, o, q: m.answer(m.encode(o)[0], q))(net, jnp.asarray(Xb[:, :N_OBS]),
                                      jnp.tile(jnp.asarray(t_q, jnp.float32), (len(Xb), 1))))
            probe[name, net_name]["rmse"] = float(np.sqrt(((pred - Xb) ** 2).mean()))
            probe[name, net_name]["pred"] = pred
print(f"question-and-answer networks and beta-VAEs ready in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

print("setup | network | KL per latent neuron | |rho| with kappa (best, second) | |rho| with b (best, second)")
rows_qa = {}
for (name, net_name), p in probe.items():
    c = p["corr"][p["active"]] if len(p["active"]) else np.zeros((1, p["corr"].shape[1]))
    srt = np.sort(c, 0)[::-1]
    second = srt[1] if len(srt) > 1 else np.zeros(c.shape[1])
    rows_qa[name, net_name] = dict(best=srt[0].tolist(), second=second.tolist(), n_active=int(len(p["active"])))
    print(f"{name:38s} | {net_name:19s} | {np.round(np.sort(p['kl'])[::-1], 2)} | {srt[0, 0]:.2f}, {second[0]:.2f} | {srt[0, 1]:.2f}, {second[1]:.2f}")
print("rms prediction error of SciNet over t in [0, 10]:", {f"{n} | {net}": round(p["rmse"], 4) for (n, net), p in probe.items() if "rmse" in p})
nums["qa"] = {f"{i}_{net}": rows_qa[n, net] for i, n in enumerate(SETUPS) for net in ("SciNet", "beta-VAE")}
nums["qa_long"] = rows_qa[list(SETUPS)[0], "SciNet, 1000 epochs"]
nums["qa_rmse"] = [probe[n, "SciNet"]["rmse"] for n in SETUPS]
nums["qa_rmse_long"] = probe[list(SETUPS)[0], "SciNet, 1000 epochs"]["rmse"]
name_ic = list(SETUPS)[2]
print(f"{name_ic}: |rho| with x0 and v0 over the active neurons (best, second)")
for net_name in ("SciNet", "beta-VAE"):
    p = probe[name_ic, net_name]
    srt = np.sort(p["corr"][p["active"]], 0)[::-1]
    print(f"  {net_name:9s} x0: {srt[0, 2]:.2f}, {srt[1, 2]:.2f}   v0: {srt[0, 3]:.2f}, {srt[1, 3]:.2f}")

  beta-VAE  x0: 0.75, 0.25   v0: 0.25, 0.15


In the setting of the paper and after 100 epochs, SciNet uses two latent neurons (3.64 and 1.23 nats) and switches the third one off (0.03 nats), as reported by Iten et al. The two active neurons, however, both follow \(\kappa\) (\(|\rho|=0.96\) and \(0.85\)), and \(b\) reaches only \(|\rho|=0.50\). The representation is good enough for predictions (root-mean-square error 0.0518 over \(t\in[0,10]\), 5% of the amplitude), but it is not disentangled. Trained for 1000 epochs, as in the paper, the same network separates the two parameters. One neuron follows \(\kappa\) with \(|\rho|=1.00\) and the other \(b\) with \(0.98\), the second-best correlations are only \(0.05\) and \(0.06\), the third neuron carries no information (0.00 nats), and the prediction error drops to 0.0275, 2.8% of the amplitude (the paper reports below 2% after 1000 epochs on 95 000 samples). This reproduces their finding of one neuron per parameter, with a prediction error still somewhat above theirs.
The \(\beta\)-VAE with \(\beta=4\) reaches the same separation after 60 epochs (\(|\rho|=0.99\) for \(\kappa\) and \(0.97\) for \(b\), second-best \(0.01\) and \(0.08\)). Its KL term is far more expensive. Per observed position, SciNet weighs a squared error of one with 1 and the KL with \(\beta=10^{-3}\), while our \(\beta\)-VAE weighs it with \(1/(2\sigma_x^2)=50\) and the KL with \(\beta=4\), a ratio of 0.08, eighty times larger. The stronger pull towards the factorised prior aligns the code with independent directions much sooner, while SciNet’s small \(\beta\) breaks the rotational symmetry of the latent space only slowly.
The random force of strength \(D=0.002\) changes nothing essential for either network at 100 epochs. SciNet again has two neurons following \(\kappa\) (\(0.98\) and \(0.84\)) and \(b\) at \(0.49\), and the \(\beta\)-VAE separates \(\kappa\) (\(0.98\)) and \(b\) (\(0.96\)). Random initial conditions change more. SciNet keeps only two of its five neurons active and stores \(\kappa\) (\(0.91\)) and \(x_0\) (\(0.86\)), but not \(b\) (\(0.30\)) or \(v_0\). For answering questions over \([0,10]\), the frequency and the starting point matter most, and at 100 epochs the network has not yet found room for the damping. The \(\beta\)-VAE keeps three active coordinates, for \(\kappa\) (\(0.90\)), \(b\) (\(0.79\), with \(0.26\) in a second coordinate) and \(x_0\) (\(0.75\)), and drops \(v_0\) (\(0.25\)), the least visible factor, as in Section 4.


Code

(_, _), (Xb0, Fb0) = paper_sets[name0]
p0 = probe[name0, "SciNet, 1000 epochs"]

axs[0].axvspan(0, t_q[N_OBS - 1], color=UJSky, alpha=0.12, lw=0); axs[0].text(2.45, 1.05, "observed", ha="center", fontsize=12)
axs[0].set_xlabel("$t$"); axs[0].set_ylabel("$x$"); axs[0].legend(loc="lower right"); axs[0].set_ylim(-1.1, 1.25)
for a, kz in zip(axs[1:], act0):
    sc = a.scatter(Fb0[:, 0], Fb0[:, 1], c=p0["mu"][:, kz], cmap="coolwarm", s=4)
    fig.colorbar(sc, ax=a, pad=0.02).set_label(rf"$\mu_{kz}$")
    a.set_xlabel(r"spring constant $\kappa$"); a.set_ylabel("damping factor $b$")
    a.set_title(rf"latent neuron {kz}: $|\rho|$ = {p0['corr'][kz, 0]:.2f} ($\kappa$), {p0['corr'][kz, 1]:.2f} ($b$)", fontsize=13)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The figure shows the SciNet trained for 1000 epochs in the setting of the paper. On the left it predicts a test trajectory over \([0,10]\) from the observed first half (shaded). In the middle and on the right every test observation is placed at its true \((\kappa,b)\) and coloured by the mean of one latent neuron. The colour of neuron 0 changes only along \(\kappa\) and that of neuron 1 only along \(b\), the analogue of Fig. 6b of the paper. Both networks, the question-and-answer network and the \(\beta\)-VAE, thus find the same physical parameters when the data contain only these two, the question-and-answer network after much longer training. With nuisance factors and short training both store the most visible parameters first.

title: Lab 028: Physical parameters from trajectories
text:
6. Two coupled oscillators

6.1 Equations of motion and normal modes
Two equal masses \(m\) are each attached to a wall by a spring \(k\) and to each other by a coupling spring \(k_c\). Both masses move in the same fluid, with friction rate \(\gamma\), and each is hit by its own random force, \[\begin{aligned}
m\ddot x_1&=-kx_1-k_c(x_1-x_2)-m\gamma\dot x_1+m\sqrt{2D}\,\eta_1(t),\\
m\ddot x_2&=-kx_2-k_c(x_2-x_1)-m\gamma\dot x_2+m\sqrt{2D}\,\eta_2(t),
\end{aligned}\] with \(\eta_1,\eta_2\) independent white noises. In matrix form \(m\ddot{\mathbf x}=-K\mathbf x-m\gamma\dot{\mathbf x}+\dots\) with the stiffness matrix \(K=\begin{pmatrix}k+k_c&-k_c\\-k_c&k+k_c\end{pmatrix}\). Its eigenvectors are the normal modes. The in-phase motion \((1,1)\), in which the coupling spring is never stretched, has \(\omega_1^2=k/m\), and the anti-phase motion \((1,-1)\), in which the coupling spring is stretched twice as much as each mass moves, has \(\omega_2^2=(k+2k_c)/m\). SymPy finds them, and numpy.linalg.eigvalsh confirms them for random spring constants.


Code
k, kc, m_ = sp.symbols("k k_c m", positive=True)
K = sp.Matrix([[k + kc, -kc], [-kc, k + kc]])            # m x'' = -K x - m gamma x' + noise
for val, mult, vecs in K.eigenvects():
    print(f"eigenvalue {sp.simplify(val)}:  omega^2 = {sp.simplify(val / m_)},  mode {list(vecs[0])}")

# numerical check for a few random spring constants (m = 1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for _ in range(3):
    kv, kcv = rng.uniform(1, 4), rng.uniform(0.2, 2)
    ev_num = np.linalg.eigvalsh(np.array([[kv + kcv, -kcv], [-kcv, kv + kcv]]))
    print(f"k = {kv:.3f}, k_c = {kcv:.3f}: eigvalsh -> omega = {np.sqrt(ev_num).round(6)},"
          f"  formulas -> {np.round([np.sqrt(kv), np.sqrt(kv + 2 * kcv)], 6)}")


eigenvalue k:  omega^2 = k/m,  mode [1, 1]
eigenvalue k + 2*k_c:  omega^2 = (k + 2*k_c)/m,  mode [-1, 1]
k = 2.911, k_c = 0.686: eigvalsh -> omega = [1.706132 2.069328],  formulas -> [1.706132 2.069328]
k = 1.123, k_c = 0.230: eigvalsh -> omega = [1.059679 1.257943],  formulas -> [1.059679 1.257943]
k = 3.440, k_c = 1.843: eigvalsh -> omega = [1.854673 2.669406],  formulas -> [1.854673 2.669406]


In the mode coordinates \(q_\pm=(x_1\pm x_2)/\sqrt2\) the two equations separate, \[\begin{aligned}
\ddot q_+&=-\omega_1^2q_+-\gamma\dot q_++\sqrt{2D}\,\eta_+,\\
\ddot q_-&=-\omega_2^2q_--\gamma\dot q_-+\sqrt{2D}\,\eta_-,\qquad \eta_\pm=\frac{\eta_1\pm\eta_2}{\sqrt2}.
\end{aligned}\] The friction is the same for both masses, so it does not couple the modes, and \(\eta_\pm\) are again independent white noises of unit strength, because \(\langle\eta_+\eta_-\rangle=\frac12(\langle\eta_1^2\rangle-\langle\eta_2^2\rangle)=0\). The two masses are therefore two independent noisy oscillators of Section 1, seen through a rotation of \(45^\circ\). A trajectory depends on the springs only through \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\). Below, the Euler–Maruyama integrator of the two masses is run without noise from \(x_1=1\), \(x_2=0.2\) at rest, and \(q_\pm\) are compared with the exact damped oscillators at \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) (with \(m=1\)).


Code
def simulate_two(k, kc, gamma, x10, x20, v10, v20, key, D=D_NOISE, dt=DT, n_sub=N_SUB, n_rec=T_POINTS):
    """Euler-Maruyama for N pairs of coupled masses (m = 1); all parameters (N,). Returns positions (N, 2, n_rec)."""
    def em_step(state, kk):
        x1, x2, v1, v2 = state
        e1, e2 = jax.random.normal(kk, (2,) + x1.shape)          # independent noises on the two masses
        a1 = -k * x1 - kc * (x1 - x2) - gamma * v1
        a2 = -k * x2 - kc * (x2 - x1) - gamma * v2
        s = jnp.sqrt(2 * D * dt)
        return (x1 + v1 * dt, x2 + v2 * dt, v1 + a1 * dt + s * e1, v2 + a2 * dt + s * e2), None
    def record(state, kk):
        state, _ = jax.lax.scan(em_step, state, jax.random.split(kk, n_sub))
        return state, state[:2]
    _, (x1s, x2s) = jax.lax.scan(record, (x10, x20, v10, v20), jax.random.split(key, n_rec - 1))
    x1 = jnp.concatenate([x10[None], x1s]).T; x2 = jnp.concatenate([x20[None], x2s]).T
    return jnp.stack([x1, x2], 1)
simulate_two = jax.jit(simulate_two, static_argnames=("n_sub", "n_rec"))

# check without noise: the mode coordinates q_+ = (x1 + x2)/sqrt2 and q_- = (x1 - x2)/sqrt2 are single damped oscillators
kv, kcv, gv = 2.0, 1.0, 0.3
one = jnp.ones(1)
X2 = np.asarray(simulate_two(kv * one, kcv * one, gv * one, 1.0 * one, 0.2 * one, 0 * one, 0 * one, jax.random.key(0), D=0.0,
                             n_sub=1, n_rec=601))[0]
t_fine = DT * np.arange(601)
q_plus, q_minus = (X2[0] + X2[1]) / np.sqrt(2), (X2[0] - X2[1]) / np.sqrt(2)
for name, q, om in [("q+", q_plus, np.sqrt(kv)), ("q-", q_minus, np.sqrt(kv + 2 * kcv))]:
    ex = np.asarray(mean_trajectory(om, gv, q[0], 0.0, jnp.asarray(t_fine)))      # both masses start at rest
    print(f"{name}: max |Euler (dt = {DT}) - damped oscillator with omega = {om:.4f}| = {np.abs(q - ex).max():.4f}")


q+: max |Euler (dt = 0.01) - damped oscillator with omega = 1.4142| = 0.0199
q-: max |Euler (dt = 0.01) - damped oscillator with omega = 2.0000| = 0.0276


The differences are of order \(\Delta t\), as expected from the Euler method. The figure shows the system, the two modes, and one trajectory started from \(x_1=1\), \(x_2=0\). Both modes are excited, and the energy moves back and forth between the masses at the beat frequency \(\omega_2-\omega_1\).


Code
import warnings
# the hand-placed axes of this figure trigger a harmless constrained-layout warning of matplotlib
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="There are no gridspecs with layoutgrids", category=UserWarning)

        ax.text(xm + 0.3, y - 0.45, f"$x_{lab}$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11, color=UJGray)
    ax.text(0.45, y + 0.2, "$k$", ha="center", fontsize=11, color=UJNavy)
    ax.text(2.1, y + 0.2, "$k_c$", ha="center", fontsize=11, color=DSOrange)
    ax.text(3.75, y + 0.2, "$k$", ha="center", fontsize=11, color=UJNavy)

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 1.75), layout="none")
    a0 = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.42, 0.5, 0.55]); draw_two_masses(a0); a0.set_xlim(-0.2, 4.4); a0.set_ylim(-0.75, 0.55)
    a0.set_aspect("equal"); a0.axis("off")
    for j, (title, sgn, om_lab) in enumerate([("in phase", 1, r"$\omega_1=\sqrt{k/m}$"), ("anti-phase", -1, r"$\omega_2=\sqrt{(k+2k_c)/m}$")]):
        a = fig.add_axes([0.0 + 0.25 * j, 0.0, 0.24, 0.36])
        for xm, s in [(0.6, 1), (1.6, sgn)]:
            a.add_patch(Rectangle((xm, -0.2), 0.4, 0.4, facecolor=UJSky, edgecolor=UJNavy, lw=1))
            a.annotate("", xy=(xm + 0.2 + 0.35 * s, 0.38), xytext=(xm + 0.2, 0.38), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=DSOrange, lw=1.3))
        a.text(1.3, -0.35, om_lab, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11, color=UJNavy)
        a.set_xlim(0.2, 2.4); a.set_ylim(-0.9, 0.6); a.axis("off")
    a1 = fig.add_axes([0.62, 0.22, 0.37, 0.62])
    X_demo = np.asarray(simulate_two(*(jnp.array([v]) for v in (2.0, 0.6, 0.25, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)), jax.random.key(3)))[0]
    a1.plot(t_grid, X_demo[0], color=UJBlue, label="$x_1$"); a1.plot(t_grid, X_demo[1], color=DSOrange, label="$x_2$")
    a1.set_xlabel("$t$"); a1.legend(loc="upper right", ncol=2, handlelength=1.0, borderaxespad=0.0)
    a1.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.4); a1.set_title(r"$x_1(0)=1$, $x_2(0)=0$")
    save(fig, "gen_traj_coupled_sketch.png"); plt.show()







6.2 Data
The spring constants are drawn uniformly, \(k\in[1,4]\) and \(k_c\in[0.2,2]\), the friction log-uniformly, \(\gamma\in[0.2,2]\), and the initial conditions uniformly, \(x_1(0)\in[0.5,1.5]\), \(x_2(0)\in[-1,1]\), \(\dot x_{1,2}(0)\in[-0.5,0.5]\). The noise strength \(D\), the time step \(\Delta t\) and the 100 recorded times are those of Section 2. The input of the network is the two-channel trajectory \(\big(x_1(t_i),x_2(t_i)\big)\), flattened to 200 numbers. Because \(k\) and \(k_c\) are drawn independently, \(\omega_1=\sqrt k\) and \(\omega_2=\sqrt{k+2k_c}\) are correlated, and \(\omega_2\) is correlated with both springs. This makes the question decidable, because a coordinate that follows \(\omega_2\) has \(|\rho|\) close to 1 with \(\omega_2\) but clearly smaller with \(k_c\), and vice versa.


Code
K_RANGE, KC_RANGE, GAMMA2_RANGE = (1.0, 4.0), (0.2, 2.0), (0.2, 2.0)
def make_two_data(n, seed):
    """n trajectories of two coupled masses, (n, 2, 100), and factors (n, 7) = (k, k_c, gamma, x1, x2, v1, v2) at t = 0."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    kk, kc_, ga = rng.uniform(*K_RANGE, n), rng.uniform(*KC_RANGE, n), np.exp(rng.uniform(*np.log(GAMMA2_RANGE), n))
    x1, x2 = rng.uniform(*X0_RANGE, n), rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, n)
    v1, v2 = rng.uniform(-V0_MAX, V0_MAX, n), rng.uniform(-V0_MAX, V0_MAX, n)
    X = simulate_two(*(jnp.asarray(a, jnp.float32) for a in (kk, kc_, ga, x1, x2, v1, v2)), jax.random.key(seed))
    return np.asarray(X, np.float32), np.stack([kk, kc_, ga, x1, x2, v1, v2], 1)

X2tr, F2tr = make_two_data(20_000, seed=11)
X2te, F2te = make_two_data(5_000, seed=12)
w1_te, w2_te = np.sqrt(F2te[:, 0]), np.sqrt(F2te[:, 0] + 2 * F2te[:, 1])
P2_springs = np.stack([F2te[:, 0], F2te[:, 1], np.log(F2te[:, 2])], 1)
P2_modes = np.stack([w1_te, w2_te, np.log(F2te[:, 2])], 1)
P2_ic = F2te[:, 3:]
print("correlations in the test data:  rho(omega_2, k) = %.2f,  rho(omega_2, k_c) = %.2f,  rho(omega_1, omega_2) = %.2f"
      % (np.corrcoef(w2_te, F2te[:, 0])[0, 1], np.corrcoef(w2_te, F2te[:, 1])[0, 1], np.corrcoef(w1_te, w2_te)[0, 1]))
nums["two_data_corr"] = {"w2_k": float(np.corrcoef(w2_te, F2te[:, 0])[0, 1]), "w2_kc": float(np.corrcoef(w2_te, F2te[:, 1])[0, 1]),
                         "w1_w2": float(np.corrcoef(w1_te, w2_te)[0, 1])}


correlations in the test data:  rho(omega_2, k) = 0.63,  rho(omega_2, k_c) = 0.75,  rho(omega_1, omega_2) = 0.63


In the test data \(\rho(\omega_2,k)=0.63\), \(\rho(\omega_2,k_c)=0.75\) and \(\rho(\omega_1,\omega_2)=0.63\). A coordinate that follows \(\omega_2\) perfectly would therefore have \(|\rho|=0.75\) with \(k_c\), and one that follows \(k_c\) perfectly \(|\rho|=0.75\) with \(\omega_2\).


6.3 Springs or normal modes
We train the same \(\beta\)-VAE with 200 inputs and \(d=10\) latent coordinates, for \(\beta=4\) and two seeds, and correlate the active coordinates with two descriptions of the same oscillator, the spring constants \((k,k_c,\ln\gamma)\) and the normal-mode frequencies \((\omega_1,\omega_2,\ln\gamma)\). The cell prints, for every model, the largest \(|\rho|\) of each parameter over the active coordinates.


Code
D2_LATENT, BETAS2, SEEDS2 = 10, [4], [0, 1]
t0 = time.time()
vaes2, ev2 = {}, {}
X2tr_flat, X2te_flat = X2tr.reshape(len(X2tr), -1), X2te.reshape(len(X2te), -1)     # (n, 200): x1(t) then x2(t)
for beta in BETAS2:
    for seed in SEEDS2:
        vaes2[beta, seed], _ = train(lambda s: TrajVAE(2 * T_POINTS, D2_LATENT, rngs=nnx.Rngs(s)), partial(beta_vae_loss, beta=beta),
                                     (X2tr_flat,), EPOCHS, seed, name=f"lab028_two_beta{beta}_seed{seed}")
        ev2[beta, seed] = evaluate(vaes2[beta, seed], X2te_flat)
print(f"{len(vaes2)} models ready in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
summary2 = {}
for key in vaes2:
    mu, lv = ev2[key][0], ev2[key][1]
    kl2 = np.asarray(kl_per_dim(mu, lv)).mean(0); act2 = np.flatnonzero(kl2 > ACTIVE_NATS)
    act2 = act2[np.argsort(kl2[act2])[::-1]]
    c_spr, c_mod, c_ic = abs_corr(mu, P2_springs)[act2], abs_corr(mu, P2_modes)[act2], abs_corr(mu, P2_ic)[act2]
    summary2[key] = dict(active=act2, kl=kl2, c_spr=c_spr, c_mod=c_mod, c_ic=c_ic)
    print(f"beta {key[0]}, seed {key[1]}: rate {ev2[key][2]:.2f}, distortion {ev2[key][3]:.2f}, active {len(act2)};"
          f"  best |rho| with k, k_c, ln gamma: {np.round(c_spr.max(0), 2)};  with omega_1, omega_2, ln gamma: {np.round(c_mod.max(0), 2)}")
nums["two"] = {f"{b}_{s}": {"n_active": int(len(v["active"])), "best_springs": v["c_spr"].max(0).round(3).tolist(),
                            "best_modes": v["c_mod"].max(0).round(3).tolist()} for (b, s), v in summary2.items()}


2 models ready in 5 s
beta 4, seed 0: rate 10.45, distortion 20.31, active 7;  best |rho| with k, k_c, ln gamma: [0.73 0.5  0.51];  with omega_1, omega_2, ln gamma: [0.74 0.59 0.51]
beta 4, seed 1: rate 10.63, distortion 19.29, active 7;  best |rho| with k, k_c, ln gamma: [0.68 0.65 0.48];  with omega_1, omega_2, ln gamma: [0.69 0.63 0.48]




Code
key2 = max(vaes2, key=lambda kk: summary2[kk]["c_mod"].max(0)[:2].sum() + summary2[kk]["c_spr"].max(0)[:2].sum())
s2 = summary2[key2]
print(f"model shown: beta = {key2[0]}, seed = {key2[1]}")
print("rows: active coordinates; columns: k, k_c, ln gamma | omega_1, omega_2, ln gamma | x1(0), x2(0), v1(0), v2(0)")
print(np.round(np.c_[s2["c_spr"], s2["c_mod"], s2["c_ic"]], 2))
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(5.5, 1.8), sharex=True)
    for a, Cm, labels in [(axs[0], s2["c_spr"].T, ["$k$", "$k_c$", r"$\ln\gamma$"]),
                          (axs[1], s2["c_mod"].T, [r"$\omega_1$", r"$\omega_2$", r"$\ln\gamma$"])]:
        a.imshow(Cm, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1, aspect="auto")
        for (r, c), v in np.ndenumerate(Cm):
            a.text(c, r, f"{v:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, color="white" if v > 0.6 else UJNavy)
        a.set_yticks(range(3)); a.set_yticklabels(labels)
        a.spines[:].set_visible(False); a.tick_params(length=0)
    axs[0].set_ylabel("springs"); axs[1].set_ylabel("modes")
    axs[1].set_xticks(range(len(s2["active"]))); axs[1].set_xticklabels([f"$z_{{{k}}}$" for k in s2["active"]])
    save(fig, "gen_traj_coupled_corr.png"); plt.show()
nums["two_show"] = {"beta": key2[0], "seed": key2[1], "c_spr": np.round(s2["c_spr"], 3).tolist(), "c_mod": np.round(s2["c_mod"], 3).tolist()}


model shown: beta = 4, seed = 1
rows: active coordinates; columns: k, k_c, ln gamma | omega_1, omega_2, ln gamma | x1(0), x2(0), v1(0), v2(0)
[[0.68 0.18 0.47 0.69 0.6  0.47 0.06 0.17 0.17 0.11]
 [0.16 0.07 0.08 0.17 0.03 0.08 0.1  0.89 0.05 0.  ]
 [0.26 0.12 0.48 0.24 0.05 0.48 0.46 0.32 0.12 0.2 ]
 [0.22 0.65 0.22 0.21 0.63 0.22 0.02 0.12 0.06 0.28]
 [0.32 0.12 0.47 0.32 0.12 0.47 0.73 0.01 0.18 0.14]
 [0.17 0.26 0.11 0.17 0.09 0.11 0.16 0.02 0.31 0.56]
 [0.08 0.09 0.09 0.09 0.13 0.09 0.15 0.09 0.71 0.3 ]]





Both seeds have seven active coordinates, one per factor (\(k\), \(k_c\), \(\gamma\) and four initial values). The figure shows seed 1. Coordinate \(z_1\) follows \(k\) (\(|\rho|=0.68\)) and \(\omega_1=\sqrt k\) (0.69), the same statement, since \(\omega_1\) is a monotonic function of \(k\). It also correlates with \(\omega_2\) (0.60) and \(\ln\gamma\) (0.47). Coordinate \(z_0\) follows \(k_c\) with \(0.65\) and \(\omega_2\) with \(0.63\). This difference is far too small to decide the question of Section 6.2. A pure \(\omega_2\) coordinate would correlate with \(k_c\) at only 0.75, and a pure \(k_c\) coordinate with \(\omega_2\) at 0.75, while \(z_0\) reaches neither value with either parameter, so it is a mixture. In seed 0 the corresponding coordinate prefers \(\omega_2\) slightly (0.59 against 0.50 with \(k_c\)). The friction is not isolated, since three coordinates correlate with \(\ln\gamma\) at 0.47–0.48, each together with an initial condition. The initial conditions themselves take four coordinates, with \(x_2(0)\) at 0.89, \(x_1(0)\) at 0.73, \(\dot x_1(0)\) at 0.71 and \(\dot x_2(0)\) at 0.56.
The answer is therefore negative on both sides. The \(\beta\)-VAE does not find the normal-mode frequencies as such, and it does not find the springs either. One coordinate tracks the in-phase frequency, a second one the coupling, in a mixture of the two descriptions. With seven factors and two channels the problem is harder than for one oscillator, and, as there, the most visible factors, here the initial positions, are captured most cleanly.


Code
ref2 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(F2te[:, 0] - 2.5) + np.abs(F2te[:, 1] - 1.0) + np.abs(F2te[:, 2] - 0.5)))
mu_ref2 = ev2[key2][0][ref2]
coords2 = list(s2["active"][:6])
fig, axs = plt.subplots(int(np.ceil(len(coords2) / 3)), 3, figsize=(16, 3.4 * np.ceil(len(coords2) / 3)), squeeze=False, sharex=True)
for a, kz in zip(axs.ravel(), coords2):

        cv = np.asarray(decode(vaes2[key2], jnp.asarray(Z[None], jnp.float32)))[0].reshape(2, T_POINTS)
        col = plt.cm.coolwarm((v + 2) / 4)
        a.plot(t_grid, cv[0], color=col, lw=1.6, label=f"$z={v}$")
        a.plot(t_grid, cv[1], color=col, lw=1.6, ls="--")
    r = list(s2["active"]).index(kz)
    best = [("k", s2["c_spr"][r, 0]), ("k_c", s2["c_spr"][r, 1]), (r"\omega_1", s2["c_mod"][r, 0]),
            (r"\omega_2", s2["c_mod"][r, 1]), (r"\ln\gamma", s2["c_mod"][r, 2])]
    nm, vv = max(best, key=lambda p: p[1])
    a.set_title(rf"$z_{{{kz}}}$: largest $|\rho|$ with ${nm}$ ({vv:.2f})", fontsize=13)
for a in axs.ravel()[len(coords2):]: a.axis("off")
axs[0, 0].legend(fontsize=11, title="solid $x_1$, dashed $x_2$", title_fontsize=11)
for a in axs[-1]: a.set_xlabel("$t$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The traversals show the two spring-related coordinates at work. Moving \(z_1\) changes the frequency of the motion of both masses together, which is the in-phase frequency \(\omega_1\). At \(z=2\) (red) both oscillate faster than at \(z=-2\) (blue). Moving \(z_0\) changes mainly the relative motion of the two masses, how far \(x_1\) (solid) and \(x_2\) (dashed) separate after the start, i.e. the anti-phase content and its frequency. \(z_8\) sets the initial position of the second mass, and \(z_4\) and \(z_9\) change the damping together with the starting values.

title: Lab 028: Physical parameters from trajectories
text:
Summary
The Langevin equation of a damped oscillator with white noise was integrated with the Euler–Maruyama scheme, whose noise step scales as \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\). The simulated mean and stationary variance agree with the exact results \(e^{At}\mathbf s(0)\) and \(\langle x^2\rangle=D/(\gamma\omega^2)\) up to an error of order \(\Delta t\) (about 5% at \(\Delta t=0.01\) for the variance).
A \(\beta\)-VAE with a Gaussian decoder, whose reconstruction term is a scaled mean squared error, trained on 20 000 noisy trajectories without labels, uses four latent coordinates for four factors at \(\beta=1\) and in two of the three seeds at \(\beta=4\) (the third has a fifth, weak coordinate of 0.13 nats). At \(\beta=8\) it drops the initial velocity, the least visible factor. The damping is the one physical parameter that ends up in a coordinate of its own (\(|\rho|=0.87\) with \(\ln\gamma\)). In the overdamped regime this coordinate follows \(\omega^2/\gamma\), the slow decay rate, which is the combination the data actually contain. The frequency is stored together with the initial position, because the encoder can measure a frequency only as accurately as the oscillation is visible. The mutual information gap stays between 0.03 and 0.07 for all \(\beta\) and seeds, against 0.92 for the true factors. The Fisher information of the trajectories explains the ranking. The visibility of a parameter decides whether it is stored, while the overlap of the sensitivity directions and the nonlinearity of the map decide whether it is stored alone.
The question-and-answer network SciNet of Iten et al. reproduces their result when trained as long as in the paper (one neuron for \(\kappa\), one for \(b\), \(|\rho|=1.00\) and \(0.98\)), and the \(\beta\)-VAE finds the same two parameters with a much stronger KL term in a fraction of the training. Noise of the size used here changes little, while nuisance initial conditions change which parameters are stored first. For two coupled masses the \(\beta\)-VAE finds one coordinate for the in-phase frequency and one that mixes the coupling constant with the anti-phase frequency, so it decides neither for the springs nor for the normal modes.
The general lesson is that a latent coordinate becomes interpretable when its parameter is visible in the data, when no other parameter changes the data in a similar way, and when the training is long enough. A coordinate has to be checked against known physics before it is given a name.

title: Lab 028: Physical parameters from trajectories
text:
Exercises

Exercise 1. Euler–Maruyama for a free Brownian particle
A free overdamped Brownian particle obeys \(\dot x=\sqrt{2D}\,\eta(t)\). (a) Write the Euler–Maruyama update and show that, for \(x_0=0\), \(\langle x_n^2\rangle=2Dn\Delta t\) for every step size \(\Delta t\). (b) Explain why the noise term must scale as \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\), by computing \(\langle x^2\rangle\) at a fixed time for a noise term that scales as \(\Delta t\). (c) Check (a) numerically for two step sizes.

Solution

\(x_{n+1}=x_n+\sqrt{2D\Delta t}\,\zeta_n\), hence \(x_n=\sqrt{2D\Delta t}\sum_{j<n}\zeta_j\) and, since the \(\zeta_j\) are independent with unit variance, \(\langle x_n^2\rangle=2D\Delta t\,n=2Dt_n\). The scheme is exact for this equation, at any \(\Delta t\). (b) With a term \(\propto\Delta t\,\zeta_n\) one would get \(\langle x_n^2\rangle\propto n\Delta t^2=t_n\Delta t\to0\) for \(\Delta t\to0\), so the particle would stop diffusing in the continuum limit. Only \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) gives a limit that does not depend on the step size. (c) The next cell checks (a) for two step sizes.



Code
# free Brownian particle: x_{n+1} = x_n + sqrt(2 D dt) zeta_n,  x_0 = 0  ->  <x_n^2> = 2 D n dt for every dt
D_ex, n_walk = 0.5, 200_000
for dt_ex in [0.5, 0.05]:
    steps = int(2.0 / dt_ex)
    x = np.zeros(n_walk)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x += np.sqrt(2 * D_ex * dt_ex) * rng.standard_normal(n_walk)
    print(f"dt = {dt_ex}: <x^2>(t = 2) = {np.mean(x**2):.4f},  exact 2 D t = {2 * D_ex * 2.0:.4f}")


dt = 0.5: <x^2>(t = 2) = 1.9908,  exact 2 D t = 2.0000
dt = 0.05: <x^2>(t = 2) = 1.9986,  exact 2 D t = 2.0000


Both step sizes reproduce \(2Dt=2\) within the sampling error, which is about 0.3% for 200 000 walkers. We obtain 1.9908 for \(\Delta t=0.5\) and 1.9986 for \(\Delta t=0.05\).



Exercise 2. Stationary variance of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process
In the overdamped limit the oscillator obeys \(\gamma\dot x=-\omega^2x+\sqrt{2D}\,\eta(t)\). (a) Check that \(x(t)=\int_0^te^{-r(t-s)}\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{\gamma}\eta(s)\,ds\) with \(r=\omega^2/\gamma\) solves it for \(x(0)=0\). (b) Using \(\langle\eta(s)\eta(s')\rangle=\delta(s-s')\), compute \(\langle x(t)^2\rangle\) and its limit \(t\to\infty\). Compare with the underdamped result of Section 1.3.

Solution

Differentiating, \(\dot x=\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{\gamma}\eta(t)-r\,x(t)\), which is the equation divided by \(\gamma\). (b) \(\langle x^2\rangle=\frac{2D}{\gamma^2}\int_0^t\!\int_0^te^{-r(t-s)}e^{-r(t-s')}\delta(s-s')\,ds\,ds'=\frac{2D}{\gamma^2}\int_0^te^{-2r(t-s)}ds\). SymPy evaluates the integral in the next cell.



Code
s_, tau, D_, g_, w_s = sp.symbols("s tau D gamma omega", positive=True)
r_ = w_s**2 / g_                                                  # relaxation rate of the overdamped particle
# x(t) = int_0^t e^{-r (t - s)} (sqrt(2D)/gamma) eta(s) ds  ->  <x^2> = (2D/gamma^2) int_0^t e^{-2 r (t - s)} ds
var_t = (2 * D_ / g_**2) * sp.integrate(sp.exp(-2 * r_ * (tau - s_)), (s_, 0, tau))
print("<x^2>(t) =", sp.simplify(var_t))
print("t -> infinity:", sp.limit(var_t, tau, sp.oo))


<x^2>(t) = D/(gamma*omega**2) - D*exp(-2*omega**2*tau/gamma)/(gamma*omega**2)
t -> infinity: D/(gamma*omega**2)


The limit is \(D/(\gamma\omega^2)\), the same as \(\langle x^2\rangle\) of the full oscillator in Section 1.3. The stationary distribution of the position does not depend on the mass, as it must for a Boltzmann distribution \(\propto e^{-\omega^2x^2/(2k_BT)}\) with \(k_BT=D/\gamma\) (units with \(m=1\)).



Exercise 3. A stronger random force
Generate the data of Section 2 with \(D\) ten times larger and train a \(\beta\)-VAE with \(\beta=4\) (60 epochs suffice for a first look). Compare the rate, the distortion, the number of active coordinates and the best correlations with the four factors with those at the original \(D\), and relate the changes to the noise-floor argument of Section 3.3.

Solution


Code
# a ten times larger noise strength
Xtr_D, _ = make_oscillator_data(20_000, seed=31, D=10 * D_NOISE)
Xte_D, Fte_D = make_oscillator_data(5_000, seed=32, D=10 * D_NOISE)
vae_D, _ = train(lambda s: TrajVAE(T_POINTS, D_LATENT, rngs=nnx.Rngs(s)), partial(beta_vae_loss, beta=4), (Xtr_D,), 60, 0,
                 name="lab028_ex_D10_beta4")
mu_D, lv_D, R_D, Drec_D = evaluate(vae_D, Xte_D)
act_D = np.flatnonzero(np.asarray(kl_per_dim(mu_D, lv_D)).mean(0) > ACTIVE_NATS)
print(f"D = {10 * D_NOISE}: rate {R_D:.2f} nats, distortion {Drec_D:.2f}, active coordinates {len(act_D)}")
print("best |rho| over active coordinates (omega, ln gamma, x0, v0):", np.round(abs_corr(mu_D, probe_factors(Fte_D))[act_D].max(0), 2))
print("for comparison, D = %.3f, beta = 4 (mean over seeds):" % D_NOISE, np.round(np.mean([best_corr[4, s] for s in SEEDS], 0), 2))


D = 0.02: rate 6.74 nats, distortion 13.96, active coordinates 5
best |rho| over active coordinates (omega, ln gamma, x0, v0): [0.44 0.76 0.67 0.43]
for comparison, D = 0.002, beta = 4 (mean over seeds): [0.55 0.82 0.6  0.56]


With \(D=0.02\) the model has five active coordinates instead of four, a rate of 6.74 nats and a distortion of 13.96 nats. The best correlations with \(\omega\), \(\ln\gamma\) and \(v_0\) drop, from 0.55, 0.82 and 0.56 (mean over the seeds at \(D=0.002\)) to 0.44, 0.76 and 0.43, while the one with \(x_0\) rises from 0.60 to 0.67. Ten times more noise raises the noise floor tenfold. The trajectories deviate from their means by about three times more, the small details by which \(\omega\) and \(v_0\) are recognised are masked first, and the code spends a coordinate on the noise. The damping and the initial position, the most visible factors, survive best. (This is a single seed with 60 epochs, and firm conclusions require several seeds.)



Exercise 4. A driving frequency as a third parameter
Add a periodic force \(F\cos(\Omega t)\) with \(F=0.5\) to the equation of motion and draw \(\Omega\) uniformly in \([0.5,2.5]\) for every trajectory. Train a \(\beta\)-VAE with \(\beta=4\) and correlate its active coordinates with \((\omega,\ln\gamma,\Omega,x_0,v_0)\). Check whether a coordinate follows the driving frequency, find which of the five factors is easiest to find, and explain why.

Solution


Code
# a third physical parameter: the frequency Omega of a driving force F cos(Omega t), F = 0.5
F_DRIVE = 0.5
def simulate_driven(omega, gamma, Omega, x0, v0, key, D=D_NOISE, dt=DT, n_sub=N_SUB, n_rec=T_POINTS):
    def em_step(state, inp):
        (x, v), (k, tn) = state, inp
        eta = jax.random.normal(k, x.shape)
        return (x + v * dt, v + (-omega**2 * x - gamma * v + F_DRIVE * jnp.cos(Omega * tn)) * dt + jnp.sqrt(2 * D * dt) * eta), None
    def record(state, inp):
        k, n0 = inp
        state, _ = jax.lax.scan(em_step, state, (jax.random.split(k, n_sub), (n0 + jnp.arange(n_sub)) * dt))
        return state, state[0]
    _, xs = jax.lax.scan(record, (x0, v0), (jax.random.split(key, n_rec - 1), n_sub * jnp.arange(n_rec - 1)))
    return jnp.concatenate([x0[None], xs]).T

def make_driven(n, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    om, ga = rng.uniform(*OMEGA_RANGE, n), np.exp(rng.uniform(*np.log(GAMMA_RANGE), n))
    Om, x0, v0 = rng.uniform(0.5, 2.5, n), rng.uniform(*X0_RANGE, n), rng.uniform(-V0_MAX, V0_MAX, n)
    X = simulate_driven(*(jnp.asarray(a, jnp.float32) for a in (om, ga, Om, x0, v0)), jax.random.key(seed))
    return np.asarray(X, np.float32), np.stack([om, np.log(ga), Om, x0, v0], 1)

Xtr_dr, _ = make_driven(20_000, 41)
Xte_dr, Pte_dr = make_driven(5_000, 42)
vae_dr, _ = train(lambda s: TrajVAE(T_POINTS, D_LATENT, rngs=nnx.Rngs(s)), partial(beta_vae_loss, beta=4), (Xtr_dr,), 60, 0,
                  name="lab028_ex_driven_beta4")
mu_dr, lv_dr, _, _ = evaluate(vae_dr, Xte_dr)
kl_dr = np.asarray(kl_per_dim(mu_dr, lv_dr)).mean(0); act_dr = np.flatnonzero(kl_dr > ACTIVE_NATS)
print("active coordinates:", len(act_dr))
print("|rho| (rows: active coordinates; columns: omega, ln gamma, Omega, x0, v0)")
print(np.round(abs_corr(mu_dr, Pte_dr)[act_dr], 2))


active coordinates: 6
|rho| (rows: active coordinates; columns: omega, ln gamma, Omega, x0, v0)
[[0.12 0.02 0.26 0.2  0.3 ]
 [0.21 0.58 0.1  0.18 0.12]
 [0.13 0.04 0.04 0.65 0.17]
 [0.57 0.55 0.25 0.13 0.16]
 [0.3  0.13 0.27 0.33 0.3 ]
 [0.2  0.35 0.5  0.16 0.15]]


The driven model has six active coordinates. The driving frequency is found only partially, since its best coordinate reaches \(|\rho|=0.50\) with \(\Omega\) and also 0.35 with \(\ln\gamma\). The initial position is again the cleanest factor of this model (0.65 in one coordinate), the damping reaches 0.58, and \(\omega\) is shared with \(\ln\gamma\) (0.57 and 0.55 in the same coordinate). With \(F=0.5\) the driving force adds a response of amplitude \(F/\sqrt{(\omega^2-\Omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\Omega^2}\) that depends on all three of \(\omega\), \(\gamma\) and \(\Omega\), and within six time units the driven oscillation is still mixed with the transient. As a result \(\Omega\) is only moderately visible and is confused with the other two frequencies.



Exercise 5 (open). Hopping in a double well
Replace the spring by the double-well potential \(V(x)=a(x^2-1)^2\), i.e. \(\ddot x=-V'(x)-\gamma\dot x+\sqrt{2D}\,\eta\), and vary the barrier height \(a\) and the temperature \(k_BT=D/\gamma\) between trajectories, with a time window long enough to see several jumps between the wells. The mean time between jumps follows Kramers’ law, \(\tau\propto e^{a/k_BT}\) [Kramers 1940; Hänggi, Talkner and Borkovec 1990]. Train a \(\beta\)-VAE on the trajectories and test whether a latent coordinate follows \(\ln\tau\), i.e. the combination \(a/k_BT\), or \(a\) and \(T\) separately. The time of the first jump is random and differs between trajectories with the same parameters, so the encoder must summarise statistics of the trajectory instead of its shape, and a summary input such as the histogram of \(x\) or the sequence of well occupations may work better than the raw positions.


Exercise 6 (open). Long training with noise and nuisance factors
Section 5.4 trains SciNet for 1000 epochs only in the noise-free setting of the paper. Train it for 1000 epochs also on the data with noise and on the data with noise and random initial conditions (five latent neurons). Check whether it then stores \(\kappa\), \(b\), \(x_0\) and \(v_0\) in separate neurons, compare with the \(\beta\)-VAE, and explain the result through the cost, by identifying the parameters that improve the answers to the questions \(t\in[0,10]\) the most.

title: Lab 033: Signal characterisation
text:
1. Signals and protocol
The generators below are shared by all time-series notebooks, so that every model is trained and tested on the same numbers. They integrate the equations with the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method (RK4) in jax.lax.scan and return \(N=4000\) samples per signal. The last lines define the common protocol of the forecasting labs, a chronological split into a training block of 3000 samples, whose last 500 serve for validation, and a test block of the final 1000 samples, with rescaling to \([0,1]\) fitted on the first 2500 samples, the part of the training block on which models are fitted.


Code
# Lorenz-63 with sigma = 10, rho = 28, beta = 8/3. RK4 with h = 0.01, one sample every 2 steps (dt = 0.02).
# Initial state (1, 1, 1); the first 2500 samples (50 time units) are discarded. We keep the x component.
def lorenz_rhs(u, sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0/3.0):
    x, y, z = u
    return jnp.array([sigma*(y - x), x*(rho - z) - y, x*y - beta*z])

def rk4_step(f, u, h):
    k1 = f(u); k2 = f(u + 0.5*h*k1); k3 = f(u + 0.5*h*k2); k4 = f(u + h*k3)
    return u + h/6.0*(k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=(0, 1, 2))
def lorenz_trajectory(n_samples, sub=2, n_discard=2500, h=0.01):
    """Returns array (n_samples, 3) sampled every `sub` RK4 steps (dt = sub*h)."""
    def one_sample(u, _):
        u = jax.lax.fori_loop(0, sub, lambda i, v: rk4_step(lorenz_rhs, v, h), u)
        return u, u
    u0 = jnp.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
    u, _ = jax.lax.scan(one_sample, u0, None, length=n_discard)
    _, traj = jax.lax.scan(one_sample, u, None, length=n_samples)
    return traj

# Mackey-Glass dx/dt = beta x(t-tau)/(1 + x(t-tau)^n) - gamma x with beta = 0.2, gamma = 0.1, n = 10.
# RK4 with h = 0.1; the delayed value at the half step is the linear interpolation of the two stored values.
# Constant history x = 1.2 on [-tau, 0]; the first 3000 fine steps are discarded and every 10th point is kept
# (unit sampling).
def mackey_glass(tau, n_samples, h=0.1, x0=1.2, transient=3000, every=10,
                 beta=0.2, gamma=0.1, n=10):
    lag = int(round(tau / h))
    f = lambda x, xd: beta * xd / (1.0 + xd**n) - gamma * x
    def step(buf, _):
        # buf = (x[i-lag], ..., x[i]) is the delay window, length lag+1
        x, xd0, xd1 = buf[-1], buf[0], buf[1]
        xdh = 0.5 * (xd0 + xd1)
        k1 = f(x, xd0); k2 = f(x + 0.5*h*k1, xdh); k3 = f(x + 0.5*h*k2, xdh); k4 = f(x + h*k3, xd1)
        xn = x + h/6.0*(k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)
        return jnp.concatenate([buf[1:], xn[None]]), xn
    n_steps = transient + n_samples * every
    _, xs = jax.lax.scan(step, jnp.full(lag + 1, x0), None, length=n_steps)
    x = np.concatenate([np.full(lag + 1, x0), np.asarray(xs)])
    return x[transient::every][:n_samples]

def santafe(path="data/santafe_laser.txt"):
    return np.loadtxt(path).astype(float)

# Common protocol of the lecture: N = 4000 samples per signal; training block = first 3000 samples
# (its last 500 = validation), test block = last 1000; rescaling to [0, 1] with the min/max of the first 2500 samples.
N_SAMPLES, N_TRAIN, N_VAL, TAU_MAX = 4000, 3000, 500, 50
def rescale01(s, n_train=N_TRAIN - N_VAL):
    lo, hi = s[:n_train].min(), s[:n_train].max()
    return (s - lo) / (hi - lo)




Code
lor_states = np.asarray(lorenz_trajectory(N_SAMPLES))          # (4000, 3): x, y, z of Lorenz-63
sf_full = santafe()                                              # all measured samples of data set A
S = {"lorenz": lor_states[:, 0],
     "mg15": mackey_glass(15, N_SAMPLES), "mg25": mackey_glass(25, N_SAMPLES), "mg35": mackey_glass(35, N_SAMPLES),
     "santafe": sf_full[:N_SAMPLES]}
DT = {"lorenz": 0.02, "mg15": 1.0, "mg25": 1.0, "mg35": 1.0, "santafe": 1.0}   # sampling interval (time units)
UNIT = {"lorenz": "time unit", "mg15": "time unit", "mg25": "time unit", "mg35": "time unit", "santafe": "sample"}
for k in KEYS:
    assert S[k].shape == (N_SAMPLES,) and np.all(np.isfinite(S[k]))
    print(f"{LABEL[k]:22s} N = {len(S[k])}  mean = {S[k].mean():8.4f}  std = {S[k].std():8.4f}  "
          f"min = {S[k].min():8.4f}  max = {S[k].max():8.4f}")
print("Santa Fe record length:", len(sf_full))
