Exercise 1.4. Autoregressive model and Koopman eigenvalues
A single sine wave obeys an exact linear recursion. From \(\sin(\omega(n+1))+\sin(\omega(n-1))=2\cos\omega\,\sin(\omega n)\), \[
s_{n+1}=2\cos\omega\;s_n-s_{n-1},
\] an AR(2) model without noise whose characteristic roots are \(e^{\pm i\omega}\). A sum of \(K\) sine waves with distinct frequencies obeys the AR(\(2K\)) recursion whose characteristic polynomial is the product of the \(K\) factors \(1-2\cos\omega_i\,z+z^2\). In the language of Lab 035, each wave is spanned by a pair of Koopman eigenfunctions with eigenvalues \(e^{\pm i\omega_i}\), the delay vector of length \(2K\) is a dictionary that is invariant under the dynamics, and the AR coefficients form the last row of its companion matrix.

Compute the eigenvalues of the companion matrix (Lab 035), plot them in the complex plane with the unit circle, and compare their moduli and angles with \(1\) and \(\omega_i\).

title: Exercise 01: Rössler system and superimposed oscillators
text:
2. Rössler system
Rössler looked for the simplest autonomous flow with chaotic motion and found a system with three variables and a single nonlinear term [O. E. Rössler, Phys. Lett. A 57, 397 (1976), doi:10.1016/0375-9601(76)90101-8], \[
\dot x=-y-z,\qquad \dot y=x+a\,y,\qquad \dot z=b+z\,(x-c).
\] The linear part in the \((x,y)\) plane is an oscillator with negative damping for \(a>0\), so trajectories near the plane spiral outwards. The variable \(z\) stays small until \(x\) exceeds \(c\). Then the product \(zx\) makes \(z\) grow quickly, and the term \(-z\) in \(\dot x\) throws the trajectory back towards the centre of the spiral, where the outward motion starts again. The stretching happens on the spiral and the folding in the excursion in \(z\), the same two ingredients as in the logistic map of Lab 033. We use the standard parameters \(a=0.2\), \(b=0.2\), \(c=5.7\), which are the defaults of ReservoirPy, and we observe only \(x(t)\).

Exercise 2.1. Equations, fixed points and the generated signal
Read the source of reservoirpy.datasets.rossler (for example with inspect.getsource). State its default parameters, initial state, sampling step h and the integrator it calls. Check how the output times are constructed from n_timesteps and h, and find the value of h that gives a sampling interval of exactly \(\Delta t=0.1\). Generate the trajectory with this sampling interval and tolerances rtol = atol = 1e-10 passed to the integrator, discard the first 500 time units as a transient, and keep \(N=4000\) samples. Plot the attractor in \((x,y,z)\) and \(x(t)\).
Find the fixed points of the flow analytically, check \(\mathbf F(\mathbf u^*)=0\) numerically, and compute the eigenvalues of the Jacobian \(J=\partial\mathbf F/\partial\mathbf u\) with jax.jacfwd (as for Lorenz-63 in Lab 033). From the complex pair at the fixed point near the origin derive the rotation frequency of the spiral in cycles per time unit. Finally write the right-hand side in JAX, integrate it with RK4 at step \(h=0.01\) from the first stored state, and compare with the ReservoirPy trajectory over the first 20 time units.

Estimate the PSD (power spectral density) with the Hann-windowed periodogram of the whole record and with Welch segments of \(L=1024\) samples (Lab 033), and plot both. 3. Forecasts
We forecast both signals with the protocol of Lab 036. The fitting origins are \(k=63,\dots,2449\), the validation origins \(k=2499,\dots,2949\) and the test origins \(k=2999,\dots,3949\), and every model returns the leads \(\tau=1,\dots,50\) at once, one output per lead. The forecast from the origin \(k\) uses only the values \(s_0,\dots,s_k\), and the input window is at most the last \(L=64\) of them, \((s_{k-63},\dots,s_k)\). The targets \(s_{k+1},\dots,s_{k+50}\) of the fitting origins end at sample 2499, before the validation block, and those of the validation origins end at sample 2999, before the test block, so no input window or target used for fitting or for a choice reaches the test block. The first code cell checks these conditions.
Persistence, AR and NVAR read the window and nothing else. Persistence repeats the last value, and AR and NVAR are ridge regressions of the 50 targets on the delay vector \((s_k,\dots,s_{k-p+1})\) and on the delay vector with its quadratic monomials. The NVAR features are fixed, and only the linear readout is fitted. The MA model forecasts from its last \(q=8\) one-step prediction errors \(e_k,\dots,e_{k-7}\), which the fitted filter computes from all values up to the origin. The RNN and the LSTM network start from a zero hidden state at the oldest value of the window and carry their state through the 64 values, so they are also functions of the window. All their weights, the recurrence and the linear readout of the last hidden state, are learned by gradient descent. The optional ESN keeps a state driven by the signal from the first sample, with a fixed random recurrence and a ridge readout. For the MSO signal, persistence and the direct AR model were computed in Exercise 1.5.
The capacity \(C(\tau)=r(\tau)^2\) is biased upwards on a finite test block. For \(n\) test origins and a forecast unrelated to the targets, \(r(\tau)\) scatters around zero with variance close to \(1/(n-1)\), so \(C(\tau)\approx1/(n-1)=0.0011\) for \(n=951\) and \(C_{\rm tot}\approx0.05\). A total of this size means no skill.

Exercise 3.1. Persistence, AR and NVAR
Compute persistence, the direct AR model and the direct NVAR model for Rössler \(x\) with ridge_model of Lab 036 (order and ridge strength chosen by the validation \(C_{\rm tot}\)), and the direct NVAR model for the MSO signal. Rebuild the selected Rössler NVAR model with ReservoirPy, NVAR(delay=p, order=2, strides=1) >> Ridge(ridge=beta), fitted on the same origins with warmup=63 as in Lab 034, and check that its test predictions agree with the JAX model.

Exercise 3.2. Moving-average model
The MA(\(q\)) model writes the signal as its mean plus a weighted sum of the present and the last \(q\) innovations, \(s_k=\mu+\varepsilon_k+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\theta_j\varepsilon_{k-j}\). Fit MA(8) to the first 3000 samples of each signal, the fitting and validation blocks (no setting of this model is chosen on the validation block), by maximum likelihood with statsmodels, ARIMA(order=(0, 0, 8), trend="c"), as in Lab 036. \hat s_{k+\tau}=\mu+\sum_{j=\tau}^{q}\theta_j\,e_{k+\tau-j},
\] which uses only errors up to the origin \(k\). The filter in apply runs forward in time, so \(e_k\) depends on \(s_0,\dots,s_k\) only. For \(\tau>q\) the forecast is the fitted mean \(\mu\), a reference level computed over the first 3000 samples. Report \(\mu\), the coefficients \(\theta_j\), the smallest modulus of the roots of the MA polynomial \(1+\sum_j\theta_jz^j\), \(C(1)\), \(C(8)\) and \(C_{\rm tot}\), and explain the value of \(C(\tau)\) for \(\tau>8\).

Exercise 3.3. Recurrent networks
Train an RNN and an LSTM network in flax.nnx as in Lab 036. The RNN updates its hidden state \(\mathbf h_k\in\mathbb R^{n_h}\) by \(\mathbf h_k=\tanh(W_h\mathbf h_{k-1}+W_xs_k+\mathbf b)\). The LSTM adds a cell state \(\mathbf c_k\) controlled by three gates, with the sigmoid \(\sigma(a)=1/(1+e^{-a})\), the elementwise product \(\odot\) and the concatenation \([\mathbf h_{k-1},s_k]\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf f_k&=\sigma\big(W_f[\mathbf h_{k-1},s_k]+\mathbf b_f\big), &
\mathbf i_k&=\sigma\big(W_i[\mathbf h_{k-1},s_k]+\mathbf b_i\big),\\
\mathbf g_k&=\tanh\big(W_g[\mathbf h_{k-1},s_k]+\mathbf b_g\big), &
\mathbf o_k&=\sigma\big(W_o[\mathbf h_{k-1},s_k]+\mathbf b_o\big),\\
\mathbf c_k&=\mathbf f_k\odot\mathbf c_{k-1}+\mathbf i_k\odot\mathbf g_k, &
\mathbf h_k&=\mathbf o_k\odot\tanh(\mathbf c_k),
\end{aligned}
\] the forget gate \(\mathbf f_k\), the input gate \(\mathbf i_k\), the candidate \(\mathbf g_k\) and the output gate \(\mathbf o_k\), with the initial forget bias \(\mathbf b_f=1\). Both networks have \(n_h=32\) hidden units, run over the window of \(L=64\) values with jax.lax.scan from \(\mathbf h=0\), and read the 50 leads from the last hidden state with a linear layer. title: Exercise 02: Stock market returns
text:
1. Prices and returns
The file contains one closing level \(P_k\) per trading day \(k\). Prices grow multiplicatively, a move of one percent means the same at any level, so the natural variable is the logarithm. The daily log-return is \[
r_k=\ln\frac{P_k}{P_{k-1}}=\ln P_k-\ln P_{k-1},
\] which for small moves is close to the relative change \((P_k-P_{k-1})/P_{k-1}\). The analysis window of this exercise is the last 5000 returns of the record, about the last fifth of it. Section 4 splits the window in time order into a fitting block, its first 3000 returns, a validation block and a test block of 1000 returns each. Every statistic of Sections 1 to 3 is computed on data up to the end of the fitting block, the fitting block of the window or the record up to its end, so that the validation and test blocks do not influence the choice of the forecast variable, of the scaling or of the models. The figures of the whole record are shown for orientation only.
Exercise 2.1. Load the closing levels, compute the log-returns of the whole record and keep the last 5000 of them as the analysis window. Print the number of trading days, and for the record up to the end of the fitting block and for the fitting block of the window the mean and standard deviation of the returns, their extreme values and the number of days with zero return. Plot the price on a logarithmic axis, the returns of the whole record and the returns of the window.


Code
# Exercise 2.1: np.loadtxt, np.log, np.diff; keep r = r_all[-5000:] and the 5001 log-prices behind it.
# Plot P_k with semilogy and mark the analysis window with axvspan.
...



Random walk and differencing
A random walk with drift is the simplest model of the log-price, \[
\ln P_k=\ln P_{k-1}+\mu+\sigma\eta_k,\qquad \eta_k\ \text{independent}\ \mathcal N(0,1),
\] with drift \(\mu\) and daily volatility \(\sigma\). It is the autoregressive model AR(1) \(\ln P_k=c+\phi\ln P_{k-1}+\varepsilon_k\) at \(\phi=1\), a unit root of the characteristic polynomial \(\Phi_1(z)=1-\phi z\) (Lab 034), and in the notation of the autoregressive integrated moving-average models it is ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift. One difference, \((1-B)\ln P_k=r_k=\mu+\sigma\eta_k\), turns it into white noise with mean \(\mu\). A model of this kind has no stationary mean, and its variance grows linearly in time. Forecasting the level then rewards persistence, \(\widehat{\ln P}_{k+1}=\ln P_k\), without saying anything about the dynamics.
Exercise 2.2. Fit AR(1) with a constant to the 3001 log-prices of the fitting block by least squares in JAX and with statsmodels AutoReg, and report \(\hat\phi\) with its standard error. Simulate three random walks with the drift and volatility of the fitting block, starting at the same log-price, and plot them together with the data. Compute the squared correlation \(C(1)\) of persistence for the log-price and for the returns over the last 1000 days of the fitting block.


Code
# Exercise 2.2: the AR(1) least-squares fit as in the AR section of Lab 034 (design matrix rows (1, ln P_{k-1})).
# Random walk: lp[0] + cumsum(mu + sigma * eta) with eta from jax.random.normal.
...




Stationarity
A process is stationary when its mean and autocovariance do not depend on the origin of time (Lab 033). A quick check slides a window of \(W=250\) trading days, about one trading year, over the record and computes the rolling mean \(\bar r^{(250)}_k\) and the rolling standard deviation \(\sigma^{(250)}_k\) of the returns \(r_{k-249},\dots,r_k\).
A formal test of the unit root is the augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test [D. A. Dickey and W. A. Fuller, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 74, 427 (1979), doi:10.1080/01621459.1979.10482531; S. E. Said and D. A. Dickey, Biometrika 71, 599 (1984), doi:10.1093/biomet/71.3.599]. It fits by least squares the regression \[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_k&=\alpha+\beta\,y_{k-1}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\gamma_i\,\Delta y_{k-i}+\varepsilon_k,\\
\Delta y_k&=y_k-y_{k-1},
\end{aligned}
\] where the lagged differences absorb short-range correlations of \(\Delta y\). A unit root means \(\beta=0\), and a stationary AR process has \(\beta<0\). The null hypothesis is the unit root, \(H_0:\beta=0\), against \(\beta<0\). The test statistic is the \(t\)-ratio \(\hat\beta/{\rm se}(\hat\beta)\). Under \(H_0\) it does not follow the Student distribution, and its critical values come from the Dickey–Fuller distribution, which statsmodels.tsa.stattools.adfuller tabulates and returns with a \(p\)-value. A strongly negative statistic rejects the unit root. Option regression="ct" adds a linear trend \(\delta k\) to the regression, and autolag="AIC" chooses \(p\) by the Akaike information criterion.
Exercise 2.3. title: Exercise 02: Stock market returns
text:
2. Distribution, correlations and spectra

Heavy tails
We standardise the returns of the fitting block, \(x_k=(r_k-\bar r)/\sigma_r\), with their mean \(\bar r\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_r\). A Gaussian variable has skewness \(\langle x^3\rangle=0\) and excess kurtosis \(\kappa=\langle x^4\rangle-3=0\). A positive \(\kappa\) means more probability in the tails and in the centre than a Gaussian of the same variance. The Student \(t\) distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom has power-law tails, \(p(x)\propto|x|^{-(\nu+1)}\) for large \(|x|\), and it is a common one-parameter model of heavy tails [R. Cont, Quant. Finance 1, 223 (2001), doi:10.1080/713665670].
Exercise 2.4. Compute the skewness and the excess kurtosis of the fitting block in JAX and compare with scipy.stats. Fit a Student \(t\) distribution with scipy.stats.t.fit. For \(a=3,4,5,6\) compare the fraction of days with \(|x_k|>a\) with the Gaussian value \(2\,\Phi(-a)\), \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function, and with the fitted \(t\) distribution. Plot the histogram on a logarithmic axis and the tail probability \(P(|x_k|>a)\) against \(a\).

# scipy.stats.t.fit(x) returns (nu, loc, scale); Gaussian tail 2 * scipy.stats.norm.sf(a).
...




Autocorrelation of returns and of their size
The autocorrelation function (ACF) is estimated as in Lab 033, \[
\hat\rho(k)=\frac{\sum_{n=0}^{N-1-k}(x_n-\bar x)(x_{n+k}-\bar x)}{\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(x_n-\bar x)^2},
\] with \(\bar x\) the mean of the \(N\) values. The sum of \(N-k\) products is divided by the sum of all \(N\) squares, which is the convention of statsmodels with adjusted=False. For \(N\) independent samples the estimates at \(k\ge1\) scatter around zero with standard deviation close to \(1/\sqrt N\), so about 95% of them lie in the band \(\pm1.96/\sqrt N\). The ACF of \(r_k\) measures linear predictability of the returns. The ACF of \(|r_k|\) and of \(r_k^2\) measures whether large moves follow large moves, whatever their sign, which is called volatility clustering.
Exercise 2.5. Compute \(\hat\rho(k)\) for \(k=0,\dots,200\) of \(r_k\), \(|r_k|\) and \(r_k^2\) of the fitting block with the JAX function of Lab 033 and check it against statsmodels. Report the values at a few lags and the number of lags in \(1,\dots,200\) outside the 95% band. Plot the ACF of \(r_k\) at small lags and the three ACFs up to lag 200.

Power spectra
By the Wiener–Khinchin theorem (Lab 033) an ACF that vanishes at all \(k\ge1\) corresponds to a flat power spectral density (PSD). For a white noise of unit variance and unit sampling interval the one-sided PSD is \(S(f)=2\) at every frequency. A slowly decaying ACF puts excess power at low frequencies.

3. Tests for deterministic structure
The chaotic signals of Lab 033 have a delay embedding of low dimension, they reject a linear Gaussian null model in a surrogate test, and their nearby trajectories separate exponentially at a rate \(\lambda_1\), the largest Lyapunov exponent. We now run the same diagnostics on the returns. Two reference signals help to read the results, the Lorenz \(x\) signal of Lab 033 (4000 samples, \(\Delta t=0.02\)), whose answers we know, and the returns in random order, which keep the distribution and destroy every time dependence.
Exercise 2.7. Copy from Lab 033 the Lorenz-63 generator, the delay embedding, the nearest-neighbour search, the mutual information \(I(\ell)\) and the false-nearest-neighbour (FNN) fractions of the ratio test. Generate the Lorenz \(x\) reference and a random permutation of the standardised returns of the fitting block. All diagnostics of this section use the 3000 returns of the fitting block.

Delay and embedding dimension
Lab 033 chose the delay \(\ell\) at the first minimum of \(I(\ell)\) and the dimension \(m\) at the point where the FNN fraction drops below 5%. The histogram estimate of \(I(\ell)\) uses 16 bins of equal width over the range of the data. With heavy tails almost all returns fall into the two or three central bins. The mutual information is invariant under a monotone change of variables, so we also compute it from the ranks \(u_k={\rm rank}(x_k)/N\), which have a uniform distribution.
Exercise 2.8. Compute \(I(\ell)\) for \(\ell=0,\dots,50\) of the returns with equal bins and with ranks, of the shuffled returns (ranks) and of Lorenz \(x\), and report \(I(1)\), \(I(10)\), the mean over \(\ell=20,\dots,50\) and the first local minimum. Compute the FNN fractions for \(m=1,\dots,10\) of the returns and of the shuffled returns with \(\ell=1\) and of Lorenz \(x\) with \(\ell=10\), and plot both diagnostics.

# Exercise 2.8: ranks with scipy.stats.rankdata(x) / N; fnn_fractions(x, lag) as in Lab 033 with Theiler window 50.

Lyapunov exponent and Kaplan–Yorke dimension
The Rosenstein estimate of \(\lambda_1\) follows the mean logarithmic distance \(\langle\ln d(k)\rangle\) of initially nearest neighbours \(k\) steps later and reads \(\lambda_1\) from the slope of a straight part of this curve (Lab 033). The Sano–Sawada estimate fits local Jacobians to the neighbourhoods of the delay vectors and returns a whole spectrum \(\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_m\), from which the Kaplan–Yorke dimension \(D_{\rm KY}=j+\Sigma_j/|\lambda_{j+1}|\) follows, \(\Sigma_j=\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_j\) and \(j\) the largest index with \(\Sigma_j\ge0\). Both algorithms return numbers for any input. Whether the numbers mean anything depends on the assumptions behind them, a deterministic low-dimensional flow sampled densely enough that nearby delay vectors evolve similarly.
Exercise 2.9. Compute the Rosenstein curve of the returns and of the shuffled returns (\(m=4\), \(\ell=1\), Theiler window 50, \(k\le50\)) and of Lorenz \(x\) (\(m=4\), \(\ell=10\), \(k\le150\)). Surrogate test (optional)
This exercise is optional, and no later exercise uses its results. The null hypothesis of the surrogate test of Lab 033 (Appendix A) is a stationary linear Gaussian process observed through a static monotone function. Iterative amplitude-adjusted Fourier-transform (IAAFT) surrogates realise it with the exact value distribution and nearly the same spectrum [T. Schreiber and A. Schmitz, Phys. Rev. Lett. 77, 635 (1996), doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.635]. The first statistic is the normalised error \(E={\rm rms}(s_{n+1}-s_{j+1})/\sigma_s\) of the nearest-neighbour forecast in the delay space, with \(\mathbf y_j\) the nearest neighbour of \(\mathbf y_n\) outside the Theiler window, and a one-sided test that rejects \(H_0\) when the data error is the smallest of 20 values (19 surrogates). A second statistic targets volatility clustering, \[
A=\sum_{k=1}^{20}\hat\rho_{|x|}(k),
\] the sum of the first 20 ACF values of \(|x_k|\), with \(H_0\) rejected when the data value is the largest of the 20.

title: Exercise 02: Stock market returns
text:
4. Forecasting the returns
We adapt the protocol of Labs 034 and 036 to the window of 5000 returns. The split is chronological, 60/20/20. The first 3000 returns form the fitting (training) block, the next 1000 the validation block and the last 1000 the test block. The returns are standardised, \(s_k=(r_k-\mu_{\rm tr})/\sigma_{\rm tr}\), with the mean and standard deviation of the fitting block. The labs rescale to \([0,1]\) with the minimum and maximum instead, which for heavy-tailed data would squeeze almost all values into a narrow band set by a few extreme days. Every model reads at most the window \(\mathbf v_k=(s_{k-63},\dots,s_k)\) of \(L=64\) values and returns the leads \(\tau=1,\dots,50\) directly. The fitting origins are \(k=63,\dots,2949\), the validation origins \(k=2999,\dots,3949\) and the test origins \(k=3999,\dots,4949\). The forecast from the origin \(k\) uses only values up to \(s_k\), the targets of the fitting origins end at return 2999, before the validation block, and those of the validation origins end at return 3999, before the test block, so no input window or target used for fitting or for a choice reaches the test block.
Persistence and the mean of the fitting block are the baselines. AR and NVAR are ridge regressions on the window, with fixed features and a fitted linear readout. MA forecasts from its last eight one-step errors, which its filter computes from all values up to the origin. The RNN and the LSTM network start from a zero hidden state at the oldest value of the window, and all their weights, recurrence and readout, are learned by gradient descent. The mean baseline is a reference level computed over a fixed period, the fitting block. Its NMSE on the test block is \(1+(\bar s_{\rm fit}-\bar s_{\rm test})^2/\sigma^2_{\rm test}\) and exceeds 1 whenever the mean of the test block differs from that of the fitting block.
The scores are those of Lab 034, \(\mathrm{NMSE}(\tau)\), the capacity \(C(\tau)=r(\tau)^2\) and \(C_{\rm tot}=\sum_{\tau=1}^{50}C(\tau)\). For returns the sign of the move matters to a trader, so we add the directional accuracy \[
\mathrm{DA}(\tau)=\frac1n\sum_{k}\mathbb 1\big[(\hat r_{k+\tau}>0)=(r_{k+\tau}>0)\big],
\] the fraction of the \(n\) test origins at which the forecast and the true return agree on up or down. If the \(n\) hits were independent with probability \(q\), their number would be binomial and DA would have the standard error \(\sqrt{q(1-q)/n}\), which for \(n=951\) is about 0.016. A forecast that always says up reaches the fraction of up days, which is above 0.5 for a rising index, so this fraction is the baseline for DA.
Exercise 2.11. Set up the standardised returns, the origins and the windows. Copy the score function of Lab 034 and add the directional accuracy with its standard error, computed on the raw returns \(r=\mu_{\rm tr}+\sigma_{\rm tr}s\). Score persistence, \(\hat s_{k+\tau}=s_k\), and the mean of the fitting block. Report the fraction of up days among the test targets.

AR and NVAR
The direct autoregressive (AR) model and the nonlinear vector autoregression (NVAR) are ridge regressions on the delay vector \((s_k,\dots,s_{k-p+1})\) and on the delay vector together with its quadratic monomials (Lab 034, Lab 036). In the labs the order \(p\) and the ridge strength \(\beta\) were chosen by the largest validation \(C_{\rm tot}\). On a signal without structure this choice rewards chance correlations, because \(C\) ignores the sign and the scale of the forecast. Here we choose \((p,\beta)\) by the smallest validation NMSE averaged over the 50 leads, from \(p\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64\}\) for AR, \(p\in\{2,4,8,12,16\}\) for NVAR and \(\beta\in\{10^{-4},10^{-2},1,10^{2},10^{4}\}\).

Fit the direct AR and NVAR models with the selection above and report \(p\), \(\beta\), \(C_{\rm tot}\), \(C(1)\), \(\mathrm{NMSE}(1)\) and \(\mathrm{DA}(1)\) on the test block.

Moving-average model
The moving-average model MA(\(q\)) writes the signal as its mean plus a weighted sum of the present and the last \(q\) innovations, \(s_k=\mu+\varepsilon_k+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\theta_j\varepsilon_{k-j}\) (Lab 034). Its autocorrelation vanishes beyond lag \(q\), so it describes a short memory of the shocks. We fit MA(8) by maximum likelihood with statsmodels, ARIMA(order=(0, 0, 8), trend="c"), on the first 4000 standardised returns, as Lab 036 fits it on its training and validation blocks. No setting of this model is chosen on the validation block, and the test block is not used. The one-step prediction errors \(e_k=s_k-\hat s_k\) of the fitted model, computed over the whole record with apply, give the forecast \[
\hat s_{k+\tau}=\mu+\sum_{j=\tau}^{q}\theta_j\,e_{k+\tau-j},
\] which uses only errors up to the origin \(k\) and equals the mean \(\mu\) for \(\tau>q\).
Exercise 2.13. Fit MA(8) to the standardised returns, report \(\mu\), the coefficients \(\theta_j\) with their standard errors, and compare the forecast from the first test origin with the forecast method of statsmodels. Report \(C_{\rm tot}\), \(C(1)\), \(\mathrm{NMSE}(1)\) and \(\mathrm{DA}(1)\) on the test block.

# forecast as in the static-model comparison of Lab 036; fit.apply(s[:k + 1]).forecast(50) for the check.
...




Recurrent networks
The recurrent neural network (RNN) updates a hidden state \(\mathbf h_k\in\mathbb R^{n_h}\) by \(\mathbf h_k=\tanh(W_h\mathbf h_{k-1}+W_xs_k+\mathbf b)\), and the long short-term memory (LSTM) network adds a cell state controlled by forget, input and output gates (Lab 036). We use the cells of Lab 036 with \(n_h=32\) hidden units, run over the window from \(\mathbf h=0\), a linear readout of the last hidden state to the 50 leads, and the training loop with Adam (learning rate \(5\times10^{-3}\), minibatches of 128 windows), gradient clipping at norm 1 and early stopping on the validation loss with patience 20 and at most 250 epochs. The hidden state is reset to zero for every window, so the networks are functions of the 64 values of the window, and all weights, recurrence and readout, are learned. A claim about a network must hold for more than one random initialisation, so both networks are trained with the seeds 0, 1 and 2.
Exercise 2.14. Train the RNN and the LSTM network on the returns for the three seeds and report the number of epochs, the test \(C_{\rm tot}\), \(\mathrm{NMSE}(1)\) and \(\mathrm{DA}(1)\) for each seed. Use seed 0 in the comparison table.

Significance
A model that is independent of the targets still produces a nonzero \(C(\tau)\) on a finite test block. For \(n\) independent pairs the expected squared correlation is close to \(1/(n-1)\), so \(C_{\rm tot}\approx50/(n-1)\approx0.05\) without any skill. A permutation test makes this concrete for each model. We randomly reorder the forecast origins, which destroys the pairing of forecasts and targets and keeps both distributions, recompute \(C_{\rm tot}\) 500 times and read off the 95th percentile. A model whose test \(C_{\rm tot}\) lies below this value shows no evidence of skill at the 5% level. The permutation also destroys the serial correlation of the forecasts, which for the returns is weak.
Exercise 2.15. Collect for all models the test \(C_{\rm tot}\) with the 95th percentile of its permutation null, \(C(1)\), \(\mathrm{NMSE}(1)\) and \(\mathrm{DA}(1)\) with its standard error and its difference from the fraction of up days. 5. Forecasting the volatility
The ACF of \(|r_k|\) in Exercise 2.5 shows that the size of tomorrow’s move depends on the sizes of the past moves. Econometrics models this conditional variance with the autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH) model [R. F. Engle, Econometrica 50, 987 (1982), doi:10.2307/1912773] and its generalisation GARCH [T. Bollerslev, J. title: Exercise 03: Koopman operator
section: 1. Closed dictionaries of a lifted map
text:
1. Closed dictionaries of a lifted map
The map \[
x_{k+1}=a\,x_k,\qquad y_{k+1}=b\,y_k+c\,x_k^2
\] with real parameters \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) becomes linear on the three observables \((x,y,x^2)\), with the matrix \[
K_3=\begin{pmatrix}a&0&0\\0&b&c\\0&0&a^2\end{pmatrix}
\] and the eigenfunctions \(\xi_a=x\), \(\xi_{a^2}=x^2\) and \(\xi_b=y+\kappa x^2\) with \(\kappa=c/(b-a^2)\). Adding the single observable \(y^2\) to this dictionary leaves a closure error in the new component, since \(y^2\) at the next step contains terms outside the span. We use \(a=0.9\), \(b=0.5\) and \(c=1\) for all numerical checks.

Exercise 1.1. A closed dictionary that contains \(y^2\)
Compute the images of \(y^2\), \(x^2y\) and \(x^4\) under one step of the map and show that the six observables \(\mathbf g=(x,\,y,\,x^2,\,y^2,\,x^2y,\,x^4)\) span an invariant subspace. Write the \(6\times6\) matrix \(K_6\) with \(\mathbf g(\mathbf x_{k+1})=K_6\,\mathbf g(\mathbf x_k)\) and check \(\mathbf g\circ\varphi-K_6\mathbf g=0\) with sympy. Find the eigenvalues of \(K_6\) and express them through \(a\) and \(b\). Show that \(\xi_b^2\) and \(x^2\xi_b\) are eigenfunctions and identify their eigenvalues.
Then verify the closure numerically. Fit EDMD with \(\beta=0\) on 500 states drawn uniformly from \([-1,1]^2\) for the dictionaries \((x,y,x^2,y^2)\) and \(\mathbf g\), and compute the root-mean-square (RMS) closure error of every component on 2000 fresh states. Compare the fitted matrix with \(K_6\), and compare the 50-step forecast of \(y^2\) by the matrix power \(K_6^n\) with direct iteration of the map from 200 random states.

# for (x, y, x^2, y^2) and the six-function dictionary; 50-step forecast of y^2




Exercise 1.2. Which polynomial dictionaries close
Show that one step maps the monomial \(x^my^n\) to a combination of the monomials \(x^{m+2j}y^{n-j}\) with \(j=0,\dots,n\). Assign the weight 1 to \(x\) and the weight 2 to \(y\) and show that the weighted degree \(m+2n\) is preserved. title: Exercise 03: Koopman operator
text:
2. DMD and the Koopman operator
DMD fits a linear map to the state itself, which for the map of Section 1 is the dictionary \((x,y)\). This dictionary does not close, since \(y\) at the next step contains \(c\,x^2\). For a dictionary that does not close, the least-squares fit is the projection of \(\mathcal K\) onto the span of the dictionary in the inner product defined by the data, \(\langle f,h\rangle=\frac1{n_p}\sum_if(\mathbf x_i)h(\mathbf x_i)\), and its result depends on where the data lie. For a closed dictionary the projection is exact and the fitted matrix is the same for any data that span the dictionary.

Exercise 2.1. DMD eigenvalues depend on the data

title: Exercise 03: Koopman operator
text:
3. Koopman eigenfunctions of the pendulum
The damped pendulum \[
\dot\theta=\omega,\qquad \dot\omega=-\omega_p^2\sin\theta-\gamma\,\omega
\] has the angle \(\theta\), the angular velocity \(\omega\), the small-amplitude frequency \(\omega_p\) and the damping rate \(\gamma\). We use \(\omega_p=1\) and \(\gamma=0.2\). The hanging position \((0,0)\) is a stable spiral and the upright position \((\pi,0)\) a saddle. The mechanical energy per unit moment of inertia is \(E=\tfrac12\omega^2+\omega_p^2(1-\cos\theta)\). The generator acts as \(\mathcal Ag=\omega\,\partial_\theta g-(\omega_p^2\sin\theta+\gamma\omega)\,\partial_\omega g\).

text:
4. Delay DMD of measured signals
A record offers only the values \(s_k=h(\mathbf x_k)\) of one observable, and the window \(\mathbf u_k=(s_k,s_{k-1},\dots,s_{k-L+1})\) is a dictionary generated by the dynamics from \(h\). A linear map fitted from \(\mathbf u_k\) to \(\mathbf u_{k+1}\) is delay DMD, and iterating it gives a recursive forecast. Its first row is the least-squares autoregressive model of order \(L\). Both signals below have \(N=4000\) samples, are rescaled to \([0,1]\) with the minimum and maximum of the first 2500 samples and centred with the mean of the first 3000, the training block. The forecasts start from every fifth origin of the test block, the last 1000 samples, for which the window and 300 forecast steps lie inside the block. The normalised root-mean-square error \(\mathrm{NRMSE}(\tau)\) is the root-mean-square difference between forecast and truth at the lead \(\tau\) over the origins, divided by the standard deviation of the test block, and the amplitude \(A(\tau)\) is the root mean square of the forecast itself divided by the same standard deviation.

title: Lab 034: Forecasting with linear models and NVAR
text:
0. Signals
We use the five signals of the characterisation notebook, generated by the same code. The Lorenz-63 model [E. N. Lorenz, J. Atmos. Sci. 20, 130 (1963), doi:10.1175/1520-0469(1963)020<0130:DNF>2.0.CO;2] is a low-dimensional chaotic flow, and we observe its \(x\) component every \(\Delta t = 0.02\). The Mackey–Glass delay equation [M. C. Mackey and L. Glass, Science 197, 287 (1977), doi:10.1126/science.267326] is sampled once per time unit at three delays. At \(\tau_{\rm MG}=15\) it settles on a limit cycle, at \(\tau_{\rm MG}=25\) it is weakly chaotic, and at \(\tau_{\rm MG}=35\) the chaos is developed. The Santa Fe record is the measured intensity of a far-infrared NH\(_3\) laser (data set A of the Santa Fe time-series competition) [H. Kantz and T. Schreiber, Nonlinear Time Series Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2003)], with slow growth of pulsations followed by sudden collapses.
Every signal has \(N=4000\) samples. Each is rescaled to \([0,1]\) with the minimum and maximum of its first 2500 samples, the fitting block defined below, so that all scores and plots share one scale.


Code
# Signal generators: Lorenz-63, Mackey-Glass and the Santa Fe laser record.

# Lorenz-63: sigma=10, rho=28, beta=8/3; RK4 with h=0.01, sampled every 2 steps (dt=0.02);
# initial state (1,1,1), first 50 time units discarded; we keep the x component.
def lorenz_rhs(u, sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0/3.0):
    x, y, z = u
    return jnp.array([sigma*(y - x), x*(rho - z) - y, x*y - beta*z])

def rk4_step(f, u, h):
    k1 = f(u); k2 = f(u + 0.5*h*k1); k3 = f(u + 0.5*h*k2); k4 = f(u + h*k3)
    return u + h/6.0*(k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=(0, 1, 2))
def lorenz_trajectory(n_samples, sub=2, n_discard=2500, h=0.01):
    """Returns array (n_samples, 3) sampled every `sub` RK4 steps (dt = sub*h)."""
    def one_sample(u, _):
        u = jax.lax.fori_loop(0, sub, lambda i, v: rk4_step(lorenz_rhs, v, h), u)
        return u, u
    u0 = jnp.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
    u, _ = jax.lax.scan(one_sample, u0, None, length=n_discard)
    _, traj = jax.lax.scan(one_sample, u, None, length=n_samples)
    return traj

# Mackey-Glass: dx/dt = beta x(t-tau)/(1+x(t-tau)^n) - gamma x, beta=0.2, gamma=0.1, n=10;
# RK4 with h=0.1, the delayed value at half steps by linear interpolation, constant history
# x=1.2 on [-tau, 0], first 3000 fine steps discarded, every 10th point kept (unit sampling).
def mackey_glass(tau, n_samples, h=0.1, x0=1.2, transient=3000, every=10,
                 beta=0.2, gamma=0.1, n=10):
    lag = int(round(tau / h))
    f = lambda x, xd: beta * xd / (1.0 + xd**n) - gamma * x
    def step(buf, _):
        # buf = (x[i-lag], ..., x[i]) : the delay window, length lag+1
        x, xd0, xd1 = buf[-1], buf[0], buf[1]
        xdh = 0.5 * (xd0 + xd1)
        k1 = f(x, xd0); k2 = f(x + 0.5*h*k1, xdh); k3 = f(x + 0.5*h*k2, xdh); k4 = f(x + h*k3, xd1)
        xn = x + h/6.0*(k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)
        return jnp.concatenate([buf[1:], xn[None]]), xn
    n_steps = transient + n_samples * every
    _, xs = jax.lax.scan(step, jnp.full(lag + 1, x0), None, length=n_steps)
    x = np.concatenate([np.full(lag + 1, x0), np.asarray(xs)])
    return x[transient::every][:n_samples]

def santafe(path="data/santafe_laser.txt"):
    return np.loadtxt(path).astype(float)

# Common protocol: N = 4000 samples per signal; train = first 3000 (last 500 of them = validation),
# test = last 1000; rescale to [0,1] with min/max of the first 2500 samples (fitting part of the training block); horizons tau = 1..50.
N_SAMPLES, N_TRAIN, N_VAL, TAU_MAX = 4000, 3000, 500, 50
def rescale01(s, n_train=N_TRAIN - N_VAL):
    lo, hi = s[:n_train].min(), s[:n_train].max()
    return (s - lo) / (hi - lo)




Code
raw = {"Lorenz": np.asarray(lorenz_trajectory(N_SAMPLES)[:, 0]),
       "MG 15": mackey_glass(15, N_SAMPLES), "MG 25": mackey_glass(25, N_SAMPLES),
       "MG 35": mackey_glass(35, N_SAMPLES), "Santa Fe": santafe()[:N_SAMPLES]}
sig = {name: rescale01(s) for name, s in raw.items()}     # each signal rescaled with its training block
NAMES = list(sig)
for name, s in sig.items():
    assert s.shape == (N_SAMPLES,)
    print(f"{name:9s} train range [{s[:N_TRAIN].min():.2f}, {s[:N_TRAIN].max():.2f}]"
          f"   test range [{s[N_TRAIN:].min():.3f}, {s[N_TRAIN:].max():.3f}]")

fig, axs = plt.subplots(5, 1, figsize=(12, 9), sharex=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, name in zip(axs, NAMES):
    ax.plot(sig[name], lw=0.8, color=UJBlue)
    ax.set_ylabel(name)
axs[-1].set_xlabel("sample index $k$")
plt.show()

The ReservoirPy library [N. Trouvain et al., ICANN 2020, doi:10.1007/978-3-030-61616-8_40] ships generators of the same systems and the Santa Fe record. Its Santa Fe file is the same data. Its Mackey–Glass generator uses an RK4 step \(h=1\) with the delayed value held fixed during a step and a random initial history around \(x_0=1.2\), and its Lorenz generator calls scipy.integrate.solve_ivp without removing the transient. The trajectories therefore differ from ours in detail, and the signals are of the same kind. The helper to_forecasting cuts a series into input–target pairs \((s_k, s_{k+\tau})\).
