title: Lab 041: Physics-informed neural networks
text:
2. Physics-informed neural network
The PINN replaces the unknown function \(x(t)\) by a multilayer perceptron \(x_\theta(t)\) with parameters \(\theta\). The input \(t\in[0,T]\) is first rescaled to \(\tau=2t/T-1\in[-1,1]\), then passes through three hidden layers of 32 tanh units each, and a linear output unit returns the number \(x_\theta(t)\), \[\mathbf h_1=\tanh(W_1\tau+\mathbf b_1),\qquad \mathbf h_{l+1}=\tanh(W_{l+1}\mathbf h_l+\mathbf b_{l+1}),\qquad x_\theta(t)=W_4\mathbf h_3+b_4 .\] Because the network is a composition of smooth functions, its derivatives \(\dot x_\theta=\partial_tx_\theta\) and \(\ddot x_\theta=\partial_t^2x_\theta\) exist at every \(t\). Automatic differentiation evaluates them by applying the chain rule to the same composition, so they are the exact derivatives of the network function up to round-off and involve no finite differences. With them we form the residual of the equation of motion, \[r_\theta(t)=\frac{m_0\ddot x_\theta(t)+c\dot x_\theta(t)+k_sx_\theta(t)}{k_s},\] which vanishes for every \(t\) when \(x_\theta\) solves the equation. Dividing by \(k_s\) gives the residual the units of a position.
The drawing shows the network as nodes and edges on the left. The boxes on the right show how the derivatives in \(t\), the residual and the initial conditions are assembled into the loss defined below.


Code
def draw_layers(ax, sizes, labels, xs, ys_span=2.2, node_r=0.11, colors=None, edge_color="0.75"):
    """Nodes-and-edges drawing of a fully connected network, columns at x = xs, labels below the columns."""
    cols = []
    for n, x in zip(sizes, xs):
        ys = np.linspace(ys_span / 2, -ys_span / 2, n) if n > 1 else np.array([0.0])
        cols.append([(x, y) for y in ys])
    for a, b in zip(cols[:-1], cols[1:]):            # edges first, so that the nodes are drawn on top
        for (x0, y0) in a:
            for (x1, y1) in b:
                ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=edge_color, lw=0.6, zorder=1)
    for i, col in enumerate(cols):
        for (x, y) in col:
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), node_r, fc=(colors[i] if colors else "#DCE6F2"), ec=UJNavy, lw=1.0, zorder=3))
    for i, lab in enumerate(labels):
        ax.text(xs[i], -ys_span / 2 - 0.25, lab, ha="center", va="top", linespacing=1.1)
    return cols

def box(ax, x, y, text, w, h, fc, **kw):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.04", fc=fc, ec=UJNavy, lw=1.0, zorder=3))
    ax.text(x, y, text, ha="center", va="center", zorder=4, **kw)

def arrow(ax, p, q, **kw):
    ax.annotate("", xy=q, xytext=p, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=UJNavy, lw=1.0, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0, **kw), zorder=2)

WIDTH, DEPTH = 32, 3
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 1.85)); ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
    cols = draw_layers(ax, [1, 5, 5, 5, 1], ["", "", "", "", ""], xs=[0, 0.65, 1.3, 1.95, 2.6], ys_span=2.0, node_r=0.09,
                       colors=["#DCE6F2", "#F6E3D3", "#F6E3D3", "#F6E3D3", "#E3F1EE"])
    for col in cols[1:4]:
        ax.text(col[0][0], 0.5 * (col[-2][1] + col[-1][1]), r"$\vdots$", ha="center", va="center", zorder=4,
                bbox=dict(fc="white", ec="none", pad=0.3))
    ax.text(-0.17, 0, "$t$", ha="right", va="center")
    ax.text(2.6, -0.2, r"$x_\theta$", ha="center", va="top")
    ax.text(1.3, -1.15, f"{DEPTH} tanh layers,\n{WIDTH} units each", ha="center", va="top", linespacing=1.1, fontsize=11)
    # automatic differentiation in t and the residual
    xm, wm = 4.85, 3.5
    box(ax, xm, 0.75, r"$\partial_t x_\theta,\ \partial_t^2 x_\theta$", wm, 0.5, "#EFEFEF", fontsize=11)
    ax.text(xm, 1.06, "automatic differentiation", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11, color=UJGray)
    box(ax, xm, -0.55, r"$r_\theta=\dfrac{m_0\ddot x_\theta+c\dot x_\theta+k_sx_\theta}{k_s}$", wm, 0.74, "#F6E3D3", fontsize=11)
    arrow(ax, (2.72, 0.06), (xm - wm / 2 - 0.05, 0.62)); arrow(ax, (2.72, -0.06), (xm - wm / 2 - 0.05, -0.45))
    arrow(ax, (xm, 0.46), (xm, -0.14))          # ends on the top edge of the residual box
    # loss terms
    xr, wr = 8.35, 2.3
    box(ax, xr, 0.75, r"$[x_\theta(0)-x_0]^2$" + "\n" + r"$[\dot x_\theta(0)-v_0]^2/\omega_0^2$", wr, 0.72, "#DCE6F2", fontsize=11)
    ax.text(xr, 1.17, "initial conditions", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11, color=UJGray)
    box(ax, xr, -0.55, r"$\frac{1}{N_r}\sum_i r_\theta(t_i)^2$", wr, 0.6, "#F6E3D3", fontsize=11)
    box(ax, xr, -1.55, r"loss $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$", wr, 0.42, "#E3F1EE", fontsize=11)
    arrow(ax, (xm + wm / 2 + 0.05, 0.75), (xr - wr / 2 - 0.05, 0.75)); arrow(ax, (xm + wm / 2 + 0.05, -0.55), (xr - wr / 2 - 0.05, -0.55))
    arrow(ax, (xr, -0.9), (xr, -1.31))
    ax.annotate("", xy=(xr + wr / 2 + 0.05, -1.5), xytext=(xr + wr / 2 + 0.05, 0.5), zorder=2,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=UJNavy, lw=1.0, connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.35"))
    ax.set_xlim(-0.45, 10.1); ax.set_ylim(-1.85, 1.5); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    save(fig, "fig_lab041_pinn_architecture"); plt.show()





The network has \(1\cdot32+32+2\,(32\cdot32+32)+32+1\) parameters. In the code, jax.grad(net, argnums=1) differentiates the network with respect to its time argument, and applying jax.grad again gives the second derivative. We compare both with central finite differences at four times on the untrained network.


Code
def init_mlp(key, sizes):
    # LeCun normal weights (variance 1/n_in) and zero biases, one (W, b) pair per layer
    params = []
    for n_in, n_out in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:]):
        key, sub = jax.random.split(key)
        params.append((jax.random.normal(sub, (n_out, n_in)) / np.sqrt(n_in), jnp.zeros(n_out)))
    return params

def make_net(t_a, t_b):
    # scalar network x_theta(t) on the window [t_a, t_b]; the input is rescaled to [-1, 1]
    def net(params, t):
        h = jnp.atleast_1d(2 * (t - t_a) / (t_b - t_a) - 1)
        for W, b in params[:-1]:
            h = jnp.tanh(W @ h + b)
        W, b = params[-1]
        return (W @ h + b)[0]
    d1 = jax.grad(net, argnums=1)          # dx_theta/dt
    d2 = jax.grad(d1, argnums=1)           # d^2x_theta/dt^2
    return net, d1, d2

def n_params(params):
    return int(sum(W.size + b.size for W, b in params))

SIZES = [1] + [WIDTH] * DEPTH + [1]
net, d1, d2 = make_net(0.0, T_END)
p_test = init_mlp(jax.random.key(0), SIZES)
# automatic derivatives against central finite differences at a few times
ts = jnp.array([0.3, 2.7, 6.1, 9.4]); e = 1e-4
fd1 = jax.vmap(lambda t: (net(p_test, t + e) - net(p_test, t - e)) / (2 * e))(ts)
fd2 = jax.vmap(lambda t: (net(p_test, t + e) - 2 * net(p_test, t) + net(p_test, t - e)) / e**2)(ts)
print(f"network {SIZES}, {n_params(p_test)} parameters")
print(f"max |d1 - finite difference| = {jnp.abs(jax.vmap(lambda t: d1(p_test, t))(ts) - fd1).max():.1e},"
      f" max |d2 - finite difference| = {jnp.abs(jax.vmap(lambda t: d2(p_test, t))(ts) - fd2).max():.1e}")
nums["n_params"] = n_params(p_test)


network [1, 32, 32, 32, 1], 2209 parameters


max |d1 - finite difference| = 2.9e-11, max |d2 - finite difference| = 6.0e-08


The network has 2209 parameters. The automatic first derivative agrees with the finite difference to \(2.9\times10^{-11}\) and the second derivative to \(6.0\times10^{-8}\), which is the size of the truncation and round-off errors of the finite differences themselves.

Loss
The training set of a PINN contains no solution values. It consists of \(N_r=200\) collocation points \(t_i\), equally spaced on \([0,10]\), at which the equation of motion is enforced, and of the two initial conditions. The loss is \[\mathcal L(\theta)=\frac{w_r}{N_r}\sum_{i=1}^{N_r}r_\theta(t_i)^2+w_0\big[x_\theta(0)-x_0\big]^2+w_1\Big[\frac{\dot x_\theta(0)-v_0}{\omega_0}\Big]^2 .\] The first term is the mean squared residual. It is zero for every solution of the equation of motion, a two-parameter family of damped oscillations, and therefore cannot select one of them. The two initial-condition terms select the solution with \(x(0)=x_0\) and \(\dot x(0)=v_0\), and the division by \(\omega_0\) gives the velocity term the units of a position. The weights \(w_r\), \(w_0\) and \(w_1\) fix the balance between the terms. A small weight of the initial conditions lets the optimiser settle on a function with a small residual that starts at the wrong state, and a large one slows down the reduction of the residual. We use \(w_r=w_0=w_1=1\), a choice that works for this problem. Wang, Teng and Perdikaris adapt the weights during training from the sizes of the gradients of the separate terms [arXiv:2001.04536]. When measurements \(x_j\) at times \(t_j\) are available, a data term \(\frac{w_d}{N_d}\sum_j[x_\theta(t_j)-x_j]^2\) is added in the same way.
Lagaris et al. satisfied the initial conditions by construction with the ansatz \(x_\theta(t)=x_0+v_0t+t^2N_\theta(t)\), where \(N_\theta\) is the network. This removes the initial-condition terms, and we keep the penalty form because it carries over to the inverse problem and to data terms without change.


Code
N_R = 200
T_COL = jnp.linspace(0.0, T_END, N_R)        # collocation points t_i

def make_osc_loss(net, d1, d2, t_col, w_r=1.0, w_ic=1.0, w_d=0.0, t_data=None, x_data=None, use_ic=True):
    """Loss of the oscillator PINN. With learn_c the damping c is the last entry of the parameter tuple."""
    def loss(params, c=C_TRUE):
        r = jax.vmap(lambda t: (M * d2(params, t) + c * d1(params, t) + K * net(params, t)) / K)(t_col)
        L = w_r * jnp.mean(r**2)
        if use_ic:
            L += w_ic * ((net(params, 0.0) - X0)**2 + ((d1(params, 0.0) - V0) / OMEGA0)**2)
        if w_d > 0:
            L += w_d * jnp.mean((jax.vmap(lambda t: net(params, t))(t_data) - x_data)**2)
        return L
    return loss

loss_osc = make_osc_loss(net, d1, d2, T_COL)
print(f"loss of the untrained network: {loss_osc(p_test):.3f}")


loss of the untrained network: 2.056




Optimisers
We minimise \(\mathcal L\) in two stages. The first is the Adam optimiser (adaptive moment estimation) [Kingma and Ba, arXiv:1412.6980]. With the gradient \(\mathbf g_n=\nabla_\theta\mathcal L\) at step \(n\) it keeps running averages of the gradient and of its componentwise square, \[\mathbf m_n=\beta_1\mathbf m_{n-1}+(1-\beta_1)\mathbf g_n,\qquad \mathbf v_n=\beta_2\mathbf v_{n-1}+(1-\beta_2)\mathbf g_n^2,\] corrects their bias from the zero initial values, \(\tilde{\mathbf m}_n=\mathbf m_n/(1-\beta_1^n)\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf v}_n=\mathbf v_n/(1-\beta_2^n)\), and updates \(\theta_{n}=\theta_{n-1}-\eta\,\tilde{\mathbf m}_n/(\sqrt{\tilde{\mathbf v}_n}+\epsilon)\) with \(\beta_1=0.9\), \(\beta_2=0.999\) and \(\epsilon=10^{-8}\). Every parameter thus moves by a step of order \(\eta\) whatever the scale of its gradient. Our implementation of these four lines in JAX and optax.adam run for 300 steps from the same initial parameters with \(\eta=3\times10^{-3}\).


Code
def adam_init(params):
    zeros = jax.tree.map(jnp.zeros_like, params)
    return dict(m=zeros, v=zeros, n=0)

def adam_update(grads, state, lr, b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8):
    # Adam: running means of the gradient and of its square, bias correction, step lr m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat)+eps)
    n = state["n"] + 1
    m = jax.tree.map(lambda m, g: b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g, state["m"], grads)
    v = jax.tree.map(lambda v, g: b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g**2, state["v"], grads)
    step = jax.tree.map(lambda m, v: -lr * (m / (1 - b1**n)) / (jnp.sqrt(v / (1 - b2**n)) + eps), m, v)
    return step, dict(m=m, v=v, n=n)

# 300 steps of our Adam and of optax.adam from the same initial parameters
lr = 3e-3
vg = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(loss_osc))
p_own, s_own = p_test, adam_init(p_test)
tx = optax.adam(lr); p_ox, s_ox = p_test, tx.init(p_test)
for _ in range(300):
    _, g = vg(p_own); u, s_own = adam_update(g, s_own, lr); p_own = optax.apply_updates(p_own, u)
    _, g = vg(p_ox); u, s_ox = tx.update(g, s_ox, p_ox); p_ox = optax.apply_updates(p_ox, u)
diff = max(float(jnp.abs(a - b).max()) for a, b in zip(jax.tree.leaves(p_own), jax.tree.leaves(p_ox)))
print(f"after 300 steps: loss own Adam {loss_osc(p_own):.6e}, optax Adam {loss_osc(p_ox):.6e},"
      f" max parameter difference {diff:.1e}")
nums["adam_check"] = diff


after 300 steps: loss own Adam 1.018542e-01, optax Adam 1.018542e-01, max parameter difference 6.7e-16


After 300 steps both optimisers reach the loss \(0.1018542\), and their parameters differ by \(6.7\times10^{-16}\), the level of round-off. optax.adam performs the same update as our four lines, and we use it from now on together with its learning-rate schedules.
The second stage is the limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno method (L-BFGS) [D. C. Liu and J. Nocedal, Math. Program. 45, 503 (1989), doi:10.1007/BF01589116], a quasi-Newton method that estimates the curvature of the loss from the differences of the last few gradients and chooses the step length by a line search. Close to a minimum it converges much faster than Adam, and Adam brings the parameters into this region first. We run 10000 Adam steps with the learning rate decreasing from \(3\times10^{-3}\) to \(3\times10^{-5}\) along a cosine, followed by 3000 iterations of optax.lbfgs. During training we record the loss and the largest deviation \(\max_t|x_\theta(t)-x(t)|\) from the closed-form solution on 2001 equally spaced times. The PINN never sees this deviation, which serves only as a diagnostic.


Code
def train(loss, params, n_adam=10000, n_lbfgs=3000, lr=3e-3, monitor=None, every=250):
    """Adam with a cosine learning-rate decay, followed by L-BFGS. Returns parameters and a history."""
    tx = optax.adam(optax.cosine_decay_schedule(lr, n_adam, alpha=1e-2))
    state = tx.init(params)
    @jax.jit
    def adam_step(p, s):
        l, g = jax.value_and_grad(loss)(p)
        u, s = tx.update(g, s, p)
        return optax.apply_updates(p, u), s, l
    lb = optax.lbfgs()
    vg_state = optax.value_and_grad_from_state(loss)
    @jax.jit
    def lbfgs_step(p, s):
        l, g = vg_state(p, state=s)
        u, s = lb.update(g, s, p, value=l, grad=g, value_fn=loss)
        return optax.apply_updates(p, u), s, l
    hist = dict(it=[], loss=[], mon=[])
    t0 = time.time()
    for it in range(n_adam + n_lbfgs):
        if it == n_adam:
            state = lb.init(params)
        params, state, l = (adam_step if it < n_adam else lbfgs_step)(params, state)
        if it % every == 0 or it == n_adam + n_lbfgs - 1:
            hist["it"].append(it); hist["loss"].append(float(l))
            if monitor is not None:
                hist["mon"].append(monitor(params))
    hist = {k: np.array(v) for k, v in hist.items()}
    hist["time"] = time.time() - t0
    hist["final_loss"] = float(loss(params))
    return params, hist

T_DENSE = jnp.linspace(0.0, T_END, 2001)
x_dense = x_exact(np.asarray(T_DENSE))
max_err = lambda p: float(jnp.abs(jax.vmap(lambda t: net(p, t))(T_DENSE) - x_dense).max())

N_ADAM, N_LBFGS = 10000, 3000
p_pinn, hist_pinn = train(loss_osc, init_mlp(jax.random.key(0), SIZES), N_ADAM, N_LBFGS, monitor=max_err)
x_pinn = np.asarray(jax.vmap(lambda t: net(p_pinn, t))(T_DENSE))
err_pinn = np.abs(x_pinn - x_dense)
i_switch = np.searchsorted(hist_pinn["it"], N_ADAM)
print(f"training {N_ADAM} Adam + {N_LBFGS} L-BFGS iterations in {hist_pinn['time']:.1f} s")
print(f"loss after Adam {hist_pinn['loss'][i_switch - 1]:.2e}, final loss {hist_pinn['final_loss']:.2e}")
print(f"max |x_PINN - x| on [0, {T_END:g}]: after Adam {hist_pinn['mon'][i_switch - 1]:.2e}, final {err_pinn.max():.2e}")
nums["pinn_osc"] = dict(time=hist_pinn["time"], loss_adam=float(hist_pinn["loss"][i_switch - 1]),
                        loss=hist_pinn["final_loss"], err_adam=float(hist_pinn["mon"][i_switch - 1]), err=float(err_pinn.max()))


training 10000 Adam + 3000 L-BFGS iterations in 24.9 s
loss after Adam 5.52e-04, final loss 1.57e-06
max |x_PINN - x| on [0, 10]: after Adam 1.50e-01, final 1.23e-03


The 13000 iterations take about 25 s on our machine. Adam lowers the loss from 2.06 to \(5.5\times10^{-4}\), while the maximal error of the network falls only to \(0.15\). L-BFGS then reduces the loss to \(1.6\times10^{-6}\) and the error to \(1.2\times10^{-3}\). A small loss therefore does not by itself guarantee a small error, since a residual that is small at every collocation point still accumulates over the window. The left panel shows the loss \(\mathcal L\) and the maximal error \(\max_t|x_\theta(t)-x(t)|\) against the iteration, with the switch from Adam to L-BFGS dotted. The right panel compares the trained network with the closed-form solution, and the grey ticks at the bottom mark the 200 collocation points.

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 2.3), layout="constrained")

title: Lab 041: Physics-informed neural networks
text:
3. Accuracy and cost
A PINN solves the same initial-value problem that a classical integrator solves, so the two can be compared directly. The classical solvers integrate the first-order system for the state \(\mathbf y=(x,\dot x)\), \[\dot{\mathbf y}=\mathbf f(\mathbf y)=\Big(\dot x,\ -\frac{c\dot x+kx}{m}\Big).\] We use our RK4 with a constant step \(h\) and two solvers of diffrax [P. Kidger, On Neural Differential Equations, PhD thesis, University of Oxford (2021), arXiv:2202.02435]. The first is RK4 itself, defined through its Butcher tableau as a diffrax solver, which must reproduce our integrator to round-off. The second is Tsitouras’ 5(4) Runge–Kutta pair (Tsit5) [Ch. Tsitouras, Comput. Math. Appl. 62, 770 (2011), doi:10.1016/j.camwa.2011.06.002] with adaptive step size. Each step of Tsit5 estimates its local error from the difference of a fifth- and a fourth-order solution, and a proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controller of diffrax shrinks or enlarges the step so that this estimate stays below the relative and absolute tolerances.


Code
f_osc = lambda y: jnp.array([y[1], -(C_TRUE * y[1] + K * y[0]) / M])     # state y = (x, xdot)

class RK4(diffrax.AbstractERK):
    """Classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method as a diffrax solver (Butcher tableau of RK4)."""
    tableau = diffrax.ButcherTableau(c=np.array([0.5, 0.5, 1.0]), b_sol=np.array([1/6, 1/3, 1/3, 1/6]),
                                     b_error=np.zeros(4),
                                     a_lower=(np.array([0.5]), np.array([0.0, 0.5]), np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])))
    interpolation_cls = diffrax.ThirdOrderHermitePolynomialInterpolation.from_k

N_EVAL = [0]                      # counter of right-hand-side evaluations inside diffrax
def _bump(n):
    N_EVAL[0] += int(n); return np.int32(0)
def rhs_counted(t, y, args):
    io_callback(_bump, jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((), jnp.int32), 1, ordered=False)
    return f_osc(y)
rhs = lambda t, y, args: f_osc(y)

def dfx_solve(solver, ctrl, dt0, ts, counted=False):
    sol = diffrax.diffeqsolve(diffrax.ODETerm(rhs_counted if counted else rhs), solver, 0.0, T_END, dt0,
                              jnp.array([X0, V0]), saveat=diffrax.SaveAt(ts=ts), stepsize_controller=ctrl, max_steps=10**6)
    return sol.ys

def timed(fn, repeat=20):
    # median wall time of a compiled function, after one call for compilation
    jax.block_until_ready(fn()); ts_ = []
    for _ in range(repeat):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); jax.block_until_ready(fn()); ts_.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return float(np.median(ts_))

# own RK4 and diffrax RK4 with the same step h = 0.01
h = 0.01; n = int(round(T_END / h))
y_own = np.asarray(rk4_solve(f_osc, [X0, V0], h, n))
y_dfx = np.asarray(dfx_solve(RK4(), diffrax.ConstantStepSize(), h, jnp.arange(n + 1) * h))
print(f"h = {h}: max |own RK4 - diffrax RK4| = {np.abs(y_own - y_dfx).max():.1e},"
      f" max |own RK4 - exact x| = {np.abs(y_own[:, 0] - x_exact(np.arange(n + 1) * h)).max():.1e}")
nums["rk4_vs_diffrax"] = float(np.abs(y_own - y_dfx).max())


h = 0.01: max |own RK4 - diffrax RK4| = 1.8e-15, max |own RK4 - exact x| = 4.9e-09


With \(h=0.01\) our RK4 and the diffrax RK4 agree to \(1.8\times10^{-15}\), and both deviate from the closed-form solution by \(4.9\times10^{-9}\).
The cost of a classical integration is measured by the number of evaluations of the right-hand side \(\mathbf f\) and by the wall time. RK4 evaluates \(\mathbf f\) four times per step. For Tsit5 we count the evaluations with a callback inside the vector field, since the number of accepted and rejected steps is chosen by the controller. The accuracy is the largest deviation of \(x\) from the closed-form solution on \([0,10]\). For the PINN the corresponding numbers are the training time and the number of residual evaluations during training, one per collocation point and iteration, each of which costs a forward pass of the network and two derivatives. L-BFGS may evaluate the loss more than once per iteration in its line search, so this count is a lower bound. The wall times are medians over repeated calls of compiled functions.


Code
rows = []
for h in (0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01):
    n = int(round(T_END / h))
    fn = jax.jit(lambda: rk4_solve(f_osc, jnp.array([X0, V0]), h, n))
    y = np.asarray(fn())
    rows.append(dict(method="RK4", setting=h, nfe=4 * n, err=float(np.abs(y[:, 0] - x_exact(np.arange(n + 1) * h)).max()),
                     time=timed(fn)))
for tol in (1e-3, 1e-5, 1e-7, 1e-9, 1e-11):
    ctrl = diffrax.PIDController(rtol=tol, atol=tol)
    fn = jax.jit(lambda: dfx_solve(diffrax.Tsit5(), ctrl, 0.1, T_DENSE))
    y = np.asarray(fn())
    N_EVAL[0] = 0; jax.block_until_ready(dfx_solve(diffrax.Tsit5(), ctrl, 0.1, T_DENSE, counted=True))
    rows.append(dict(method="Tsit5", setting=tol, nfe=N_EVAL[0], err=float(np.abs(y[:, 0] - x_dense).max()), time=timed(fn)))

# PINN: one residual evaluation = network and its two time derivatives at one collocation point
t_eval_pinn = timed(jax.jit(lambda: jax.vmap(lambda t: net(p_pinn, t))(T_DENSE)))
rows.append(dict(method="PINN", setting="training", nfe=(N_ADAM + N_LBFGS) * N_R, err=float(err_pinn.max()),
                 time=hist_pinn["time"]))
print(f"{'method':7s} {'setting':>9s} {'evaluations':>12s} {'max error':>10s} {'time [s]':>10s}")
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r['method']:7s} {str(r['setting']):>9s} {r['nfe']:12d} {r['err']:10.1e} {r['time']:10.2e}")
print(f"evaluating the trained PINN on {len(T_DENSE)} times takes {t_eval_pinn:.1e} s")
nums["cost"] = rows; nums["pinn_eval_time"] = t_eval_pinn


method    setting  evaluations  max error   time [s]
RK4           0.4          100    1.3e-02   1.59e-05
RK4           0.2          200    8.0e-04   1.67e-05
RK4           0.1          400    5.0e-05   1.90e-05
RK4          0.05          800    3.1e-06   2.27e-05
RK4          0.02         2000    7.9e-08   3.35e-05
RK4          0.01         4000    4.9e-09   6.12e-05
Tsit5       0.001           97    4.4e-03   1.36e-04
Tsit5       1e-05          229    2.1e-05   1.79e-04
Tsit5       1e-07          596    1.1e-07   3.32e-04
Tsit5       1e-09         1406    8.9e-10   6.50e-04
Tsit5       1e-11         3459    8.0e-12   1.34e-03
PINN     training      2600000    1.2e-03   2.49e+01

The left panel plots the maximal error against the number of evaluations, the right panel against the wall time. Each RK4 point belongs to one step size, \(h=0.4\) down to \(0.01\), and each Tsit5 point to one tolerance, \(10^{-3}\) down to \(10^{-11}\). The PINN is a single point.


Code
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 2.4), layout="constrained", sharey=True)
    for meth, mk in (("RK4", "o-"), ("Tsit5", "s-"), ("PINN", "*")):
        rr = [r for r in rows if r["method"] == meth]
        lab = {"RK4": "own RK4", "Tsit5": "diffrax Tsit5", "PINN": "PINN training"}[meth]
        axs[0].loglog([r["nfe"] for r in rr], [r["err"] for r in rr], mk, color=COL[meth], ms=(10 if meth == "PINN" else 4), label=lab)
        axs[1].loglog([r["time"] for r in rr], [r["err"] for r in rr], mk, color=COL[meth], ms=(10 if meth == "PINN" else 4))
    axs[0].set_xlabel("evaluations"); axs[0].set_ylabel(r"max $|x_{\rm num}-x|$")
    axs[1].set_xlabel("wall time [s]")
    fig.legend(*axs[0].get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="outside upper center", ncol=3, handlelength=1.5)
    save(fig, "fig_lab041_cost_accuracy"); plt.show()





The RK4 error falls by a factor of about 16 whenever \(h\) is halved, from \(8.0\times10^{-4}\) at \(h=0.2\) to \(5.0\times10^{-5}\) at \(h=0.1\) and \(3.1\times10^{-6}\) at \(h=0.05\), the convergence of a fourth-order method. Tsit5 reaches \(8.0\times10^{-12}\) with 3459 evaluations. The trained PINN deviates from the solution by \(1.2\times10^{-3}\), after \(2.6\times10^{6}\) residual evaluations and about 25 s of training. RK4 with \(h=0.2\) is already more accurate, \(8.0\times10^{-4}\), with 200 evaluations in about \(2\times10^{-5}\) s, about \(1.5\times10^{6}\) times faster. Even evaluating the trained network at 2001 times, about \(7\times10^{-4}\) s, takes longer than the RK4 integration with \(h=0.05\), which is more than a hundred times more accurate. For the initial-value problem of a low-dimensional ODE the PINN is a slow and inaccurate solver. Its construction pays off when the equation is combined with data, which the next experiments show.

Sparse data with and without the residual
The residual term is what distinguishes a PINN from an ordinary fit. To isolate its effect we give the network 12 exact, noise-free values of the closed-form solution at equally spaced times in the window \(0\le t\le4\), about the first 1.3 periods, and train the same architecture with the same optimiser twice. The first loss contains only the data term, \(\frac1{N_d}\sum_j[x_\theta(t_j)-x_j]^2\). The second adds the mean squared residual at the 200 collocation points on the whole interval \([0,10]\). Neither loss contains the initial conditions, which the data at \(t=0\) already fix.


Code
T_DATA_END, N_DATA = 4.0, 12
t_data = jnp.linspace(0.0, T_DATA_END, N_DATA)
x_data = jnp.asarray(x_exact(np.asarray(t_data)))       # noise-free samples of the exact solution

loss_data = make_osc_loss(net, d1, d2, T_COL, w_r=0.0, w_d=1.0, t_data=t_data, x_data=x_data, use_ic=False)
loss_phys = make_osc_loss(net, d1, d2, T_COL, w_r=1.0, w_d=1.0, t_data=t_data, x_data=x_data, use_ic=False)
p_data, h_data = train(loss_data, init_mlp(jax.random.key(0), SIZES), N_ADAM, N_LBFGS)
p_phys, h_phys = train(loss_phys, init_mlp(jax.random.key(0), SIZES), N_ADAM, N_LBFGS)
inside = np.asarray(T_DENSE) <= T_DATA_END
res_dp = {}
for name, p in (("data only", p_data), ("data + residual", p_phys)):
    e = np.abs(np.asarray(jax.vmap(lambda t: net(p, t))(T_DENSE)) - x_dense)
    res_dp[name] = dict(err_in=float(e[inside].max()), err_out=float(e[~inside].max()))
    print(f"{name:16s} max error for t <= {T_DATA_END:g}: {e[inside].max():.1e}, for t > {T_DATA_END:g}: {e[~inside].max():.1e}")
nums["data_vs_phys"] = res_dp


data only        max error for t <= 4: 2.6e-02, for t > 4: 1.2e+00
data + residual  max error for t <= 4: 3.6e-05, for t > 4: 3.0e-04


Inside the data window both networks follow the solution, with maximal errors of \(2.6\times10^{-2}\) for the data-only fit and \(3.6\times10^{-5}\) with the residual. Beyond the window the data-only network has no information. It continues smoothly and drifts away from the oscillation, with a maximal error of 1.2. The residual carries the solution through the remaining two periods with a maximal error of \(3.0\times10^{-4}\), so the equation of motion turns 12 exact samples of the first 1.3 periods into the whole trajectory. The figure shows the exact solution, the 12 data points (blue) in the shaded data window and the two trained networks.


Code
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 2.3), layout="constrained")
    ax.axvspan(0, T_DATA_END, color="#DCE6F2", lw=0, zorder=0)
    ax.text(T_DATA_END / 2, 1.33, "data window", ha="center", va="bottom")
    ax.plot(T_DENSE, x_dense, color=COL["exact"], lw=1.0, label="exact $x(t)$")
    ax.plot(T_DENSE, jax.vmap(lambda t: net(p_data, t))(T_DENSE), color=DSOrange, ls="-.", label="data only")
    ax.plot(T_DENSE, jax.vmap(lambda t: net(p_phys, t))(T_DENSE), "--", color=COL["PINN"], label="data + residual")
    ax.plot(t_data, x_data, "o", color=COL["data"], ms=4, label="data", zorder=5)
    ax.set_xlim(0, T_END); ax.set_ylim(-2.6, 1.6); ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$x$")
    ax.legend(loc="lower right", ncol=2, fontsize=11, handlelength=1.6)
    save(fig, "fig_lab041_data_vs_physics"); plt.show()

title: Lab 041: Physics-informed neural networks
text:
4. Inverse problem
In an experiment the parameters of the equation are often unknown, and the measurements are noisy. The PINN treats an unknown parameter like a weight of the network. We assume that \(m_0\) and \(k_s\) are known and the damping coefficient \(c\) is unknown, and we measure the position at 25 equally spaced times \(t_j\in[0,10]\) with independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma=0.02\), \[y_j=x(t_j)+\sigma\varepsilon_j,\qquad \varepsilon_j\sim\mathcal N(0,1).\] The initial state is treated as unknown as well, so the loss contains no initial-condition terms, \[\mathcal L(\theta,c)=\frac1{N_{\rm obs}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\rm obs}}\big[x_\theta(t_j)-y_j\big]^2+\frac1{N_r}\sum_{i=1}^{N_r}r_{\theta,c}(t_i)^2,\] where the residual \(r_{\theta,c}\) uses the trainable \(c\). Both terms are in units of a squared position, so equal weights penalise a violation of the equation of motion like a deviation from the data of the same size. We write \(c=e^{s}\) and train \(s\), which keeps \(c\) positive, and start from \(c=1.0\), two and a half times the true value \(0.4\).
The classical reference is a least-squares fit of the closed-form solution \(x(t;c,x_0,v_0)\) to the same data with scipy.optimize.least_squares. Its standard error of \(c\) follows from the Jacobian \(J\) of the normalised residuals \((x(t_j)-y_j)/\sigma\) as the square root of the diagonal element of \((J^\top J)^{-1}\). We repeat both estimates for five independent noise realisations.


Code
N_OBS, SIGMA_NOISE, C_INIT = 25, 0.02, 1.0
t_obs = jnp.linspace(0.0, T_END, N_OBS)

def inverse_loss(t_obs, y_obs):
    # parameters = (network parameters, log c); the residual uses the trainable damping c = exp(log c)
    def loss(q):
        params, logc = q
        c = jnp.exp(logc)
        r = jax.vmap(lambda t: (M * d2(params, t) + c * d1(params, t) + K * net(params, t)) / K)(T_COL)
        fit = jnp.mean((jax.vmap(lambda t: net(params, t))(t_obs) - y_obs)**2)
        return fit + jnp.mean(r**2)          # both terms in units of x squared, equal weights
    return loss

inv = []
for seed in range(5):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    y_obs = jnp.asarray(x_exact(np.asarray(t_obs)) + SIGMA_NOISE * rng.normal(size=N_OBS))
    q0 = (init_mlp(jax.random.key(seed), SIZES), jnp.log(C_INIT))
    q, h_inv = train(inverse_loss(t_obs, y_obs), q0, N_ADAM, N_LBFGS, monitor=lambda q: float(jnp.exp(q[1])))
    # classical reference: least-squares fit of (c, x0, v0) in the closed-form solution
    ls = least_squares(lambda z: (x_exact(np.asarray(t_obs), z[0], z[1], z[2]) - np.asarray(y_obs)) / SIGMA_NOISE,
                       x0=[C_INIT, 0.5, 0.5])
    cov = np.linalg.inv(ls.jac.T @ ls.jac)
    inv.append(dict(seed=seed, c_pinn=float(jnp.exp(q[1])), c_ls=float(ls.x[0]), c_ls_err=float(np.sqrt(cov[0, 0])),
                    hist=h_inv, q=q, y_obs=y_obs))
    print(f"noise seed {seed}: c_PINN = {inv[-1]['c_pinn']:.4f}, c_least-squares = {ls.x[0]:.4f} +- {np.sqrt(cov[0, 0]):.4f},"
          f" {h_inv['time']:.0f} s")
cp = np.array([r["c_pinn"] for r in inv]); cl = np.array([r["c_ls"] for r in inv])
print(f"true c = {C_TRUE}; PINN mean {cp.mean():.4f}, std {cp.std(ddof=1):.4f};"
      f" least squares mean {cl.mean():.4f}, std {cl.std(ddof=1):.4f}; max |c_PINN - c_LS| = {np.abs(cp - cl).max():.4f}")
nums["inverse"] = dict(c_true=C_TRUE, c_init=C_INIT, n_obs=N_OBS, sigma=SIGMA_NOISE, c_pinn=cp.tolist(), c_ls=cl.tolist(),
                       c_ls_err=[r["c_ls_err"] for r in inv], pinn_mean=cp.mean(), pinn_std=cp.std(ddof=1),
                       ls_mean=cl.mean(), ls_std=cl.std(ddof=1), max_diff=float(np.abs(cp - cl).max()))


noise seed 0: c_PINN = 0.4000, c_least-squares = 0.4035 +- 0.0099, 26 s


noise seed 1: c_PINN = 0.3977, c_least-squares = 0.3971 +- 0.0098, 26 s


noise seed 2: c_PINN = 0.4006, c_least-squares = 0.3975 +- 0.0098, 25 s


noise seed 3: c_PINN = 0.4103, c_least-squares = 0.4048 +- 0.0099, 25 s


noise seed 4: c_PINN = 0.3958, c_least-squares = 0.3962 +- 0.0099, 25 s
true c = 0.4; PINN mean 0.4009, std 0.0056; least squares mean 0.3998, std 0.0040; max |c_PINN - c_LS| = 0.0054


The left panel shows the estimate of \(c\) during the training for the five noise realisations, with the true value dotted and the switch from Adam to L-BFGS marked by the vertical line. The right panel shows the noisy data of the first realisation, the trained network and the exact solution.


Code
r0 = inv[0]
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 2.3), layout="constrained", gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.3]})
    ax = axs[0]
    for r in inv:
        ax.plot(r["hist"]["it"], r["hist"]["mon"], color=COL["PINN"], lw=1.0, alpha=0.7)
    ax.axhline(C_TRUE, color="k", ls=":", lw=1.0); ax.text(200, C_TRUE + 0.03, "true $c$", va="bottom")
    ax.axvline(N_ADAM, color="0.5", ls=":", lw=1.0)
    c_top = max(float(np.max(r["hist"]["mon"])) for r in inv)
    ax.set_xlabel("iteration"); ax.set_ylabel("estimate of $c$"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05 * c_top)
    ax = axs[1]
    ax.plot(T_DENSE, x_dense, color=COL["exact"], lw=1.0, label="exact")
    ax.plot(T_DENSE, jax.vmap(lambda t: net(r0["q"][0], t))(T_DENSE), "--", color=COL["PINN"], label=r"PINN $x_\theta$")
    ax.plot(t_obs, r0["y_obs"], "o", color=COL["data"], ms=3.5, label="noisy data")
    ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$x$"); ax.set_xlim(0, T_END); ax.set_ylim(-1.0, 1.45)
    fig.legend(*ax.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="outside upper center", ncol=3, fontsize=11, handlelength=1.6)
    save(fig, "fig_lab041_inverse"); plt.show()





In the first few hundred Adam steps all five estimates rise above the starting value \(c=1.0\), then they fall to the neighbourhood of the true value within the Adam stage and stay there under L-BFGS. For the first noise realisation the PINN gives \(c=0.4000\) and the least-squares fit \(0.4035\pm0.0099\). Over the five realisations the PINN estimates have the mean 0.4009 and the standard deviation 0.0056, the least-squares estimates 0.3998 and 0.0040. On the same data the two estimates differ by at most 0.0054, less than the statistical error 0.0099 of the least-squares fit. The spread of the PINN estimates, 0.0056, is somewhat larger than that of the fit, 0.0040, and five realisations are too few to decide whether this difference is significant. The PINN thus recovers the damping within the noise of the data, with a precision at most comparable to that of the classical fit. The least-squares fit uses the closed-form solution, while the PINN needs only the equation of motion, which makes the same procedure applicable to equations without a solution formula.

title: Lab 041: Physics-informed neural networks
text:
5. Heat equation

Diffusion in a rod
A thin rod conducts heat along its axis, and its two ends are held at the same fixed temperature. We measure the position \(x\) along the rod in units of its length and the temperature \(u(x,t)\) relative to that of the ends. Fourier’s law states that the heat current is proportional to \(-\partial_xu\), and the conservation of energy then gives the heat equation \[\partial_tu=D\,\partial_x^2u,\qquad 0<x<1,\quad 0<t\le t_{\max},\] with the boundary and initial conditions \[u(0,t)=u(1,t)=0,\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x).\] The thermal diffusivity \(D\) sets the time scale of the conduction. The same equation describes every diffusion process, with \(u\) a concentration and \(D\) the diffusion coefficient. Integrating the equation over the rod gives \[\frac{d}{dt}\int_0^1u\,dx=D\big[\partial_xu(1,t)-\partial_xu(0,t)\big],\] so the heat content of the rod changes only through the heat currents at its ends.
The product ansatz \(u=X(x)\,T(t)\) separates the equation into \(X''/X=\dot T/(DT)=-\lambda\). The boundary conditions admit only \(X_n(x)=\sin n\pi x\) with \(\lambda_n=n^2\pi^2\), \(n=1,2,\dots\), and every such mode decays exponentially in time, \[\begin{aligned}
u(x,t)&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\,e^{-t/\tau_n}\sin n\pi x,\\
\tau_n&=\frac{1}{Dn^2\pi^2},\qquad b_n=2\int_0^1u_0(x)\sin n\pi x\,dx .
\end{aligned}\] A mode with \(n\) half-wavelengths along the rod decays \(n^2\) times faster than the lowest mode, so fine structure in the temperature profile disappears first and the profile approaches the shape \(\sin\pi x\) while its amplitude decays.
We take \(D=0.1\), \(t_{\max}=1\) and the initial profile \(u_0(x)=\sin\pi x+\tfrac12\sin3\pi x\), for which \(b_1=1\), \(b_3=\tfrac12\) and all other coefficients vanish. The code evaluates \(\tau_1\) and \(\tau_3\) and checks with central finite differences that the series solves the heat equation.


Code
D_TRUE, T_MAX = 0.1, 1.0              # thermal diffusivity and end of the time window
B_HEAT = {1: 1.0, 3: 0.5}             # Fourier coefficients b_n of the initial profile

def u0_heat(x):
    return sum(b * jnp.sin(n * jnp.pi * x) for n, b in B_HEAT.items())

def u_heat(x, t, D=D_TRUE):
    # separation of variables: every sine mode decays with the rate D n^2 pi^2
    return sum(b * np.exp(-D * n**2 * np.pi**2 * t) * np.sin(n * np.pi * x) for n, b in B_HEAT.items())

tau = {n: 1 / (D_TRUE * n**2 * np.pi**2) for n in B_HEAT}
# residual of the series solution with central finite differences on a grid of test points
xx, tq = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19), np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19)); e = 1e-4
res_fd = ((u_heat(xx, tq + e) - u_heat(xx, tq - e)) / (2 * e)
          - D_TRUE * (u_heat(xx + e, tq) - 2 * u_heat(xx, tq) + u_heat(xx - e, tq)) / e**2)
print(f"tau_1 = {tau[1]:.4f}, tau_3 = {tau[3]:.4f}; amplitudes at t = {T_MAX:g}:"
      f" mode 1 {np.exp(-T_MAX / tau[1]):.3f}, mode 3 {0.5 * np.exp(-T_MAX / tau[3]):.1e}")
print(f"max |finite-difference residual of the series solution| = {np.abs(res_fd).max():.1e}")
nums["heat"] = dict(D=D_TRUE, t_max=T_MAX, tau1=tau[1], tau3=tau[3], amp1_end=float(np.exp(-T_MAX / tau[1])),
                    amp3_end=float(0.5 * np.exp(-T_MAX / tau[3])))


tau_1 = 1.0132, tau_3 = 0.1126; amplitudes at t = 1: mode 1 0.373, mode 3 6.9e-05
max |finite-difference residual of the series solution| = 5.8e-07


The mode \(n=1\) decays with the time \(\tau_1=1.013\) and the mode \(n=3\) with \(\tau_3=0.113\), nine times faster. At \(t=1\) the amplitude of the first mode has dropped to 0.373 and that of the third to \(6.9\times10^{-5}\). The finite-difference residual of the series is \(5.8\times10^{-7}\), the size of the truncation error of the differences. The left panel shows the temperature \(u(x,t)\) as a colour map in the plane of the position \(x\) and the time \(t\), and the middle panel the profiles \(u(x,t)\) at five times. The two maxima of the initial profile, which come from the mode \(n=3\), have almost merged into a flat top at \(t=0.2\), and afterwards the profile keeps the shape \(\sin\pi x\) while it decays. The right panel shows the amplitudes \(b_ne^{-t/\tau_n}\) of the two modes on a logarithmic axis, straight lines with the slopes \(-1/\tau_n\).


Code
XH, TH = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, 1, 101), np.linspace(0, T_MAX, 101))     # evaluation grid, rows = times
UH = u_heat(XH, TH)
T_PROF = (0.0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0)
prof_cols = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0.0, 0.85, len(T_PROF)))
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 2.1), layout="constrained", gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1, 1]})
    im = axs[0].pcolormesh(XH, TH, UH, cmap="inferno", vmin=0, vmax=1.1, shading="auto", rasterized=True)
    axs[0].set_xlabel("$x$"); axs[0].set_ylabel("$t$"); axs[0].set_title("$u(x,t)$")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=axs[0], ticks=[0, 0.5, 1], fraction=0.08, pad=0.03)
    for tk, cc in zip(T_PROF, prof_cols):
        axs[1].plot(XH[0], u_heat(XH[0], tk), color=cc, lw=1.3, label=f"$t={tk:g}$")
    axs[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axs[1].set_ylabel("$u$"); axs[1].set_xlim(0, 1)
    tt_h = np.linspace(0, T_MAX, 201)
    for n, b in B_HEAT.items():
        axs[2].semilogy(tt_h, b * np.exp(-tt_h / tau[n]), color=(UJNavy if n == 1 else DSOrange), label=f"$n={n}$")
    axs[2].set_xlabel("$t$"); axs[2].set_ylabel(r"$b_n e^{-t/\tau_n}$"); axs[2].set_xlim(0, T_MAX); axs[2].set_ylim(5e-5, 2)
    axs[2].legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=11, handlelength=1.2, borderaxespad=0.2)
    fig.legend(*axs[1].get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="outside upper center", ncol=len(T_PROF), fontsize=11,
               handlelength=1.2, columnspacing=1.0)
    save(fig, "fig_lab041_heat_exact"); plt.show()







Crank–Nicolson solver
The classical reference is a finite-difference solution on the grid \(x_i=i\,\Delta x\), \(\Delta x=1/N_x\), and \(t^n=n\,\Delta t\), \(\Delta t=t_{\max}/N_t\). The numbers \(U_i^n\) approximate \(u(x_i,t^n)\), and the second derivative is replaced by the second difference \(\delta^2U_i=U_{i+1}-2U_i+U_{i-1}\). The Crank–Nicolson scheme averages this difference over the old and the new time level [J. Crank and P. Nicolson, Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 43, 50 (1947), doi:10.1017/S0305004100023197], \[\frac{U_i^{n+1}-U_i^n}{\Delta t}=\frac{D}{2\Delta x^2}\big(\delta^2U_i^{n+1}+\delta^2U_i^n\big),\qquad U_0^n=U_{N_x}^n=0 .\] Every time step solves a tridiagonal linear system for the \(N_x-1\) interior values, which costs a number of operations proportional to \(N_x\). The error decreases as \(\Delta x^2+\Delta t^2\), and the scheme is stable for every \(\Delta t\). The explicit scheme with the forward difference in time needs no linear solve but is stable only for \(D\Delta t/\Delta x^2\le\tfrac12\). We solve on grids with \(N_x=N_t=10,20,\dots,160\), measure the error as the largest deviation \(\max_{i,n}|U_i^n-u(x_i,t^n)|\) from the series solution over all grid nodes, and record the median wall time of the compiled solver.


Code
def cn_solve(D, nx, nt):
    # Crank-Nicolson for u_t = D u_xx with u(0,t) = u(1,t) = 0; returns U[n, i] at t^n = n dt, x_i = i dx
    dx, dt = 1.0 / nx, T_MAX / nt
    a = 0.5 * D * dt / dx**2
    m = nx - 1                                             # number of interior nodes
    dl = jnp.full(m, -a).at[0].set(0.0); du = jnp.full(m, -a).at[-1].set(0.0); dd = jnp.full(m, 1 + 2 * a)
    def step(u, _):
        rhs = (1 - 2 * a) * u + a * (jnp.pad(u[1:], (0, 1)) + jnp.pad(u[:-1], (1, 0)))   # (1 + D dt/2 delta^2) U^n
        u = jax.lax.linalg.tridiagonal_solve(dl, dd, du, rhs[:, None])[:, 0]           # (1 - D dt/2 delta^2) U^{n+1} = rhs
        return u, u
    u_in = u0_heat(jnp.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nx + 1)[1:-1])
    _, us = jax.lax.scan(step, u_in, None, length=nt)
    return jnp.pad(jnp.concatenate([u_in[None], us]), ((0, 0), (1, 1)))     # add the boundary nodes

rows_heat = []
for nx in (10, 20, 40, 80, 160):
    fn = jax.jit(lambda: cn_solve(D_TRUE, nx, nx))
    U = np.asarray(fn())
    xg_, tg_ = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, 1, nx + 1), np.linspace(0, T_MAX, nx + 1))
    rows_heat.append(dict(nx=nx, err=float(np.abs(U - u_heat(xg_, tg_)).max()), time=timed(fn)))
    print(f"N_x = N_t = {nx:3d}: max |U - u| = {rows_heat[-1]['err']:.2e}, wall time {rows_heat[-1]['time']:.1e} s")
nums["heat_fd"] = rows_heat


N_x = N_t =  10: max |U - u| = 2.73e-03, wall time 3.4e-05 s
N_x = N_t =  20: max |U - u| = 6.81e-04, wall time 5.2e-05 s


N_x = N_t =  40: max |U - u| = 1.70e-04, wall time 1.1e-04 s
N_x = N_t =  80: max |U - u| = 4.25e-05, wall time 4.3e-04 s


N_x = N_t = 160: max |U - u| = 1.06e-05, wall time 9.5e-04 s


The error falls by a factor of four whenever the grid spacing and the time step are halved, from \(2.7\times10^{-3}\) at \(N_x=10\) to \(1.1\times10^{-5}\) at \(N_x=160\), the second-order convergence of the scheme. The wall time stays at the level of a millisecond or below on all grids, from \(3\times10^{-5}\) s at \(N_x=10\) to \(8\times10^{-4}\) s at \(N_x=160\).


PINN of the heat equation
The network \(u_\theta(x,t)\) now has two inputs. Both are rescaled to \([-1,1]\), and the hidden layers are those of the oscillator, three layers of 32 tanh units. The residual of the heat equation is \[r_\theta(x,t)=\partial_tu_\theta(x,t)-D\,\partial_x^2u_\theta(x,t),\] where jax.grad with respect to \(t\) gives the time derivative and jax.hessian with respect to \(x\) the second space derivative. The loss contains three terms, \[\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L(\theta)={}&\frac1{N_r}\sum_{i=1}^{N_r}r_\theta(x_i,t_i)^2+\frac1{N_0}\sum_{k=1}^{N_0}\big[u_\theta(x_k,0)-u_0(x_k)\big]^2\\
&+\frac1{N_b}\sum_{l=1}^{N_b}\big[u_\theta(0,t_l)^2+u_\theta(1,t_l)^2\big].
\end{aligned}\] The first term is the mean squared residual at \(N_r=41\times41=1681\) collocation points \((x_i,t_i)\) on a regular grid of the domain \([0,1]\times[0,t_{\max}]\). The second term enforces the initial profile at \(N_0=101\) equally spaced positions \(x_k\), and the third term the boundary conditions at \(N_b=51\) equally spaced times \(t_l\) at both ends. All weights equal one. Every loss evaluation costs about eight times as many network passes as for the oscillator, and we shorten the training to 5000 Adam steps with the cosine schedule and 2000 L-BFGS iterations. The error is the largest deviation \(\max|u_\theta-u|\) from the series solution on a grid of \(101\times101\) points.


Code
SIZES_H = [2] + [WIDTH] * DEPTH + [1]

def heat_net(params, x, t):
    # network u_theta(x, t); both inputs rescaled to [-1, 1]
    h = jnp.array([2 * x - 1, 2 * t / T_MAX - 1])
    for W, b in params[:-1]:
        h = jnp.tanh(W @ h + b)
    W, b = params[-1]
    return (W @ h + b)[0]
heat_ut = jax.grad(heat_net, argnums=2)              # du_theta/dt
heat_uxx = jax.hessian(heat_net, argnums=1)          # d^2u_theta/dx^2

N_XC = 41
XC, TC = [jnp.asarray(a.ravel()) for a in np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, 1, N_XC), np.linspace(0, T_MAX, N_XC))]
X_IC = jnp.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 101); U_IC = u0_heat(X_IC)
T_BC = jnp.linspace(0.0, T_MAX, 51)

def make_heat_loss(split, x_obs=None, t_obs=None, y_obs=None):
    # split(q) returns (network parameters, D); the data term is added when observations are given
    def loss(q):
        params, D = split(q)
        r = jax.vmap(lambda x, t: heat_ut(params, x, t) - D * heat_uxx(params, x, t))(XC, TC)
        L = jnp.mean(r**2)
        L += jnp.mean((jax.vmap(lambda x: heat_net(params, x, 0.0))(X_IC) - U_IC)**2)
        L += jnp.mean(jax.vmap(lambda t: heat_net(params, 0.0, t)**2 + heat_net(params, 1.0, t)**2)(T_BC))
        if y_obs is not None:
            L += jnp.mean((jax.vmap(lambda x, t: heat_net(params, x, t))(x_obs, t_obs) - y_obs)**2)
        return L
    return loss

heat_field = jax.jit(lambda p: jax.vmap(lambda x, t: heat_net(p, x, t))(jnp.asarray(XH.ravel()), jnp.asarray(TH.ravel())).reshape(XH.shape))
heat_err = lambda p: float(np.abs(np.asarray(heat_field(p)) - UH).max())

N_ADAM_H, N_LBFGS_H = 5000, 2000
p_heat0 = init_mlp(jax.random.key(0), SIZES_H)
p_heat, hist_heat = train(make_heat_loss(lambda q: (q, D_TRUE)), p_heat0, N_ADAM_H, N_LBFGS_H, monitor=heat_err)
U_pinn = np.asarray(heat_field(p_heat))
i_sw = np.searchsorted(hist_heat["it"], N_ADAM_H)
fd_better = [r for r in rows_heat if r["err"] < hist_heat["mon"][-1]]
print(f"network {SIZES_H}, {n_params(p_heat0)} parameters; {N_ADAM_H} Adam + {N_LBFGS_H} L-BFGS iterations in {hist_heat['time']:.1f} s")
print(f"final loss {hist_heat['final_loss']:.1e}; max |u_PINN - u|: after Adam {hist_heat['mon'][i_sw - 1]:.1e}, final {heat_err(p_heat):.1e}")
print(f"coarsest Crank-Nicolson grid more accurate than the PINN: N_x = {fd_better[0]['nx']},"
      f" error {fd_better[0]['err']:.1e}, {fd_better[0]['time']:.1e} s")
nums["heat_pinn"] = dict(n_params=n_params(p_heat0), time=hist_heat["time"], loss=hist_heat["final_loss"],
                         err_adam=float(hist_heat["mon"][i_sw - 1]), err=heat_err(p_heat), n_col=N_XC**2,
                         fd_nx=fd_better[0]["nx"], fd_err=fd_better[0]["err"], fd_time=fd_better[0]["time"])


network [2, 32, 32, 32, 1], 2241 parameters; 5000 Adam + 2000 L-BFGS iterations in 43.5 s
final loss 2.6e-06; max |u_PINN - u|: after Adam 6.8e-03, final 9.5e-04
coarsest Crank-Nicolson grid more accurate than the PINN: N_x = 20, error 6.8e-04, 5.2e-05 s


The network has 2241 parameters, and the 7000 iterations take 44 s. At the end of the Adam stage the maximal error is \(6.8\times10^{-3}\), and L-BFGS lowers it to \(9.5\times10^{-4}\) at the final loss \(2.6\times10^{-6}\). The left panel compares the PINN (dashed) with the series solution (black) at three times. The middle panel shows the absolute error \(|u_\theta-u|\) over the domain, multiplied by \(10^3\). The right panel shows the maximal error \(\max|u_{\rm num}-u|\) against the wall time, for the Crank–Nicolson solutions on the five grids and for the training of the PINN (star).


Code
def label_profiles(ax, times, place):
    # time labels of the profiles; place[t] = (x, y) of the label and, optionally, the end point of a leader line
    for tk in times:
        p = place[tk]
        ax.annotate(f"$t={tk:g}$", xy=p[2] if len(p) > 2 else p[:2], xytext=p[:2], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11,
                    zorder=4, arrowprops=(dict(arrowstyle="-", color="0.4", lw=0.8, shrinkA=1, shrinkB=0) if len(p) > 2 else None))

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 2.2), layout="constrained", gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.15, 1]})
    ax = axs[0]
    for j, tk in enumerate((0.0, 0.3, 1.0)):
        k = int(round(tk / T_MAX * 100))
        ax.plot(XH[0], UH[k], color="k", lw=1.0, label=("exact" if j == 0 else None))
        ax.plot(XH[0], U_pinn[k], "--", color=COL["PINN"], lw=1.4, label=("PINN" if j == 0 else None))
    label_profiles(ax, (0.0, 0.3, 1.0), {0.0: (0.22, 1.2), 0.3: (0.5, 0.95, (0.5, 0.72)), 1.0: (0.5, 0.26)})
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$u$"); ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.35)
    ax = axs[1]
    im = ax.pcolormesh(XH, TH, 1e3 * np.abs(U_pinn - UH), cmap="magma_r", shading="auto", rasterized=True)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$t$")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.08, pad=0.03)
    ax.set_title(r"$10^3\,|u_\theta-u|$")
    ax = axs[2]
    ax.loglog([r["time"] for r in rows_heat], [r["err"] for r in rows_heat], "o-", color=COL["RK4"], ms=4, label="Crank–Nicolson")
    ax.loglog([hist_heat["time"]], [hist_heat["mon"][-1]], "*", color=COL["PINN"], ms=10, label="PINN training")
    ax.set_xlabel("wall time [s]"); ax.set_ylabel(r"max $|u_{\rm num}-u|$")
    ax.set_xticks([1e-4, 1e-1, 1e2])
    fig.legend(*[a + b for a, b in zip(axs[0].get_legend_handles_labels(), axs[2].get_legend_handles_labels())],
               loc="outside upper center", ncol=4, fontsize=11, handlelength=1.5, columnspacing=1.0)
    save(fig, "fig_lab041_heat_pinn"); plt.show()





The error of the PINN is largest close to the corners \(x=0\) and \(x=1\) at \(t=1\) and along the initial line \(t=0\), where the loss balances the initial profile, the boundary conditions and the residual against each other. The Crank–Nicolson solution on the grid \(N_x=N_t=20\) is already more accurate, with the error \(6.8\times10^{-4}\), and takes about \(5\times10^{-5}\) s, about \(1\times10^{6}\) times less than the training. For the forward problem of the heat equation with known \(D\) and known initial and boundary conditions the finite-difference solver is the better tool, as the RK4 integration was for the oscillator. A grid in one space dimension is cheap. The mesh-free formulation of a PINN can matter for many space dimensions or irregular domains, which this notebook does not test.


Thermal diffusivity from four thermometers
In the inverse problem the diffusivity \(D\) is unknown, and four thermometers at the fixed positions \(x_s=0.1,\,0.3,\,0.55,\,0.8\) record the temperature at the 20 times \(t_j=0.05\,j\), \(j=1,\dots,20\). The readings carry independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma=0.01\), \[y_{sj}=u(x_s,t_j)+\sigma\varepsilon_{sj},\qquad \varepsilon_{sj}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).\] The initial profile and the temperature of the ends are known. The loss of the forward problem receives the data term \[\mathcal L_{\rm data}(\theta)=\frac1{N_{\rm obs}}\sum_{s,j}\big[u_\theta(x_s,t_j)-y_{sj}\big]^2,\qquad N_{\rm obs}=80,\] and the residual uses the trainable diffusivity \(D=e^{s}\), written through its logarithm \(s\) so that it stays positive. Training starts from \(D=0.3\), three times the true value, with the same budget as the forward problem. The trained network is at the same time an estimate of the whole temperature field \(u(x,t)\) that is consistent with the heat equation and with the sparse readings, a simple example of data assimilation.
The classical reference fits \(D\) through the Crank–Nicolson solver. On the grid \(N_x=100\), \(N_t=200\) the thermometer positions and reading times are grid nodes, and scipy.optimize.least_squares minimises the sum of the squared normalised deviations \([U(x_s,t_j;D)-y_{sj}]/\sigma\) over \(D\). Its standard error follows from the Jacobian as for the oscillator. We repeat both estimates for five noise realisations.


Code
X_SENS = np.array([0.1, 0.3, 0.55, 0.8]); T_READ = 0.05 * np.arange(1, 21); SIGMA_HEAT, D_INIT = 0.01, 0.3
XO, TO = [jnp.asarray(a.ravel()) for a in np.meshgrid(X_SENS, T_READ)]    # readings ordered by time, then position
NX_LS, NT_LS = 100, 200
IX = np.round(X_SENS * NX_LS).astype(int); IT = np.round(T_READ / T_MAX * NT_LS).astype(int)
cn_at_sensors = jax.jit(lambda D: cn_solve(D, NX_LS, NT_LS)[IT][:, IX].ravel())
jax.block_until_ready(cn_at_sensors(D_INIT))                                 # compile once

inv_heat = []
for seed in range(5):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(100 + seed)
    y_h = jnp.asarray(u_heat(np.asarray(XO), np.asarray(TO)) + SIGMA_HEAT * rng.normal(size=XO.shape))
    q0 = (init_mlp(jax.random.key(seed), SIZES_H), jnp.log(D_INIT))
    q, h_h = train(make_heat_loss(lambda q: (q[0], jnp.exp(q[1])), XO, TO, y_h), q0, N_ADAM_H, N_LBFGS_H,
                   monitor=lambda q: float(jnp.exp(q[1])))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    ls = least_squares(lambda z: (np.asarray(cn_at_sensors(z[0])) - np.asarray(y_h)) / SIGMA_HEAT, x0=[D_INIT])
    t_ls = time.perf_counter() - t0
    inv_heat.append(dict(D_pinn=float(jnp.exp(q[1])), D_ls=float(ls.x[0]), D_ls_err=float(np.sqrt(np.linalg.inv(ls.jac.T @ ls.jac)[0, 0])),
                         field_err=heat_err(q[0]), time=h_h["time"], t_ls=t_ls, nfev=int(ls.nfev), hist=h_h, q=q, y=y_h))
    r = inv_heat[-1]
    print(f"noise seed {seed}: D_PINN = {r['D_pinn']:.5f}, D_least-squares = {r['D_ls']:.5f} +- {r['D_ls_err']:.5f},"
          f" max |u_PINN - u| = {r['field_err']:.1e}, PINN {r['time']:.0f} s, least squares {t_ls:.2f} s ({r['nfev']} solver calls)")
dp = np.array([r["D_pinn"] for r in inv_heat]); dl_ = np.array([r["D_ls"] for r in inv_heat])

In all five realisations the estimate of \(D\) falls from its starting value 0.3 below the true value early in the Adam stage, then approaches the true value and stays there under L-BFGS. For the first realisation the PINN gives \(D=0.10008\) and the least-squares fit \(0.09987\pm0.00051\). Over the five realisations the PINN estimates have the mean 0.09983 and the standard deviation 0.00057, the least-squares estimates 0.09978 and 0.00052. On the same data the two estimates differ by at most 0.00021, less than half of the statistical error of the fit, so for this problem the PINN and the classical fit give the same diffusivity within the noise. The reconstructed field deviates from the series solution by at most \(1.6\times10^{-3}\) for the first realisation and by at most \(3.3\times10^{-3}\) over all five, compared with \(9.5\times10^{-4}\) for the forward PINN with known \(D\).
The cost differs by orders of magnitude. One PINN training takes 46 s on average, while the least-squares fit needs 8 Crank–Nicolson solutions and about 0.06 s. The Crank–Nicolson solution with the fitted \(D\) also gives the whole field, so in this setting with a known initial profile the PINN offers no advantage in accuracy or cost. The advantage of the PINN lies in the form of its loss. An unknown initial profile, readings at arbitrary positions and times or a different equation enter by adding, removing or changing terms, while the classical route requires adapting the solver or the fitting procedure to each such change. This notebook does not test these extensions.

title: Lab 041: Physics-informed neural networks
text:
6. Pendulum over several periods
For the pendulum the network \(\theta_{\rm PINN}(t)\) has the residual \(r(t)=\ddot\theta_{\rm PINN}(t)+\omega_p^2\sin\theta_{\rm PINN}(t)\), and the loss contains its mean square and the initial conditions \(\theta_{\rm PINN}(0)=\theta_0\), \(\dot\theta_{\rm PINN}(0)=0\) with unit weights. We keep the network, the optimiser and the training budget of the oscillator, place 100 collocation points per period and train on windows of one, two and four periods \(T_p\), each with three random initialisations (seeds). A second experiment trains in time order, one network per period, each started from the end state \((\theta_{\rm PINN},\dot\theta_{\rm PINN})\) of the previous one. The error is measured against the RK4 reference with step \(10^{-3}\).


Code
def pend_pinn(t_a, t_b, y0, n_col, seed=0):
    # PINN theta_PINN(t) for theta'' + omega_p^2 sin(theta) = 0 on [t_a, t_b] with theta(t_a), theta'(t_a) = y0
    net_p, d1_p, d2_p = make_net(t_a, t_b)
    t_col = jnp.linspace(t_a, t_b, n_col)
    def loss(p):
        r = jax.vmap(lambda t: d2_p(p, t) + OMEGA_P2 * jnp.sin(net_p(p, t)))(t_col)
        return jnp.mean(r**2) + (net_p(p, t_a) - y0[0])**2 + (d1_p(p, t_a) - y0[1])**2
    p, h = train(loss, init_mlp(jax.random.key(seed), SIZES), N_ADAM, N_LBFGS)
    th = lambda t: np.asarray(jax.vmap(lambda s: net_p(p, s))(jnp.asarray(t)))
    om = lambda t: np.asarray(jax.vmap(lambda s: d1_p(p, s))(jnp.asarray(t)))
    return th, om, h

N_COL_PER = 100                       # collocation points per period
t_ref = t_pend[::10]; th_ref = Y_pend[::10, 0]          # RK4 reference on a grid of spacing 0.01
pend_runs = {}
for n_per in (1, 2, 4):
    for seed in (0, 1, 2):
        th, om, h = pend_pinn(0.0, n_per * T_PEND, (TH0, 0.0), N_COL_PER * n_per, seed)
        m = t_ref <= n_per * T_PEND + 1e-9
        e = np.abs(th(t_ref[m]) - th_ref[m])
        bad = np.nonzero(e > 0.1)[0]
        pend_runs[(n_per, seed)] = dict(err=float(e.max()), loss=h["final_loss"], time=h["time"], th=th,
                                        t_fail=float(t_ref[m][bad[0]]) if len(bad) else None)
        print(f"window {n_per} period(s), seed {seed}: final loss {h['final_loss']:.1e}, max |theta_PINN - theta_RK4| ="
              f" {e.max():.1e}, first time with error > 0.1: {pend_runs[(n_per, seed)]['t_fail']}, {h['time']:.0f} s")
nums["pend_windows"] = {f"{k[0]} {k[1]}": dict(err=v["err"], loss=v["loss"], t_fail=v["t_fail"]) for k, v in pend_runs.items()}

On one period all three seeds reach maximal errors between \(3.7\times10^{-5}\) and \(6.9\times10^{-5}\). On two periods all three seeds converge to the same function with the loss \(3.1\times10^{-3}\), which leaves the solution at \(t=1.95\) and settles at the upright position \(\theta=-\pi\). This equilibrium satisfies the equation of motion at almost every collocation point, so the loss is small although the function is far from the solution. On four periods seeds 0 and 1 reach errors of \(6.5\times10^{-2}\) and \(5.2\times10^{-2}\), and seed 2 fails in the same way with an error of 5.1. Failures of this kind are documented for PINNs and attributed to the optimisation of the residual loss [Krishnapriyan et al., NeurIPS 2021, arXiv:2109.01050]. Training one network per period removes the failure, and the error grows from \(6.9\times10^{-5}\) in the first window to \(1.4\times10^{-3}\) in the fourth, since every window starts from the slightly wrong end state of the previous one. The four trainings take 61 s, and RK4 with \(h=0.01\) integrates the same four periods in about \(3\times10^{-4}\) s. Wang, Sankaran and Perdikaris reach a similar ordering in time within a single network by weighting the residual at later times by the size of the residual at earlier times [arXiv:2203.07404]. The figure shows the deviation \(|\theta_{\rm PINN}-\theta_{\rm RK4}|\) on a logarithmic axis for the networks of seed 0 trained on two and on four periods and for the training with one network per period, whose first window is the one-period network. The thin vertical lines mark multiples of \(T_p\).

title: Lab 041: Physics-informed neural networks
text:
Summary
A physics-informed neural network represents the solution of a differential equation by a multilayer perceptron and trains it on the mean squared residual of the equation at collocation points, with the derivatives from automatic differentiation, plus penalty terms for the initial and boundary conditions and for data. On the damped oscillator the network with 2209 parameters reaches a maximal error of \(1.2\times10^{-3}\) after 10000 Adam and 3000 L-BFGS iterations. A fourth-order Runge–Kutta integration with \(h=0.2\) is more accurate and more than a million times faster, and the adaptive Tsit5 solver of diffrax reaches \(8\times10^{-12}\) with a few thousand evaluations, so for a forward initial-value problem of a low-dimensional ODE the PINN does not compete with a classical solver.
The residual pays off in combination with data. Twelve exact samples of the first 1.3 periods suffice to reconstruct the oscillation over the whole window with an error of \(3.0\times10^{-4}\), where a fit of the same network to the data alone drifts away by 1.2 outside the data window. With noisy observations and an unknown damping the same loss estimates \(c\) together with the trajectory, \(0.4009\pm0.0056\) over five noise realisations for the true value 0.4, against \(0.3998\pm0.0040\) for a least-squares fit of the closed-form solution.
The heat equation \(\partial_tu=D\partial_x^2u\) in a rod repeats both findings for a partial differential equation. With known \(D\) the PINN reaches \(9.5\times10^{-4}\), while a Crank–Nicolson solver on a grid of \(20\times20\) points is more accurate in a time about a million times shorter. With \(D\) unknown and four thermometers read at 20 times with noise \(\sigma=0.01\), the PINN estimates \(D=0.09983\pm0.00057\) for the true value 0.1, the same within the noise as a least-squares fit through the Crank–Nicolson solver, \(0.09978\pm0.00052\), and returns the whole temperature field with an error of a few times \(10^{-3}\). The classical fit is again much faster.
The pendulum shows the main weakness of the method. On one period the PINN agrees with RK4 to below \(10^{-4}\), while on longer windows the training can converge to the upright equilibrium, a function with a small residual far from the solution. Training one network per period removes this failure at a cost many orders of magnitude above that of RK4. These conclusions refer to the networks, budgets and problems of this notebook.

title: Lab 042: Neural ordinary differential equations
text:
1. Euler steps and residual networks
The explicit Euler method integrates \(\dot{\mathbf x}=\mathbf F(\mathbf x)\) by replacing the derivative with a forward difference over the step \(\Delta t\), \[\mathbf x_{k+1}=\mathbf x_k+\Delta t\,\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k).\] The new state is the old state plus a correction computed from the old state. A residual network (ResNet) has the same structure [K. He, X. Zhang, S. Ren, J. Sun, arXiv:1512.03385]. Its hidden representation \(\mathbf h_l\) passes from layer \(l\) to layer \(l+1\) through a block that adds a learned correction to its input, \[\mathbf h_{l+1}=\mathbf h_l+\mathbf f_l(\mathbf h_l),\] where \(\mathbf f_l\) is a small network with its own parameters. The identity path lets the signal and its gradient pass through many layers, which made networks with more than a hundred layers trainable. Weinan E and, independently, Haber and Ruthotto read the ResNet as an Euler discretisation of a continuous dynamical system, with the layer index playing the role of time [W. E, Commun. Math. Stat. 5, 1 (2017), doi:10.1007/s40304-017-0103-z; E. Haber, L. Ruthotto, Inverse Probl. 34, 014004 (2018), arXiv:1705.03341].
Writing \(\mathbf f_l(\mathbf h)=\Delta t\,F_\theta(\mathbf h)\) with a single network \(F_\theta\) shared by all layers and letting the number of layers grow as \(L=T/\Delta t\) with fixed total time \(T\), the sequence \(\mathbf h_0,\mathbf h_1,\dots,\mathbf h_L\) approaches the solution of \[\dot{\mathbf x}(t)=F_\theta(\mathbf x(t)),\qquad \mathbf x(0)=\mathbf h_0,\] at the times \(t=l\,\Delta t\). The global error of Euler’s method is proportional to \(\Delta t\), so the limit exists for a smooth \(F_\theta\). In this limit the depth of the network is replaced by the integration time, and any ODE solver can perform the forward pass. A Neural ODE uses this continuous form directly. We check the first-order convergence on the harmonic oscillator \(\ddot x=-x\), integrated over one period \(T=2\pi\) from \((x,\dot x)=(1,0)\) with decreasing \(\Delta t\).


Code
f_ho = lambda y: jnp.array([y[1], -y[0]])          # harmonic oscillator x'' = -x, state (x, v)
def euler_path(f, y0, dt, n):
    # explicit Euler x_{k+1} = x_k + dt f(x_k); returns x_0, ..., x_n
    ys = [np.asarray(y0, float)]
    for _ in range(n):
        ys.append(ys[-1] + dt * np.asarray(f(ys[-1])))
    return np.array(ys)

T_HO = 2 * np.pi
rows_e = []
for dt in (0.5, 0.2, 0.05, 0.01):
    n = int(round(T_HO / dt))
    ys = euler_path(f_ho, [1.0, 0.0], T_HO / n, n)
    err = float(np.linalg.norm(ys[-1] - np.array([1.0, 0.0])))
    rows_e.append(dict(dt=T_HO / n, n=n, err=err, r_end=float(np.linalg.norm(ys[-1]))))
    print(f"dt = {T_HO / n:.4f} ({n:4d} steps): |x_n - x(2 pi)| = {err:.3e}, radius at t = 2 pi {np.linalg.norm(ys[-1]):.4f}")
slopes = np.diff(np.log([r["err"] for r in rows_e])) / np.diff(np.log([r["dt"] for r in rows_e]))
print("local slopes d log(error) / d log(dt):", np.round(slopes, 2))
nums["euler"] = dict(rows=rows_e, slopes=slopes.tolist())

Over one period the error of the final state falls from 3.03 at \(\Delta t=0.48\) to \(3.2\times10^{-2}\) at \(\Delta t=0.01\), and the local slope of \(\log({\rm error})\) against \(\log\Delta t\) approaches one (1.43, 1.17, 1.04), the first-order convergence of Euler’s method. The radius \(\sqrt{x^2+\dot x^2}\) at \(t=2\pi\) is 3.91 for the coarsest step and 1.032 for the finest, against the exact value 1. The left part of the figure draws three residual blocks. Each block feeds \(\mathbf h_l\) both into the network \(\mathbf f_l\) and along the identity path to the sum node, which returns \(\mathbf h_{l+1}\). The right panel shows the Euler polygons of the harmonic oscillator in the phase plane \((x,\dot x)\) for three step sizes, together with the exact circle.

    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 2.6), layout="constrained", gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.35, 1]})
    ax = axs[0]
    # a stack of three residual blocks h_{l+1} = h_l + f_l(h_l)

    ax.text(2.4, -1.0, r"$h_{l+1}=h_l+f_l(h_l)$", ha="center", va="top")
    ax.text(2.4, -1.5, r"$x_{k+1}=x_k+\Delta t\,F(x_k)$", ha="center", va="top")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 5.1); ax.set_ylim(-1.95, 1.0); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    ax = axs[1]
    th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
    ax.plot(np.cos(th), -np.sin(th), color="k", lw=1.0, label="exact")
    for dt, c in ((0.5, "0.65"), (0.2, DSOrange), (0.05, UJBlue)):
        n = int(round(T_HO / dt)); ys = euler_path(f_ho, [1.0, 0.0], T_HO / n, n)
        ax.plot(ys[:, 0], ys[:, 1], ".-", color=c, lw=0.9, ms=3, label=rf"$\Delta t={T_HO / n:.2f}$")
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\dot x$"); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlim(-4.2, 4.2); ax.set_ylim(-4.2, 4.2); ax.set_xticks([-4, 0, 4]); ax.set_yticks([-4, 0, 4])
    fig.legend(*ax.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="outside upper center", ncol=4, fontsize=10, handlelength=1.4, columnspacing=1.0)
    save(fig, "fig_lab042_resnet_euler"); plt.show()





Every Euler step of the oscillator multiplies the radius \(\sqrt{x^2+\dot x^2}\) by \(\sqrt{1+\Delta t^2}\), so the polygon spirals outwards, and the spiral approaches the circle as \(\Delta t\) decreases. A ResNet with few layers corresponds to a coarse step, and the continuous limit removes this discretisation from the model. In practice the forward pass of a Neural ODE uses an accurate solver such as RK4, and the network \(F_\theta\) is called four times per step.

title: Lab 042: Neural ordinary differential equations
text:
2. Forward pass, loss and gradients
The forward pass of a Neural ODE maps a measured initial state \(\mathbf y_0\) to predictions at the observation times \(t_1<t_2<\dots<t_K\), \[\tilde{\mathbf x}(t_k)=\mathbf y_0+\int_0^{t_k}F_\theta(\tilde{\mathbf x}(t))\,dt ,\] evaluated with an ODE solver. The loss is the mean squared distance between the integrated and the measured trajectory, \[\mathcal L(\theta)=\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\big\|\tilde{\mathbf x}(t_k)-\mathbf y_k\big\|^2 .\] The drawing shows the vector-field network \(F_\theta\) as nodes and edges inside the solver loop. Each RK4 step calls the network four times, at the stages \(\mathbf k_1,\dots,\mathbf k_4\), and combines the four velocities into the next state, \(\mathbf x_{n+1}=\mathbf x_n+\frac h6(\mathbf k_1+2\mathbf k_2+2\mathbf k_3+\mathbf k_4)\). The loop runs until the observation times, where the states enter the loss.


Code
def draw_layers(ax, sizes, labels, xs, ys_span=2.2, node_r=0.11, colors=None, edge_color="0.75"):
    """Nodes-and-edges drawing of a fully connected network, columns at x = xs, labels below the columns."""
    cols = []
    for n, x in zip(sizes, xs):
        ys = np.linspace(ys_span / 2, -ys_span / 2, n) if n > 1 else np.array([0.0])
        cols.append([(x, y) for y in ys])
    for a, b in zip(cols[:-1], cols[1:]):
        for (x0, y0) in a:
            for (x1, y1) in b:
                ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=edge_color, lw=0.6, zorder=1)
    for i, col in enumerate(cols):
        for (x, y) in col:
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), node_r, fc=(colors[i] if colors else "#DCE6F2"), ec=UJNavy, lw=1.0, zorder=3))
    for i, lab in enumerate(labels):
        ax.text(xs[i], -ys_span / 2 - 0.22, lab, ha="center", va="top", linespacing=1.1)
    return cols

def box(ax, x, y, text, w, h, fc, **kw):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.04", fc=fc, ec=UJNavy, lw=1.0, zorder=3))
    ax.text(x, y, text, ha="center", va="center", zorder=4, **kw)

def arrow(ax, p, q, **kw):
    ax.annotate("", xy=q, xytext=p, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=UJNavy, lw=1.0, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0, **kw), zorder=2)

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.8)); ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
    # the vector-field network F_theta: state in, velocity out
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((1.55, -1.25), 2.9, 2.55, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05", fc="#FAFAFA", ec="0.6", lw=0.8, zorder=0))
    cols = draw_layers(ax, [2, 5, 5, 2], [r"$\mathbf{x}$", "", "", r"$F_\theta(\mathbf{x})$"], xs=[1.85, 2.65, 3.4, 4.15],
                       ys_span=1.7, node_r=0.09, colors=["#DCE6F2", "#F6E3D3", "#F6E3D3", "#E3F1EE"])
    for col in cols[1:3]:
        ax.text(col[0][0], 0.5 * (col[-2][1] + col[-1][1]), r"$\vdots$", ha="center", va="center", zorder=4,
                bbox=dict(fc="white", ec="none", pad=0.3))
    ax.text(3.0, 1.38, r"vector field network $F_\theta$", ha="center", va="bottom")
    # solver loop
    box(ax, 0.35, 0.0, r"$\mathbf{x}_n$", 0.6, 0.4, "#DCE6F2")
    box(ax, 6.0, 0.0, "RK4 step\n" + r"$\mathbf{x}_{n+1}=\mathbf{x}_n+\frac{h}{6}\sum_s b_s\mathbf{k}_s$", 2.2, 0.75, "#EFEFEF", fontsize=10)
    arrow(ax, (0.65, 0.0), (1.7, 0.0))
    ax.text(1.15, 0.12, "4 calls\nper step", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=10, color=UJGray)
    arrow(ax, (4.3, 0.0), (4.9, 0.0)); ax.text(4.6, 0.12, r"$\mathbf{k}_s$", ha="center", va="bottom")
    # feedback path below the network: the new state is the input of the next step
    ax.plot([6.0, 6.0, 0.35], [-0.38, -1.55, -1.55], color=UJNavy, lw=1.0, zorder=2)
    arrow(ax, (0.35, -1.55), (0.35, -0.2))
    ax.text(3.2, -1.62, r"$n\to n+1$, repeated until the observation times $t_k$", ha="center", va="top")
    box(ax, 6.0, 1.1, r"$\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_k\|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(t_k)-\mathbf{y}_k\|^2$", 2.2, 0.45, "#E3F1EE", fontsize=10)
    arrow(ax, (6.0, 0.38), (6.0, 0.87)); ax.text(6.08, 0.6, r"$\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(t_k)$", ha="left", va="center")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.05, 7.15); ax.set_ylim(-2.0, 1.6); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    save(fig, "fig_lab042_node_architecture"); plt.show()






Two ways to compute the gradient
The first way treats the solver as a program. With a fixed step \(h\) the prediction is a composition of RK4 steps, each a composition of network calls, and reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backpropagation) through all of them gives the exact gradient of the discretised loss. This is called discretise-then-optimise. Backpropagation needs the intermediate values of the forward pass, so its memory grows in proportion to the number of steps.
The second way, optimise-then-discretise, derives an equation for the gradient of the continuous problem and solves it numerically. Consider first a loss \(\mathcal L(\mathbf x(T))\) that depends on the final state only. A small change \(\delta\theta\) of the parameters changes the trajectory by \(\delta\mathbf x(t)\), which obeys the linearised equation \[\delta\dot{\mathbf x}=J(t)\,\delta\mathbf x+\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\theta}\delta\theta,\qquad J(t)=\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\mathbf x}\Big|_{\mathbf x(t)},\qquad \delta\mathbf x(0)=0 .\] Let the adjoint state \(\mathbf a(t)\) solve \[\dot{\mathbf a}(t)=-J(t)^\top\mathbf a(t),\qquad \mathbf a(T)=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf x(T)} .\] Then \(\frac{d}{dt}\big(\mathbf a^\top\delta\mathbf x\big)=\mathbf a^\top\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\theta}\delta\theta\), since the two terms with \(J\) cancel. Integrating from \(0\) to \(T\) and using \(\delta\mathbf x(0)=0\) gives \(\delta\mathcal L=\mathbf a(T)^\top\delta\mathbf x(T)=\int_0^T\mathbf a^\top\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\theta}dt\,\delta\theta\), hence \[\frac{d\mathcal L}{d\theta}=\int_0^T\mathbf a(t)^\top\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\theta}\Big|_{\mathbf x(t)}dt .\] The adjoint is integrated backwards from \(t=T\) to \(t=0\). With observations at several times the loss is a sum of terms, and by linearity \(\mathbf a\) receives the jump \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf x(t_k)\) whenever the backward integration passes an observation time. The state \(\mathbf x(t)\) needed in \(J(t)\) is recomputed by integrating the Neural ODE backwards together with \(\mathbf a\) and the running integral \(\mathbf g(t)\) of the gradient, so the augmented system \[\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf x\\ \mathbf a\\ \mathbf g\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}F_\theta(\mathbf x)\\ -J^\top\mathbf a\\ -\big(\partial F_\theta/\partial\theta\big)^\top\mathbf a\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf g(T)=0,\qquad \mathbf g(0)=\frac{d\mathcal L}{d\theta},\] is solved from \(T\) to \(0\). The products \(J^\top\mathbf a\) and \((\partial F_\theta/\partial\theta)^\top\mathbf a\) are vector–Jacobian products, which jax.vjp evaluates at the cost of about one backward pass through the network, and the memory no longer depends on the number of steps. The same equations are the costate equations of Pontryagin’s optimal control theory. Their use for Neural ODEs, with the backward recomputation of \(\mathbf x(t)\), is due to Chen et al., and Kidger reviews the method and its variants.
The adjoint gradient is the gradient of the continuous loss computed with a numerical error, and it differs from the exact gradient of the discretised loss by an amount that vanishes with the step size. The backward reconstruction of \(\mathbf x(t)\) is also a source of error, since a contracting forward flow expands when integrated backwards [A. Gholami, K. Keutzer, G. Biros, arXiv:1902.10298].


Code
GAMMA_P = 0.2                                       # damping of the pendulum used in this section and in Section 3
f_dp = lambda y: jnp.array([y[1], -jnp.sin(y[0]) - GAMMA_P * y[1]])
DT_OBS, N_OBS = 0.1, 50                             # observations every 0.1 time units, 50 of them
x0_g = jnp.array([1.0, 0.0])
Y_g = rk4_path(f_dp, x0_g, 0.01, N_OBS, sub=10)     # observed states y_k = x(t_k), t_k = 0.1 k, k = 1..50
p_g = init_mlp(jax.random.key(0), [2, 32, 32, 2])   # an untrained vector-field network
F = lambda p, x: mlp(p, x)

def loss_direct(p, sub):
    # discretise-then-optimise: RK4 with `sub` steps per observation interval; jax.grad differentiates through all steps
    xs = rk4_path(lambda x: F(p, x), x0_g, DT_OBS / sub, N_OBS, sub)
    return jnp.mean(jnp.sum((xs - Y_g)**2, 1))

def grad_adjoint(p, sub):
    # optimise-then-discretise: forward solve, then the adjoint system integrated backwards with the same RK4 step
    h = DT_OBS / sub
    xs = rk4_path(lambda x: F(p, x), x0_g, h, N_OBS, sub)
    dLdx = 2 * (xs - Y_g) / N_OBS                     # dL/dx(t_k), the jumps of the adjoint at the observation times
    flat, unravel = ravel_pytree(p)
    def aug(s):
        # augmented system for (x, a, g): dx/dt = F, da/dt = -(dF/dx)^T a, dg/dt = -(dF/dtheta)^T a
        x, a, g = s
        fx, vjp = jax.vjp(lambda x, q: F(unravel(q), x), x, flat)
        ax, aq = vjp(a)
        return (fx, -ax, -aq)
    def rk4_tree(s, h):
        add = lambda s, k, c: jax.tree.map(lambda u, v: u + c * v, s, k)
        k1 = aug(s); k2 = aug(add(s, k1, h / 2)); k3 = aug(add(s, k2, h / 2)); k4 = aug(add(s, k3, h))
        return jax.tree.map(lambda y, a, b, c, d: y + h / 6 * (a + 2 * b + 2 * c + d), s, k1, k2, k3, k4)
    def interval(s, k):
        # integrate backwards from t_{k+1} to t_k, then add the jump dL/dx(t_k) (no observation at t_0)
        s = jax.lax.fori_loop(0, sub, lambda i, s: rk4_tree(s, -h), s)
        a = s[1] + jnp.where(k > 0, 1.0, 0.0) * dLdx[jnp.maximum(k - 1, 0)]
        return (s[0], a, s[2]), None
    s0 = (xs[-1], dLdx[-1], jnp.zeros_like(flat))
    s, _ = jax.lax.scan(interval, s0, jnp.arange(N_OBS - 1, -1, -1))
    return unravel(s[2])

T_OBS = DT_OBS * np.arange(1, N_OBS + 1)               # observation times as a numpy array (static for diffrax)
def loss_diffrax(p, sub, adjoint=diffrax.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint()):
    # the same loss with diffrax: our RK4 tableau, constant step, states saved at the observation times;
    # the default RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint backpropagates through the solver steps with checkpointing
    sol = diffrax.diffeqsolve(diffrax.ODETerm(lambda t, y, args: F(args, y)), RK4(), 0.0, float(T_OBS[-1]), DT_OBS / sub,
                              x0_g, args=p, saveat=diffrax.SaveAt(ts=jnp.asarray(T_OBS)), stepsize_controller=diffrax.ConstantStepSize(),
                              adjoint=adjoint)
    return jnp.mean(jnp.sum((sol.ys - Y_g)**2, 1))
