The spectral radius matters most. At \(\rho=1.2\) only 1 of 80 runs is Lorenz-like, and the median one-step NMSE rises to \(1.5\times10^{-5}\), against \(6.0\times10^{-9}\) at \(\rho=0.5\), with a median valid time of 0.7 Lyapunov times. At \(\rho=0.5\) and \(0.9\) the larger reservoir succeeds more often, 32 and 25 of 40 for \(N=300\) against 25 and 13 for \(N=100\). The weak input \(\sigma_{\rm in}=0.1\) gives 59 Lorenz-like runs out of 120 and the strong input \(\sigma_{\rm in}=0.5\) gives 37. The stronger ridge \(\beta=10^{-4}\) gives 53 Lorenz-like runs against 43 for \(10^{-8}\), but it raises the median one-step NMSE by a factor of 55, from \(2.2\times10^{-9}\) to \(1.2\times10^{-7}\), and lowers the median valid time of the runs with \(N=300\) and \(\rho\le0.9\) from 6.55 to 3.43 Lyapunov times. In this scan the smoother readout helps the climate and roughly halves the length of the forecasts. The setting of the reservoir above succeeds for 7 of its ten seeds. Without the bias the same ten reservoirs give 0 Lorenz-like runs, and 8 of them diverge. These counts hold for the Lorenz-63 data and the settings of this scan, with ten seeds per setting, so a single count carries an uncertainty of about one or two runs.
Where the free run is Lorenz-like, its largest exponent has the median 0.904 and lies between 0.621 and 0.930 over the 96 runs, against \(\lambda_1=0.904\). The periodic runs have the median exponent \(-2.6\times10^{-4}\), zero within the accuracy of a 300-time-unit estimate, and the aperiodic runs with a wrong climate have the median 1.00. The maxima test is a coarse criterion. Of the 62 runs it labels periodic, 3 have \(\lambda_1>0.1\) and are aperiodic with maxima in a few narrow bands, and 5 have \(\lambda_1<-0.1\) and are slowly decaying oscillations, so the class counts carry an uncertainty of a few runs. A small one-step error is needed for a long forecast. The median valid time is 6.6 Lyapunov times for the runs with a one-step NMSE below \(10^{-10}\) and 0.4 for those above \(10^{-5}\), and every Lorenz-like run has a one-step NMSE of at most \(2.15\times10^{-6}\). The figure shows the two failures with the smallest one-step errors. The left panels show \(x\) over the whole free run, the right panels the last 5000 steps in the \((x,z)\) plane on top of the true attractor (grey), with the last point marked.

fail = {c: best_of(c) for c in ("fixed point", "periodic")}

title: Lab 049: Weather and climate of an echo state network
text:
7. Autoregression in closed loop
The same test applies to models without a reservoir. A linear autoregressive (AR) model and a nonlinear vector autoregression (NVAR) predict the increment from the last two states, \[\mathbf u_{k+1}=\mathbf u_k+W_{\rm out}^\top\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf u_k,\mathbf u_{k-1})+\mathbf b ,\] where \(\boldsymbol\phi\) is the six numbers of \((\mathbf u_k,\mathbf u_{k-1})\) for AR and these six numbers plus their 21 quadratic monomials for NVAR, the form used by Gauthier, Bollt, Griffith and Barbosa for the Lorenz system [Nat. Commun. 12, 5564 (2021), doi:10.1038/s41467-021-25801-2]. Both are fitted by ridge regression on the training block and closed in a loop like the reservoir, for three ridge strengths.


Code
IU, JU = np.triu_indices(6)
def ar_feat(a, b, quad):
    # (u_k, u_{k-1}) and, for NVAR, all 21 quadratic monomials of these six numbers
    v = jnp.concatenate([a, b], -1)
    return jnp.concatenate([v, v[..., IU] * v[..., JU]], -1) if quad else v

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=(4, 5))
def ar_free(a, b, Wq, bq, quad, n):
    # closed loop u_{k+1} = u_k + W^T phi(u_k, u_{k-1}) + b
    def step(carry, _):
        a, b = carry
        n_ = a + ar_feat(a, b, quad) @ Wq + bq
        return (n_, a), n_
    return jax.lax.scan(step, (a, b), None, length=n)[1]

k = np.arange(1, N_TRAIN)
ar_res = {}
for quad in (False, True):
    for beta in (1e-8, 1e-6, 1e-4):
        Wq, bq = ridge_fit(ar_feat(jnp.asarray(Un[k]), jnp.asarray(Un[k - 1]), quad), jnp.asarray(Un[k + 1] - Un[k]), beta)
        F_te = ar_feat(jnp.asarray(Un[k_te]), jnp.asarray(Un[k_te - 1]), quad)
        e1 = float(np.mean(np.mean((np.asarray(Un[k_te] + F_te @ Wq + bq) - Un[k_te + 1]) ** 2, 0) / Un[k_te + 1].var(0)))
        P = np.asarray(ar_free(jnp.asarray(Un[-1]), jnp.asarray(Un[-2]), Wq, bq, quad, N_FREE))
        cls, w1 = classify(P, Un_long)
        bad = ~np.isfinite(P).all(1) | (np.abs(np.nan_to_num(P, nan=1e9)).max(1) > 10)
        t_div = float(np.argmax(bad) * DT / T_LYAP) if bad.any() else None
        name = ("NVAR" if quad else "AR") + f"_{beta:.0e}"
        ar_res[name] = dict(nmse_one=e1, cls=cls, w1=w1, t_div=t_div, P=P)
        if not quad:
            A1, A2 = np.asarray(Wq[:3]).T, np.asarray(Wq[3:]).T
            Mc = np.block([[np.eye(3) + A1, A2], [np.eye(3), np.zeros((3, 3))]])
            ar_res[name]["spec_rad"] = float(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(Mc)).max())
        print(f"{name:10s} one-step NMSE {e1:.1e}, free run: {cls}" + (f", W1 {w1:.3f}" if np.isfinite(w1) else "")
              + (f", leaves |u|<10 at lambda_1 t = {t_div:.1f}" if t_div is not None else "")
              + (f", spectral radius of the linear map {ar_res[name]['spec_rad']:.6f}" if not quad else ""))
nums["ar_nvar"] = {k_: {kk: v for kk, v in d.items() if kk != "P"} for k_, d in ar_res.items()}


AR_1e-08   one-step NMSE 4.0e-04, free run: fixed point, W1 0.832, spectral radius of the linear map 0.991202
AR_1e-06   one-step NMSE 4.0e-04, free run: fixed point, W1 0.832, spectral radius of the linear map 0.991202
AR_1e-04   one-step NMSE 4.0e-04, free run: fixed point, W1 0.832, spectral radius of the linear map 0.991198


NVAR_1e-08 one-step NMSE 1.7e-09, free run: diverged, leaves |u|<10 at lambda_1 t = 3.8
NVAR_1e-06 one-step NMSE 2.0e-09, free run: Lorenz-like, W1 0.025


NVAR_1e-04 one-step NMSE 8.2e-09, free run: Lorenz-like, W1 0.036


The AR model has the one-step NMSE \(4.0\times10^{-4}\) and relaxes to a fixed point for every ridge strength. A closed-loop linear model is a linear map of \((\mathbf u_k,\mathbf u_{k-1})\), and its largest eigenvalue modulus, 0.9912, is below one, so every trajectory converges to its fixed point. A linear map can decay, grow or oscillate, and it has no bounded chaotic motion at all. NVAR reaches a one-step NMSE of \(1.7\times10^{-9}\) at \(\beta=10^{-8}\) and leaves the attractor after 3.8 Lyapunov times of free run, after which it runs away. At \(\beta=10^{-6}\) and \(10^{-4}\) the free run is Lorenz-like, with the largest Wasserstein distances 0.025 and 0.036. The figure shows the first 20000 steps of three of these free runs on top of the true attractor (grey), with the last plotted point marked.


Code

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 2.3), sharex=True, sharey=True, layout="constrained")
    for ax, name, lab in zip(axs, ("AR_1e-06", "NVAR_1e-08", "NVAR_1e-04"),
                             (r"AR, $\beta=10^{-6}$", r"NVAR, $\beta=10^{-8}$", r"NVAR, $\beta=10^{-4}$")):
        Q = ar_res[name]["P"] * sd + mu
        ok = np.isfinite(Q).all(1) & (np.abs(Q - mu).max(1) < 60)
        Q = Q[: np.argmin(ok) if not ok.all() else len(Q)]
        ax.plot(U_long_p[:20000, 0], U_long_p[:20000, 2], color="0.85", lw=0.15)
        ax.plot(Q[:20000, 0], Q[:20000, 2], color=CCOL[ar_res[name]["cls"]], lw=0.3)
        ax.plot(Q[min(len(Q), 20000) - 1, 0], Q[min(len(Q), 20000) - 1, 2], "o", color=CCOL[ar_res[name]["cls"]], ms=4)
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=11); ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
    axs[0].set_ylabel("$z$"); axs[0].set_xlim(-25, 25); axs[0].set_ylim(0, 55)
    save(fig, "fig_lab049_ar_nvar"); plt.show()





The quadratic features contain the quadratic nonlinearity of the Lorenz equations, and with a moderate ridge two delays are enough here. The free run of NVAR still depends on the ridge strength, as that of the reservoir does, and its smallest one-step error, at \(\beta=10^{-8}\), again comes with the worst free run.

title: Lab 049: Weather and climate of an echo state network
text:
8. Forecasting from \(x\) alone
In an experiment usually only one coordinate is measured. Takens’ delay embedding replaces the missing coordinates by past values of the measured one [F. Takens, Lect. Notes Math. 898, 366 (1981), doi:10.1007/BFb0091924], and we feed the reservoir the delay vector \((x_k,x_{k-8},x_{k-16})\), with a delay of 8 samples or 0.16 time units, or only \(x_k\) as a scalar input. The readout predicts \(x_{k+1}\), and in the closed loop the prediction is appended to the record of past values from which the next delay vector is formed. We use \(N=500\), \(\rho=0.5\), \(\sigma_{\rm in}=0.3\) and \(\beta=10^{-6}\) and ten seeds for each input. This setting was fixed by a short trial on the first seed whose record is not part of this notebook, so it is not a validated choice, and the counts below hold for this setting only. The classification is the one of the scan, applied to \(x\) alone, with the maxima of \(x\) in place of those of \(z\).


Code
D_LAG, M_DEL = 8, 3                                                   # delay 8 samples = 0.16 time units
x_n = Un[:, 0]
def delay_input(x, m):
    # rows (x_k, x_{k-d}, ..., x_{k-(m-1)d}); the first (m-1)d rows repeat x_0 for the missing past
    return np.stack([np.r_[np.full(i * D_LAG, x[0]), x[:len(x) - i * D_LAG]] for i in range(m)], 1)

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=(2, 3))
def free_run_delay(r0, p, m, n, buf0):
    # closed loop with a delay input: the predicted x is appended to the buffer of past values
    def step(carry, _):
        r, buf = carry
        x_hat = r @ p["W_out"] + p["b"]                       # shape (1,)
        buf = jnp.concatenate([buf[1:], x_hat])
        u = buf[::-1][::D_LAG][:m]
        r = (1 - p["alpha"]) * r + p["alpha"] * jnp.tanh(p["W"] @ r + p["W_in"] @ u + p["theta"])
        return (r, buf), x_hat[0]
    return jax.lax.scan(step, (r0, buf0), None, length=n)[1]

XO = dict(N=500, rho=0.5, sigma_in=0.3, sigma_theta=0.1, beta=1e-6)
x_res = {}
for m in (1, M_DEL):
    Uin = delay_input(x_n, m)
    x_res[m] = []
    for s in SEEDS:
        p = esn_draw(XO["N"], s, XO["rho"], XO["sigma_in"], XO["sigma_theta"], dim=m)
        R = esn_states(p, jnp.asarray(Uin), jnp.zeros(XO["N"]))
        kk = np.arange(N_WASH, N_TRAIN)
        W_out, b = ridge_fit(R[kk], jnp.asarray(x_n[kk + 1, None]), XO["beta"])
        p = dict(p, W_out=W_out, b=b)
        e1 = float(np.mean((np.asarray(R[kk] @ W_out + b)[:, 0] - x_n[kk + 1]) ** 2) / x_n[kk + 1].var())
        buf0 = jnp.asarray(x_n[-((m - 1) * D_LAG + 1):])
        P = np.asarray(free_run_delay(R[-1], p, m, N_FREE, buf0))[:, None]
        cls, w1 = classify(P, Un_long[:, :1])
        x_res[m].append(dict(seed=s, cls=cls, w1=w1, nmse_one=e1, P=P[:, 0]))
    cnt = Counter(d["cls"] for d in x_res[m])
    print(f"x only, m = {m}: " + ", ".join(f"{c} {cnt[c]}" for c in CLASSES if cnt[c])
          + " | one-step NMSE " + f"{min(d['nmse_one'] for d in x_res[m]):.1e}-{max(d['nmse_one'] for d in x_res[m]):.1e}")
    print("   per seed: " + ", ".join(f"{d['seed']} {d['cls']} (W1 {d['w1']:.3f})" for d in x_res[m]))
    nums[f"xonly_m{m}"] = dict({c: cnt[c] for c in CLASSES}, nmse_min=min(d["nmse_one"] for d in x_res[m]),
                               nmse_max=max(d["nmse_one"] for d in x_res[m]),
                               w1=[d["w1"] for d in x_res[m]])
nums["xonly"] = dict(XO, d_lag=D_LAG, m=M_DEL)
w_good = [d["w1"] for d in x_res[M_DEL] if d["cls"] == "Lorenz-like"]
if w_good:
    nums["xonly"].update(w1_good_min=min(w_good), w1_good_max=max(w_good))

x only, m = 3: Lorenz-like 1, aperiodic, wrong climate 7, periodic 1, fixed point 1 | one-step NMSE 1.5e-10-2.9e-10

With the scalar input, none of the ten free runs is Lorenz-like. 5 are periodic, 3 end on a fixed point and 2 diverge, although the one-step NMSE is between \(6.5\times10^{-10}\) and \(1.5\times10^{-9}\). With the delay input only 1 of the ten runs is Lorenz-like, seed 3 with the Wasserstein distance \(W_1=0.011\) of the \(x\) density. Of the others 7 are aperiodic with a wrong climate, 1 periodic and 1 at a fixed point. Five of these nine runs have \(W_1\) between 0.10 and 0.16, just above the threshold 0.1, so the count of Lorenz-like runs depends strongly on the threshold. The figure shows the delay plot \((x(t),x(t-0.32))\) for the true run and for the free run with the smallest distance (seed 3, \(W_1=0.011\)).


Code
ex = min(x_res[M_DEL], key=lambda d: d["w1"] if np.isfinite(d["w1"]) else 1e9)
nums["xonly"]["example_seed"] = ex["seed"]; nums["xonly"]["example_w1"] = ex["w1"]
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 2.6), sharex=True, sharey=True, layout="constrained")
    xt = U_long_p[:20000, 0]
    axs[0].plot(xt[2 * D_LAG:], xt[:-2 * D_LAG], color=UJNavy, lw=0.15); axs[0].set_title("Lorenz-63", fontsize=11)
    xe = ex["P"][-20000:] * sd[0] + mu[0]
    axs[1].plot(xe[2 * D_LAG:], xe[:-2 * D_LAG], color=CCOL[ex["cls"]], lw=0.15)
    axs[1].set_title(f"ESN from $x$ only, seed {ex['seed']}", fontsize=11)
    for ax in axs: ax.set_xlabel("$x(t)$")
    axs[0].set_ylabel(r"$x(t-0.32)$")
    save(fig, "fig_lab049_xonly"); plt.show()





The free run reproduces the shape of the delay plot. Measuring one coordinate makes the task harder than measuring all three, since the reservoir has to rebuild \(y\) and \(z\) from the past of \(x\), and in our runs the success rate drops from 7 of ten for the full state, at \(N=300\), \(\rho=0.9\), \(\sigma_{\rm in}=0.1\) and \(\beta=10^{-8}\), to 1 of ten with a delay input and to zero with the scalar input, both at \(N=500\), \(\rho=0.5\), \(\sigma_{\rm in}=0.3\) and \(\beta=10^{-6}\). The settings differ, so the comparison mixes the effect of the input with that of the setting. The numbers for the input \(x\) come from one unvalidated setting and leave open whether a better setting exists.

title: Lab 049: Weather and climate of an echo state network
text:
Summary
An echo state network trained one step ahead on the Lorenz-63 state becomes an autonomous dynamical system once its prediction is fed back as the input. For the reservoir with \(N=300\) units studied in detail, the short-term forecast, the weather of the model, stays below the error threshold 0.4 for a median of 6.9 Lyapunov times over 190 origins. The error grows at the rate 0.93\(\,\lambda_1\) after a short initial stage, and the predictability time \(T_p=\ln(\varepsilon/\delta_{\rm eff})/\lambda_1=7.5\,T_\lambda\) accounts for the measured valid time. The long free run, about 1988 Lyapunov times, reproduces the climate. The invariant densities differ from the truth by Wasserstein distances of 0.015 to 0.016 standard deviations, the Lorenz map and the power spectrum agree within the difference between two true runs or close to it, and the largest Lyapunov exponent of the reservoir map, 0.909, matches \(\lambda_1=0.904\) of the Lorenz flow. The strongly negative exponent \(\lambda_3=-14.57\) is not reproduced, most likely because the data on the attractor carry no information about the contraction towards it.
The success is a property of the random draw and of the setting. Of 240 reservoirs, 96 reproduce the Lorenz climate and the rest end on periodic orbits, on fixed points, on wrong aperiodic attractors or diverge. The spectral radius 1.2 fails almost always. A larger reservoir and a stronger ridge raise the number of runs with the right climate, while the stronger ridge also raises the median one-step error by a factor of 55 and roughly halves the median valid time. Without the bias of the units, tested at the base setting only, none of ten reservoirs reproduces the climate. A small one-step error is necessary for a long forecast and is not sufficient for a good climate, and the free run is the test that decides. Linear autoregression in closed loop relaxes to a fixed point for all three ridge strengths, quadratic autoregression reproduces the attractor for a moderate ridge and runs away for a weak one, and a reservoir that sees only \(x\) recovers the attractor in one of ten runs with a delay input and in none with the scalar input. All results refer to the Lorenz-63 data, settings and random draws of this notebook.

title: Lab 050: Cellular automaton reservoir
Lab 050: Cellular automaton reservoir
text:
2. Cellular automata
A cellular automaton consists of a lattice, a set of cell states, a neighbourhood and a local rule.

A lattice of cells \(j=0,1,\dots,L-1\), here a ring of \(L\) cells with periodic boundary conditions, so that cell \(L-1\) is the left neighbour of cell 0.
A finite set of cell states, here the integers modulo \(q\), \(\mathbb Z_q=\{0,1,\dots,q-1\}\), with \(q=2\) for binary cells.
A neighbourhood of radius \(a\), the \(n=2a+1\) cells \(j-a,\dots,j+a\).
A local rule \(f:\mathbb Z_q^n\to\mathbb Z_q\) that returns the new state of a cell from the states of its neighbourhood.

The state of cell \(j\) at iteration \(i\) is \(c_j^{(i)}\). The global map \(F\) applies \(f\) to all cells at once, \[c_j^{(i)}=f\big(c_{j-a}^{(i-1)},\dots,c_{j+a}^{(i-1)}\big)\quad\text{for all }j,\qquad \mathbf c^{(i)}=F\big(\mathbf c^{(i-1)}\big),\] and the evolution is the iteration of \(F\) from an initial configuration \(\mathbf c^{(0)}\). Space, time and states are discrete, and the update is deterministic and local.

Elementary cellular automata
The elementary cellular automata have \(q=2\) and \(a=1\) [S. Wolfram, Rev. Mod. Phys. 55, 601 (1983), doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.55.601]. A neighbourhood \((c_{j-1},c_j,c_{j+1})\) is one of the \(2^3=8\) patterns \(111,110,\dots,000\), and a rule assigns an output bit to each. Writing the 8 output bits in this order gives a binary number between 0 and 255, the Wolfram rule number, so there are 256 elementary rules. The figure shows the tables of rules 90 and 30. Rule 90 returns \(c_{j-1}\oplus c_{j+1}\), the exclusive or (XOR) of the two neighbours, and its output bits 01011010 form the number 90. Rule 30 returns \(c_{j-1}\oplus(c_j\lor c_{j+1})\).


Code
def eca_table(rule):
    # output bit for the 8 neighbourhoods (l, c, r) with index 4l + 2c + r: bit number index of the rule number
    return jnp.asarray((rule >> np.arange(8)) & 1, jnp.int32)

def linear_table(w, q):
    # table of the linear rule c_j <- (w_{-1} c_{j-1} + w_0 c_j + w_1 c_{j+1}) mod q, index q^2 l + q c + r
    l, c, r = np.meshgrid(np.arange(q), np.arange(q), np.arange(q), indexing="ij")
    return jnp.asarray(((w[0] * l + w[1] * c + w[2] * r) % q).ravel(), jnp.int32)

def ca_step(c, table, q=2):
    # one synchronous update of all cells, periodic boundary conditions (jnp.roll)
    return table[jnp.roll(c, 1) * q * q + c * q + jnp.roll(c, -1)]

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=(2, 3))
def ca_run(c0, table, q, n_steps):
    # space-time diagram: rows c^(0), c^(1), ..., c^(n_steps)
    def one(c, _):
        c = ca_step(c, table, q)
        return c, c
    return jnp.concatenate([c0[None], jax.lax.scan(one, c0, None, length=n_steps)[1]])

# rule 90 equals the linear rule (1, 0, 1) over Z_2, rule 150 the linear rule (1, 1, 1)
assert np.array_equal(eca_table(90), linear_table((1, 0, 1), 2))
assert np.array_equal(eca_table(150), linear_table((1, 1, 1), 2))
print("rule 90 table (patterns 111 ... 000):", np.asarray(eca_table(90))[::-1])




Code
PATTERNS = [(n >> 2 & 1, n >> 1 & 1, n & 1) for n in range(7, -1, -1)]          # 111, 110, ..., 000
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(5.5, 1.9), layout="constrained")
    for ax, rule in zip(axs, (90, 30)):
        tab = np.asarray(eca_table(rule))
        for i, p in enumerate(PATTERNS):
            x0 = 1.15 * i
            for j, bit in enumerate(p):
                ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0 + 0.3 * j, 0.45), 0.3, 0.3, fc=UJNavy if bit else "white", ec="0.3", lw=0.7))
            out = tab[4 * p[0] + 2 * p[1] + p[2]]
            ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0 + 0.3, 0.05), 0.3, 0.3, fc=DSOrange if out else "white", ec="0.3", lw=0.7))
            ax.text(x0 + 0.45, -0.12, str(out), ha="center", va="top")
        ax.text(-0.25, 0.4, f"rule {rule}", ha="right", va="center")
        ax.text(9.25, -0.12, rf"$={rule}$", ha="left", va="top")
        ax.set_xlim(-1.6, 10.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 0.8); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    save(fig, "fig_lab050_rule_table"); plt.show()


Wolfram sorted the behaviour of cellular automata from random initial states into four classes [S. Wolfram, Physica D 10, 1 (1984), doi:10.1016/0167-2789(84)90245-8]. Class I evolves to a homogeneous fixed state, class II to isolated stable or periodic structures, class III to aperiodic, random-looking patterns, and class IV to localised structures that move and interact over long times. The space-time diagrams show six rules with their class in brackets, iteration \(i\) running downwards and black cells in state 1, from a single seed cell (top) and from a random configuration (bottom) on a ring of \(L=101\) cells. Rule 32 empties every configuration within a few iterations, a number set by the longest alternating run 0101… of the start, which shrinks at both ends at every iteration. On 1000 random rings of 101 cells the lattice is empty after a median of 3 and at most 8 iterations. Rule 4 keeps isolated cells and nothing else. Rules 90 and 150 draw self-similar triangles from a single seed and random patterns from random starts, rule 30 grows a random-looking triangle, and rule 110 shows the moving localised structures of class IV.


Code
ST_RULES = [(32, "I"), (4, "II"), (90, "III"), (30, "III"), (110, "IV"), (150, "III")]
L_ST, T_ST = 101, 60
seed_state = jnp.zeros(L_ST, jnp.int32).at[L_ST // 2].set(1)
rand_state = jnp.asarray(np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, 2, L_ST), jnp.int32)
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(5.5, 2.75), layout="constrained")
    for col, (rule, cls) in enumerate(ST_RULES):
        for row, c0 in enumerate((seed_state, rand_state)):
            axs[row, col].imshow(np.asarray(ca_run(c0, eca_table(rule), 2, T_ST)), cmap="Greys", interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
            axs[row, col].set_xticks([]); axs[row, col].set_yticks([])
        axs[0, col].set_title(f"{rule} ({cls})")
    axs[0, 0].set_ylabel("one seed"); axs[1, 0].set_ylabel("random")
    fig.supylabel(r"iteration $i$ $\downarrow$", fontsize=11); fig.supxlabel("cell $j$", fontsize=11)
    save(fig, "fig_lab050_spacetime"); plt.show()

# rule 32 (only 101 -> 1): iterations until a random ring of 101 cells is empty, and the longest alternating run 0101...
C32 = jnp.asarray(np.random.default_rng(3).integers(0, 2, (1000, L_ST)), jnp.int32)
S32 = np.asarray(jax.vmap(lambda c: ca_run(c, eca_table(32), 2, 50))(C32))          # (starts, 51, L)
t_erase = np.argmax(S32.sum(2) == 0, axis=1)                                          # first empty iteration
def longest_alternating(c):
    # longest run of cells in which neighbours alternate, on the ring
    a = np.r_[c != np.roll(c, -1)]; a = np.r_[a, a]; best = cur = 0
    for x in a:
        cur = cur + 1 if x else 0; best = max(best, cur)
    return min(best, len(c) - 1) + 1
alt_run = np.array([longest_alternating(c) for c in np.asarray(C32)])
nums["rule32_erase"] = dict(median=float(np.median(t_erase)), max=int(t_erase.max()), all_empty=bool((S32[:, -1].sum(1) == 0).all()),
                            corr_with_run=float(np.corrcoef(t_erase, alt_run)[0, 1]))
print(f"rule 32 on 1000 random rings of {L_ST} cells: empty after a median of {np.median(t_erase):.0f} and at most {t_erase.max()} iterations;"
      f" correlation with the longest alternating run {nums['rule32_erase']['corr_with_run']:.2f}")
for t_ in range(t_erase.min(), t_erase.max() + 1):
    sel = t_erase == t_
    if sel.any():
        print(f"  empty after {t_} iterations: {sel.sum():4d} rings, longest alternating run {alt_run[sel].min()} to {alt_run[sel].max()} cells")


The six rules fall into three kinds of long-time behaviour, which the next figure shows side by side on a ring of 81 cells over 60 iterations, from a single cell in state 1 (top) and from a random configuration (bottom). The code also measures, for the random start, the iteration after which the lattice repeats itself and the period of the repetition. Rule 32 is trivial. The single cell disappears at the first iteration, and the random configuration is empty from iteration 3 on, after which nothing changes. Rule 108 is regular. The single cell stays where it is, and the random configuration settles into vertical stripes, some fixed and some blinking, so that the whole lattice repeats with period 2 from iteration 2 on. Rule 30 is chaotic. The single cell grows into an irregular triangle, and the random configuration does not repeat within the 60 iterations. A change of a single cell spreads through the lattice under rule 30, as the damage-spreading figure further below shows, so that its long-time evolution can be known only by running it.


Code
# three kinds of behaviour on a ring of 81 cells: a trivial, a regular and a chaotic rule
L_TB, T_TB = 81, 60
seed_tb = jnp.zeros(L_TB, jnp.int32).at[L_TB // 2].set(1)
rand_tb = jnp.asarray(np.random.default_rng(5).integers(0, 2, L_TB), jnp.int32)
def settle(S_):
    # first iteration t0 and period p with c^(t) = c^(t+p) for all t >= t0 within the run (None if not periodic yet)
    for t0_ in range(len(S_)):
        for p_ in range(1, (len(S_) - t0_) // 2 + 1):
            if all(np.array_equal(S_[t], S_[t + p_]) for t in range(t0_, len(S_) - p_)):
                return t0_, p_
    return None, None
nums["three_behaviours"] = {}
for r_ in (32, 4, 108, 50, 30):
    S_ = np.asarray(ca_run(rand_tb, eca_table(r_), 2, T_TB))
    t0_, p_ = settle(S_)
    S1_ = np.asarray(ca_run(seed_tb, eca_table(r_), 2, T_TB))
    nums["three_behaviours"][str(r_)] = dict(t_settle=t0_, period=p_, live_end=int(S_[-1].sum()),
                                             seed_live=[int(S1_[i].sum()) for i in (1, 10, T_TB)])
    print(f"rule {r_:3d}, single seed: live cells at i = 1, 10, {T_TB}: {S1_[1].sum()}, {S1_[10].sum()}, {S1_[-1].sum()}")
    print(f"rule {r_:3d}, random start: " + (f"periodic with period {p_} from iteration {t0_} on" if p_ else "not periodic within"
          f" {T_TB} iterations") + f", live cells at the end {S_[-1].sum()}")
TB_RULES = [(32, "trivial"), (108, "regular"), (30, "chaotic")]
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(5.5, 3.6), layout="constrained")
    for col, (r_, lab) in enumerate(TB_RULES):
        for row, c0 in enumerate((seed_tb, rand_tb)):
            axs[row, col].imshow(np.asarray(ca_run(c0, eca_table(r_), 2, T_TB)), cmap="Greys", vmin=0, vmax=1,
                                 interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
            axs[row, col].set_xticks([]); axs[row, col].set_yticks([])
        axs[0, col].set_title(f"rule {r_}, {lab}")
        axs[1, col].set_xlabel("cell $j$")
    axs[0, 0].set_ylabel("one seed\niteration $i$ $\\downarrow$"); axs[1, 0].set_ylabel("random\niteration $i$ $\\downarrow$")
    save(fig, "fig_lab050_three_behaviours"); plt.show()


The functions of the next cell let you run any elementary rule yourself. The function run_elementary iterates a rule on a ring with numpy and uses the convention of the rule table above, the new state of a cell being bit number \(4c_{j-1}+2c_j+c_{j+1}\) of the rule number, and the cell checks that it reproduces the patterns of rules 90 and 30 computed with JAX. The function plot_rules draws a grid of space-time diagrams with one row per initial condition and one column per rule. An initial condition is written as a string of 0 and 1, and its length is the number of cells of the ring, so "00000010000000" is a ring of 14 cells with a single 1 in the middle. The words "single" and "random" give a single 1 in the middle or a random configuration on a ring of \(L\) cells. Change the parameters at the top of the cell and run it again, for example to compare a rule with its mirror image or its complement, or to watch rule 90 erase a random configuration on a ring of 64 cells.


Code
# ---------------- exploration cell: change the parameters below and run the cell again ----------------
rules = [32, 4, 30, 90, 110, 180]       # Wolfram rule numbers, 0 ... 255
initial = ["00000000000000000000100000000000000000000", "100101100101010101011", "0000000110100000000"]
# each string is one initial condition; its length is the number of cells of the ring
# "single" (one 1 in the middle of L cells) and "random" (L cells, each 1 with probability 0.5, drawn with seed) are also allowed
L = 81                                  # number of cells for "single" and "random"
generations = 30                        # number of iterations of the rule
seed = 0                                # random generator seed for "random"
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def run_elementary(rule, initial, generations):
    # space-time array (generations + 1, number of cells) of an elementary rule on a ring; plain numpy, same rule-table
    # convention as eca_table: the new state of a cell is bit number 4 c_{j-1} + 2 c_j + c_{j+1} of the rule number
    c = np.asarray(initial, int); rows = [c]
    for _ in range(generations):
        c = (rule >> (4 * np.roll(c, 1) + 2 * c + np.roll(c, -1))) & 1
        rows.append(c)
    return np.array(rows)

def make_initial(entry, L=81, seed=0):
    # one initial condition: a bit string (its length is the ring size), "single" or "random" (L cells)
    if entry == "single":
        c0 = np.zeros(L, int); c0[L // 2] = 1
        return c0
    if entry == "random":
        return np.random.default_rng(seed).integers(0, 2, L)
    if not isinstance(entry, str) or set(entry) - {"0", "1"} or len(entry) < 3:
        raise ValueError(f"initial condition {entry!r}: use 'single', 'random' or a string of at least 3 characters 0 and 1")
    return np.array([int(ch) for ch in entry])

def plot_rules(rules, initial, L=81, generations=30, seed=0):
    # grid of space-time diagrams, one row per initial condition and one column per rule; iteration runs downwards,
    # black cells are in state 1, and the top row of every panel is the initial condition
    starts = [make_initial(e, L, seed) for e in initial]
    with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
        fig, axs = plt.subplots(len(starts), len(rules), figsize=(1.25 * len(rules) + 1.6, 1.5 * len(starts) + 0.4),
                                layout="constrained", squeeze=False)
        for row, (e, c0) in enumerate(zip(initial, starts)):
            for col, rule in enumerate(rules):
                ax = axs[row, col]
                ax.imshow(run_elementary(rule, c0, generations), cmap="Greys", vmin=0, vmax=1, interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
                ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
                if row == 0: ax.set_title(f"rule {rule}")
            text = e if len(e) <= 12 else e[:11] + "…"
            axs[row, 0].set_ylabel(f"{len(c0)} cells\n{text}")
        plt.show()

# check: the same patterns as the JAX implementation of the notebook for rules 90 and 30
for r_ in (90, 30):
    assert np.array_equal(run_elementary(r_, np.asarray(seed_tb), T_TB), np.asarray(ca_run(seed_tb, eca_table(r_), 2, T_TB)))
    assert np.array_equal(run_elementary(r_, np.asarray(rand_tb), T_TB), np.asarray(ca_run(rand_tb, eca_table(r_), 2, T_TB)))
plot_rules(rules, initial, L, generations, seed)




Game of Life
This part and the traffic model of rule 184 below are optional reading. They show cellular automata as physical models and are not needed for the reservoir. The best-known two-dimensional automaton is Conway’s Game of Life [M. Gardner, Sci. Am. 223 (4), 120 (1970), doi:10.1038/scientificamerican1070-120]. Each cell of a square lattice is dead (0) or alive (1), and its neighbourhood is the Moore neighbourhood of the 8 surrounding cells. A dead cell with exactly three live neighbours becomes alive, a live cell with two or three live neighbours survives, and every other cell is dead in the next step. The neighbour count is a two-dimensional convolution with a \(3\times3\) kernel of ones and a zero in the centre, which is how the JAX implementation computes it on a periodic grid. The snapshots show a glider, five live cells that return to their shape shifted by one cell diagonally after 4 steps, and a random soup of 0.352 live cells per site that leaves 0.042 after 200 steps, mostly in small still and oscillating objects.


Code
LIFE_K = jnp.array([[1, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 1]])

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=1)
def life_run(g0, n_steps):
    # Game of Life on a periodic grid: neighbour count by a 3x3 convolution, birth on 3, survival on 2 or 3
    def one(g, _):
        gp = jnp.pad(g, 1, mode="wrap")
        n = jax.scipy.signal.convolve2d(gp, LIFE_K, mode="valid")
        g = ((n == 3) | ((g == 1) & (n == 2))).astype(jnp.int32)
        return g, g
    return jnp.concatenate([g0[None], jax.lax.scan(one, g0, None, length=n_steps)[1]])

glider = jnp.zeros((12, 12), jnp.int32).at[jnp.array([1, 2, 3, 3, 3]), jnp.array([2, 3, 1, 2, 3])].set(1)
G_gl = np.asarray(life_run(glider, 8))
soup = jnp.asarray((np.random.default_rng(1).random((64, 64)) < 0.35).astype(np.int32))
G_soup = np.asarray(life_run(soup, 200))
print("glider after 4 steps equals the glider shifted by (1, 1):",
      np.array_equal(G_gl[4], np.roll(np.roll(G_gl[0], 1, 0), 1, 1)))
nums["life_alive"] = dict(t0=float(G_soup[0].mean()), t200=float(G_soup[200].mean()))
print(f"random soup: fraction of live cells {G_soup[0].mean():.3f} at t = 0, {G_soup[200].mean():.3f} at t = 200")
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(5.5, 1.35), layout="constrained")
    for ax, (G, t, lab) in zip(axs, [(G_gl, 0, "glider"), (G_gl, 2, ""), (G_gl, 4, ""), (G_gl, 8, ""),
                                       (G_soup, 0, "soup"), (G_soup, 200, "")]):
        ax.imshow(G[t], cmap="Greys", interpolation="nearest")
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_title(f"$t={t}$")
        if lab: ax.set_xlabel(lab)
    save(fig, "fig_lab050_life"); plt.show()




Linear cellular automata over \(\mathbb Z_q\)
A rule is linear when the new state is a weighted sum of the neighbourhood modulo \(q\), \[c_j^{(i)}=\sum_{l=-a}^{a}w_l\,c_{j+l}^{(i-1)}\bmod q,\qquad w_l\in\mathbb Z_q .\] Rule 90 is the linear rule with \(q=2\) and weights \((w_{-1},w_0,w_1)=(1,0,1)\), and rule 150 has \((1,1,1)\). For a linear rule the global map is a circulant matrix acting on \(\mathbb Z_q^L\), and the superposition principle holds, \(F(\mathbf c+\mathbf c')=F(\mathbf c)+F(\mathbf c')\) modulo \(q\). Many properties of linear rules can be computed exactly from their weights, which is why they are used for reservoirs [J. Kantic, F. C. Legl, W. Stechele, J. Hermann, Complex Intell. Syst. 10, 3593 (2024), doi:10.1007/s40747-023-01330-x, arXiv:2308.11522]. The figure shows rule 90 and two linear rules over \(\mathbb Z_4\), from a single cell in state 1 and from a random configuration, with darker blue for larger states. The rule with weights \((0,2,1)\), \(c_j\leftarrow2c_j+c_{j+1}\bmod4\), moves the content of every cell one site to the left per iteration and mixes it with its neighbour, a shift register with interaction. The rule \((1,2,1)\) spreads a seed in both directions.


Code
imp = jnp.zeros(L_ST, jnp.int32).at[L_ST // 2].set(1)
rnd4 = jnp.asarray(np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, 4, L_ST), jnp.int32)
LIN_RULES = [((1, 0, 1), 2), ((0, 2, 1), 4), ((1, 2, 1), 4)]
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):

                                 interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
            axs[row, col].set_xticks([]); axs[row, col].set_yticks([])
        axs[0, col].set_title(rf"$\mathbb{{Z}}_{q}$, $w={w}$".replace(" ", ""))

Traffic flow, rule 184
Rule 184 is the simplest model of traffic on a one-lane ring road, and like the Game of Life this part is optional reading. A cell in state 1 holds a car and a cell in state 0 is empty. The rule number \(184=10111000_2\) lists the new state for the neighbourhoods \(111,110,\dots,000\), and the next cell prints this table with the car reading of every row. A cell becomes 1 if a car arrives from the left (\(c_{j-1}=1\), \(c_j=0\)) or if its car is blocked and stays (\(c_j=c_{j+1}=1\)), and becomes 0 otherwise. Each car therefore moves one cell to the right when the cell ahead is empty, and the number of cars is conserved. The density \(\eta\) is the fraction of cells in state 1, and the flux \(\Phi\) is the number of cars that move per cell and step. Rule 184 is the deterministic limit with maximum speed 1 of the traffic model of Nagel and Schreckenberg [K. Nagel, M. Schreckenberg, J. Phys. I France 2, 2221 (1992), doi:10.1051/jp1:1992277]. For \(\eta<1/2\) every car eventually finds an empty cell ahead, all cars move and \(\Phi=\eta\), the free-flow phase. For \(\eta>1/2\) the empty cells are the minority, each of them lets one car through per step, and \(\Phi=1-\eta\), the jammed phase. The fundamental diagram \(\Phi(\eta)=\min(\eta,1-\eta)\) has a cusp at \(\eta=1/2\), the transition between the two phases.
We start from random configurations of 1000 cells at densities \(\eta=0.05,\dots,0.95\), discard 1000 steps and average the flux over the next 500. The measured flux agrees with \(\min(\eta,1-\eta)\) to four decimals on this grid. The space-time diagrams on 100 cells show the free flow at \(\eta=0.3\), where cars move to the right in parallel lines once the initial clusters have dissolved, and the jammed phase at \(\eta=0.7\), where queues of standing cars travel to the left.


Code
# the table of rule 184 read as traffic: 1 = car, 0 = empty cell
t184 = np.asarray(eca_table(184))
for n in range(7, -1, -1):
    l, m, r = n >> 2 & 1, n >> 1 & 1, n & 1
    why = ("car blocked, stays" if m and r else "car moves on" if m else "car arrives from the left" if l else "stays empty")
    assert t184[n] == ((l and not m) or (m and r))
    print(f"{l}{m}{r} -> {t184[n]}   {why}")

def traffic_flux(eta, L=1000, T_wash=1000, T_avg=500, seed=0):
    # rule 184: a car (1) moves one cell to the right if the cell ahead is empty; flux = moving cars per cell and step
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    c = np.zeros(L, np.int32); c[rng.choice(L, int(round(eta * L)), replace=False)] = 1
    S = np.asarray(ca_run(jnp.asarray(c), eca_table(184), 2, T_wash + T_avg))
    moving = S[T_wash:-1] * (1 - np.roll(S[T_wash:-1], -1, axis=1))
    return float(moving.mean()), S

ETA_TR = np.round(np.arange(0.05, 0.96, 0.05), 2)
flux = np.array([traffic_flux(e_)[0] for e_ in ETA_TR])
nums["rule184"] = dict(eta=ETA_TR.tolist(), flux=flux.tolist(),
                       max_dev_from_min=float(np.abs(flux - np.minimum(ETA_TR, 1 - ETA_TR)).max()))
print(f"rule 184: max |Phi - min(eta, 1 - eta)| over the density grid = {nums['rule184']['max_dev_from_min']:.4f}")
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.4), layout="constrained")
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 3, width_ratios=[1, 1, 1.4])
    for col, e_ in enumerate((0.3, 0.7)):
        ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[col])

        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_title(rf"$\eta={e_}$")
        if col == 0: ax.set_ylabel(r"time $\downarrow$")
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2])
    ax.plot(ETA_TR, flux, "o", ms=4, color=UJBlue, label="rule 184")
    ax.plot([0, 0.5, 1], [0, 0.5, 0], color="0.5", ls="--", lw=1.0, label=r"$\min(\eta,1-\eta)$")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"density $\eta$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"flux $\Phi$")
    ax.legend(loc="lower center", handlelength=1.2, borderaxespad=0.2)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 0.62)
    save(fig, "fig_lab050_rule184"); plt.show()




Damage spreading
For a reservoir, two copies that start in different states and are driven by the same input should end up in the same state, the echo state property. Without input the related property of a cellular automaton is damage spreading. We flip one cell of a random configuration on a ring of \(L=257\) cells and follow the set of cells where the two copies differ, the damage. The left panels show this difference pattern (orange) for one run over 64 iterations, and the right panel the damaged fraction of the lattice on a logarithmic scale, averaged over 20 random starts.


Code
def damage(rule, L=257, T=128, n_runs=20, seed=0):
    # cells that differ between two copies whose initial states differ in one cell, (runs, T+1, L)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); out = []
    for _ in range(n_runs):
        c0 = jnp.asarray(rng.integers(0, 2, L), jnp.int32)
        D = ca_run(c0, eca_table(rule), 2, T) ^ ca_run(c0.at[L // 2].set(1 - c0[L // 2]), eca_table(rule), 2, T)
        out.append(np.asarray(D))
    return np.array(out)

# rule 90 on a ring of 2^n cells sends every state to zero (nilpotent map); on 257 cells it does not
for L_ring in (256, 257):
    c_r = jnp.asarray(np.random.default_rng(2).integers(0, 2, L_ring), jnp.int32)
    alive = [int(np.asarray(ca_run(c_r, eca_table(rl), 2, 256))[-1].sum()) for rl in (90, 150)]
    nums.setdefault("ring_live_after_256", {})[str(L_ring)] = alive
    print(f"ring of {L_ring} cells, random start: live cells after 256 iterations, rule 90: {alive[0]}, rule 150: {alive[1]}")
DMG_RULES = (4, 90, 30, 110)
dmg = {r: damage(r) for r in DMG_RULES}
nums["damage_fraction_t128"] = {str(r): float(d[:, -1].mean()) for r, d in dmg.items()}
nums["damage_kept_t128"] = {str(r): float((d[:, -1].sum(1) > 0).mean()) for r, d in dmg.items()}
for r, d in dmg.items():
    print(f"rule {r:3d}: damaged fraction at i = 32, 128: {d[:, 32].mean():.3f}, {d[:, -1].mean():.3f};"
          f" runs with damage left at i = 128: {(d[:, -1].sum(1) > 0).mean():.2f}")
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.6), layout="constrained")
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 5, width_ratios=[1, 1, 1, 1, 1.9])
    for col, r in enumerate(DMG_RULES):
        ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[col])
        ax.imshow(dmg[r][0][:64, 96:161], cmap="Oranges", interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_title(f"rule {r}")
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[4])
    for r, col in zip(DMG_RULES, (UJNavy, UJBlue, DSOrange, Teal)):
        ax.semilogy(np.arange(129), dmg[r].mean(axis=(0, 2)), color=col, lw=1.6 if r == 4 else 1.2, label=f"{r}")
    ax.set_xlabel("iteration $i$"); ax.set_ylabel("damaged fraction"); ax.set_ylim(1e-3, 1)
    ax.legend(loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0), handlelength=1.0, ncol=4, columnspacing=0.6, handletextpad=0.3)
    save(fig, "fig_lab050_damage"); plt.show()

def damage_edges(d, i_max=100):
    # right edge, left edge, mean position and width of the damage at iteration i_max, relative to the flipped cell
    c = d.shape[2] // 2; out = []
    for run in d:
        idx = np.nonzero(run[i_max])[0] - c
        if len(idx):
            out.append((idx.max(), -idx.min(), idx.mean(), idx.max() - idx.min() + 1))
    return np.array(out, float), len(d) - len(out)
ITER_EDGE = 100
nums["damage_edges"] = {}
for r_ in (30, 180, 210):
    d_ = dmg[r_] if r_ in dmg else damage(r_)
    E, n_dead = damage_edges(d_, ITER_EDGE)
    nums["damage_edges"][str(r_)] = dict(right=float(E[:, 0].mean() / ITER_EDGE), left=float(E[:, 1].mean() / ITER_EDGE),
                                         drift=float(E[:, 2].mean() / ITER_EDGE), width=float(E[:, 3].mean()),
                                         width_max=float(E[:, 3].max()), runs_without_damage=int(n_dead))
    e_ = nums["damage_edges"][str(r_)]
    print(f"rule {r_:3d}, after {ITER_EDGE} iterations: right edge {e_['right']:.2f} and left edge {e_['left']:.2f} cells per iteration,"
          f" drift of the mean position {e_['drift']:+.2f} per iteration, width {e_['width']:.1f} cells (largest {e_['width_max']:.0f}),"
          f" runs in which the damage vanished {n_dead} of {len(d_)}")


Under rule 4 the damage stays on one cell, a fraction of 0.002 after 128 iterations. Under rule 90 the difference of two configurations evolves by rule 90 itself, because the rule is linear over \(\mathbb Z_2\), so the damage is the Sierpinski triangle of the single seed for every background, and the damaged fraction oscillates with the self-similar pattern, 0.008 after 128 iterations. Under rule 30 the damage fills an asymmetric cone. Over the first 100 iterations its right edge moves by 1.00 cell per iteration and its left edge by 0.23 cells per iteration, since the exclusive or with the left neighbour passes every difference on to the right, and the damaged fraction reaches 0.323 of the lattice after 128 iterations. Under rule 110 it reaches 0.158. The width of the damaged region grows linearly in time for rules 90, 30 and 110, the cellular automaton counterpart of a positive Lyapunov exponent, while rule 4 keeps a perturbation where it was.
For a reservoir this has a consequence. On the ring of 257 cells a flipped cell is still visible after 128 iterations in 100% of the 20 runs under rules 90, 30 and 110, which spread it, and in 50% of the runs under rule 4, which keeps every isolated cell in state 1, so the difference survives when the flip creates or removes such a cell. Without input nothing removes such a difference. This damage test has no input, so it is not a test of the echo state property. In a CA reservoir the initial state can be forgotten only through the input, which overwrites the mapped cells at every step, and we test this with two copies of the forecasting reservoir driven by the same input further below. A second effect matters for linear rules on rings. Rule 90 on a ring of \(2^n\) cells sends every configuration to zero, while on 257 cells it does not. From a random start, after 256 iterations rule 90 leaves 0 live cells on 256 cells and 120 on 257 cells, and rule 150 leaves 133 and 138. On a ring whose size is a power of two rule 90 erases all information, which matters for the size of the reservoir lattice.
Langton related the computational ability of cellular automata to the transition between ordered and chaotic rules, the edge of chaos [C. G. Langton, Physica D 42, 12 (1990), doi:10.1016/0167-2789(90)90064-V], and the first CA reservoirs were motivated by it. We treat this as a hypothesis and test it with the forecasting reservoirs further on.

title: Lab 050: Cellular automaton reservoir
text:
3. Cellular automaton reservoir
Yilmaz replaced the echo state network by a cellular automaton [O. Yilmaz, arXiv:1410.0162 (2014), arXiv:1410.0162]. The input is written into cells of the automaton, the rule is applied a fixed number of times between two inputs, and all configurations of these applications are read by a linear readout. We follow Kantic et al., who split one input step into an encoding, an evolution and a readout [Kantic et al., Complex Intell. Syst. 10, 3593 (2024), doi:10.1007/s40747-023-01330-x]. They write a single value of \(\mathbb Z_q\) into one cell per compartment, so their number of levels equals the number \(q\) of cell states. Writing \(B\) digits per compartment is our extension, which allows more levels than cell states.
The JAX implementation runs the whole record as one jax.lax.scan. A step writes the code digits into the mapped cells, applies the rule \(N_{\rm gen}\) times through a lookup table indexed by the neighbourhood, and returns the concatenated configurations. The reservoir state has integer entries between 0 and \(q-1\), so the matrix \(X^\top X\) of the readout is computed exactly in single precision, and the solve is done in double precision.


Code
def quantise(s, Q):
    # levels l = 0..Q-1 of equal width 1/Q on [0, 1]; values outside [0, 1] go to the end levels
    return np.clip(np.floor(s * Q), 0, Q - 1).astype(int)

def ca_digits(s, Q, q):
    # quantise s to Q levels and write the level in base q as B digits, Q = q^B, least significant digit first
    l = quantise(s, Q)
    B = int(round(np.log(Q) / np.log(q)))
    return np.stack([(l // q ** b) % q for b in range(B)], 1).astype(np.int32)

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=(3, 4, 5, 6, 7))
def ca_reservoir(table, digits, cells, q, L, N_generation_steps, additive, with_input):
    # digits: (T, B) input code per step; cells: (R, B) lattice cells that receive the B digits in each compartment.
    # Per step: write the digits (replacement, or addition mod q), run N_gen iterations, return the concatenated states.
    def step(c, d):
        vals = jnp.broadcast_to(d, cells.shape)
        c = c.at[cells].set((c[cells] + vals) % q if additive else vals)
        outs = [c] if with_input else []
        for _ in range(N_generation_steps):
            c = ca_step(c, table, q)
            outs.append(c)
        return c, jnp.concatenate(outs)
    return jax.lax.scan(step, jnp.zeros(L, jnp.int32), digits)[1]

def compartment_cells(R, Lc, B, seed):
    # one fixed random choice of B distinct cells in each of the R compartments of Lc cells
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return jnp.asarray(np.stack([j * Lc + rng.choice(Lc, B, replace=False) for j in range(R)]), jnp.int32)

def ridge_int(X, Y, betas):
    # centred ridge regression for integer-valued features; X^T X in float32 is exact for these counts
    n = X.shape[0]; fm = X.mean(0, dtype=np.float64); ym = Y.mean(0)
    G = (X.T @ X).astype(np.float64) - n * np.outer(fm, fm)
    XtY = X.T.astype(np.float64) @ Y - n * np.outer(fm, ym)
    out = []
    for beta in betas:
        W = np.linalg.solve(G + beta * np.eye(G.shape[0]), XtY)
        out.append((beta, W, ym - fm @ W))
    return out



One input step
The reservoir runs on two clocks. The input step \(k\) advances by one sample \(s_k\) of the record. Inside one input step the rule is applied \(N_{\rm gen}\) times, and the generations \(i=0,1,\dots,N_{\rm gen}\) count these applications, with \(i=0\) the configuration right after the input is written. The ring has \(L=RL_c\) cells, divided into \(R\) compartments of \(L_c\) cells.
The next cell runs a small reservoir with the functions above and draws three of its input steps, rule 180, \(R=2\) compartments of \(L_c=8\) cells, \(Q=8\) levels written as \(B=3\) binary digits and \(N_{\rm gen}=3\). Time runs down, every block of four rows is one input step, cells in state 1 are blue, and the input cells are framed in orange in the row where the code word is written. The next three subsections explain the three operations on this figure.


Code
import matplotlib.patheffects as mpl_pe

# one input step of a CA reservoir, drawn from the reservoir itself: rule 180, R = 2 compartments of L_c = 8 cells,
# Q = 8 levels in binary code (B = 3 bits), N_gen = 3 generations per input step, a ring of zeros before the first sample
OS_RULE, OS_R, OS_LC, OS_Q, OS_NGEN, OS_SEED = 180, 2, 8, 8, 3, 0
os_s = np.array([0.68, 0.90, 0.16, 0.61, 0.10])            # five samples; the figure shows the last three input steps
OS_K, OS_J = 3, 5                                          # step k with s_k = 0.61, and the traced cell j
OS_L = OS_R * OS_LC
os_cells = compartment_cells(OS_R, OS_LC, 3, OS_SEED)       # B = 3 input cells per compartment, the same at every step
def os_run(s):
    X = ca_reservoir(eca_table(OS_RULE), jnp.asarray(ca_digits(s, OS_Q, 2)), os_cells, 2, OS_L, OS_NGEN, False, True)
    return np.asarray(X).reshape(len(s), OS_NGEN + 1, OS_L)       # [input step, generation i = 0 ... N_gen, cell]
os_X = os_run(os_s)
bits = lambda c: "".join(map(str, np.asarray(c)))
for k in range(OS_K - 1, OS_K + 2):
    for i in range(OS_NGEN + 1):
        print(f"step {k}, i = {i}: {bits(os_X[k, i][:OS_LC])} | {bits(os_X[k, i][OS_LC:])}")
# the traced product: cell j receives the bit a of s_k, its right neighbour keeps a bit b that s_(k-1) left there,
# its left neighbour is 0, and one generation of rule 180 gives a XOR ab = a(1 - b)
a_, b_, left_ = os_X[OS_K, 0, OS_J], os_X[OS_K, 0, OS_J + 1], os_X[OS_K, 0, OS_J - 1]
assert OS_J in np.asarray(os_cells) and OS_J + 1 not in np.asarray(os_cells) and left_ == 0
assert os_X[OS_K, 1, OS_J] == (a_ ^ (a_ & b_)) == a_ * (1 - b_)
s_alt = os_s.copy(); s_alt[OS_K - 1] = 0.9                  # another value of s_(k-1) changes b, so b carries s_(k-1)
assert os_run(s_alt)[OS_K, 0, OS_J + 1] != b_
print(f"input cells {sorted(np.asarray(os_cells)[0].tolist())} and {sorted(np.asarray(os_cells)[1].tolist())}")
print(f"cell {OS_J}: a = {a_} written from s_k, right neighbour b = {b_} left by s_(k-1), left neighbour 0;"
      f" one generation later the cell holds {os_X[OS_K, 1, OS_J]} = a(1 - b)")

ONE = "#5C8FC4"                                           # colour of a cell in state 1
def draw_one_step(show=("encode", "evolve", "readout"), name=None):
    steps = range(OS_K - 1, OS_K + 2)                     # input steps k-1, k, k+1
    inj = np.asarray(os_cells).ravel()
    lab_k = {OS_K - 1: "k-1", OS_K: "k", OS_K + 1: "k+1"}
    with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.3, 3.9))
        ry = {}
        for n_, k in enumerate(steps):
            for i in range(OS_NGEN + 1):
                y = -(n_ * (OS_NGEN + 1) + i) - 0.5 - 0.35 * n_          # small gap between input steps
                ry[(k, i)] = y
                for j, v in enumerate(os_X[k, i]):
                    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((j + 0.14 * (j >= OS_LC), y - 0.5), 1, 1, fc=ONE if v else "white", ec="0.55", lw=0.4))
            if "encode" in show:
                for j in inj:
                    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((j + 0.14 * (j >= OS_LC) + 0.06, ry[(k, 0)] - 0.44), 0.88, 0.88, fc="none",
                                               ec=DSOrange, lw=1.8, zorder=4))
                l = int(quantise(np.array([os_s[k]]), OS_Q)[0])
                ax.text(-0.95, ry[(k, 0)], rf"$s_{{{lab_k[k]}}}={os_s[k]:.2f}$", ha="right", va="center", color=DSOrange)
                ax.text(-0.95, ry[(k, 0)] - 1.1, rf"$\ell={l}$, {format(l, '03b')}", ha="right", va="center", color=DSOrange)
                ax.annotate("", xy=(-0.05, ry[(k, 0)]), xytext=(-0.7, ry[(k, 0)]),
                            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=DSOrange, lw=1.2))
        x_end = OS_L + 0.14
        y_bot = ry[(OS_K + 1, OS_NGEN)] - 0.5
        ax.annotate("", xy=(-10.3, y_bot), xytext=(-10.3, 0.0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="k", lw=1.0))
        ax.text(-10.6, y_bot / 2, r"time, input step $k$", rotation=90, ha="right", va="center")
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x_end, y_bot - 0.6), xytext=(0, y_bot - 0.6), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="k", lw=1.0))
        ax.text(x_end / 2, y_bot - 0.8, r"cell $j=0,1,\dots,15$", ha="center", va="top")
        ax.text(OS_LC - 0.2, 0.2, "compartment 1", ha="right", va="bottom", color=UJGray)
        ax.text(OS_LC + 0.34, 0.2, "compartment 2", ha="left", va="bottom", color=UJGray)
        for i in range(OS_NGEN + 1):
            ax.text(x_end + 0.3, ry[(OS_K, i)], rf"$i={i}$", ha="left", va="center", color=UJGray)
        if "evolve" in show:
            for dj, lab in ((0, "a"), (1, "b")):
                ax.text(OS_J + dj + 0.5, ry[(OS_K, 0)], lab, ha="center", va="center", color="white", fontweight="bold", zorder=5)
            ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((OS_J + 0.06, ry[(OS_K, 1)] - 0.44), 0.88, 0.88, fc="none", ec="#C44E52", lw=2.0, zorder=5))
            ax.annotate(r"$a\oplus ab=a(1-b)$", xy=(OS_J + 0.1, ry[(OS_K, 1)] - 0.3),
                        xytext=(-0.75, ry[(OS_K, 3)] + 0.15), ha="right", va="center", color="#C44E52",
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#C44E52", lw=1.4, shrinkA=2,
                                        path_effects=[mpl_pe.withStroke(linewidth=3.5, foreground="white")]))
        if "readout" in show:
            y0, y1 = ry[(OS_K, 0)] + 0.5, ry[(OS_K, OS_NGEN)] - 0.5
            xb = x_end + 3.1
            ax.plot([xb, xb + 0.3, xb + 0.3, xb], [y0, y0, y1, y1], color="k", lw=1.2)
            ym = (y0 + y1) / 2
            ax.annotate("", xy=(xb + 1.9, ym), xytext=(xb + 0.4, ym), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="k", lw=1.2))
            ax.text(xb + 2.1, ym + 0.35, r"$\mathbf{r}_k$" + f", {(OS_NGEN + 1) * OS_L} bits", ha="left", va="bottom")
            ax.text(xb + 2.1, ym - 0.35, r"$\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k=W_{\rm out}^{\top}\mathbf{r}_k+\mathbf{b}$", ha="left", va="top", color=DSOrange)
        ax.set_xlim(-12.0, x_end + 12.3); ax.set_ylim(y_bot - 1.9, 1.2); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
        if name: save(fig, name)
        plt.show()
draw_one_step(name="fig_lab050_one_step")
draw_one_step(("encode",), name="fig_lab050_one_step_encode")
draw_one_step(("encode", "evolve"), name="fig_lab050_one_step_evolve")




Encoding
The interval \([0,1]\) is cut into \(Q\) bins of width \(1/Q\), the quantisation levels, and the sample \(s_k\in[0,1]\) becomes the number of its bin, the level \(\ell_k=\lfloor Qs_k\rfloor\), clipped to \(0,\dots,Q-1\). The level is written as a binary number, the code word \(\mathbf e_k\) of \(B\) bits, \(Q=2^B\), so \(Q=8\) in the figure and the worked example has \(B=3\), and the forecasts use \(Q=16\) and \(B=4\). For \(s_k=0.61\) and \(Q=8\) the sample lies in the bin from 0.5 to 0.625, so \(\ell_k=\lfloor4.88\rfloor=4\) and the code word is \(100\). In each compartment \(B\) input cells were chosen once at random, and they are the same at every input step. The \(R\) compartments are therefore \(R\) independent random placements of the same code word. The bits of the code word overwrite the input cells. Every other cell keeps what the earlier inputs and the rule left there, and this kept content is the memory of the reservoir.
In the figure the code word 100 of \(s_k=0.61\) is written into the framed cells. Compare the row \(i=0\) of step \(k\) with the row just above it, the last generation of step \(k-1\). Only framed cells differ between the two rows.
Quantisation is the price of a discrete state. With \(Q\) levels of width \(1/Q\) the rounding error of a uniformly spread value has the standard deviation \(1/(Q\sqrt{12})\), and on the Santa Fe signal the measured root-mean-square error is 0.069 for \(Q=4\), 0.018 for \(Q=16\) and 0.0045 for \(Q=64\). The left panel of the next figure shows the signal \(s_k\) and its quantised values \((\ell_k+1/2)/Q\) for \(Q=4\) and \(16\). The right panel shows the code words of the levels \(\ell=0,\dots,7\) as rows of three bits (grey for 1).


Code
seg = sig["SantaFe"][:100]
with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.4), layout="constrained")
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, width_ratios=[2.3, 0.8])
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])
    ax.plot(np.arange(100), seg, color="k", lw=1.0, label="$s_k$")
    for Q, c in ((4, DSOrange), (16, UJBlue)):
        ax.step(np.arange(100), (quantise(seg, Q) + 0.5) / Q, where="mid", color=c, lw=1.0, label=f"$Q={Q}$")
    ax.set_xlabel("step $k$"); ax.set_ylabel("value"); ax.legend(loc="upper left", ncol=3, handlelength=1.2)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.25)
    axc = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
    Mb = np.array([[(l >> b) & 1 for b in range(2, -1, -1)] for l in range(8)])
    axc.imshow(Mb, cmap="Greys", vmin=0, vmax=1.6, interpolation="nearest")
    axc.set_xticks([]); axc.set_yticks(range(8)); axc.set_title("binary"); axc.set_ylabel(r"level $\ell$")
    save(fig, "fig_lab050_encoding"); plt.show()
q_err = {Q: float(np.sqrt(np.mean(((quantise(sig["SantaFe"], Q) + 0.5) / Q - sig["SantaFe"]) ** 2))) for Q in (4, 16, 64)}
nums["quant_rms_SantaFe"] = q_err
print("rms quantisation error on Santa Fe: " + ", ".join(f"Q = {Q}: {v:.4f} (1/(Q sqrt 12) = {1 / (Q * np.sqrt(12)):.4f})"
                                                       for Q, v in q_err.items()))




Evolution
Between two inputs the rule is applied \(N_{\rm gen}\) times to the whole ring, across the compartment boundaries as well. Rule 180 updates every cell as \[c_j\leftarrow c_{j-1}\oplus c_j\oplus c_jc_{j+1},\] where \(\oplus\) is the exclusive or (XOR) and \(c_jc_{j+1}\) the logical AND. It moves the new bits away from the input cells, on average one cell to the right per generation, and combines them with the bits of earlier inputs that they meet. After \(N_{\rm gen}\) generations the ring is a record of the recent input history that also contains products of past bits.
Look at the cell marked \(a\) in the row \(i=0\) of step \(k\). It has just received the most significant bit of \(s_k\), \(a=1\). Its right neighbour, \(b=1\), was left there by \(s_{k-1}\), and the cell checks that another value of \(s_{k-1}\) changes it. Its left neighbour is 0. One generation later the cell (red frame) holds \(0\oplus a\oplus ab=a(1-b)=0\), a product of a bit of \(s_k\) and a bit of \(s_{k-1}\).
The next cell prints the bit operations on all pairs of bits, two updates of rule 180 against its rule table, and one row of the figure updated cell by cell. XOR is addition modulo 2, and AND is the ordinary product of two bits. The column \(a\oplus ab\) is 1 only for \(a=1\), \(b=0\), the logical \(a\) and not \(b\), which in ordinary arithmetic is \(a(1-b)=a-ab\).


Code
# the bit operations of the rules on all pairs of bits: XOR is addition modulo 2, AND is the product of two bits
print(" a  b | a XOR b | ab (AND) | a XOR ab")
for a in (0, 1):
    for b in (0, 1):
        assert a ^ b == (a + b) % 2 == a + b - 2 * a * b and a & b == a * b and a ^ (a & b) == a * (1 - b)
        print(f" {a}  {b} |    {a ^ b}    |    {a & b}     |    {a ^ (a & b)}")
# no weighted sum w0 + w1 a + w2 b equals a XOR ab on all four rows: the least-squares residual is not zero
A_ = np.array([[1, a, b] for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1)], float)
t_ = np.array([a ^ (a & b) for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1)], float)
w_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A_, t_, rcond=None)[0]
print(f"best w0 + w1 a + w2 b: w = {np.round(w_, 2)}, largest error {np.abs(A_ @ w_ - t_).max():.2f}")

# two updates of rule 180, c_j <- c_(j-1) XOR c_j XOR c_j c_(j+1), against its rule table
t180 = np.asarray(eca_table(180))
print(f"\nrule 180 = {180:08b} in binary, the new states for the neighbourhoods 111, 110, 101, 100, 011, 010, 001, 000")
for l, c, r in ((0, 1, 1), (0, 1, 0)):
    v = l ^ c ^ (c & r)
    assert v == t180[4 * l + 2 * c + r]
    print(f"(c_j-1, c_j, c_j+1) = ({l}, {c}, {r}):  {l} XOR {c} XOR {c}*{r} = {v}, table entry for {l}{c}{r}: {t180[4 * l + 2 * c + r]}")

# one row of the figure updated cell by cell: step k, generation 0 -> 1, cells 3 ... 7 (cell 5 is the traced cell)
row0, row1 = os_X[OS_K, 0], os_X[OS_K, 1]
print(f"\nstep k, i = 0: {bits(row0[:OS_LC])} | {bits(row0[OS_LC:])}")
for j in range(3, 8):
    l, c, r = row0[j - 1], row0[j], row0[j + 1]
    v = l ^ c ^ (c & r)
    assert v == row1[j]
    print(f"  cell {j}: {l} XOR {c} XOR {c}*{r} = {v}")
print(f"step k, i = 1: {bits(row1[:OS_LC])} | {bits(row1[OS_LC:])}")




Readout and training
The \(N_{\rm gen}+1\) configurations of one input step, the row \(i=0\) after the writing and the rows after each generation, are concatenated into the feature vector \(\mathbf r_k=(\mathbf c_k^{(0)},\dots,\mathbf c_k^{(N_{\rm gen})})\) of \((N_{\rm gen}+1)L\) bits, 64 in the figure, read as the numbers 0 and 1. The forecast of the next 50 values is \(\tilde{\mathbf y}_k=W_{\rm out}^\top\mathbf r_k+\mathbf b\). The weights \(W_{\rm out}\) and the offset \(\mathbf b\) are fitted once by ridge regression over all training steps, and they are the only trained numbers. The last configuration \(\mathbf c_k^{(N_{\rm gen})}\) is carried over and receives the code word of \(s_{k+1}\), so step \(k+1\) starts where step \(k\) ends.
The next cell lets you drive an elementary automaton with a piece of a real signal and look at the result. The left panel shows the signal and its quantised values against the input step, and the right panel the ring after the bits are written and after each of the \(N_{\rm gen}\) generations, with the input steps separated by thin grey lines, the compartments by blue lines, and the input cells in orange, dark for a 1 and light for a 0. Encoding by addition modulo 2 in place of replacement is available as an option. The cell runs the same reservoir twice, once from a ring of zeros and once from a hand-written random-looking ring, and prints the input step from which the two runs agree. The number of bits sets a trade-off that the parameters let you explore. More bits give a finer amplitude, with a rounding error of \(1/(2^B\sqrt{12})\) for a uniformly spread signal, but they overwrite \(B\) of the \(L_c\) cells of each compartment at every step, which leaves fewer cells to carry the past.


Code
# ---------------- exploration cell: a CA reservoir driven by a signal; change the parameters and run again ----------------
signal = sig["SantaFe"][:40]            # the input s_k, values in [0, 1]
B = 4                                   # bits per sample, Q = 2**B levels
rule = 180                              # Wolfram rule number
R = 4                                   # number of compartments
N_generation_steps = 4                                   # iterations of the rule per input step
mode = "replace"                        # "replace": the bits overwrite the input cells; "xor": they are added modulo 2
initial = "0" * 64                      # initial is the starting ring as a bit string; its length is the number of cells
                                        # "zeros" or "random" give a ring of R * L_c cells
L_c = 16                                # cells per compartment for initial = "zeros" or "random"
input_cells = None                      # None: B random cells per compartment (drawn with seed);
                                        # or a list of B positions 0 ... L_c - 1, used in every compartment
seed = 0                                # seed of the random input cells and of initial = "random"
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def encode(s, B):
    # bit string of one sample, most significant bit first: level l = floor(Q s) clipped to 0 ... Q - 1, in binary code
    l = int(quantise(np.array([s]), 2 ** B)[0])
    return format(l, f"0{B}b")

def run_driven(signal, rule, B=4, R=4, N_generation_steps=4, mode="replace", initial="zeros", L_c=16, input_cells=None, seed=0):
    # space-time array (len(signal) * (N_gen + 1), L): for every input step the ring right after the bits are written
    # and its N_gen iterations; also the positions (R, B) of the input cells, digit b of the code in column b
    if initial in ("zeros", "random"):
        c = np.zeros(R * L_c, int) if initial == "zeros" else np.random.default_rng(seed).integers(0, 2, R * L_c)
    else:
        if set(initial) - {"0", "1"}:
            raise ValueError("initial must be 'zeros', 'random' or a string of the characters 0 and 1")
        c = np.array([int(ch) for ch in initial])
        if len(c) % R:
            raise ValueError(f"the ring of {len(c)} cells cannot be divided into R = {R} compartments")
        L_c = len(c) // R
    if L_c < B:
        raise ValueError(f"a compartment of L_c = {L_c} cells cannot hold B = {B} input bits")
    if input_cells is None:
        cells = np.asarray(compartment_cells(R, L_c, B, seed))           # the same random choice as the CA reservoir
    else:
        if len(input_cells) != B or len(set(input_cells)) != B or not all(0 <= x < L_c for x in input_cells):
            raise ValueError(f"input_cells needs B = {B} distinct positions between 0 and {L_c - 1}")
        cells = np.array([[j * L_c + x for x in input_cells] for j in range(R)])
    rows = []
    for s in signal:
        d = np.array([int(ch) for ch in encode(s, B)[::-1]])      # least significant bit first, as in the CA reservoir
        c = c.copy()
        c[cells] = d[None, :] if mode == "replace" else (c[cells] + d[None, :]) % 2
        rows.append(c)
        for _ in range(N_generation_steps):
            c = (rule >> (4 * np.roll(c, 1) + 2 * c + np.roll(c, -1))) & 1
            rows.append(c)
    return np.array(rows), cells

def plot_driven(signal, ST, cells, B, rule, R, N_generation_steps):
    # left: signal and quantised values against the input step; right: the driven ring, injected cells in orange
    L_ = ST.shape[1]; n_ = len(signal)
    img = np.ones(ST.shape + (3,)) * (1 - ST[..., None])                 # white for 0, black for 1
    inj = np.zeros(ST.shape, bool); inj[::N_generation_steps + 1][:, cells.ravel()] = True # rows where the bits are written
    img[inj & (ST == 1)] = mpl.colors.to_rgb(DSOrange); img[inj & (ST == 0)] = mpl.colors.to_rgb("#F6C9A6")
    y_step = np.arange(n_) * (N_generation_steps + 1) + N_generation_steps / 2                             # centre of each input step on the row axis
    with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE_RC):
        fig, (a0, a1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 6.0), sharey=True, layout="constrained", gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 2.6]})
        a0.plot(signal, y_step, color="k", lw=1.0, label="$s_k$")
        a0.step((quantise(signal, 2 ** B) + 0.5) / 2 ** B, y_step, where="mid", color=UJBlue, lw=1.0, label="quantised")
        a0.set_xlim(-0.05, 1.05); a0.set_xlabel("value"); a0.set_ylabel(r"input step $k$, iterations $\downarrow$")
        a0.set_yticks(y_step[::10], [str(k) for k in range(0, n_, 10)])
        a0.legend(loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0), handlelength=1.2)
        a1.imshow(img, interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
        for k in range(1, n_):
            a1.axhline(k * (N_generation_steps + 1) - 0.5, color="0.6", lw=0.4)
        for j in range(1, R):
            a1.axvline(j * L_ // R - 0.5, color=UJBlue, lw=0.8)
        a1.set_xticks([]); a1.set_xlabel("cell $j$")
        a1.set_title(f"rule {rule}, $B={B}$, binary code\n$R={R}$, $L_c={L_ // R}$, $N_{{\\rm gen}}={N_generation_steps}$")
        plt.show()

# checks: encoding as in the notebook, and the same features as the CA reservoir (replacement, zero start, same cells)
digits_ref = np.stack([(quantise(signal, 16) >> b) & 1 for b in range(4)], 1)          # bits of the level, least significant first
assert all(encode(s, 4)[::-1] == "".join(map(str, row)) for s, row in zip(signal, digits_ref))
ST_chk, cells_chk = run_driven(signal, 180, 4, 4, 4, "replace", "zeros", 16, None, 0)
X_chk = np.asarray(ca_reservoir(eca_table(180), jnp.asarray(digits_ref, jnp.int32), jnp.asarray(cells_chk, jnp.int32), 2, 64, 4, False, True))
assert np.array_equal(ST_chk.reshape(len(signal), -1), X_chk)

ST_a, cells_a = run_driven(signal, rule, B, R, N_generation_steps, mode, initial, L_c, input_cells, seed)
plot_driven(signal, ST_a, cells_a, B, rule, R, N_generation_steps)
# a second start, a hand-written random-looking ring of the same size, driven by the same signal
initial_b = "0100001111001000100001111001100001111100001010111000110000001010"
ST_b, _ = run_driven(signal, rule, B, R, N_generation_steps, mode, initial_b, L_c, input_cells, seed)
plot_driven(signal, ST_b, cells_a, B, rule, R, N_generation_steps)
end_a, end_b = ST_a[N_generation_steps::N_generation_steps + 1], ST_b[N_generation_steps::N_generation_steps + 1]                           # ring at the end of every input step
differ = np.nonzero((end_a != end_b).any(1))[0]
if len(differ) == 0:
    print("the two runs agree from the first input step on")
elif differ[-1] < len(signal) - 1:
    print(f"the two runs agree from input step {differ[-1] + 1} on (steps counted from 0, {len(signal)} steps)")
else:
    print(f"the two runs still differ after the last of the {len(signal)} input steps, in {(end_a[-1] != end_b[-1]).sum()} cells")

title: Lab 050: Cellular automaton reservoir
text:
4. Forecasting with a CA reservoir
We forecast all five signals with the protocol of the ESN, the same origins, targets, scores and validation-only selection. The ring has \(L_c=16\) cells per compartment, the input is quantised and written in binary code, it is encoded by replacement, which Kantic et al. found the most stable encoding against changes of the other hyperparameters in their study of linear rules, and the readout reads all \(N_{\rm gen}+1\) configurations. The ridge strength is chosen from \(\{10^{-4},10^{-2},1,10,100\}\). We first check our ridge solve for integer features against scikit-learn Ridge on one reservoir, and the test predictions agree to \(6.0\times10^{-14}\). A worked example of one input step and of the readout comes first, and before the full search we look at the space of rules.


Code
CA_RULES = {"32": (eca_table(32), 2, "I"), "4": (eca_table(4), 2, "II"), "90": (eca_table(90), 2, "III"),
            "150": (eca_table(150), 2, "III"), "30": (eca_table(30), 2, "III"), "110": (eca_table(110), 2, "IV"),
            "Z4(0,2,1)": (linear_table((0, 2, 1), 4), 4, "lin."), "Z4(1,2,1)": (linear_table((1, 2, 1), 4), 4, "lin.")}
CA_BETA = (1e-4, 1e-2, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0)

def ca_states(s, rule, Q, R, Lc, N_generation_steps, additive=False, seed=0):
    table, q, _ = CA_RULES[rule]
    d = ca_digits(s, Q, q)
    cells = compartment_cells(R, Lc, d.shape[1], seed)
    return np.asarray(ca_reservoir(table, jnp.asarray(d), cells, q, R * Lc, N_generation_steps, additive, True), np.float32)

def ca_eval(s, cfg, test=False):
    # validation C_tot for one configuration, ridge strength chosen on validation; optionally test scores
    X = ca_states(s, *cfg)
    Yv = targets(s, K_VAL)
    best = (-1.0, None)
    for beta, W, b in ridge_int(X[K_FIT], targets(s, K_FIT), CA_BETA):
        v = score(X[K_VAL].astype(np.float64) @ W + b, Yv)["Ctot"]
        if v > best[0]:
            best = (v, (beta, W, b))
    out = dict(val=best[0], beta=best[1][0], n_feat=X.shape[1])
    if test:
        P = X[K_TEST].astype(np.float64) @ best[1][1] + best[1][2]
        out.update(pred=P, **score(P, targets(s, K_TEST)))
    return out

# check of the ridge solve for integer features against scikit-learn Ridge (rule 90, Q = 16, 4 compartments, N_gen = 4)
X_chk = ca_states(sig["SantaFe"], "90", 16, 4, 16, 4).astype(np.float64)
(_, W_c, b_c), = ridge_int(X_chk[K_FIT].astype(np.float32), targets(sig["SantaFe"], K_FIT), (1.0,))
sk = SkRidge(alpha=1.0, fit_intercept=True).fit(X_chk[K_FIT], targets(sig["SantaFe"], K_FIT))
nums["sklearn_diff"] = float(np.abs(sk.predict(X_chk[K_TEST]) - (X_chk[K_TEST] @ W_c + b_c)).max())
print(f"CA readout, beta = 1: max |prediction of our ridge solve - prediction scikit-learn| = {nums['sklearn_diff']:.1e}")



One input step with numbers
The next cells carry one sample through the three operations with numbers, calling the functions of the reservoir itself. The ring is smaller than in the figure, \(R=2\) compartments of \(L_c=5\) cells, the rule is rule 90, \(c_j\leftarrow c_{j-1}\oplus c_{j+1}\), and \(N_{\rm gen}=2\). The sample is \(s_k=0.61\) with \(Q=8\) levels and \(B=3\) bits. The level is \(\ell_k=\lfloor 8\cdot0.61\rfloor=\lfloor4.88\rfloor=4\), and its binary code word is the bit string 100.


Code
# encoding, quantisation and binary code: one sample, Q = 8 levels, B = 3 bits
s_ex, Q_ex = 0.61, 8
l_ex = int(quantise(np.array([s_ex]), Q_ex)[0])               # level floor(Q s), clipped to 0 ... Q - 1
d_ex = ca_digits(np.array([s_ex]), Q_ex, 2)[0]               # digits as the reservoir receives them, least significant first
print(f"s_k = {s_ex}, Q = {Q_ex}: level l = floor({Q_ex} * {s_ex}) = {l_ex}")
print(f"binary code: {l_ex} written with B = 3 bits as {format(l_ex, '03b')}")
print(f"digits in the order of the code (column b holds bit b): {d_ex.tolist()}")


The function ca_digits returns the digits with the least significant bit first, the order in which the reservoir hands them to the input cells, so the code word 100 appears as 0, 0, 1.
The input cells are 0, 2 and 3 in the first compartment and 6, 7 and 9 in the second, and cells 0 and 6 receive the most significant bit. In the code this order is set by the columns of the array of input cells, whose column \(b\) receives bit \(b\). The previous step left the state 1001101001. The writing overwrites the six input cells and leaves cells 1, 4, 5 and 8 as they were, which gives 1000101000.


Code
# encoding, writing into the input cells: a ring of R = 2 compartments of L_c = 5 cells
R_ex, Lc_ex = 2, 5
cells_ex = jnp.asarray([[3, 2, 0], [9, 7, 6]], jnp.int32)    # row = compartment, column b receives bit b
prev_ex = jnp.asarray([int(ch) for ch in "1001101001"], jnp.int32)    # state c_{k-1}^(N_gen) left by the previous step
c0_ex = prev_ex.at[cells_ex].set(jnp.broadcast_to(jnp.asarray(d_ex), cells_ex.shape))   # the write of the CA reservoir
bits = lambda c: "".join(map(str, np.asarray(c)))
print("input cells:", sorted(np.asarray(cells_ex[0]).tolist()), "and", sorted(np.asarray(cells_ex[1]).tolist()))
print(f"previous state c_(k-1)^(N_gen) = {bits(prev_ex)}")
print(f"after replacement c_k^(0)      = {bits(c0_ex)}")
assert bits(c0_ex) == "1000101000"


Rule 90 now acts \(N_{\rm gen}=2\) times on the whole ring with periodic boundary conditions, so cell 0 has cell 9 as its left neighbour, and the cell checks the lookup-table update of the reservoir against the formula. The three rows \(\mathbf c_k^{(0)}\), \(\mathbf c_k^{(1)}\) and \(\mathbf c_k^{(2)}\), concatenated, form the feature vector \(\mathbf r_k\) of \((N_{\rm gen}+1)L=30\) bits.


Code
# evolution by rule 90 and the feature vector, N_gen = 2
def draw_row(ax, x0, y0, row, size=0.22, q=2, hi=None, ec="0.35"):
    # one lattice configuration as a row of squares; cells in `hi` get an orange edge (injected cells)

Training the readout
Training uses the feature vectors of all fitting origins at once. The rows of the matrix \(X\) are \(\mathbf r_k\) for the origins \(k=63,\dots,2449\), and the rows of \(Y\) are the targets \(\mathbf y_k=(s_{k+1},\dots,s_{k+50})\) of the same origins. With the column means \(\bar{\mathbf r}\) of \(X\) and \(\bar{\mathbf y}\) of \(Y\) and the centred matrices \(X_c\) and \(Y_c\), from which these means are subtracted, the ridge regression gives
\[W_{\rm out}=\big(X_c^\top X_c+\beta I\big)^{-1}X_c^\top Y_c,\qquad \mathbf b=\bar{\mathbf y}-W_{\rm out}^\top\bar{\mathbf r}.\]
This is one linear solve for all 50 horizons, since column \(\tau\) of \(W_{\rm out}\) belongs to horizon \(\tau\). The ridge strength \(\beta\) is the value of the grid with the largest validation \(C_{\rm tot}\). The forecast at an origin is \(\tilde{\mathbf y}_k=W_{\rm out}^\top\mathbf r_k+\mathbf b\), and \(C(\tau)\) is computed from the forecasts at the test origins. The next cell runs the reservoir of the example, rule 90 with \(Q=8\), the two compartments above and \(N_{\rm gen}=2\), over the whole Santa Fe record from a ring of zeros, checks the first feature vector against a hand computation, and prints the shapes and the first forecasts.

How \(N_{\rm gen}\) is chosen
The number of generations per input step \(N_{\rm gen}\) is a hyperparameter. In the comparison of single rules below it is chosen on the validation block together with the ridge strength \(\beta\), from \(N_{\rm gen}\in\{1,2,3,4,6,8\}\). What one generation does makes the choice understandable. Under a transport rule such as 180 a bit moves about one cell per generation, so between two writings the record shifts by about \(N_{\rm gen}\) cells and consecutive inputs lie about \(N_{\rm gen}\) cells apart. The trail behind the input cells of one compartment then holds roughly \(L_c/N_{\rm gen}\) past inputs before it runs into the next compartment, where it meets newer bits, and a bit that sits on an input cell at a writing is erased. \(N_{\rm gen}\) thus trades the spacing of the record against its length, and it also sets the number of features \((N_{\rm gen}+1)L\). Under a spreading rule such as 90 or 30 every generation mixes each bit with more of its neighbours, and many generations scramble the record.
