title: Lab 071: Barren plateaus
section: 5. Global and local costs of the hardware-efficient circuit
text:
5. Global and local costs of the hardware-efficient circuit
We measure \(\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\partial_1C]\) for the HEA in three cases, the global cost at depth \(L=N\), the global cost at fixed depth \(L=2\), and the local cost at \(L=2\). At \(N=2\) the two depths coincide. For each case we fit \(\log_2\mathrm{Var}=\alpha-cN\) to the points \(N=4\) to \(10\), so that \(\mathrm{Var}\propto2^{-cN}\), and compare with the 2-design value \(1/[2d(d+1)]\) of the global cost, which corresponds to \(c\approx2\).
For the local cost at fixed depth, the angle \(\theta_1\) rotates qubit 0 in the first block, and each \(\widehat{\mathrm{CZ}}\) layer passes its influence on by one qubit. After \(L=2\) layers it reaches only qubits 0, 1 and 2, so only \(\langle\hat Z_0\rangle\), \(\langle\hat Z_1\rangle\) and \(\langle\hat Z_2\rangle\) depend on \(\theta_1\), and these three expectation values depend only on the angles of qubits 0 to 4. For \(N\ge5\) the distribution of their derivative does not change with \(N\), and the prefactor \(1/N\) of \(C_L\) in equation (3) gives \[\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\partial_1C_L]=\frac{\mathrm{const}}{N^2}\qquad(L=2,\ N\ge5) , \tag{7}\] a power law in \(N\). The code tests equation (7) through the products \(N^2\,\mathrm{Var}\) at \(N=6,8,10\). The sketch shows such a light cone for a brickwork circuit, which grows by one qubit per layer in the same way.



sketch_entanglement_capacity


Light cone of the first two-qubit gate in a brickwork circuit, growing by one qubit per layer, and the entanglement across the middle cut, which grows by at most one bit per layer.


Code
t_start = time.perf_counter()
CURVES = {}            # name -> list of (variance, standard error) over N_LIST
SIGMA2 = {}            # name -> mean single-shot variance of the energy at the sampled states
mean_over_sem = []
def record(name, g):
    CURVES.setdefault(name, []).append(var_with_error(np.asarray(g)))
    mean_over_sem.append(abs(np.mean(g)) / (np.std(g) / np.sqrt(g.size)))

for N in N_LIST:
    # HEA at depth L = N: global cost and energy from the same circuit
    def deep(t, N=N):
        psi = hea_state(t, N, N)
        E, var = energy_and_variance(psi)
        cg = cost_global(psi)
        return jnp.stack([cg, E]), (var, cg * (1 - cg))          # single shot of C_G is a yes-or-no outcome
    G, var = batched_gradients(deep, random_angles(10 + N, 2 * N * (N + 1)))
    record("HEA L=N, global", G[:, 0, 0]); record("HEA L=N, energy", G[:, 1, 0])
    SIGMA2.setdefault("HEA L=N, energy", []).append(float(np.mean(var[0])))
    SIGMA2.setdefault("HEA L=N, global", []).append(float(np.mean(var[1])))
    # HEA at depth L = 2: global and local cost from the same circuit
    def shallow(t, N=N):
        psi = hea_state(t, N, 2)
        p = jnp.abs(psi) ** 2
        ones = 0.5 - tables(N)[0].sum(axis=0) / (2 * N)        # single-shot value of C_L: fraction of bits equal to 1
        var_local = jnp.sum(p * ones ** 2) - jnp.sum(p * ones) ** 2
        return jnp.stack([cost_global(psi), cost_local(psi)]), var_local
    G, var = batched_gradients(shallow, random_angles(20 + N, 2 * N * 3))
    SIGMA2.setdefault("HEA L=2, local", []).append(float(np.mean(var)))
    record("HEA L=2, global", G[:, 0, 0]); record("HEA L=2, local", G[:, 1, 0])
    # HVA at depth L = N: energy, derivative with respect to gamma_1
    def hva(t, N=N):
        E, var = energy_and_variance(hva_state(t, N, N))
        return jnp.stack([E]), var
    G, var = batched_gradients(hva, random_angles(30 + N, 2 * N))
    record("HVA L=N, energy", G[:, 0, 0])
    SIGMA2.setdefault("HVA L=N, energy", []).append(float(np.mean(var)))
    print(f"N = {N:2d} done after {time.perf_counter() - t_start:5.1f} s")
assert max(mean_over_sem) < 4                     # mean gradient zero within the statistical error
print(f"largest |mean gradient| / standard error over all {len(mean_over_sem)} samples: {max(mean_over_sem):.2f}")

def fit_exponent(values, Ns=np.array(N_LIST, dtype=float)):
    # log2 Var = alpha - c N over N = 4..10
    return -np.polyfit(Ns[1:], np.log2(np.asarray(values)[1:]), 1)[0]

print(f"\n{'curve':>18s} " + " ".join(f"{'N=' + str(N):>18s}" for N in N_LIST) + f" {'c':>6s}")
FITS = {}
for name, rows in CURVES.items():
    v = [r[0] for r in rows]
    FITS[name] = fit_exponent(v)
    print(f"{name:>18s} " + " ".join(f"{a:9.2e} +-{b:7.1e}" for a, b in rows) + f" {FITS[name]:6.2f}")
haar_global = np.array([haar_formula(N, "global") for N in N_LIST])
haar_energy = np.array([haar_formula(N, "energy") for N in N_LIST])
print(f"{'2-design global':>18s} " + " ".join(f"{a:18.2e}" for a in haar_global) + f" {fit_exponent(haar_global):6.2f}")

# equation (7): N^2 Var constant for the local cost at L = 2, N >= 5
n2var = np.array([N ** 2 * CURVES["HEA L=2, local"][i][0] for i, N in enumerate(N_LIST) if N >= 5])
n2err = np.array([N ** 2 * CURVES["HEA L=2, local"][i][1] for i, N in enumerate(N_LIST) if N >= 5])
mean_n2 = np.sum(n2var / n2err ** 2) / np.sum(1 / n2err ** 2)
chi2 = float(np.sum((n2var - mean_n2) ** 2 / n2err ** 2))
assert chi2 < 13.8                                 # chi^2 with 2 degrees of freedom, P = 0.001
assert FITS["HEA L=N, global"] > 1.5 and FITS["HEA L=2, global"] > 1.0 and FITS["HEA L=2, local"] < 0.6
print(f"N^2 Var of the local cost at L = 2 for N = 6, 8, 10: {np.round(n2var, 4).tolist()} +- {np.round(n2err, 4).tolist()}, chi^2 = {chi2:.1f} (2 degrees of freedom)")

styles = {"HEA L=N, global": ("o", "-", COL["hea"], "white", r"global, $L=N$"),

               FitLocalShallow=f"{FITS['HEA L=2, local']:.2f}", FitTwoDesignGlobal=f"{fit_exponent(haar_global):.2f}",
               VarGlobalDeepTen=sci(CURVES['HEA L=N, global'][-1][0]), VarLocalShallowTen=sci(CURVES['HEA L=2, local'][-1][0]),
               NsqVarLocal=f"{mean_n2:.3f}", RatioLocalGlobalTen=f"{CURVES['HEA L=2, local'][-1][0] / CURVES['HEA L=2, global'][-1][0]:.0f}")





The global cost decays exponentially at both depths. At \(L=N\) the fitted exponent is close to two, the value of a 2-design, and the variance falls by more than four orders of magnitude between \(N=2\) and \(N=10\). A shallow circuit gives the global cost no protection, since at \(L=2\) it decays at a similar rate. The global cost compares the whole bit string with \(0\dots0\), and its value is the probability of a single bit string out of \(2^N\), which is exponentially small for almost all angles, whatever the depth. This dependence on the cost was proved for layered circuits of local 2-designs in Ref. [5], and our HEA, which is not of that form, shows the same behaviour.
The local cost at \(L=2\) decays slowly, and \(N^2\,\mathrm{Var}\) is constant for \(N\ge6\) within the statistical errors, as equation (7) predicts. At \(N=10\) its gradient variance is several hundred times larger than that of the global cost of the same circuit. The derivative of a local cost at fixed depth sees only the qubits inside the light cone of the differentiated gate, and the number of these qubits does not grow with \(N\). For local costs and depths growing as \(\log N\) the variance decays at most polynomially [5], whereas circuits deep enough to form 2-designs bring back the exponential decay of equation (6) for local costs too.

section: 6. The energy for the hardware-efficient and the Hamiltonian-variational circuits
text:
6. The energy for the hardware-efficient and the Hamiltonian-variational circuits
The energy (1) is the cost of a variational eigensolver. We measure the variance of its derivative for the HEA at depth \(L=N\), with respect to \(\theta_1\), and for the HVA at depth \(L=N\), with respect to \(\gamma_1\), and compare with the 2-design value of equation (6), \(\mathrm{Var}\approx[(N-1)J^2+Nh^2]/2^{N+1}\).

The 2-design curve falls by about a factor of two per qubit. The energy gradient of the HEA at depth \(L=N\) decays far more slowly over these sizes and lies more than an order of magnitude above the 2-design value at \(N=10\). The energy is a sum of terms on one or two neighbouring qubits, and each term is affected only by the gates inside its light cone. A \(\widehat{\mathrm{CZ}}\) chain spreads information by one qubit per layer, so at depth \(N\) the circuit has only just connected the two ends of the chain and is still far from a random unitary. These sizes cannot fix the asymptotic decay rate of the HEA, which approaches equation (6) once the circuit is deep enough to form a 2-design.
The variance of the HVA grows with \(N\). Each of its angles multiplies a sum over all bonds or all qubits, so one angle changes all \(2N-1\) terms of the energy together, and the derivative adds up contributions from the whole chain. The HVA also never approaches a random unitary. Its gates commute with the parity \(\hat\Pi\) and, more restrictively, they generate only a small family of unitaries whose dimension grows polynomially with \(N\), so the states it prepares fill a small part of the \(2^N\)-dimensional space. Mild or absent barren plateaus for this ansatz were reported in Ref. [4]. The size of the set of unitaries generated by the gates of a circuit, its dynamical Lie algebra, determines the gradient variance in general [6,7].

title: Lab 071: Barren plateaus
section: 7. Shots needed to resolve a gradient
text:
7. Shots needed to resolve a gradient
A device estimates a gradient component with the parameter-shift rule from two energies, each measured with \(M\) shots per setting. When the angle \(\theta_k\) enters a single gate, as in the HEA, the error propagation of the two estimates gives the statistical variance \(\sigma^2/(2M)\) of the estimated component, where \(\sigma^2=\sigma_Z^2+\sigma_X^2\) is the single-shot variance of the energy. The typical gradient becomes visible above the shot noise when this variance equals \(\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\partial_kE]\), which requires \[M^\star=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\,\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\partial_kE]} \tag{8}\] shots per setting and per shifted circuit. In a random state \(\sigma^2\approx\sum_jc_j^2=(N-1)J^2+Nh^2\), and with equation (6) for the variance the 2-design value is \(M^\star\approx d-1=2^N-1\). Every added qubit then doubles the number of shots for one gradient component.
An angle of the HVA enters many gates. The angle \(\gamma_1\) appears in the \(N-1\) gates \(\hat R_{zz}(\theta_g)\) of the first layer, each with \(\theta_g=2\gamma_1\), so the chain rule gives \(\partial E/\partial\gamma_1=\sum_g2\,\partial E/\partial\theta_g\). Each of the \(N-1\) terms is measured with the two-point rule by shifting the angle of one gate alone, which takes \(2(N-1)\) circuits. The terms are estimated independently, and their variances add with the squared factors \(c_g^2=4\), so the variance of the estimated derivative is \(4(N-1)\,\sigma^2/(2M)\). For an angle that enters gates with factors \(c_g\), equation (8) becomes \[M^\star=\frac{\sigma^2\sum_gc_g^2}{2\,\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\partial_kE]} , \tag{9}\] with \(\sum_gc_g^2=4(N-1)\) for \(\gamma_1\). The code first checks the chain rule for \(\gamma_1\) at \(N=6\) against jax.grad, with each gate shifted separately, and then evaluates equations (8) and (9) with the measured variances and the measured \(\sigma^2\), averaged over the sampled states.


Code
def hva_state_bond_shift(theta, N, L, bond, shift):
    # the HVA with the angle 2 gamma_1 of the single gate R_zz on (bond, bond + 1) shifted by `shift`
    z, zz, _ = tables(N)
    psi = jnp.ones((2,) * N, dtype=CDTYPE) / 2 ** (N / 2)
    for l, (gamma, beta) in enumerate(theta.reshape(L, 2)):
        psi = psi * jnp.exp(-1j * gamma * zz)
        if l == 0:
            psi = psi * jnp.exp(-1j * shift / 2 * z[bond] * z[bond + 1])     # extra R_zz(shift) on one bond
        psi = rotate_all(psi, jnp.broadcast_to(rotation(X, 2 * beta), (N, 2, 2)))
    return psi

The figure collects \(M^\star\) for all circuits and costs, with the single-shot variance of the global cost, \(C_G(1-C_G)\), and of the local cost, the variance of the fraction of bits equal to 1, measured at the sampled states. The global cost of the deep HEA needs a number of shots that grows exponentially with \(N\), whereas the local cost at \(L=2\) and the HVA need few. At \(N=10\) a typical energy gradient of the deep HEA is resolved with about sixty shots per setting, while a 2-design would need about a thousand. For the 2-design the count doubles with every qubit and reaches about \(10^6\) shots at \(N=20\) and \(10^{15}\) at \(N=50\), for a single component of a single gradient. The gradient of the HVA with respect to \(\gamma_1\) is resolved with a few shots per setting in each of its \(2(N-1)\) shifted circuits, about one shot at \(N=2\) and seven at \(N=10\). The growth is slow and set by the number of gates that share the angle. These numbers describe the start of training at uniformly random angles, where the optimiser must first find a direction downhill. A barren plateau cannot be removed by a better optimiser, because every optimiser on a device has to resolve the gradient, or differences of energies, above the shot noise, and equations (8) and (9) set the cost of doing so. The core route ends here.

title: Lab 071: Barren plateaus
section: 8. Noise and ways around barren plateaus
text:
8. Noise and ways around barren plateaus
Noise on a device produces a second kind of plateau. Depolarising noise after each layer replaces part of the state by the maximally mixed state, on which every traceless observable has expectation value zero. The whole cost landscape therefore contracts towards a constant by a factor that decays exponentially with the depth. For circuits whose depth grows linearly with \(N\) the gradient then vanishes exponentially in \(N\), independently of the random-unitary argument of Section 4 and also for structured ansätze [8]. The only remedy within the circuit is a smaller depth or lower error rates.
The known ways of keeping the gradient measurable change the cost, the circuit or the starting point.

Local costs, built from terms that act on few qubits, decay at most polynomially for circuits of logarithmic depth [5], as Section 5 shows for the HEA at \(L=2\).
Shallow circuits keep the light cone of each gate small, and they also limit the effect of noise [5,8].
Structured ansätze that respect the symmetries of the problem, such as the HVA, prepare states in a small part of the state space and keep large gradients, as Section 6 shows [4]. The dimension of the dynamical Lie algebra of the circuit predicts when this happens [6,7].
Initial angles chosen so that the circuit starts as the identity [9], or circuits trained layer by layer [10], start training away from the random region.

All of these measures restrict the set of states that the circuit explores. A circuit that can prepare almost any state, a highly expressive ansatz, has small gradients, and expressibility and trainability have to be balanced [11].

title: Lab 071: Barren plateaus
text:
9. Exercises

Show that the derivative \(-b\sin(\theta_k-c)\) averages to zero over \(\theta_k\in[-\pi,\pi]\), and check numerically that the mean gradient of Section 5 is zero within its standard error.
Derive \(\mathrm{Var}\,\langle\hat Z_0\rangle=1/(d+1)\) for random states, starting from the fact that the vector of probabilities \(|\psi_{\mathbf b}|^2\) of a random state is uniformly distributed on the probability simplex.
Measure the variance for the local cost of the HEA at depth \(L=N\) and compare it with \(L=2\) and with the 2-design value \(2^{-N}/(8N)\).
Differentiate with respect to the last angle of the HEA instead of the first, and explain the result for the local cost at \(L=2\) with the light-cone argument.
Draw the HEA angles uniformly from \([-\epsilon,\epsilon]\) with \(\epsilon=0.1\) and measure the variance of the global cost against \(N\).
Show that equations (6) and (8) give \(M^\star=d-1\) for a 2-design, using \(\sigma^2=d\sum_jc_j^2/(d+1)\) for a random state.
For the global cost a single shot is a yes-or-no outcome with variance \(C_G(1-C_G)\). Estimate \(M^\star\) for the global cost of the deep HEA at \(N=10\).

title: Lab 071: Barren plateaus
text:
10. Summary
For angles drawn at random, the mean of every gradient component vanishes and its variance measures the typical gradient. In a random state every expectation value concentrates around its mean, with a variance of order \(2^{-N}\). A circuit that acts as a random unitary gives gradient variances that decay exponentially with \(N\), at a rate set by the size of the cost observable. Global costs decay exponentially for the hardware-efficient circuit at every depth considered, with the 2-design exponent at depth \(N\). A local cost at fixed depth keeps a gradient variance that decreases only as \(1/N^2\), because the derivative sees only the qubits inside the light cone of the differentiated gate. The energy of the Ising chain decays slowly for the hardware-efficient circuit at the sizes studied. Its gradient grows with \(N\) for the Hamiltonian-variational circuit, whose shared angles and symmetry keep it in a small part of the state space. The number of shots needed to resolve a gradient is the ratio of the single-shot variance to the gradient variance, and for a random unitary it doubles with every qubit.

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
2. State-vector simulator
The simulator stores the state of \(N\) qubits as a tensor \(\psi[b_0,\dots,b_{N-1}]\) with one axis of length 2 per qubit, and qubit 0 is the most significant bit, so the amplitude of the bit string \(b_0b_1\dots b_{N-1}\) sits at the flat index \[k=\sum_{q=0}^{N-1}b_q\,2^{N-1-q}. \tag{1}\] A rotation generated by a Pauli matrix \(\hat P\) is \[\hat R_P(\theta)=e^{-i\theta\hat P/2}=\cos\frac\theta2\,\hat I-i\sin\frac\theta2\,\hat P , \tag{2}\] and a one-qubit gate acts on qubit \(q\) by a contraction with axis \(q\) of the state tensor. The controlled-\(Z\) gate \(\widehat{\mathrm{CZ}}\) on the pair \((q,q+1)\) multiplies the amplitude of every bit string with \(b_q=b_{q+1}=1\) by \(-1\). It is diagonal in the computational basis, so a chain of such gates is one vector of signs \(\pm1\) multiplied element-wise into the state. The last check compares the contraction with the Kronecker-product matrix \(\hat I\otimes\hat U\otimes\hat I\) on three qubits.


Code
# recap: one-qubit matrices, rotations (2), gates on a state tensor, CZ chain as a sign vector
I2 = jnp.eye(2, dtype=CDTYPE)
X = jnp.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], dtype=CDTYPE)
Y = jnp.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]], dtype=CDTYPE)
Z = jnp.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]], dtype=CDTYPE)

def rot(P, theta):
    return jnp.cos(theta / 2) * I2 - 1j * jnp.sin(theta / 2) * P

def apply_1q(psi, U, q):
    # psi has shape (2,)*N; contract the gate with axis q and put the new axis back at position q
    return jnp.moveaxis(jnp.tensordot(U, psi, axes=([1], [q])), 0, q)

def bit_table(N):
    # row k holds the bits b_0 ... b_{N-1} of index k, qubit 0 most significant, equation (1)
    k = np.arange(2 ** N)
    return (k[:, None] >> (N - 1 - np.arange(N))) & 1

def cz_chain_signs(N):
    b = bit_table(N)
    return np.prod([1 - 2 * b[:, q] * b[:, q + 1] for q in range(N - 1)], axis=0)

U_test = rot(Y, 0.7) @ rot(Z, -1.1)
psi3 = jax.random.normal(jax.random.PRNGKey(7201), (8,)) + 0j
psi3 = psi3 / jnp.linalg.norm(psi3)
assert jnp.allclose(apply_1q(psi3.reshape(2, 2, 2), U_test, 1).reshape(-1), jnp.kron(jnp.kron(I2, U_test), I2) @ psi3, atol=TOL)
assert jnp.allclose(rot(X, jnp.pi), -1j * X, atol=TOL)
assert list(bit_table(3)[3]) == [0, 1, 1]
CZ01 = jnp.diag(jnp.array([1, 1, 1, -1], dtype=CDTYPE))
assert np.allclose(np.diag(np.kron(CZ01, np.eye(2)) @ np.kron(np.eye(2), CZ01)), cz_chain_signs(3))
print("simulator ready: contraction = Kronecker matrix, CZ chain = sign vector", cz_chain_signs(3))

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
3. Generative modelling
We consider an unknown probability distribution \(p\) over a space of outcomes and a data set \[\mathcal D=\{x^{(1)},x^{(2)},\dots,x^{(|\mathcal D|)}\} \tag{3}\] of \(|\mathcal D|\) independent samples drawn from it. The learner sees the samples and never the distribution \(p\) itself. A generative model is a family of distributions \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\), labelled by parameters \(\boldsymbol\theta\). New samples can be drawn from \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\), and \(\boldsymbol\theta\) is adjusted so that \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) comes close to \(p\) in a measure of distance between distributions. Training means choosing \(\boldsymbol\theta\) from the data, and a trained model produces new samples that look like the data without copying them.
Classical machine learning offers many such families. A histogram of the data is the simplest one, and it can be sampled by picking a bin with the stored frequency. A Boltzmann machine assigns the probability \(e^{-E_{\boldsymbol\theta}(x)}/Z\) through an energy function with trainable couplings. An autoregressive network writes the probability of a vector as a product of conditional probabilities, one component after another. Generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders transform random noise into samples with a neural network. The quantum model studied here addresses the same task and differs in how the probabilities arise.
The sketch summarises the task, a model trained on samples of an unknown distribution that produces new samples, and the Born machine as one such model.



generative modelling

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
4. Data as bit strings
A register of \(N\) qubits returns bit strings \(\mathbf b=b_0b_1\dots b_{N-1}\), so the data must be written as bit strings before a circuit can model them. Discrete data such as spin configurations or binary images are bit strings already. A continuous variable \(x\in[x_{\min},x_{\max}]\) is first discretised. We cut the interval into \(2^N\) bins of equal width \[w=\frac{x_{\max}-x_{\min}}{2^N}, \tag{4}\] and number them from left to right by the bin index \[k(x)=\left\lfloor\frac{x-x_{\min}}{w}\right\rfloor\in\{0,1,\dots,2^N-1\}, \tag{5}\] where \(\lfloor\cdot\rfloor\) rounds down to an integer and the right end \(x=x_{\max}\) is assigned to the last bin. The index written in binary, \[k=\sum_{q=0}^{N-1}b_q\,2^{N-1-q}, \tag{6}\] is the bit string \(\mathbf b\), with \(b_0\) the most significant bit, which is the ordering (1) of the amplitudes. Every value of \(x\) in bin \(k\) therefore corresponds to the computational basis state \(|\mathbf b\rangle\), and every measured bit string corresponds back to a bin. When a value of \(x\) is needed, we take the centre of the bin, \[x_k=x_{\min}+\Big(k+\frac12\Big)w . \tag{7}\]
For \(N=3\) and the interval \([-4,4]\), \(w=1\) and there are eight bins labelled \(000,001,\dots,111\). The value \(x=-0.37\) lies in the bin \([-1,0)\) with index \(k=\lfloor 3.63\rfloor=3\), and \(3=0\cdot4+1\cdot2+1\cdot1\) is the bit string \(011\). The value belongs to the basis state \(|011\rangle\), and a measurement that returns \(011\) is read as the bin centre \(x_3=-0.5\). The discretisation loses the position of \(x\) inside its bin, an error of at most \(w/2\). Each added qubit doubles the number of bins and halves the width \(w\), so the resolution improves exponentially with the number of qubits.
The code implements equations (5) to (7) and runs the example in both directions.


Code
def x_to_index(x, N, xmin, xmax):
    k = np.floor((np.asarray(x) - xmin) / (xmax - xmin) * 2 ** N).astype(int)
    return np.clip(k, 0, 2 ** N - 1)                    # x = xmax goes into the last bin

def index_to_bits(k, N):
    return [(int(k) >> (N - 1 - q)) & 1 for q in range(N)]

def bits_to_index(bits):
    N = len(bits)
    return sum(b * 2 ** (N - 1 - q) for q, b in enumerate(bits))

def bin_centre(k, N, xmin, xmax):
    return xmin + (np.asarray(k) + 0.5) * (xmax - xmin) / 2 ** N

x_example = -0.37
k_example = int(x_to_index(x_example, 3, -4.0, 4.0))
b_example = index_to_bits(k_example, 3)
assert k_example == 3 and b_example == [0, 1, 1] and bits_to_index(b_example) == 3
print(f"x = {x_example} -> bin k = {k_example} -> bit string {''.join(map(str, b_example))}"
      f" -> bin centre x_k = {bin_centre(k_example, 3, -4.0, 4.0):+.2f}")
for N_ in (3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10):
    print(f"N = {N_:2d}: {2**N_:5d} bins of width {8 / 2**N_:.4f} on [-4, 4]")
for k in range(8):
    assert bits_to_index(index_to_bits(k, 3)) == k

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
section: 5. The target distribution and the data set
text:
5. The target distribution and the data set
The target is a mixture of two Gaussian peaks on \(x\in[-4,4]\), \[p(x)\propto\sum_{j=1}^{2}w_j\,\exp\!\Big[-\frac{(x-\mu_j)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big], \tag{8}\] with weights \(w_1=0.4\) and \(w_2=0.6\), centres \(\mu_{1,2}=\mp1.6\) and the common width \(\sigma=0.6\). On \(N=6\) qubits the interval is cut into 64 bins of width \(w=0.125\). The exact bin probability \(p(\mathbf b)\) is the integral of \(p(x)\) over bin \(k\), which follows from the error function. We know \(p(\mathbf b)\) only because we chose the target. A learner sees the data set, \(|\mathcal D|=3000\) values of \(x\) drawn from equation (8), each converted to a bit string with equation (5). The data define the empirical distribution \[\tilde p(\mathbf b)=\frac{n(\mathbf b)}{|\mathcal D|}, \tag{9}\] where \(n(\mathbf b)\) counts how often the bit string \(\mathbf b\) occurs in the data set. The tilde marks an estimate obtained from samples. The model is trained on \(\tilde p\), and the exact \(p\) serves only to judge how well the trained model generalises beyond the finite data set.
The two peaks make the bits strongly correlated. The left peak sits around bin 19, bit string \(010011\), and the right peak around bin 44, bit string \(101100\), so a value near the left peak has \(b_0=0\), \(b_1=1\), \(b_2=0\), whereas a value near the right peak has the opposite bits.


Code
N = 6
K = 2 ** N
XMIN, XMAX = -4.0, 4.0
W_MIX, MU_MIX, SIG_MIX = np.array([0.4, 0.6]), np.array([-1.6, 1.6]), 0.6
edges = np.linspace(XMIN, XMAX, K + 1)
xk = bin_centre(np.arange(K), N, XMIN, XMAX)

def mixture_cdf(x):
    return sum(w * 0.5 * (1 + erf((x - m) / (np.sqrt(2) * SIG_MIX))) for w, m in zip(W_MIX, MU_MIX))

p_exact = np.diff(mixture_cdf(edges)); p_exact /= p_exact.sum()     # exact bin probabilities p(b)

rng = np.random.default_rng(72)                                       # seed of the data set
D_SIZE = 3000
comp = rng.choice(2, size=2 * D_SIZE, p=W_MIX)
x_draw = rng.normal(MU_MIX[comp], SIG_MIX)
x_data = x_draw[(x_draw >= XMIN) & (x_draw <= XMAX)][:D_SIZE]
k_data = x_to_index(x_data, N, XMIN, XMAX)
p_data = np.bincount(k_data, minlength=K) / D_SIZE                     # empirical distribution (9)
BITS = bit_table(N)

assert len(x_data) == D_SIZE and abs(p_data.sum() - 1) < TOL
tv = lambda a, b: 0.5 * float(np.abs(np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)).sum())
print("first five data values:", np.round(x_data[:5], 3))
print("as bit strings        :", ["".join(map(str, BITS[k])) for k in k_data[:5]])
print(f"bins never seen in the data: {int((p_data == 0).sum())} of {K}")
print(f"peak bins of p: {int(np.argmax(p_exact[:32]))} = {''.join(map(str, BITS[np.argmax(p_exact[:32])]))},"
      f" {32 + int(np.argmax(p_exact[32:]))} = {''.join(map(str, BITS[32 + np.argmax(p_exact[32:])]))}")
NUMBERS["DataSize"] = str(D_SIZE)
NUMBERS["TVDataTarget"] = f"{tv(p_data, p_exact):.3f}"
NUMBERS["EmptyBins"] = str(int((p_data == 0).sum()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 3.2))
ax.bar(xk, p_data, width=0.125, color=COL["data"], edgecolor="white", lw=0.3, label=r"data $\tilde p(\mathbf{b})$")
ax.step(np.r_[edges[0], edges[1:]], np.r_[p_exact[0], p_exact], where="pre", color=COL["target"], lw=1.3, label=r"target $p(\mathbf{b})$")
ax.set_xlabel(r"bin centre $x_k$"); ax.set_ylabel("probability"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=11)
save(fig, "fig_lab072_target"); plt.show()

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
6. The Born machine
A circuit \(\hat V(\boldsymbol\theta)\) with gate angles \(\boldsymbol\theta\) acts on the register prepared in \(|0\rangle^{\otimes N}\) and produces the state \(|\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)\rangle=\hat V(\boldsymbol\theta)|0\rangle^{\otimes N}\). A measurement of every qubit in the computational basis returns the bit string \(\mathbf b\) with the Born-rule probability \[q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf b)=\big|\langle\mathbf b|\hat V(\boldsymbol\theta)|0\rangle^{\otimes N}\big|^2 . \tag{10}\] These probabilities are non-negative and sum to one for every \(\boldsymbol\theta\), because the state is normalised, so equation (10) is a family of distributions over the \(2^N\) bit strings. A model whose probabilities are squared amplitudes is called a Born machine. The idea was introduced with matrix product states as the source of the amplitudes [1] and compared with Boltzmann machines in Ref. [2]. With a parametrised circuit as the source, the model is the quantum circuit Born machine [3, 4], whose sampling hardness and training were studied in Ref. [5].
The sketch shows the Born machine, a circuit \(\hat V(\boldsymbol\theta)\) acting on \(|0\rangle^{\otimes N}\) and followed by a measurement of every qubit, which returns one bit string \(\mathbf b\) per run.



quantum circuit Born machine


Sampling needs no further computation, since one run of the circuit followed by a measurement of all qubits draws one bit string from \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) and, through equation (7), one value of \(x\). The probabilities themselves are not directly accessible on a device. An experiment estimates \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf b)\) only as a frequency over many runs, \(\tilde q(\mathbf b)=n(\mathbf b)/M\) for \(M\) shots, and a bit string of small probability may not appear at all. A simulation, by contrast, stores all \(2^N\) amplitudes and gives the exact \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\).
The circuit is the same object that prepares trial states in the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). In VQE the measured bit strings serve only to estimate an energy, and the goal is the state that minimises it. In a Born machine the distribution of the bit strings is the goal, and the samples themselves are the output.
In the circuit used throughout, a rotation block applies \(\hat R_z(\phi_q)\hat R_y(\vartheta_q)\) to every qubit \(q\), and an entangling layer is the chain of \(\widehat{\mathrm{CZ}}\) gates on the pairs \((0,1),(1,2),\dots,(N-2,N-1)\). The circuit with \(L\) layers is \[\hat V(\boldsymbol\theta)=\hat B_L\,\widehat{\mathrm{CZ}}_{\rm chain}\cdots\hat B_1\,\widehat{\mathrm{CZ}}_{\rm chain}\,\hat B_0,\qquad \hat B_\ell=\bigotimes_{q=0}^{N-1}\hat R_z(\phi_{\ell q})\,\hat R_y(\vartheta_{\ell q}), \tag{11}\] with \(n=2N(L+1)\) angles. The array theta has the shape \((L_{\max}+1,N,2)\), and a mask switches off the layers beyond \(L\), so that circuits of every depth \(0\le L\le L_{\max}\) share one compiled function. At \(L=0\) only the block \(\hat B_0\) remains, the product circuit of Section 8. We check that \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) sums to one and draw a record of bit strings from a random circuit.


Code
L_MAX = 5
CZ_SIGNS = jnp.asarray(cz_chain_signs(N), dtype=CDTYPE)

def rotation_block(psi, angles):
    # angles[q] = (vartheta_q, phi_q): R_z(phi) R_y(vartheta) on qubit q
    for q in range(N):
        psi = apply_1q(psi, rot(Z, angles[q, 1]) @ rot(Y, angles[q, 0]), q)
    return psi

def born_state(theta, mask):
    # equation (11); mask[l] = 1 keeps layer l + 1, mask[l] = 0 removes its CZ chain and its rotations
    psi = jnp.zeros((2,) * N, dtype=CDTYPE).at[(0,) * N].set(1.0)
    psi = rotation_block(psi, theta[0])
    def layer(psi, inputs):
        angles, m = inputs
        psi = (psi.reshape(-1) * jnp.where(m > 0, CZ_SIGNS, 1.0)).reshape((2,) * N)
        return rotation_block(psi, angles * m), None
    psi, _ = lax.scan(layer, psi, (theta[1:], mask))
    return psi.reshape(-1)

@jax.jit
def born_probs(theta, mask):
    return jnp.abs(born_state(theta, mask)) ** 2            # equation (10)

def depth_mask(L):
    return jnp.asarray((np.arange(L_MAX) < L).astype(float))

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=2)
def sample_bits(key, q, shots):
    # shots measurements of all qubits: bin indices drawn with probabilities q, by inverting the cumulative sum
    u = jax.random.uniform(key, (shots,)) * jnp.sum(q)
    return jnp.minimum(jnp.searchsorted(jnp.cumsum(q), u), q.shape[0] - 1)

def counts_to_freq(idx, size=K):
    return jnp.bincount(idx, length=size) / idx.shape[0]

theta_rand = jax.random.uniform(jax.random.PRNGKey(7202), (L_MAX + 1, N, 2), minval=0, maxval=2 * np.pi)
q_rand = born_probs(theta_rand, depth_mask(2))
assert abs(float(q_rand.sum()) - 1) < TOL
shots_demo = sample_bits(jax.random.PRNGKey(7203), q_rand, 5)
print("q sums to", float(q_rand.sum()), "| five measured bit strings:",
      ["".join(map(str, BITS[int(i)])) for i in shots_demo], "-> x =", np.round(xk[np.asarray(shots_demo)], 3))
idx_big = sample_bits(jax.random.PRNGKey(7204), q_rand, 200_000)
print(f"total variation between q and the frequencies of 200000 shots: {tv(counts_to_freq(idx_big), q_rand):.4f}")


q sums to 1.0000000000000007 | five measured bit strings: ['101011', '001011', '100100', '100100', '101100'] -> x = [ 1.438 -2.562  0.562  0.562  1.562]
total variation between q and the frequencies of 200000 shots: 0.0078


The frequencies of 200 000 shots agree with the exact probabilities up to the statistical error of the record, which confirms that sample_bits draws from \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\).

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
7. The loss function
Training needs a number that measures how far \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) is from the data. The Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence [6] of \(q\) from \(p\) is \[D_{\rm KL}(p\,\|\,q_{\boldsymbol\theta})=\sum_{\mathbf b}p(\mathbf b)\,\ln\frac{p(\mathbf b)}{q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf b)} , \tag{12}\] with the convention \(0\ln0=0\), and it is measured in nats because of the natural logarithm. It is non-negative and vanishes only for \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}=p\). It is asymmetric in its arguments and therefore not a distance in the mathematical sense. The weight \(p(\mathbf b)\) makes it most sensitive to the bit strings that are frequent in the data.
When \(p\) is replaced by the empirical distribution (9), the KL divergence becomes the negative log-likelihood of the data, the standard loss of statistics. Splitting the logarithm gives \[D_{\rm KL}(\tilde p\,\|\,q_{\boldsymbol\theta})=\sum_{\mathbf b}\tilde p(\mathbf b)\ln\tilde p(\mathbf b)-\sum_{\mathbf b}\tilde p(\mathbf b)\ln q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf b) . \tag{13}\] The first sum is minus the Shannon entropy \(H(\tilde p)\) of the data, in nats, which does not depend on \(\boldsymbol\theta\). In the second sum each bit string occurs with the weight \(n(\mathbf b)/|\mathcal D|\), so the sum over bit strings is a sum over the data points, \[-\sum_{\mathbf b}\tilde p(\mathbf b)\ln q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf b)=-\frac1{|\mathcal D|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal D|}\ln q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\big(\mathbf b^{(i)}\big)\equiv\mathcal L_{\rm NLL}(\boldsymbol\theta), \tag{14}\] and therefore \[D_{\rm KL}(\tilde p\,\|\,q_{\boldsymbol\theta})=\mathcal L_{\rm NLL}(\boldsymbol\theta)-H(\tilde p). \tag{15}\] Minimising the KL divergence to the data and maximising the likelihood of the data are the same task with the same gradient.
The loss (14) contains \(\ln q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf b)\) for every bit string in the data. If the model gives a data bit string a vanishing probability, the loss diverges, so the training must start from a model that covers all bit strings. We start from angles close to \(\vartheta_q=\pi/2\), for which each qubit is near \(|+\rangle\) and \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) is close to the uniform distribution \(1/64\). On a device the loss is harder to use, because it needs the probability of each data bit string, which can only be estimated from shot frequencies. A zero frequency, common for small probabilities, makes the estimate of \(\ln q\) infinite.
We judge a trained model by the KL divergence (12) from the exact target, \(D_{\rm KL}(p\,\|\,q_{\boldsymbol\theta})\), which tests generalisation beyond the data, and by the total variation distance \[d_{\rm TV}(p,q)=\frac12\sum_{\mathbf b}\big|p(\mathbf b)-q(\mathbf b)\big| \tag{16}\] which is the largest difference between the probabilities that the two distributions assign to any set of bit strings. It lies between 0 and 1 and stays finite when \(q\) vanishes on some bit strings.
The gradient of the loss is computed by automatic differentiation of the simulator with jax.grad. On a device the gradient comes from the parameter-shift rule. It gives the derivative of each probability \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf b)\) from two circuits whose angle \(\theta_j\) is shifted by \(\pm\pi/2\), because \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf b)\) is the expectation value of the projector \(|\mathbf b\rangle\langle\mathbf b|\). The probabilities of both circuits are estimated from shots. The angles are updated with the Adam optimiser [7], implemented in a few lines, and lax.scan runs the whole training loop inside one compiled function.


Code
P_DATA = jnp.asarray(p_data)

def kl_div(p, q):
    # equation (12) in nats; terms with p = 0 contribute zero
    p, q = jnp.asarray(p), jnp.asarray(q)
    return jnp.sum(jnp.where(p > 0, p * (jnp.log(jnp.where(p > 0, p, 1.0)) - jnp.log(q + 1e-300)), 0.0))

def nll(q, k_samples):
    return -jnp.mean(jnp.log(q[k_samples]))               # equation (14)

def kl_loss(theta, mask):
    return kl_div(P_DATA, born_probs(theta, mask))

def adam(loss, theta0, steps, lr):
    # Adam with the standard moment decay rates 0.9 and 0.999; returns the final angles and the loss history
    value_and_grad = jax.value_and_grad(loss)
    def step(carry, i):
        th, m, v = carry
        l, g = value_and_grad(th)
        m = 0.9 * m + 0.1 * g
        v = 0.999 * v + 0.001 * g ** 2
        th = th - lr * (m / (1 - 0.9 ** (i + 1))) / (jnp.sqrt(v / (1 - 0.999 ** (i + 1))) + 1e-8)
        return (th, m, v), l
    (th, _, _), hist = lax.scan(step, (theta0, jnp.zeros_like(theta0), jnp.zeros_like(theta0)), jnp.arange(steps))
    return th, hist

# equation (15): KL to the data = negative log-likelihood - entropy of the data
q_check = born_probs(theta_rand, depth_mask(2))
S_data = -float(jnp.sum(jnp.where(P_DATA > 0, P_DATA * jnp.log(jnp.where(P_DATA > 0, P_DATA, 1.0)), 0.0)))
assert abs(float(kl_div(P_DATA, q_check)) - (float(nll(q_check, jnp.asarray(k_data))) - S_data)) < 1e-10
print(f"random circuit: KL to the data = {float(kl_div(P_DATA, q_check)):.4f} = NLL {float(nll(q_check, jnp.asarray(k_data))):.4f}"
      f" - entropy of the data {S_data:.4f}")


random circuit: KL to the data = 1.7221 = NLL 5.3552 - entropy of the data 3.6331


The check confirms equation (15) on a random circuit to numerical precision.

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
8. The product circuit
Without entangling gates, \(L=0\) in equation (11), the circuit is a product of one-qubit gates and prepares a product state. Each qubit \(q\) ends in its own state \(\cos(\vartheta_q/2)|0\rangle+e^{i\phi_q}\sin(\vartheta_q/2)|1\rangle\) up to a global phase, and the amplitude of a bit string is a product of one-qubit amplitudes. The Born probability then factorises, \[q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf b)=\prod_{q=0}^{N-1}q_q(b_q),\qquad q_q(0)=\cos^2\frac{\vartheta_q}2,\quad q_q(1)=\sin^2\frac{\vartheta_q}2 , \tag{17}\] so every bit is an independent biased coin, and the phases \(\phi_q\) have no effect on the outcomes. A product circuit cannot represent any correlation between bits.
The sketch contrasts the product circuit, whose bits are independent biased coins, with a circuit whose \(\widehat{\mathrm{CZ}}\) gates correlate the bits.



product circuit versus circuit with entanglers


The best product model of a given distribution follows from equation (12). With \(q\) of the form (17), the logarithm of \(q\) splits into a sum over qubits, and \[D_{\rm KL}\Big(p\,\Big\|\,\prod_q q_q\Big)=-H(p)-\sum_{q=0}^{N-1}\sum_{b_q\in\{0,1\}}p_q(b_q)\ln q_q(b_q), \tag{18}\] where \(p_q(b_q)\) is the marginal probability that bit \(q\) takes the value \(b_q\) under \(p\). Each inner sum is smallest for \(q_q=p_q\), by the non-negativity of the KL divergence between the two one-bit distributions. The best product model is therefore the product of the marginals of the data, and no training of the angles can go below the value of equation (18) at \(q_q=p_q\).
For the two-peak target the marginals mix the bits of the two peaks. The product of marginals spreads probability over many bit strings that combine the leading bits of one peak with the trailing bits of the other, which puts probability into bins between and outside the peaks. We first verify the factorisation (17) for random angles and then train the product circuit with the KL divergence to the data.


Code
theta_prod = jax.random.uniform(jax.random.PRNGKey(7205), (L_MAX + 1, N, 2), minval=0, maxval=2 * np.pi)
q_prod = np.asarray(born_probs(theta_prod, depth_mask(0)))
marg = np.array([[np.cos(theta_prod[0, q, 0] / 2) ** 2, np.sin(theta_prod[0, q, 0] / 2) ** 2] for q in range(N)])
q_fact = np.prod(marg[np.arange(N), BITS], axis=1)                   # equation (17)
assert np.allclose(q_prod, q_fact, atol=1e-12)

m1 = (p_data[:, None] * BITS).sum(0)                                  # marginals P(b_q = 1) of the data
q_marg = np.prod(np.where(BITS == 1, m1, 1 - m1), axis=1)             # best product model
kl_bound = float(kl_div(p_data, q_marg))
print("factorisation (19) holds for random angles")
print("data marginals P(b_q = 1):", np.round(m1, 3))
print(f"lower bound of the product circuit, KL(p_data || product of marginals) = {kl_bound:.4f}")
NUMBERS["KLProductBound"] = f"{kl_bound:.3f}"

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
9. Layered circuits with entanglers
Entangling gates between the rotation blocks make the amplitudes, and therefore the bits, correlated. We train circuits (11) of depth \(L=0,1,\dots,5\), with \(n=12,24,\dots,72\) angles, each from three random starts with \(600\) Adam steps and the learning rate \(0.05\). The starting angles are \(\vartheta=\pi/2\) and \(\phi=0\) plus uniform noise of amplitude \(0.3\), so every start lies near the uniform distribution. The mask lets one compiled function, vectorised with jax.vmap, train all eighteen circuits at once. For each depth we record the KL divergence to the data, which is the training loss, and the KL divergence to the exact target, which tests generalisation.


Code
SEEDS, STEPS, LR = 3, 600, 0.05
depths = np.repeat(np.arange(L_MAX + 1), SEEDS)
masks = jnp.asarray((np.arange(L_MAX)[None, :] < depths[:, None]).astype(float))
theta0 = jax.random.uniform(jax.random.PRNGKey(7206), (len(depths), L_MAX + 1, N, 2), minval=-0.3, maxval=0.3)
theta0 = theta0.at[..., 0].add(np.pi / 2)
t_train = time.perf_counter()
train_all = jax.jit(jax.vmap(lambda th, m: adam(lambda x: kl_loss(x, m), th, STEPS, LR)))
theta_tr, hist_tr = train_all(theta0, masks)
hist_tr = np.asarray(hist_tr)
q_tr = np.asarray(jax.jit(jax.vmap(born_probs))(theta_tr, masks))
print(f"training of {len(depths)} circuits: {time.perf_counter() - t_train:.1f} s")

kl_train = hist_tr[:, -1]
kl_target = np.array([float(kl_div(p_exact, q)) for q in q_tr])
tv_target = np.array([tv(p_exact, q) for q in q_tr])
best = {L: int(np.where(depths == L)[0][np.argmin(kl_train[depths == L])]) for L in range(L_MAX + 1)}
print(" L   n  | KL(data||q) best  | KL(p||q) of best | TV(p,q) of best")
for L in range(L_MAX + 1):
    i = best[L]
    print(f" {L}  {2 * N * (L + 1):3d} |     {kl_train[i]:.4f}        |      {kl_target[i]:.4f}      |     {tv_target[i]:.3f}")
assert abs(kl_train[best[0]] - kl_bound) < 1e-4          # the product circuit reaches the product-of-marginals bound
WORDS = ["Zero", "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five"]
for L in range(L_MAX + 1):
    NUMBERS[f"KLDataL{WORDS[L]}"] = f"{kl_train[best[L]]:.4f}"
    NUMBERS[f"KLTargetL{WORDS[L]}"] = f"{kl_target[best[L]]:.4f}"
    NUMBERS[f"TVTargetL{WORDS[L]}"] = f"{tv_target[best[L]]:.3f}"

The product circuit converges from all three starts to the bound of equation (18), so its remaining error is the missing correlation between the bits. One entangling layer lowers the KL divergence from 0.5 to below 0.1, and every further layer lowers the training loss again. The figure shows the training curves of the best start at each depth and the final divergences against depth.


Code
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.0, 3.6))
cmap = plt.get_cmap("viridis")
for L in range(L_MAX + 1):
    axs[0].semilogy(hist_tr[best[L]], color=cmap(L / (L_MAX + 0.5)), lw=1.3, label=f"$L={L}$")

axs[0].axhline(kl_bound, color="0.4", ls=":", lw=1.0)
axs[0].set_xlabel("Adam step"); axs[0].set_ylabel(r"$D_{\rm KL}(\tilde p\,\|\,q_{\theta})$")
axs[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=10, ncol=3, loc="lower right")
Ls = np.arange(L_MAX + 1)
axs[1].semilogy(Ls, [kl_train[best[L]] for L in Ls], "o-", color=COL["model"], label=r"to the data, $D_{\rm KL}(\tilde p\,\|\,q_{\theta})$")
axs[1].semilogy(Ls, [kl_target[best[L]] for L in Ls], "s--", color=COL["target"], label=r"to the target, $D_{\rm KL}(p\,\|\,q_{\theta})$")
axs[1].set_xlabel(r"number of entangling layers $L$"); axs[1].set_ylabel("KL divergence (nats)")
axs[1].set_ylim(top=3); axs[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=10, loc="upper right")
for a, lab in zip(axs, "ab"):
    a.text(0.03, 0.92, f"({lab})", transform=a.transAxes)
save(fig, "fig_lab072_depth"); plt.show()





Panel (a) shows the loss against the Adam step for the best start at each depth, and the dotted line marks the product bound (18), which the \(L=0\) curve reaches. Panel (b) shows the final KL divergence against the number of entangling layers, measured against the data (circles) and against the exact target (squares). Both fall quickly up to \(L=2\). Beyond it the loss on the data keeps decreasing by an order of magnitude, while the divergence from the target stays near \(0.014\). The deeper circuits start to reproduce the statistical fluctuations of the 3000 data values, including empty bins, and these fluctuations are not part of \(p\). Fitting these fluctuations is called overfitting, and the divergence from a target that the training never sees detects it. If this picture holds, the saturation level is set by the size of the data set and drops for a larger one. We test this with a second data set of 30 000 values drawn from the same target, and train the circuits with \(L=2\), 3 and 5 from the first of their three starts. In practice \(p\) is unknown, and a part of the data set held back from training plays the role of the target.


Code
rng_big = np.random.default_rng(7272)                                   # seed of the larger data set
D_BIG = 30_000
comp_b = rng_big.choice(2, size=2 * D_BIG, p=W_MIX)
x_big = rng_big.normal(MU_MIX[comp_b], SIG_MIX)
x_big = x_big[(x_big >= XMIN) & (x_big <= XMAX)][:D_BIG]
p_big = jnp.asarray(np.bincount(x_to_index(x_big, N, XMIN, XMAX), minlength=K) / D_BIG)
sel = np.array([SEEDS * L for L in (2, 3, 5)])                          # first start of each depth
train_big = jax.jit(jax.vmap(lambda th, m: adam(lambda x: kl_div(p_big, born_probs(x, m)), th, STEPS, LR)))
th_big, hist_big = train_big(theta0[sel], masks[sel])
q_big = np.asarray(jax.jit(jax.vmap(born_probs))(th_big, masks[sel]))
print(f"TV(data, p): 3000 values {tv(p_data, p_exact):.3f}, 30000 values {tv(np.asarray(p_big), p_exact):.3f}")
print(" L | KL(p||q), 3000 values | KL(p||q), 30000 values   (same starting angles)")
kl_big = {}
for L, i, q in zip((2, 3, 5), sel, q_big):
    kl_big[L] = float(kl_div(p_exact, q))
    print(f" {L} |        {kl_target[i]:.4f}         |        {kl_big[L]:.4f}")
    NUMBERS[f"KLTargetBigL{WORDS[L]}"] = f"{kl_big[L]:.4f}"
NUMBERS["TVDataBigTarget"] = f"{tv(np.asarray(p_big), p_exact):.3f}"

With ten times more data the empirical distribution lies closer to the target, at the total variation distance 0.015 instead of 0.065. From the same starting angles, the divergence of the trained circuits from the target then drops from about 0.016 to about 0.002 at \(L=3\) and \(L=5\). title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
10. Evaluation from samples
A trained circuit on a device is used and tested through its samples. We measure the \(L=3\) model \(M=10^4\) times, convert the bit strings to bin frequencies \(\tilde q(\mathbf b)\) and values of \(x\), and compare them with the target. The total variation distance (16) can be computed from the frequencies directly. The KL divergence (12) from the target requires \(\ln\tilde q(\mathbf b)\) in every bin where \(p(\mathbf b)>0\) and is infinite as soon as one such bin received no shot, so a sampled model is judged by the total variation distance.


Code
L_EVAL, M_EVAL = 3, 10_000
q_eval = jnp.asarray(q_tr[best[L_EVAL]])
idx_eval = sample_bits(jax.random.PRNGKey(7207), q_eval, M_EVAL)
q_freq = np.asarray(counts_to_freq(idx_eval))
x_gen = np.asarray(xk[np.asarray(idx_eval)])            # generated values of x at the bin centres
tv_exact, tv_sampled = tv(p_exact, q_eval), tv(p_exact, q_freq)
empty = int(np.sum((q_freq == 0) & (p_exact > 0)))
print(f"L = {L_EVAL}: TV(p, q) exact = {tv_exact:.3f}, from {M_EVAL} shots = {tv_sampled:.3f}")
print(f"bins with p > 0 and no shot: {empty} -> KL(p || q~) from the shots is infinite")
print(f"mean and standard deviation of x: data {x_data.mean():+.3f} {x_data.std():.3f} | generated {x_gen.mean():+.3f} {x_gen.std():.3f}"
      f" | target {np.sum(p_exact * xk):+.3f} {np.sqrt(np.sum(p_exact * xk**2) - np.sum(p_exact * xk)**2):.3f}")
print(f"fraction of generated x > 0: {np.mean(x_gen > 0):.3f}  (weight of the right peak 0.6)")
NUMBERS["EvalShots"] = str(M_EVAL)
NUMBERS["TVEvalExact"] = f"{tv_exact:.3f}"
NUMBERS["TVEvalSampled"] = f"{tv_sampled:.3f}"

ax.step(np.r_[edges[0], edges[1:]], np.r_[p_exact[0], p_exact], where="pre", color=COL["target"], lw=1.2, label=r"target $p(\mathbf{b})$")

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
11. An example from the literature
The circuits of Section 9 train every gate angle, including the angles of rotations placed between entangling layers. Deep circuits of this kind become hard to train, because their gradients become very small as the number of qubits grows [8]. One remedy fixes the entangling part of each layer and trains only single-qubit rotations. The quantum scrambling Born machine [9] follows this design. Each of its layers applies trainable rotations of every qubit around a fixed, non-trainable entangling unitary that spreads correlations over the whole register. Ref. [9] considers three choices of this unitary, a Haar-random unitary, a finite-depth brickwork circuit of random two-qubit gates, and evolution for a fixed time under a spin-chain Hamiltonian with nearest-neighbour couplings. Once the fixed unitary creates entanglement close to that of a random state, the trained model reaches a similar accuracy for all three, and only one-qubit angles need to be optimised on a device. A variant treats the couplings and fields of the spin-chain Hamiltonian as trainable parameters as well. Some of the circuits also contain ancilla qubits, which take part in the evolution but are not measured. Ignoring their outcomes sums the Born probabilities over their bits \(\mathbf a\), \(q(\mathbf b)=\sum_{\mathbf a}|\langle\mathbf b,\mathbf a|\psi\rangle|^2\), so the measured qubits follow a mixture of Born distributions, given by their reduced density matrix. Such mixtures, which require extra qubits, can represent distributions that a pure state of the measured qubits alone cannot.
The sketch shows a register split into measured system qubits and unmeasured ancillas, whose outcomes are summed over to give a mixture of Born distributions.



ancilla qubits traced out


The figure below is a published result of Ref. [9], shown without change and not produced by our simulation. The circuit has ten qubits. Two registers of four qubits encode two continuous variables \(x\) and \(y\) on a grid of \(16\times16\) bins, and the remaining two qubits are ancillas that are traced out. The target is a mixture of four Gaussian peaks. Panel (a) shows the target distribution, panel (b) the distribution learned by the variant with trainable Hamiltonian parameters. Panel (c) shows slices through the peak positions (the dashed lines in panels (a) and (b)), with the target in black and the learned model in red. All four peaks are reproduced with their weights.



Published result of Ref. [9], not our simulation: target and learned two-dimensional distribution with four peaks

title: Lab 072: Modelling probabilities with a quantum circuit
text:
13. Summary
A Born machine models a probability distribution over bit strings by the squared amplitudes of a state prepared by a parametrised circuit, and a measurement of all qubits draws one sample from it. Continuous data enter through a discretisation into \(2^N\) bins. The bin indices, written in binary with qubit 0 as the most significant bit, are the measured bit strings, and each added qubit halves the bin width. Training minimises the KL divergence to the data, which equals the negative log-likelihood up to the entropy of the data and needs the model probabilities. On a device these probabilities are estimated from shots, and the gradient follows from the parameter-shift rule. A circuit without entangling gates gives independent bits and cannot go below the KL divergence of the product of the marginals, which fails for a two-peak target. Entangling layers create the correlations, and a few layers reproduce the target to within the statistical error of the data set, beyond which deeper circuits fit the fluctuations of the data.

title: Lab 073: QUBO and QAOA
text:
2. State-vector simulator
The simulator stores the state of \(N\) qubits as a tensor \(\psi[b_0,\dots,b_{N-1}]\) with one axis per qubit, and qubit 0 is the most significant bit, so the amplitude of the bit string \(b_0b_1\dots b_{N-1}\) sits at the flat index \[k=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}b_i\,2^{N-1-i}. \tag{1}\] A rotation generated by a Pauli matrix \(\hat P\) is \[\hat R_P(\theta)=e^{-i\theta\hat P/2}=\cos\frac\theta2\,\hat I-i\sin\frac\theta2\,\hat P , \tag{2}\] and a one-qubit gate acts on qubit \(i\) by a contraction with axis \(i\) of the state tensor. The two-qubit rotation \(\hat R_{zz}(\theta)=e^{-i\theta\hat Z_i\hat Z_j/2}\) is diagonal in the computational basis. Since \(\hat Z_i\hat Z_j|\mathbf b\rangle=(-1)^{b_i+b_j}|\mathbf b\rangle\), it multiplies the amplitude of each bit string by the phase \(e^{-i\theta(-1)^{b_i+b_j}/2}\). The checks compare the contraction with the Kronecker-product matrix and the phase form of \(\hat R_{zz}\) with the matrix exponential.


Code
# recap: one-qubit matrices, rotations (2), gates on a state tensor, diagonal R_zz as a phase vector
I2 = jnp.eye(2, dtype=CDTYPE)
X = jnp.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], dtype=CDTYPE)
Z = jnp.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]], dtype=CDTYPE)

def rot(P, theta):
    return jnp.cos(theta / 2) * I2 - 1j * jnp.sin(theta / 2) * P

def apply_1q(psi, U, q):
    return jnp.moveaxis(jnp.tensordot(U, psi, axes=([1], [q])), 0, q)

def bit_table(n):
    k = np.arange(2 ** n)
    return (k[:, None] >> (n - 1 - np.arange(n))) & 1          # row k = bits of index k, equation (1)

def zz_signs(n, i, j):
    b = bit_table(n)
    return (-1.0) ** (b[:, i] + b[:, j])                        # eigenvalue of Z_i Z_j on every bit string

psi3 = jax.random.normal(jax.random.PRNGKey(7301), (8,)) + 0j; psi3 /= jnp.linalg.norm(psi3)
U_test = rot(X, 0.9)
assert jnp.allclose(apply_1q(psi3.reshape(2, 2, 2), U_test, 2).reshape(-1), jnp.kron(jnp.kron(I2, I2), U_test) @ psi3, atol=TOL)
ZIZ = jnp.kron(jnp.kron(Z, I2), Z)
assert jnp.allclose(expm(-1j * 0.7 / 2 * ZIZ) @ psi3, jnp.exp(-1j * 0.7 / 2 * zz_signs(3, 0, 2)) * psi3, atol=1e-12)
print("simulator ready: contraction = Kronecker matrix, R_zz = phase vector")


simulator ready: contraction = Kronecker matrix, R_zz = phase vector

title: Lab 073: QUBO and QAOA
text:
3. Quadratic unconstrained binary optimisation
A QUBO problem has \(N\) binary variables \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), collected in the vector \(\mathbf x=(x_0,\dots,x_{N-1})\), and a real symmetric \(N\times N\) matrix \(Q\). Each variable will be stored in one qubit, so \(N\) is also the number of qubits, and in a graph problem the number of vertices. The problem asks for the vector that minimises the quadratic cost \[C(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^{T}Q\,\mathbf x=\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}\,x_ix_j . \tag{3}\] A binary variable satisfies \(x_i^2=x_i\), so the diagonal elements \(Q_{ii}\) act as linear costs, and every quadratic function of binary variables has the form (3) up to a constant. The word unconstrained means that all \(2^N\) vectors are allowed. Constraints, such as a fixed number of ones, are added to the cost as penalty terms.
The sketch evaluates the cost (3) for one bit string, where only the entries of \(Q\) in rows and columns with \(x_i=1\) contribute.



QUBO cost of a bit string


Checking every vector costs \(2^N\) evaluations of \(C\), about \(10^{15}\) for \(N=50\). QUBO is NP-hard, so no known algorithm solves every instance in a time that grows only polynomially with \(N\), and practical solvers for large instances are heuristics. A greedy method flips one variable at a time as long as the cost decreases. Simulated annealing also accepts some cost increases, with a probability that decreases during the run, in order to leave local minima. For the instance studied here, \(2^8=256\) candidates are checked in a fraction of a second, which gives the exact answer against which the quantum algorithm is compared.

title: Lab 073: QUBO and QAOA
text:
4. MaxCut
A graph consists of \(N\) vertices and a set \(E\) of edges, each joining a pair of vertices \((i,j)\). As an analogy, the vertices can be people and the edges conflicts between them, and the task is to split the people into two rooms so that as many conflicting pairs as possible end up in different rooms. A split of the vertices into two groups is called a cut, because drawing a line between the groups cuts every edge that crosses it. We label the groups by a binary variable per vertex, \(x_i=0\) for the first group and \(x_i=1\) for the second, so a cut is a bit string \(\mathbf x=x_0x_1\dots x_{N-1}\). The size of the cut is the number of edges whose two ends carry different labels, and the maximum-cut problem (MaxCut) asks for the bit string with the largest cut size.
On a square, four vertices \(0,1,2,3\) are joined in a ring by the edges \((0,1)\), \((1,2)\), \((2,3)\) and \((3,0)\). The bit string \(0000\) puts everyone in one group and cuts no edge. The string \(1000\) moves vertex \(0\) to the other group and cuts its two edges \((0,1)\) and \((3,0)\), so its cut size is two. The string \(1010\) alternates the groups around the ring, so every edge joins vertices of different groups and all four edges are cut. No string can do better, so the maximum cut of the square is four, reached by \(1010\) and by its complement \(0101\). Exchanging the two groups never changes a cut, so the optimal bit strings always come in such complementary pairs. A triangle behaves differently, because around a cycle of three vertices the labels cannot alternate, and at most two of its three edges can be cut. Odd cycles in a graph make some edges impossible to cut.
The sketch shows the optimal cut \(1010\) of the square, which cuts all four edges, and the triangle, where one edge always stays uncut.



MaxCut of a square and a triangle


For a square the answer is evident, but in general the only sure method is to compare candidates, and their number \(2^N\) doubles with every vertex. MaxCut is one of the problems that Karp proved NP-complete in its decision form [4], so no algorithm is known that finds the optimum of every graph in a time that grows polynomially with \(N\). Approximate algorithms are therefore judged by the approximation ratio, the cut they find divided by the maximum cut. The best known polynomial-time classical algorithm, based on semidefinite programming, guarantees a ratio of at least \(0.878\) on every graph [5]. MaxCut appears in the partitioning of networks and circuits, in clustering, where the edges carry the dissimilarities of items, and in physics as the ground-state problem of an Ising antiferromagnet, where a cut edge is a satisfied bond.
An edge \((i,j)\) is cut when exactly one of \(x_i\), \(x_j\) equals one, and the expression \(x_i+x_j-2x_ix_j\) equals one in that case and zero otherwise. The cut size is therefore \[\mathrm{cut}(\mathbf x)=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}\big(x_i+x_j-2x_ix_j\big). \tag{4}\] Maximising the cut is minimising \(C(\mathbf x)=-\mathrm{cut}(\mathbf x)\), a QUBO with the matrix \[Q_{ii}=-d_i,\qquad Q_{ij}=Q_{ji}=\begin{cases}1 & (i,j)\in E\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}\quad(i\neq j), \tag{5}\] where the degree \(d_i\) is the number of edges at vertex \(i\). Each edge contributes \(Q_{ij}+Q_{ji}=2\) to the product term \(2x_ix_j\) of equation (4), and the linear terms \(x_i\) collect on the diagonal.
Our graph has \(N=8\) vertices and twelve edges. It is a ring of eight vertices in which each vertex is also joined to the opposite vertex, so every vertex has three neighbours. It contains cycles of odd length, such as \(0\)–\(1\)–\(2\)–\(3\)–\(4\)–\(0\), and on a cycle of odd length at least one edge stays uncut, so no division cuts all edges. The code builds \(Q\), checks equation (5) against the direct count of cut edges for all 256 bit strings, and finds the maximum cut by exhaustive search. The bit string \(\mathbf b=b_0\dots b_7\) of a candidate is \(\mathbf x\) itself, \(b_i=x_i\).


Code
n = 8
EDGES = [(0, 1), (0, 4), (0, 7), (1, 2), (1, 5), (2, 3), (2, 6), (3, 4), (3, 7), (4, 5), (5, 6), (6, 7)]
Q = np.zeros((n, n))
for i, j in EDGES:
    Q[i, j] += 1; Q[j, i] += 1; Q[i, i] -= 1; Q[j, j] -= 1          # equation (5)
BITS = bit_table(n)                                                   # all 256 candidate bit strings x = b
cost = np.einsum("ki,ij,kj->k", BITS, Q, BITS)                        # C(x) = x^T Q x for every candidate
cut = np.array([sum(int(b[i] != b[j]) for i, j in EDGES) for b in BITS])
assert np.array_equal(cost, -cut)
assert np.all(np.diag(Q) == -3)

cut_max = int(cut.max())
opt_idx = np.flatnonzero(cut == cut_max)
fmt = lambda k: "".join(map(str, BITS[k]))
print("QUBO matrix Q:\n", Q.astype(int))
print(f"maximum cut = {cut_max} of {len(EDGES)} edges, reached by {len(opt_idx)} bit strings:", [fmt(k) for k in opt_idx])
print("number of bit strings with cut size 0, 1, ..., 12:", np.bincount(cut, minlength=len(EDGES) + 1))
print(f"mean cut of a uniformly random bit string = {cut.mean():.2f} = |E|/2")
for nn in (8, 20, 50, 100):
    print(f"n = {nn:3d}: 2^n = {2.0 ** nn:.2e} candidates")
NUMBERS["NumVertices"] = str(n)
NUMBERS["NumEdges"] = str(len(EDGES))
NUMBERS["MaxCut"] = str(cut_max)
NUMBERS["NumOptimal"] = str(len(opt_idx))
NUMBERS["RandomMeanCut"] = f"{cut.mean():.1f}"

title: Lab 073: QUBO and QAOA
section: 5. The Ising Hamiltonian of a QUBO
text:
5. The Ising Hamiltonian of a QUBO
A qubit measured in the computational basis gives the bit \(b_i\), and its Pauli operator \(\hat Z_i\) has the eigenvalue \(z_i=1-2b_i=\pm1\). We identify each binary variable with the bit of one qubit, \(x_i=b_i\), so that \[x_i=\frac{1-z_i}2 . \tag{6}\] Inserting equation (6) into the cost (3) and using \(z_i^2=1\) for the diagonal terms gives \[C=\frac14\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}(1-z_i)(1-z_j)=\underbrace{\frac14\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}+\frac14\sum_iQ_{ii}}_{\text{constant }c_0}\;\underbrace{-\;\frac14\sum_i\Big[\sum_j(Q_{ij}+Q_{ji})\Big]z_i}_{\text{fields }h_i}\;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{i<j}\frac{Q_{ij}+Q_{ji}}{4}\,z_iz_j}_{\text{couplings }J_{ij}} . \tag{7}\] Equation (7) is the energy of classical Ising spins \(z_i=\pm1\) with couplings \(J_{ij}=(Q_{ij}+Q_{ji})/4\), fields \(h_i=-\sum_j(Q_{ij}+Q_{ji})/4\) and a constant \(c_0\). Replacing each spin by its Pauli operator gives the cost Hamiltonian \[\hat{\mathcal H}_C=\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\,\hat Z_i\hat Z_j+\sum_ih_i\,\hat Z_i+c_0\,\hat I . \tag{8}\] It contains only \(\hat Z\) operators and is therefore diagonal in the computational basis, \[\hat{\mathcal H}_C|\mathbf b\rangle=C(\mathbf b)\,|\mathbf b\rangle . \tag{9}\] Every basis state \(|\mathbf b\rangle\) is a candidate solution, its energy is the cost of that candidate, and the ground state of \(\hat{\mathcal H}_C\) is the optimal bit string. A degenerate ground level holds all optimal bit strings. For MaxCut the fields vanish, since \(\sum_j(Q_{ij}+Q_{ji})=-2d_i+2d_i=0\), and equation (7) becomes \[\hat{\mathcal H}_C=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in E}\hat Z_i\hat Z_j-\frac{|E|}2\,\hat I , \tag{10}\] so an uncut edge raises the energy by \(1/2\) and a cut edge lowers it by \(1/2\).
The sketch summarises the chain from the QUBO through the Ising energy to the diagonal cost Hamiltonian, with the energy levels of MaxCut on the square, whose ground states are the optimal cuts.



from QUBO to the cost Hamiltonian


The code applies the general formulas (7) to the matrix \(Q\), builds the diagonal of \(\hat{\mathcal H}_C\) for all 256 bit strings, and compares it with the cost. It also builds the full \(256\times256\) matrix of equation (8) from Kronecker products and checks that it is diagonal.


Code
def qubo_to_ising(Q):
    # equation (7): constant c0, fields h_i, couplings J_ij (i < j)
    S = Q + Q.T
    c0 = Q.sum() / 4 + np.trace(Q) / 4
    h = -S.sum(axis=1) / 4
    J = np.triu(S, k=1) / 4
    return c0, h, J

c0, h, J = qubo_to_ising(Q)
Zsign = 1 - 2 * BITS                                                  # z_i = 1 - 2 b_i, equation (6)
diag_H = c0 + Zsign @ h + np.einsum("ki,ij,kj->k", Zsign, J, Zsign)   # diagonal of equation (8)
assert np.allclose(diag_H, cost, atol=TOL)                            # equation (9) for all 256 bit strings
assert np.allclose(h, 0) and np.isclose(c0, -len(EDGES) / 2)          # equation (10)

def z_on(i):
    ops = [Z if q == i else I2 for q in range(n)]
    out = ops[0]
    for o in ops[1:]:
        out = jnp.kron(out, o)
    return out

Zops = [z_on(i) for i in range(n)]
H_dense = c0 * jnp.eye(2 ** n) + sum(J[i, j] * Zops[i] @ Zops[j] for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n) if J[i, j] != 0)
assert jnp.allclose(H_dense, jnp.diag(jnp.diag(H_dense)), atol=TOL) and np.allclose(np.diag(H_dense), cost)
print(f"c0 = {c0}, all h_i = 0, J_ij = 1/2 on the {len(EDGES)} edges")
print("ground energy of H_C =", diag_H.min(), "= -(maximum cut); ground states:", [fmt(k) for k in np.flatnonzero(diag_H == diag_H.min())][:4], "...")
DIAG = jnp.asarray(diag_H)


c0 = -6.0, all h_i = 0, J_ij = 1/2 on the 12 edges
ground energy of H_C = -10.0 = -(maximum cut); ground states: ['00101101', '01001011', '01011010', '01101001'] ...


The diagonal of the Hamiltonian agrees with the QUBO cost on all 256 bit strings, and the Kronecker-product matrix has no off-diagonal element. The lowest energy is \(-10\), the negative of the maximum cut.

title: Lab 073: QUBO and QAOA
text:
6. Answers from measured bit strings
A quantum algorithm for a QUBO prepares some state \(|\psi\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf b}\psi_{\mathbf b}|\mathbf b\rangle\) and measures all qubits in the computational basis. Each shot returns one bit string \(\mathbf b\) with probability \(|\psi_{\mathbf b}|^2\), which is one candidate solution, and its cost \(C(\mathbf b)\) is evaluated on a classical computer in a time that grows only polynomially with \(N\). From \(M\) shots we keep the best bit string. The state is useful when its weight on optimal or near-optimal bit strings is much larger than the uniform weight \(2^{-N}\) of random guessing. If the optimal bit strings together carry the probability \(P_{\rm opt}\), at least one of \(M\) independent shots is optimal with probability \[P_{\rm hit}(M)=1-(1-P_{\rm opt})^M , \tag{11}\] and the number of shots needed for a chance of 95 per cent is \(M_{95}=\lceil\ln0.05/\ln(1-P_{\rm opt})\rceil\), about \(3/P_{\rm opt}\) for small \(P_{\rm opt}\).
The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) uses the same circuits and measurements for a different purpose. There the answer is the ground-state energy, a number estimated as an average over many shots. Here the answer is one sampled bit string. Its cost is known exactly as soon as it has been measured, and the average energy serves only as the training signal for the circuit.
The uniform superposition \(|+\rangle^{\otimes N}\), prepared by a Hadamard gate on every qubit, gives every bit string the probability \(2^{-N}\), so its shots are uniformly random guesses. We sample 100 shots from it.


Code
@partial(jax.jit, static_argnums=2)
def sample_bits(key, probs, shots):
    # shots measurements of all qubits: indices of bit strings drawn with the given probabilities
    u = jax.random.uniform(key, (shots,)) * jnp.sum(probs)
    return jnp.minimum(jnp.searchsorted(jnp.cumsum(probs), u), probs.shape[0] - 1)

P_OPT_RANDOM = len(opt_idx) / 2 ** n
uniform = jnp.full(2 ** n, 1.0 / 2 ** n)
shots_rand = np.asarray(sample_bits(jax.random.PRNGKey(7302), uniform, 100))
print("first five shots of |+>^n:", [fmt(k) for k in shots_rand[:5]], "cuts", cut[shots_rand[:5]])
print(f"best of 100 random shots: cut {cut[shots_rand].max()}, optimal shots: {int(np.sum(cut[shots_rand] == cut_max))}")
M95 = lambda p: math.ceil(math.log(0.05) / math.log(1 - p))
print(f"random guessing: P_opt = {P_OPT_RANDOM:.4f}, shots for a 95% chance of one optimum: {M95(P_OPT_RANDOM)}")
NUMBERS["POptRandom"] = f"{P_OPT_RANDOM:.4f}"
NUMBERS["MNinetyFiveRandom"] = str(M95(P_OPT_RANDOM))


first five shots of |+>^n: ['10001111', '10101100', '00001010', '00010000', '00001010'] cuts [5 8 6 3 6]
best of 100 random shots: cut 10, optimal shots: 2
random guessing: P_opt = 0.0312, shots for a 95% chance of one optimum: 95


For eight qubits random guessing is still an effective strategy, since about 95 random shots find an optimum with a probability of 95 per cent. The probability of an optimum falls as \(2^{-N}\) times the number of optimal strings. A useful quantum state must concentrate its weight on low-cost bit strings so that the number of shots stays small for large \(N\).

title: Lab 073: QUBO and QAOA
Lab 073: QUBO and QAOA
text:
8. Depth one
At \(p=1\) the expected cost \(E(\gamma,\beta)\) depends on two angles and can be drawn as a map. Three symmetries restrict the angles that need to be scanned. The eigenvalues of \(\hat{\mathcal H}_C\) are integers, so \(\hat U_C(\gamma+2\pi)=\hat U_C(\gamma)\). A shift \(\beta\to\beta+\pi/2\) multiplies the mixing layer by \((-i)^N\prod_i\hat X_i\), which flips every bit, leaves \(|+\rangle^{\otimes N}\) and every cut unchanged, and therefore leaves \(E\) unchanged. Reversing both angles, \((\gamma,\beta)\to(-\gamma,-\beta)\), complex-conjugates the state and leaves all probabilities unchanged. The rectangle \(0\le\gamma\le\pi\), \(-\pi/4\le\beta\le\pi/4\) therefore contains every value of \(E\). We evaluate \(E\) on a grid of \(101\times101\) angles with jax.vmap.


Code
gam = jnp.linspace(0, np.pi, 101)
bet = jnp.linspace(-np.pi / 4, np.pi / 4, 101)
land = jax.jit(jax.vmap(jax.vmap(lambda g, b: energy(jnp.array([g, b])), (None, 0)), (0, None)))(gam, bet)
land = np.asarray(land)                                       # land[i, j] = E(gamma_i, beta_j)
ig, ib = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(land), land.shape)
print(f"grid minimum: E = {land.min():.4f} at gamma = {float(gam[ig]):.3f}, beta = {float(bet[ib]):.3f}; expected cut {-land.min():.3f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 3.4))
im = ax.pcolormesh(np.asarray(bet), np.asarray(gam), -land, cmap="cividis", shading="auto")
ax.plot(float(bet[ib]), float(gam[ig]), "w*", ms=10)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\beta$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\gamma$")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label=r"expected cut $-E(\gamma,\beta)$")
save(fig, "fig_lab073_landscape"); plt.show()


grid minimum: E = -8.3083 at gamma = 0.628, beta = -0.393; expected cut 8.308





The colour shows the expected cut \(-E(\gamma,\beta)\) of the depth-one state, and the star marks the best grid point. At \(\gamma=0\) or \(\beta=0\) the state keeps the uniform distribution and the expected cut equals the random value of six edges. The expected cut has its maxima at negative \(\beta\), near \(\gamma\approx0.6\) and \(\gamma\approx2.5\), and its minima at positive \(\beta\), where the angles move probability towards small cuts. The best depth-one state cuts slightly more than eight edges on average.

title: Lab 073: QUBO and QAOA
section: 9. Deeper circuits trained by gradient descent
text:
9. Deeper circuits trained by gradient descent
For \(p>1\) a grid is too expensive, since its size grows as the number of grid points per angle to the power \(2p\). We minimise \(E(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)\) with gradients from jax.grad and the Adam optimiser [2], with 400 steps and the learning rate 0.02. The landscape has several local minima at larger \(p\), so we train 16 starting angle sets in parallel with jax.vmap and keep the best. Fifteen are random, with \(\gamma_\ell\in[0,\pi/2]\) and \(\beta_\ell\in[0,\pi/4]\). The sixteenth is a linear ramp, \[\gamma_\ell=s_\ell\,\delta t,\qquad\beta_\ell=-(1-s_\ell)\,\delta t,\qquad s_\ell=\frac{\ell-1/2}{p}, \tag{17}\] with \(\delta t=0.8\), in which the cost angles grow and the mixing angles shrink in magnitude from the first layer to the last. On a device the gradient comes from the parameter-shift rule, with the energy estimated from shots. Each QAOA angle is shared by several gates. The angle \(\gamma_\ell\) enters every gate \(\hat R_{zz}(2\gamma_\ell J_{ij})\) of the gate form (15), and \(\gamma_\ell\) also enters \(\hat R_z(2\gamma_\ell h_i)\) when there are fields, while \(\beta_\ell\) enters the \(N\) gates \(\hat R_x(2\beta_\ell)\). If gate \(g\) has the angle \(\theta_g=c_g\varphi\) for a shared angle \(\varphi\), the chain rule gives \(\partial_\varphi E=\sum_gc_g\,\partial_{\theta_g}E\), and each term follows from the two shifted circuits of the parameter-shift rule. For MaxCut, \(c_g=2J_{ij}=1\) for the twelve \(\hat R_{zz}\) gates of a layer and \(c_g=2\) for its eight \(\hat R_x\) gates, so the two derivatives of one layer need \(2\times(12+8)=40\) circuits and a full gradient \(40p\) circuits, each measured with many shots. We judge the trained state by the approximation ratio \[r=\frac{-E(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)}{\mathrm{cut}_{\max}} \tag{18}\] which compares the expected cut with the optimum and equals \(6/10\) for random guessing. We also use the probability \(P_{\rm opt}\) of an optimal bit string, which enters equation (11), and the number \(M_{95}\) of shots for a 95 per cent chance of measuring an optimum.


Code
def adam(loss, theta0, steps, lr):
    # Adam with the standard moment decay rates 0.9 and 0.999
    value_and_grad = jax.value_and_grad(loss)
    def step(carry, i):
        th, m, v = carry
        l, g = value_and_grad(th)
        m = 0.9 * m + 0.1 * g
        v = 0.999 * v + 0.001 * g ** 2
        th = th - lr * (m / (1 - 0.9 ** (i + 1))) / (jnp.sqrt(v / (1 - 0.999 ** (i + 1))) + 1e-8)
        return (th, m, v), l
    (th, _, _), hist = lax.scan(step, (theta0, jnp.zeros_like(theta0), jnp.zeros_like(theta0)), jnp.arange(steps))
    return th, hist

def fold(angles):
    # map gamma into (-pi, pi], beta into (-pi/4, pi/4] using the symmetries of Section 8
    p = len(angles) // 2
    g = (np.asarray(angles[:p]) + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi
    b = (np.asarray(angles[p:]) + np.pi / 4) % (np.pi / 2) - np.pi / 4
    if g[0] < 0:
        g, b = -g, -b                                     # time reversal
    return g, b

OPT_MASK = jnp.asarray(cut == cut_max)
STARTS, STEPS, LR, RAMP_DT = 16, 400, 0.02, 0.8
results, states, curves = {}, {}, {}
t_train = time.perf_counter()
for p in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    key = jax.random.PRNGKey(7310 + p)
    th0 = jax.random.uniform(key, (STARTS, 2 * p)) * jnp.r_[jnp.full(p, np.pi / 2), jnp.full(p, np.pi / 4)]
    s_l = (np.arange(1, p + 1) - 0.5) / p
    th0 = th0.at[0].set(jnp.r_[s_l * RAMP_DT, -(1 - s_l) * RAMP_DT])     # linear ramp start, equation (17)
    th, hist = jax.jit(jax.vmap(lambda t: adam(energy, t, STEPS, LR)))(th0)
    hist = np.asarray(hist)
    E_final = np.asarray(jax.vmap(energy)(th))
    i_best = int(np.argmin(E_final))
    g_b, b_b = fold(th[i_best])
    psi = qaoa_state(jnp.asarray(g_b), jnp.asarray(b_b))
    probs = np.asarray(jnp.abs(psi) ** 2)
    E_best = float(np.sum(probs * diag_H))
    assert abs(E_best - E_final[i_best]) < 1e-10               # folding the angles leaves E unchanged
    p_opt = float(probs[np.asarray(OPT_MASK)].sum())
    results[p] = dict(E=E_best, ratio=-E_best / cut_max, P_opt=p_opt, M95=M95(p_opt),
                      gammas=g_b.tolist(), betas=b_b.tolist(), starts_within_1e3=int(np.sum(E_final < E_best + 1e-3)))
    states[p], curves[p] = probs, hist[i_best]
print(f"training of 4 x {STARTS} circuits: {time.perf_counter() - t_train:.1f} s")
assert results[1]["E"] <= land.min() + 1e-9                   # depth one: at least as good as the best grid point
print(" p | expected cut | ratio r | P_opt  | M_95 | gamma_l                       | beta_l")
print(f" random guess |   {cut.mean():.3f}     |  {cut.mean() / cut_max:.3f}  | {P_OPT_RANDOM:.4f} | {M95(P_OPT_RANDOM):4d} |")

10. Sampling the trained circuits
A device gives the distribution of panel (b) only through shots. We measure the trained \(p=4\) state \(M=1000\) times, compute the cut of every measured bit string, and keep the best one. From the same shots we estimate the expected cost (16) as the mean \(\bar C=\frac1M\sum_{s=1}^MC(\mathbf b^{(s)})\) with its standard error \(\sigma_{\bar C}=\sigma_C/\sqrt M\), where \(\sigma_C\) is the sample standard deviation of the costs. The same number of uniformly random bit strings serves as the comparison. Finally we follow the cut of the best bit string found so far as the number of shots grows, for both sources.
